title: Iran War Updates: U.S. reduces troop footprint in Mideast as indirect talks with Iran continue
description: The U.S. military has quietly reduced its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing threats from Iran and its Houthis allies in Yemen, sources tell CBS News.
author_name: Duarte  Dias, Khaled  Wassef, Frank  Andrews
content:
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Thursday that it had struck four vessels transferring oil ship-to-ship in the Persian Gulf after they used a route through the Strait of Hormuz that Iran rejects. Ship-to-ship cargo transfers have become more common as tankers and other commercial vessels try to avoid Iranian detection and strikes in the strategic waterway.
In a statement, the IRGC Navy said it "monitored and pursued four violating vessels that had previously passed through an illegal route," referring to shipping lanes in the strait that the Trump administration has encouraged vessels to use to avoid Iranian fees and controls. Tehran considers those southern routes, close to Oman's coast, unauthorized and has targeted vessels trying to use them for months.
"They discovered the vessels transferring oil cargoes from ship to ship in the north-central part of the Persian Gulf," the bulletin read. "All four ships were hit simultaneously and are burning."
The IRGC said three other ships attempting to use routes not recognized by Iran "suffered accidents and caught fire after striking mines west of the Strait of Hormuz, and were brought to a halt."
The IRGC said the U.S. "encouraging vessels to pass through an illegally mined passage has led to an increasing number of maritime incidents day by day."
"If this course continues," the group warned, "the confrontation will extend to the bases of the aggressors in the region."
Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said Thursday that the latest attack on the kingdom's airports, a strike on the eastern city of Dammam's King Fahd International Airport, had risen to two.
"The number of deaths resulting from the attack has risen to two, after confirming an additional death. The deceased were a Saudi citizen and a resident of Indian nationality," the General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement shared on social media.
It said eight others, "a Saudi citizen, two residents each of Indian, Yemeni, and Bangladeshi nationalities, and a resident of Nepalese nationality," were injured in the attack.
The statement did not assign blame for the attack, but Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen have attacked Saudi airports and other infrastructure for weeks in retaliation for the Saudi government's backing of Yemeni state forces in the neighboring nation's decade-long civil war.
GACA said in its statement that it was continuing work in conjunction with other security authorities "to assess the damages, and to take all necessary measures to ensure the safety of passengers and employees, and to maintain the security and safety of the civil aviation system in the Kingdom."
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent weeks have inflicted severe losses on the kingdom and prompted the U.S. to quietly reduce its military footprint in the region as missiles hit energy infrastructure and civilian airports, killing more than 20 people.
Saudi Arabia, despite its size, wealth and a substantial military, has appeared to be on the back foot as it faces the Yemeni rebels.
Saudi Arabia spent $83 billion on defense last year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute — far more than any other country in the Middle East , including Israel.
So, why has the kingdom struggled to stop the Houthi barrage? Read our full story here .
An attack targeting the King Fahd International Airport in the eastern Saudi Arabian city of Dammam killed one person and injured eight others Wednesday evening, the kingdom's civil aviation authority said.
The authority said in a statement that injuries from the attack ranged from "minor to serious" and that material damage to the airport was also being assessed.
It did not describe what type of attack occurred, but the kingdom's airports have been targeted repeatedly by projectiles in recent days by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militants.
A U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official told CBS News on Wednesday the military has been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing regional threats from the Houthis and direct threats from Iran.
NBC News was first to report on the drawdowns.
Asked about the reports, U.S. Central Command spokesperson Capt. Tim Hawkins told CBS News: "We regularly move U.S. service members and assets to optimize mission readiness. We do not discuss related movements for operational security reasons. U.S. forces remain vigilant and ready to protect American personnel and interests across the region."
The U.S. State Department has also ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel and their families to depart Saudi Arabia, citing threats posed by the Iran-backed Houthis.
CBS News has learned several U.S. embassies in the Middle East have adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status.
The restricted operations status, which the department introduced in August amid flare-ups in the war with Iran, allows embassies to reduce staffing and services without fully suspending operations.
The Saudi energy ministry said that falling debris from the interception of a drone targeting an oil facility killed two people and injured two others on Wednesday.
"The attempted attack resulted in the deaths of two individuals, a Filipino and a Nepali, and injuries to two others," the ministry said in a statement. It did not say who launched the drone aimed at the Shaybah oil field near the UAE border.
The U.S. has ordered all non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as the kingdom faces escalating attacks by Houthi militants.
"Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a social media post Wednesday.
The order came a few days after the U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia , Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and several other countries warned that hostilities could rapidly and without warning spread beyond areas already affected by the fighting.
"The safety and security of Department personnel and their families remain our highest priority, and we will continue to take all necessary steps to protect and support them," Pigott added.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi issued a warning to the U.S. on Wednesday afternoon, saying it should choose diplomacy over returning to war.
"Iran is prepared to give diplomacy another chance if we see strong evidence of a sincere desire by US to build trust & reach a just solution," he wrote on X , sharing a link to an opinion piece in the Financial Times. "But if US chooses war over diplomacy, it'll certainly result in an even greater strategic failure."
Araghchi said earlier in the day that Iran and the U.S. were still involved in indirect negotiations via mediators over the seven-day ceasefire proposal from September. The proposal was outright rejected by President Trump, but Araghchi said the U.S. was trying to add further clauses to the agreement.
The U.S. Treasury announced new sanctions on the Panamanian-Greek law firm Karnakis and Karnakis for involvement in Iran's "shadow fleet" as part of its Operation Economic Outcast .
The U.S. accuses Karnakis and Karnakis of being indirectly involved in Iran's illicit shipping operations for years. A "shadow fleet" refers to oil tankers that hide their true ownership in order to evade sanctions.
"Whether you are conducting illegal oil transfers at sea or sitting in the corner office of a law firm, if you are supporting the Iranian regime, we will find you and sanction you," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. "Iran's facilitators must make a choice: Either you are with us or against us. We know who you are, we know what you're doing, and we will continue to take action."
The Treasury also said it sanctioned Singapore- and UAE-based shipping agents, including a fleet of cargo vessels that has directly taken part in Iran's "shadow fleet" and "helped generate substantial revenue for the Iranian regime."
A limited number of Saudi airlines took off and landed at the country's main airport on Wednesday, two days after authorities notified airlines that they could resume operations with prior permission.
Saudia and FlyNas were operating flights Wednesday, according to flight-tracking data published by FlightAware. Major carriers, including Lufthansa and Air France, have canceled flights through mid-November.
Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport has been hit multiple times this month by Yemen's Houthi rebels and shut down on Oct. 10. A strike two weeks ago killed 13 people and injured hundreds more.
The Houthis have acknowledged attacking the airport, claiming without evidence that Saudi Arabia provided military equipment to government forces through the facility.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said any interference in the Yemen war by Egypt or any other country would make the situation "more difficult."
"Egypt has sufficient experience to avoid entangling itself in such a highly complex conflict," said Iran's top diplomat in an interview with Iraqi state broadcaster Al-Iraqiya aired on Tuesday.
"We believe that any foreign presence or interference will only make resolving this issue more difficult," Araghchi noted.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Wednesday that Cairo's proposed military support for Riyadh was to "defend Saudi territory, and does not include an attack on Yemen," according to a statement from his office.
At a government event titled Egypt Forum 2026, Sisi said the "objective is to defend the kingdom's lands and borders, as well as those of any other Arab state, should it be requested of Egypt," his spokesman said in a statement.
Sisi on Saturday had asked parliament to authorize support for Saudi Arabia in its war with the Houthis, "if requested."
The parliament, which is stacked with supporters of the president, has since held two rare secret sessions, before postponing deliberations until next week.
Iran's newly appointed defense minister, Mehrdad Akhlaghi, said Wednesday his first hours in office were devoted to meeting the requirements of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' Aerospace Force and the army's air defense units.
"We are not in a war of rhetoric in response to repeated threats; we are turning threats into greater readiness and more effective defensive power," he wrote in his first post on X since taking office.
Akhlaghi added Iran was concentrating on its objectives through the use of new technologies.
"We may eat dirt, but we will not give up our soil," he concluded.
President Trump blocked a planned Israeli multiday operation that would have resumed strikes against Iran on the weekend of Oct. 10, according to the Financial Times .
The plan was designed to exceed the intensity of the joint U.S.-Israeli military offensive launched in February, three people familiar with the matter told the paper, and would have struck Iranian nuclear sites, regime targets and civilian infrastructure such as power plants.
The president blocked the strike to avoid escalating conflict before the U.S. midterm elections, according to the report.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Wednesday he had directed the Israeli army and intelligence services to topple the Iranian regime.
"The regime in Iran has still not learned the lesson," Netanyahu told a graduation ceremony at an officer training school in the country's southern Negev desert.
"Mojtaba Khamenei, the current tyrant, has decided to follow in his father's footsteps," he said, referring to the country's supreme leader, who replaced his father Ali Khamenei after he was killed in a U.S.-Israeli airstrike on Feb. 28.
"He has taken the safety off, and Iran is once again attempting to develop 'death bombs,'" he added, without giving details on what exactly he was referring to.
"There is only one way to remove this threat once and for all," Netanyahu said, "by toppling the regime in Iran. And that is my directive to the [Israel Defense Forces], the Mossad, and the security services."
He did not expand on how he expected the military or intelligence services to carry out the directive.
Saudi Arabia has held talks with a senior Syrian military delegation on arrangements to transfer up to 10,000 Syrian fighters to take part in the war against Yemen's Houthi movement, according to a report by the Lebanese Hezbollah-owned Al-Akhbar newspaper, citing Yemeni intelligence sources.
The report claims Syrian military officials visited Saudi Arabia's southern regions of Najran and Asir to inspect sites prepared to receive the fighters, while discussions in Riyadh covered transport logistics, financing and military assignments.
The Syrian delegation included Brig. Gen. Khaled Khattab, former commander of the Ansar al-Tawhid faction and current commander of the 82nd Division in the new Syrian army; and Brig. Gen.Haitham al-Ali, also known as Abu Muslim, commander of the army's Third Corps and a former leader in Hayat Tahrir al-Sham.
Khattab reportedly spent four days in southern Saudi Arabia, accompanied by Saudi officers, visiting sites in the regions of Asir and Najran being prepared to receive Syrian fighters. Meanwhile, al-Ali held several meetings with Saudi officers at the Defense Ministry in Riyadh to discuss the costs of transferring around 10,000 fighters, financial arrangements, additional benefits and their intended military tasks. The delegation reportedly finalized logistical arrangements for the transfer.
The report also raises the possibility that foreign fighters currently in Syria, including Uyghurs, Uzbeks, Tajiks and other nationalities, could be transferred to Yemen.
A missile industry veteran has been tapped as Iran's new defense minister, replacing the previous minister who was killed on Feb. 28, the first day of U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran.
Iranian parliamentarians overwhelmingly approved the appointment of Mehrdad Akhlaghi Ketabchi, 68, as the country's new defense chief on Sunday.
Akhlaghi studied chemical engineering at Amirkabir University of Technology and then spent more than four decades working in Iran's military industries, holding senior positions in the Shahid Bagheri Industrial Group, the Aerospace Industries Organization – which has worked on missile development in cooperation with Russia, China and North Korea – and the Defense Industries Organization.
He worked with Hassan Tehrani Moghaddam, a senior Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commander widely regarded as the father of Iran's missile industry.
Akhlaghi has been under international sanctions since 2007 because of his involvement in Iran's missile programs.
His appointment comes as Iran works to rebuild its military facilities and replenish weapons lost during the war. He has pledged to strengthen domestic arms production, and his background suggests rebuilding Iran's missile programs will be a priority for the ministry.
Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia has claimed repeatedly since late August that Iran has rebuilt its weapons manufacturing capacity, including last week, when it said the country was now able to make more arms than " even before it [the war] began ."
Early in the war, the U.S. military said it had destroyed more than 85% of Iran's "defense industrial base," and President Trump had previously claimed Iran's military capabilities were destroyed by U.S. strikes, but experts have questioned that assessment, and Iran has demonstrated an ongoing capacity to launch attacks on ships in the region.
A Qatari aircraft arrived in Tehran Tuesday just minutes after a plane carrying Pakistan's army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, departed. The Qatari plane left the Iranian capital approximately 30 minutes later, according to aviation tracking data cited by Iran's semi-official Fars News agency.
The aircraft's short stay raised questions about whether it might have been carrying a diplomatic message amid ongoing indirect negotiations between the U.S. and Iran. Qatar is among the nations that have acted as mediators between the two sides for months.
No information about the aircraft's passengers or why it was in Tehran for only half an hour was provided in the Fars report.
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels said they had targeted a Saudi military operations room at Badr Camp in Aden, in southwest Yemen, with a ballistic missile on Wednesday.
Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, in a post on X , called the strike a direct hit.
"Our armed forces successfully targeted the enemy Saudi operations room at Badr Camp in Aden with a ballistic missile. The strike was accurate and direct," he said.
Aden is the de facto seat of power of Yemen's Saudi-backed government, which was forced to decamp after the Houthis occupied the national capital Sanaa more than a decade ago.
The attack claimed by the Houthis Wednesday was the third in a week on Aden.
A police official in Aden told the French news agency AFP earlier that there had been a blast "caused by a Houthi missile." Two other security sources told AFP the strike targeted a site near the city's airport.
A senior official from Iran's Revolutionary Guard threatened to target undersea internet cables in the Strait of Hormuz if Iranian infrastructure comes under attack.
Brig. Gen. Yadollah Javani, the IRGC's deputy for political affairs, warned Iran would use its full capabilities to retaliate if the U.S. and its allies launch new attacks against Iranian infrastructure. He said various investments and assets, including undersea cables carrying internet data in the strategic waterway, could be among the targets of Iranian retaliation if hostilities resume.
"The Americans and their allies have significant investments, and if they want to damage our infrastructure, it is natural that the Islamic Republic will use all its capabilities and easily destroy their investments and assets, including the internet cables that pass beneath the waters of the Strait of Hormuz," he said.
Analysts say cutting the cables in the waterway would most likely affect internet connectivity in Persian Gulf countries .
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday that Tehran and Washington were still engaged in indirect negotiations via mediators over the seven-day ceasefire proposal presented by Iran in September.
Araghchi said the U.S. was seeking to add further clauses to the Iranian proposal, which Mr. Trump rejected last month.
The proposal called for the end of the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports and vessels, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil sales, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the release of frozen Iranian assets.
He said Pakistan and Qatar were among the nations facilitating the indirect talks between Iran and the U.S., as they have been for months.
"The negotiating table remains in place," Araghchi said. "It is the American side that is closing the path, not Iran."
U.S. diplomatic missions across the Middle East have issued a new round of security warnings to Americans amid escalating attacks by Iran-backed Houthi militants against Saudi Arabia, including an Oct. 10 strike on Riyadh's international airport that killed an American citizen.
The alerts, issued Sunday by U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and several other countries, warned that hostilities could rapidly and without warning spread beyond areas already affected by the fighting. The advisories urged Americans to exercise vigilance and prepare for possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and other travel disruptions.
"We are actively warning U.S. citizens about the very real threat the Houthis pose and urging them to heed official guidance," Edgar Vasquez, the State Department's deputy assistant secretary for press, told CBS News.
"These alerts are part of a proactive effort by the Trump administration to ensure Americans are aware of potential risks," Vasquez said, adding that the safety and security of American citizens remain the department's "top priority."
President Trump said the U.S. is "doing very well with Iran" and he's just deciding how he wants to win the war.
"As you know, we're doing very well with Iran," Mr. Trump said as he took questions from reporters in the Oval Office at an unrelated executive order signing. "We just have to make a final decision of which way do we want to win? Do we want to win the nice way or the not nice way? But we're doing very well."
The war, which Mr. Trump said would take only a few weeks in March, has now dragged on for almost eight months with no apparent end in sight. Iran said on Tuesday it would not return to the negotiating table unless the U.S. drops its sanctions, threats and pressure campaign — an unlikely demand.
The president also discussed Europe not helping the U.S. with the war with Iran, saying, "We don't need any help. But I was testing them."
"I just called individual presidents and prime ministers to ask, would they like to help us? And they said, 'No,'" Mr. Trump said. "I said, 'Well, that's not nice.' You know, we spend hundreds of billions a year on NATO. And they said no."

title: Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield, and what they mean to Ukraine in the war against Russia
description: Here's what to know about Starlink and Starshield, the technologies Ukraine is relying on in the war against Russia.
content: Over the past week, Ukraine has received a stark reminder of its growing dependence on uninterrupted access to Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield networks in its drone-heavy war against Russia, now in its fifth year.Ukraine has a fraction of Russia's resources, but its aggressive development of drone warfare on defensive and offensive fronts has helped it endure an onslaught from its much bigger adversary, which invaded Ukraine in early 2022. That was true until last week, when Ukraine reported a throttling of the Starshield network that was causing its drones to stop midflight and fall out of the sky.The two SpaceX networks operate on a constellation of thousands of low-Earth satellites — Starlink is the commercial version, while Starshield is a military product licensed to the U.S. government and its partners, among them Ukraine.Kyiv's reliance on drones has made Starlink and Starshield nearly indispensable to its arsenal. When Ukraine experienced a disruption to those networks, it lost the shield of interceptors and drones that offered some protection against Russian drone and missile strikes.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy believes Musk throttled Starshield at the request of U.S. officials, though the world's richest man has denied any role and said it's the U.S. government that controls the military-grade network. President Trump has also denied he's responsible for slowing the network. However, CBS News reported Tuesday that Musk was behind the disruption, though a number of questions remain unanswered. There has also been conflicting information about whether full access to the networks has been restored. As of Wednesday afternoon, Starlink remained throttled, Zelenskyy's office confirmed. Here's what's known about Starshield and Starlink — and their role in the Ukraine war.What happened in Ukraine?On Oct. 13, Ukraine's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment, making it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones, officials and soldiers told CBS News. Ukrainian soldiers said they noticed "speed limits" had been imposed on their use of SpaceX's Starshield internet dishes, the military-grade Starlink dishes that Ukrainians strap onto their drones so remote pilots can maintain their connection with the unmanned aircraft as they fly toward Russian targets.Access was restricted by turning off dishes on Ukrainian drones flying above a certain speed, causing them to fall out of the sky. Ukraine's Ministry of Defense sources said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions without informing them beforehand.Zelenskyy said Saturday the speed limits had prevented Ukraine from using Starshield to shoot down Russian Shahed attack drones.What are Starshield and Starlink?Starshield, the military-grade satellite network, runs on the same constellation of satellites as its civilian sister, Starlink, but has fewer technical limitations and more advanced security features. Both are operated by Musk's company SpaceX.The U.S. government pays SpaceX to license the use of Starshield and controls who can access the technology. Its use has been limited to Ukraine and occupied territories. It is not available in Russia.There is no working alternative to Starlink, as no direct competitor approaches Starlink's coverage of 11,150 satellites. Amazon Leo aims to compete, but at this point, it has under 400 satellites in low Earth orbit and has been hampered by the launchpad explosion of a Blue Origin rocket in May.Regular Starlink terminals have a 70 km/hr (43.5 mph) speed cap, which is the speed at which internet can be used in a vehicle in motion. At rates exceeding the cap, the internet degrades and is no longer usable. Starshield has no artificial speed cap and is known to work at speeds of at least 160 km/hr (99.4 mph). Starshield-equipped strike drones cruise at 160 km/h or more, and they're the backbone of Ukrainian mid-range strikes. During the throttling over the last week, Ukrainian units reported link drops at speeds as low as 90 km/hr (55.9 mph), making those drones inoperable. The degradation of Starshield is estimated to have cost Ukraine tens of millions of dollars in losses, according to an analysis by Dimko Zhluktenko, a drone pilot and analyst in the Armed Forces of Ukraine.On Oct. 15, some Ukrainian officials said that the Starshield restrictions had been lifted. But Zelenskyy told NBC News on Sunday the maximum speed was still 161 km/hr.Zelenskyy told Fox News on Wednesday that the service was "still limited," but he added that Secretary of State Marco Rubio told him he would "work with his team on this to unblock" it.Is Ukraine using Starshield or Starlink? It uses both. Starlink has been providing internet service to Ukrainian civilians and military forces since 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, according to Reuters.Initially funded by private donors and a U.S. foreign aid contract, SpaceX won a Pentagon contract to pay for Starlink for Ukraine in 2023, along with a contract for 500 Starshield terminals. In August 2024, SpaceX signed another Defense Department contract to expand Starshield usage to 3,000 terminals for the front lines, Bloomberg reported.Beyond communicating with and guiding drones over long distances, Starshield also serves another function: It connects every sensor and weapon system on the battlefield. Disruptions to the service have an impact that can be compared to an office having to function without being able to connect to Wi-Fi. Ukraine's military uses Starlink for general battlefield communications, and Ukrainian civilians rely on it for communications needs, too.On the Russian side, the Kremlin had also been using Starlink until February, when SpaceX cut off its access. As a result, Ukraine gained more than 150 square miles of territory.Musk and throttling Ukraine's access to StarshieldCBS News reported Tuesday that a decision by Musk led to restrictions on Ukraine's use of SpaceX's satellite communications network, though it remains unclear how Musk's order to curtail service was executed. Musk had spoken with administration officials multiple times, seeking clarity on the president's thinking on the matter. He has in the past expressed distaste for the perception that his company could be seen as profiting from the Ukraine war.The temporary restrictions came as a surprise to some Trump administration officials, who said neither Mr. Trump nor the Pentagon had specifically ordered any limits meant to deliberately disrupt drone operations and battlefield communications. The president said Monday he was seeking information about who had ordered the slowdown. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday denied the Pentagon had manipulated the service, saying, "We haven't made any directives or anything like that." Can Elon Musk stop the use of Starlink and Starshield?Musk has not admitted to imposing restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starshield."Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," the world's richest person wrote on X.He added that Starlink is a "commercial service," writing that it is "limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action."Rubio, however, seemed to attribute the network constraints to Musk."The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr. Musk," Rubio told reporters in Mumbai on Wednesday.Within a few minutes, though, he seemed to concede that Starshield was different: "We don't control what a private company — how they decide their product can be used. Now, if they're in a contract with the United States military, like Starshield, that's a different matter, because that's something we are purchasing and using for our use."Intelligence-sharingAt around the same time as the Starlink and Starshield disruptions, Ukraine also did not receive warnings from U.S. intelligence about major Russian strikes.Ukraine relies on a mixture of American sensors, aircraft, surveillance and human intelligence to map Russian positions and launch sites. The early warning system, which is distinct from the SpaceX products, notifies Ukraine when Russia has launched a ballistic missile in its direction. It failed in at least two instances, on Oct. 13 and Oct. 18. On Oct. 13, Zelenskyy said Ukraine "received no advance warning" when Russia launched a ballistic missile barrage. That overnight attack targeted energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv and Kharkiv, killing six people and leaving some 600,000 without power. Ukrainian sources said U.S. officials said the warning system had failed due to "bad weather." Ukrainian officials expressed doubt about that explanation and accused the U.S. of "playing" with the system. By 3 a.m., that system seemed to have been restored.Then on Monday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had been hit by another wave of Russian missile and drone strikes, "and again, there was no warning from partners."A senior Pentagon official told CBS News Monday there had been "no change to Department of War policy regarding intelligence sharing or any capabilities we are enabling Europeans to provide to Ukraine."By Wednesday, however, the warning system appeared to have been restored: "Now intelligence works. Thank you so much. That was crucial for us," Zelenskyy said on Fox News.Rising pressure to end the warDeliveries of key Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine have also slowed, Ukraine has said. Rubio on Tuesday called interceptors the "most in-demand product right now in the defense field," and said that "when a country doesn't get interceptors from the United States, it's not because we're denying. We have our own needs, too.""There's nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine," he said. "It's simply a balance between our obligations."Mr. Trump has grown impatient with the more than four-year-long war. He has sought to portray the ongoing Ukraine war as the reason for high energy prices and has vented his frustration with Zelenskyy more frequently in recent weeks, accusing him of not doing enough to end it.He waived restrictions on buying Russian diesel earlier this month in an effort to ease pressure on the price of the commodity, a move Zelenskyy argued could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin. And Mr. Trump also waived sanctions on Russia last week.Mr. Trump said earlier this month that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop striking each other's energy infrastructure — announcing an "energy ceasefire." Zelenskyy initially said Ukraine was willing to abide by such an agreement, but that Russia's strikes never ceased, and several days later he told the Financial Times his country would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries because Russia was still attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.The Russian government never confirmed that it had agreed to a ceasefire.Mr. Trump told reporters Tuesday that Russia keeps "grinding away" and is more capable of sustaining casualties than Ukraine, arguing "it's time" for Zelenskyy to make a deal.

title: Chemical leak in Toledo forces hazardous materials evacuation, shelter-in-place orders
description: A massive chemical leak in Toledo, Ohio, is forcing some people out of their homes while others have been told to shelter in place.
content: A massive chemical leak in Toledo, Ohio, is forcing some people out of their homes while others have been told to shelter in place.A plume of smoke full of chemicals erupted from the MC Tank terminal. One injury has been reported so far. According to officials, a Lucas County sheriff's deputy who responded to the scene wasn't feeling well and drove himself to a hospital. Toledo Fire and Rescue ordered everyone within a 1-mile radius of 1266 Progress Ave. to evacuate, and everyone within a 3-mile radius to shelter in place due to a hazardous materials release. In an update Wednesday, Toledo officials say the evacuation and shelter-in-place zone has been reduced to half a mile. The orders beyond that zone have been lifted."There is still concern that the tank is emitting this chemical, and it has the potential within 12 hours of the incident to be explosive," said Toledo Mayor Wade Kapszukiewicz. "As a result, our first responders and hazmat teams and safety teams are not approaching the tank." The evacuation orders were issued at 10:48 p.m. Tuesday, and the shelter-in-place orders were issued at 4:24 a.m. Wednesday. Those within the shelter-in-place area were asked to stay indoors, close windows and doors and turn off ventilation that draws in outside air. They were also asked to keep pets inside.MC Tank Transport Inc. said in a statement that equipment associated with its operations is involved in the incident.According to the statement and as the City of Toledo confirmed, the chemical involved in this incident is glycidyl methacrylate, an industrial chemical used to make certain plastics, paints and coatings perform better.Who is in the evacuation zone?According to the City of Toledo, the zone is a 1-mile radius around 1266 Progress Ave. Those living or working within 1 mile of that address were asked to evacuate and can go to:Shoreland Elementary School — temporary shelter.Meijer parking lot (off East Alexis) — Red Cross and TARTA buses are stationed to provide shelter as needed.The shelter-in-place zone is a 3-mile radius around 1266 Progress Ave. No injuries have been reported. Toledo public schools were closed on Wednesday.

title: Community remembers two Monroe High Schools students killed in separate incidents
description: Students at Monroe High School came together Wednesday night to remember two of their classmates who recently died.
content: Students at Monroe High School came together Wednesday night to remember two of their classmates who recently died. One of them was 15-year-old Trenton Grant, who died tragically after an assault and fire on Saturday. The other, Garrett Siffer, 18, of Ida, was killed in a single-vehicle crash last Thursday morning in Raisinville Township. "Because I know right now they're smiling down on us right now," said principal Steve Pollzzie to all his students on the football field.Students filled the football field as they shared memories and said prayers for those who knew Trenton and for his family there on Wednesday."He was an amazing, amazing young man. He had a smile that can light up a room. He was talented in many, many ways," said Pollzzie.Polizzi said he has known Trenton since kindergarten. Early Saturday morning, the Monroe County Sheriff's Office was called for an assault and a house fire. Multiple people were hurt, including Grant, who died from his injuries. Investigators originally said it was an isolated incident, but now they're calling it a homicide, and they have even taken a suspect into custody.Deputies have not released any information about the suspect, how they were caught, or when they will be arraigned. For now, the community's focus is on each other, especially those who knew Grant."I see people that are hurting, and that's what I saw this weekend," said event organizer Deb Starlgraeve.Starlgraeve and other business owners helped put on the vigil. A local pizzeria donated food while local mental health resources and service dogs supported and comforted anyone who needed it."It's encouraging to see the community come together this way," said event organizer, Tino Amaya.The Monroe County Sheriff's Office says this is still an active investigation and is seeking any tips. If you know anything, call police or 800-SPEAK UP

title: Angel Reese, Dream overpower Valkyries 97-71 to take 2-1 WNBA Finals lead
description: The Atlanta Dream​ found their shooting touch and took a 2-1 lead in the WNBA Finals on Wednesday, pulling away from the Golden State Valkyries for a 97-71 win at State Farm Arena.
content: The Atlanta Dream found their shooting touch and took a 2-1 lead in the WNBA Finals on Wednesday, pulling away from the Golden State Valkyries for a 97-71 win at State Farm Arena.Angel Reese finished with 21 points and 12 rebounds. The Dream set a franchise record for points in a Finals game and had five players score in double figures.Rhyne Howard added 16 points and five steals, while Naz Hillmon scored 15 and made three 3-pointers. Isobel Borlase contributed 12 points off the bench, and Jordin Canada finished with 10 points, eight assists and six rebounds.Golden State erased Atlanta's 46-40 halftime lead early in the third quarter, but the Dream answered. After the teams were tied at 49, Atlanta closed the quarter on a 22-8 run to take a 71-57 lead into the fourth. "I'm most proud of the second half because the first few possessions were a little sloppy. I was really close to using a timeout," Dream coach Karl Smesko said. "They pulled together on their own and got it worked out, cleaned it up themselves."Borlase and DeWanna Bonner helped Atlanta build separation late in the third, combining for nine consecutive Dream points while Reese was on the bench. Atlanta continued to stretch its lead in the fourth and finished with a 26-point victory. After shooting below 35% in each of the first two games, Atlanta made 49.3% of its shots Wednesday, including nine of 22 from 3-point range. The Dream also outscored Golden State 44-20 in the paint.Reese made seven of 12 shots, both of her 3-point attempts and all five free throws. She became the youngest player to record double-doubles in three consecutive WNBA Finals games. Howard followed her Finals-record six steals in Game 2 with five more, becoming the first player with at least five steals in consecutive Finals games. Gabby Williams led Golden State with 15 points and eight assists. Tiffany Hayes scored 14, while Cecilia Zandalasini and Janelle Salaün added 13 apiece.Game 4 is scheduled for 1 p.m. Saturday at State Farm Arena. Atlanta needs two more victories to win its first WNBA championship.

title: As Kansas Senate race tightens, Marshall argues opponent is just another Democrat, while Hamilton says he's "independent-minded"
description: GOP Sen. Roger Marshall and Pastor Adam Hamilton debated tariffs, war and high fuel prices, and also addressed the most controversial issues in each of their campaigns.
content: The candidates in Kansas' surprisingly competitive Senate race faced off in a debate Wednesday evening, as Republicans fight to head off the possibility of their first loss in a Kansas Senate contest in nearly a century.Incumbent GOP Sen. Roger Marshall hammered away at what it would mean if he were to lose — that it could help hand control of the Senate to Democrats: "My opponent's going to say anything he can to lie to get into that office and give control to Chuck Schumer."Marshall's Democratic challenger, megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton, tried to convince voters that he's not too progressive for Kansans and went on the offensive against Marshall over the impact of tariffs, the Iran war and other Trump administration policies on the state.Marshall hewed closely to many of President Trump's views, and like him, blamed rising diesel costs on the war in Ukraine, rather than the Iran war."The real problem with the cost of diesel, in particular, is No. 1, is the Ukraine war, and because of that, diesel production has gone down," Marshall said. But at the same time, he said of Mr. Trump's recent announcement that the U.S. would purchase Russian diesel, "it doesn't sound like a great idea to me." He added, "If this brings Russia to the bargaining table and it ends the war, then I'm all for it right now."While Marshall implored Trump voters to come out and vote for him, he said he does not always align with the president and has "objected" to him multiple times before, specifically citing the ICE raids in Kansas and Mr. Trump's short-term waiver on beef imports, both of which have hurt Kansas farmers.Hamilton described himself as a "moderate or independent-minded Democrat" and vowed to "work across the aisle to try to bring people together to solve problems." Hamilton largely sought to distance himself from mainstream Democrats. He promised not to vote for Schumer to be majority leader if Democrats win the Senate, called the Biden administration's border policies a "disaster" and said during a discussion on transgender participation in sports: "I have a 12-year-old granddaughter. I don't want biological men or boys competing against her that could harm her."Marshall argued Hamilton leans further to the left than he has let on. The Republican senator also questioned how independent Hamilton would be."He's going to say he's going to vote against these things, but every Democrat stands up, and when Schumer tells them to jump, they say, 'how high?'" Marshall said during the sports discussion. "So why is he going to be any different once he gets to Washington? He can tell us one thing, but let's see what his actions would be like."Hamilton said he would try to "force" Mr. Trump to end the Iran war. High gas prices and tariffs are putting many farms in the state in dire economic straits, with many voters telling CBS News that they aren't sure if they will survive past next year if conditions continue. "It was not a good decision to go to war in Iran, and we need to get out," said Hamilton.Marshall said he "want[s] this war to be over … as soon as possible, but we cannot let Iran have a nuclear weapon." He described Hamilton's views as "war through weakness, as opposed to peace through strength."Hamilton slammed Mr. Trump's tariffs, arguing they have led to chaos and uncertainty. Marshall said the president's tariffs have led to a "manufacturing renaissance."Mr. Trump's immigration policies have also drawn scrutiny in Kansas, including a string of Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids that agricultural leaders warned could cause workforce disruptions. Marshall pushed back last month, saying in a post on social media that ICE "needs to coordinate with our local law enforcement."During Wednesday's debate, Hamilton called ICE's practices "militarized" and "politicized." Marshall said "all this discussion starts with a secure border," arguing Democrats could loosen border enforcement.Polling suggests a tight race, and millions of dollars have gushed into Kansas, flooding the state's airwaves with anti-Marshall and anti-Hamilton ads.The debate's moderator wasted no time in asking both candidates about their biggest controversies. For Marshall, that's the New York Times report about how the OB/GYN aggressively pursued his former patients — many of whom struggled economically — for medical debts and in some cases had them arrested. Hamilton faced questions regarding his church's response to an incident of child sex abuse at a youth summer camp in 2005. Marshall said "we did everything possible to take good care of people" and that many of his patients got free care. He conceded that some patients were turned over to collections agencies, which he called a fairly rare occurrence that is standard in the medical industry. At his rally in Wichita on Monday, Mr. Trump defended Marshall against these allegations, saying he was required by law to report the debt, and that he's been unfairly "made out to be some kind of Shylock character." (The Anti-Defamation League later said the term "Shylock," a reference to a Jewish moneylender in William Shakespeare's "The Merchant of Venice," is "rooted in a longstanding antisemitic stereotype.")On the abuse scandal, Hamilton said his church subsequently changed its policy on handling allegations of abuse, and "ultimately, we helped get this man put behind bars." Still, Hamilton admitted, "I should have checked to make sure that he wasn't going back (to the youth camp). That was a mistake on my part." Cathy Bien, a spokesperson for Hamilton's United Methodist Church, told CBS News on Wednesday that the incident was "handled the best way [they] knew how 20 years ago." Kansas could decide which party controls the Senate, and even before the debate, early voting numbers were skyrocketing in the state. Election officials say that they are fielding numbers that rival the 2024 presidential election. The race could hinge on how many Republicans cross party lines to vote for Hamilton. At least 100 Kansas Republican leaders have endorsed Hamilton, including former governors, state officials and Mr. Trump's own former White House press secretary, Stephanie Grisham.But many are voting early to ensure Republicans maintain control of the Senate. One early voter in Wichita, Tim Higgins, told CBS News that he's backing Marshall because "it's important to keep the progress that the nation is currently on since the presidential election." However, for many, the race is about state issues. "Rural Kansas is struggling, urban Kansas is struggling," said former Republican state Rep. Terrie Huntington, who is voting for Hamilton. "I think people are looking for change."

title: NYC officials release 40,000 additional unseen post-9/11 documents
description: New York City officials have released an additional 40,000 documents that had previously been withheld from the public, shedding more light on air quality concerns at Ground Zero after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.
content: New York City officials have released an additional 40,000 documents that had previously been withheld from the public, shedding more light on air quality concerns at Ground Zero after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.The latest release is the second set of documents made public under a court agreement between 9/11 Health Watch and Mayor Zohran Mamdani's administration. The move also settled a multi-year legal battle over air quality and health concerns following the attacks. Documents released show health officials were still finding evidence of asbestos nearly 10 months after the attacks, even though government officials repeatedly assured New Yorkers the air around Ground Zero was safe to breathe. Mamdani said the city made "an enduring promise" last month when it launched the public records portal and released the first 170,000 pages of documents. "It wasn't a box-check. It was the first of many steps we are taking to bring closure and clarity to millions of New Yorkers," he said. "I am proud to release these next 40,000 documents and look forward to the work to come."First responders, elected officials and families of people who developed 9/11-related illnesses pushed for the records to be made public for over 20 years.The database now contains more than 200,000 pages of records, including the long-discussed Harding Memo and files known as the "68 Boxes.""Our commitment to honoring the victims of the horrific terror attacks of Sept. 11 and delivering accountability and transparency to survivors cannot begin or end on the anniversary," Mamdani said."The first responders, family members and survivors of that terrible day deserve transparency and accountability from their city government every day," he added.Additional documents are expected to be released in the coming months.

title: Video captures North Brunswick burglary, family says thieves stole $100K safe
description: The homeowners say four masked thieves kicked in their front door, disabled security cameras and made off with a safe containing cash, jewelry and passports in a break-in that lasted about six minutes.
content: A North Brunswick family says four masked burglars broke into their home and stole a safe containing an estimated $100,000 worth of cash, jewelry and important documents.The burglary happened around 7:45 p.m. Friday at a home on Aspen Drive, according to the family."They basically kicked the door open, and they broke this entire frame," Kinjal Patel, the victim's brother, said.Patel said surveillance footage shows four suspects forcing their way into the home before heading directly upstairs.The thieves then searched room after room until they found the family's safe."They basically took the safe and they dragged it," Patel said.According to the family, the entire break-in lasted about six minutes.The homeowner, Chirag Patel, said the safe contained cash, jewelry and critical documents, including passports."I felt like my life was over," Patel said. He estimated the loss at "close to like $100K."The family believes the suspects may have been watching the house before the break-in. They shared video from a neighbor's security camera that they say shows a suspicious vehicle driving near the home about 15 minutes after the family left.Patel said the family's Ring camera captured only a still image of the suspects.The family also believes the burglars may have jammed the home's Wi-Fi signal, disabling security cameras during the break-in."We feel like this was a targeted attack," Kinjal Patel said.It's unclear why the home may have been targeted, but the family said detectives are actively investigating leads.The family has provided investigators with footage of what they believe is a silver Mercedes-Benz that may be connected to the burglary."I just hope justice is served and I hope to see them in court," Chirag Patel said.The Patel family is offering a $2,000 reward for information that leads to an arrest.Anyone with information is asked to contact the North Brunswick Police Department at 732-247-0922 or online.

title: Naz Reid has 20 points and 11 rebounds in his Charlotte debut as the Hornets beat the Nets 110-103
description: Naz Reid had 20 points and 11 rebounds in his Charlotte debut, Grayson Allen added 21 points off the bench and the Hornets beat the Brooklyn Nets 110-103 on Wednesday night.
content: Naz Reid had 20 points and 11 rebounds in his Charlotte debut, Grayson Allen added 21 points off the bench and the Hornets beat the Brooklyn Nets 110-103 on Wednesday night.Dennis Schroder scored eight of his 19 points in the fourth quarter, Brandon Miller had 18 and Moussa Diabate added 17 for the short-handed Hornets.Charlotte, which was eliminated from the Eastern Conference play-in tournament last season, was without starters Coby White (left calf strain) and shooting guard Kon Knueppel (right hamstring strain), who led the NBA last season in 3-pointers made.The Hornets dealt star point LaMelo Ball to Minnesota after the season in the deal that brought Reid to Charlotte.Julius Randle scored 33 points on 11-for-18 shooting from the field in his debut for the Nets. Michael Porter Jr. shot 10 for 21 from field to finish with 26 points.None of Brooklyn's other three starters scored in double figures. The Nets, celebrating their 60th season, wore white uniforms with red and blue in a nod to their ABA days.The Hornets had their 10-point lead trimmed to five heading in the final period. Porter cut the deficit to 94-90 with a floater with 7:20 left in regulation, but Schroder, who debuted for his 12th different NBA team, then outscored the Nets 8-2. He capped it with a finger roll layup that extended the lead 102-92 with 5:38 to play.Brooklyn had a chance to make it a one possession game after a three-point play from Randle with 1:16 remaining but Egor Demin's turnover led to a 3-pointer from Allen that sealed the game.Mikel Brown Jr., who the Nets took with the No. 6 pick in the draft, had six points and three assists in 20 minutes off the bench.Up nextHornets: Welcome the Atlanta Hawks for their home opener Friday.Nets: Visit the Cleveland Cavaliers on Saturday.

title: A return of 70s in Philadelphia as coastal flooding concerns diminish. Here's the weather forecast.
description: Thursday will be another dry but breezy day across the Philadelphia region as Subtropical Storm Josephine moves farther away from the East Coast.
content: Thursday will be another dry but breezy day across the Philadelphia region as Subtropical Storm Josephine moves farther away from the East Coast.While we're not expecting any direct impacts from the storm, rough surf and some lingering minor coastal flooding will remain concerns along parts of the Jersey Shore and Delaware beaches.Otherwise, expect a mix of sun and just a few clouds with a noticeable northwest breeze. title: 3 people, including toddler, found dead from gunshots in Ohio home
description: A man, a woman and a toddler were found dead with gunshot wounds in a home in Gnadenhutten, Tuscarawas County, authorities in Ohio said.
content: A man, a woman and a toddler were found dead with apparent gunshot wounds in a home in Tuscarawas County, Ohio, authorities said. The Tuscarawas County Sheriff's Office said in a news release on Facebook that a 67-year-old male, a 51-year-old female and a 22-month-old boy were found dead at a home on North Cherry Street in the Village of Gnadenhutten on Wednesday morning. They all appeared to have gunshot wounds, and a gun was found at the scene.The sheriff's office said the 911 dispatch center received a 911 hang-up call around 4:15 a.m. on Wednesday. The phone call did not reveal a location because it was disconnected almost immediately, the sheriff's office said. Dispatchers tried to call back several times, and the sheriff's office said it appears a voice "softly" said "help" during one of the attempted call-backs to the phone. The sheriff's office said officials reached the phone's owner, who said it was a spare device he had loaned to an "associate." The phone was then tracked to the 200 block of North Cherry Street, according to the sheriff's office. A family member was located, and they unlocked the door and found the three people dead inside. The identities of the three people were not released on Wednesday. Tuscarawas County Coroner Jeff Cameron will perform autopsies to determine the cause and manner of death."There are many people to interview and much to do with evidence from the scene but I feel strongly that the community is in no danger," the sheriff's office said. More information will be provided once "we are confident that we have gathered and verified all the necessary facts," according to the sheriff's office. Gnadenhutten is about 62 miles south of Akron.

title: Retired NYPD detective faces murder charge in deadly George Washington Bridge shooting
description: A retired NYPD detective is charged with murder in the deadly shooting on the George Washington Bridge Tuesday night, police said.
author_name: Tony  Aiello, Jesse  Zanger, Naveen  Dhaliwal
content: A retired NYPD detective is charged with murder in the deadly shooting on the George Washington Bridge Tuesday night, police said. Victor Romero, 62, retired from the NYPD 25 years ago, police said. Police believe he fatally shot Koran Irvine in an apparent road rage incident. Irvine, 46, was fatally shot just after 7 p.m. Tuesday night. Port Authority Police officers were responding to reports of a single-vehicle crash in the middle of the bridge and found Irvine with a gunshot wound. He was rushed to a nearby hospital where he later died. Investigators have recovered a gun and it is being tested to determine if it is connected to the shooting. Romero's vehicle is in custody, police sources said. The NYPD was at Romero's home in Haverstraw, New York waiting to execute a search warrant, according to police sources.Technology at the George Washington Bridge and license plate readers helped in the investigation. Detectives are also reviewing surveillance footage as they work to establish what happened on the bridge before the gunfire erupted. Romero joined the NYPD in 1994. He worked for seven years and retired as a narcotics detective on disability after being shot by robbers at his family's coin laundry in Brooklyn. In 2000, the Civilian Complaint Review Board received a complaint about Romero firing a weapon. Romero retired before the CCRB could complete its investigation. Meanwhile, relatives have been gathering at Irvine's home in Valley Cottage in Rockland County. "It's senseless. It's senseless," Irvine's friend Anthony Hodges said. "He became almost like a brother to me. He's just so vibrant. He always had a smile on his face. It was never a time I didn't have a conversation with him and he didn't smile. He was just such a lively person." "He was a very nice man. We're new to the neighborhood. I remember when we first came, he would help us out. They have some chickens in the back. He brought us eggs to welcome us," neighbor Hope Dorcelly said. "I'm very shocked. We just heard about it this morning actually and we're just completely devastated for the family."Irvine was married for 15 years to his wife Patricia, and has a teen girl and younger boy. In a statement posted on GoFundMe, the Irvine family said his "family was his world ... he loved deeply ... and always strived to give his family the best life possible." Irvine was a 20-year employee of Con Edison. "We are heartbroken by the tragic loss of a member of the Con Edison family in this senseless act of violence. Our deepest condolences go out to his family, friends, colleagues, and everyone who knew and loved him," the utility said in a statement.

title: Allegheny County's mandate on paid parental leave draws strong reactions from small businesses
description: Some Allegheny County small businesses are looking at laying people off or moving out of the county due to the just-passed mandatory paid parental leave policy.
content: Some Allegheny County small businesses are looking at laying people off or moving out of the county due to the just-passed mandatory paid parental leave policy, according to a tax professional whose company specializes in working with small businesses. Total Business Solutions in Warrendale represents 250 small businesses across the area. The businesses' president, Kelly Bender, has already spoken with a number of them about the tough decisions they are facing since the policy passed county council on Tuesday night. "The immediate conversations that I had were how will we afford to pay 100% leave if an employee has to take off that much time," she said. "And right now we're really trying to figure out how that is without having to lay people off. Or I have actually a couple business owners who have said, 'I think I'm going to move and relocate my business outside of the county.'"The businesses the policy will hit, she explained, are the ones that are already on tight margins. She mentioned hearing concerns from labor- and service-based businesses like restaurants, hairdressers and landscapers. One of her clients is Body by Design Holistic Wellness Spa in the North Hills. Just Wednesday, the spa hired its ninth employee. As it stands, it will be one of its last."It's frustrating," spa owner Heather Brown said. "It's hard to be a business owner already. We already have a lot of financial obligations."She explained that after moving into a new space, she's been planning to grow the business in the next three to four years. Now, she said she is changing the way she thinks about the future of the spa. As a direct result of the parental leave policy, she said she will have to cap the number of employees at 14, one shy of 15 â which is when the paid leave policy kicks in. Just a single employee on full paid parental leave would make her business unsustainable, she explained."The profit margins are already very tight, and to mandate paid leave for six or eight weeks at a time would be catastrophic if funded by small businesses," she said. "As a mother, I hate to even think about how that might be a hardship for someone in the future, but it's just such an impractical piece of legislation when small businesses are expected to take that financial burden."Bender explained what she said makes the policy different from parental leave policies in other parts of the country. "What most other states who have done these types of policies have done is set up some type of taxation system in which employers are paying on a per-employee basis into some type of shared insurance pool. Or they have access to a shared insurance pool," Bender said. "I think that the idea of the paid parental leave policy is a good one and noble, but to put the burden of the financial impact entirely on the backs of the employers is misguided." Business owners considering layoffs told Bender they either can't afford to pay the workers due to the impact of the paid parental leave policy or laying off workers would allow them to get under the 15-person threshold. "In my experience, if a business is already struggling, they will try to hold on until it ends in closure, eliminating all the jobs at once," Bender said. "The 15 mark is not some magic number that leads to great profitability. That's still a pretty small business. Supporters of paid parental leave said it will protect workers and their families.

title: LA County woman who was allegedly watching porn charged for deadly 15 Freeway crash in Utah
description: A Los Angeles County woman was charged in connection with a deadly crash in Utah in June, which allegedly happened after she was watching pornography while driving.
content: A Los Angeles County woman was charged in connection with a deadly crash in Utah, which allegedly happened after she was watching pornography while driving. Christine Chao, 44, of Rosemead, was charged with second-degree felony text messaging or email automobile homicide on Tuesday for the June 12 crash in Juab County, Utah, according to documents from Juab County's Fourth District Court. Utah Highway Patrol troopers were called to the spot of the three-car crash, where traffic was slowing due to ongoing construction, the court documents said. Prosecutors said two cars were traveling "at a slower speed" when Chao's vehicle struck the rearmost car, causing it to crash into the vehicle in front of it. "All three vehicles subsequently left the road due to the collision," the court documents said. "After the crash, the defendant told officers she was at fault."Investigators seized Chao's phone and obtained a search warrant to examine it. "Officers did not observe any brake marks on the road to indicate the defendant slowed before the crash," the document said. "An examination of the phone ... showed that the defendant had accessed the website ... less than two minutes before the crash occurred. This website is commonly used to view pornographic videos."Utah Highway Patrol Trooper Richard Tinoco, one of several who were called to the scene, said that the passenger in the rearmost car was in critical condition after the crash, but was later pronounced dead at the scene. Chao was ordered to appear in Utah for a November 17 court date, according to Juab County prosecutors.

title: El-Sayed, Rogers touch on Michigan jobs, auto industry and education in final Senate debate
description: In their final debate ahead of the midterm election, Michigan U.S. Senate candidates Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers discussed local topics that have become hot-button issues among voters in the state.
content: In their final debate ahead of the midterm election, Michigan U.S. Senate candidates Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers discussed local topics that have become hot-button issues among voters in the state.The candidates are in the final stretch of a contentious race that has drawn national attention, with El-Sayed fighting to maintain Democratic control in the state alongside Sen. Elissa Slotkin and Rogers, who was endorsed by President Trump, hoping to become the first Republican elected to a Michigan U.S. Senate seat in more than 30 years.Aside from clashing over national topics like tariffs, the Iran war, artificial intelligence and Social Security, the candidates were asked about jobs in Michigan, the auto industry and education.El-Sayed called for an end to stock buybacks and pointed to General Motors, which the Detroit Free Press reports is authorizing a $20 billion share repurchase program. He also pushed for Michigan to become the "world's leader in internal combustion engine research and manufacturing." At the state level, Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who dropped out of the U.S. Senate race ahead of the August primary, introduced Senate Bill 783 in February 2026, which aims to amend the Michigan Strategic Fund Act and restrict stock buybacks.El-Sayed mentioned electric vehicles, saying, "We also can't see the future of auto to China, so I think we need to say what would happen if we decided to throw the gauntlet down and build a 300-mile-range, $25,000 EV? We tariff around EVs, we invest in that and then we can continue to win both the future of internal combustion and EVs."Rogers also brought up China, arguing that the first federal policy to implement is banning the country from building cars in the U.S.In September, Zhao Chunlin, vice president of manufacturing at Chinese EV maker Zeekr, told CBS News that their vehicle would soon be sold in North America following a trade deal signed between Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Chinese President Xi Jinping.The U.S. government, on the other hand, has so far refused to allow Chinese vehicles into the market, for example, through prohibitive tariffs."That (Chinese vehicles built in the U.S.) is the single No. 1 existential threat to our automobile industry here. Remember, China doesn't come here to make profits; they come here to steal market share," Rogers said. "When they talk about showing up, or they build them in Canada and try to talk to them about coming across the bridge, we need to stop that at the border, and we need to make sure that it is very clear in the law that those Chinese cars can't be built right here in the United States."On education, the moderators asked both candidates what they would do to help expand opportunities for students in Michigan, which is 44th in the nation in fourth-grade reading.Rogers called that ranking "unacceptable" and proposed using Title I funds to support a "phonics-based" reading program between third and fourth grades and bringing skilled trades back into schools. Meanwhile, El-Sayed pointed to a funding issue and pushed to fund the Department of Education, which is being dismantled following executive orders signed in 2025.In a rebuttal, Rogers says El-Sayed uses "flowery language" and will find ways to blame Mr. Trump. El-Sayed responded, saying that he is going to blame the president because "this is Donald Trump's economy. We are living in it."

title: Lavender Heights businesses form alliance to push for changes to Sacramento parking rules
description: Small business owners in Sacramento's Lavender Heights neighborhood have formed a new alliance to address concerns about parking costs and public safety, calling on city leaders to make changes they say are hurting local businesses.
content: Small business owners in Sacramento's Lavender Heights neighborhood have formed a new alliance to address concerns about parking costs and public safety, calling on city leaders to make changes they say are hurting local businesses.More than 20 businesses have signed on to the newly formed Lavender Alliance, which was established this week. The group plans to hold a community meeting next Wednesday and says it has invited Sacramento Mayor Kevin McCarty and Councilmember Phil Pluckebaum, who represents District 4, including Midtown and Lavender Heights.The effort follows an Oct. 7 town hall hosted by McCarty to discuss public safety and economic development in Midtown, where business owners raised concerns about the city's parking policies."It's 8 a.m. to 10 p.m. The meters get more expensive every night. You've got a meter maid sitting out there at 9:58 to nail every car," said Jill Osur, owner of Teneral Cellars wine lounge in Lavender Heights, during the town hall.In July, Sacramento extended metered parking hours to run from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m. Osur said her business has seen sales decline by about 20% since the change."People are literally spending 30 dollars out front before they ever spend a dime to buy a glass of wine," Osur said. "Imagine that, you've already spent 28 dollars on parking. You're two minutes late and now you've got a $92 ticket. Why would you come back?"Dan Chapin, a Roseville resident, said he recently received a $92 parking ticket while visiting Midtown."Popped into some meetings and totally forgot. It was an expensive adventure downtown," Chapin said.He said the cost could make visitors reconsider spending time at local businesses."I think it might make you think twice about coming to a restaurant or a bar location," he said.In a statement, McCarty said the city faced difficult budget decisions earlier this year."Earlier this year, we had to make tough budget choices between laying off police, fire, and parks workers or increasing fees and parking rates. There were no good options," McCarty said.Osur said she left the town hall feeling that city leaders were not adequately addressing the concerns of Midtown businesses."I was very disappointed. I really felt, and left, feeling that the mayor is not concerned at all with the high number of businesses leaving Midtown," Osur said. "Following that meeting, we had a business meeting here with a lot of local business owners and we created the Lavender Alliance."The city said it has improved parking signage in the area to make the changes clearer. It also reported that parking citations declined by nearly 7% from July through September compared with April through June.The Lavender Alliance says it plans to address several issues affecting the neighborhood. Its parking demands include reducing metered hours to 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., making parking free on holidays and eliminating Sunday parking fees.The group plans to discuss its concerns and priorities at its meeting next Wednesday.

title: Valkyries fans pack Oakland bar to cheer on team as playoff series shifts to Atlanta
description: Despite it being an away game, fans were still sporting violet and went to mini Ballhallas around the Bay Area to cheer on their team.
content: The Golden State Valkyries left Ballhalla to take on the Dream in Atlanta for game 3 of the WNBA Finals. Despite it being an away game, fans were still sporting violet and went to mini Ballhallas around the Bay Area to cheer on their team.Oakland United Beerworks was packed with Valkyrie fans. It was a busy night as 12 different brews were flowing from the tap."Tonight is about as busy as I've seen it," Chris Ritter, a co-owner of Oakland United Beerworks, said.Oakland United is in the Valkyries bar network. This place started showing games last year and over time has developed a following.Now, it's partnered with the Valks and has team gear to hand out for all the postseason games. Ritter says that while the team plays at Chase Center in San Francisco, they embody the spirit of the Town."Oakland is a state of mind," Ritter said. "Oakland is one of those places that it is never easy. You're always working, but you really live this place. You have to really love this place. Most people who stay here for a period of time really understand how unique it is. And the Valkyries, it's hard to express. They have that spirit."Fans have made Oakland United their home away from home. People bring their pooches and gather with friends to watch their favorite team."Oakland United really feels like a neighborhood bar," Jessica Chesnutt said. "Feels like a Cheers. We have regulars come here all the time."Oakland United originally was located closer to the proposed waterfront ballpark for the Athletics. When that fell through, it moved more into the heart of Jack London Square. Teaming up with the Valkyries has been one of the keys to this brewery's success."They've been incredible in helping the small business in Oakland really bring in a lot of people," Ritter said. "You know, small businesses never easy. When you get people who are backing you, like the Valkyries, it means a lot to us and will always be loyal to them as a result."With the Game 3 loss, the Valkyries are now down 2-1 in the series, but fans say the finals are far from over."I feel like you get back the energy you put in," Allyson Yuen said. "We're not going to put out that negative energy. We'll get it. We're fine."Win or lose, Ritter is grateful for the lively crowd."We're going to miss everyone when the season is over," Ritter said. "We're hoping they'll still keep coming, right?"

title: Suspended Broward officer accused of taking over deceased man's identity and home bonds out of jail
description: Brian Louis Sguros left the Broward County Jail after posting his $25,000 bond on Wednesday afternoon, wearing two surgical masks and saying nothing to cameras.
content: A suspended Lauderhill police officer faces five criminal charges after allegedly stealing the identity of a deceased man and taking over his home.Brian Louis Sguros left the Broward County Jail after posting his $25,000 bond on Wednesday afternoon, wearing two surgical masks and saying nothing to cameras. Investigators said the scheme began in 2022 when Sguros conducted a welfare check at the home of 71-year-old Dennis West and found him dead. Sguros allegedly lied to the medical examiner, claiming West had no family and identifying himself as a friend. He then had West's body cremated and moved into the residence.According to officials, Sguros also used West's identity to file permits for home renovations."What's so upsetting is officers are supposed to uphold the law, and instead he's defrauding people," Broward Property Appraiser Marty Kair said.Kair noted that property scams happen hundreds of times a year, usually targeting seniors and typically involving realtors or lawyers. However, he said this is the first time a law enforcement officer has been implicated.Kair offered advice for homeowners looking to protect their estates."If you have a property, do a will, name heirs," Kair said. "It's much less likely your loved ones will be defrauded.""I kind of asked the question why and how he got the house so quickly," neighbor Lethel Hey said.Detectives said they were alerted to the situation when the original homeowner's relatives sold the home.

title: Eagles fans flood Jalen Hurts with letters of support after blood clots diagnosis
description: Eagles fans are writing letters to Jalen Hurts in the aftermath of his blood clots diagnosis to show him they will have his back.
content: Philadelphia Eagles fans are showing nothing but love to quarterback Jalen Hurts in the aftermath of his blood clots diagnosis.Fans are flying to flood his mailbox with well wishes and letters to show Hurts that they will always have his back."We're behind you 100%," Sabrina Barker of Pottstown said. "We're looking out for you and keeping you in our thoughts and prayers.""We really appreciate him beyond what he does at the grass at the Linc," Michael Feldman of Morristown said, "that we care about him as a human being and his health foremost. And number two, what he does for us on Sundays, Mondays and Thursdays."Feldman is one Eagles fan who wrote one of the letters. He said he felt compelled to join in."I figured if I am going to be sending a letter to one of my favorite NFL players ever, I might as well thank him for winning a Super Bowl in addition to wishing him a speedy recovery," Feldman said.The idea all started on the Philadelphia Eagles Fan Group Facebook page, which has 464,000 followers. Moderators said the idea took off and stretched far beyond Philadelphia."It's actually been tremendous to see that the whole NFL community just rounding up to be behind him, to just show him all the support," Barker said.Eagles fans said they hope the letters help lift Hurts up, and they are urging others to keep sending them — the more, the merrier."He gets criticized so much, and it often seems like the voices that criticize have so much more reach than the voices who want to support him," Jake Tribble of Sicklerville said. "So that's our only hope out of this, that this outpouring of love reaches him because there are a lot of us out there. ... He has a lot of support behind him, and there are a lot of people that want him to know we love him and are wishing him well."Birds fans said they hope Hurts knows they care, like they know he does."I think he cares about this community more than just where he gets his paycheck," Feldman said, "and I would say a lot of Philly athletes are like that. The Kelces, Harper, Schwarber. The list can go on and on."
