title: Fellow officer says she was concerned by Matthew Farwell's demeanor days before Sandra Birchmore's death
description: A woman who worked with Matthew Farwell at the Stoughton Police Department​ testified that she was concerned about his demeanor just days before Sandra Birchmore was found dead.
content: A woman who worked with Matthew Farwell at the Stoughton Police Department testified Wednesday at his federal trial in Massachusetts that she was concerned about his demeanor just days before Sandra Birchmore was found dead.Sandra Barrett, a veteran Stoughton police detective, took the stand as Farwell is standing trial accused of killing 23-year-old Sandra Birchmore and her unborn baby in 2021.Barrett has worked at the Stoughton Police Department since 2001 and became a detective in 2016. Farwell became a detective about two years after her."We were very good friends," said Barrett, adding the two would spend time together outside of work, and she knew his wife and children.Barrett also said she knew Sandra Birchmore from around town, adding that Birchmore was often where police officers were. "She was nice. I felt that she was a little immature," Barrett said. "Even when I spoke to her in her older years, I felt like I was talking with a juvenile. I felt she was just a little immature. Socially awkward."The prosecutor asked Barrett if she ever believed Birchmore was in a sexual relationship with Farwell before her death. Barrett said she did not.In January 2021, Barrett said Farwell's demeanor changed. She testified that he seemed agitated, stressed, and was frequently going outside to take phone calls. Barrett said she attempted to address her concerns with Farwell at the end of that month while at a restaurant."I asked the defendant if everything was okay," Barrett said. "He explained to me that he was having problems with a female partner in his life, someone other than his wife."Barrett said Farwell told her the female was threatening to tell his wife."He told me that he was fine and that he believed the problem was going to take care of itself," Barrett said.Barrett testified that a day or two after the conversation, she learned Birchmore had died.According to Barrett, Massachusetts State Police did not interview her after Birchmore's death.Police originally ruled Birchmore's death a suicide. Later, federal investigators arrested Farwell and accused him of killing Birchmore then attempting to stage the scene as a suicide. On cross-examination, Barrett was asked if she was surprised to initially learn Birchmore had died by suicide. "I didn't have much feeling about it either way," she said. Farwell faces a mandatory sentence of life in prison if convicted. He has pleaded not guilty to charges of killing a witness or victim and causing the death of an unborn child. Jason Pickard is scheduled to take the stand on Thursday. He is a U.S. Army recruiter who had a sexual relationship with Sandra. After her death, DNA results revealed that Pickard was the father of Birchmore's unborn fetus, not Farwell.

title: Baltimore mayor signs executive order ahead of Baby Bonus ballot question
description: Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott signed an executive order Wednesday establishing an advisory board to oversee a program that would give families with newborns a financial jump-start.
content: Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott signed an executive order Wednesday establishing an advisory board to oversee and help shape a program that would give families with newborns a financial jump-start.The mayor says the measure would be "life-changing" for these families. Baltimore Baby Bonus would provide $1,000 paymentsIf voters approve Question 1, the Baltimore Baby Bonus, in the November midterm elections, new and expecting parents would receive a one-time payment of $1,000. Qualifying low-income families would also receive additional monthly cash assistance and contributions to a college savings account."We are here today because this fall, Baltimore residents are voting on a ballot measure that would make this kind of support available to families across our city," Scott said Wednesday. The mayor has been a vocal supporter of the measure, which was first proposed in 2024. Since then, Baltimore has established a pilot program that provided $1,000 monthly payments to 200 young families for two years.Scott said the pilot program was successful, with participants experiencing less food insecurity and stress and missing fewer hours of work."They used money to continue their education, pay down debt, save for emergencies and invest in their families," he said.Advisory board will oversee Baby FundThe advisory board will include researchers, funders and community partners, including Healthcare Access Maryland and the Center for Urban Families. It will also include a representative from the Baltimore Baby Fund Coalition and a member of the Baltimore City Council."Together, they will work to ensure this fund has the greatest possible impact," said the mayor. Scott, who chairs Mayors for Guaranteed Income, said pilot programs across the country have shown that families use guaranteed income to meet basic needs."We know from experience, here in the city, and as the chair of Mayors for Guaranteed Income across the United States of America, where there have been dozens of pilots proven that guaranteed income goes to stuff that right-wingers think it is going to go to," he said. "They are not spending it to go on vacation or to go on luxury vacations. They are spending it on food for their families or a car so they can spend more time with their families or having a place to live."How would Baltimore fund the Baby Bonus?The proposed amendment would require the city's annual budget to include a contribution to the Baby Fund. The required annual contribution would be 3 cents for every $100 in taxable property value in Baltimore.The fund could also accept grants and donations. Any unspent money would remain in the fund for the benefit of families with newborns and could not be transferred to other city purposes.Scott said national research has linked guaranteed income programs for families to improved academic outcomes, higher future incomes and fewer referrals to Child Protective Services.The mayor is urging voters to approve Question 1 on the November ballot. "I know first-hand how fast monthly costs add up, especially for newborns," he said. "I also know how critical the early months are for our children's life-long success. We want to make sure we are setting our families and our babies up for success in life."

title: New York man charged with illegally capturing, dragging great white shark onto Cape Cod beach
description: Christopher Stefanou is charged with animal cruelty for allegedly catching a great white shark​ and dragging it onto a Cape Cod beach.
content: A New York man is accused of illegally catching a great white shark and dragging it onto a Cape Cod beach.Christopher Stefanou of Long Island is charged with animal cruelty and breaking rules about shark fishing, Cape & Islands District Attorney Robert Galibois said Wednesday.Galibois said that in October of 2025, "Stefanou and his crew embarked on a days-long excursion on the eastern shore of Cape Cod with a European client with the goal of capturing a great white shark, resulting in the capture of 'Aaron the Shark.'""Authorities were alerted to the illegal activity when Stefanou publicly posted video footage of the capture on social media showing the men using prohibited equipment, including a drone, to capture and drag the shark onto the beach, where they proceeded to celebrate and photograph themselves with the shark prior to releasing it," Galibois said.Aaron the Shark is listed in the Atlantic White Shark Conservancy's white shark logbook. The 9-and-a-half-foot male shark was tagged by researchers in 2024 and has been detected up and down the outer Cape thousands of times by acoustic sonar. The 30-year-old Stefanou was arraigned in Barnstable Superior Court Wednesday on charges of animal cruelty to shark, fishing for shark, mechanical deployment of bait, attempt to capture a shark and possession of protected species shark. Bail was set at $10,000.He's due back in court on Dec. 11. Galibois said until then, he's been ordered to surrender his fishing license, not post any shark fishing videos to social media, and stay out of Massachusetts except for legal reasons. In a statement to WBZ, Stefanou's attorney said his client is "a skilled and accomplished angler with more than a decade of experience." "There can be no question that Chris respects the sport, actively participates in conservation practices, assists in marine tagging and research efforts, and volunteers his time to educate enthusiasts on safe and responsible angling," Stefanou's attorney Jon A. Ciraulo said. "The charges against Chris are allegations only. He maintains his innocence and intends to fully challenge the allegations against him."

title: Dog on the loose after girl suffers multiple bites in northwest Miami-Dade, deputies say
description: Deputies say the dog is a family pet, and it ran off after a deputy tried to use a Taser on it, while the girl is being treated at Jackson Memorial Hospital.
content: A dog that bit a young girl several times in northwest Miami-Dade was still on the loose Wednesday night, Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office deputies said.The attack happened around 4:40 p.m. behind a home off Northwest 66th Street near Liberty City. Deputies said the dog is a family pet. A damaged, empty cage sat behind the main house, all that remained of the incident. The girl is being treated at Jackson Memorial Hospital. Investigators are still working out what led to the attack.When deputies arrived, the dog was aggressive toward them, deputies said. One deputy tried to use a Taser on the dog, which sent the animal running away."We have an aggressive dog, chasing kids and biting them," a caller said in a recording of a call about the attack.Signs are posted outside the home. Neighbors told CBS News Miami to watch for the dog.The girl's age and condition are currently unknown.No additional information has been released.

title: In final Michigan Senate debate, El-Sayed ties Rogers to Trump, while Rogers says El-Sayed is untrustworthy
description: Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed clashed onstage Wednesday during the second debate in the increasingly bitter Michigan Senate race.
content: Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed clashed onstage Wednesday during the second, and final, debate in the increasingly bitter Michigan Senate race. El-Sayed repeatedly argued his opponent is and would be a "sock puppet" for President Trump in the Senate, while Rogers cast his opponent as untrustworthy and trying to run from past, further-left positions. The neck-and-neck race is one of the nation's most closely watched contests in the November midterms and could help determine which party wins control of the Senate. Democrats hope to take advantage of Mr. Trump's unpopularity and voters' frustration with inflation and the Iran War. Republicans have sought to capitalize on divisions between progressives like El-Sayed and more moderate Democrats on Middle East policy and Medicare for All. El-Sayed called Rogers' platform a "MAGA vision" and argued the former congressman "stand[s] hip-to-hip with Donald Trump on all of his worst policies, the policies that are raising the price of your gas, making it impossible to afford your groceries." The Democratic former health official responded to attack lines by inviting the audience to play "MAGA bingo.""He's going to bend to Donald Trump because he is a sock puppet for the man," said El-Sayed.Rogers pushed back at one point, saying: "He wants to make this about Donald Trump. The bingo game ought to be: 'How many times can he put Trump in any answer?'" Asked by reporters after the debate if he's planning to attend Mr. Trump's Michigan rally on Sunday, which El-Sayed brought up, Rogers said he'd go but didn't know all the final details yet.During the debate, Rogers argued El-Sayed has not been honest about his platform, accusing him of engaging in a "pattern of deception.""Think about this: there are so many Democrats who are coming out today and saying they can't vote for Abdul El-Sayed because he's too extreme," Rogers said. He also claimed he's "doing exceptionally well with Jewish Democrats who are literally afraid," alluding to some community members' reluctance to support El-Sayed, a frequent critic of the Israeli government.The debate was somewhat tamer than the two candidates' first faceoff earlier this month, which featured insults and interruptions in virtually every answer. But it was still testy.One of the more contentious moments came after Rogers tried to link El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood and suggested he had the same supporters as terror groups like Hamas — allegations El-Sayed has vehemently pushed back against.Earlier this month, several news outlets reported on social media posts by El-Sayed's half sister suggesting the Democratic candidate's mother had supported the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist group and political movement founded in her home country of Egypt. El-Sayed has disavowed any connection to the organization, and has noted that he wasn't raised by his birthmother since his parents divorced when he was young. Rogers said El-Sayed was trying to make himself look like "a victim.""You can grin and you can smile and you can talk real pretty, but I'm going to tell you what, that is a risk to our national security," Rogers said. He told reporters after the debate that he questions whether El-Sayed can get a security clearance if elected. El-Sayed called the allegations "shameful.""He keeps raising this question about this association with an organization I've never been a part of, because [of] my mom, who's a nurse in Missouri?" the Democrat said. "It doesn't make any sense, and it's actually really quite beneath you, Mike."El-Sayed pressed Rogers on the Iran war, pointing to the conflict as the cause of high consumer prices and casting the Republican as a hawk who has "a war for everything.""We need a War Powers Resolution, rather than a senator who is going to stand hip-to-hip with Donald Trump on this war that made no sense when it started and certainly makes no sense now," El-Sayed said when asked how he would bring costs down.Rogers has called on the war to end, but also said on the debate stage that if Iran is allowed to control the Strait of Hormuz or build a nuclear weapon that gas could rise even higher. The moderators asked El-Sayed whether he views Iran as a significant threat to U.S. national security. It was a variation on a question during the first debate, when El-Sayed was asked whether Iran or Israel is a bigger threat, which he called a "ridiculous hypothetical."El-Sayed said Wednesday that "there's no doubt that Iran has posed a threat," but he argued "that threat had been contained" by the Obama-era deal that limited Iran's nuclear program. Mr. Trump ended that deal during his first term in office.Rogers said Iran is "absolutely" a threat and argued El-Sayed's previous answers on Iran were "an absolute nonstarter if you're going to send somebody … to the United States Senate."Meanwhile, Rogers pushed El-Sayed on some of his progressive policy views, including his support for Medicare for All, a single-payer healthcare plan."Money in your pocket? You'll be lucky to have a damn pair of pants when you're done," said Rogers, arguing El-Sayed's policies would require significant tax hikes.El-Sayed responded by saying: "Right now, the folks pulling the money out of your pocket are the big corporations who are buying his campaign." Asked by CBS News after the debate about how much the plan would cost, El-Sayed argued if implemented it'd be less expensive than the costs of healthcare currently, and said the platform has bipartisan support. On tariffs, El-Sayed criticized Mr. Trump's tariffs but said he is open to some import duties. He said, "You don't give all the chemo all at once, all at the same time."Rogers called the president's tariffs a "mixed bag," questioning the trade war with Canada but saying the "reshoring of manufacturing is underway."

title: Parents, teachers raise concerns about AI use in Anne Arundel County schools
description: The Anne Arundel County Board of Education is working to develop a policy governing the use of artificial intelligence in schools following a state mandate requiring local districts to establish responsible-use guidelines.
content: The Anne Arundel County Board of Education is working to develop a policy governing the use of artificial intelligence in schools following a state mandate requiring local districts to establish responsible-use guidelines.The board held the first reading of its draft policy during Wednesday night's meeting, where parents and teachers voiced concerns about AI's potential impact on students' learning and critical thinking skills."Let kids think for themselves. Let kids problem solve for themselves. Let them compose a sentence for themselves," parent Hillary Klemmt said.That sentiment was echoed by educators who urged the district to prioritize students' creativity, communication and independent thinking as it develops its policy."School is meant to be a place to build our creativity, our communication, as well as develop critical thinking skills," said Amanda Nickelson, an art teacher at Brooklyn Park Middle School. "And we all know the ability for students to use AI diminishes any and all of those skills."Parents call for caution as district develops AI policyThe discussion follows legislation passed by the Maryland General Assembly requiring the Maryland State Department of Education to establish statewide guardrails, tool-evaluation rubrics and educator training for AI use. The law also requires local school districts to adopt customized responsible-use policies.The deadline for those policies is Oct. 22, but Anne Arundel County's board is continuing to work through the details as it considers how AI should be used in classrooms.Board member Dr. Joanna Tobin said the rapid pace of technological change makes it difficult to predict the potential consequences of AI in education."We're now faced with looking into a future that we have absolutely no idea what it's going to be, but that future is like weeks away, months away. Maybe a year away, not decades away," Tobin said. "And it's going to require the best thinking that we all have to consider this and try to understand where the harms we might not even imagine might be without eliminating the necessary and at times developmentally appropriate moment where our students need not be walled off from this."Some parents are asking the district to consider a moratorium on AI use in schools rather than rush to adopt a policy. They said they do not want students to become guinea pigs as educators and administrators navigate the technology."A student is going to get a quick fix; they get that quick information that they need but there's no actual learning happening. There's no long-term memory," Klemmt said. "The work that we're putting in, that the kids are putting in, that struggle is how they're going to learn."More meetings planned before policy adoptionThe board has scheduled a second reading of the proposed policy for Dec. 2, with adoption planned for Dec. 16.In the meantime, the district will hold a series of community meetings to discuss the responsible use of AI in schools. Each meeting will begin at 6 p.m.Tuesday, Oct. 27 â North County High SchoolMonday, Nov. 2 â Glen Burnie High SchoolThursday, Nov. 5 â Northeast High SchoolTuesday, Nov. 10 â Arundel High SchoolThursday, Nov. 12 â Southern High SchoolTuesday, Nov. 17 â Annapolis High SchoolThursday, Nov. 19 â Meade High School

title: Anthony Edwards scores 45 with nine 3-pointers as Timberwolves rout Heat 131-106 in Giannis Antetokounmpo's debut
description: Anthony Edwards hit nine 3-pointers and scored 45 points to join an elite club, LaMelo Ball scored 21 in his Minnesota debut and the Timberwolves spoiled Giannis Antetokounmpo's first game with Miami by beating the Heat 131-106.
content: Anthony Edwards hit nine 3-pointers and scored 45 points to join an elite club; LaMelo Ball scored 21 in his Minnesota debut, and the Timberwolves spoiled Giannis Antetokounmpo's first game with Miami by beating the Heat 131-106 on Wednesday night.Edwards, who scored 41 in last season's opener at Portland, joined only Wilt Chamberlain and Michael Jordan as players with at least 40 points in multiple openers. Chamberlain did it four times — consecutively from 1959 through 1962 — and Jordan did it in 1986, 1989 and 1995.Jaden McDaniels scored 17, Ayo Dosunmu had 16, and Jonathan Kuminga added 12 for the Timberwolves, who won for the sixth time in their last eight season openers. Rudy Gobert grabbed 15 rebounds, and Edwards had 10 for Minnesota, which outscored Miami 63-24 on 3-pointers and outrebounded the Heat 52-34.Antetokounmpo scored 35 before fouling out of his Heat debut, 21 of those points coming in the first half. Bam Adebayo scored 15 for Miami, which has dropped three consecutive season-openers — the third time in franchise history that's happened.Antetokounmpo was 13 for 19 from the floor and had six rebounds. It still wasn't anywhere near enough to keep the Heat close in the opener.Minnesota took command with a six-minute burst that started late in the second quarter and continued early into the third. It wound up as a 23-7 run, one that turned a one-point Timberwolves lead into a 78-61 edge. Edwards and Ball combined for 17 points during that spurt, while the Heat missed six of nine shots and turned the ball over on four possessions.Miami was within eight midway through the third quarter, before Minnesota went on a 45-23 run. Edwards had 18 in that burst, while Miami missed on 11 of 12 3-point tries.Up nextTimberwolves: Visit Orlando on Friday.Heat: Host Detroit on Friday.___See AP's full NBA coverage here

title: Judge rules against DHS's policy of knocking on doors to track down possible noncitizen voters
description: A federal judge ruled DHS's practice of knocking on doors and asking people about their immigration status — and whether they have voted in recent elections — likely violates the Voting Rights Act.
content: A federal judge ruled late Wednesday that the U.S. Department of Homeland Security's practice of knocking on doors and asking people about their immigration status — and whether they have voted in recent elections — likely violates the Voting Rights Act.The ruling took aim at an operation that was documented by a CBS News investigation earlier Wednesday. Homeland Security Investigations has posted photos and videos of agents approaching homes in multiple states. The Trump administration says the practice is part of an effort to crack down on voting by noncitizens, but critics say it could intimidate legal voters. In her ruling, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin ordered federal immigration authorities to stop carrying out "elections-related field operations and field interviews" in nine states, including California and New York, if the operations are likely to involve people who government officials "know, suspect, or should reasonably know or suspect are U.S. citizens."Her order will remain in effect until polls close on Election Day. She stayed the ruling until 5 p.m. on Friday, which will give the government a chance to seek appeal. Martinez-Olguin sided with groups that sued over the noncitizen voting investigation surge, including the California Nurses Association and National Nurses United. She found the policy likely ran afoul of a section of the Voting Rights Act that makes it illegal to "intimidate, threaten, or coerce" those who assist people with voting or engage in voter mobilization efforts."Plaintiffs do not claim, nor does the Court find, that it is unlawful for federal officials to undertake investigations into unlawful voting in federal elections," the judge wrote. "Rather, Plaintiffs seek to stop DHS from continuing to investigate U.S. citizens, who have a legal right to vote, in a way that intimidates and threatens the participation of CNA/NNU members from urging or aiding others to vote."Martinez-Olguin also pointed to the "high likelihood of error" in the government's process for assembling a list of potential targets, which includes data from government agencies and commercially available data.Protect Democracy, one of the groups that sued over the policy, celebrated the ruling."It was clear from the start that DHS built its lists on bad data, never checked how often it was wrong, and recklessly sent agents to people's homes weeks before an election," Beau Tremitiere, counsel at Protect Democracy, said in a statement to CBS News. "Today's ruling should remind us that American citizens hold the ultimate power in our democracy, not the government–no matter what the administration says otherwise."CBS News has reached out to DHS for comment.President Trump has prioritized cracking down on voter fraud during his second term, although there has been little evidence to back up his claims of widespread voting by noncitizens. Just 156 people have been charged with voting-fraud related offenses since the beginning of the Trump administration, according to the Justice Department. The Justice Department reported earlier this week that it arrested several dozen green card holders in California on allegations they illegally registered to vote in U.S. federal elections.

title: First women cohort graduates with degrees through Northwestern Prison Education Program
description: They're the first incarcerated women to earn degrees from a Top 10 university through the program.
content: Education can open doors in the most unlikely places. That's the belief behind a university program committed to empowering students who are in prison.It's just one example of efforts to reduce recidivism in the criminal justice system.Prison seems an unlikely place for pomp and circumstance, but this circumstance in Kewanee, Illinois, is singular.Chelsea Raker has reason to celebrate, even while serving a 40-year sentence for armed robbery."I've never seen so many strong women. I've never had an example of a strong woman until now and I'm surrounded by them."Seventeen women imprisoned by one institution feel liberated by one another. They're the first incarcerated women to earn degrees from a Top 10 university."Northwestern fostered my imagination and granted me access to knowledge," Raker said.For six years, the women from Logan County Correctional Center have been students with the Northwestern Prison Education Program led by Jennifer Lackey, who says she has seen growth in the women."I've seen a tremendous amount of resilience and strength. So much loss. So many challenges and so much courage," she said.She's also seen dedication on the part of Northwestern University professors."That's a heavy ask because it's a seven-hour round-trip drive plus a three-hour class," Lackey said.Women who've accepted their past mistakes aren't used to accepting accolades. Their achievement is worthy of commencement speakers from the local, state and federal level â including Nancy Pelosi."They told me I was supposed to convey some wisdom. I think I could learn some wisdom from all of you," she said.As grateful as graduates are to shake hands with politicians, Raker cares most about the hug â from her son."My son. My son's my motivation for breathing," she said. "I've been locked up for ten years, and since then, I've seen him once."With a diploma in hand, graduates hold onto hope that commencement is not an end, but a new beginning.Northwestern started the prison education program in 2018. Since then, two cohorts of men have graduated through the program.Do you hear the Heartbeat of Chicago? We want to know about it. Click here to submit an idea for a Heartbeat of Chicago story

title: Burglars hit at least 4 businesses on Chicago's 95th Street
description: Burglars hit at least 4 businesses on Chicago's Street
content: Burglars hit no fewer than four businesses on 95th Street in Chicago's Beverly, Washington Heights, and Roseland neighborhoods early Wednesday morning.All of the burglaries happened in a span of 30 minutes. Thieves hit Legacy Cutz Barbershop at 332-334 E. 95th St. at Calumet Avenue. They broke the front glass door to get inside, grabbed equipment, and ran from the scene.Owner Johnnie Akons said he got the call about the crime around 3:30 a.m. His alarm alerted him that someone had entered his shop through a smashed front door."I would've said naw, I don't think that'll happen at our shop. We've been there for a while, like five years at that location and we never had any problems ... it was really shocking," Akons said. "We have it hard enough with the things that going on keeping our business running, for people to break into them."Legacy Cutz was one of the four businesses that were targeted on Wednesday morning.Workers at the GlowÂ³ MedSpa, at 1306 W. 95th St. near Throop Street, were also left to clean up Wednesday morning after thieves broke the front window to get in.They grabbed electronics and ran away from the scene.Police had information about another burglary a few blocks away at JoJo The Balloon and Flower Lady, at 1116 W. 95th St., right off Vincennes Avenue. Police said at 3:39 a.m., a burglar broke the front glass window, took a cash box and money, and ran away.Three people also broke the front door at a business at the K.A.M. Alliance mental health and substance abuse treatment clinic, at 2215 W. 95th St. near Leavitt Street. The burglars got inside, but did not appear to have taken anything."The same individuals that are targeting these businesses. It's not beneath them to target an individual as well. They're opportunist," said former Chicago police first superintendent Anthony Riccio, who is now the director of public safety at Monterrey Security.He points out how important it is for businesses to have layers of security, starting with bright lighting after hours. It can keep thieves away. If they do break in, it helps to have better surveillance images."They have these rooms now where they analyze the video that they've recovered. There's comparisons made between all these cases," Riccio said.Police haven't said if one crew is behind the burglaries, but Akons hopes other businesses can survive until the crime is under control â because he's staying put. "Just because a few people do something silly like this, that don't mean the whole city is like that," he said.

title: McGeorge law students break down California ballot measures to help voters make informed decisions
description: Students at UOP's McGeorge School of Law spent the semester examining the statewide propositions on the November ballot, researching their potential effects and compiling their findings into a 268-page report available online.
content: With Election Day approaching, California voters are facing a crowded ballot and competing claims about what the state's propositions would do.A group of University of the Pacific students is working to make those decisions easier by offering a detailed, nonpartisan analysis of the measures.UOP's McGeorge School of Law offers a special course on California propositions every election year. Students spent the semester examining the statewide propositions on the November ballot, researching their potential effects and compiling their findings into a 268-page report available online.The students presented their research at a free public forum Wednesday night, where community members could hear their explanations and ask questions.For some voters, the amount of information surrounding ballot measures can make the process difficult."The advertisements, all the text messages and the phone calls, all those things can be really overwhelming," law student Nikki Adkins said.Another voter, Art Fong, said competing messages can make the decision even more challenging."You read the materials and one says one thing and the other says the opposite," Fong said.The students said understanding the measures can be difficult even for people who have spent months studying them."We've really taken everything apart and it's even difficult for us to understand after working on it for two months," Adkins said.McGeorge law professor Mary-Beth Moylan said California has 14 statewide ballot propositions this election, creating a substantial amount of material for voters to review.Among the measures drawing attention are Propositions 40, 41 and 42, which involve competing proposals related to a so-called "billionaires tax.""There's a lot of buzz about that and there's a lot of buzz about 41 and 42, which are countermeasures," Moylan said.Law student Andrew Dale added, "If one of them receives more affirmative yes votes than 40, 40 is null and void even if it passes."The course also gives students an opportunity to examine what goes into drafting a statewide initiative.

title: Denver Water issues 450 citations for water restriction violations
description: Denver residents have been restricted from lawn watering since October 1st, and some are playing the price for violations.
content: Denver Water customers are saving millions of gallons amid ongoing drought restrictions, but hundreds of others are facing thousands of dollars in fines for violating the rules.Since the beginning of the month, Denver Water has issued 450 violations totaling about $265,000.A first time violation carries a fine of at least $500, and Denver Water says hundreds of customers are now facing those penalties.A green, lush lawn may look beautiful, but in Denver, it could come with a hefty price tag. Current water restrictions, which took effect Oct. 1, ban lawn watering.Greg Fisher with Denver Water said that helped with violations."By October, we saw that increase, and honestly, it's also easier for us to see the violation in October because we banned all spray irrigation," said Fisher.The fine for a first violation is $500, increasing to as much as $1,000 for subsequent violations. For multifamily customers, fines start at $1,000.Denver Water says it sent a postcard to every customer warning them about the restrictions, which is why fines began sooner."It's much easier for us to pick out violations. There are no more assigned days, so if we saw spray irrigation at all, we could assess a violation."Denver Water says customers reduced water use by 33% during the first 18 days, saving billions of gallons. But hundreds of others are paying the price.Some Denver residents disagree with the fines."The city keeps giving leniency to big businesses and continues to punish the residents. They shouldn't be responsible for it. It's turning neighbors against neighbors," said Denver resident Mads Delgado.Meanwhile, others say the fines are justified, like Denver resident, Jeff Huffman."Yeah, yeah, I do. There was a very, very dry winter, and the summer has also been dry, so we are going to need the water."Denver Water anticipates reservoirs will be about 60% full by next spring, well below the 85% target. That's why customers are expected to continue conserving water."We are definitely not past the drought. We will not be past the drought until we get a good snow year. So we're really hopeful that that's this coming winter," said Fisher.Through September, Denver Water says it received more than 7,500 reports of water waste and issued more than 2,000 formal warnings.

title: Maryland students react to Mike Locksley's departure as football coach
description: On campus, students expressed support for the coaching change, though some questioned whether it came too late.
content: The University of Maryland has parted ways with head football coach Mike Locksley following a five-game losing streak that dropped the Terrapins to 2-5 this season.The university described the move as a mutual decision, ending Locksley's tenure after more than seven seasons.On campus, students expressed support for the coaching change, though some questioned whether it came too late."Thank God he's gone. Football team is on the rise. The Big Ten is ours next year without him," student Ryan Leif said.Locksley was hired in 2018 and led Maryland to three consecutive bowl victories from 2021 through 2023. He finished his tenure with a 38-49 overall record and a 16-47 record in Big Ten play.For some students, the team's struggles made the decision feel overdue."Watching those games has just been so rough because we have the talent. The play calling just hasn't been great," Ethan Brezden said.Others agreed that a coaching change was necessary but questioned the timing."I think it's the right move. I think it's too little, too late," Iris Whiteman said.Aazaar Abdul-Rahim named interim head coachAssistant coach Aazaar Abdul-Rahim will lead the Terrapins on an interim basis.A Washington, D.C., native, Abdul-Rahim is in his third season with the program. Since 2024, he has served as co-defensive coordinator, associate head coach of the defense and cornerbacks coach. He previously coached at Maryland from 2016 to 2018.Maryland has a bye week to prepare under its new leadership before hosting Illinois on Halloween.

title: Ringgold Elementary School South teacher caught with marijuana vape pen at school, police say
description: A Ringgold Elementary School South teacher is facing misdemeanor charges after allegedly bringing a marijuana vape pen to school.
content: A Ringgold Elementary School South teacher is facing misdemeanor charges after allegedly bringing a marijuana vape pen to school.Investigators said 58-year-old Tami White had a marijuana vape on her on school grounds on Oct. 14. According to the criminal complaint, the assistant superintendent found White with the device. When he turned it over to the district police department, investigators pulled it apart, and it allegedly smelled of marijuana.The vape was then tested, and it came back positive for marijuana, which is not permitted on school grounds, according to the criminal complaint. White's current employment status is unclear.In a statement, Ringgold School District Superintendent Randall Skrinjorich said, in part, that it is aware of the allegations and does "not permit or condone the alleged conduct reported with regard to any employee.""The District takes these matters very seriously and is committed to maintaining a safe, respectful, and appropriate environment for all students and staff," Skrinjorich added. Ryan Painter said his 10-year-old sister is a student at Ringgold Elementary School South "What if she dropped it and my sister picked it up?" Painter told KDKA-TV on Wednesday. "She shouldn't of brought that. Honestly, in my opinion, personally, zero tolerance."Makena Gregory lives in the area and understands the outrage from some in the community. "I can understand why people are angry about it," Gregory said. "I guess because it is in a school building with children. But at the end of the day, she is an adult. I'm a weed smoker. I just don't think it's that big of a deal."

title: Minnesota gubernatorial candidates try to separate themselves from party leaders during final debate
description: In the race for Minnesota governor between Democratic U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar and Republican Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth, the recurring theme of their final televised debate was seeing who could distance themselves further from leaders of their own respective parties.
content: In the race for Minnesota governor between Democratic U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar and Republican Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth, the recurring theme of their final televised debate was seeing who could distance themselves further from leaders of their own respective parties. While moderators with FOX9 and Gray Media brought up topics ranging from gang violence to health care, Klobuchar made repeated attempts to tie Demuth to President Donald Trump, who is deeply unpopular in Minnesota according to public opinion polls. "I don't think we need a rubber stamp for Donald Trump in the governor's office," Klobuchar said. Demuth had a similar attack line of her own, arguing that Klobuchar is in lock-step with Gov. Tim Walz. He bowed out of the race in January after facing mounting criticism for the way that fraud has exploded in social programs during his tenure. "A vote for Amy Klobuchar is a vote for a Tim Walz third term," Demuth said. It was these barbs that brought the most contentious moments in Wednesday evening's debate at KTTC/KXLT's studio in Rochester. Klobuchar said repeatedly that she believed Walz could have done far better when it came to reigning in the fraud sooner; she also said she disagreed with the pardon of an immigrant in Minnesota who sexually abused a 10-year-old girl. That man was pardoned by The Board of Pardons, which consists of Walz, Attorney General Keith Ellison and Supreme Court Justice Natalie Hudson. "I disagree with Tim Walz on fraud, I wouldn't have pardoned the sex offender, I would have put the money into infrastructure," Klobuchar said. Klobuchar challenged Demuth to explain how she differed from Mr. Trump given the widespread economic impact of both the war in Iran and his tarrif policies."As far as the war in Iran I've been very clear about talking about that it needs to come to an end soon. I have also separated when it comes to bringing foreign beef and some of the other tariffs. Our top trading partner is Canada," Demuth said. The debate comes less than two weeks from election day. On paper, Klobuchar has the upper hand as Demuth attempts to become the first Republican to win a statewide election in Minnesota in decades.According to their most recent filings, Klobuchar has nearly six times the cash on-hand that Demuth has; Real Clear Politics gives Klobuchar an advantage of about eight points in the polls. On fraud, Demuth made the case that she has been fighting to correct apparent issues since she first joined the state legislature in 2019. Klobuchar pointed to her experience as a prosecutor, once again critical of Walz's actions. A WCCO review of their respective fraud plans found similarities. On healthcare, housing, and the economy, Demuth argued that democratic policies have lead to overregulation and high costs; Klobuchar said that she's committed to building 100,000 new housing units statewide and said she will not raise taxes. Both candidates also faced questions on the relatively new issue of violence related to Somali-gangs in the Twin Cities Metro. Demuth touted her endorsement from The Police Officers Federation of Minneapolis as she argued that officers and judges need to be allowed to go after criminals aggressively. She said that she would support an ongoing gang-violence task force. Klobuchar said that, through her experience as a prosecutor, she understands what it takes to take on gangs and end the problem by working with the Minnesota BCA.

title: ICE agents seen near early voting sites in two Florida counties; election supervisors contact FBI
description: Supervisors of elections in Leon and Monroe counties say they contacted the FBI, and immigration advocates called the presence of agents at polling places inappropriate.
content: Two Florida counties have reported seeing immigration enforcement at or near polling places open for in-person early voting hours.In Leon County, Supervisor of Elections Mark Earley said two U.S. Customs and Border Protection vehicles were seen at the Northeast Branch Library, the busiest polling site in the county, on Monday.And in Monroe County, Supervisor of Elections Sherri Hodies told the news media in a statement that she has launched an investigation after reports of masked federal agents conducting a stop at a polling place in Key Largo on Tuesday.Both supervisors of elections said they have contacted the FBI. "To their credit, they are taking it seriously," Earley said in a released statement.In his statement, Earley noted the two Customs and Border Patrol vehicles stayed at the polling place for 10 minutes before leaving, and that his office didn't receive any calls about the incident.Federal law prohibits armed federal agents from conducting activities in and around polling places unless force is necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States.U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Florida Department of State, the agency overseeing the state's elections, did not immediately respond to requests for comment Tuesday evening.The FBI reassured supervisors of elections at this year's statewide elections conference that there would be no immigration enforcement at polling places, one of the biggest rumors circulating about this year's midterm elections.Brevard County Supervisor of Elections Tim Bobanic has said they were being told: "time and time again that there are no plans for any of that kind of stuff to happen in Florida."Early told the News Service of Florida that seeing Border Patrol agents at one of his county polling places was "very unfortunate," but he would be "very surprised if it happened again.""Voters should never experience intimidation from anyone when they are voting, and that includes being intimidated by law enforcement or any other governmental officials," Early said in his statement. "This nation belongs to the people. Government works for them. I will do everything in my power to ensure that our voters can cast their ballots in a fair election free from intimidation or implied threats.Immigration advocates called the presence of border patrol at polling places "completely inappropriate."Thomas Kennedy, a spokesperson for the Florida Immigrant Coalition, said he hoped it wouldn't happen but expected it."To me and to immigration advocacy groups, it smells and feels like an intimidation tactic. It's completely unnecessary," Kennedy said.Earley said voters with concerns or questions should contact their supervisor of elections."Get up, make your voice heard, and get out there and vote," he said.

title: House Speaker Mike Johnson campaigns for Kevin Lincoln in competitive Central Valley congressional race
description: House Speaker Mike Johnson traveled to Stockton on Wednesday to campaign for Republican Kevin Lincoln, stepping up GOP efforts to reclaim California's 13th Congressional District less than two weeks before the 2026 midterm election.
content: House Speaker Mike Johnson traveled to Stockton on Wednesday to campaign for Republican Kevin Lincoln, stepping up GOP efforts to reclaim California's 13th Congressional District less than two weeks before the 2026 midterm election.Johnson's visit marked his second trip to the Central Valley in less than a month and was part of a six-week campaign effort he said would take him to more than 40 congressional districts across 22 states."Hello, Central Valley, it's so great to be back," Johnson said at the rally.Lincoln, a Marine Corps veteran and former Stockton mayor, is challenging Democratic Rep. Adam Gray in the race."Kevin Lincoln is not running for Congress to be famous. He is running to serve his country, as he's been doing his whole life," Johnson said.The district has been closely contested in recent elections. Gray won his seat in 2024 by a margin of about 190 votes, while Republican John Duarte defeated Gray by 564 votes in 2022. Duarte attended Wednesday's rally.Republican state Sen. Alexandra Macedo, the minority leader, argued that voters in the Central Valley prioritize policy over party affiliation."This isn't a partisan vote. Voters here in the valley vote policy," Macedo said.Lincoln has focused his campaign on affordability, public safety and border security as he seeks to unseat Gray."We build, we serve, and we sacrifice. But you better believe the people of the Central Valley never give up," Lincoln said.He also emphasized the importance of continuing to connect directly with voters as Election Day approaches."I have to continue to do what I've done over this entire campaign cycle, and that's knock on doors, talk to voters, be accessible to them, and to demonstrate to them that I'm the candidate that they can trust," Lincoln said.Johnson's appearance underscores the Republican Party's effort to invest time and resources in competitive congressional districts ahead of the midterms. The outcome in California's 13th District could hinge on whether Lincoln can attract moderate and swing voters beyond the Republican base.We reached out to Gray's campaign for comment but did not immediately hear back.

title: Jonathon Cooper returns to Denver Broncos, says, "I do hold myself accountable," following domestic violence charges
description: Broncos outside linebacker Jonathon Cooper was back practicing with the team Wednesday after his leave due to arrest in the summer.
content: Denver Broncos outside linebacker Jonathon Cooper was back practicing with the team Wednesday after his leave due to an arrest for domestic violence in June.Cooper spoke during a press availability inside the team locker room and said he takes accountability for the legal process he is being put through in the state. "Relationships are difficult, no excuses on my end," Cooper said during media availability. "I do apologize for anyone's feelings. truthfully, because they have to be associated with me. I'm a grown man ... I understand the concern. I understand the level of awareness, how serious these matters are ... But I do hold myself accountable."Cooper is facing charges of domestic violence and felony assault related to an incident involving his then-girlfriend. He has pleaded not guilty to those charges. As he resumes activity with the Broncos, the linebacker still awaits his trial for those charges. It was rescheduled and moved to March, 2, 2027. Cooper thanked his teammates and the organization for the steps he has taken to return to the team at this point. "I put a lot of work in this offseason on myself and for my family and for this team, and just really excited to be back and really excited to get to work," Cooper said.Cooper does remain under investigation by the NFL as well, and he could be suspended once the league finishes its review.Cooper's first game of eligibility will come when the Broncos go on the road to play the Arizona Cardinals on Sunday, Oct. 25.

title: University of Chicago public safety meeting held amid sexual assault allegations at fraternity houses
description: UChicago to hold public safety meeting amid sex assault allegations
content: The University of Chicago held a public safety meeting Wednesday evening, just after one alleged sexual assault at one fraternity party this month and another at a different frat house earlier this year that is the subject of a new lawsuit.The Wednesday evening meeting was not scheduled in response to the fraternity house sexual assault allegations. The agenda was set in September before the allegations hit the headlines and before one of the alleged assaults happened. Still, sexual misconduct support and education are among the topics on the agenda for the meeting.The meeting will give students and neighbors in the Hyde Park community a chance to weigh in on safety and interact with UChicago's campus police chief.On Tuesday, a woman filed a lawsuit against the Alpha Delta Phi fraternity at the University of Chicago, alleging that she was raped at a fraternity party in February and that the fraternity and the university were aware of years of sexual assault reports.According to the complaint, the victim, identified only as Jane Doe, attended a party at the Alpha Delta Phi house, 5747 S. University Ave., on Feb. 7, 2026. According to the complaint, at the party Doe was given a shot of unidentified alcohol by one of the fraternity members, which the complaint identifies as student Kevin Shim, and was encouraged to drink it. The lawsuit says "almost immediately" after she drank the alcohol, Doe began to feel "unsteady and lightheaded."At that point, according to the complaint, Shim coerced her upstairs to a bedroom, led her to a bed, and sexually assaulted her. The complaint states Doe told him multiple times that she felt unsteady and lightheaded, but he ignored her. The complaint also says that while in the room, Doe "lost all physical and verbal ability to refuse" the frat member.The complaint states Doe was raped while unable to consent or to verbally or physically refuse Shim, but she did plead with him to wear a condom. According to the complaint, he refused.After the assault, Jane Doe alleges Shim left her in the room, and another frat brother blocked her friends from going upstairs to find her. The lawsuit alleges her friends were not allowed to go upstairs until her assailant told his frat brother that it was OK.Doe alleges she was still unconscious when her friends found her and she struggled to speak and walk as they helped her out of the house. She reported the assault to Chicago police the next morning when she discovered bloodstains in her underwear, according to the lawsuit.The woman's attorney said she had a rape kit performed and reported the assault to police the next day.The lawsuit accuses the local chapter and national organization of Alpha Delta Phi of ignoring previous sexual assault reports and failing to enforce safety rules.Doe's attorneys said the effects of the alleged assault have continued for months."She is working through this," said attorney Georgia Booth. "A sexual assault, what she experienced, alters a person in ways that unless you've gone through it yourself personally, you can never imagine."Chicago police said the investigation into the Alpha Delta Phi incident remains open more than eight months after the reported assault.At this time, Shim has not been criminally charged. CBS News Chicago reached out to him for comment, but has not heard back. Alpha Delta Phi says it has suspended him from the fraternity.Meanwhile, at UChicago, a sexual assault was also reported at the Alpha Epsilon Pi fraternity house on the next block at 5625 S. University Ave., during a party early on the morning of Sunday, Oct. 11.According to a University of Chicago report, a 21-year-old woman reported she was sexually assaulted in a bathroom during a frat party at 1:50 a.m. Sunday. A UChicago alert issued this week said the woman was not affiliated with the university.The woman did not know her attacker, the university said. They said when someone intervened, the unidentified suspect ran off.Video has surfaced online showing a woman, who identified herself as a friend of the 21-year-old victim, chasing down a man she claimed to be her friend's attacker and yelling that he assaulted her friend in a bathroom at a frat party.Later, the friend commented that the 21-year-old woman was "drugged and taken away from us against her will … practically incapacitated, being held to the ground with a man over her, kissing her and taking her clothes off."In the alleged AEPi incident, a person of interest has been identified through witness statements and video evidence, all of which have been shared with the Chicago Police Department, the university said. The person has not been taken into custody.The incidents at the UChicago frat houses are making headlines amid the fallout from separate sexual assault allegations at the Chi Phi fraternity house at Cornell University, which is also raising questions about fraternity culture.University of Chicago police Chief Kyle Bowman was set to provide an update.The meeting touched on other topics, including Halloween events in Hyde Park.

title: From WWII to the Super Bowl, the St. Paul Airport has served the Twin Cities for 100 years
description: The St. Paul Airport turns 100-years-old this month. In the last century, the airport helped with the war effort and also played a major role in Twin Cities flight.
content: The St. Paul Airport turns 100-years-old this month. In the last century, the airport helped with the war effort and also played a major role in Twin Cities flight. "We've got California, Florida, Alaska. We've had international flights from Spain, Portugal," said Jack Carroll, general manager of the St. Paul Flight Center.At the St. Paul Airport, no two days are the same. Military and private aircraft bring in service members and celebrities. And when the Super Bowl was here, it was all hands on deck."It was the busiest day in the airport's history. Literally, they shut down two of the three runways. There were airplanes parked on every available piece of laptop," said Carroll.It's just part of the airport's long runway of memories."Air mail. That's the overriding story," said Bruce Kitt, Northwest Airlines History Center.Kitt said a century ago, Minneapolis and St. Paul were competing to be the air mail destination from Chicago to the Twin Cities."Neither one of them could agree so they both built up their airports, and like a ping pong ball, service bounced between each one. And then it eventually wound up at MSP," said Kitt.But St. Paul's success was only slightly delayed. In 1930, Northwest Airways moved its fleet to the airport, which was also known as Holman Field â named after Charles "Speed" Holman. He was the first pilot hired by the airline and also doubled as a stunt pilot.Sadly, Holman died in 1931 while performing a stunt at an airshow in Omaha, Nebraska. But his name lives on. In 1939, the Holman terminal was built, and three years later the Riverside Hangars were added. The government took those over during World War II so they could modify B-24 bomber planes.When it was really busy, they would run four lines of bombers. Two in each hangar. They modified over 3,300 B-24s during the war," said Kitt.Kitt says when the war ended, things changed. Legacy carriers were going to Minneapolis St. Paul International Airport because of the longer runways, while Holman Field attracted regional airlines. Over the decades, St. Paul has proven resilient. More than once in the 1990's, flooding temporarily grounded operations, but they always came back.As a result, years ago they built a flood wall to keep the rising waters of the Mississippi River from getting on the runway.It's held up well. Kitt often wonders what might have been for Holman Field if history hadn't gotten in the way."It would be interesting to speculate, what if the war never occurred? Then what would have the city rivalries have been?"Like MSP, the St. Paul Airport is run by the Metropolitan Airports Commission. Each year there more than 40,000 takeoffs and landings happen in St. Paul.

title: Rookie Cole Knuble pots 1st 2 NHL goals to help Flyers beat Sabres for 3rd straight win
description: Rookie Cole Knuble scored his first two career NHL goals, and the Flyers beat the Sabres, 3-1, for their third straight win.
content: Rookie forward Cole Knuble scored twice to help the Philadelphia Flyers beat the Buffalo Sabres 3-1 on Wednesday night.Knuble, playing his second career game, scored his first two goals in front of his father, former NHL forward Mike Knuble, who played 1,068 games with five teams.Trevor Zegras also scored and Dan Vladar made 27 saves to give the Flyers their third straight win after starting 0-6-3.Jason Zucker made his season debut following sports hernia surgery and scored for Buffalo. Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen stopped 23 shots for the Sabres, who are 1-1-2 in their last four games.Sabres captain Rasmus Dahlin returned to the lineup after missing four games with an upper-body injury.The Flyers grabbed a 2-0 lead late in the first period after Knuble's first career goal at 14:49 and a power-play goal from Zegras at 19:17 when he batted a rebound of Matvei Michkov's shot out of the air past Luukkonen.Zucker's power-play goal at 19:25 of the second cut it to 2-1.Knuble's second of the game, 3:03 into the third, made it 3-1 after he banked in the puck off Luukkonen's skate.Flyers forward Tyson Foerster returned to the lineup after a one-game absence because of an undisclosed injury.Both teams are in action again Saturday. The Sabres open a four-game trip against the Washington Capitals, while the Flyers return home to host the Anaheim Ducks.

title: County in southwestern Colorado prepares for rain
description: Communities in southwestern Colorado are preparing for several inches of rain through Friday morning.
content: Communities in southwestern Colorado are preparing for several inches of rain through Friday morning, with officials around Pagosa Springs drawing on lessons learned from historic flooding last year.Archuleta County Sheriff Mike Le Roux said recent weeks have already brought unusually wet conditions to the region."The contrast in seasons over the last 60 days has been significant," Le Roux told CBS Colorado.Heavy rain has already caused problems in the county, including a washout on County Road 500 late last month."The last six to eight weeks have been unprecedented, or much like last year, which again created historic flood data," Le Roux said.Last September, five days of rain sent the San Juan River to two dangerous peaks, causing damage in areas east of Pagosa Springs and around the community's well-known hot springs."Some river restoration work has been done. Certainly, our Public Works Department has worked hard over the last year to restore everything back to where we would like to see it, but over the last 6 weeks, we've had an inundation of rainfall that has created certain issues," he said.Le Roux said that experience has helped emergency officials prepare for the latest round of storms."We've had the benefit of that foresight," he said. "We've made face-to-face contact with everybody that was affected by the floods last year. We've identified a sheltering location ahead of time so that we're not dealing with that if and when we do need to make those evacuations."Archuleta County has also brought in a machine capable of producing about 100 sandbags an hour as officials prepare for possible flooding."We procured a piece of equipment from the Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management that has made Mass sandbagging a lot easier, and so, using volunteer search and rescue members yesterday, our Public Works Department and the Sheriff's Office, we started ... pre-bagging, and we've got, you know, groups of sandbags delivered to key areas within the county ahead of time, and made that available for the residents. And, in addition to that, the self-serve option is always available, so you can bring your own shovel. The bags are free, the sand is free. But the pre-filled bags are there for those that aren't able necessarily to do that as an individual," Le Roux said.Attention is also focused upstream, where the San Juan River descends from the Wolf Creek Pass area. Le Roux said monitoring conditions about 12 to 13 miles away can provide officials with some early warning."We do have some snow in the high country," Le Roux said. "I understand it's going to be warm, potential for rain up there, and so there's potential for additional snowmelt to increase that level."The San Juan River is currently expected to peak Friday morning.

title: Suspect faces charges in alleged road rage shooting outside Rangeview High School
description: Luis Melendez is charged after shooting outside of a high school.
content: The man who shot a gun in a road rage dispute outside Rangeview High School Tuesday has a history of violent road rage encounters, as alleged in arrest documents.35-year-old Luis Melendez is currently in custody at the Aurora Detention Center. He's charged with first-degree attempted murder, violation of a protection order, both possession and prohibited use of a weapon by a previous offender."My first thought was, 'Oh my God, we're gonna get shot,'" said Maryam, a Rangeview High School student. "I was really scared...like I was shaking."Rangeview High School students are still shaken up by a secure perimeter that was called just minutes before the end of the school day Tuesday."All I heard was like this loud bang for some reason," said Nazan, a Rangeview student. "I heard this loud noise, and I thought someone fell. So I didn't think much of it until we got like to secure perimeter, and then one of my teachers told me that he saw like in the parking lot two people like arguing."About 15 minutes later, students were let go."I went to my mom's car and she told me the whole incident," said Rangeview student Matias Barela.Aurora Police say two men who were at Rangeview to pick up students got into a fight over a road rage incident. That fight escalated when one of the men took out a gun and fired it.No one was hurt."That's a very far extreme," Rangeview student Aaron Gailey said."I've heard from a lot of people that this is the best school in APS, so I wouldn't expect that from a school like this," said Matias.Aurora Police used Flock license plate readers and drones to find the suspect after he sped away. They arrested 35-year-old Luis Melendez.Melendez is already facing charges in another road rage case.An affidavit says on Sept. 28, he waved a gun and threw up gang signs at a pregnant woman and her boyfriend after being frustrated they slowed for traffic.At the time of that incident, Melendez was on probation for menacing and burglary and had three protection orders against him, all prohibiting him from having a gun."Gun on school grounds ... even if someone was walking by that could have been like their life," said Aaron.At school the next day, students are still shocked by what happened."There was like a whole bunch of like rumors and stuff," said Aaron."I heard a lot of people making jokes about it. I just want to say, like, a lot of people like lose their family members to stuff like this. I don't think it's like funny to be making jokes about that," Matias said.Melendez is being held on a $25,000 bond. He's due in court Thursday morning.

title: Pennsylvania lawmakers pass bell-to-bell cellphone ban for schools, send to Shapiro for signature
description: A bill to ban student cellphone use in Pennsylvania schools is headed to Gov. Josh Shapiro's desk for his signature.
content: Pennsylvania state lawmakers have passed a "bell-to-bell" ban on students using cellphones in schools. The bill requires schools to adopt policies prohibiting student cellphone use during the school day. It allows school districts to set their own policies and applies to school districts, intermediate units, career and technical schools, private schools, charter schools and cyber charter schools. The bill now goes to Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, to sign into law. Shapiro expressed support for the legislation Wednesday on social media."I called for this in my Budget Address and repeatedly urged the legislature to act — and now, we've brought Democrats and Republicans together to get this done for our students and our educators," his post said in part. State Sen. Devlin Robinson, who sponsored the bill in the Senate, said teachers shouldn't have to compete with smartphones."I'm a big proponent that while you're in school, it should be dedicated to reading, writing and arithmetic," Robinson said. "School is really, let's call it what it is, yes, you're supposed to be learning, but this is practice for the real world. We're trying to make good citizens who are going to enter the workforce and become productive members of society. And if we allow them to just be distracted by their cellphones all day while they're supposed to be learning, it's counterproductive to those goals." The bill allows exceptions for a handful of reasons, including:Students or immediate family members with certain medical conditions.Students learning English who use a phone for translation.Special occasions such as field days and science fairs.Students with individualized education plans who need a personal device. Teachers who want to use phones for educational purposes may be able to do so with approval from their principals.Under the bill, the "school day" includes instructional time as well as recess, homeroom, lunch and time between classes.The Pennsylvania State Education Association, a teachers union, praised the bill in a statement."This bill takes an essential step toward reducing distractions for students during class time and keeping lessons and teaching on track. We are confident that this change to the school day will have a positive impact on student behavior, academic performance, and mental health," Aaron Chapin, president of the Pennsylvania State Education Association, said in the statement. If the bill is signed into law, Pennsylvania will join 40 states that already restrict cellphone use in schools, including 19 that have bell-to-bell bans. Pennsylvania schools would be required to implement policies by the beginning of the 2027-2028 school year.

title: 2 Miami-Dade residents sue to require countywide vote on Miami Seaquarium marina development plan
description: The plaintiffs say the plan to add more than 300 boat slips extends into Biscayne Bay, and the developer says its plans are consistent with the county charter.
content: Two Miami-Dade County residents are suing to require a countywide vote on whether a new marina can be built at the Miami Seaquarium site on Virginia Key, arguing that voters, not just county commissioners, should decide.Aaron Stauber and Gregory Frankel filed the lawsuit under the county charter's citizen enforcement provision, specifically Article 7. They say the future of the Seaquarium site should be up to every county resident."If they were simply going to go ahead and modernize that… we wouldn't be here today, but that's not what's on the table," Stauber said.The Seaquarium itself is exempt from Article 7 of the county charter. The suit claims the development extends beyond the existing Seaquarium site and into Biscayne Bay, where Resilient Aquarium LLC plans to build more than 300 boat slips that do not currently exist.The developer said in a statement that the plan follows the rules."The plan was very carefully designed to be consistent with the property's allowable use, and with Article 7 of the County Charter," the developer said. "We are confident we will be able to move forward with transforming the site once our plans are approved by Miami-Dade County."Frankel said the lawsuit is about process."Really, this is about process. It's about good governance. It's about the citizens, residents of Miami-Dade County having a voice in the redevelopment process," Frankel said.County Commissioner Raquel Regalado, whose District 7 includes Virginia Key, hosted a webinar with the developer into the evening on Wednesday.

title: Kawhi-less Clippers roll past the Kings 121-96 in a wire-to-wire season-opening rout
description: The Clippers dominated the Sacramento Kings 121-96 in their first season opener without Kawhi Leonard since 2019.
content: Darius Garland scored 30 points and the Clippers routed the Sacramento Kings 121-96 on Wednesday night in Los Angeles' first season opener without Kawhi Leonard since 2019.Brook Lopez added 17 points and 11 rebounds off the bench. Rookie guard Keaton Wagler had 15 points, five rebounds and five assists, and Rui Hachimura had 10 points and eight rebounds in his debut after coming over from the Lakers. The Clippers never trailed and their bench outscored the Kings' reserves 53-34.Zach LaVine led the Kings with 28 points and Domantas Sabonis added 14 points and 18 rebounds. The Clippers have the largest decrease in the NBA in average age between their current roster and the group that was active for last year's season opener, according to the Elias Sports Bureau.That's partly due to the team trading James Harden and Chris Paul last season and sending Leonard to the Toronto Raptors last month after the NBA found the Clippers guilty of violating salary cap-circumvention rules involving him. Leonard scored 23 points to lead the Raptors in a season-opening win over Chicago on Wednesday.Clippers owner Steve Ballmer wasn't in his usual baseline seat near the team's bench. He's serving a one-year suspension from all league and team activities "for knowingly seeking to help Mr. Leonard obtain off-court income opportunities." The team was fined $30 million and lost five consecutive draft picks from 2029 through 2033 as punishment.The Clippers were without key players Bradley Beal (right knee injury management), Brandon Ingram (right heel surgery) and Max Strus (right plantar fascia partial tear). Also out are Jordan Miller (left rotator cuff surgery) and Yanic Konan Niederhauser (right foot surgery).Up nextKings: Host Portland on Friday.Clippers: Visit the Lakers on Friday.

title: Walker Kessler has perfect Lakers debut with 12-for-12 shooting in 127-105 win over Warriors
description: Luka Doncic scored 28 points in three quarters and Walker Kessler had 26 points on 12-for-12 shooting during his auspicious debut for the Los Angeles Lakers in a 127-105 victory over the Golden State Warriors.
content: Walker Kessler scored 26 points on 12-for-12 shooting and grabbed nine rebounds during his auspicious debut for the Los Angeles Lakers in a 127-105 victory over the Golden State Warriors on Wednesday night.Luka Doncic scored 28 points in three quarters and Austin Reaves added 23 as the Lakers began life after LeBron James with a thrashing of the Warriors, who got 23 points from Stephen Curry to begin his 18th season.The 7-foot-2 Kessler was an immediate force around both rims for the Lakers, who traded a bounty of draft capital to Utah to fill Doncic's desire for a top center. Kessler's 12 shots without a miss were the second-most in Lakers history, trailing only a 14-for-14 performance by Wilt Chamberlain in March 1969.Although Kessler hadn't played in a competitive game since last Halloween due to injury, he slammed down a lob from Doncic on LA's opening possession and never slowed down, repeatedly finishing his teammates' passes while the Lakers rolled away.Doncic scored 23 points in the first half while engaging in a prolonged physical and verbal confrontation with Warriors rookie Yaxel Lendeborg, who got a technical foul for something he said during their exchanges. Doncic capped the chippy matchup with flair, banking in a half-court shot at the buzzer and then gleefully pointing at the fuming rookie.Doncic also had eight rebounds and seven assists before getting to sit out the fourth quarter of his first competitive game since April 2. He has returned as the Lakers' clear centerpiece with James' departure for Philadelphia â and with Kessler as a compelling teammate.Lendeborg scored 12 points in the 11th overall pick's debut. Brandon Williams added 14 points.Golden State opened without Brandin Podziemski (back), along with veterans Jimmy Butler, Kristaps Porzingis and Moses Moody, who all have long-term injuries. The Lakers were without new guard Collin Sexton (calf) and first-round pick Cameron Carr (oblique), and swingman Jake LaRavia left the court limping in the fourth quarter.Up nextWarriors: Host Memphis on Friday.Lakers: Host Clippers on Friday.

title: Nithya Raman walks back "gold standard" comment about former LAPD Chief Daryl Gates
description: Los Angeles City Council member and mayoral candidate Nithya Raman is walking back recent comments about controversial former LAPD Chief Daryl Gates.
content: Los Angeles City Council member and mayoral candidate Nithya Raman is walking back recent comments about controversial former LAPD Chief Daryl Gates."This city used to be the gold standard in terms of non-cooperation with immigration enforcement, years ago under the era of Daryl Gates," Raman said during last week's mayoral debate. "And now, under this mayor, we've actually lost trust from our immigrant community in our city and in our law enforcement."Raman referenced Gates because he was the first LAPD chief to implement a rule restricting officers from checking Angelenos' immigration status. However, Gates, who resigned in the wake of the 1992 LA Riots, was also viewed as leaving a legacy of police brutality and racial tension.During an interview with CNN that aired Wednesday, Raman apologized for the reference and said she never should have mentioned him. "It was a mistake to reference his name at all. I was trying to make a point, and I fumbled that point," Raman said during the interview. "That point was not to praise Daryl Gates in any way, shape or form, and I sincerely apologize."After the comment, Bass' campaign said Raman's apology was "too little, too late" and proof that she isn't ready to lead Los Angeles. Raman's campaign said Bass is trying to manufacture controversy in order to distract from her own failed record as mayor with just weeks left until the election. She went on to say that she's met with leaders of LA's Black community and owned her mistake.

title: Bulls fall 135-92 to Raptors, spoiling Chicago rookie Caleb Wilson's NBA debut
description: The Raptors routed the Chicago Bulls 135-92 on Wednesday night in the season opener for both teams.
content: Kawhi Leonard scored 23 points in his return to Toronto, Scottie Barnes and Immanuel Quickley also had 23 apiece and the Raptors routed the Chicago Bulls 135-92 on Wednesday night in the season opener for both teams.RJ Barrett added 20 points and Ja'Kobe Walter had 10 for the Raptors, who never trailed.Leonard shot 5 for 17, including 2 of 6 from 3-point range, but went 11 for 11 at the free-throw line. The two-time NBA Defensive Player of the Year had four of Toronto's 15 steals before checking out with 8:12 remaining in the final quarter.The Bulls committed 27 turnovers, leading to 35 points for the Raptors. Chicago rookie Caleb Wilson had nine turnovers in his NBA debut.Toronto scored almost as many points in the first quarter (43) as the Bulls had in the opening half (44).Matas Buzelis scored 17 points for the Bulls and Wilson had 16. Norman Powell and Jaylin Smith each added 15.Wilson shot 7 for 21 and went 1 for 8 from long distance.The Bulls combined to shoot 4 for 36 from 3-point range. Powell, who went 2 of 6, was the only Chicago player to make more than one.Leonard connected for a 3 on his first shot, then missed his next eight attempts before hitting a pull-up jumper late in the second.Leonard was traded from San Antonio to Toronto before the 2018-19 season. He helped the Raptors win the NBA championship that season before signing with the Los Angeles Clippers.Toronto reacquired Leonard in an offseason trade after a salary cap-circumvention scandal that led to massive sanctions against the Clippers.Former NBA star Serge Ibaka, Leonard's teammate on that 2019 Raptors championship team, watched from a courtside seat opposite the Toronto bench.Up nextBulls: At Milwaukee on Friday.Raptors: At Washington on Friday.

title: Florida Bar fires employee over racist messages to University of Miami football player
description: The Florida Bar says it has fired an employee over online messages that were sent to a Miami football player after the Hurricanes beat Florida State last weekend.
content: The Florida Bar has fired an employee following a brief investigation into Instagram direct messages sent to a Miami football player after the Hurricanes beat Florida State last weekend.The employee, who worked at the Bar for about two years as a computer technician, was fired on Wednesday, the Bar said.
