An account from a person using the employee's name sent a number of messages to Miami's Damon Wilson II after the Hurricanes' 43-35 victory, including several racist and homophobic slurs.Wilson, who is Black, shared a screenshot of the messages publicly Sunday, calling it a "glimpse into the life of a black student athlete." The Bar said Tuesday that the employee was under investigation."Those messages were reprehensible and inconsistent with the mission, values, and policies of The Florida Bar," the group's statement said Wednesday. "While [he] denies sending the messages, he did not provide evidence sufficient to demonstrate to The Florida Bar's satisfaction that his Instagram account had been compromised. As of today, The Florida Bar has terminated his employment."It's unclear why the private messages were sent to Wilson, who is in his first season at Miami after previously playing at Georgia and Missouri."That's my brother, and I embrace him," Miami offensive lineman Ryan Rodriguez said Tuesday when asked about Wilson and the online comments. "It's more than a game. That's my brother."Miami, the No. 1-ranked team in the AP Top 25, next plays Saturday at home against Pittsburgh.___Sign up for Top 25 poll alerts here, visit the Top 25 here, and see AP's full college football coverage here

title: Breast cancer survivors are turning pain into purpose at Comedy in Harlem
description: Breast cancer survivors are taking the stage in Harlem, using humor to raise awareness about the disease.
content: Cancer is not the easiest thing to talk about, but some breast cancer survivors say laughter can make it a little easier."Although it is serious, if we can laugh about it, we can talk about it," said stand-up comic Meshelle "the Indie-Mom of Comedy" Foreman. "[Comedy] has healed me, and I believe there are so many women who can benefit from having it shared with them in a lighter way and not making it so heavy."Foreman has been telling jokes on stages across the U.S. since the 1990s but was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2021. Her first thought was about not being there to see her children grow up, but Foreman says an early diagnosis saved her life. "I have had, in the last five years, the most courageous comedy, because I realized that it makes no sense for me not to share my story," Foreman said.Foreman can often be seen making audiences laugh at Comedy In Harlem, which held a comedy show for Breast Cancer Awareness in October where 10% of the proceeds go toward breast cancer research and awareness. Local comics say humor can be both a creative outlet for the performer and a way to connect with others."Onstage, I talk about how a mammogram saved my life. I talk about how weird and uncomfortable it is. I talk about the medicine of laughter," said Foreman.Comedy In Harlem first opened in 2021 in East Harlem by comic and actress Nicky Sunshine and her husband, Jaime Roberts, who spent years producing shows at places like Broadway Comedy Club. The duo had noticed an absence of comedy clubs in upper Manhattan. They also felt that they and fellow performers of color were not receiving opportunities in other neighborhoods known for comedy around NYC. The space now operates directly above the 147th Street exit at the 145th Street subway station on St. Nicholas Avenue in West Harlem. Harlemites are just as likely to attend a grassroots community meeting at the cellar as they are a live show."We knew so many funny friends that weren't getting enough stage time downtown. ... We're about putting people on stage, but also amplifying community voices and really amplifying the needs of the community," said co-owner Nicky Sunshine. "For example, one of the first and most successful regular shows that we do is Ladies Night."Now cancer-free, Foreman encourages other women to share their stories. From motherhood to breast cancer, she recalls writing jokes while pumping breastmilk, then later while recovering from the disease."There are so many women who don't get the opportunity to live their dreams, to do what they've been sent here to do, and there are systems in place to make you feel some kind of way about pursuing your goals and your dreams, and having the audacity to be somebody's wife and mother, and then being a working artist," said Foreman.They say you never know who in the audience might be laughing to keep from crying."Maybe [Meshelle's] narrative or her jokes will help somebody else who's going through a similar experience. That's what [stand-up] is about: just making that connection and really kind of touching humanity with our personal narratives," said Sunshine.The American Cancer Society reports that 1 in 8 women will be diagnosed with breast cancer in their lifetime. Early detection can save lives, especially for Black women, who are more likely to die from the disease.Have a story idea or tip in Harlem? Email NoÃ«lle by CLICKING HERE.

title: Rev the Runway in Denver combines high end fashion with luxury vehicles
description: Rev the Runway is a premier charity fashion and luxury car event benefitting National Jewish Health.
content: Rev the Runway is a premier charity fashion and luxury car event benefitting National Jewish Health."The fashion show really is the highlight of the evening. It is being produced by Margaret Merritt. She has produced shows for Nieman Marcus before. She's also produced shows for Michael Kors, and she did the Phoenix Fashion Week. She really brings incredible, beautiful stages," said Kiki Sebring, a member of the Rev the Runway planning committee. Neiman Marcus provides a curated collection of designer clothes from London, Paris, and Milan. Mercedes-Benz of Denver puts it's most luxurious vehicles on display. In addition to the fashion show, attendees can do a F1 driving simulator, try a new color at the Tom Ford lip bar, and enjoy music spun by DJ Simone. The event features handcrafted cocktails, tequila tastings, and cuisine from local Denver restaurants. There will also be some exciting auction items for attendees to bid on including an opportunity to meet the new Thunder, the Broncos mascot. "Nieman Marcus has helped us procure tickets to this year's Paris Fashion Week. So it will including flights. It will include two nights of hotels and a couple of great restaurants," Sebring explained. All the proceeds from Rev the Runway go to support patient care and medical research for respiratory, cardiac, and immune diseases at National Jewish Health. "It's incredibly important that we help fundraise so that they can provide charity patient care. Last year alone they did $43 million in charity patient care. That means if you cannot afford to pay but you need help...you need their amazing doctors by your side, they will treat you," said Kristen Holtzman, event chair for Rev the Runway.LINK: For Tickets to Rev the RunwayRev the Runway is Thursday, November 5, 2026 at Mercedes-Benz of Denver. CBS Colorado Meteorologist Lauren Whitney will emcee the event.

title: Lamar Jackson returns to Ravens practice, but still limited because of his ankle injury
description: Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson was able to do limited work at practice Wednesday, according to Baltimore coach Jesse Minter.
content: Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson was able to do limited work at practice Wednesday, according to Baltimore coach Jesse Minter.Jackson has missed the past two games with an ankle injury. He was not at practice during the portion open to reporters Wednesday, but the Ravens listed him as limited afterward."Lamar was actually able to get a little bit of limited work in today, in preparation," Minter said. "That's where that's at. Again, it's a day-by-day thing. But he was able to get a little bit of work in and be involved in the preparation."Baltimore hosts Cincinnati on Sunday.Jackson was hurt in a Week 4 victory over Tennessee, and he had not practiced since. The Ravens are 1-1 in his absence after losing at Cleveland last weekend."There's nobody that wants to be out there more than Lamar," Minter said. "I understand all the stuff and what people say, but Lamar wants to play. But at the same time, you have to be healthy enough to play and that's how we would really treat any player."Center Cam Jurgens (concussion) was a full participant in practice after missing the two games since his trade from Philadelphia to Baltimore.

title: Michigan school official, business speak on impact of Toledo chemical leak
description: Several school districts with students living within the shelter-in-place area canceled school and activities, including Bedford Public Schools and Mason Consolidated Schools.
content: The city of Toledo issued an emergency evacuation order after confirming the release of a toxic chemical late Tuesday night.Officials issued a shelter-in-place order for a three-mile radius around the site of the chemical leak. That includes parts of Southeast Michigan. In an update Wednesday, Toledo officials said the evacuation and shelter-in-place orders were reduced to a half-mile radius of the facility. The orders beyond that zone have been lifted.Officials say no injuries or fatalities have been reported.CBS News Detroit spoke with school districts and businesses on the Michigan side of that zone to learn how the chemical leak in Toledo affected them on Wednesday.Several school districts with students living within the shelter-in-place area canceled school and activities, including Bedford Public Schools and Mason Consolidated Schools, and posted updates on their websites and Facebook."Out of an abundance of caution and making sure we are maintaining our priority of our kids being healthy and safe, we needed to cancel for the day. We monitored that all day," said Mason Consolidated Schools Superintendent Kelli Tuller.Tuller says canceling school on Thursday wasn't off the table."The EPA is closely monitoring that, and the situation isn't fully under control. I'm going to be alerting our parents this afternoon or early evening that we should be on call and prepare some contingency plans for child care and the change in our schedule tomorrow possibly," she said.Some businesses kept their doors open along Telegraph Road just north of the state line. An employee told us he didn't notice any chemical fumes when he got to work."No, I haven't noticed anything, at least not here. I take Detroit Ave. on my way up into work. A little bit [of smell] on my commute in, but once I got here, really no issue," said the Fish Market employee, Cam Micheau.CBS News Detroit asked Micheau whether the emergency affected the business."Maybe a little slower at some points, especially around that 11-12, slower than we typically see, but as for the morning, a lot of the morning was business as usual. Only difference was a lot of people wearing masks really," he said.

title: Cow gets loose in Pikesville, makes its way to I-695
description: A cow got loose in a Pikesville neighborhood and eventually made its way onto I-695 on Wednesday, prompting multiple calls to Baltimore County police.
content: A cow got loose in a Pikesville neighborhood and eventually made its way onto I-695 on Wednesday, prompting multiple calls to Baltimore County police.Around 1 p.m., officers received a report of a cow walking along Hambleton Court. Additional calls followed as the animal was spotted along Old Court Road, Greenmount Avenue and I-695.Officers D. Royster and D. Bailey joined the cow's owner in tracking down the animal. Using rope from a patrol car, they were able to wrangle the cow, load it into a trailer and arrange for its return home.The cow remained in police custody until another farmhand arrived with a trailer to transport the animal.No injuries were reported.Police said the cow belongs to a local farmer whose property is in the 3200 block of Old Court Road."The Baltimore County Police Department would like to thank everyone who assisted in bringing this call to a safe conclusion," the department said.

title: Video of woman's arrest raises more questions about use of force by Donora police
description: Another video is raising more questions about the use of force in the Donora Police Department.
content: Another video is raising more questions about the use of force in the Donora Police Department. Video from last year shows an officer identified as Bob Cunningham handcuffing and dragging a woman down steps after she called police for help. According to the criminal complaint, the woman called police for help retrieving belongings from a friend's house. The officer wrote that he warned her to stop screaming and yelling. She was arrested for disorderly conduct."I'm just getting havoc every day from these officers," said concerned resident Kelsha Barnes. "It takes one time for them to know who you are and they just continue and continue to keep targeting you."Around the same time as this arrest, KDKA-TV reported on a video that appeared to show Cunningham knocking a cellphone from a man's hand.It raises questions about whether officials reviewed the woman's arrest."There is a right way to arrest people and there's a wrong way," said Donora borough councilmember Roderick Wilson. "We need to look at that. But I will say step one is everybody, including council, we need some sensitivity training as far as dealing with these cases and in particular the police in my opinion."Last week, KDKA reported on a different Donora officer seen punching a man twice and tasing him. More people have since come forward with their own encounters with both officers. Their concerns put borough leaders under scrutiny, including Council President Casey Perrotta, who was fired as an Elizabeth Borough police officer and convicted in a case involving forged psychological evaluation paperwork for another officer. He was permanently barred from working as a police officer. Now he leads a council making decisions about Donora police, a role some residents question since he can't be an officer himself."That's something that needs to be taken up by the powers that be, and I'll just leave it at that," Wilson said. "That would fall into he hands of the solicitor and how that may go forward," he added. Wilson said he was going to sit down with the police chief Wednesday afternoon and look at the videos together. He said he wants the borough to address these concerns locally without having to call for a federal investigation.

title: Baltimore City Schools CEO Jermaine Dawson reflects on first 100 days, outlines goals
description: Baltimore City Public Schools CEO Dr. Jermaine Dawson reflected on his first 100 days leading the district Wednesday, highlighting community feedback and outlining his goals for the months ahead.
content: Baltimore City Public Schools CEO Dr. Jermaine Dawson reflected on his first 100 days leading the district Wednesday, highlighting community feedback and outlining his goals for the months ahead.Dawson said he spent his first few months listening to students, families, educators and community members to better understand their needs and priorities.The new CEO, who succeeded Dr. Sonja Santelises, said three messages consistently emerged from those conversations: protect what works, make the everyday run smoothly and build schools every neighborhood believes in.Dawson turned the feedback into a visual installation featuring hundreds of handwritten words on sticky notes representing the community's hopes and aspirations. The words were collected during listening sessions and school visits.He said the installation serves as a tangible reflection of the voices, ideas and experiences that will help shape the district's work moving forward."I've spent my first 100 days as the City Schools CEO listening to Baltimoreans, both inside and outside our schools," Dawson said. "These words reflect many different hopes, but they come back to something we all share: the belief that every student deserves to be known, valued, challenged and supported."Transition team to help shape district's futureDawson said he is now focused on turning those conversations into action.The next phase will include a transition team of more than 200 people, ranging from students to senior staff members. The group will work to translate community feedback into tangible progress for the district.The transition team will meet three times between November and January to review the feedback collected and help establish the district's strategic direction."My word is possibility because I want every student in Baltimore to see a future filled with opportunities and know that City Schools is committed to helping them achieve it," Dawson said.

title: Takedown of "large-scale" cocaine trafficking ring in Pittsburgh area leads to charges against 8
description: The takedown of a "large-scale" cocaine trafficking ring has led to charges against eight people who authorities called a "scourge" on the state of Pennsylvania.
content: The takedown of a "large-scale" cocaine trafficking ring has led to charges against eight people whom authorities called a "scourge" on the state of Pennsylvania.Eight Pittsburgh-area residents were indicted by a federal grand jury on charges of violating drug laws, United States Attorney Troy Rivetti announced on Wednesday. The indictment, which was unsealed after the arrests of seven of the defendants Wednesday morning, follows a 15-month Homeland Security Task Force investigation into what Rivetti called an "extensive" cocaine trafficking organization between June 2025 and September of this year. Multiple other agencies were also involved. "Great collaboration led to the takedown of these upper-level cocaine traffickers who were a scourge to the Commonwealth, as their conduct fueled addiction and endangered neighborhoods," Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday said in a press release. "We, along with our partners, are committed to combatting a surge in cocaine-dealing across the Commonwealth." Pittsburgh Bureau of Police Chief Jason Lando said the indictment is a testament to what law enforcement agencies can accomplish when they work together. "This partnership is also one of the reasons why we continue to see a decrease in shootings and homicides in our region, making Pittsburgh a safer place for all," Lando said in a statement. Authorities identified those charged as Terrance Bonner, 45; Martin Langford, 59; Roddell Smalls, 53; Maurice Tinsley, 45; Justin Rumble, 47; Oscar Stokes, 45; and Rashawdi Pugh, 47. Tinsley is from Bellevue, Stokes is from Uniontown, Pugh is from Aliquippa and the rest are from Pittsburgh.Langford is the president of the Westside Mustangs Youth Athletic Association. His program, based in Pittsburgh's West End, received Stop the Violence grant funding under the Gainey administration. News of the bust comes less than a week after the Pennsylvania Office of Attorney General announced charges against 13 other people accused of running "a major cocaine trafficking pipeline" from Youngstown, Ohio, to Butler County.

title: GetGo now charges $3 to put air in your tires
description: People used to be able to fill up their tires for free at GetGo, but now the gas station chain charges $3.
content: It's the time of year when you'll likely need to fill up your tires because cold temperatures play with air pressure. But just as the price of everything is going up, so too is the cost of air.People used to be able to fill up their tires for free at GetGo, but now the gas station chain charges $3. KDKA-TV reached out to GetGo on Wednesday about why it's now charging for air. "We appreciate feedback from our customers and understand that air service is valued by many," the statement said. "After testing the change at select locations over the summer, we began transitioning to paid air service in September to coincide with the installation of new, more reliable equipment. We remain focused on delivering a convenient, high-quality experience for our customers." Gwendolyn Dolyn was at GetGo to fill up her tires on Wednesday, but when KDKA-TV told her it would be $3, she said she'd be going home to use her own pump. When GetGo customer Curtis Ramey learned about the new charge, he called it "robbery." "That's kind of crazy," he said. "You can breathe air for free." Some gas stations have been charging for air for a while, though it's cheaper. At one Sunoco station, it costs 75 cents. GetGo has 279 locations throughout several states. Not all have the new machines yet, but they will soon. "That's insane," said GetGo customer Callie Munch. "It's always been free. It's air. Air is all around us. Why should we have to pay for it?"

title: East Texas deputy killed, police officer injured during exchange of gunfire with assault suspect, officials say
description: The sheriff's office said that the suspect had outstanding felony warrants for aggravated assault and aggravated assault on a peace officer.
content: A Van Zandt County deputy has died, and an officer is in the hospital following an exchange of gunfire with a suspect overnight, officials say. The suspect was later found dead. According to the Van Zandt County Sheriff's Office, at about 10 p.m. Tuesday, deputies were called to assist the Canton Police Department to serve a warrant in the 4300 block of State Highway 198, just south of the city of Canton. The sheriff's office said that the suspect had outstanding felony warrants for aggravated assault and aggravated assault on a peace officer. At about 10:20 p.m., law enforcement on scene reported shots being fired from inside the home toward deputies and officers outside, which prompted them to return fire. During that exchange, a Canton police officer and a Van Zandt County deputy were struck, the sheriff's office confirmed. The deputy, identified by his mother as Adam Sherifi, was pronounced dead. The police officer, whose name has not been released, was transported to a Plano hospital with a gunshot wound to the arm and is expected to be okay, officials told CBS News Texas.Officials said the suspect, who has not been identified, was found dead inside the home from a gunshot wound. However, officials have not confirmed if the wound was self-inflicted or from the exchange of gunfire with law enforcement. Brenda Haley, who lives near the suspect, describes what happened last night as an ambush. "They didn't even get to get out of that car before all this went on," Haley said. "The sound of that won't ever leave my heart or my mind. It was just so unnecessary." During an interview with CBS affiliate KYTX in Tyler, Canton Mayor Lou Ann Berry said the suspect was wanted after they allegedly were involved in an assault with a sword at a Walmart the day before. Following the news of the deputy's death, condolences from law enforcement agencies and city leaders began pouring in on Wednesday. "Our hearts are heavy as we mourn the tragic loss of a Van Zandt County Deputy who made the ultimate sacrifice in the line of duty," the Van Zandt County Peace Officers' Association said in a statement. "Please join us in praying for the family, friends, and fellow officers of our fallen hero. We also ask for continued prayers for the officer who was wounded, praying for healing, strength, and a full recovery." A prayer vigil was held outside the Van Zandt County Courthouse on Wednesday afternoon in honor of the fallen deputy. Watch below: Outside the Van Zandt County Justice Center, a growing memorial now honors Sherifi's sacrifice. "He was a joy. He was laughter," said Nancy White, a relative of Sherifi's. "He was fun. He loved his wife and his children."For his family, the heartbreak also comes with uncertainty."He was the man," White said. "He did the providing and the protection, and they don't have that now."Haley says neighbors never really knew a lot about the suspect."He stayed to himself," said Haley. "He had two kids that got off the bus right there."The sheriff's office said the investigation is ongoing and the Texas Rangers will be the lead agency.

title: In the cutthroat world of online dating, men use AI to put their best face forward
description: How much AI is too much when it comes to finding love on the apps? "It's very subtle," one dating app user said of his AI-enhanced photos.
content: Marissa, a 31-year-old Boston resident, downloaded dating apps because she is looking for love. But more and more, she finds herself looking for something else: AI-free photos.The marketing professional said she routinely comes across dating app profiles that appear to be digitally altered. Usually, the changes are minor and can be easily made using tools like Photoshop, such as editing someone out of a photo. Sometimes, however, the photo appears to be completely AI-generated, she told CBS News, citing a photo she came across on Bumble of a man dressed in a suit tiling a bathroom wall. "AI aside, I'm not sure what the appeal is there," she said (Marissa asked to withhold her surname for privacy reasons).Numerous women on TikTok also report spotting photos of men on dating apps that appear to be AI-generated. Their accounts demonstrate how AI is blurring the line between what's real and what's fake in the already fraught arena of online dating. They also raise ethical questions about how far is too far when it comes to manipulating your online persona."People want authentic connections and conversations," Kathryn Coduto, an assistant professor at Boston University who studies dating apps, told CBS News in an email. "I think AI has made people more wary and skeptical of others, especially people they don't know."Of course, dating app users have long relied on filters and other editing tools to polish their photos. But AI tools are upping the ante, allowing people to create high-quality images within seconds, and in some cases, fabricate fake scenes. "A dater has to think about how they're going to capture someone's attention in a few seconds or less," Coduto told CBS News. "This might mean making your photo look a little better than it might have before."To be sure, this practice isn't exclusive to men. However, they appear more likely to use AI to spruce up their dating profiles than women, Coduto added."So far, men are more interested in AI in the dating space, which isn't surprising," Coduto said. "Women tend to receive more matches and messages, so men have a harder time standing out."The "digital stylist" who helps men AI their photosAI can create obvious distortions when it generates photos, such as omitting a finger from someone's hand. For Marissa, a telltale sign is the person's face, which sometimes looks "waxy" in AI-generated photos, she said. Still, as technology improves, it's becoming harder to distinguish a real photo from one created by AI models. Lana Li, a Brooklyn, New York, dating consultant who runs the Substack "Love Me Like a Robot," calls herself a "digital stylist." She uses AI to help men level up their dating app photos, and defends using the technology as long as the photos still genuinely represent who they are. "I can take a picture of somebody and then put them in a different outfit or change their hairstyle a little bit, or put different shoes on them," she told CBS News. "Or if I think their body language doesn't look confident in the picture, I will have [ChatGPT] change that."The 37-year-old also uses FaceApp to change men's facial expressions. She said the edits are subtle, such as slightly lifting the corner of someone's mouth to make them look "friendlier."Despite her liberal approach to using AI, there are lines Li is unwilling to cross. For example, one client asked her to digitally alter a photo so that his head was on a marathon runner's body â a request she declined."I told him, 'I can't work with you if you want to not represent yourself accurately,'" she said.Two men who spoke to CBS News on the condition of anonymity to maintain their privacy told CBS News they've used AI in their online dating photos, but in ways they feel stop short of being misleading and remain true to who they are.A ban on HingeOne man, a 30-year-old tech employee and client of Li's, said she used ChatGPT to digitally clothe him in more professional garb and to tame his frizzy hair."It's very subtle," the New York City resident said, saying he still looked like himself, even with the edits. He emphasized that he doesn't want to "catfish" anyone â a concern for singles even in the absence of AI.Another man is pulling back after one of his AI photos backfired. The 50-something-year-old New York City resident said he fed photos of himself into Aragon.ai, an AI headshot generator, which produced a picture of him standing on a Manhattan roof with a sunset in the background. It immediately drew hits on his Hinge profile."This picture generally got the most likes," he told CBS News. "Now that could just be because it was the first thing they saw. But regardless, it was proving to be effective, and women seemed to like it."That was, until Hinge banned him. He managed to get his account back but ultimately decided to delete the sunset photo, suspecting it was the reason for his removal from the app."How much AI am I OK with?"Most popular dating apps have policies that limit the use of AI-generated images in people's profiles. Hinge emphasizes the importance of authenticity on its website, noting that people should be able to discern "fact from fiction.""If you decide to include generative AI images, audio, or video in your profile, it should not be used to misrepresent yourself or your intentions," the company says on its AI policy page.Hinge also uses automated tools and human reviewers to detect and remove "prohibited material," according to the company's terms of service. If users see suspicious AI material, they can confidentially report it through the app or online. A spokesperson for Match Group, which owns Hinge, Tinder and a handful of other dating apps, told CBS that as generative AI evolves, the company is "watching closely and listening to daters, who tell us they want more transparency, more authenticity, and more confidence that a real person is on the other end."Bumble also uses tools to detect and weed out AI-generated content, and lets users report profiles that feature such images. A spokesperson said the company prohibits inauthentic profiles, and Bumble's community guidelines bar the use of "artificially generated photos or enhanced photos to deceive others.""We enforce this through a combination of AI-powered tools, human moderation, verification features and member reporting, and we take action based on the severity of a violation, up to and including permanently banning accounts," the spokesperson said. Marissa, the 31-year-old who lives in Boston, said that when she sees a person's profile whose photos bear the hallmarks of AI, she chooses to move along. "The dating pool is already challenging, and this is just another thing we have to grapple with," she said. "How much AI am I OK with?"

title: Texas turnout more Democratic in first two days of early voting than in 2024, VoteHub says, but too early to draw conclusions
description: Nearly 1.5 million Texans voted in the first two days of early voting, with Democratic-leaning voters showing stronger early participation than in 2024. Analysts caution that turnout trends don't necessarily predict election results.
content: Nearly 1.5 million Texans cast ballots during the first two days of early voting, according to VoteHub, as candidates in major statewide races make a final push to get their supporters to the polls.In Allen on Wednesday, Gov. Greg Abbott urged supporters to vote as soon as possible and encouraged family and friends to do the same."Tell them they got to go vote today or tomorrow to make sure their vote counts in this election. Are you with me?" Abbott said. His Democratic challenger, Gina Hinojosa, has also urged her supporters to vote. In addition to meeting directly with voters, Hinojosa said she is spending heavily to get her message out."People are turning out," Hinojosa said. "We are on broadcast TV. This is an expensive state to run in, and we're playing at the high rollers table, but that's because the payout is so high."Zachary Donnini, head of data science at VoteHub, which is working with the CBS News Data Desk, said the electorate during the first two days of early voting appeared more Democratic-leaning than during the same period in 2024."For the people who voted on the first day, on Monday, in Texas, we think that the electorate was about 10 points more Democratic than it was the first day of the 2024 in-person early voting," Donnini said. "But we think the second day was a little bit better for Republicans in the sense that maybe it was only eight or nine points more blue than the same day in 2024."VoteHub estimates that 32% of Texans with a history of voting in Democratic primaries cast ballots during the first two days of early voting, compared with nearly 21% of those with a history of voting in Republican primaries.Tracking partisan turnout in Texas is more difficult because voters do not register by party, unlike in some other states. Donnini cautioned that it is too early to draw conclusions from the turnout trends.President Donald Trump won Texas by 14 percentage points in 2024. This year, Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico has led Republican Ken Paxton in most polls.A CBS News poll conducted Oct. 8-16 showed Talarico leading Paxton 51% to 49%. The RealClearPolitics average of polls conducted Oct. 5-19 showed Talarico ahead by 1.9 percentage points, 48.2% to 46.3%.Despite Democratic enthusiasm this year, Donnini cautioned that polling numbers do not automatically translate into election victories."To win a Trump-plus-14 state like Texas, you need two things: If you're James Talarico or Hinojosa, you need one, a good electorate," Donnini said. "You need your people to be mobilized and come out just to make the job easier. Then, the job is win over people who voted for Donald Trump. It's that simple."Meanwhile, Abbott maintains a lead in the governor's race.The CBS News poll showed Abbott leading Hinojosa 52% to 48%. The RealClearPolitics polling average showed Abbott ahead by 2.2 percentage points, 49.1% to 46.9%.As of Wednesday night, nine days of early voting remained in Texas.VoteHub projects that two-thirds of Texas voters will cast their ballots during early voting this year and that total turnout could approach the number of ballots cast in the 2024 presidential election.Watch Eye on Politics at 7:30 a.m. Sunday on CBS News Texas, on air and streaming.Follow Jack on X and Instagram: @cbs11jack

title: Son says Stephen Hubbard was experiencing "extreme tiredness with life" before release from Russian jail
description: In an interview with CBS News after Stephen Hubbard was released from Russian custody, his son, Fr. Joseph Coleman, said his father might have made a mistake in staying in Ukraine when the war began.
content: Washington — Fr. Joseph Coleman feared he would never again see his father, Stephen Hubbard, when they had a brief phone conversation last year while Hubbard was in a Russian prison."He was expressing a very extreme tiredness with life, the life that he was experiencing at that time. I don't want to say suicidal thoughts, but the conversation hinted it leaned in that direction," Coleman, a Greek Orthodox priest, told CBS News on Wednesday in his first television interview since his father's release.Hubbard's release was announced earlier Wednesday during a meeting between U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Hubbard, a U.S. citizen, was imprisoned in Russia for more than four years after being accused of fighting for Ukraine. The U.S. government had deemed Hubbard wrongfully detained.President Trump said Putin had agreed to release Hubbard at his request, with "no 'swap' necessary," though he also said that his decision to waive new sanctions against Russia played a role in Hubbard's release. In a one-minute phone call with his father before Hubbard took off from St. Petersburg, Coleman said he sounded better than he had during their last conversation in May 2025. Witkoff was also present, leaving little opportunity for a private exchange."I want to embrace him as a son embraces his father. I want to personally assess his health to make sure he's well," Coleman said. He said he would also give his dad space to adjust to freedom and expected to see Hubbard later that evening.Coleman, who lives in Cyprus, did not grow up in the same home as Hubbard, who was divorced from Coleman's mother. He said the family had lost track of Hubbard entirely for roughly three years after his detention.Martin De Luca, Hubbard's U.S.-based attorney, told CBS News that when his legal team took on the case in February 2025, neither the family nor the U.S. Embassy knew precisely where Hubbard was being held.Lawyers in Russia eventually located him and arranged for legal visits, money for food and basic necessities, and the brief phone call with his son.De Luca said the isolation had taken an enormous toll."It's just being isolated from everybody you've ever known and just from the outside world," he said.After Putin granted Hubbard's release, Witkoff praised the Russian president as a "humanitarian," prompting swift backlash from Republican and Democratic lawmakers. Putin is wanted by the International Criminal Court for alleged war crimes involving the deportation of Ukrainian children, and Russian forces have been accused of widespread abuses during the war.Asked about Witkoff's description of Putin, Coleman called his father's release "a small step toward peace in this greater conflict" and thanked Putin for signing off on the deal.He described the decision as an act of "compassion and even mercy."Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired schoolteacher, was captured in Ukraine shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022 and accused of manning a checkpoint for mercenaries. He was later sentenced to almost seven years in a penal colony following a closed-door trial.His family has consistently disputed the charges.De Luca said his legal team conducted its own investigation, interviewing people who knew Hubbard and examining his circumstances before the invasion. He said they found no evidence that Hubbard had served in the Ukrainian military or was physically capable of doing so at roughly 70 years old."We have not seen any evidence to support those allegations," De Luca said. He added that the Russian case file was largely sealed and that his team had repeatedly sought evidence substantiating the charges.De Luca and Coleman both credited the Trump administration's diplomatic engagement with Moscow for securing Hubbard's freedom.Asked whether recent U.S. decisions benefiting Russia — including sanctions relief and purchases of Russian diesel — were connected to Hubbard's release, De Luca said he did not believe there was a direct link, though he acknowledged that bilateral relationships involve multiple overlapping interests.Mr. Trump, however, has explicitly said that allowing new sanctions to take effect would have prevented Hubbard's release.And despite Hubbard's release, as many as 20 Americans remain imprisoned in Russia, including some whose families dispute the charges against them. The State Department continues to warn Americans against traveling to Russia because of the risk of wrongful detention.De Luca said he was not concerned that the administration's engagement with Moscow would encourage further detentions, arguing that diplomatic dialogue had helped secure several Americans' freedom.But Russia has not been designated a state sponsor of wrongful detention under a new Trump administration policy, despite its history of imprisoning Americans on questionable charges. Iran and Afghanistan have both received the designation.Coleman stopped short of blaming his father for his circumstances but acknowledged he might have made a mistake by remaining in Ukraine as Russian forces advanced."The Russian forces told foreign nationals to leave and he did not," Coleman said. "I do not like what happened to my father. I am ecstatic that he is free. But he was living in an area that was a war zone.""I'm not saying his detainment was justifiable. I'm not saying that," he said. "But these things happen in war."

title: Minnesota governor candidates pledge anti-fraud plans. What changes are already underway?
description: DFL Sen. Amy Klobuchar and GOP House Speaker Lisa Demuth pledge to fight fraud that has flourished in state government in recent years if elected to be the next governor, which is a top issue this fall.
content: DFL Sen. Amy Klobuchar and GOP House Speaker Lisa Demuth pledge to fight fraud that has flourished in state government in recent years if elected to be the next governor, which is a top issue this fall.More than one quarter of Minnesota's likely voters said solving the problem will be top of mind when deciding who should be the state's next chief executive, according to the latest Minnesota Star Tribune poll.Klobuchar has said she would do a "top to bottom" audit of state government and close gaps in enforcement, so fraud can be better prosecuted. She wants regular, in-person inspections and promises to implement a "do not pay" database to block anyone convicted of fraud from every grant, contract or program in state government.Demuth similarly said she would crosscheck convicted criminals across state programs so they aren't stealing from multiple funds and instruct her agencies to conduct unannounced site visits. She also said she would replace all the commissioners leading those departments with experts committed to ending the "culture of fraud."But any of their plans would be an addition to policy changes the legislature implemented over the last few years.What anti-fraud measures did the Minnesota Legislature approve?On a bipartisan basis in a closely divided capitol these last two years, lawmakers passed a slate of new anti-fraud measures, including increasing criminal penalties for fraudsters and boosting the Medicaid Fraud Control Unit in the attorney general's office.They also added protections for whistleblowers and made it easier to stop payments for suspected fraud, which was a request of Gov. Tim Walz's administration as it grapples with the social services scandal.Outdated technology beleaguers county governments tasked with implementing the programs and the Legislature earmarked $75 million for upgrades.A significant change is a new Office of Inspector General, an independent watchdog tasked with investigating waste, fraud and abuse. The next governor will choose who leads the agency from a list of recommendations from a legislative commission. The group has begun that work and plans to have the candidates by January.

title: Zac Brown Band founding member raising awareness of ALS with "Hop on a Cure" nonprofit
description: Grammy Award-winning Zac Brown Band plays Target Center on Friday. A founding member will be on stage with a message.
content: Grammy Award-winning Zac Brown Band plays Target Center on Friday. A founding member will be on stage with a message.John Driskell Hopkins often wears a hat that says: Hop on a Cure. His guitar strap says it too. It's what's behind it that he wants you to listen to.John Driskell Hopkins and his wife Jen founded the nonprofit Hop on a Cure after his ALS diagnosis. "Our mission is number one â awareness. So, I think that John sharing his story and highlighting other people with ALS is really showing people what this disease is and what it does, and then of course research dollars. Like it's so underfunded. It costs so much to get a drug from trial to FDA approval. Not only does it take time, but lots of financial resources," Jen Hopkins said.The couple spoke about how fans can help with their mission. "Give us all your money," John Driskell Hopkins joked."Wear a T-shirt. Educate yourself. Tell people about it," they said."It's all about being a billboard all the time. When I look out into the crowd and see a lot of blue Hop on a Cure shirts, it really is moving to me to see that support. So everyone in our crowd needs to know that I see that and I appreciate it," John Driskell Hopkins said."When you're here playing, what does it mean to you to be on the road with the band and playing while you're navigating this journey?" WCCO's Jennifer Mayerle asked."Truly hope that I can do this forever, but my challenges are growing, and I'm very blessed to have a slow progression, and there may come a day where I can't be on the road. I do find myself pausing and like scanning the whole crowd like I'm trying to imprint it on my brain. And I've done that every week this tour. I forget some shows, but every week I remember to just make a photograph in my mind. I'm trying to embrace all of those moments," John Driskell Hopkins said.He will be creating those memories on stage with Zac Brown Band Friday at Target Center.Tickets are still for sale. If you'd like to support Hop on a Cure, click here. John Driskell Hopkins is still releasing new music on his own. His song, "I Love You Forever," is written for his family.

title: Man who fired stolen gun at officer during chase in St. Paul pleads guilty
description: A St. Paul, Minnesota, man pleaded guilty Wednesday for fleeing police and firing a stolen gun​ at an officer last January.
content: A St. Paul, Minnesota, man who fled from police and fired a stolen gun at an officer last January pleaded guilty Wednesday.Samuel Flowers, 28, originally faced eight counts, including second-degree attempted murder, first-degree assault, two counts of prohibited firearm and ammunition possession, a dangerous weapons charge, fifth-degree drug possession, fleeing a peace officer and refusing to submit to a chemical test.He pleaded guilty to one dangerous weapons charge.Documents say police officers tried to make a traffic stop after witnessing Flowers speeding in a Chevrolet Impala. Flowers eventually fired at the officer from inside the Impala during the pursuit. The officer was not hurt, but his vehicle was damaged. A separate car belonging to a civilian was also damaged by gunfire, charges said.Flowers crashed into a parked car on the 800 block of Fuller Avenue, and police arrested him. They found an "AR-style rifle" and more than a dozen spent casings inside the Impala, the criminal complaint said. The gun had been reported stolen in Minneapolis in 2018.Flowers is scheduled to be sentenced on Dec. 21, 2026.

title: Giants going with J.J. McCarthy as their starting quarterback
description: The Giants are turning to J.J. McCarthy to start at quarterback in their next game Sunday at Houston.
content: John Harbaugh and the New York Giants are turning to J.J. McCarthy to start at quarterback for their game Sunday at Houston.McCarthy got the nod over Jameis Winston, who started the previous four games since Jaxson Dart was sidelined for the foreseeable future because of a knee injury."It's all things considered what gives us the best chance to be our best, give us the best chance to play the best offense we can," Harbaugh said upon making the announcement following practice on Wednesday. "I thought Jameis has done a tremendous job: won us games, played well, but as we go forward here, this is going to be our direction. We think it gives us some good options on offense."The Giants (3-2-1) are in the middle of the pack on offense league-wide as they start a third player in seven games at football's most important position. They have their bye week after playing the Texans but are making the change to McCarthy now that he has fully grasped offensive coordinator Matt Nagy's system."He's got the game plan down," Harbaugh said. "He can throw it. He's picked up the offense really quickly. He's an athletic guy, obviously, and he's going to play some good football."Harbaugh said there was no debate over Winston starting against New Orleans last weekend. Winston threw two interceptions before getting replaced by McCarthy early in the fourth quarter with New York down 34-10."Last game, it wasn't what it was capable of being," said Winston, who has completed 57% of his passes for 957 yards, seven touchdowns and five interceptions this season. "Every single week as a football team, you're defined off of the last time you stepped foot on the field, so I believe that, based off last game and my job is to lead the New York Football Giants to a win, that didn't happen."Facing little resistance from the Saints given the score, McCarthy was 11 of 21 for 243 yards and led multiple scoring drives, getting to within seven before an incomplete pass on fourth down in the final minute."It was really fun to just be out there with this group and be able to execute the plays and Coach Nags trusting me to run his offense and just super thrilled to be back out there playing again," McCarthy said. "There was some good things. There was some bad things."McCarthy is more mobile than Winston but has only been around just over three weeks since being acquired from Minnesota for a fifth-round draft pick in a late-September trade. Sunday's game is set to be the 23-year-old's 11th NFL start, after he made 10 for the Vikings last season, and he feels more prepared this time around."I believe just experience does wonders: being able to be in that same situation where you might have made a mistake the last time," McCarthy said. "This time, you're just going to react better and make a more well-rounded-response decision in that situation."His Giants debut is taking place in the same stadium in Houston where McCarthy won the national title with Michigan on Jan. 8, 2024. His coach at the time was Jim Harbaugh, John's younger brother.McCarthy had 11 TD passes and 12 interceptions with Minnesota. He lost the starting job there in training camp to free agent addition Kyler Murray.Sitting in first place in the NFC East, the Giants are banking on McCarthy making good on his growing confidence. He ran his first practice with the starters on Wednesday, and teammates are getting used to having someone new at the helm."He has to know how fast this guy is, how slow this guy is and how he likes to run his routes," receiver Darnell Mooney said. "There's some things we've still got to work on. If it works out well, it works out well. If it doesn't, we still have to continue to build that chemistry."

title: Rep. Keith Self says he was never in danger from alleged assassination plot by McKinney teen
description: The North Texas congressman says federal authorities had already arrested the 17-year-old when he learned of the alleged threat. Self praised the FBI for taking action.
author_name: Doug  Myers, S.E.  Jenkins, Amelia  Mugavero
content: U.S. Rep. Keith Self says he was never in any real danger from an alleged assassination plot involving a 17-year-old boy from his hometown of McKinney.By the time U.S. Capitol Police notified him of the threat, federal authorities had already arrested the teenager, Self said."When we knew about it, they had him," Self, R-McKinney, told CBS News Texas. "... It's more routine than you would think with members of Congress."Self said he did not know the wording of the threat or how or where it was made.He said law enforcement informed him that the McKinney teenager had planned to make waves, "perhaps try to shoot at me," and carry out a terrorist attack. He said it was unclear exactly what that meant."The FBI, through the Capitol Police, only tells us so much," Self said.Self said he did not know how the FBI uncovered the alleged assassination plot, but believed authorities had been aware of the teenager before his arrest."I understand that they've known about this kid for a while," he said.Self declined to speculate about what motivated the alleged plot but said the teenager was "somehow under the influence of the things that we see happening in Texas and certainly in McKinney.""It's a very unsettled time," Self said. "We see it, we feel it."Self said he had received threats before, "but not to this degree and not any that action was taken by law enforcement."Still, he said he was not fazed by the threat."I was in the military for 25 years, deployed multiple times," he said. "I also knew that the law enforcement had him under control. Now, it would have been a little different if they had said, 'There's an unknown threat out there.'"Meanwhile, Self said he was "very grateful" to the FBI for acting before the alleged threat could be carried out."So often we hear that somebody does something and then you find out later that the FBI had him on some sort of watch list and didn't take action," Self said. "So I am very grateful that the FBI took action in this case."Efforts to reach the FBI and Capitol Police for comment have been unsuccessful.CBS News Texas will provide updates as more information becomes available.

title: Colorado commissary owner in dispute with landlord over extra charges
description: Local commissary, where about 50 small businesses operate, is in a dispute that could shut it down.
content: The owners of a food truck commissary said that they are fighting to stay open because they're in a legal dispute with their landlord, who they say is charging them thousands of dollars in fees they don't believe they are responsible for.Both sides have hired lawyers to work out the dispute. The landlord told CBS Colorado the tenants are disputing costs they agreed to. The Foothills Commissary owners say as the dispute drags on it's costing them a lot of money, and they're concerned about the dozens of businesses who depend on them.About 50 small, locally owned businesses and food trucks operate out of the Foothills Commissary.Many are female or minority owned, including La Baja Fish Tacos & Grill."It's a small kitchen, you can see, but this is where the magic happens," said Rene Jimarez, the owner of the food truck.On Wednesday morning, Jimarez was getting his food truck ready for an inspection. His food truck is one of about 15 food trucks, parked at the commissary which serves as home base."This is our kitchen. This is our commissary. This is where we do everything, prepping, cleaning, cooking," said Jimarez. "It's like a community. We help each other. We look out for each other.""We're all kind of tight knit. We help each other out. We borrow things. We borrow employees. We share ingredients if we're out or something kind of a thing, so very family-oriented," said Randall Baldwin, the co-owner of Foothills.Food trucks in Colorado are required to operate from a licensed commissary kitchen.Baldwin says a landlord dispute is pushing them to the financial limit."We've been experiencing some landlord issues, of course, some amounts that they're saying we owe for certain items that are not valid in our opinion," said Baldwin.Baldwin says they were told they're past due $35,000 in fees."It came out of nowhere. We pay our rent on time every month, as far as we knew, we were caught up in paying on everything. This was a big surprise for us," said Randall. "We're a small business, and that amount is not something we're sitting on."In a statement to CBS Colorado, the landlord said:"Per the terms of the Lease, the tenant agrees to pay base rent plus its share of operating costs and expenses. The tenant has disputed certain of those costs. We continue to work in good faith with the tenant's legal representation to resolve these issues amicably."As the dispute goes on, Baldwin added that as a small business, they're already working on thin margins."Having this kind of linger over our heads is not a lot of fun for us," said Baldwin. "We just want to take care of these pending issues, so we don't have further concerns.""We are concerned about the whole situation," said Jimarez.The Commissary owners say they're working with their lawyers to take a closer look at the charges and where they're coming from.The Commissary is raising money and crowdsourcing to help cover lawyers' costs and have emergency funding until the dispute is resolved.

title: Former Chicago Bears kicker Robbie Gould resigns as Saint Viator High School's head coach
description: Gould served as head coach for two seasons after taking over the position in 2024.
content: Saint Viator High School announced on Wednesday that its head football coach and former Chicago Bears kicker Robbie Gould has resigned from the position. According to Saint Viator, Gould decided to resign as coach in order to spend more time with his family following the 2026 season."We are grateful to Coach Gould for his leadership, dedication, and commitment to our student-athletes," said Saint Viator President Ryan Aiello. "We appreciate his contributions to Saint Viator football, respect his decision to prioritize his family and wish him all the best."The school says it's already searching for its next head coach who will "strengthen the program, support the recruitment and development of student-athletes, and position the Lions for long-term success.""We are investing in the future of this program, and our student-athletes will remain our top priority. We are focused on finding the right leader to guide the next chapter of Saint Viator football," said Athletic Director Nick Sobieszczyk.Gould played for the Bears for 11 seasons, from 2005 through 2015, when he was released by the team. He appeared in 166 games. He played for one season with the New York Giants, then for the San Francisco 49ers until he retired in December 2023.He was announced as Saint Viator's head coach in December 2024 after a nationwide search, according to the school's president.Saint Viator ended the 2026 season with a 2-7 overall record and a 53-6 win over Chicago De La Salle on Friday, Oct. 16.The school says he will continue to support senior student-athletes with their college recruiting efforts and assist with the leadership transition as needed.The school added that they will provide updates as the search progresses.

title: 2 Staten Island adult day care operators charged in Medicaid fraud probe
description: The arrests came as federal and state investigators executed search warrants at several adult day care locations across the city.
content: A mother and daughter who operate a Staten Island adult day care center were arrested Tuesday and charged with allegedly defrauding Medicaid and long-term care providers, authorities said.The arrests came as federal and state investigators executed search warrants at several adult day care locations across the city.Officials said Yangsim Oum and Juyoung Choe were taken into custody at their adult day care center on Forest Avenue.Oum and Chloe allegedly billed government programs and long-term care companies for services that were never provided, according to Staten Island District Attorney Michael McMahon."They stole upwards of $530,000, billing our government partners and long-term care companies for senior services never provided," McMahon said.Prosecutors allege the fraud occurred between April and August 2026. Oum and Choe were indicted on hundreds of counts, including health care fraud and falsifying business records. Investigators said some claims were submitted for seniors who were deceased or no longer in the United States.A neighboring business owner said the allegations were surprising."I thought they were running a very good business here," Wale Osinuga said. "If they're doing that, that's very bad." Both women were released on their own recognizance.Attorney Yan Katsnelson, who represents Oum, said his client denies the allegations and has retained accountants to review the records."Ms. Oum denies these allegations and any wrongdoing," Katsnelson said in a statement. "My office is investigating the allegations and retaining accountants. Ms. Oum looks forward to having her name cleared."Attorney Mark Fonte, who represents Choe, said his client also denies the charges."My client adamantly denies these charges and refuses to be lumped together with the day care scandals currently in the news,"Fonte said in a statement. "My firm has hired forensic accountants to verify every dollar involved."The U.S. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said it comes one day after officials from their office were in Flushing, Queens speaking with several adult day care center employees and reviewing operations.Kim Brandt, chief operating officer and deputy administrator at CMS, said one operator told officials a nearby center was paying up to $1,000 per person in kickbacks to recruit seniors."When one operator is complaining that the place down the street is outbidding her for seniors, that tells you how this market really works," Brandt said.Federal officials say New York's Medicaid program has become a focus of scrutiny. The FBI said Medicaid spending per enrollee in New York is 40% to 60% higher than the national average.On Wednesday, CMS sent a letter to New York's Medicaid director demanding a corrective action plan within 30 days.The letter states that New York has an obligation to maintain "an effective monitoring system" to detect and prevent fraud."If we're funding criminal organizations, they're using that money to do other things that are bad for us," CMS Administrator Dr.Mehmet Oz said. "It's also clear that the social adult day care program, as it stands right now, is a plague on the state."Earlier Wednesday, before the letter became public, the New York State Health Commissioner Dr. James McDonald was asked at the press conference announcing Staten Island arrests how much of New York state's rising Medicaid costs stem from fraud. He said he didn't have an exact number but said since 2021, the state has recovered more than $15 billion Medicaid dollars through efforts to fight fraud and abuse. "The investigation our administration has worked on has strengthened oversight of Medicaid and taken steps to protect taxpayer dollars," McDonald said.McDonald added that more than 100 cases of suspected fraud have been referred to the New York attorney general's office.McMahon said he believes "countless other adult day care centers" may be engaged in similar schemes and said his office's investigation is ongoing.CBS News New York reached out to Gov. Kathy Hochul's office for comment and had not received a response as of Wednesday evening.

title: Long Island man says phone scammers knew his exact account number, balance due
description: Utilities are warning their customers that criminals have been posing as electric company workers, and they have been armed with information a customer would think only the utility would know.
content: Utilities are warning their customers that criminals have been posing as electric company workers, and they have been armed with information a customer would think only the utility would know. Staffing company founder Steven Weinstein says he's vigilant about spam calls. His guard was up when he got a call Friday from PSEG's phone number. "We are shutting your power off. I'm alerting you it's going to be sometime today," Weinstein said he was told. Weinstein didn't buy it until the caller revealed something that seemed to prove he was legit. "I said 'So how much do I owe?' He knew the exact amount - exact. He knew my account number," Weinstein said. "It matched perfectly." The caller had Weinstein make a $500 cash payment at a 7/11. "The guy's still on the phone, supposedly PSEG. He said 'You're done, I'll send you a confirmation.' And he had my email - no confirmation," Weinstein said.Weinstein called PSEG himself. "I tell the story. She goes, 'I think you were scammed,'" he said. PSEG Long Island has been warning customers about caller ID spoofing, but this incident raises troubling questions about how the caller knew Weinstein's account number and balance due. "We have seen this before," PSEG LI asset protection specialist Robert Vessichelli said. "You have people involved in identity theft that literally drive down streets and open up mailboxes." PSEG Long Island says it has found no evidence its systems were hacked or customer accounts breached. "Sometimes they're just going into your garbage to find out what your bills are," said Vinny Minhas of Corsearch, a company that works to combat online impersonation. Minhas has the following advice. "Don't trust an incoming phone call. Hang up, and make sure you can call yourself," he said. "In 20 seconds, I can replicate any phone number. I can even replicate your loved ones and family members." Weinstein says he's speaking out to warn others because he's not just concerned about the money he lost, it's what else the scammers who called him knew. "That's the worrisome part. That's the part that could make people not sleep at night," Weinstein said. The utility says it will never call and threaten to shut off power in a day if you don't pay. That sense of urgency is exactly what scammers rely on to get your money.

title: Minnesota man who jumped onto runaway school bus credits "Grey's Anatomy" for inspiring his actions
description: A quick-thinking bystander came to the rescue of the students and driver aboard a runaway school bus in Saint Paul, Minnesota.
content: A quick-thinking man who came to the rescue of the students and driver aboard a runaway school bus in Saint Paul, Minnesota, on Monday afternoon credited the television series "Grey's Anatomy" for inspiring his actions. Ebro Ahmed, 27, told CBS News that he leaped into action after noticing the Battle Creek Middle School bus rolling down the street at about 10 mph with its doors wide open and its lights flashing. Ahmed said it caught his attention because the lights of a school bus normally don't flash unless it is at a complete stop. "When he drove past me, it really shook me," Ahmed told CBS News Wednesday. "I was like, 'What is going on?'"As captured on nearby security cameras, Ahmed, who works at a nearby store, sprinted from the sidewalk and jumped onto the moving bus."I saw the bus driver obviously having a medical emergency," Ahmed said. "All I looked at was the gear control and I was trying to put it into park."Ahmed, who told CBS News he had never been behind the wheel of a bus before, said he briefly got confused between the reverse and park selections on the gear shift and accidentally put the bus into reverse. "I started hearing beeps and we were going backwards," Ahmed explained. "And then I said, 'That is not right,' and I threw it into neutral and pulled the [parking] brake." He went on: "When I looked behind me, I saw all of the kids kind of a little scared, crying with their phones out getting ready to call the police." Saint Paul Public Schools said there were 19 students aboard the bus at the time. None of them were hurt in the incident. The district did not provide information on the condition of the driver. "After everything, he was coming to, but he's still kind of out of it," Ahmed said of the driver. "And so I just let him be. Even when the police came, he was already done having his medical emergency. He was getting a little bit better, but I just didn't want to rush and start asking him questions." Ahmed doesn't have any medical experience, but he does credit his favorite TV show, "Grey's Anatomy," for inspiring him. "In 'Grey's Anatomy,' you never see doctors panic. I know it is all acting and stuff, so I just knew to be calm and just think everything through," Ahmed said. The district said a second bus eventually came to pick up the students and continue the route.Asked if he feels like a hero, Ahmed responded, "I feel like any person in my situation would have done the same thing."

title: Six more Orange County parents charged with child endangerment for letting kids ride e-motorcycles
description: Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer charged six more parents with child endangerment charges for allegedly letting their children ride illegal e-motorcycles, marking the latest in a series of similar charges in the area.
content: Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer charged six more parents with child endangerment charges for allegedly letting their children ride illegal e-motorcycles, marking the latest in a series of similar charges in the area. In a news release from the DA's Office, prosecutors said their task force dedicated to cracking down on the illegal activity has resulted in charges against 12 parents. The news comes just a day after similar charges were filed against the parents of a 13-year-old Garden Grove boy who died while riding an e-moto in May. Earlier this year, the DA also filed charges against an Aliso Viejo mother, who faces more than seven years in prison, after her 14-year-old son crashed into an 81-year-old Vietnam veteran, resulting in his death in April. In August, Spitzer's office charged a Yorba Linda father with felony child endangerment for a crash that left his then 12-year-old son with severe injuries after he was hit by a car when he allegedly ran a red light.According to Spitzer's office, injuries connected to e-bikes and e-motos are the "number one reason" children in Orange County end up in the emergency room. In the last four years, injuries have jumped more than 430% across Southern California."We don't want to have to prosecute parents – we want to save kids' lives," said a statement from Spitzer. "When parents refuse to parent and tell their kids 'no' when it comes to riding something that is dangerous and illegal, then I have no choice but to hold parents accountable and file criminal charges. Kids are getting seriously injured and killed and I refuse to allow another child to be hurt or killed because I didn't do everything I could to send a message that these vehicles are not child's play. If you're going to hand the keys to a deadly weapon to your child, then be prepared to face the consequences of your actions."Yorba LindaNew charges include those against Yorba Linda father Alex Li, who allegedly allowed his11-year-old son to ride an e-moto with a 1200-watt motor. In June, Li's son suffered broken bones and an arterial bleed after he collided with a pickup truck. If convicted as charged, Li faces up to one year in Orange County Jail for his misdemeanor count of child endangerment.Spitzer's office charged Yorba Linda mother Maria Roehling with one felony count of child endangerment and an infraction for letting a child under 18 drive a motor vehicle without a license. Her charges come in connection with a May 23 incident during which her 8-year-old son was "speeding on his E-Moto capable of going speeds more than 47 miles per hour when he was hit by a pickup truck in Yorba Linda." If convicted as charged, Roehling faces up to six years in a state prison. "The 9-year-old's Instagram accounts show him doing wheelies on the E-Moto on residential streets and posting about a crash he had on the E-Moto just a few weeks before being hit by the pickup truck," the DA's Office release said.OrangeProsecutors have also charged Dan Rezmives with one misdemeanor count of child endangerment, one misdemeanor count of contributing to the delinquency of a minor and an infraction for allowing a child under 18 to drive a motor vehicle without a license. He faces up to one year in prison if convicted of those charges, which are connected to an incident on March 22, during which an Orange Police Department officer allegedly saw his son riding a Surron Light Bee E-Moto on a public street, while Rezmives was riding a bicycle. "The officer had previously warned Rezmives and the 12-year-old that it was illegal to operate an E-Moto on city streets," the release said. "The Surron, which Rezmives claimed was a Christmas present for his son, is capable of going up to 50 miles per hour."Newport BeachTwo Newport Beach parents, Hulin Guo and Xiaomin Wang, each face up to a year in prison after they were each charged with misdemeanor counts of child endangerment and contributing to the delinquency of a minor, as well as allowing a child under 18 to drive a motor vehicle without a license. Prosecutors said both parents were "repeatedly warned" of the dangers for allowing their 17-year-old son to ride an e-moto, which had been impounded at least twice.The charges stem from a May 9 incident during which the couple's teenage son led Newport Beach police on a pursuit on his Surron E-Moto, "while driving around pedestrians in sidewalks and driving the wrong direction on public streets after refusing to pull over for a traffic stop."Though police ended the chase at the time, they later identified the boy as the e-moto rider after serving a search warrant at their home. Prosecutors also said that on Halloween in 2024, the couple's son, who was 15 at the time, was tackled off his e-moto by an officer after he and another boy were spotted riding recklessly and doing wheelies on residential streets filled with trick-or-treaters."When the boy's parents came to the police station to pick up their son, they were reminded by officers of the dangers of allowing their son to ride the E-Moto," the DA's office said. "On September 23, 2023 an officer found the couple's son hiding in the bushes after he and other children riding E-Motos ignored the officer's amplified commands to stop following reports of reckless riding."Garden GroveTuan Nguyen was charged with one misdemeanor count of child endangerment for an April 8 incident, during which is 13-year-old son allegedly led Garden Grove police on a pursuit while speeding and running red lights while riding a Surron Light Bee X, prosecutors said. At times, the boy also allegedly drove the wrong way in traffic after he refused to pull over for officers. The pursuit ended when the boy crashed the e-moto into a police car, the release said.La PalmaJose De Jesus Ramirez Barragan, 33, was charged with one misdemeanor count of contributing to the delinquency of a minor and faces up to one year in prison after he allegedly allowed his 15-year-old brother to ride his e-motorcycle. "When La Palma police attempted to pull the 15-year-old over, he refused and instead ignored the officer's amplified commands and began a police pursuit while driving 40 miles per hour, running red lights, and nearly crashing into several cars before losing control and crashing into several bushes," the release said. "

title: First case of New World screwworm in U.S. wildlife confirmed in Texas elk, USDA says
description: The New World screwworm was detected in an elk that was discovered on a game ranch in Pecos County, Texas.
content: The first case of New World screwworm in wildlife in the United States has been found in an elk in Texas, the U.S. Department of Agriculture announced Wednesday.The elk was discovered on a game ranch in Pecos County and was reported after being harvested by a hunter, the USDA's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service said.The detection prompted additional wildlife surveillance in the area by the USDA and the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department. The Texas Animal Health Commission will also modify a previously established infested zone.Officials said hunters should watch for signs of infection, including visible maggots in wounds, foul-smelling injuries and animals that appear weak or distressed.Other warning signs include open or enlarging wounds and infestations around an animal's nose, mouth, ears, eyes or genital areas.Officials urged anyone who notices suspicious signs of infestation to report them immediately.The USDA in June confirmed the presence of a flesh-eating New World screwworm in a 3-week-old Texas calf.New World screwworm is a parasitic fly that lays eggs in open wounds or body openings of warm-blooded animals, including livestock and, in rare cases, humans. Once hatched, the larvae feed on living tissue, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.While the USDA says New World screwworm doesn't affect food safety, it can impact meat production.Typically found in South America and parts of the Caribbean, the parasite has spread north into Central America and Mexico in recent years. The first human case in the U.S. was confirmed last year, though the patient recovered and officials found no evidence of further transmission.

title: Video shows police actions leading up to fatal shooting of 1-year-old in car outside Mississippi Walmart
description: The Mississippi attorney general announced the police officer will not be charged in connection with the killing of 1-year-old Kohen Wiley.
content: Body camera and surveillance footage from the fatal police shooting of a 1-year-old boy show the moments several police officers rush out of a Mississippi Walmart and open fire as a driver accused of shoplifting tries to pull out of the parking lot.Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch announced this week that no charges would be filed against the officer who opened fire on the car, striking and killing Kohen Wiley in the June 14 incident."Today, the Office of the Attorney General announced it has completed the review of a June 14, 2026 incident in Senatobia involving one officer with the Senatobia Police Department," Fitch said in a statement. "In this incident, the Attorney General's Office found the use of force was justified."The video shows five law enforcement officers running out of the Walmart after being informed a shoplifter is attempting to drive away. When they reach the silver-colored sedan, they surround it and shout repeatedly to "stop the car." The woman driving the car, a friend of Wiley's mother, instead drives forward and nearly hits one of the officers. It is at this point that one of the officers opens fire on the car.The video, which was posted online by Darkhorse Press, has been verified but not independently obtained by CBS News.Wiley was taken to a local hospital, where he was pronounced dead, according to police. Wiley's mother and her friend reject accusations they were shoplifting, according to their lawyer, Ben Crump. They have not been charged with any crime. The friend was driving the car, while his mother held Wiley in her lap in the vehicle, Crump said."I watched my baby take his first breath and I watched my baby take his last breath," the boy's mother, Vellesiya Wiley, said at a press conference alongside Crump in June. She alleges she held up Kohen to show they had a child in the car and stop them from shooting, according to Crump.The Mississippi Bureau of Investigation immediately launched an investigation into the incident, which then presented the findings to the attorney general."Before anything else, I want to acknowledge the tremendous pain our community is experiencing," Senatobia Mayor Greg Graves said in a statement after the shooting. "The child lost their life. That heartbreaking loss has touched every corner of our community. My thoughts and prayers remain with all those involved. We are committed to transparency throughout this investigation."Crump and Wiley's family called for body camera to be released after the attorney general decided Monday the officer would not be charged."A 1-year-old baby was shot and killed by a police officer, and now the state of Mississippi says that use of force was justified. How can anyone accept that conclusion when Kohen's family and the public still have not been allowed to see the body-camera footage?" Crump said in a statement earlier this week, also noting the Senatobia police chief was recently fired for allegedly using racial slurs. "If the footage supports the state's decision, release it," he added.
