"We will not stop fighting until this family gets the truth."The Mississippi Department of Public Safety said it would officially release the video at the end of the week after the family views it.CBS News reached out to the family's lawyer, Crump, about the video and whether the family has seen it, but he hasn't responded.

title: Boo at the Zoo returns to Philadelphia with extended dates, seasonal activities for families
description: Boo at the Zoo is open every weekend in October at the Philadelphia Zoo.
content: The Philadelphia Zoo is getting into the Halloween spirit with Boo at the Zoo, a family-friendly event featuring trick-or-treating, carnival games and spooky surprises.For the first time, the zoo is hosting the event every weekend in October.Visitors can watch animals enjoy pumpkin treats and take part in twice-daily costume contests. Winners can receive free admission to the zoo for a year."I've taken my son to Boo at the Zoo many, many years and I expect to take my daughter this year," Regla Perez from Olney said.The celebration features 10 trick-or-treat stations, a haunted train ride and the Trick-or-Tree House, an indoor play area normally reserved for zoo members that is open to all guests during the event.Visitors can also explore the Cryptic Creatures exhibit, which celebrates legendary creatures such as the Kraken, Bigfoot and the Jersey Devil."Everybody comes in costume," Dani Hogan, the zoo's director of mission integration, said. "We get to see so many original ideas and we just love seeing people have fun at our favorite place, the Philadelphia Zoo."For 11-year-old Charli Gonzalez, one of the zoo's real-life animals is a favorite."Giraffe," Gonzalez said.The ticketed event is expected to draw up to 10,000 visitors per day.Boo at the Zoo gives families a chance to celebrate Halloween while enjoying the Philadelphia Zoo's animals and seasonal activities.

title: Colorado's Adams 14 School District adds e-buses to its fleet
description: Adams 14 School District added 14 new electric buses to its fleet.
content: Diesel fuel has hit record prices and that's putting the squeeze on public school districts all across the country. Many districts are making the move to electric fleets, not only because of the price of gas, but also because it's a greener option. Adams 14 School District is the latest to unviel new electric buses. The District is adding 14 new e-buses to it's fleet with the help of Xcel Energy and Veregy. Xcel provided nearly $2.4 million through its Electric School Bus (ESB) Program. The district also received a $2.86 million award from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's Clean School Bus Rebate Program. Veregy guided the District through the funding process, designed the infrastructure, and built the project.Adams 14's bus fleet is now fully electric. "We are demonstrating that we invest in our children, that our community is worth investing in," said Dr. Karla Loría , Adams 14 Superintendent.The District said that the change to electric is saving them ore than $77,000 a year in fuel and maintenance. Federal tax credits and utility rebates could give the District another million dollars.

title: Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office $132,000 cowboy hat order draws mixed reactions: "This is all part of the rebranding"
description: The agency says the hats are optional and will come from its existing uniform budget, while some residents question the spending.
content: The Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office has ordered 1,000 cowboy hats for deputies at a total cost of $132,000, drawing mixed reactions from voters and prompting officials to defend the purchase.The hats cost $132 each. The sheriff's office says they are optional and will be paid for from its existing uniform budget.A social media video of deputies putting on a cowboy hat and passing it along drew attention to the new uniform option. Sheriff Rosie Cordero Stutz appears at the end."We've always worn a badge. Now we're adding a sheriff style to it," Cordero Stutz says in the video.Some residents questioned the spending."My paycheck, our taxes, and as a 20-plus-year resident, I'm very disappointed," said Eliseo Abreus, a Miami-Dade voter.Voter Beatriz Morejon Paniaga, speaking in Spanish, acknowledged the cost but said she did not think the hats were a bad idea if they help protect deputies.Stedman Stahl, president of the South Florida Police Benevolent Association, supports the purchase and called it part of the agency's rebranding."This is all part of the rebranding," Stahl said.He also pointed to the practical benefits of a wider brim for deputies who work outdoors, particularly those directing traffic in the heat. Comparing the cowboy hat with a baseball cap, he said the hat gives more coverage."Your ears are going to burn up, your neck will get burned up," he said of wearing a baseball cap in the sun. "This gives you a lot more protection."Stahl also said Cordero Stutz has saved the county money through other uniform decisions. At a news conference with Gov. Ron DeSantis, Cordero Stutz said that keeping the agency's existing brown uniforms, rather than switching to green, avoided about $4.8 million in costs. She said the hats fall within the uniform funds deputies receive each year.In a statement to CBS News Miami, the sheriff's office repeated that the purchase does not require a new budget allocation."The cowboy hat is an optional addition to our deputies' authorized uniforms, not a new budget item," the statement reads. "It is purchased using funds already allocated in our existing uniform budget."The agency said deputies may also choose to wear no hat.

title: Kick the Vape campaign aims to get Philadelphia teens off e-cigarettes
description: The Philadelphia Department of Health kicked off its "Kick the Vape​" campaign in an attempt to curb vaping among teens.
content: A new campaign launched Wednesday in Philadelphia aims to reduce the number of teenagers who use e-cigarettes.The Philadelphia Department of Health kicked off its "Kick the Vape" campaign in an attempt to curb vaping among teens, which it says is up dramatically.Harmony Ellis, a high school senior in Philadelphia, is on a mission to get other students to kick the popular habit of vaping."I didn't like it. I thought, you know, that was really harmful, and I have asthma," Ellis said.The 17-year-old said there is a lot of peer pressure to vape, and the product flavors and designs are enticing for teens."They feel like it's cool, trendy," Ellis said. "They feel like it is something that they just want to do because they see their friends do it and they don't understand the true health risk about it."Research has shown that e-cigarettes that contain nicotine and other chemicals can be addictive and cause lung, brain and heart damage."Smoking nicotine remains the number one cause of preventable death, disease, and disability in the United States," Dr. Samara Jinks-Chang, Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, said. And because Philadelphia leads the country in the number of youngsters who are vaping, the city health department is kicking off a new anti-vaping campaign."The rates of vaping for high school students has risen by 300% between 2017 and 2025," Ryan Coffman with the health department said."The tobacco industry wants youth to be hooked," Philadelphia Health Commissioner Dr. Palak Raval-Nelson said. "That is their model right back in the day with cigarettes, and people are hooked for life. Now, it's vaping, and you're hooked for life." Raval-Nelson said that, in addition to raising awareness about the dangers, the city will also target enforcement. Stores are only allowed to sell approved vaping products and not to minors."End up trying these products," Raval-Nelson said, "and they don't realize the hidden danger and how they're going to get hooked and addicted for life."The new Kick the Vape campaign will have a number of resources to help people stop, and the city will also ramp up enforcement.

title: In Pennsylvania's 1st District, incumbent Brian Fitzpatrick faces tough reelection fight: "All hands on deck"
description: The Fitzpatrick-Harvie race is tightening in the district that includes Bucks County and part of Montgomery County.
content: Pennsylvania has once again become the battleground to watch in a major election. In this year's midterms, the commonwealth is host to four congressional races — for seats currently held by Republicans — that could determine which party controls the U.S. House.Pennsylvania's 1st Congressional District, encompassing all of Bucks County and part of Montgomery County, was thought to be Democrats' longest shot of the four. Now, experts say the race between Republican Brian Fitzpatrick, the incumbent, and Democrat Bob Harvie has tightened."For Republicans, this is all hands on deck," John Kennedy, professor of political science at West Chester University, said. "This is the Democrats' best opportunity since 2018 to try to take this seat."But Kennedy notes the seat will by no means be an easy pickup. Fitzpatrick has represented the politically purple region for nearly a decade, with deep family ties to the area. He, more than other Republican candidates in contested races, has kept President Trump at arm's length. Two years ago, Fitzpatrick won reelection by nearly 13 percentage points, in a district Mr. Trump narrowly lost to Kamala Harris."It makes him a very formidable incumbent," Kennedy said. "One [who is] very difficult to defeat."But like other Republicans, experts say Fitzpatrick will have to deal with a poor national environment for the GOP. Mr. Trump's approval rating was down to 37% in Pennsylvania in an October Quinnipiac University poll. The same data showed Pennsylvania voters favored Democrats on a generic ballot, 54% to 39%. Kennedy also pointed to millions of dollars being pumped into this race on both sides, saying each party sees the seat as in play.Earlier this month, the Cook Political Report moved its rating of this race from "Likely Republican" down to "Lean Republican," still giving the edge to Fitzpatrick.But the GOP, which has controlled Congress for the last two years, is also facing poor marks on the economy. High prices remain the number one concern for most voters who spoke to CBS Philadelphia, regardless of who they're backing."It's the economy," Clint Pagano of Springtown said. "I think that's a hot button for a lot of people, frankly.""Prices. Cost of gas, food, and just about everything," Jane Gable of Riegelsville said."The prices are too high. Gas is too high. Everything's too high," Andrew London said.True to its politically purple nature, we spoke with many voters who said they're backing each of the candidates. But it did appear the national environment was weighing on at least some. Two people who said they backed Fitzpatrick in the past are at least considering voting in the other direction this year."I was a Republican, pretty Republican. But I think I'm leaning more toward Democrat," London said."I'm leaning toward the Democrats. And I generally don't lean that way," Andy Huberegsen of Springtown said. "I think we need something to kind of counterbalance what's going on in the White House right now."Another challenge Kennedy pointed out could be the presence of the governor's race at the top of this year's ticket. Democratic incumbent Josh Shapiro led Republican State Treasurer Stacy Garrity by a wide margin in the October Quinnipiac poll, 59% to 34%.Kennedy said that to win, Fitzpatrick may have to entice some voters who also plan to back Shapiro in November."He's going to need a significant number of ticket-splitters in order to survive this election season," Kennedy said.

title: Pennsylvania's 12th Congressional District features rematch between Summer Lee and James Hayes
description: Incumbent Democrat Summer Lee is facing a challenge from Republican James Hayes in Pennsylvania's 12th Congressional District.
content: Incumbent Democrat Summer Lee is facing a challenge from Republican James Hayes in Pennsylvania's 12th Congressional District.Lee believes that if midterm elections are a referendum on the sitting president, President Trump's economy and the issue of affordability should return her to Congress for the third time. "Prices, affordability is the thing we hear most about," Lee told KDKA-TV in an interview. "Whether that be gas prices or groceries, housing, childcare, healthcare. Poor working people are just being left behind. So, I think that is the referendum."Lee blames those costs on the war in Iran and tariffs and said the Republican majority has sat idly by while the president has abused his power in other areas â taking the administration to task on the Epstein files and what she calls the Justice Department's targeting of political enemies. "In so many ways, norms have been violated that we just have not seen," Lee said. "We've heard about the unprecedented erosion of our checks and balances and presidential overreach."A former member of the Democratic Socialists of America, Lee has gained a national profile during her two terms in Congress as a member of the "Squad," a group of young left-wing Democrats, including Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York. Lee's politics stand in sharp contrast to Hayes, her second-time challenger. He is a pro-business, free-market conservative who said Lee's focus is elsewhere. "Maybe the radicals in Michigan, maybe the radicals in California, maybe she's representing them," Hayes said. "But I want to represent this area."Hayes, a Shadyside businessman with postgraduate degrees from Princeton University and the University of Chicago, said he's forwarding a conservative agenda including strong support of police and things like school choice. And he doesn't shy away from unpopular stances, calling the intervention in Iran necessary. He believes the development of refineries will bring down gas and diesel prices. He also supports the responsible development of data centers, which he said could foster a new artificial intelligence economy in southwestern Pennsylvania. "We need to be creative and think about how we can make this thing happen in a way that everybody prospers," Hayes said.One matter of strong contention is Lee's opposition to the war in Gaza and her condemnation of the policies of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu."She's not only anti-Israel. To me, when you look at her rhetoric, she seems to be anti-white people, which would make her a racist. And she seems to have some issue with the Jewish people in general, which would make her antisemitic," Hayes said.Lee rejects the notion that her stance amounts to antisemitism."The majority of Americans have the perspective that Israel has gone way too far in Gaza," Lee said. "Whether you call it genocide or you point out war crimes or you call it tragedy, the majority of Americans take that stance."But even if Lee loses the support of Jewish voters in Squirrel Hill and the city's 14th Ward, KDKA political analyst Jon Delano said Hayes' bid to unseat Lee is an uphill fight. "It's a tough year for a Republican challenger against an incumbent Democrat," Delano said.

title: Mother sues Maryland officials after daughter's death in foster care, lawyers plan to subpoena Gov. Moore
description: The mother of a foster child who died in the state's care in 2025 is suing the governor and other officials and accusing them of inaction and multiple failures that led to her vulnerable daughter's death.
content: The mother of a foster child who died in state care in 2025 is suing Maryland Gov. Wes Moore and other officials, accusing them of inaction and multiple failures that contributed to her daughter's death.Sixteen-year-old Kanaiyah Ward died in September 2025 at a Marriott Residence Inn just steps from the Johns Hopkins Hospital campus in Baltimore.Her case prompted Maryland to end its practice of housing some foster children in hotels.The lawsuit Kanaiyah Ward died alone in a room on the 11th floor of the Marriott Residence Inn off North Wolfe Street, with pink Benadryl pills scattered by her side along with a suicide note. She was a foster child assigned to live in the hotel by the state, something her mother's legal team told WJZ Investigates was dangerous and never should have happened.Her mother Brooke Ward's new federal lawsuit names the governor and other state leaders and contractors."Every institution with a hand in Kanaiyah's care knew what she needed, and every one of them failed her," the complaint said. The lawsuit noted the teenager's mother "brings this action to hold every one of them accountable for what they did, for what they failed to do, and for the death of a child who had no one else to protect her."DeMaurice Smith is not only a lawyer representing Ward's mother but also a relative. "I'm coming out of retirement as a former federal prosecutor to try this case, and they need to understand that we are coming to get them," Smith told WJZ Investigator Mike Hellgren. "Someone needs to be held accountable for this. Kanaiyah died alone, but this family is in no way, shape, or form alone now."Smith said that because of Ward's mental health challenges, her mother could no longer care for her without help from the state but never expected they would leave her daughter alone with access to medication. "For all the families who face the horrible situation where they have to turn to the state to provide care for their loved one, no one deserves the call that Brooke Ward got," Smith said. The lawsuit detailed how Ward's contracted caretaker was working a 53-hour shift after her co-worker called out sick. It alleged she failed to check on the 16-year-old for more than 4 hours and left medication unsecured despite Ward's documented history as a suicide risk—and was unable to help revive her."The 911 call is absolutely chilling. The woman didn't know CPR. When the dispatcher was trying to walk her through it, she refused. She couldn't find a defibrillator. It's just egregious," said Thomas Doyle, who is also a member of the Ward family's legal team. State responds While the state Department of Human Services (DHS) declined to comment on specific allegations in the lawsuit, the agency told WJZ Investigates it stopped the practice of housing children in hotels shortly after Ward's death.DHS said it also worked to pass legislation to strengthen protections for vulnerable children.Here is the full DHS statement from agency press secretary Lillian Price: "We cannot comment on the specifics of this ongoing litigation due to important privacy protections. In December 2025, the Department released all records that could be legally disclosed, including a finding of child neglect for employees of a one-on-one service provider tasked with caring for Kanaiyah. After dramatically reducing the number of children in hotels over the past three years, DHS ceased the practice entirely in November 2025. We also worked closely with the General Assembly to pass Kanaiyah's Law, which will further strengthen the state's child welfare system. We remain committed to strengthening and reforming child welfare in Maryland and will not rest until every child in our state is safe, thriving in a permanent home, and surrounded by a loving family."Demanding accountability The Ward family's lawyers said the state's actions were too little too late. "When the state assumes the solemn responsibility of placing a child in foster care, that child should be placed in a loving, safe home—not warehoused in a hotel room," said Scott Lerner with Dechert, LLC, who also represents Ward's mother. "Hotels are for guests, and they're not foster homes. They should not be treated as such."Just days before Ward's death, state officials were updated on the number of foster children still living in hotels at a Board of Public Works meeting, but attorneys for the family allege top leaders failed to act. "Had Governor Moore used his emergency powers that he always had on September 10th, she would be alive," said Smith. Ward's lawyers said they can and will subpoena Governor Wes Moore to answer questions about this case under oath. WJZ Investigates reached out to the governor's office for further comment but received no immediate response. The lawsuit also names Marriott International, which franchises the hotel.

title: How the Greater Pittsburgh Community Food Bank plans to attack food insecurity
description: Food insecurity is a year-round reality for a lot of people. So how do we get to the core of it and eliminate it?
content: Every year since 1982, you've been helping us make sure our neighbors in need have a warm Thanksgiving meal. But food insecurity is a year-round reality for a lot of people. So how do we get to the core of it and eliminate it? Or at least take a big bite out of it?The Greater Pittsburgh Community Food Bank has a new plan of attack."We cast a vision going all the way out to 2035 to cut hunger in half," said Charla Irwin-Buncher, the food bank's chief external affairs officer.The food bank is refocusing its mission with a new strategy to better help our neighbors."The food bank is really stepping up into a role of being a convener and a catalyst for change in a different way," said Irwin-Buncher.The new strategy has three main pillars. First is "food for today." "So that's emergency food assistance and being there for folks who need us to be there as part of their regular grocery solution," Irwin-Buncher said. Second is "stability for tomorrow." "So that's connections to other benefits and other resources here locally," she said. "Because it's never just only food insecurity. There are other things going on in the household — either underemployment, childcare issues, transportation, someone in the household might be sick. So really thinking through all those other supports that are available."And the third is "opportunity for a lifetime." "That is really looking at policy changes, workforce development, things that are really going to make an impact on people's lives, so they don't ultimately need the services of the food bank or any of our partners anymore," said Irwin-Buncher.She says it's no secret that it takes a village, but she says it's really time to start putting that into action by being proactive instead of reactive."There are a lot of silos within the human services' safety net," Irwin-Buncher said. "So we're all doing really great work, but we're not necessarily collaborating as much as we could. That's really where the food bank is standing up and taking on a leadership role to convene those groups and bring those people together."She says recent research shows 26% of our neighbors struggle in some way with food insecurity. Of that, she says 15% are deemed food secure but only because they receive help from the government or food banks. The other 11% experience real hunger at some level, either because they're not getting enough resources or none at all.Irwin-Buncher says the impact of that cannot be underestimated."It's really hard to think about your bigger aspirations and your dreams if you're really focused on just getting by day to day," she said.But she says all of this is about way more than food."All of the charitable food in the world will not solve food insecurity," she added.Which is why the food bank has gone back to the drawing board."To be able to catalyze our community to really come together to actually get at the real issue and not just solve someone's immediate need for food," she said. "If we can start moving in this way, maybe we can finally really solve food insecurity. Food insecurity has been a problem in our country for many, many years. So this actually feels like we're making steps to truly make a difference and ultimately reduce the need for our services over the long term. Having a community where people are not struggling with food insecurity and folks have a roof over their head, I think that's something we can all get behind."And the KDKA Turkey Fund is just one of the many ways you can do your part to help the food bank help our neighbors.And here's how you can donate to it. You can go to any PNC Bank. If you donate in person, they'll match all donations, up to $100,000. You can donate online at kdkaturkeyfund.com. You can text "kdturkey" to 50155. Or you can mail a check to P.O. Box Thanks, Pittsburgh, PA 15230.From all of us at KDKA-TV, thank you!

title: Norcross family buys former Trump Plaza site along Atlantic City boardwalk
description: Atlantic City Mayor Marty Small announced that George Norcross and his family bought the former Trump Plaza Hotel and Casino​ site.
author_name: Tom  Dougherty, CBS News Philadelphia  Staff
content: South Jersey power broker George Norcross and his family are now the owners of the former Trump Plaza Hotel and Casino site along the Atlantic City boardwalk.Atlantic City Mayor Marty Small on Wednesday announced that Norcross and his family bought the property.It's unclear what the Norcross family plans to build on the property, but it will not be another casino. Small said no additional casinos are permitted in Atlantic City."The Norcross team's continued investment reflects what I keep saying, that investor confidence in Atlantic City is at an all-time high right now," Small said in a statement. "When successful business leaders like Mr. Norcross choose Atlantic City, it sends a strong message and helps attract additional investors who recognize the opportunities here."The property has been empty since the building was demolished in 2021.

title: 2 Fayette County corrections officers fired, another suspended after alleged inmate beating
description: Two corrections officers have been fired and a third has been suspended for 10 days after the alleged beating of an inmate.
content: Two corrections officers have been fired and a third has been suspended for 10 days after the alleged beating of an inmate left him with "severe" injuries, officials said.Fayette County District Attorney Mike Aubele confirmed the news to KDKA-TV on Wednesday. The inmate, Robert Stimmel, suffered a brain bleed that required treatment at Ruby Memorial Hospital in Morgantown, West Virginia, after the alleged beating. In an interview with KDKA-TV on Oct. 13, Aubele called the man's injuries "severe.""He was days in the hospital for what happened," Aubele said. Officers with the Uniontown Police Department picked Stimmel up on Oct. 8 on a bench warrant related to terroristic threats. The officers brought him to the jail and turned him over to corrections officers. The alleged beating happened during intake, where inmates undress, shower and receive jail clothing. There are no cameras in the Fayette County Jail's intake area. "I would say he suffered severe bodily injury," Aubele said on Oct. 13. It was not immediately known if the corrections officers would face any criminal charges in connection with the incident.

title: U.S. ordering some government staff to depart Saudi Arabia, reducing military footprint in Middle East
description: The U.S. military has also been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to regional threats from the Houthis and direct threats from Iran, CBS News has learned.
content: The U.S. State Department has ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel to depart Saudi Arabia, following an uptick in attacks on the kingdom by Iran-backed Houthi militants.The U.S. military has also been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing regional threats from the Houthis and direct threats from Iran, a U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official told CBS News on Wednesday.The State Department "issued an ordered departure for non-emergency U.S. government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia only," spokesperson Tommy Pigott wrote in a Wednesday X post, pushing back on a report that orders could apply to other Gulf states.CBS News has learned several other embassies adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status, but have not gone on ordered departure, which involves the mandatory evacuation of designated diplomatic staff and accompanying family due to security risks.The restricted operations status, which the department introduced in August amid flare-ups in the war with Iran, allows embassies to reduce staffing and services without fully suspending operations.The decision to draw down personnel in Saudi Arabia comes after U.S. embassies in the kingdom, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and other countries issued warnings over the weekend, urging Americans in the region to exercise caution and prepare for travel disruptions due to Houthi attacks.Why can't Saudi Arabia stop the Houthis' deadly attacks?"Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," Pigott said Wednesday.The Houthis have launched drones and missiles at airports and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, including a strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport earlier this month that killed 12 people and injured more than 300 others. One American was among those killed.The attacks have continued, with a Saudi-led military coalition reporting that it intercepted multiple Houthi drones on Monday and Tuesday.Saudi Arabia's energy ministry said Tuesday that air defenses blocked a drone attack on the country's Shaybah oil field. Two people were killed and two were injured by falling debris, according to the agency, which did not specify who launched the drone.Meanwhile, the Houthis have sought to expand their territorial control in Yemen. The group has controlled a large swath of the country for more than a decade, including the capital of Sanaa.Some Saudi officials have blamed Iran for the conduct of the Houthis, which are aligned with the Islamic Republic. Iran has denied any role in the escalation.The conflict could cause problems beyond Saudi Arabia due to the Houthis' proximity to the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a key maritime chokepoint that a large share of the world's oil flows through. The strait has become more important in recent months due to disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz wrought by the U.S.-Iran war.Ambassador Marwan Ali Noman, political adviser to the Foreign Minister of Yemen, warned in an interview with CBS News on Tuesday that the Houthis could continue their attacks unless confronted."We are fighting on behalf of everyone, because the threat and risk of the Houthis will expand," Noman said, adding that the Yemeni government is seeking international assistance.The United Kingdom has offered support to Saudi Arabia, including defensive air operations. It's not clear whether the Trump administration is also planning to assist Saudi Arabia. President Trump did not rule out strikes on the Houthis after the group's deadly Oct. 10 attack on the Riyadh airport, telling reporters: "We may."Mr. Trump said earlier this month: "We have communication with the Houthis, and we'll see what happens. But what they did was very bad."

title: Cedar Hill's brotherhood fuels Longhorns ahead of rivalry showdown with DeSoto
description: Separated by just minutes along Belt Line Road, the Longhorns and Eagles share a rivalry built on pride, brotherhood, and tradition.
content: At Cedar Hill High School, there's a different level of pride in putting on that red uniform, and it shows on the football field."We're about Cedar Hill," Longhorn's quarterback Jaiden Mitchell said. "We die; we bleed Cedar Hill. We go through the boot camp. We go through everything in the offseason. We build that bond; we build that brotherhood.""Brotherhood is what we really just got to work on," Cedar Hill safety Jeremiah Hobbs said. "That's really the standard. As long as we keep the brotherhood, we make everything strive better."This week, the Longhorns take on a familiar foe in the DeSoto Eagles, considered one of the great rivalries in DFW high school football."They've got some great football players," Cedar Hill coach Brice Musgrove said. "We're just going to have to pay hard, and we're going to let the scoreboard take care of itself. 6 seconds of explosion every play."To understand how big this rivalry is, look no further than Belt Line Road. If you stop at the intersection of Belt Line and N Duncanville, Longhorn Stadium is just 10 minutes away. Right on the other side is Desoto, Texas, where Eagle Stadium is only seven minutes away. It doesn't matter what the records or classifications are. This game is and always will be the Battle of Belt Line."I've been around this rivalry since I was a little boy," Mitchell said. "Now that I'm finally able to be on the field and actually be able to play, it's a blessing."The Longhorns have captured three state championships and made their most recent appearance in the title game in 2020.Despite some adversity, this current generation is determined to live up to the expectations set by teams of the past."When you go to the local Walmart, the local grocery store, and you have on Cedar Hill attire...people know your name," Musgrove said. "It's just been a hub for football. You've had somewhat of a downfall in recent years, just as far as the standard that had been set in the years prior. But we're definitely trying to take an opportunity to rebuild the culture.""We're working," Mitchell said. "We're going to prove everybody wrong. Everybody that's not on our back...we're working."

title: DeSoto football learned hard lesson from 0-2 start. Now the Eagles are having fun again
description: After opening with two losses, the defending Class 6A Division II state champions say a humbling start helped them rediscover the intensity, consistency, and joy that fueled last year's title run.
content: The DeSoto Eagles are an example of a team that prepares the way they play.Intense, physical, fast, but it all culminates into one thing."Having fun..you got to have fun," DeSoto head coach Claude Mathis said. "That's what we weren't having at first, and they're having a lot of fun right now with consistency. How we practice is how we take it to the field, and they get it."The Eagles are the defending 6A Division II state champions, but they've faced plenty of adversity this season.Much like their championship run a year ago, DeSoto started 0-2, falling to St. Thomas Aquinas and Allen."We got a lot of players with a lot of offers and stars. and felt like based on who we had on our team, plus the name Desoto, that we were just going to come in and beat everybody," Desoto linebacker Quentin Billings said. "I felt like those two losses really taught us to play the game. It humbled us.""I kind of just had to tell them that we've been here before," DeSoto quarterback/running back SaRod Baker said. "We were here last year, and in December, we were holding up the state championship."Since that 0-2 start, DeSoto has been nothing short of dominant. The Eagles have been clicking on both sides of the ball, and they look poised for another state title run. But Mathis says success isn't automatic. It starts and ends with how they prepare."We always say to each other....this is hard," Mathis said. "Friday nights, Thursday nights and Saturday is easy. If we can't do it out here, we can't do it on Saturdays, we can't do it on a Friday or Thursday. They understand now that this is their own legacy. They got to build their own legacy.""This year's team is a new team just like last year's team is a new team," Desoto safety Rickshown Hanks Jr. said. "Majority of the guys this year are not the same guys. We have to all just gel together and just buy in...not listening to what the outsiders say.""We're coming along, getting better and better every week," Baker said. "That's all you can ask for. Nobody is perfect, so all you can ask for is to get 1 percent better every day."

title: Head coach Mike Locksley to depart Maryland after 2-5 start to season
description: Head coach Mike Locksley is departing the University of Maryland after the team got off to a 2-5 start to the 2026 season.
content: Head coach Mike Locksley is departing the University of Maryland after the team got off to a 2-5 start to the 2026 season. The decision came four days after the Terrapins lost at home to Rutgers for their fifth straight defeat. Locksley began as head coach at Maryland during the 2019 season. "In a mutual decision, Maryland Athletics announced that Michael Locksley is stepping down as the head coach of the football program, effective immediately. Aazaar Abdul-Rahim has been named interim head coach," said a statement issued by the University of Maryland on Wednesday. "Following thoughtful conversations with Coach Locksley, we agreed that a coaching change was in the best interest of Coach Locksley and the Maryland football program," said Jim Smith, Barry P. Gossett Director of Athletics. Locksley was seven games into his eighth season at the helm. He led the Terps to three straight bowl victories â a first for the program â from 2021-23, but since then Maryland is 10-21 in two-plus seasons. Locksley already was under pressure to reverse that decline. Then he dropped back-to-back home games to teams with first-year coaches â Virginia Tech and UCLA â before falling to Nebraska and Ohio State on the road.On Saturday, Maryland hosted the Scarlet Knights for homecoming â with plenty of empty seats â and blew a 10-point halftime lead in a 37-30 loss. It was Rutgers' first win of the season over an Football Bowl Subdivision team.Locksley went 38-49 during this stint at Maryland and just 16-47 in Big Ten play. The Terps had a 20-game winning streak against nonconference opponents snapped when they lost to Virginia Tech.Maryland hired Locksley in December 2018, about a month after coach DJ Durkin was fired in the aftermath of offensive lineman Jordan McNair's death of heatstroke in an offseason workout."On behalf of the University of Maryland, I want to thank Michael for his dedication to our football program and the genuine care he showed our student-athletes," Smith added. "Michael represented Maryland with pride, strengthened our connection throughout the state and the region, and made a lasting impact on the young men he coached. We are grateful to Michael, Kia, and his family for everything they have contributed to our university."Locksley's replacement, Abdul-Rahim, is a Washington, D.C., native in his third season of his second stint with the Terrapins. He has served as co-defensive coordinator, associate head coach of the defense and the team's cornerbacks coach since 2024. He previously coached at Maryland from 2016-18. He played three seasons at San Diego State, graduating in 1998.

title: Broadway musical SIX returns to the Hippodrome in Baltimore
description: The Broadway musical was last at the Hippodrome in 2023.
content: King Henry VIII's wives are coming to Baltimore with the return of the show SIX.It's the first stop of a national tour that includes stops in Detroit, Michigan, and San Francisco, California.The Broadway musical was last at the Hippodrome in 2023. SIX won two Tony Awards in 2022 for Best Original Score and Best Costume Design of a Musical.The show runs from Oct. 25 to Nov. 1.SIX is a modern retelling of the lives of each of King Henry VIII's wives.They form a girl group and stage a contest to see who suffered the most under their shared husband.The winner of that contest becomes the group's leader.The cast includes Christina Jones as Catherine of Aragon, Brittany Smithson as Anne Boleyn, Melina Savannah Cruz as Jane Seymour, Shelby Griswold as Anna of Cleves, Thabitha Moruthane as Katherine Howard, and Nina Anne Nelson as Catherine Parr."It's a 90 minute marathon, I will say, [but] I love to perform," Nelson said. "From start to finish, we get to have fun on stage together."While there is a competition, the cast said the show is really about empowerment and how each queen really owns their story."All of their lives are basically centered around Henry, this is their opportunity to tell the world this is who I am," said Moruthane.

title: Dodgers say Shohei Ohtani's knee and biceps injuries require offseason rest, not surgery
description: Shohei Ohtani needs offseason rest, not surgery, for knee and biceps injuries that led to his worst offensive numbers since he joined the Los Angeles Dodgers.
content: Shohei Ohtani needs offseason rest, not surgery, for knee and biceps injuries that led to his worst offensive numbers since he joined the Los Angeles Dodgers before the 2024 season."It was just an unfortunate game of whack-a-mole," Andrew Friedman, president of baseball operations, said Wednesday. "The knee got to a better spot, and then just kind of the biceps area was bothering him. Some of that would calm down for some period, some of that would get re-irritated. It was just a lot of different things he was trying to contend with at once."Ohtani and the Dodgers are equally enthused about him returning to two-way duties next season. What both sides need to figure out is how to keep him healthy while hitting and pitching into October."I'm not only expecting him to pitch," Friedman said, "we're excited about him pitching."Ohtani didn't pitch after July 3 this year due to injuries that also affected his hitting. He had his worst offensive numbers since joining the Dodgers in December 2023, and his 30 home runs were his fewest since 2019 with the Los Angeles Angels. His three-run drive in Game 4 of the National League Championship Series against Milwaukee snapped a 25-game homerless streak.Ohtani turns 33 next July and has undergone two Tommy John surgeries on his right elbow during his MLB career. Friedman said how to better manage Ohtani's two-way workload for a potential full season next year had yet to be discussed since the season ended last week with a four-game sweep at the hands of the Brewers in the NLCS."I expect us to throw our heads together and figure out both in the batter's box, on the mound, just how we marry all that together to have him impact us as much as he can during the regular season and then also be in a really good spot going into October," Friedman said.

title: Costumes set the mood for "Disney's Beauty & the Beast"
description: CBS Colorado's Dillon Thomas got a behind the scenes look at the iconic costumes of "Disney's Beauty & the Beast."
content: The classic Disney story of "Beauty and the Beast" is taking the stage at the Denver Center for the Performing Arts, bringing its beloved characters to life through elaborate costumes, including the iconic gold dress worn by Belle.Among the most memorable costumes is the formal outfit worn by the Beast near the end of the musical, as his character transforms both physically and emotionally."When I put on this outfit, I actually really start to feel how much of his character has actually developed throughout the entire show," said Fergie Philippe, who plays the Beast.Philippe said the costume helps convey the character's emotional journey as the story unfolds."This is my favorite look in the show," Philippe said. "We really get to see the Beast transformation from not only from Beast to human, but we also get to see his emotional arc kind of get laid out."The wardrobe also helps communicate the personalities and stories of the musical's other characters, from the villagers to the enchanted objects.Maya Patrick, who works in the production's wardrobe department, said each character has a distinct look designed to help bring the story to life."I wish I could show you all of these. All of the different villagers have such unique, specific looks that bring them all to life in a different way," Patrick said.But one costume that continues to draw attention from audiences is Belle's iconic gold dress.Patrick said that the audience's reaction when Belle first appears in the gown is a highlight for the wardrobe team."One of my favorites is when she does the reveal and the audience just gasps or applauds and it's like, 'Ah, yes, our work is shining,'" Patrick said.The dress sparkles on stage inspiring audience members to ask whether the gown contains LED lights. Patrick has an answer for that."There are not. There are about 30,000 rhinestones, though.""Beauty and the Beast" plays the Denver Center for the Performing Arts through Nov. 7. For ticket information, click here. CBS Colorado is a proud partner of the DCPA.

title: Woodland police dispute DHS account of ICE agent's collision with pedestrian
description: The Woodland Police Department is disputing the Department of Homeland Security's account of a collision involving an ICE vehicle and a pedestrian, saying video evidence contradicts claims made by the federal agency.
content: The Woodland Police Department is disputing the U.S. Department of Homeland Security's account of a collision involving an Immigration and Customs Enforcement vehicle and a pedestrian, saying video evidence contradicts claims made by the federal agency.In a statement Wednesday, Woodland police said investigators reviewing footage of the Oct. 20 incident determined the pedestrian, Antonio Moreida, did not jump onto the hood of the ICE vehicle or slide off it, contradicting DHS' description of what happened.The department said the video shows the pedestrian was struck by a vehicle driven by an ICE agent. Investigators also determined the driver applied the brakes before the collision."We believe our community deserves accurate, factual information about this incident, particularly given the concerns it has raised," the department said.One of the various angles of footage of the incident was taken from a home Ring camera. CBS News Sacramento obtained and reviewed the footage, which corroborates what Woodland police said.The police department's statement marks a direct rebuttal to DHS, which said Wednesday, "An agitator jumped onto the hood of an ICE vehicle and the officer driving applied the brakes. The agitator slid off the hood. ICE immediately contacted EMS and the Woodland Police Department. Flopping for the camera is dangerous, especially when it interferes with a federal law enforcement operation." Democratic U.S. House Rep. Mike Thompson, whose district includes Woodland, also sharply criticized the DHS statement as a lie."It's just nonsense," Thompson said. "You know it, and I know it. The local police know it. Our community knows it, and they're not going to get away with lying to our community."Moreida also offered his own response to the DHS, saying its statement doesn't describe what happened "whatsoever.""DHS definitely has a way of framing things to their benefit," Moreida said.Moreida, a volunteer with immigrant advocacy organization NorCal Resist, told CBS News Sacramento that he went to the neighborhood after hearing reports of an ICE operation, intending to document the activity and alert nearby residents.He said he began recording people he believed were federal immigration officers and asked them to identify themselves.CBS News Sacramento obtained footage recorded by Moreida that shows the front end of the vehicle striking him as he recorded in the street."I took the corner of the car to the chest," Moreida told the station. "When I first hit the ground, I had the wind knocked out of me. That was my first reaction."Moreida said that while he was in the hospital, a family member took a photo they said shows an ICE vehicle parked outside his home across town from where the collision happened."Later, when he was fortunate to come home from the hospital, this car was across the street, staking out his house," Woodland Mayor Tom Stallard said. "I mean, what does that sound like to you?"CBS News Sacramento reached back out to the DHS for a response to Moreida and the mayor's claim but has not heard back.Woodland police said it is conducting an active criminal investigation into the collision and would forward that investigation to the Yolo County District Attorney's Office once complete.

title: Driver charged with murder after fatal crash at Ventura County Costco gas pumps
description: A driver has been charged with murder after a crash near Costco gas pumps in Camarillo that left a 28-year-old man dead on Tuesday.
content: A driver has been charged with murder after a crash near Costco gas pumps in Camarillo that left a 28-year-old man dead on Tuesday. In a news release, the Ventura County Sheriff's Office said deputies were called to the Costco parking lot, in the 400 block of W. Ventura Boulevard, after learning that a man had been struck by a car. Upon arrival, witnesses pointed deputies to the suspect, 35-year-old Agoura Hills resident Abba Bryski, who was detained at the scene. The victim of the crash, only identified as a man from Modesto, was pronounced dead after being taken to a nearby hospital, deputies said. "Detectives with the Sheriff's Major Crimes Bureau assumed responsibility for the investigation and are actively investigating the incident as a homicide," the news release said.Bryski was booked at the Ventura County Jail on one count of murder, according to the news release. Investigators did not provide further details on the circumstances leading up to the crash or Bryski's charge. "The cause and manner of the death will be determined by the Ventura County Medical Examiner's Office," deputies said. "This investigation is ongoing."Anyone who knows more was urged to contact Detective Erik Hernandez at 805-384-4729 or Detective Gerardo Cruz at 805-384-4726.

title: Former NYC building commissioner traded favors for cash, Mets tickets, prosecutors say
description: Prosecutors played recorded phone calls and displayed text messages on Wednesday as they argued former New York City Buildings Commissioner Eric Ulrich allegedly exchanged political favors for cash, Mets tickets and other benefits.
content: Prosecutors played recorded phone calls and displayed text messages on Wednesday as they argued former New York City Buildings Commissioner Eric Ulrich allegedly exchanged political favors for cash, Mets tickets and other benefits.Ulrich, 41, is accused of accepting more than $150,000 in bribes in exchange for political favors while serving as a City Council member, senior adviser to Mayor Eric Adams and later as buildings commissioner.In one recorded phone call played in court, Ulrich is heard discussing someone seeking a city job."Not everything has a price attached to it," Ulrich said.Prosecutors argue some of Ulrich's political influence did come with a price. They displayed surveillance photos from their investigation and presented text message exchanges they say show Ulrich asking for and receiving money.In one message shown in court, a person told Ulrich he would help him whenever he needed."Even if you wanted to say no you wouldn't do it, because we are like family. Love you," the message read.Prosecutors allege Ulrich promised to steer contracts and expedite inspections for several Queens business owners in exchange for cash and other benefits.One of his co-defendants, Michael Mazzio, is accused of providing Mets season tickets to Ulrich. Prosecutors allege Ulrich helped Mazzio's daughter obtain a higher-paying city job and also attempted to assist Mazzio, who operates a Brooklyn towing company, with licensing issues.Ulrich's defense attorney argued the former commissioner was struggling with alcoholism and gambling and borrowed money from friends and others during that period. But the defense maintains the payments were loans, not bribes.Mazzio's attorney said the two men are longtime friends and contends their actions were legal.Brothers Anthony and Joseph Livreri pleaded guilty last month to giving Ulrich cash in exchange for lifting a vacate order on a bakery.Ulrich and Mazzio have pleaded not guilty. When leaving court, Ulrich declined to comment on the evidence presented.The case is being heard as a bench trial, meaning a judge, not a jury, will decide the outcome. The trial is expected to last about a month.

title: St. Paul council members pass three part plan to combat homelessness
description: Residents living near the Shepard Road encampment say they've noticed the increase in activity in the area since August.
content: When St. Paul, Minnesota, cleared the city's largest homeless encampment at Pig's Eye Park this summer, officials cited serious safety concerns, including fires, sexual assaults and fatal drug overdoses.But the closure did not end homelessness. Instead, it shifted it.More than 400 people are now living in an encampment along Shepard Road, where the population has surged since the Pig's Eye closure.St. Paul City Council members say they don't think shuffling around homeless camp residents is a solution."Instead of a plan that connected neighbors to housing, we've been told to fear our neighbors who've turned to living in tents because they cannot afford their homes," Council Member Hwa Jeong Kim said.Residents living near the Shepard Road encampment say they've noticed the increase in activity in the area since August.One resident who lives in the apartments nearby told WCCO that incidents, including fires, have become more common. He also said thieves stole the wheels from his vehicle a few days ago.With winter approaching, the St. Paul City Council has approved a new approach to managing homeless encampments.The plan includes a 60-day outreach period before an encampment can be closed, unless there is an immediate threat to public safety. It also calls for a temporary indoor shelter for six months this winter, and development of a permanent shelter modeled after Avivo Village in Minneapolis."We must expand access to shelter, examine city policies that displace families and take full responsibility for what happens after we tell someone to leave," Council Member Anika Bowie said.A legislative aide to Kim said the temporary shelter and efforts to connect people with housing alone could cost more than $2 million. The city would need financial support from county and state partners to make the plan a reality.Whether people living outdoors will accept those options remains an open question."You've got people that are homeless, people that are mentally ill," said Michael, who lives at the Shepard Road camp. "You've got all kinds of issues from people being out here. It's not just one group. It's a bunch of different groups, and at least if you're out here or somewhere like this, you can separate yourself a little bit."A spokesperson for Mayor Kaohly Her shared this statement:"We share the goal of moving people from encampments into safe and stable housing. Our administration is looking into the viability and affordability of these proposals. Every spending choice we make comes at the expense of other priorities and essential services our residents depend on. We continue to plan for the coordinated transition of the encampments at Randolph and l'Orient, with outreach teams connecting each individual at the encampment to shelter, housing, and services. I remain committed to bringing all levels of government and partners to the table to address this systemic problem."

title: Austin Lemieux and Neal Shipley grouped together for PGA Tour event in Bermuda
description: Two popular names with deep ties to the Pittsburgh region will be grouped together at the Butterfield Bermuda Championship.
content: Two popular names with deep ties to the Pittsburgh region will be grouped this week at the PGA Tour's event in Bermuda. The Butterfield Bermuda Championship will get underway on Thursday at the Port Royal Golf Course in Bermuda, and when the tournament begins, Neal Shipley will be playing alongside Austin Lemieux, the son of former Pittsburgh Penguins owner Mario Lemieux.Shipley, 25, a native of Mt. Lebanon, has made a name for himself in the golf world over the past few years after making a meteoric rise to popularity in 2024 when he earned low amateur honors at both the Masters and the U.S. Open. Since then, Shipley won two events on the Korn Ferry Tour and has earned his PGA Tour card. Earlier this year, Shipley made history when he made the first-ever hole-in-one in the TGL, an indoor, professional golf league based out of Florida.Lemieux, 30, is making his PGA Tour debut this week after shooting a 66, the number synonymous with his father's illustrious NHL career, in a qualifying event in Florida last week.Following in his father's footsteps, Lemieux initially took up hockey, playing at the collegiate level at Arizona State University. He is now pursuing a career in the game of golf. "I'm already pretty nervous, a little bit," Lemieux said Monday. "Everyone gets nerves, and I'm just trying to deal with them as best as I can."The two Pittsburgh-area natives will be joined in their group by Luke Clanton, who was a TGL teammate of Shipley. The trio is set to tee off at 7:52 a.m. Thursday.

title: Farmington farm installs ramp to make hayride accessible to people who use wheelchairs
description: Pumpkins, corn mazes, and hayrides are fall traditions for many Minnesotans. But for people who use wheelchairs, those experiences can be out of reach.
content: Pumpkins, corn mazes, and hayrides are fall traditions for many Minnesotans. But for people who use wheelchairs, those experiences can be out of reach. A new ramp at Crazy Legs Farm is helping people with mobility challenges enjoy a fall tradition that can otherwise be difficult to access: a hayride.Living Well Disability Services brought residents, families and staff together at the Farmington farm for an afternoon of fall activities, made more accessible with help from local partners.Jenny Ackerley, a program manager at Living Well Disability Services, said uneven terrain can make it difficult for people who use wheelchairs or have trouble walking to participate in outdoor activities."It's not often that people, especially in wheelchairs, or those that have difficulty walking, can navigate these kind of uneven, rocky grounds," Ackerley said.The event came together with help from the KDK Foundation, founded by Dennis Klose, whose daughter receives care at Living Well.The foundation partnered with Crazy Legs Farm to make the experience possible, while Dakota Lumber donated materials for the ramp.Klose said helping make experiences like this accessible aligns with the foundation's mission."Oh, it's truly amazing. I mean, it is written in part of our mission statement is to make dreams a reality," Klose said.He praised the Farmington community for its generosity and willingness to help bring the project to life."It's just amazing what this community can and will do. And all you have to do is ask them," Klose said.For Living Well Disability Services, the event was about more than enjoying the fall season. Ackerley said creating opportunities for people to participate helps foster a sense of belonging."We really value belonging, and it's important that everybody gets to come together and feel valued," Ackerley said.

title: San Jose begins installing speed cameras along Saratoga Avenue
description: San Jose is installing 33 automated speed cameras across the city as officials look for ways to reduce dangerous driving and prevent traffic fatalities.
content: San Jose is installing 33 automated speed cameras across the city as officials look for ways to reduce dangerous driving and prevent traffic fatalities. But as the cameras go up, residents have mixed reactions to the new enforcement effort.One of the cameras now stands along Saratoga Avenue, near the site of a motorcycle crash that killed a woman several weeks ago. Three of the first four cameras installed in San Jose are along Saratoga Avenue, where some residents say speeding has long been a concern."Dude, cars are just zooming by, shaking my car. It's crazy," said Brandon, a San Jose resident who works at a coffee shop near Saratoga Avenue and Latimer Avenue.Brandon said he believes something needs to be done to address the problem."Something needs to happen," he said.Asked why he thinks speeding is so common in the area, Brandon said, "I don't know, like everyone around here just wants to drive fast and has somewhere to be, I guess."At Saratoga Avenue and Williams Road, another newly installed camera sits near a preschool. Himi Pearl, a San Jose resident and teacher who works nearby, supports the effort, saying the cameras could encourage drivers to follow traffic rules and drive safely."I think it's necessary to put [them] on to make sure we are following our rules and be safe," Pearl said.Still, she is unsure how effective the cameras will be."Um, no, I'm not sure. I'm looking forward to seeing how the camera will help people," she said.Not everyone is welcoming the change. On Curtner Avenue, resident Myra said she was surprised when crews installed a speed camera near her front porch. She initially thought the workers were making a different kind of improvement."I thought they were doing something with a light bulb, and then my son pulled up from work and said it's a camera," Myra said.She said she would have appreciated advance notice."A knock on the door or a letter would have been nice, saying, 'Hey, we're posting this,'" she said.The cameras are part of a five-year pilot program authorized under California's AB 645, which allows select cities to use automated speed enforcement to address dangerous driving.San Jose has recorded 41 traffic fatalities this year, underscoring the challenge facing city officials as they look for ways to make streets safer.December 6 is when warning period begins. February 4 is when they start actually fining drivers.

title: Mexican man convicted after using dead infant's identity for more than 40 years, prosecutors say
description: Vidal Blanco-Blas, 62, obtained a U.S. passport and other government documents under the stolen name and has a history of drug convictions.
content: A Mexican man who used a deceased American infant's identity for more than 40 years, obtaining a U.S. passport and committing multiple drug offenses under the stolen name, has been convicted of federal identity theft and passport fraud, prosecutors said.Vidal Blanco-Blas, 62, was convicted Friday in federal court in Dallas of making false statements on a U.S. passport application and aggravated identity theft, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Texas."Exploiting the identity of a deceased American infant to sneak into the U.S and conceal a decades-long life of crime and fraud is an appalling act that undermines the integrity of our immigration system and erodes trust in our nation's most vital security documents," said U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould.In a news release, prosecutors said Blanco-Blas assumed the identity of Julio Cesar Torres, an American citizen who died in Mexico at about 3 months old, and used the stolen name for more than four decades after entering the U.S.Under the false identity, Blanco-Blas obtained a Social Security number, a Texas driver's license, a voter registration card, and a U.S. passport, authorities said.Witnesses testified that Blanco-Blas instructed his daughter to pretend he was her uncle, Julio Cesar Torres, when they were in public.Prosecutors said the deception even extended to his own family. Witnesses testified that Blanco-Blas told his daughter to pretend he was her uncle, Julio Cesar Torres, whenever they were in public.Blanco-Blas also had a lengthy criminal record under the stolen name. According to prosecutors, he previously received an 84-month prison sentence for conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute a controlled substance, a 120-month sentence for marijuana possession, and a 21-month sentence for possession with intent to distribute up to 30 kilograms of marijuana.He now faces up to 12 years in federal prison. Sentencing is scheduled for March 22, 2027, before U.S. District Judge Sam A. Lindsay.CBS News Texas will provide updates as more information becomes available.

title: Mariah Fredericks on her latest New York City novel, "Murder on 34th Street"
description: Mariah Fredericks' new fictional mystery imagines a murder leading up to the Thanksgiving Day Parade.
content: Please consider joining our Facebook group by CLICKING HERE. Find out more about the books below.Listen to the Club Calvi Podcast by CLICKING HERE November is around the corner, and a new mystery is adding a sinister twist to a holiday tradition. Mary Calvi talked to author Mariah Fredericks about her new historical novel "Murder on 34th Street." In the book, it's the 1930s and a young assistant tries to save Santa from a threat at the Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade, but she still discovers a body on the float. Fredericks told Mary the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is one of the iconic events in the New York City calendar and that she has always loved it. "You have 100-foot floats filled with gas, tons of kids from warm states balancing tubas and trumpets and bass drums, and the hundreds of thousands of people who come to watch all over the world," Fredericks said. "Everything has to go perfectly. And it just seemed like a terrific scenario that really belonged in a book." Mary asked Fredericks about the book's dedication: "To Nina and Julie 70's kids sitting on a curb watching the parade go by." "When I was, I think, 10, my best friend, Nina, lived on Central Park West," Fredericks remembered. "I lived about four blocks from the parade route. [Nina] said, my parents say if my older sister Julie comes with us, we can go watch the parade in person. And I remember getting up early and finding a spot on the curb. This was in the 1970s, and I remember the amazing sight of these hundred-foot characters that I love floating overhead, and you felt like you were in the center of the world." The main character in "Murder on 34th Street" is Grace, an assistant who's the person employees turn to when there's a problem. "The day before the parade, a real doozy lands on her desk when Harry Gardner, playing Santa, says, 'I've received a note that says Santa won't live to see Christmas,'" Fredericks said. "So Grace has to leap into action to protect not just Harry and Santa Claus, but the Macy's holiday shopping season." With Thanksgiving approaching, Fredericks says the parade is part of her plans. "I am going to try and sneak out early and see if I can find a spot on the curb," Fredericks says. "But if there is no pavement, I'll definitely be watching at home."Club Calvi books may contain adult themes. _______________________________________________________________________________________ "Murder on 34th Street" by Maria Fredericks From the publisher: New York, 1932. Grace Verlander is the secret beating heart of Macy's. She's the "assistant to the assistant to the someone who's in charge", the go-to person for keeping everything running smoothly behind-the-scenes at the famous, bustling store.It's not every day you get a letter from Santa Claus, but three days before the Macy's annual Thanksgiving Day Parade, Grace arrives at work to find a note from the store Santa Claus in her locker: someone has sent him a death threat. Shocked, Grace promises to look into it and speaks to the store detective about the parade's security, confident that they've found a solution that will keep everyone safe. But on the day of the parade, despite all their precautions, a dead body is found on one of the floats.Using her wits and deep knowledge of the ways of the place, Grace is determined to find the killer and seek justice—not just for the dead man, but to save the reputation of this iconic store from ruin.Mariah Fredericks lives in New York CityCLICK HERE to read an excerpt "Murder on 34th Street" by Mariah Fredericks (ThriftBooks) $23_________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Excerpt: "Murder on 34th Street" by Mariah Fredericks It is blue skies and a balmy 30 degrees. There are thousands of Macy's employees crowding the streets, starting at 110th and Amsterdam. Facing them from the other side of the cordon, like someone on the wrong end of a firing squad, is yours truly. Every last one of my colleagues would happily skin me alive and wear my hide for warmth. Only Jerry the Pig seems content. Sixty feet high, he bobs overhead, patiently awaiting the whistle.Which will come the moment I hear from Detective Halsey that Santa's sleigh is unsabotaged and safe to ride. As I step from side to side, wondering what is taking the good detective so long, one of Felix's minders growls, "When do we get to move?""Soon!" I trill."What's the holdup?" calls Lil, shivering among her fellow lollipop gals.Andy the Alligator hisses, the sound provided by a recording of bacon frying in a pan. "The alligator." I point. "It's passing gas. Anyone got an antacid?"Stony faces all around. Felix looms. He has it in for me, I can tell.I hope he gets snagged on the Empire State Building."Miss Verlander!" Helen Schonbrun charges into view, resplendent in sable coat. "What is the problem?""Final checks on Santa's float. Making sure our ho ho hos are in order."I smile, inviting Helen to do the same. She does not."If you persist in this tinkering," she warns, "I will not be held responsible.""I understand." And I do. Helen is adept at shifting blame, and a wise woman realizes when she is outgunned. Tossing a hasty "Excuse me" at her and the mutinous masses, I hurry down the line, past Andy and Jerry the Pig, past the regimental marching band and the wooden cannon mounted on a wagon that will shoot lucky balloons into the crowds, past a grinning Fritz the Dachshund and Willie Red Bird, with a forty-foot wingspan, and finally to Santa's float, which stands at the end of the parade line, set back behind a rope and protected by the most fearsome balloon of all, the Terrible Tiger, a colossus of bold stripes and big teeth. Ducking under the rope, I see Stu and Stockroom Moe seated at the front of the float in the driver's seat. Stu may have worked rodeo, but Moe drove a milk wagon for years, and the horses, Jingle and Belle, seem content.Crossing around the side, I take a moment of pleasure in Raymond's creation. Depictions of St. Nick's domain tend toward the jolly olde or outright bizarre—one year's Santa Blimp, for example. But Raymond's float conjures a child's dream of Christmas morning, if the child had just ridden the Cyclone and was feeling a bit woozy. In the center is Santa's workshop, where a dizzying array of toys loops through, around, and above the darling little building. Teddy bears and trains, baseballs and dolls dance through the air into Santa's enormous sack, which sits at Santa's feet, or rather Harry's, who is perched high on the throne at the back of the float, magnificent in white whiskers and red velvet. Thankfully, someone has laid a blanket over his legs to keep out the cold. In addition, the workshop serves as a warmth station, with more blankets and probably a flask of something. There is also a wee door with a wee window facing Harry, which means Halsey can keep an eye on him even from inside the workshop.At the moment, the good detective is strutting around the float, kicking the wheels and pounding the floorboards. Raymond follows close behind, rage barely held in check. I have the sinking feeling Halsey is one of those people who puts more effort into looking like he's doing his job rather than actually doing it.Stepping in front of him, I say, "All ready to go, Detective?" Halsey has been sniffing at the underside of the float. Now he straightens. "Security takes time, Miss Verlander. Patience and time.""Why is there an elf?" Raymond demands.To Raymond, I say, "I'll explain . . ." Then, to Halsey, "You've had men stationed by the float all night, haven't you?""Yes."Raymond interrupts, "Nobody told me about an elf.""Last-minute decision, very high up." I point to the hut on the float. "You've checked the workshop, inside and out?"Halsey nods. "Several times."Irene taps her watch. "Burnt bird, Grace.""I remember, Irene. Detective, if everything's all right with the float . . .""Everything's not all right," insists Raymond. "He's too tall to be an elf. The proportions are all wrong."Raymond is correct, of course. Halsey looks ridiculous in a green jacket with a red scarf for a sash. Someone has even managed to get him into a pair of turned-up booties and a pointed elf's hat, complete with bell. But the absurdity of Halsey the elf is not my main concern. "If the float is sound and Mr. Gardner and Mrs. O'Malley are secure . . .""It's my professional judgment that Santa Claus is exposed."I'm about to say of course he's exposed, that's the whole point, when I hear my name howled. Mr. Bascomb has found me."Why are we standing here, Miss Verlander? We have to be in Herald Square by three thirty!""And I have to be in Queens by four o'clock," Irene reminds us."If we are not in Herald Square by three thirty, the Straus brothers will want to know why," says Bascomb. "I will have to tell them why!""I'd like to take a look at the sight lines one more time," Halsey announces.Raymond folds his arms. "If the elf is on the float, he stays in the workshop.""I don't like telling things to the Straus brothers!" shrieks Bascomb."Not even Mr. Herbert!"The three men close in on me, each making his boneheaded argument. I look up at Harry, who mouths, I'm sorry. Which makes me angry. Harry is the last person who should be sorry."Right!" I punch the air. "Let's start the parade!"Bascomb hurries off to give Helen Schonbrun the good news.Raymond asks, "And the elf stays in the workshop?""No." Raymond's aesthetics and the aesthetics of Raymond are near and dear to my heart. But in this, I can't give way. "The elf stays where he belongs, which is by Santa's side. Isn't that right, Detective Halsey?"Halsey jerks his jaw. He doesn't appreciate the assistant to the head of personnel, who is wearing a skirt, of all things, dictating to him in matters of security. He nods to the workshop. "Fellow's got to warm up occasionally.""One break, five minutes, every mile. And while you're in there, you keep watch through that window, understood?"Halsey narrows his eyes at understood. I have a feeling I have gone on some list he keeps in his head.I'm about to tell him he needs to keep a special lookout for a scrawny balding man with brown hair and a mustache when I hear the shriek of a whistle, the blare of brass, and the sarcastic cheering of my colleagues. Slowly, a mass of nearly one thousand people begins to move. The ninth annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is underway.Copyright © 2026 from MURDER ON 34TH STREET by Mariah Fredericks.
