title: NYPD officer faces disciplinary trial in 2016 fatal shooting of Delrawn Small
description: More than a decade after an off-duty NYPD officer fatally shot a man during a Brooklyn road rage confrontation, Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch has ruled that a long-delayed disciplinary case can move forward.
content: The disciplinary case against an off-duty NYPD officer who fatally shot a Brooklyn man during a road rage encounter is moving forward after more than a decade of waiting.Police Commissioner Jessica Tish has determined that the Civilian Complaint Review Board has jurisdiction to prosecute disciplinary charges against Officer Wayne Isaacs, clearing the way for a department trial scheduled for Jan.13.The decision stems from the 2016 fatal shooting of 37-year-old Delrawn Small on Atlantic Avenue in Brooklyn. Prosecutors said Small was killed following a confrontation with Isaacs after a traffic dispute. Isaacs testified during his criminal trial that he opened fire after Small punched him in the face, though surveillance video did not clearly show the alleged assault. In 2017, a jury acquitted Isaacs of murder and manslaughter charges.The CCRB's disciplinary case has remained unresolved for years amid legal challenges and questions over whether the agency had the authority to prosecute conduct that occurred while Isaacs was off duty.Last year, the NYPD's trial commissioner recommended dismissing the disciplinary case, arguing that the CCRB lacked jurisdiction because the incident occurred while Isaacs was not on duty.However, in a letter to the CCRB obtained by CBS News New York, Tisch rejected that argument."It is undisputed that [Isaacs] was taking police action when he used that force," Tisch wrote. "While I am expressing no view on the ultimate merits of the case, CCRB has jurisdiction. The matter should proceed to trial forthwith."The decision was welcomed by Small's family."I don't think there's a chance for justice. I think there's a chance for accountability," Small's brother, Victor Dempsey, said.After learning of Tisch's decision, Dempsey said it could signal a shift in the department's approach to police discipline."I feel like she made the right decision. Hopefully, that's a step in the right direction, that accountability looks different under this administration," he said.Advocates who have supported the family said the case has faced repeated delays over the years."Delrawn's family has had to get through so many delays, attempts to get the whole process canceled," said Yul-san Liem of the Justice Committee."First, he wasn't a cop, then he is a cop," Public Advocate Jumaane Williams said. "He lied about what happened. We know all of this, and he's still an officer."In a statement, Patrolmen's Benevolent Association President Patrick Hendry defended Isaacs and criticized the CCRB."CCRB is continuing to push this case without a single shred of new evidence," Hendry said. "We will continue to fight this case and every instance of CCRB's blatant overreach."A CCRB spokesperson praised Tisch's decision, saying the agency is pleased the commissioner "recognizes the importance of a trial in this case."

title: Family, friends of two men charged in Miami-Dade cockfighting case say allegations are false
description: Deputies say a search of a lot turned up fighting rings, an arena and hundreds of roosters, while relatives and friends of the two men say no fights happen there.
content: Family members and friends of two men facing animal cruelty charges in connection with an alleged cockfighting operation in Miami-Dade County are pushing back against the allegations.Investigators said Angel Ponce-Maqueda, 29, and Jesus Fabian Oliva were involved in the operation after authorities executed a search at the property Tuesday morning.According to arrest reports from Miami-Dade Sheriff's deputies, a detective originally arrived at the lot to investigate environmental crimes but discovered cockfighting training rings, an arena, numbered seats, a scoreboard, syringes, medicine, vitamins, rooster agitators, and hundreds of roosters. Some of the roosters had injuries.Detectives located Ponce-Maqueda in an RV near rooster cages. Investigators reported that the 29-year-old admitted to feeding and watering the roosters but denied owning any of the animals.In court, Oliva also denied having any role in cockfighting. Investigators said Oliva initially claimed ownership of all the roosters before changing his story during questioning.Oliva's family said he owns the property and collects rent from 13 to 15 people living in RVs on the lot, most of whom saw deputies rush through the gates Tuesday morning.However, relatives and friends of the suspects maintain that investigators are wrong."They are posting false things," said a woman related to Ponce-Maqueda who asked not to be identified.A friend of both suspects, who also spoke on condition of anonymity, said no animal fighting takes place on the site."There were no rooster fights or anything happening on this property, and it hasn't happened since [Oliva's] father died," the friend said. "The arena is decaying. It's falling apart. The roof has holes in it. The arena itself is breaking down. You can't stand in there, or it will break down on you. There are no rooster fights."

title: Water main break disrupts service to Darling Way homes in Roseville
description: A water main break has temporarily disrupted water service to several homes in Roseville and prompted a road closure, officials said Wednesday.
content: A water main break has temporarily disrupted water service to several homes in Roseville and prompted a road closure, officials said Wednesday.Shortly before 5:30 p.m., the City of Roseville said service was disrupted to homes at 601 to 919 Darling Way, as utility crews were preparing to begin repairs. The city also said a single classroom at George Cirby Elementary school was impacted as well.A one-block closure of Darling Way was put in place between Clarice Lane and Keehner Avenue. City officials have urged drivers to use alternate routes.The city said there was no estimated time for the repairs to be complete but said it would provide additional information when it becomes available.

title: Pittsburgh youth football program president charged in cocaine trafficking ring
description: The president of a Pittsburgh youth football program is one of more than a half dozen local people indicted on drug charges, accused of being part of a cocaine trafficking ring.
content: The president of a Pittsburgh youth football program is one of eight people indicted on drug charges, accused of being part of a cocaine trafficking ring. This federal indictment was unsealed this morning, charging four men from Pittsburgh and three others from Bellevue, Uniontown and Aliquippa. One of the Pittsburgh men charged is Martin Langford, who started the Westside Mustangs Youth Athletic Association. Langford is accused in the federal indictment of possession with intent to distribute cocaine on three separate occasions. Langford's program, based in the city's West End, received Stop the Violence grant funding from the city under the Gainey administration. That taxpayer money was passed out throughout the city to help tackle violence. According to the Pittsburgh Courier, Langford's football program grew from 80 kids in its inaugural season to 240. According to his LinkedIn, Langford is also the owner of 412 Entertainment and J/G Trucking. U.S. Attorney Troy Rivetti announced the indictment on Wednesday, calling it a takedown of a "large-scale" cocaine trafficking organization in the Pittsburgh area. The 15-month Homeland Security Task Force investigation spanned from June 2025 to September of this year. "This office and our law enforcement partners will continue to stand together in investigating and prosecuting those who conspire to harm our communities and destroy lives through the distribution of illegal controlled substances," U.S. Attorney Troy Rivetti said in a press release. Authorities identified the others charged as Terrance Bonner, 45; Roddell Smalls, 53; Maurice Tinsley, 45; Justin Rumble, 47; Oscar Stokes, 45; and Rashawdi Pugh, 47.

title: Federal immigration vehicle hits pedestrian in Woodland, police say
description: Woodland police are investigating a traffic collision involving a vehicle operated by federal immigration authorities and a pedestrian Tuesday morning.
content: Woodland police are investigating after a vehicle operated by federal immigration authorities struck a pedestrian Tuesday morning.Officers responded shortly after 9:30 a.m. to the area of Locust and Clover streets, the Woodland Police Department said.The pedestrian suffered minor injuries and was treated at the scene before being taken to an area hospital, police said. NorCal Resist, an immigrant advocacy organization, said the person was stable but described them as being "scraped up."Woodland police said the agents in the vehicle were conducting a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operation in the area when the collision happened. The driver alerted local authorities and remained cooperative, police added.NorCal Resist posted footage of the collision to their social media pages, showing a man, Antonio Moreida, being knocked to the ground. Woodland police said it has since reviewed multiple angles of footage of the incident, including the minutes of interaction between Moreida and federal personnel leading up to it.Woodland police said the actions of both parties are under review. The department said the federal agency has been notified of the investigation and that it has requested ICE's full cooperation."I've seen the video myself, and I find it very troubling. I understand why people in our community are upset and worried," Woodland Police Chief Kinnan said in a statement. "Our responsibility is to conduct a thorough and impartial investigation to establish the facts. We recognize the concerns surrounding federal law enforcement activity in Woodland, and the safety and well-being of our community members remain a priority." Moreida is a student at Woodland Community College and a volunteer with NorCal Resist. He told CBS News Sacramento that he went to the neighborhood after hearing reports of an ICE operation with the hopes of documenting it and alerting nearby residents.He said he began recording people he believed were federal immigration officers and asked them to identify themselves. CBS News Sacramento obtained additional footage recorded by Moreida showing the front end of the vehicle striking him as he was recording in the middle of the street."I took the corner of the car to the chest," Moreida told CBS News Sacramento. "When I first hit the ground, I had the wind knocked out of me. That was my first reaction."In a statement to CBS News Sacramento Wednesday morning, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said ICE did not hit a pedestrian. "An agitator jumped onto the hood of an ICE vehicle and the officer driving applied the brakes. The agitator slid off the hood. ICE immediately contacted EMS and the Woodland Police Department," the spokesperson said. "Flopping for the camera is dangerous, especially when it interferes with a federal law enforcement operation."Tuesday's Woodland City Council meeting ended up being a packed house with community members voicing their concerns and showing support for Moreida, who was also in attendance and spoke.The incident prompted criticism from state and federal lawmakers, who called for accountability and a thorough investigation. "California has taken action to strengthen legal protections for Californians and will keep fighting for the safety of its communities against the federal government's campaign of terror and weaponized incompetence. Their tactics continue to harm our families every day, " Governor Gavin Newsom's office said Wednesday in a statement. Democratic U.S. House Rep. Mike Thompson, whose district includes Woodland, said he was in communication with local law enforcement, who informed him that federal immigration authorities were operating the vehicle involved."ICE cannot continue to terrorize our communities ... No one is above the law," Thompson said in a statement. Thompson also said the incident highlights the need for transparency and accountability, citing what he described as growing distrust and fear within communities."Members of our community need to feel safe," he said.California Assembly Majority Leader Cecilia Aguiar-Curry, whose District 4 also includes Woodland, called for "a full investigation by local and state authorities because we can't rely on this federal administration to investigate itself.""This kind of behavior is unacceptable and falls short of the standards of professionalism and restraint our communities have every right to expect from law enforcement," Aguiar-Curry said.The Yolo County District Attorney's Office released a statement saying it was aware of the incident but could not comment further due to the investigation being active. Woodland police said that, once complete, a full investigation would be sent to the district attorney's office for review.

title: Breast cancer diagnosis upends lives of younger women navigating motherhood
description: Two survivors share their experiences with breast cancer, from treatment during pregnancy to a diagnosis after preventive surgery, and their efforts to raise awareness.
content: Jenna Tomasiewicz was 28 weeks pregnant with her second son when she noticed something that brought her to her doctor's office."I was putting on lotion and I found a lump on my right breast," Tomasiewicz said.At 34, she was diagnosed with stage 2 breast cancer that had spread to the lymph nodes in her armpit."I was like the epitome of health. I was so fit. I was always eating so healthy. I have no family history of breast cancer. I even tested negative for the BRCA gene. So cancer wasn't even on my radar," she said.Doctors recommended that Tomasiewicz begin chemotherapy while pregnant. She went for a second opinion and she was told it would be safe."I was induced at 37 weeks and, gosh, it was just the most blissful moment of my life when he was born," she said.Her husband, John Tomasiewicz, recalled the uncertainty of that time."We were just starting our family, just starting our life together. So it was very difficult," he said.For Margot Casino, learning she carried a BRCA mutation through a 23andMe test prompted a series of difficult decisions. The mutation put her at a much higher risk of breast cancer, and she risked passing the gene to their children."My husband and I at the time decided to do IVF to ensure that our children didn't inherit this mutation and wouldn't have to face the same difficult choices that I faced, and am still facing today," Casino said.She also underwent preventive surgeries, including a double mastectomy and hysterectomy, in an effort to reduce her cancer risk."I thought that I had some sort of leg up in this metaphorical race against cancer, essentially. And it really felt like someone pulled the rug out from under me," she said.While recovering from one of the surgeries, Casino felt a lump. A week later, she found another. Her doctor urged her to undergo an ultrasound and biopsy."That confirmed the diagnosis of stage 3C invasive ductal carcinoma. In eight weeks, it had grown and spread through my axillary lymph nodes into my internal mammary nodes," Casino said.According to the American Cancer Society, about 1 in 10 women diagnosed with breast cancer is younger than 45.This Breast Cancer Awareness Month, Casino says she has reached a milestone in her treatment."I feel great. I was told that there is no evidence of disease at this time on the one-year anniversary of my diagnosis," she said.Tomasiewicz is now a social worker and cancer coach. Her son is healthy, and she is in remission."Having cancer didn't matter. I was in a lot of pain, that didn't matter. I was bald, that didn't matter. Like nothing in the world mattered," she said.Both women are involved with the Susan G. Komen Foundation, raising awareness and supporting funding for advances in breast cancer treatment.CBS News New York is partnering with the Komen Foundation for this year's Race for the Cure, taking place Saturday.Have a story idea or tip in Brooklyn? title: The Atlanta Bucks, city's inclusive gay rugby team, builds family on and off the field
description: The Atlanta Bucks, reportedly Georgia's first inclusive gay rugby team, have grown from a group of players who meet for practice into a strong support system.
content: The Atlanta Bucks, reportedly Georgia's first inclusive gay rugby team, have grown from a group of players who meet for practice into a support system that helps members face isolation, rejection, and the challenges many in the LGBTQ community still carry.On a Monday night, the team gathered at a park in East Atlanta to practice for their first game of the season.At practice, veterans teach rookies the plays and run them through drills."They welcomed me with open arms," said Atlanta Bucks player Manny Baza-Fainn.Not every player on the team is gay. Some players are allies."I feel like this is just a wonderful place for people to step out of their comfort zone," said Baza-Fainn.Several players said sports did not feel safe for them growing up. Some said they faced bullying. They said the team gives them the opposite experience."Rugby is not about, like, you have to be fit," said Baza-Fainn.Baza-Fainn joined the team in 2023. He said he hoped to make friends."I've struggled with social anxiety," said Baza-Fainn.Soon after he joined, his husband, Anthony, faced a medical emergency."My husband actually just had open-heart surgery the day before the one-on-one," said Baza-Fainn.He said he was new to the team and worried he would lose his spot."My heart was torn because I wasn't sure if I was going to be able to make it," he adds.He said the team kept his place and stood by him."We really do support each other on and off the pit," he said.The players also spend time together away from the field. They meet at a bar for trivia nights. Anthony Baza-Fainn manages the team's sponsor and said the team has changed his husband."Being that Manny is an introvert, it's really helped him come out a little bit," he said.Some players found love on the team."My current boyfriend and I actually met on the team," said Atlanta Bucks co-captain Colin Mackey.The team said it has had a busy year. The Bucks traveled to Brisbane, Australia, for the Bingham Cup and placed third in their tier of 16 teams. The team also placed third out of eight teams at the Pride Cup Scrum in the Sun tournament in Orlando in June.The club said it has a new president, new leadership and new jersey kits. Its new season is underway.You can learn more about the team and see their upcoming matches on their website.

title: CPD warns of thieves posing as charity fundraisers, stealing belongings from patrons at restaurants
description: The incidents occurred at restaurants in the Loop, West Loop and Near South Side during various hours of the day between Oct. 7 and 18.
content: Chicago police issued an alert on Wednesday about a string of thefts involving people posing as charity fundraisers. The incidents occurred at restaurants in the Loop, West Loop and Near South Side during various hours of the day between Oct. 7 and 18.Police said in each instance, the thieves approached diners seated in a restaurant or coffee shop, posing as fundraisers and placing a flyer or newspaper directly on top of the victims' wallet/purse or cell phone. While engaging in conversation with the victim, they would slide the victims' belongings underneath the paper and walk away with the items. Police said in some incidents, the stolen bank and/or credit cards were used shortly after at nearby department stores.Incident dates and locations:500 block of South Dearborn Street on Oct. 7 at 10:35 a.m. - Loop500 block of South Dearborn Street on Oct. 7 at 10:45 a.m. - Loop2000 block of South Clark Street on Oct. 12 at 6:54 p.m. - Near South Side700 block of South Dearborn Street on Oct. 14 at 10:45 a.m. - Loop200 block of South Wacker Drive on Oct. 14 at 3 p.m. - Loop0-100 block of South Canal Street on Oct. 16 at 3:30 p.m. - West Loop200 block of South Wabash Avenue on Oct. 17 at 7:10 p.m. - Loop1300 block of South Michigan Avenue on Oct.18, 2026 at 7:15 p.m. - Near South SideChicago police are advising the public to never leave their phone, wallet, or keys sitting loose on a restaurant table or counter where a stranger can easily cover them with paper. They also recommend investing in a Bluetooth tracker and placing it either in their wallet or bag, or attaching it to their cell phones.Anyone with information is asked to contact Area 3 detectives at 312-744-8263 or submit an anonymous tip at CPDTIP.com, using reference No. 263041.

title: Gubernatorial candidate Dan Cox calls for Maryland ban on new mega data centers
description: Republican gubernatorial candidate Dan Cox called Wednesday for a statewide ban on new mega data centers.
content: Republican gubernatorial candidate Dan Cox is calling for a statewide ban on new mega data centers. Standing at a news conference near a massive data center development Wednesday in Adamstown, Maryland, Cox demanded the statewide ban as well as a moratorium on current development.Cox was joined by residents who said the development in Frederick County has disrupted their community. "I mean, I want to stay local. I love the area. I love my kids to love the area, but it's just hard to be close to something like that" said Adamstown resident Jean Butler. Some residents also raised concerns about air pollution and water quality. "We noticed it smelled funny, it tasted funnyâ¦and we're drinking this, we're bathing in thisâ¦" said Casey, a local resident. Cox blames Gov. Wes Moore and Frederick County leaders for allowing "fast-tracked permits" for new data centers to move forward. "Immediately today, this governor, Gov. Moore could issue an executive order providing a moratorium on protecting the land, while we make sure that we pursue this process that protects all of our residents, and bans the data centers on Maryland soil," Cox said. But the Moore administration says the governor has imposed strict requirements on data centers â including making them pay for their own energy infrastructure.It also points to Cox's own record. In 2020, the candidate co-sponsored legislation offering tax breaks for data centers. When asked about that during the press conference, Cox said the industry has changed."The data centers of seven years ago are not today's data centers. They never were, and we never knew that this was going to happen with the 20 super Walmart sized data centersâ¦that's outrageous," Cox said.

title: Oakland high school dedicates podcast studio in honor of student killed in 1997
description: All Tied Up Academy, an Oakland non-profit that provides mentorship for youth of color, debuted a podcast studio at McClymonds High School named after Lo'Eshe Lacy, a student whose life was cut short by gun violence in 1997.
content: Nearly three decades after losing his daughter to gun violence, Donald Lacy returned to the Oakland high school where she once studied for a dedication honoring her life and giving a new generation of students a platform to share their stories."The ATU Academy x Lo'Eshe Lacy Podcast Studio" at McClymonds High School was dedicated in memory of Lo'Eshe, who was 16 when she was killed in 1997. She and her best friend, Maya McGhee-Nelson, were shot outside the school in an incident of youth gun violence. They were innocent bystanders. McGhee-Nelson survived."She was my first born child. My only daughter," Donald Lacy said.Lo'Eshe loved to rap, dance and sing. Her father, who recently retired after 48 years in radio, recalled how she would visit his radio show and deliver her own reports.Now, 29 years after her death, her voice is inspiring students to find their own.The dedication ceremony brought an emotional surprise when McGhee-Nelson walked into the room. Seeing his daughter's childhood friend again moved Lacy, who recalled the girls growing up together."You all gotta give me a little grace," he told the audience through tears. "To see my girl Maya walking through that door. Whew. I still see y'all's snotty noses running around the house!"Addressing McGhee-Nelson, he added, "God don't make mistakes. You were here because he wanted you here."The moment underscored how the loss of Lo'Eshe continues to shape the lives of those who knew her.But the ceremony also marked a new beginning.When Lacy was invited to unveil the podcast studio bearing his daughter's name, he reacted with visible emotion as he entered and saw the space for the first time.The ATU Academy's founder Armand Carr, who helped lead the dedication, said the studio ensures Lo'Eshe's legacy will continue."Her voice is still being heard," Carr said. "Just because you're not here physically, your spiritual voice still carries on."The studio is designed to give students a place to express their ideas, creativity and perspectives through podcasting.For 16-year-old Yasmin Taylor, the opportunity means being able to share her thoughts with others and hear different points of view."I'm able to share my ideas and my creativity with others," Taylor said. "I think it's important to get everybody's perspective."During the ceremony, Taylor interviewed Lacy inside the new studio, asking what he hoped people would take away from the space.His answer focused on the next generation."That... young people need these vehicles," Lacy said. "Old guys like me, we had our time, so what can I do to help empower you?"For Lacy, the studio is more than a memorial. It is a way to ensure his daughter's story is remembered not only for how her life ended, but for the promise she carried and the impact she hoped to make.Addressing the students, he offered a final message of encouragement."All three of y'all got an impact you gonna make," he said. "Believe that, believe that."

title: Massachusetts ballot question guide for the 2026 election
description: There are nine ballot questions for Massachusetts​ voters to decide in the 2026 election, the most in over three decades.
content: There are nine ballot questions for Massachusetts voters to decide in the 2026 election, the most in over three decades.The issues covered by the questions range from guns to marijuana policy to taxpayer refunds.Election officials expect long lines at the polls as voters flip through pages of information, but here's what to know about each ballot question before you vote.Question 1: Public RecordsA "yes" vote would expand the public records law to include the governor's office and the state Legislature, which are currently exempt. A "no" vote would not make any changes to the law.The ballot question is being spearheaded by state Auditor Diana DiZoglio, who has long sought to audit the Legislature."You have a right to see what your government is doing with your hard-earned taxpayer dollars," DiZoglio argues.While there is no formal opposition group to Question 1, some lawmakers say the ballot question is overly broad and creates privacy risks. The House of Representatives passed their own bill earlier this year to increase public access to legislative records, but DiZoglio has called it unconstitutional. Question 2: CPCS collective bargainingA "yes" vote would allow public defenders and other employees of the Committee for Public Counsel Services to unionize. A "no" vote would make no changes to the labor relations law.Supporters say these workers deserve the right to form a union if they choose to do so. Opponents argue it could hamper the agency's ability to respond to staffing needs and other court demands.Question 3: Eliminating political party primariesA "yes" vote would eliminate separate party primaries for state elections. Instead, there would be one primary where all candidates, regardless of party, would appear on one ballot and the top two candidates would advance to the general election.A "no" vote would make no changes to the law."This is about making sure that every voter has a vote that matters," said Harvard University political philosophy professor Danielle Allen, who supports the change. "We have the fewest competitive elections in Massachusetts of any state in the country and when there's no choice, voters get taken for granted."Massachusetts Democratic Party chair Steve Kerrigan said changing the rules would benefit the richest candidates."We are the birthplace of democracy and anything that says that we should limit our choices for people come November is wrong for Massachusetts," he said. Watch the full debate on Question 3.Question 4: Same-day voter registrationA "yes" vote would let eligible citizens register to vote or update their voter registration address at their polling place on Election Day. A "no" vote would keep the current law in place.If Question 4 passes, Massachusetts would join 17 other states that allow for same-day registration. Currently, Massachusetts residents must register to vote or change their registration 10 days before an election. Question 4 supporters say it would give voters the same opportunity that others in New England have. Opponents say it raises fraud concerns. Question 5: State revenue limit & rebateA "yes" vote would limit how much revenue Massachusetts could collect in a year, and provide a refund to taxpayers the next year if collections go over that limit. A "no" vote would make no changes to the law.Supporters say it would put more money back in the pockets of Massachusetts families. Opponents say it would reduce the state's "Rainy Day" fund and force major budget cuts.Question 6: Natural Resource Conservation FundA "yes" vote would put state taxes generated from the sale of sporting goods, recreational vehicles and golf courses into a fund for natural resource conservation. A "no" vote would not establish a fund.Supporters say it would raise tens of millions to protect clean drinking water, prevent flood damage, reduce pollution and improve parks, trails and other green spaces. Opponents say it could take away funding from other priorities, and note the Legislature ultimately has authority over appropriations.Question 7: Single family homesA "yes" vote would allow single-family homes to be built on lots of 5,000 square feet or more across the state. A "no" vote would make no changes to the law.Proponents of Question 7 say this would allow for the creation of more affordable homes. "We've heard people reach out, say they can't afford a home with even a dual income," Andrew Mikula, founder of the group "Legalize Starter Homes" told WBZ-TV. "Opponents say it's a "one-size-fits-all" plan that would take away local control over zoning."There's many communities that are questioning whether they have enough water to serve their communities, never mind an expansion," said Adam Chapdelaine, executive director of the Massachusetts Municipal Association. Question 8: Prohibit sale of adult recreational use marijuanaA "yes" vote would repeal the 2016 law that legalized adult recreational marijuana use, and change penalties for possession. A "no" vote would make no changes to the marijuana law.Supporters of Question 8 say marijuana contributes to car crashes, crime and lost productivity. Opponents say making recreational marijuana use illegal again would kill jobs in the cannabis industry and result in arrests that disproportionately target minorities. Question 9: Gun lawsA "no" vote would repeal the gun reform law enacted in 2024. A "yes" vote would keep it in place.The law tightened regulation of firearms, including "ghost guns," machine guns and assault-style weapons. It also expanded "red flag" provisions and mandated an electronic registration system to track guns.Toby Leary, speaking for the "no" side, says Massachusetts already had the strictest gun control laws in the nation and said the new law is trying to "scare people." "At the end of the day, this is a constitutional issue," Leary said. "Does the Legislature have the privilege to erode or restrict or encumber any of our constitutional rights?"On the "yes" side, Ruth Zakarin said the legislation is about safety. "We're asking people to vote yes on 9 this November to preserve this critically important law and to make sure we're doing everything we possibly can to keep our community safe from gun violence," she said. Watch the full debate on Question 9.

title: No timeline for reopening Great Allegheny Passage after deadly rockslide, officials say
description: A portion of the Great Allegheny Passage trail in Fayette County remains closed after a deadly rockslide over the weekend.
content: A portion of the Great Allegheny Passage trail in Fayette County remains closed after a deadly rockslide over the weekend.The Great Allegheny Passage posted on Facebook that Pennsylvania State Police and the Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources are investigating."It's heartbreaking because that is not an area on the trail that I was ever concerned with," said Jen Sigado, a resident and avid biker. "There's a bench right across from where it happened. I sit on the bench almost every day and look at the river. Never once would have thought that particular hillside would go."In the post, GAP announced there will be a shuttle service to get bikers from one side of the trail to the other in the meantime. The shuttle costs $20."I understand them charging money because it's a business, and gas is expensive, and insurance, and everything else," Sigado said. "But to take advantage of such a tragedy when we have hundreds of people on this trail every day. Considering the rockslide fell on Ohiopyle State Park — I used to work for the state. Don't tell me there isn't money to provide a shuttle."Sigado said she disagrees with making bikers have to pay for a shuttle, especially when bikers can get around it themselves."Right up the road, across from Walmart, is Wheeler Bottom," Sigado said. "You can take it straight down. There's a bike trail parking lot, and you get right on the trail there. The way they're going, the shuttle, it's five miles. Now, if they went to the closest one, the turn's a mile and a half up the road, and then a mile back to the trail."KDKA-TV reached out to the Great Allegheny Passage for comment on the fee but did not hear back.The DCNR told KDKA-TV on Wednesday that it's in uncharted territory because of the size and volume of the rockslide. A spokesperson said there is no set timeline for when the trail could reopen but stressed it could be a while before it does."Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources (DCNR) staff are working with stakeholders, geologists, and engineers to determine the cause of the incident," said Wesley Robinson, the press secretary for the DCNR. "The trail section will remain closed until the necessary excavation work is completed, technical crews have stabilized the area, and the trail is deemed safe for public use."DCNR staff are also working with the Great Allegheny Passage Conservancy to help trail users safely detour around the closure. Updates on the closure are available on the Ohiopyle State Park website."KDKA-TV talked to a professor and the head of the Department of Geosciences at Penn State who said a study will need to be completed to determine if another rockslide could happen."Often you'll see, even in really small failures like along a stream bank, or big ones on cliffs, if there are open fractures at the top of the cliff, that's an indication that there's greater potential for failure if those cracks are already there," said professor Eric Kirby.In KDKA drone video, to the left of the rockslide, what appears to be a visible crack in the hillside can be seen. Kirby said that could be concerning."If there's a fracture there, and this thing already failed behind once, if that end is open, and the failure just came off this end, now both ends of the block are no longer connected, so the only thing still holding it in is what's behind in the trees back into the hillside," Kirby said.As far as what potentially caused the rockslide, Kirby said that's up to a geotechnical engineer on site to determine."But from what I can see and judge at, there's a prominent horizontal ledge that is at the base of the cliff where the vegetation then starts above the trail, and it looks like what happened is that the hillside failed behind that and down to it," Kirby said. "That ledge looks to me like what we would call a bedding plane, but one of the old depositional layers in the sedimentary rocks themselves. So probably a weaker layer to begin with, which is why below that point the slope is more just rubbly and holds vegetation, and above that point it's stronger and steeper, right? So, from a standpoint of how these events likely evolve, there could be small rocks and gravel and stuff that comes off where the slide is, as that rock mass adjusts to the fact that this piece just popped off."Kirby said it's hard to determine if the rockslide was caused by recent weather."That's a really hard question because, in a general sense, we do see associations between hillside failures and rain, right? Because as the water percolates in, it can increase the sort of pore pressures, the pressures in the spaces in the soil and the fractures and things, but we don't always know what that threshold is for a failure to happen, and so, the unsatisfying answer is that it's possible, but we couldn't know for sure."The DCNR said technical crews have stabilized the area but said that section of the trail will remain closed until the investigation is complete.

title: LeBron James mania hits Philadelphia ahead of Sixers' home opener: "This is going to be our year"
description: There was a certain buzz Wednesday in Philadelphia after the Sixers kicked off the LeBron James era with a win in New York.
content: With the countdown to the Sixers' home opener in South Philadelphia, there was a buzz in the city Wednesday, especially after the team's win the night before."The team has great chemistry. You can see it," Les Hamilton from West Oak Lane said. "They started off a little bit slow, but I'm super happy that they won on ring night because why would you play us on ring night anyway? They should've known they were gonna lose."Justin Dahlman flew in from Calgary, Alberta, Canada, to see Thursday's game against the Cleveland Cavaliers."I'm a Raptors fan 'cause I'm from Canada," Dahlman said. "Some people might not like that here because of the history, but after seeing LeBron just tear apart the Raptors in the Eastern Conference for my whole life pretty much, just have to be here to see him."He's not the only one going to the game Thursday who spoke to CBS News Philadelphia on Wednesday."Sixers, the greatest team in the NBA," Keith Franklin II from Drexel Hill said.He became a first-time season ticket holder this year."Grabbed those earlier this year once I heard the great news about LeBron James and I can't wait. That's my favorite player," Franklin said.During lunchtime, a steady stream of people came to Rally House Center City to look specifically for Sixers merchandise."We've seen a lot of people come in for Sixers," Julian Maloney, assistant manager at Rally House Center City, said. "We've seen a lot of people who don't even know anything about basketball, being able to talk to them about different players, seeing a lot of people buy presents for kids."Lori Miceli works in the city but lives in Havertown."I'm going to a second birthday party this weekend," Miceli said. "I don't think he has any Sixers stuff, so I wanted to get him something. All my kids were in their jerseys yesterday and then their shirts today, and then they're like, 'Mom, wash it cause we're wearing it again.'"Dion Cole from West Philly was decked out head to toe in Sixers gear, literally down to his socks."I truly believe this is going to be our year," Cole said.The hype around the team, several fans told the CBS News Philadelphia crew, is not only warranted but welcomed after recent news surrounding the Eagles."They were holding the city down. Seriously, shout out to all the Eagles players, especially Jalen Hurts, for what he's going through, right? Prayers up," Hamilton said. "And everything like that. But I think that the Sixers have a high expectation to live up to.""With, like, Jalen Hurts, that news, that disappointing news," Miceli said. "I feel like we really needed this win last night, LeBron energy and everything, so I think it's a cool time to be in the city."

title: What are the ballot questions for Maryland's 2026 midterm elections? Question 3 and more explained.
description: As Maryland starts hitting the polls for early voting in the 2026 midterm elections, voters will be asked to weigh in on a handful of ballot questions, including the highly anticipated Question 3.
content: As Maryland starts hitting the polls for early voting in the 2026 midterm elections this week, voters will be asked to weigh in on a handful of ballot questions, including the highly anticipated Question 3. Voters across the state will face the same three questions, and then some counties will face additional questions. The statewide questions are labeled Question 1, Question 2 and Question 3, while the county specific questions are labeled alphabetically. Here's a look at what the statewide questions say, and how to learn more about your county questions.Question 3: Congressional redistrictingQuestion 3 essentially paves the way for Maryland lawmakers to redraw the state's congressional maps. If approved, it would eliminate the state constitution requirement that says congressional districts must be compact and connected. Gov. Wes Moore and the state's top Democrats say the redistricting is necessary to fight back against the Trump administration's efforts to redraw other congressional districts across the country in favor of Republicans. The move would further gerrymander the state, and it could eliminate the only Republican congressional seat on the Eastern Shore.While the ballot measure would not automatically redraw the districts, it would allow the Democrat-controlled General Assembly to do so next session. That could spell the end of GOP control and Rep. Andy Harris' tenure over District 1, which covers the Eastern Shore and parts of Baltimore, Carroll and Harford counties.The fight to redraw the congressional maps has been messy. The Democrat-led state legislature held a special session in August to add Question 3 to the November ballot. It passed the House 96-38 and the Senate 32-13.But Republican groups sued to block the question from appearing on the ballot, arguing that the legislature had missed a deadline and that the language was confusing. The legal battle reached the state's highest court, and the Maryland Supreme Court ultimately ruled that Question 3 could appear before voters but it needed to be rewritten to be more clear. Based on the court's ruling, Question 3 now reads: FOR the purpose of clarifying that certain requirements apply only to districts for the election of members of the Senate of Maryland and the House of Delegates; authorizing the General Assembly to grant original jurisdiction to the Supreme Court of Maryland to review the congressional districting plan of the State; and providing that nothing in the Maryland Constitution provides applicable criteria for the boundaries of a congressional districting plan.Many voters appear to be against the measure, with 53% of likely voters saying they were opposed in a UMBC poll last month. Only 25% said they supported it, and 19% were still undecided. Question 3 appears to be especially unpopular with independent voters, with 59% saying they would vote "no."Statewide ballot Questions 1 and 2The other two statewide ballot questions have been somewhat less controversial. Question 1 asks voters whether the state budget should have to cover agreements stemming from arbitration between the state and its employees. Those agreements could include things like changes to wages, hours, fringe benefits, health benefits and other terms and conditions of employment. Providing that each budget submitted by the Governor shall include proposed expenditures necessary to implement wages, hours, fringe benefits, health benefits, and other terms and conditions of employment in each collective bargaining memorandum of understanding with State employees, whether the State and State employees reached those terms and conditions by mutual agreement or through a neutral decider's order.A vote in favor of Question 1 would mean the governor has to include that funding in his or her proposed budget."The Governor must put enough money in the State budget to cover the agreed upon pay and benefits for employees, whether those terms were negotiated or decided by a neutral decision-maker," the question continues. A vote against Question 1 would mean the current law stays the same. Question 2 relates to filling positions on the Commission on Judicial Disabilities, in the event that a member is no longer able to serve. This would apply when a member is recused, disqualified or when their term expires. Authorizing temporary substitute appointments to the Commission on Judicial Disabilities when a member is recused or disqualified, or when a member's term expires. In these situations, the Commission Chair may recall a former member of the Commission, or the Governor, at the request of the Commission Chair, may appoint a temporary substitute member or extend the term of a current member until a permanent replacement is appointed. Only individuals who meet the constitutional eligibility requirements may be recalled or appointed to the Commission.A vote in favor of Question 2 would authorize the commission chair to temporarily fill the opening -- either by appointing a former member, or by asking the governor to pick a substitute or to extend the current member's term until a replacement can be appointed."Only individuals who meet the constitutional eligibility requirements may be recalled or appointed to the Commission," the question says. A vote against Question 2 would mean the current rules stay the same, and temporary appointments are not allowed. County-by-county ballot questionsThen come the county-by-county ballot questions. Some counties have several additional questions, while some have none. Here's a look at how many additional ballot questions each county has in our area:Anne Arundel County: Questions A-CBaltimore County: Questions A-NCarroll County: N/AFrederick County: Question AHarford County: N/AHoward County: Questions A-BPrince George's County: Questions A-JQueen Anne's County: N/AIn Baltimore City, voters will be asked to weigh in on Questions A through H. Question I has drawn particular interest, regarding the creation of something called the "Baltimore Baby Fund." The newly created fund would be used to "enhance the economic stability of families with newborns" in the city, and it would be separate from similar funding that is already set aside in this year's budget. "The amendment would require each year's City budget to include a contribution to the Baby Fund. The City's required annual contribution to the Baby Fund will be $0.03 for every $100 in taxable property value in the City," Question I continues. "The Baby Fund will also be able to accept grants and donations. Money in the Baby Fund will stay in the Baby Fund until the City spends it for the benefit of families with newborns. The City could not transfer money in the Baby Fund to any other purpose."Mayor Brandon Scott has said he supports the measure, calling it "an opportunity to provide innovative, evidence-based support to families of newborns while reducing childhood poverty."Another high-interest ballot question is Question A in Howard County. If approved, it would change the language in the county's charter to replace gender-specific words, like "he" and "she," with gender-neutral words, like "they" and "them." Anne Arundel, Baltimore and Prince George's counties have made similar changes to their charters in recent years. The Maryland State Board of Elections has a breakdown of all the ballot questions, including for each county, on its website here.

title: N.Y. congressional candidate Brad Lander detained by the Israeli military during West Bank trip
description: Brad Lander said he was released after being detained by the Israel Defense Forces while on a trip in the West Bank.
content: New York Democratic congressional candidate Brad Lander was detained by the Israel Defense Forces while on a trip in the West Bank.The former New York City comptroller posted on social media Wednesday, saying he was detained while "harvesting olives in a grove near Nehalim."Lander said on social media that he was eventually released with a warning because of his public profile."I was detained for a couple of hours and then released with a warning, but it's now about eight hours later and many of the others are still in detention and facing a risk of deportation," Lander said.Lander spoke with CBS News New York after he was detained along with about 60 volunteers and rabbis from the Protect the Harvest Coalition who went to help guard Palestinian olive farmers who have been under attack for weeks by West Bank settlers."We were harvesting in a field between a Palestinian village and a big Israeli settlement. After a couple hours, a van, a security van from the settlement, sort of drove down and saw us, and they seem to have put in a phone call, and then shortly after that a bunch of IDF soldiers and Israeli police showed up," Lander said."People are still detained, including many of whom are rabbis. And we are figuring out what is the plan. There were rumors about deporting them," said Aziz Abu Sarah of Protect the Harvest.Israel Defense Forces issued a statement defending its actions and insisted the group did not get permission to be there and posed a security risk."Harvesting in this area requires a request to be submitted to the relevant authorities in advance of the start of the olive harvest season. This coordination is necessary to ensure the security of the area and maintain public order," the IDF said in its statement."It's a bald-faced lie, and I saw it with my own eyes," Lander said. "This was a private field owned by a Palestinian farmer who invited us to come. You don't need a permit to harvest your own field and invite volunteers to join."This is part of an effort to ethnically cleanse them from their land by making it impossible to harvest their fields or drive on their roads or live in their homes," Lander added.New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani denounced the move and told CBS News New York he appreciated Lander's moral clarity."The Israeli military found that as an offense worthy of detention. It begs a larger question of their conduct over the course of not just this week, not just this month, not just this year, but so many years prior to this. And it is unacceptable," Mamdani said. "And we should also be calling for the end to a genocide that that same military that has detained him has perpetrated against Palestinians over the last few years."Lander arrived in the region over the weekend, according to his team. He said he plans to stay in the West Bank until Friday and will meet with Israelis and Palestinians. For right now, he's concerned about the other members of his group that haven't yet been released.Lander has previously been critical of Israel's military action in Gaza and has called for an end to U.S. military aid."What I'm angry about as an American Jew and a human being is the violence that is being done to Palestinians, an effort to push them off their land and out of their homes," Lander said.

title: Windows smashed at iconic bar in South Boston, several cars vandalized in neighborhood
description: Boston police are investigating numerous reports of vandalism in South Boston.
content: Boston police are on the hunt after they received numerous reports of vandalism in South Boston. The damage has City Councilor Ed Flynn urging people on social media to scour their surveillance cameras for anything that can generate leads.One incident happened on Telegraph Street. Neighbors say a man wearing all black picked up a rock and smashed in a car windshield."I come up and down this street multiple times a day, and I keep walking by that car, and it's scary," said Amanda Gordon, who lives nearby. "I'm surprised at the damage that was done."A neighbor spoke to WBZ off camera. She says her husband and another neighbor yelled at the suspect before he fled. They awoke to the noise just before 6 a.m. Matt Elias lives on the block and somehow didn't hear the destruction."I'm a heavy sleeper, so I kind of just slept right through it, but obviously saw the news in the morning," said Elias. "I'm parked around the corner today, so I kind of lucked out."Recently, Boston police have received numerous reports of break-ins or vandalism, including two on Telegraph Street. A man on Ewer Street had the passenger window of his truck smashed in, and there were also incidents on Gold and West 4th."Cars were hit in all different neighborhoods, so it's not like I can just go hide somewhere," explains Elias.As the vandalism spreads, neighbors have now started to learn about damage at Murphy's Law. The iconic bar known from the movie "Gone Baby Gone," now has numerous windows that are smashed or poked through."It didn't look like something someone in a bar would do," said Elias."They are still open or they're open limited hours, they're still serving drinks, which good to know," said Gordon.Boston police say they don't currently have a police report from the bar, so details are limited as to what happened.

title: Baltimore State's Attorney plans to retry James Barnett in 2022 rowhome fire that killed 3 firefighters
description: The Baltimore City State's Attorney's Office announces plans to retry the man accused of setting a vacant Stricker Street rowhome on fire back in 2022.
content: The Baltimore City State's Attorney's Office has announced plans to retry the man accused of setting a vacant Stricker Street rowhome on fire back in 2022.Meanwhile, family members of the three firefighters — Lt. Kelsey Sadler, Lt. Paul Butrim and Kenny Lacayo -- who were killed in the fire are holding onto hope after the judge declared a mistrial in the case against James Barnett."We're just going to keep fighting for Kelsey, Paul and Kenny because they deserve that," said Lacey Marino, the sister of Sadler. "You know, this, this is about them."A new hearing is set for Nov. 6. That's when the state and the defense will decide on a new trial date. The jury in the trial of James BarnettThe jury could not come to a unanimous decision on whether to convict Barnett of second-degree arson, involuntary manslaughter and reckless endangerment charges in the case. One juror told CBS News Baltimore that some jurors led with emotion, leading to a six-to-six split."That's the ultimate conundrum, if you will," said legal expert Warren Alperstein. "If it was 11 to 1 to convict, it's probably an easier decision to re-try."Alperstein said, for some, it's hard to eliminate emotion inside the deliberation room."Given the fact that these jurors are human beings, it's very difficult to remove the human side, emotional side, of it away from the deliberations," he said.Some jurors expressed frustration during deliberations, saying some did not take a good look at the evidence presented in trial. "As a former prosecutor, now practicing criminal defense attorney, I've seen cases and have been on different sides of this where you think it's going to be a conviction," Alperstein said. "For some reason, you can't convince all 12 as a prosecutor and, vice versa, as a defense attorney."Looking to a new trialAlperstein said there may not be new evidence to be uncovered in a new trial, but prosecutors may develop a new approach to the case.He said, for the defense, a mistrial is better than a conviction. It gives the defense another shot to convince a new jury that Barnett is innocent. Though, a new trial could bring challenges for both the prosecution and the defense."The events that underly the charges, that happened five years ago," Alperstein said. "So, it's been publicized since then. It was publicized obviously now, again, during this trial. The more publicity that is out there, the more folks that could be potential jurors are going to hear it."

title: Sen. Susan Collins enlists Manchin to woo Maine moderates as she distances herself from Trump
description: Republican Sen. Susan Collins campaigned Wednesday with an unusual ally: Democrat-turned-independent Joe Manchin.
content: Lewiston, Maine — Republican Sen. Susan Collins is campaigning on a simple idea: She can sit across the table from anyone. On Wednesday, she did it literally, sharing breakfast sandwiches with Democrat-turned-independent Joe Manchin and a roomful of Maine voters as she makes her case to people of every political stripe."She's not a Trump senator. She's not a Republican senator or a Democrat senator," Manchin told reporters after dining with Collins in the morning. "She's an American senator that represents her state of Maine."Collins is the only Republican senator up for reelection in a state that President Trump lost. CBS News rates the race a toss-up. But Collins, who is running for a sixth term, has a history of surviving tough reelection battles and outrunning other Republicans. In 2020, she won by more than 8 points, even as Mr. Trump lost Maine by 9 points.Both Collins and Manchin — who represented deep-red West Virginia in the Senate before leaving the Democratic Party and retiring in 2024 — have a history of clashing with their respective parties.Collins worked to distance herself when pressed on Mr. Trump on Wednesday. While touring a local New Balance factory, she was asked about Trump envoy Steve Witkoff calling Russian President Vladimir Putin a "humanitarian" for releasing a jailed U.S. citizen. The question drew a visible reaction from Manchin, who shook his head. Collins responded with a flat "no.""I would describe Putin as a warmonger, a thug. He's certainly not a humanitarian. He is the aggressor in the war against Ukraine," she said. She also said she does not support Mr. Trump's decision to waive new sanctions on Russia and strike a diesel deal with Moscow to import Russian diesel, arguing it will give Russia more funding to attack Ukraine.Collins, who has long defected from parts of Mr. Trump's agenda, has also criticized the president's handling of the Iran war. In debates, she has said the president did not have a good plan and that the conflict should end. Her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, doesn't believe she's sincere in her rebukes."She's the chair of appropriations. If she wants to stop the war, she can cut the funding off for the war," Jackson said at a debate last week. "But she's not willing to do that because Donald Trump wants this and that's what is going to happen."Similar skepticism popped up outside of Collins' breakfast stop. A group of protesters shouted for the incumbent to retire and held signs and cutouts of Brett Kavanaugh's face, a reference to her vote to confirm the Supreme Court justice. Collins' supporters, dressed in bright red, drowned them out with chants of "six more years," when she stepped outside to talk to the press and her tour bus blocked the demonstrators from view.Elaine Makas, a Lewiston Democrat who served in the state legislature from 2002 to 2008, joined the protest. She said she's grateful for Collins' service and calls her "genuinely a nice person," but argued that is not enough. "She's just voting wrong," Makas told CBS News. "She's fallen completely in line with the president."Collins has argued that she frequently votes against Mr. Trump's wishes.Makas echoed Jackson's line of attack. "She only disagrees with him when her vote doesn't matter," she said. She said she personally knows Jackson, a former state Senate president, from their time in the legislature and believes he'll "listen" to Mainers.

title: Denver breaks ground on new river front park near Empower Field
description: Denver is breaking ground on a new park along the South Platte River.
content: Denver is breaking ground on a new park along the South Platte River which will eventually become one of Denver Parks and Recreation's newest spaces. The Denver Housing Authority has been working to redevelop the Sun Valley neighborhood for more than a decade now. The apartment complexes are up and open, and now construction is officially beginning on the final project - an 11-acre river front park. City leaders gathered Wednesday to put shovels in the ground- a symbol of an important milestone for West Denver and the Sun Valley neighborhood. "To have a wonderful place for everyone to be able to play together and grow together, this is a tremendous gift for us all," said Sabrina Douse, who lives in the area.Douse moved to Sun Valley with her family three years ago and has seen an enormous change as the area roughly tripled in density."Everyone is finally coming out of their apartments and getting to know everyone," said Douse.The Sun Valley Riverfront Park will be built in two separate phases and eventually span more than 10 acres along the South Platte River."That means there's room to walk, run, to bike, to take the dog, and to explore the river corridor for everyone," said Denver Parks and Rec's executive director, Jolon Clark. "And there will be a large central pavilion that will be able to welcome and accommodate small festivals, live music, private parties, farmers markets, and more. All of those things, the community came forward and said, 'This is what we want.'"And according to Douse, the neighborhood kids have spoken with the one thing they're looking forward to the most. "The splash pad is one of the biggest things that everybody's excited about," she said. "So, I'm excited that those kids will have a place to really enjoy their summers together and have this safe area to play in.""This is exactly what we want the experience for every Denverite to be," said Denver Mayor Mike Johnston. "You live in a neighborhood where you have an apartment or a house you can afford, you're right next to great walkways and waterways, and you have outside your home a great public park and public space where you can come and play."This project is supported by $2 million from the Elevate Denver Bond Program, approved by voters in 2017 as well as the 2025 Vibrant Denver Bond for the second phase. The first half of the park is expected to open to the public sometime next year.

title: Suspicious packages sent to offices of U.S. Reps. Quigley, Schakowsky, Schneider
description: Police are investigating after suspicious mail was delivered to the district offices of at least three members of Congress from Illinois on Wednesday.
content: Police are investigating after suspicious mail was delivered to the district offices of at least three members of Congress from Illinois on Wednesday. It's the second such incident for all three lawmakers in the past week. U.S. Rep. Jan Schakowsky received a suspicious letter at her district office in Skokie, U.S. Rep. Mike Quigley received a suspicious piece of mail at his district office in Chicago, and U.S. Rep. Brad Schneider received suspicious mail at his district office in Lincolnshire.Suspicious packages delivered to U.S. Rep. Jan Schakowsky's office in Skokie and U.S. Rep. Mike Quigley's office in Chicago prompted hazardous materials responses on Wednesday. It was the second such incident for both lawmakers in the past week."Today, my Skokie office received another suspicious letter. When my staff noticed something unusual about the envelope, they once again immediately alerted authorities out of an abundance of caution," Schakowsky said in a statement. Schakowsky said her office worked with Skokie Police and U.S. Capitol Police to respond to the situation. An employee at her Skokie office said they immediately evacuated the office and called Skokie police, who sent a hazmat team along with their officers. The congresswoman said all of her staff are safe, and her office has been given the all clear to reopen. Skokie police confirmed they were investigating a suspicious package delivered to Schakowsky's office, but did not provide any further information.Schneider said his office also received a piece of suspicious mail on Wednesday in Lincolnshire, prompting them to close the office and contact Lincolnshire Police and U.S. Capitol Police. The office was later given the "all clear" after the letter was safely removed from the office.Meantime, Quigley's office in the Lincoln Park neighborhood in Chicago confirmed they received a suspicious piece of mail on Wednesday. Quigley was not in the office at the time. The building was evacuated, and police and hazardous materials teams were on the scene on Wednesday afternoon."I am always grateful for the extraordinary commitment of our local police and fire departments to the safety of my team and our community. I know the FBI is already investigating last week's letter, and I am confident they will do the same for the most recent incident. Those responsible, once identified, must be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law," Schneider said in a statement.For all three members of Congress, it was the second time in the past week that their offices had received suspicious mail."This is clearly another effort to scare and intimidate elected officials, public servants, and voters in the lead-up to the coming midterm elections. I am again calling on my colleagues and political leaders on both sides of the aisle to condemn political violence in the strongest of terms and turn down the temperature of political discourse," Quigley said in a statement.Schakowsky similarly said she and her team "will not be deterred.""We will keep showing up, doing our jobs, and fighting for the people of Illinois' 9th Congressional District. Nothing changes that commitment," Schakowsky said.Last week a suspicious letter with white powder inside delivered to Maria Pappas' office prompted a hazmat response at the Cook County government building in downtown Chicago. She said she did not believe it was related to the mailings that had been reported nationwide, but instead believed it to be a disgruntled taxpayer angry about their property taxes.Federal authorities have been investigating letter and packages containing white powder substances sent to election offices and the offices of elected officials starting last week, as the 2026 midterm election approaches.

title: Man charged with firing shots outside Kluczynski Federal Building in downtown Chicago
description: A man has been charged with federal weapons violations after he allegedly fired shots outside the John C. Kluczynski Federal Building in downtown Chicago on Tuesday.
content: A man has been charged with federal weapons violations after he allegedly fired shots outside the John C. Kluczynski Federal Building in downtown Chicago on Tuesday.Edmund Horvath, 36, of Lynwood, has been charged with illegal possession of a firearm by an individual previously convicted of misdemeanor domestic violence. According to the charges shortly after 4 a.m. Tuesday, Horvath rode a bicycle down the vehicle ramp leading to the Kluczynski Building's parking garage, at 230 S. Dearborn St. in the Loop.A federal security officer approached Horvath and asked him to leave the area. Moments later, the security officer heard multiple gunshots.Chicago police responded to the scene and found Horvath alone near the Kluczynski Building's garage entrance. Officers spotted multiple shell casings and recovered a 9mm handgun.After he was taken in for questioning, Horvath admitted to firing the handgun and said "he was shooting due to people purportedly chasing him."A bullet hole was also seen in the window of the Central Standard Building, which spans the square block from Clark Street west to LaSalle Street and from Quincy Street south to Jackson Boulevard and houses Wintrust financial offices. Its Clark Street frontage, lined with Ionic columns, is right across from Federal Plaza.Horvath was due to make his first court appearance on Wednesday afternoon.According to the charges, he was previously convicted of misdemeanor domestic battery charges in Cook County in 2024, and was sentenced to 30 days' time served.

title: Late April frost costs Maryland farm $1 million in lost apple, peach crops
description: A late April frost is costing a Maryland farm more than $1 million this fall after freezing temperatures destroyed most of its apple and peach crops.
content: A late April frost is costing a Maryland farm more than $1 million this fall after freezing temperatures destroyed most of its apple and peach crops.Baugher's Orchard and Farm in Westminster said the frost wiped out 90% of its apple and peach crop in a matter of hours.This year has been one of the worst for the five-generation family farm's apple harvest. Farm officials said they have never experienced a frost that cold so late in the spring."Your entire apple and peach crop can come down to one morning in April, and it could just completely wreck it all. And there's nothing you can do about it," Emmitt Baugher told WJZ.Frost leaves orchard with few apples to harvestThe unpredictable weather has forced the farm to adjust to get through the season. Despite using several methods to protect the crops, including windmills and small bonfires near the trees, the farm couldn't overcome the freezing temperatures.Bins that are usually full of apples this time of year are sitting idle as the farm waits for next year's harvest. There simply aren't enough apples left on the trees to pick."This should be empty. The cold storage should be full of apples, but this year it's reversed," Baugher said.The farm has 135 acres of apple orchards and is struggling to find enough fruit to make products for its market, including apple cider."Our packing line would be running pretty much nonstop about this time of year, packing orders, but we run maybe two or three times a week," Baugher said. "We're struggling just to get enough apples to even make the weekly quota for cider."Farm brings in apples as prices riseTo keep up with demand, the farm is bringing in apples from out of state, paying $13 to $15 per bushel â a significant increase from last year.The farm has also had to send home about 20% of its day laborers.Normally, the orchard's trees would be full of apples for customers to pick themselves this time of year. Instead, many trees are bare. Some of the apples that did grow have rotted, contributing to an estimated $1.5 million loss from the apple crop alone."We haven't picked any EverCrisps this year. We haven't been in here at all," Baugher said.Buying apples from outside the farm has also driven up prices for customers. A gallon of apple cider now costs several dollars more than it did last year.Farm looks to next year's harvestDespite the losses, the farm still has to maintain its orchards in hopes of a better harvest next year."Whether it had 100 apples on it, whether it had zero, you still have to take care of it, still have to prune it, still have to mow under it," Baugher said. "You have to do all the same stuff as if you had a crop, but you're doing it all knowing. You're not really going to get anything at the end of it."Some apples that survived the frost and were harvested are misshapen, which Baugher said can happen after exposure to cold temperatures. The apples can resemble small pumpkins and contain few seeds.The farm is hoping to bounce back next year and is asking for more cooperative weather."Try to keep that frost a little earlier. We don't want to have that frost in late April. A little bit of warmer temperatures will be good for sure," Baugher said.To help make ends meet this season, the farm has turned its attention to other crops, including watermelon, sweet corn and pick-your-own pumpkins.The farm said it is grateful for its loyal customers, whose support is helping it get through one of the most challenging years in its history.

title: Maryland man arrested at Fort Lauderdale airport after saying he had bombs, report says
description: A judge set bond at $25,500 for Michael Knight, 31, who, an arrest report says, told a federal officer he was joking.
content: A 31-year-old Maryland man was arrested Tuesday night after allegedly claiming he had bombs inside Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport.Michael Knight is charged with making a false report about a bomb and disorderly intoxication.According to an arrest report, Knight was inside Terminal 4 around 8:30 p.m. when he approached a U.S. Customs and Border Protection officer near Gate G5 and said, "I got bombs." Deputies said Knight told the officer he was joking and tried to walk away before being arrested."It's mind-blowing, but we can't let that happen," traveler Andrew Greco said.A federal officer reported seeing Knight earlier dancing throughout Terminal 4 and displaying "extremely intoxicated" behavior, according to the report. After being read his Miranda rights, Knight told a detective he drank four alcoholic beverages inside the terminal while waiting for his flight, adding that he "never drinks.""Everybody knows that you can't really use that terminology anymore," traveler Ron Sherry said. "It's just disrespectful whether you're drunk or not."Knight appeared in bond court Wednesday, where a judge set his total bond at $25,500. The judge ordered that Knight cannot return to Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport or possess any firearms or ammunition.

title: Columbia Association awarded grant to bolster fitness for those impacted by cancer
description: With the help of a national grant, the Columbia Association now has staff trained to help those impacted by cancer stay fit.
content: Mounting evidence for years has shown that exercise can make a difference for cancer patients.Not only patients, though, but also cancer survivors.With the help of a national grant, the Columbia Association now has staff trained to help those impacted by cancer stay fit.Exercise oncology supportThe Columbia Association was one of ten organizations to get an Exercise Oncology Grant from the Health & Fitness Association.The grant pays for the organizations to train staff in exercise oncology, to develop or expand programs to help those who have had, or survived cancer.CA got $4,800 from the grant. It's meant to train at least three staff members to get an exercise oncology credential.All of the grants are funded by the American Cancer Society.Selected staff will participate in three facilitated learning sessions and receive a best practices guide, according to HFA's announcement of the grants. Meeting people where they're atFitness hasn't always been Joe Richard Saunders's top priority.But things changed with his first cancer diagnosis. Saunders's journey started in 2023 with back pain, he said doctors couldn't figure it out at first."My lung collapsed and I ended up in the ER," Saunders recalled.He ended up having stage 4 diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. He had surgery to remove it under the recommendation of his doctors.Not long after that, though, Saunders was diagnosed with central nervous system (CNS) lymphoma. He had a bone marrow transplant and has been in remission since 2024.Saunders said one of his doctors said his commitment to exercise helped."My doctor kind of flipped the script around and [said] 'You gave youself the best odds going into this fight with cancer,'" he said.CA personal trainer Steve Madewell is also a cancer survivor. He has made it his mission to share the benefits exercise can have at any point of one's cancer journey.When Madewell learned about CA getting one of HFA's grants, he signed up for the training right away.A big benefit from the training, Madewell said, is learning more about the different types of cancers and their effects on the body.It's helped him learn more red flags and other signs to look out for in people impacted by cancer."If anyone has bone metastases, they should not be lifting heavy because you don't wanna injure their bones. That's one case," Madewell said.He adds he learned more about virtual personal training and how to be prepared for a broad range of exercises.Madewell said it can make a big difference having a personal trainer who has not only been through a cancer diagnosis, but also has seen the other side of one."I would've absolutely loved having a trainer that I could meet with and that I could unload on. I could vent to," he said.Having something like this so close to home means the world to Saunders."[The fact someone like Steve can go] I can meet you where you're at and then go from there, to me that's amazing," Saunders said.

title: Denver Nuggets, Colorado Avalanche seasons bring new food vendors and options to Ball Arena
description: Nuggets and Avalanche fans will find nearly 100 new food and drink options on the menu at ball arena.
content: As the Denver Nuggets and Colorado Avalanche return to Ball Arena for their new seasons, fans will find nearly 100 new food and drink items on the menu, including offerings from local businesses joining the arena's lineup of vendors.Kroenke Sports & Entertainment invited CBS Colorado staff to sample some of the new options ahead of the busy season, with an emphasis on offering something for every taste and budget."We've got nearly 100 new items across the whole arena this season," said Bret Workman, Ball Arena's executive chef.Among the additions is a taco salad designed to look like a taco rather than the traditional bowl of lettuce and toppings.The arena staff says they are also keeping affordability in mind as fans look for food during games. Several traditional concessions, including popcorn, nachos, pretzels and hot dogs, are available for $5 each.The new menu received positive reviews from reality television personalities Joe Ferrucci and Jordan Keltner from "Love Is Blind," who sampled some of the offerings."The dumplings were pretty good. We had some chicken tenders. They were pretty good," Ferrucci said."I like the chicken tenders. The pizza was good. Yeah, everything was very good," Keltner said.This season also brings new local businesses into Ball Arena, including Maria Empanada.Lorena Cantarovici, founder of Maria Empanada, said the opportunity carries special meaning for her as a Latina business owner."As a Latina, and for the first time empanadas in Ball Arena, so it's the honor that Maria Empanada is being that first one," Cantarovici said. "We are super excited to be here."Food is a major part of the game-night experience at Ball Arena. An estimated 70% of the arena's 20,000 fans on a typical night purchase food, according to the information provided by the arena.With the Nuggets back on the basketball court and the Avalanche returning to the ice, the expanded menu gives fans more options to enjoy before the action begins and throughout the game.

title: Denver renters want action against cockroach infestation
description: A Denver couple says their apartment complex has not done enough to battle a cockroach infestation.
