content: A Colorado couple said that ongoing maintenance issues, inconsistent pest control treatments and changes in property management have left them frustrated and searching for a way out of their lease.What was supposed to be an exciting new chapter for Colorado native Ashton Dechant and his girlfriend, Loren, quickly turned into a nightmare. The couple moved into ReNew Kennedy Park apartments, located along South Parker Road in Denver, on May 1. But less than three weeks later, they spotted their first cockroach. "It's just been a nightmare since we got here, to be 100% honest," Dechant said.Dechant said that the cockroach infestation is just one of several problems they've experienced since moving in. He claimed their apartment has broken windows, damaged door frames, plumbing issues and air conditioning that wasn't working as summer approached. Meanwhile, he said that the complex has prioritized renovations to shared amenities, including the gym and pool. But his biggest concern remains the cockroaches, which he says are growing in both number and size.Dechant said that he's repeatedly contacted the leasing office about the infestation. Although pest control workers have come out to spray, he said that treatments have been inconsistent and the problem persists. A recent change in property management has only added to his frustration, leaving him feeling like the process is starting over. "Since we moved here, it's been a runaround circle game," Dechant said.Colorado landlord-tenant attorney Steven Flaxman said that state law requires landlords to take prompt action when notified of an infestation. He explained that tenants may have legal options if landlords fail to adequately address the problem, including arranging extermination services and potentially deducting eligible costs from rent if they follow the required legal procedures.For Dechant, however, the goal is no longer another pest control treatment. He wants to leave ReNew Kennedy Park. He says management offered to move the couple into another building, but only if they signed a new yearlong lease."I'm like, no, I want my last six months because I'm going to leave after this," he said.Flaxman said Colorado's warranty of habitability law may allow tenants to terminate their lease if a qualifying habitability issue is repaired but reoccurs within six months, provided the legal requirements are met.For now, Dechant and his girlfriend remain in their apartment, hoping for a resolution to a problem they say has overshadowed what was supposed to be a fresh start.CBS Colorado reporter Kennedy Cook reached out to the leasing office and the property managers, but got no response.

title: Video shows quick-thinking bystander stop runaway St. Paul school bus
description: A bystander's split-second decision saved a school bus driver and the kids on board Monday on the east side of St. Paul, Minnesota.
content: A bystander's split-second decision saved a school bus driver and the kids on board Monday on the east side of St. Paul, Minnesota.It happened outside Ya Bricks Snacks and Tobacco off North Mendota Street and Fremont Avenue East in the Dayton's Bluff neighborhood.Surveillance camera footage from the store shows Ebro Ahmed sprint toward the bus. He had just seen the driver drop off some kids when the bus kept rolling forward with the doors still opened.Ahmed saw the driver was having a medical issue, jumped inside and stopped the bus. "It caught me by surprise because I was kind of confused about the door open," Ahmed said. "So then I ran towards the bus and noticed he was having an emergency so I just hopped on there."Ahmed said that at first, he wasn't able to stop the bus. He tried to throw it in park but then it went in reverse. After he was able to put the bus into stop, he looked behind him."I see all the kids kind of a little scared, crying, you know, with their phones out, getting ready to call the police," he said.Ahmed said he was in part inspired by "Grey's Anatomy," because the doctors are calm amid chaotic situations. "It's something you would never think would happen in real life," the 27-year-old said.A spokesperson with St. Paul Public Schools told WCCO Wednesday the driver was transporting students from Battle Creek Middle School, located about 3 miles southeast of the crash site. There were 19 students on the bus at the time."Another bus came to pick the students up to continue on their route home," the spokesperson said. "Students were likely late arriving home, and some may have been upset at the situation."St. Paul Public Schools said Wednesday evening that the driver has been released from the hospital and is resting at home.

title: Stockton widow keeps comic book artist Tony DeZuniga's legacy alive
description: Tina DeZuniga is carrying on her late husband Tony DeZuniga's legacy by keeping his artwork, which was recently on display at the Haggin Museum in Stockton.
content: Tony DeZuniga helped pave the way for Filipino artists in the American comic book industry, becoming the first Filipino artist to work for DC Comics. More than a decade after his death, his wife, Tina DeZuniga, is continuing to share his legacy with the community where their love story began.DeZuniga, who died in 2012, was survived by his wife and five children. His artwork was featured in an exhibit at Stockton's Haggin Museum over the summer, giving fans and visitors a chance to celebrate his contributions to comics and the arts.For Tina, seeing her late husband's work displayed is a reminder of both his talent and the impact he had on generations of Filipino artists."Oh, it's always exciting to see his workâ¦he did almost everything: Batman, Superman, Spider-Man, X-Men," Tina said.DeZuniga's career spanned iconic superheroes and multiple artistic mediums. But his influence extended beyond the pages of comic books.When he entered the industry, the Philippines faced a shortage of paper that affected its comic book business. Tina said the circumstances helped create an opportunity for Tony to connect Filipino artists with international publishers.Tina said Tony helped bring a publisher to the Philippines, opening doors for artists who wanted to work with major comic book companies."So that's why now, even the young artists are enjoying (working) for DC, Marvel, and other publishers. It'ss because of Tony. He's the one who started the whole thing (for) the Filipino artists. That's why he's like a hero for all these artists."Although the two grew up near each other in Manila, the capital of the Philippines, they did not meet until their paths crossed in Stockton.Tina was running Best Lumpia, a restaurant she owned for 35 years, when Tony approached her about catering a house blessing for a home he had recently purchased. At first, she said, she wasn't convinced by his claim that he was an artist. That changed when she visited his home and saw his work."You know how men try to impress women?" she said. "Like, 'Oh, I'm an artist.' I said, 'OK, OK,' and then one day, because he just moved here from San Francisco, he asked me, 'Can you cater for my house blessing, because I just bought a house?' I said, 'OK.' So I went to check on the place, and I saw the artwork and said, 'He's really an artist.'"In 2009, the couple walked a red carpet in Los Angeles for a movie premiere, an experience Tina remembers as a departure from their everyday lives."Oh, it's something different," she said. "I mean, you really feel like you're a celebrity."Tony also explored art beyond comic books, working with different materials and mediums, including work with Sega."Tony is a real artist because no matter what medium he used or whatever things he would do in art, he's doing it so magnificently," she said. "I mean, it's really good. Drawing with pencil or painting, everything, he does everything so well."So much so that Tina encouraged him to pursue painting after they married. One of his paintings depicted a sabongero, or a man involved in cockfighting, a subject Tony worried might be too culturally specific for an art competition."I entered it in one of the art competitions," Tina said. "And he said, 'Oh, that's too Filipino. I don't think it's gonna work.' But guess what? It became the best of show at Delicato."The Haggin Museum exhibit was another milestone for Tina, who said it had long been a dream to see Tony's work displayed there.Museum CEO Susan Obert told CBS News Sacramento the museum offered to bring food to honor the family at the exhibit's grand opening. Tina, however, chose to cater the event herself, serving Filipino food and dessert.Best Lumpia is still in business after Tina sold it to her brother. She said the barbecue sauce is her mother's recipe.

title: Baby who had 50 seizures a day now seizure-free after surgery at Children's Minnesota
description: For two parents in St. Paul, Minnesota, the birth of their daughter was supposed to be one of the happiest moments in their lives. But soon after Loralei was born, Nkaujfuah and Jonathan knew something was wrong.
content: For two parents in St. Paul, Minnesota, the birth of their daughter was supposed to be one of the happiest moments in their lives. But soon after Loralei was born, Nkaujfuah and Jonathan knew something was wrong."The seizures progressively got worse," Loralei's mother Nkaujfuah said. "I felt scared. I didn't know what was going on with her. I just knew something was wrong and I just needed to get her help."Lorelei was having up to 50 seizures a day. Medication wasn't working. "Seizures at that young age, especially five weeks of age, can be catastrophic in nature," said Dr. Nitin Agarwal, a pediatric epileptologist at Minnesota Epilepsy Group.Agarwal and a team of neurosurgeons at Children's Minnesota got together to come up with a plan."We all sat down and had a discussion about the things and decided to proceed with this procedure called a hemispherectomy," Agarwal said. It's a surgery where the neural pathways between the left and right hemisphere of the brain are separated. Lorelei would be one of the youngest patients to have it done. Something that worried her parents."She was just so young," Nkaujfuah said. "I was just really scared of the outcome and the process."Doctors knew the surgery wasn't going to be easy."It's still one of the more challenging surgeries that we as neurosurgeons perform. But in a two-month-old it's even more challenging," Medical Director of Neurosciences at Children's Minnesota Dr. Meysam Kebriaei said.But the surgery proved to be a success. Lorelei has been seizure-free ever since. And at her three month post-op check in, she was all smiles."All the developmental milestones are catching up," Agarwal said. "The family is very pleased, we are very pleased and we are very hopeful that she will have a very good outcome from here.""She's dealing with normal baby stuff," Kebriaei said. "She's keeping her parents awake at night but not because of seizures."Lorelei's parents look forward to her living a happy and healthy life. "We made it out to the other side," Nkaujfuah said. "It's just amazing seeing her grow and seeing her smile."

title: Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson to give head tax another shot in 2027 budget proposal
description: Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson to give head tax another shot in 2027 budget proposal
content: Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson unveiled his $17.6 billion 2027 budget proposal for the city on Wednesday, relying on a head tax that most aldermen have already rejected."My 2027 budget ensures that every Chicagoan receives their fair share of the investments, services, and opportunities that define our city, funded by responsible spending cuts that protect essential services and by asking wealthy corporations to pay their fair share," Johnson said in his budget address at City Hall.The mayor wants to take another crack at his controversial corporate head tax to help offset an $882 million shortfall, despite most aldermen warning him ahead of time that they would reject any such proposal. Johnson is looking to charge companies with 125 or more full-time employees $25 per worker per month. Companies whose employees work in parts of Chicago officially designated as Socioeconomically Disadvantaged Areas would qualify for credits to cover the cost of the tax for each employee in those areas.While this tax is often called a head tax, Mayor Johnson prefers to think of it as the "equitable employer tax."Mayor Johnson's office estimates the head tax would raise $101 million a year. He said it would affect less than 3% of Chicago's businesses. The revenue would go toward pothole repairs, libraries, and gun violence reduction. As he prepares to run for re-election in 2027, the mayor is clearly reaching out to his progressive base, arguing corporations need to chip in more to help the city balance its budget.Johnson said Chicagoans tell him they want corporate America to help with the heavy lift of erasing the city's $882 million budget deficit."There is no reason to coddle or feel sorry for corporations. They are doing just fine," Johnson said. "Large corporations can and should contribute more to the city whose people, infrastructure, and neighborhoods make their success possible."But the same City Council coalition that passed the 2026 budget without a head tax over Johnson's objections said his second bid for the tax is a non-starter.Last month, the 29 alders who are part of the City Council Budget Accountability Coalition sent a joint letter to the mayor declaring their willingness to work together on a budget plan. However, the group specifically requested no head tax, and said they would not support any move that increases costs for companies that keep or create jobs in Chicago."It was disingenuous for the mayor to put the head tax into the budget. Twenty-nine of us signed that letter. Clearly that part of it's dead on arrival," Ald. Bill Conway (34th) said after Johnson's budget address.The mayor's opponents argue the head tax is a job killer that would discourage companies from relocating to Chicago."The majority of council will not support, so the fact that it was proposed in here feels very much like a political tactic," Ald. Nicole Lee (11th) said.Johnson proposed a $21-per-employee monthly head tax on companies with more than 100 employees as part of his 2026 budget proposal last year, and later revised it to a $33-per-employee monthly head tax on companies with more than 500 employees. The City Council voted it down, and the mayor's opponents passed an alternate budget plan over his objections.There is no indication that the parliamentary arithmetic in the City Council has shifted in favor of a head tax this year. Some Chicago aldermen warned weeks ago that a head tax proposal would be dead on arrival.The alders wrote to the mayor that while the current budget gap forecast is lower than previously estimated, "it remains a fiscal challenge of the first order," one which they believe three principles should anchor. One of those principles is rejecting a head tax or any other "tax on job growth."The other two principles the alders are endorsing are rejecting an increase in property taxes and avoiding relying on "Springfield revenues that have not been approved."Meanwhile, Johnson also proposed a 15-cent packaging waste tax that would expand the city's existing retail bag tax to include all forms of packaging for carry-out or delivery, bringing in an estimated $9 million.He also wants sports betting companies to pay a 20% tax, up from 10.25% to bring in $37 million, although the city's sports betting tax is facing a court challenge, with opponents arguing only the state of Illinois is authorized to impose such a tax.The mayor also plans to increase personal property lease taxes from 15% to 20%. The tax rate for car leases would remain at 15%, while leases for film production equipment would see their tax reduced to 11%. The mayor's office estimates the changes to the personal property lease tax would generate $234 million.Johnson also estimates the city will bring in an additional $18 million in parking ticket revenue from the plan to expand the Smart Streets program citywide. The program uses automated cameras to ticket drivers who block bus lanes, bike lanes, and crosswalks.On top of the required $2.97 billion payment to cover the costs of city employee pensions, Johnson is proposing a $364 million supplemental pension payment.The mayor also plans to declare a $520 million surplus in tax increment finance revenue. Of that, the city will net roughly $100 million, and $285 million will go to the Chicago Public Schools. The rest will go to various other government bodies in Chicago. Johnson's team also suggests taking out a loan of $480 million to help pay off police misconduct claims sooner, which the team says would cut down on legal costs.The mayor's acting budget director, Jonathan Ernst, said his office has been through every department line by line — shaving what it can without impacting city services.The City Council Budget Committee will hold a series of meetings over the next three weeks to allow alders to question each city department about the mayor's budget plan. The City Council has until the end of the year to pass a 2027 spending plan.This year is an election year, leaving some alders on the fence on the mayor's budget proposal, and prepared for a long fight over the 2027 spending plan."The politics of it are challenging, right? The way it was presented last year kind of left folks pretty entrenched, and so trying to figure out how to get to 26 [votes] is going to be, I think, harder this time," said Ald. Andre Vasquez (40th), who voted against the 2026 budget passed by the mayor's City Council opponents.

title: Northwestern University student dies after being pulled out of Lake Michigan in Evanston
description: A Northwestern University student was pronounced dead after she was pulled from Lake Michigan on Wednesday morning near the school's Evanston campus.
content: A Northwestern University student was pronounced dead after she was pulled from Lake Michigan on Wednesday morning near the school's Evanston campus.Around 7 a.m., Evanston police and firefighters responded to the lakefront near the university's southern lakefill area, just north of Clark Street Beach, after a person spotted a person in the water.Rescue divers pulled an unresponsive woman out of the water and began performing CPR. She was taken to Endeavor Health Evanston Hospital, where she was pronounced dead. Police said she had been in the water for about 30 minutes.The Cook County Medical Examiner's office said the victim is a 19-year-old woman. Northwestern University officials confirmed she was a student. CBS News Chicago is not identifying the woman out of respect for her family's wishes. Sources said she is from out of state."Our thoughts are with the student's family and friends. The University is providing support services to impacted community members," a Northwestern spokesperson said.The woman's death is under investigation, but police said there is no danger to the public.Jackie Ovalles said she was taking her husband to work at Northwestern when she saw the commotion on the lakefront on Wednesday morning."It's sad. I'm sure there's students from all over the world, and we have a lot of visitors not from Illinois near Lake Michigan, and Lake Michigan can be dangerous, and a lot of people aren't aware of how dangerous it can be," she said.Police also warned that Lake Michigan can be dangerous. "Hazard warnings and signs prohibiting swimming and fishing are posted along Northwestern University's lakefront property. Evanston Police urge people to follow posted warnings, check lake conditions before approaching the water and follow instructions from city or university officials to stay out of the water and off break walls and rocks," police said.Evanston's beaches have been closed since Labor Day, the traditional end of the swimming season on Lake Michigan, so no lifeguards were on duty.

title: Police say 2 teen girls arrested for planning Riverside County school shooting may have had motive of revenge
description: Two teenage girls were arrested this month in connection with their alleged plans to carry out a shooting at Corona High School, according to police, who were contacted by the FBI earlier in October.
content: Police say that the two teenage girls who were arrested this month in connection with their alleged plans to carry out a school shooting at Corona High School may have had a hit list and were potentially planning some sort of revenge.In a news release shared Tuesday, Corona Police Department officers said they were contacted by the FBI on October 6 after "they had identified online social media communications regarding a possible threat" at the high school, which is located on W. 10th Street. Corona police told CBS LA on Wednesday, just hours after the arrests were announced, that Meta, the platform that owns several social media sites including Facebook and Instagram, alerted the FBI of the planned attack."A collaborative investigation led to the immediate arrest of a 15-year-old female Corona High School student," according to the release.Corona PD detectives executed numerous search warrants for electronic devices and communications and searched multiple Riverside County residences, the release said. Through their investigation, police identified and arrested a second suspect, a 15-year-old female student from Norco High School who previously attended Corona High. "The evidence obtained showed the two suspects had spent several months researching school shootings and discussed how they could carry out a potential attack at Corona High School on an unspecified future date," police said. "Communications showed the suspects discussed methods to obtain weapons, but had not yet been able to do so."Police said no weapons were discovered throughout the course of their investigation, which remains ongoing and in collaboration with the FBI, Riverside County Sheriff's Office and the Corona-Norco Unified School District. "Parents and students are reminded to immediately report anything they see or hear that could be concerning, as awareness plays a vital role in keeping everyone safe," police said.Both suspects remain in custody on charges of conspiracy to commit murder, and the Riverside County District Attorney's Office is reviewing the case, police said. The DA's Office said it couldn't confirm the charges or the suspects' identities because of their ages. "The average suspect that commits a crime like this is gonna do it independently or by themselves, and it is not very common for them to be females," said Corona PD Lt. Robert Montanez, who added that the suspects had a map of the high school campus, ways to skirt the law and acquire firearms and "specifics how they would carry out the attack." They also allegedly had a list of targets that included both students and teachers.In a statement, the Corona-Norco Unified School District said the two suspects haven't returned to school since their arrests."We are grateful for the swift response of the Corona Police Department and their continued partnership throughout this investigation," the district said. "We understand that hearing news like this can be unsettling for families, and we want our parents to know that the safety and well-being of our students and staff remain our highest priority."FBI Director Kash Patel addressed the incident on social media on Wednesday morning, thanking local authorities for their quick work in preventing tragedy. "Outstanding work by our agents and law enforcement partners," Patel's post said. "Protecting our kids is non-negotiable."As the investigation continues, police asked anyone with more information to contact Corona PD Detective Edwards at George.Edwards@CoronaCA.gov or 951-279-3656.

title: Sacramento County officials urge residents to get flood insurance as 'Super El Niño' looms
description: Sacramento County District 5 Supervisor Pat Hume is urging residents to prepare for heavy rain and possible flooding.
content: Sacramento County District 5 Supervisor Pat Hume is urging residents to prepare for heavy rain and possible flooding, with the possibility of a 'Super El NiÃ±o' looming. The district, which consists of multiple communities, including Wilton, Elk Grove, and Isleton, is no stranger to dangerous flooding. In the winter of 2022-2023, several consecutive powerful storms led to a levee breach, which caused significant flooding along the Cosumnes River, killing three people. Physical preparations for possible flooding have already begun. Reclamation District 800, responsible for levee maintenance along the Cosumnes River in the area, says it has invested tens of millions of dollars into repairs and upgrades."RDA is going to be as ready as possible," said Leland Schneider, a member of the Board of Directors for the reclamation district. "We've all joined forces to be ready for this when it does come."The county also wants people to be prepared insurance-wise. According to Hume, over 80% of properties identified as 'at-risk' in unincorporated Sacramento County do not have flood insurance â and because new policies often have a 30-day waiting period before coverage takes effect, Hume says the time to act is now."This is a good time to start looking at that," said Harold Newbill, an insurance agent at McClatchy Insurance Agency. Newbill said that the agency has seen an uptick in activity in flood insurance quotes on their website.Homeowners who are concerned about if their home is at risk of flooding can visit the Floodsmart website to check its status.

title: San Jose couple's foundation works to improve youth literacy levels
description: Two-thirds of children who cannot read by the time they're in fourth grade will wind up in jail or on welfare, according to the World Literacy Foundation. A San Jose couple is working to break that disturbing trend.
content: Two-thirds of children who cannot read by the time they're in fourth grade will wind up in jail or on welfare, according to the World Literacy Foundation. A San Jose couple is working to break that disturbing trend.Alicia and Darrell Cortez recently arrived at Shirakawa Elementary School in San Jose bearing books and the promise of prizes."We're going to reward them with this experience of a lifetime, a holiday shopping spree," Darrell Cortez said. He and his wife Alicia started Shop with a Cop Foundation Silicon Valley in 2008. Just before Darrell retired from 30 years on the San Jose police force, he was looking for way to serve the community.He said he liked the concept behind the national Shop with a Cop. Although they're not affiliated with the nationwide initiative, the couple started taking underserved kids on a shopping spree for the holidays."The joy for me is the actual day of the event - to see the joy on the faces of the children," said Alicia, a retired educator.In 2015, they added a 10-week literacy program in underperforming San Jose schools targeting third graders."It's the turning point. It's where they're learning to read and they make that transition to reading to learn," Alicia said.The couple knows reading can transform a child's path in life. The Literacy Project Foundation says 85% of youth in juvenile court system struggle to read."The juvenile hall-to-prison pipeline begins in the classroom so we have to do what we can to put a stop to that," Darrell said.On their recent visit to Shirakawa Elementary, the Cortezes and their volunteers introduced books to celebrate Hispanic Heritage Month. The nonprofit helped raise reading scores at the school by 18% last year, so more than half of the students can read at or above grade level.Isaac's test scores jumped last year."Then I started doing that program and actually locked in and I passed and I was excited and got all the prizes," he said.Martin now reads for entertainment."When I went on vacation, I bring one of my favorite books and it helps me," said the fourth grader.The 200 students in the literacy program receive a Shop with a Cop Foundation Silicon Valley shopping spree during the holiday season. They each receive a gift card for $300. Top readers get to spend $50 more.Take Samantha. She not only bought herself a Hello Kitty plushie during last year's shopping festivities, but she also found that she enjoyed the required 20 minutes of reading a day."I think I just want to read because I want to, not because I want something," she beamed.Peter Diaz. California Community President of Citizens Equity First Credit Union (CEFCU) helps sponsor the Cortez's service projects."They're all in," Diaz said. "They help build that foundation which helps improve educational success, so it's an investment for the future.""It's rewarding and humbling at the same time to know that these students are excelling," Darrell said.

title: Demand for home energy bill assistance soaring in Massachusetts: "More panic than usual"
description: With colder weather approaching and high oil prices already here, Massachusetts families are increasingly seeking financial help for their energy bills.
content: With colder weather approaching and high oil prices already here, Massachusetts families are increasingly seeking financial help for their energy bills, as the state prepares to launch a new relief program aimed at expanding assistance to middle-income households.Earlier this month, Gov. Maura Healey announced $15 million in supplemental funding for the existing federal Home Energy Assistance Program, along with $34 million for a new, one-time relief program aimed at middle-income families who heat their homes with oil."Many could pay as much as $700 more for a single fill up," Healey said of heating oil prices.Frustrating process to get assistanceHowever, the new program will not launch until December, and some residents say a lack of clarity surrounding the assistance has made navigating the process frustrating.Jennifer McGrath has been trying to help her retired elderly parents on the South Shore access financial assistance but says she has already encountered hurdles."It was just frustrating, and if it was my parents doing it, you know, they would have probably given up," McGrath said, noting her parents were wary about seeking help to begin with."We're living through times where people are legitimately financially stressed out, and I'm talking across all income brackets. This kind of stuff provides like a glimmer of hope. So, it can be frustrating if that isn't something that's easily accessible or easy to figure out," McGrath said, explaining the number of people she has called trying to get information.The Massachusetts Office of Housing and Livable Communities say they've received more than 13,000 submissions through its interest form. Residents are asked to visit Mass.gov/heatinghelp to see if they are eligible for assistance.For now, applications are only open for the longtime federal Home Energy Assistance Program for low-income qualifiers. State officials say more than 6,400 first-time applicants have already applied, as well as 53,000 returning applicants.In the meantime, officials are encouraging residents struggling to pay their bills to contact their local community action agency for guidance."More than 200 calls daily"Action for Boston Community Development (ABCD), one of the local organizations helping residents access financial assistance in Boston and 10 surrounding communities, says inquiries about the Home Energy Assistance Program have more than doubled since last winter."We're seeing more than 200 calls daily," said ABCD CEO Sharon Scott-Chandler. "This early in the season, that's unusual."Scott-Chandler says many families are already worried about how they will afford to heat their homes this winter."We've talked to a lot of people on the phone who are very concerned about the high price of oil, high price of energy, and so we're seeing more demand and more panic than usual," she said.Scott-Chandler says assistance will be available for those who qualify and encourages families not to hesitate to seek help."Everyone is welcome to and should be calling if they're having difficulty making ends meet and paying energy bills, putting food on the table, paying their rent. I mean, that's what this really is about, it's an entire affordability crisis," Scott-Chandler added.

title: 72-year-old Commerce man denies federal voter fraud allegations
description: At 72 years old, Omar Muñoz said he never expected to find himself in handcuffs and at the center of a federal voter fraud investigation.
content: At 72 years old, Omar Muñoz said he never expected to find himself in handcuffs and at the center of a federal voter fraud investigation."Six police cars, 18 police officers," Muñoz said, recalling his arrest on Monday. "We had a helicopter over here, and they threatened to do damage if I don't open the door."Prosecutors accuse the Belize-born lawful permanent resident of registering to vote in Los Angeles County in 2019 and voting in four elections. Muñoz denies the claims and says he has never registered or voted. "That is fraud to me," he said. He also suggested someone else could have used his personal information, pointing to a past incident."There was an Omar Muñoz who used my name and social that was working at the Cheesecake Factory in Calabasas," Muñoz said. "The IRS was the one who fixed that for me."The case is part of "Operation Protect the Vote," which resulted in charges against 28 people in California. Reacting to the charges, State Attorney General Rob Bonta said there is no widespread voter fraud in California but that there are, at times, one-off examples of voter fraud. Muñoz said he's had six surgeries and suffers from diabetes, a heart murmur, neuropathy and high blood pressure. "Right now, I'm apprehensive, feeling a lot of pain and my body is trembling," he said. While the charges against him remain allegations, Muñoz said he's confident that he will be found innocent in the end. "At the same time, your name gets dragged," he said. The U.S. Attorney's Office has not responded to CBS LA's request for comment.

title: Maryland man guilty in $18 million Medicare fraud case involving nursing homes during COVID-19 pandemic
description: A Maryland man has been convicted by a federal jury of fraudulently billing Medicare for expensive respiratory tests for nursing home patients during the COVID-19 pandemic.
content: A Maryland man has been convicted by a federal jury of fraudulently billing Medicare for expensive respiratory tests for nursing home patients during the COVID-19 pandemic. The man found guilty was 42-year-old Patrick Britton-Harr of Annapolis, said a news release issued Tuesday by the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ). Britton-Harr provided COVID-19 testing kits to nursing homes across the country during the pandemic, court documents and evidence presented at trial showed, according to the DOJ. But in addition to the COVID-19 specimens collected and billed to Medicare, Britton-Harr also requested reimbursement "for separate, high-priced respiratory pathogen panel (RPP) tests purportedly conducted in a laboratory he owned in Arizona," the release said. The RPP tests are designed to screen for over 30 respiratory pathogens. The defendant falsely claimed to Medicare that physicians who treated patients ordered the RPP tests. But in reality, the physicians never ordered the tests for their nursing home patients, and several testified at trial that they had never ordered an RPP test for any patient during their entire medical careers, the DOJ said.As a result, Britton-Harr's company, Provista Health, "fraudulently billed Medicare $18.7 million for RPP testing purportedly performed in just six months, of which Medicare paid more than $7.2 million," the release noted. "Mr. Britton-Harr's decision to exploit elderly nursingâhome residents and inexperienced interns for personal gain during a global pandemic is unconscionable," said a statement by U.S. Attorney Kelly O. Hayes for the District of Maryland. "This verdict reinforces our message: there is nowhere to hide for those who commit fraud. We will find you and prosecute you to the fullest extent of the law." The fraud scheme involving Britton-Harr permitted him to "fund a lavish lifestyle," which, among other things, included him buying a $112,500 Porsche 911 and making $25,000 monthly mortgage payments on a waterfront mansion in Annapolis, the DOJ said.

title: Pope Leo won't need further treatment after lung cancer surgery, doctors say
description: Pope Leo XIV will not need any further treatment after having lung cancer surgery, his doctors said in a statement.
content: Pope Leo XIV will not need any further treatment after having lung cancer surgery, his doctors said in a statement Wednesday.Test results confirmed that the pope's cancer was localized, Dr. Luigi Carbone, the pope's physician, and Dr. Stefano Margaritora, his surgeon, said in a statement."A subsequent oncological evaluation has confirmed that no further therapy is required," the doctors said.Leo's cancer diagnosis was revealed last week after he was admitted to a Rome hospital for what was initially described as a surgery to remove a lung nodule. The pontiff was diagnosed with the common cancer of lung adenocarcinoma, and doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung during a procedure that lasted about 90 minutes.In an interview with Vatican News published over the weekend, Margaritora said the discovery of the malignant lung tumor was "entirely accidental." A small spot was found at the base of the lung during a routine exam, he said, adding that doctors wouldn't have found it if it was located a little higher up."The Holy Father falls into the category of people who discover they have lung cancer entirely by chance – not because they are undergoing preventive screening, but because they undergo examinations for other reasons," Margaritora told Vatican News.On Saturday, four days after his surgery, the 71-year-old pope left the hospital and was greeted by a large crowd cheering for him. He delivered his traditional Sunday noon prayer at the Vatican, thanking the faithful for their prayers and the hospital staff for their care."This experience has made me feel particularly close to all those who are living with illness or infirmity," Leo said. "Now that I have overcome this delicate phase, as you know, I will gradually resume my activities, always with God's help and your prayers."Leo is continuing his recovery at the Vatican and hosted his usual general audience Wednesday, waving from the popemobile to the large crowd of the faithful gathered in St. Peter's Square and blessing children raised up to him.The pope is expected to travel to South America in early November, the Vatican said.

title: Teacher who survived Oregon school shooting recounts being shot, pretending to be dead to survive
description: Becky Drury, the 54-year-old teacher wounded in the shooting at an Oregon elementary school last week, says she was shot before she had "any chance to act."
content: Becky Drury, the 54-year-old teacher wounded in the shooting at an Oregon elementary school last week, is sharing a statement about her experience, saying the gunman shot her before she had "any chance to act."In the statement Wednesday, Drury recalled running to see what was happening outside her classroom at Silver Rail Elementary School before spotting the shooter."I turned to shut the door behind me, but the shooter was already there," Drury wrote. "Before I could do anything more, he shot me at close range and I fell to the ground.""Lying on the floor, I saw that my left hand was almost completely severed from the gunshot, and my other arm was also severely injured," she continued. "I could not get up, defend myself, or protect anyone else. So, I did the only thing I could do, which was to pretend to be dead in the hope he would not shoot me again."Drury suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries from the Oct. 15 shooting that killed three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and a 25-year-old teacher. Another student, a 7-year-old, was also seriously wounded.The suspect was identified as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, a former student at the school. Police said he shot through the school's locked doors before entering a special needs classroom and opening fire.The gunman was tackled by another teacher and fatally shot by an armed bystander, 36-year-old Kaylub Giamanco, who followed him into the school, according to police. Drury said Wednesday she was sharing what happened to her because "I want to make sure the events of that day and my actions in particular are reported accurately.""I know there has been contradictory reporting about my actions that day, but the truth is I was shot before I had any chance to act," she wrote.She thanked those who have supported her since the shooting, and said, "What happened in that classroom was unimaginable, and like so many in this community, my heart is broken for everyone affected by this tragedy."

title: Ukraine supporters rally at Minnesota Capitol amid news of US prisoner release, possible negotiations
description: A small group of demonstrators rallied on the steps of the Minnesota State Capitol in St. Paul Wednesday morning to show their support of Ukraine amid its yearlong war with Russia.
content: A small group of demonstrators rallied on the steps of the Minnesota State Capitol in St. Paul Wednesday morning to show their support of Ukraine amid its yearslong war with Russia.Demonstrators were joined by members of the Ukrainian American Community Center, who say this support means everything to them.The rally comes amid news early Wednesday that Russia freed Stephen Hubbard, a U.S. citizen who had been in jail for more than four years on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine. Also early Wednesday, Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to resume three-way negotiations with Ukraine and the U.S. aimed at ending the war.Rally participants WCCO spoke with Wednesday say they're cautiously optimistic that all of this news could mean things are trending in the direction of peace."So many people are hurt, killed, families destroyed, cities," said Iryna Petrus, with the Ukrainian American Community Center. "And it's not about infrastructure, it's not about industry, but it's humanity. It comes very deeply."Petrus spends her days in constant communication with family and friends overseas. She was joined Wednesday by Wendy Morris, who spent the summer delivering vehicles from Scotland to Ukraine to be used to evacuate people.Petrus says for her, the end of war means one thing: hope."We are divided by language, by nation, but we are not divided in our hearts if we truly understand why we are here on this earth," she said.

title: 6 charged with organizing dozens of "sham marriages" to help immigrants get green cards in Massachusetts
description: Six people are facing federal charges after they allegedly charged thousands of dollars to organize "sham marriages" in Massachusetts.
content: Six people are facing federal charges after they allegedly charged thousands of dollars to organize "sham marriages" in Massachusetts to help undocumented immigrants get green cards and U.S. citizenship.Jennifer Gonzalez, Amara Pugh, Erica Daniels, Cherice Alejandro, Jessica Tavares and Jalyn Hill are each charged with harboring illegal aliens, conspiracy to harbor illegal aliens and marriage fraud. Hill is currently serving a state prison sentence for a firearms offense. The five women were arrested Wednesday morning.U.S. Attorney for Massachusetts Leah Foley said at a news conference that Gonzalez was the mastermind of the scam. Foley said Gonzalez charged about $40,000 per marriage and arranged 18-20 sham marriages per year for the last decade.Gonzalez, who is a U.S. citizen, has a criminal history with convictions that include assault and battery, identity fraud, and fraud.Foley alleged that Gonzalez netted about $6 million throughout the course of the 10 years, and was heard on a recording telling a cooperating witness that she used the money to buy land in the Dominican Republic. "Every time I have a spare dollar I just invest in new property in my country. That's what I really do. I like to buy land. Like, I have a lot of land in my country," Gonzalez said in the recording.Pugh served as the secretary for the plan, Foley said, while the other four women were paid by Gonzalez and "customers" to participate in one or more fake marriages "for the sole purpose that customers could get citizenship." The women would enter fraudulent marriages with the men and stay married for several years to avoid suspicion. Foley said the women and their "customers" would take "couples photos" on the day the marriage became official to make the relationship look real. The undocumented immigrants would use the pictures while applying for citizenship.Gonzalez was heard in one recording saying she "stopped doing weddings at the end of 2024 because that's when Trump was becoming president" and immigration in 2025 was "a little harsh."The cooperating witness also captured Gonzalez saying Massachusetts is a "sanctuary" for immigrants."Massachusetts is the best place for you to be. That is a fact," Gonzalez said. "You get health insurance. You get a lot of help as an immigrant here."Foley said Gonzalez also fraudulently collected over $124,000 in Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits.The defendants face potential sentences totaling 25 years in prison on the three charges combined. Two of the women declined comment while leaving court, attempting to use their shirts to cover their faces as they passed WBZ-TV reporter Logan Hall. "No. Leave me alone," one of them said. "This case sends a clear message. Marriage is not a loophole, it is not a shortcut, and it is not a tool for gaming U.S. immigration laws. Marriage fraud is not victimless," said Shawn Saucier, northeast regional chief of U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

title: Silver Diner appeals to Maryland Gov. Moore to keep its restaurant at BWI
description: The Silver Diner has appealed to Maryland Gov. Wes Moore in a renewed effort to keep its restaurant open at Baltimore-Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport (BWI).
content: The Silver Diner has appealed to Maryland Gov. Wes Moore in a renewed effort to keep its restaurant open at Baltimore-Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport (BWI). The state of Maryland has the authority to require BWI's Germany-based concessions manager, Fraport USA, "to place an independent, locally owned restaurant like Silver Diner in this space," said a press release about a letter sent to Moore by Silver Diner CEO Bob Giaimo. "By utilizing the authority at the state's disposal, and instructing Fraport to renew its lease agreement with Silver Diner, you would be acting in the best interests of BWI Airport and the Maryland economy," Giaimo says in his letter to Moore.The Maryland-based restaurant chain sued airport concessions manager Fraport USA last month, alleging breach of contract and fraudulent misrepresentation. Silver Diner claims Fraport demanded an $8 million to $10 million rebuild as a condition for renewing its lease at BWI.The lawsuit alleges that the requirement could jeopardize the diner's future at BWI. Silver Diner is asking a court to enforce a 10-year sublease that would allow the restaurant to continue operating at the airport. The Rockville-based Silver Diner opened its restaurant at BWI in 2007. "The financially prohibitive condition was invented by Fraport, which falsely blamed the State of Maryland," the press release said. "The unauthorized gutting requirement would close Silver Diner BWI for more than a year and result in the loss of more than 120 local jobs," it added."Prices would increase substantially for families who are already struggling to meet the rising costs of groceries, electricity and other household essentials," Giaimo wrote in the letter. "Fraport, which generated nearly $5 billion in revenues during the last fiscal year, would reap another windfall for its Wall Street and global investors." Last month, Silver Diner launched a letter-writing campaign in an effort to keep the restaurant at BWI. A spokesperson for Silver Diner, Len Foxwell, claimed at the time that the campaign had resulted in more than 1,000 letters being sent to Moore and other officials.The letters call on the Maryland Aviation Administration (MAA) to support the effort to renew Silver Diner's lease at BWI.

title: After 75 years, remains of North Texas soldier missing in Korean War finally come home
description: Sonny Tischler was 21 when he disappeared during the Korean War. Now, his family finally has answers and the chance to give him a proper burial.
content: A Denton County family is preparing to do something Thursday that they have waited 75 years to do: bury the remains of a loved one who went missing during the Korean War.Sonny Tischler grew up outside Celina in the 1930s and '40s, helping his father on the family farm until he enlisted in the Army just before the start of the Korean War."He said I'm going to go ahead and volunteer, and then I can get it over with and then get my own farm," said Melva Doris Faulk, Tischler's sister.But shortly after beginning his tour of duty as a bazooka and machine gun specialist, the 21-year-old went missing. Word soon reached his large, heartbroken family."Two army officers came to our house," she said. "It was very sad, you know, our only brother. Losing Sonny was hard, but not knowing what happened to him made the family's pain even worse. For years, I wondered, maybe did the communists get him? Was he tortured?"And if my dad could've only known that, because every day I would see him pray and ask us to pray that we would hear something. My dad died in 1965, and he never knew what happened to his son."Thanks to a Korean farmer who discovered human remains decades ago and DNA testing that took years to complete, Tischler's family now knows how he died. His remains were returned to North Texas this month."The phone rang, and I looked at my phone, and it said US Army," said Mary Ann Turner, Tischler's niece. "I was so happy, and I knew that the rest of the family would be happy.Turner learned that her uncle likely died the day he disappeared."It was a blessing to find that he had evidently met his end from a sniper's bullet, so he didn't suffer," she said.The military returned not only Tischler's remains but also his helmet, belt buckle, and combat boots.Faulk, 89, is one of only three surviving siblings who will have the opportunity to say a proper goodbye to their only brother on Thursday. His funeral will be held in Pilot Point, more than 75 years after his death."It was just hard to believe and really overwhelming to know after 75 years how he could really be identified," she said. "It was such a happy feeling, though. Why was it a happy feeling? You know, I think we'd just finally given up."I think we had acknowledged that he would not be coming home alive, so this is homecoming."

title: Galleria of Mt. Lebanon is not closing despite online rumors, property owners say
description: The Galleria in Mt. Lebanon's property owners said a social media rumor saying the mall is closing next month is false.
content: The Galleria in Mt. Lebanon's property owners said a social media rumor saying the mall is closing next month is false.The rumor claimed the mall is closing on Nov. 30, right in the middle of the holiday season. Roadside, the Galleria's management, told KDKA-TV on Wednesday that the rumors are false."We are aware of the rumors posted on Facebook," a spokesperson for Roadside said. "Those reports are false and the mall remains open and will continue to welcome visitors." The rumor also said the site will be redeveloped into a Wegmans grocery store. Mt. Lebanon leaders said on Wednesday that they've received no permits for any demolition and construction at the site.However, like most rumors, there is some truth about where this is all coming from. Earlier this year, when Roadside bought the mall, there were media reports that the company was looking to bring a Wegmans to the South Hills. This would be as a Wegmans store is being built in Cranberry Township, Butler County. KDKA-TV reached out to Wegmans about the location and did not hear back on Wednesday. KDKA-TV also asked Roadside about any plans for Wegmans and did not get a response.

title: Abdul El-Sayed visits Detroit exhibit displaying documents from Epstein files
description: Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed was in Detroit for a tour of a new exhibit at the Norwood, where the Donald Trump and Jeffrey Epstein Memorial Reading Room currently sits.
content: Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed was in Detroit for a tour of a new exhibit at the Norwood, where the Donald Trump and Jeffrey Epstein Memorial Reading Room currently sits.El-Sayed joined survivors of Epstein to view the traveling exhibit, which opened in Detroit this week."What they've chosen to do is to try to make meaning by making justice, holding accountable for people who did this to them and hundreds of other young women," El-Sayed said.The Reading Room features millions of pages of partially redacted documents released by the Department of Justice."We must make sure that every credible lead is pursued, and where the evidence supports collusion, those cases must move forward regardless of title, wealth, status, or political affiliation. As a survivor, I know that justice can't be measured by the number of pages released," said survivor Liz Stein.Survivors say there are still 3 million pages from the Epstein files that haven't been released. Survivors, advocates and lawmakers have raised questions after the DOJ said it had collected more than 6 million pages of material from its investigation but had released only half of it.The DOJ told CBS News that it released "every document required by the Epstein Files Transparency Act.""We must create a democracy that future generations can be proud of, one rooted in accountability and justice, rather than the shameful division and indifference we are experiencing today," said survivor Sharlene Rochard.El-Sayed claims the White House and the Department of Justice are trying to cover up what happened, a claim that President Trump has denied."I'll tell you that as I think about what needs to happen next, we need to make sure that that Department of Justice in that White House does not have handmaidens in Congress and in the Senate who are going to serve to snuff out these candles, and that's a choice we all get to make," El-Sayed said. "I think all of us have a responsibility to lift up our voices. And yes, that means at the ballot box, but that also means in the 13 days before everybody gets to the ballot box. All that we will do is on the line. Justice for the survivors is on the line. In America, where something like this is allowed to happen, is on the line."El-Sayed writes a message to survivors and adds it to the reflection wall. His message says, "Thank you for turning your pain into a world that is safer for all of our girls. It shouldn't be this hard."When asked if he would make it a priority to see that all of the files are released if he gets elected to Congress, he said, "You need to understand what happened, and too often there are unwritten traditions that get in the way of doing the things that need to be done. And I have a habit of trying to do away with unnecessary, ineffective, unhealthful traditions."The last day to see the Donald Trump and Jeffrey Epstein Memorial Reading Room at the Norwood is Thursday, Oct. 22.

title: What early voting numbers say about Michigan's 2026 midterm election
description: Voting before Election Day has become more common, particularly after the COVID-19 pandemic, so a big early number doesn't necessarily indicate higher overall turnout.
content: With Election Day now less than two weeks away, more than 2 million absentee ballots have been requested across Michigan.As of Wednesday morning, more than 860,000 Michiganders have returned their ballots.With the addition of early in-person votes, nearly 11.6% of the state's active registered voters have already voted, but those numbers only tell part of the story."We're running ahead of where we were in 2022, which is the most comparable cycle. I think what we're seeing, we're about 17% ahead in terms of where that vote was in 2022," said Peter Trumbore, Political Science Professor, Oakland University.Voting before Election Day has become more common, particularly after the COVID-19 pandemic, so a big early number doesn't necessarily indicate higher overall turnout.The next test starts Saturday when in-person early voting opens statewide, and Trumbore says the beginning and end of that window could be the busiest."For a lot of reasons, you're probably going to see heavier traffic at the very beginning, and then, as the window starts to close, you'll have people who want to try to get in before it's too late," said Trumbore.In Southeast Michigan alone, more than 1.1 million absentee ballots have been requested, with parts of Metro Detroit accounting for more than 300,000 of those requests.Once in-person voting begins, Trumbore says, where those voters show up will be the next number to watch, especially in Wayne and Oakland counties."If we see strong in-person early voting in Wayne County and in the city of Detroit in particular, I think that that's going to bode well for Democrats," said Trumbore.In-person early voting has already started in several counties within the Upper Peninsula, but statewide early voting begins on Oct. 24 and runs through Nov. 1.

title: Organization fights to preserve Stockton's Little Manila neighborhood
description: A local organization is doing what it can to preserve the history of the Little Manila neighborhood in Stockton.
content: Little Manila, a four-block section of Stockton, was once home to the largest Filipino population in the world outside of the Philippines. The area is now on a national registry of endangered historic sites â but a local organization is doing what it can to preserve the history of the neighborhood.Hannah Divino works with Little Manila Rising, a community-based organization focused on preserving the historical footprint of Little Manila in Stockton. The Little Manila Rising Center is set to open its physical location by the end of the year â right in the heart of the historical neighborhood.The area started as a safe place for Filipino migrants in the early 1900s, who faced racism as they tried to integrate into the city."There were signs that said, literally, 'positively no Filipinos allowed,'" Divino said.Little Manila continued to grow and flourish, becoming the largest Filipino community outside of the Phillipines by the 1930s. The neighborhood had a diner, churches, and dance halls â but construction of the Crosstown freeway in the late 1960s would lead to an exodus of Filipino residents. Over 1,000 people were forced out of their homes, which would be replaced by fast food chain restaurants and a gas station. "When I look at this, my heart really breaks, because this, again, was a huge part of Filipino history," Divino said. She learned the powerful, yet painful history of the neighborhood through the Little Manila After School Program, as one of the first high school students to go through the program. Quincel Quiambao is also part of the movement to establish the Little Manilla Rising Center. Quiambao is not from Stockton, but said that the welcoming community has made the city feel like home."That sense of belonging really means a lot to me," Quiambao said.The center will serve as a community hub, advocating for both the Filipino community as well as other marginalized communities.

title: Florida GOP drops lawsuit against Democrats, TV stations stopping ad citing Hope Florida grand jury report
description: Attorneys representing RPOF stated that the lawsuit had achieved its objective after multiple State Attorneys weighed in on the issue following its filing.
content: The Republican Party of Florida (RPOF) has voluntarily dismissed its lawsuit against the Florida Democratic Party, several Democratic figures, and major news broadcasting organizations without prejudice, according to court documents filed late Wednesday afternoon in the Tenth Judicial Circuit Court of Florida.The lawsuit aimed to stop the airing of a political ad that highlights the leaked Hope Florida grand jury report. One of the Democratic figures targeted in the lawsuit was Attorney General candidate Jose Javier Rodriguez, who is running against incumbent Attorney General James Uthmeier in the 2026 midterm elections, which are less than two weeks away. RPOF had argued that the ads should have been pulled because the Court of Appeals had expunged the report, but this was met with accusations that the party was violating the First Amendment. State statutes "make it unlawful for any person to knowingly broadcast the content, gist, or import of testimony of a witness examined before a grand jury. The advertisement does exactly that," the lawsuit states. "It tells viewers that 'a leaked grand jury report found' that '$10 million was misappropriated' – a conclusion the First District held was wrong as a matter of law, based on a document that no longer lawfully exists."Attorneys representing RPOF stated that the lawsuit had achieved its objective after multiple State Attorneys weighed in on the issue following its filing. "RPOF is dismissing this case so that the work of the State Attorneys can continue without distraction," the notice stated, acknowledging that criminal investigations and charging decisions ultimately rest with law enforcement officials.The Florida Democratic Party issued a statement to CBS News Miami, following the dismissal of the lawsuit. The statement noted that Tuesday a judge denied RPOF's request to immediately pull the ad without hearing from the Democrats. "Well, that didn't take long," said Florida Democratic Party Chair Nikki Fried in the statement. "Republicans raced to court in the middle of the night to silence us, threatened TV stations, and tried to scare Floridians out of talking about Hope Florida. After a judge denied their emergency request to pull our ad, they walked away from their own case. Their stunt backfired. Thanks to this lawsuit, more Floridians are paying attention, and the pressure for answers keeps mounting. Who decided to send $10 million from a Medicaid settlement to the first lady's charity? Why did $8.5 million of it end up in a political committee run by James Uthmeier? And what did the Republican Party of Florida do with its share? Those questions aren't going away just because Republicans dropped their lawsuit."What does the Hope Florida grand jury report reveal? The report was finalized in January. It found that, in 2024, the diversion of $10 million from a $67 million Medicaid settlement ended up in a political committee headed by Uthmeier, then-Gov. Ron DeSantis' chief of staff, meant the money was "misappropriated"; no one could be indicted in the case.The money was first given to the Hope Florida Foundation as part of the settlement with Centene to resolve overpayments. That group then gave the money to two nonprofits, which in turn gave it to Uthmeier's political committee, which opposed two measures on the 2024 ballot. The proposals would have legalized recreational marijuana and installed a right to an abortion in the state constitution, but failed to pass.The lack of an indictment means that, under state law, the report can be sealed and blocked from public view. Those named in the report petitioned a trial court to prevent its publication, and the court partially agreed, allowing some redactions to be made public.Those named in the report appealed to the 1st DCA, which originally ruled on Aug. 25 that the grand jury presentment should be expunged, but that ruling was kept hidden from public view. Within 24 hours, CBS News Miami published the unredacted report.

title: "This is me on a plate": How one dish shows what a new Wisconsin restaurant is about
description: Local growers supply the beef, lamb, mushrooms, honey, cheese and vegetables at Fiddlehead Kitchen in St. Croix Falls, Wisconsin. One is the vegetable farm Marlee Crave and her husband established in 2020.
content: Marlee Crave served a summer dish at Fiddlehead Kitchen made from her husband's tomatoes and greens, her homemade sourdough bread and her family's cheese."Here you go, this is me on a plate," she said.Crave and Sarah Mittelstadt call plates like that their "heart dishes." The two women opened Fiddlehead Kitchen at the end of August in downtown St. Croix Falls, Wisconsin, just across the border from Minnesota, with a menu built around local farms.Local growers supply everything from beef and lamb to mushrooms, honey, cheese and vegetables. Crave and her husband established a vegetable farm in 2020, and it grows most of the vegetables the restaurant uses.The menu changes with the seasons. Crave said that once something is no longer available from her farmers, it comes off the menu. That's why the burger has no tomato right now, she said. The tomatoes "just died."Surprises from farmers shape the menu, too. When a farmer shows up with a "bumper crop of parsnips," Mittelstadt said, that becomes inspiration for her and Crave.Mittelstadt studied food systems at the University of Minnesota, then worked on a mushroom farm before cooking in Minnesota and Wisconsin kitchens. Crave grew up around her family's Wisconsin dairy farm and cheese business. After working with chefs in the Twin Cities, she landed at the same restaurant as Mittelstadt, and the two bonded over local food.When that restaurant closed, they kept cooking, doing pop-ups and working out of a smaller kitchen before opening Fiddlehead Kitchen.For Mittelstadt, the payoff is seeing familiar and new faces gather around food grown close to home. Inviting people in and feeding them food from the area "fills me every time," she said.Fiddlehead Kitchen is open Wednesdays for Burger Night. It serves a full lunch and dinner menu Thursday through Saturday.

title: Basketball Museum of Illinois hosts Leadership Academy for Chicago area student athletes
description: More than 100 athletes from Chicago area schools gathered under one roof on Wednesday morning for a day not focused on competition, but for a meeting of the minds.
content: More than 100 athletes from Chicago area schools gathered under one roof on Wednesday morning for a day not focused on competition, but for a meeting of the minds.The Basketball Museum of Illinois hosted its 5th Leadership Academy at the Wintrust Sports Complex in Bedford Park.Student athletes hit the hardwood, not for competition, but cooperation. Organizers said those who attended the academy were chosen because they show the potential to influence and inspire.Christ The King Jesuit College Prep School senior Isaiah Steins said he was proud to have been selected."I mean, of course, because they've seen something in me that I didn't see in myself for like a good long time. St. Laurence High School junior Clancy Bowen, who plays volleyball, said she was excited to see how other teams may work."We all put our ideas together to make everything work. I thought that was pretty cool," she said.Running tabletops and drills on the court, they were just feet from something new â the Basketball Museum of Illinois, set to open in late 2027, with a focus on kids' access and outreach."They are able to hear different voices. That's a key component to this; different voices from other campuses, different voices in our leadership academy presenters, and the opportunity to have time and space outside of the high school bubble," said the museum's executive director, Jason Ronai.The museum seeks to put a spotlight not only on where the sport's been, but where it is going with this next generation."Having good leadership can take you a long way," Steins said.

title: North Philadelphia shooting leaves 3 injured after nearly 2 dozen shots were fired, police say
description: Three people were injured after a shooting inside and outside a North Philadelphia home Wednesday morning, police said.
content: Three people were injured when nearly two dozen shots were fired at a North Philadelphia home Wednesday morning, police said.Police said the shooting occurred inside and outside a home around 10 a.m. on the 2800 block of North 20th Street. Two women and a man were riddled with bullets.Authorities said a 49-year-old woman was shot 11 times and a 29-year-old man was shot three times in the leg. They were both taken to a local hospital in stable condition.A 27-year-old woman who was shot six times was also taken to the hospital in critical condition.The shooting left neighbors shaken and raised broader concerns about gun violence and safety in the community."It's a tragedy," a relative of the victims said.The relative asked not to be identified. She said she arrived at the scene after the shooting and saw bullet casings and blood on the street."Bullet casings, blood. That's pretty much all I gotta say," she said. "The streets of Philadelphia. We need help. We need some help. I just hope that everybody recovers."For some residents, the violence is frightening. For others, it has become an all-too-familiar part of life in the neighborhood."It's not surprising," Arlacey Chambers, who has lived in the neighborhood for eight years, said. "You witness people get shot all the time."Chambers said she has witnessed gun violence before, including a shooting at a nearby store. Despite those experiences, she said residents continue to work to maintain a sense of community."We try to keep it clean, we try to keep it organized," she said. "You just never know."For Elyce Rivera, the threat of gun violence is concerning because of her three children, ages 14, 8 and 3."It's kind of like alarming, honestly," Rivera said.Rivera said the possibility of gunfire puts her family on edge."That's scary because my husband is outside all the time as well," she said. "Bullets have no names on them, have no names on them."Police have not released details about what led to the shooting or said whether anyone has been taken into custody.Investigators are asking anyone with information about the shooting to come forward and contact police.

title: Rain creates concerns as Altadena continues to rebuild after Eaton Fire
description: The rain is raising concerns in Altadena once again for families devastated by the Eaton Fire.
content: The rain is raising concerns in Altadena once again for families devastated by the Eaton Fire."We're really concerned about the foundation being too wet and the soil moving and shifting," Eaton Fire survivor Raya Reynaga said. "As you can see, there's a lot of dirt in the back that we're concerned with, the mudslides and so forth. We're concerned that it's going to go underneath the house and mess up all the footings."Reynaga's home for 28 years burned in the Eaton Fire, and she lost everything. Now, her new prefab house in Altadena rests on a pile of dirt as she waits for more permits, leaving her worried about what will happen when the storm rolls in. Nearby, a group gathered to push for more state and federal fire recovery funding, while also preparing for the possibility of a wet winter. "We are rebuilding. We are very concerned about the El NiÃ±o," resident Mary Landau said. "We just started. The first beam of the roof went up last week. They're at our house right now, tarping."Altadena Town Councilmember Anton Anderson, who had more than a dozen family members lose their homes in the fire, says that with every delay comes another expense they can barely afford."They're all rebuilding, which is great news," he said. "With the rain and everything else, that's one of the concerns I have."Residents can pick up as many as 25 pre-filled sandbags at the Los Angeles County Public Works yard on Mountain View Street during daylight hours. Officials urged displaced residents to check on their properties, clear gutters and remove debris before the rain arrives.

title: Malibu takes extra precautions as storm hits Southern California
description: Malibu, already dealing with coastal erosion from previous storms, is taking extra precautions as a storm hits Southern California.
content: Malibu, already dealing with coastal erosion from previous storms, is taking extra precautions as a storm hits Southern California. "In two years, we've had four brush fires. We've had multiple earthquakes, blackouts," resident Scott McKay said.McKay moved from Calabasas to live the Malibu dream, but he said the last couple of years have felt more like a nightmare."It's just been difficult," he said. "Now, to see our beach washing away is depressing."What was once a sandy stretch of paradise is now a shoreline scarred by powerful surf and high tides. "It came all the way up and it picked away at the edge of the road here," Malibu city spokesperson Matt Meyerhoff said. "It also broke a water main. That became a public safety concern."The damage occurred near Point Dume, where crews are now placing large boulders to protect the road from further erosion and flooding. With the storm moving in, the city is racing to shore up its coastline before more damage is done."The boulders work," Malibu Public Works spokesperson Wade Major said. "They work as a temporary solution."The danger isn't just along the coast. Recent wildfires have stripped vegetation from nearby hillsides, leaving the ground more vulnerable to mudslides. City crews are clearing drains and monitoring roads for trouble spots. For the people who have already weathered so much, they say the uncertainty is exhausting."Who knows what's going to happen," McKay said. "I don't know. It's nerve-wracking, and it's a shame."

title: What is glycidyl methacrylate? Toledo warns residents after chemical leak
description: After a chemical leak in Toledo, Ohio, forced people out of their homes and others to shelter in place, the city of Toledo confirmed that the released chemical is glycidyl methacrylate and is providing guidance on it.
content: After a chemical leak in Toledo, Ohio, forced people out of their homes and others to shelter in place, the city of Toledo confirmed that the released chemical is glycidyl methacrylate and is providing guidance on it.What is glycidyl methacrylate?Glycidyl methacrylate is an irritant that can cause burning of the eyes, nose, mouth and skin, according to the city of Toledo. If exposure occurs, it is recommended to shower or rinse the affected area. Symptoms of overexposure include headache, dizziness, tiredness, nausea and vomiting. Toledo CBS affiliate WTOL reported that Lucas County Health Commissioner Karim Baroudi said in a news conference Wednesday morning that the chemical is mostly an irritant at this stage."There is no immediate danger as far as the release that happened," Baroudi said. "For the people sheltering in place, close the windows. For people driving through the 3-mile radius, make sure you circulate the vent in your car. Don't bring in outside air."Baroudi said that long-term exposure to the compound can cause cancer."It is a toxic chemical," Baroudi said. "It's really toxic if you touch it, if you ingest it. Now we're trying to determine how much toxicity is in the air that the people are breathing so we can give better guidance." It is recommended that you contact a medical professional if you believe you're experiencing a reaction to exposure. Where is the evacuation zone?The City of Toledo's Fire and Rescue ordered everyone within a 1-mile radius of 1266 Progress Ave. (MC Tank Terminal) to evacuate the area.Toledo Fire and Rescue is also asking everyone within a 3-mile radius to shelter in place. This means staying indoors, closing windows and doors and turning off ventilation.How did the Toledo chemical leak happen?MC Tank Transport Inc. said in a statement that equipment associated with its operations is involved in the incident.According to the statement, glycidyl methacrylate is an industrial chemical used to make certain plastics, paints and coatings perform better."At this moment, we are working with the American Red Cross to arrange emergency lodging and transportation assistance for displaced residents," MC Tank Transport Inc. says.

title: Bystander rescues woman from burning Modesto home before firefighters arrive
description: A bystander pulled a woman from a burning home in Modesto after finding her in a wheelchair inside the residence, officials say.
content: A bystander pulled a woman from a burning home in Modesto after finding her in a wheelchair inside the residence, officials said Wednesday.The Modesto Fire Department said the fire happened at a residence in the area of East Roseburg Avenue and Sunrise Avenue.Before crews arrived, officials said a passerby stopped his vehicle and attempted to reach the woman inside but was initially unable to enter because of the intense heat.The bystander told the woman to get down on the floor before crawling into the home beneath the heaviest heat and dragging her to safety, according to the fire department.The woman was taken to Doctors Medical Center in Modesto, but the nature of her injuries and her condition were not known.Fire officials also reported downed live power lines in the area while the fire was active.The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

title: Witkoff faces backlash for calling Putin a "humanitarian": "Embarrassing and outrageous"
description: After special envoy Steve Witkoff told Putin he was a "humanitarian" for releasing a U.S. citizen deemed to have been wrongfully detained, GOP Sen. John Cornyn responded, "No. Putin is a stone cold killer."
content: Washington — U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff faced immediate backlash Wednesday for praising Russian President Vladimir Putin as a "humanitarian" after he released 74-year-old Stephen Hubbard, an American who had been imprisoned in Russia for four years and who had been determined to be wrongfully detained."You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian," Witkoff told Putin Wednesday in response to Hubbard's release. "You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that, I commend you, and I thank you again."Witkoff made the comment in St. Petersburg during a visit with the Russian president that was aimed at moving toward a resolution of the Ukraine war that Putin started four and a half years ago. Over the past month, Russia has been intensifying its strikes against civilian and energy infrastructure to try to cripple the power grid before the brutal Ukrainian winter. Mr. Trump was asked later in the day if he would describe Putin the same way Witkoff did. "Well, I guess you have to say for that particular purpose, for the purpose of allowing a man who was thinking he was going to be in prison for life out," Mr. Trump said during a White House roundtable on cyber crime. "But I wouldn't say anything one way or the other." Witkoff's "humanitarian" comment sparked pushback from Republicans, some of whom have openly criticized the president and his administration in recent months.
