title: Trump administration asks Supreme Court to allow border wall construction to resume in Big Bend region
description: The Justice Department asked the Supreme Court to lift a lower court injunction that temporarily blocked the Trump administration from building a border wall and related infrastructure in the Big Bend Sector.
content: Washington — The Trump administration on Wednesday asked the Supreme Court to allow it to resume for now construction of a border wall and other infrastructure through a remote area of West Texas that includes Big Bend National Park.The Justice Department urged the high court to lift a lower court injunction that temporarily bars the Department of Homeland Security from building the barrier or related infrastructure in the Big Bend Sector, which covers more than 500 miles of the U.S.-Mexico border and 77 counties in Texas. "The district court's injunction significantly frustrates the government's ability to stop the flow of illegal aliens and drugs across the southern border," Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote in the request for emergency relief. "The Secretary identified the Big Bend project areas at issue because of the high rates of illegal-alien crossings and drug smuggling in the region over the past several years."President Trump's promise to build a wall along the southern border has been a hallmark of his immigration agenda for the last decade. But earlier this year, the president's plans were met with significant pushback from lawmakers in both parties, cattle ranchers and local law enforcement officials in Texas when photos and videos shared to social media showed bulldozers arriving at Big Bend National Park.In response to the backlash, Customs and Border Protection Commissioner Rodney Scott paused construction inside the park until the end of September. The agency has said that the proposed border wall will not cut through Big Bend National Park, but other infrastructure would, including patrol roads, detection technology and roughly 17 miles of vehicle barriers.Construction of a 47-mile-long stretch of wall in the Big Bend region began last month, according to CBP. The government has awarded contracts for five border-barrier projects in that area along the U.S.-Mexico border, the Justice Department said.The Trump administration announced in February that the Department of Homeland Security would build barriers and roads in the Big Bend Sector. The project includes the construction of 30-foot-tall bollard walls stretching from Fort Quitman, Texas, to Closed Canyon, which is located in Big Bend Ranch State Park. Border walls and roads would span more than 300 miles, according to the government. Because of the project's impact on cultural, recreational, wildlife and environmental resources, the federal government would typically have to ensure compliance with federal environmental protection and historical preservation laws before moving forward. But when then-Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem announced the project earlier this year, she invoked a 1996 federal immigration law that gives the secretary the authority to waive all legal requirements deemed necessary to ensure quick construction of physical barriers and roads in the vicinity of the southern border to "deter illegal crossings in areas of high illegal entry." Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who succeeded Noem after her firing, issued two more waivers allowing CBP to construct barrier systems.In response to the move, an environmental nonprofit, a professional riverboat guide and a religious organization dedicated to preserving the Sacred Heart of the Church of Jesus along the Rio Grande filed a lawsuit in April seeking to stop the Trump administration from implementing the project.The Trump administration argued that the stretch of land at issue in the case is an area of "high illegal entry" given the rates of illegal crossings and drug smuggling. The government said more than 89,000 people were apprehended trying to cross into the U.S. illegally in the Big Bend Sector between 2021 and 2025.But the plaintiffs said that the Big Bend Sector ranks last for apprehensions compared to the other six sectors along the southern border. While the area covers more than 25% of the U.S.-Mexico border, annual apprehensions in the Big Bend Sector ranged between 0.3% and 2.2% of total border-wide apprehensions, according to court filings.Earlier this month, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone granted the challengers' request for a preliminary injunction and barred the Department of Homeland Security from building border barriers or related infrastructure, or engaging in "any construction or ground disturbing activities" in the Big Bend Sector.Cardone found that Noem and Mullin exceeded their authorities when issuing the waivers between February and July that allowed construction to proceed. Just before the Justice Department sought the Supreme Court's intervention, Cardone rejected the Trump administration's request to pause her decision.

title: Ex-Atlanta halfway house employee sentenced to prison for sexually assaulting inmate during shift
description: A former employee of an Atlanta halfway house has been sentenced to more than a year in prison for sexually abusing an inmate and lying during an investigation into the act.
content: A former employee of an Atlanta halfway house has been sentenced to prison for sexually abusing an inmate and lying during an investigation, officials say.Tristan Cox, a contract employee who worked at the Atlanta Residential Reentry Center as a residence monitor in 2024, pleaded guilty to violating the inmate's civil rights and making false statements to a federal agent.Under federal law, corrections staff are prohibited from having sexual contact, and any such contact is a civil rights violation.Cox was accused of sexually assaulting an inmate in a supply room during one of his overnight shifts, authorities said. When interviewed by federal agents, Cox denied having any sexual contact with the inmate then said that the victim assaulted him after being told that DNA evidence corroborated the victim's account."Cox exploited his position to sexually assault an inmate and lied about it to a federal agent," stated Special Agent in Charge Eric Fehlman of the Department of Justice Office of the Inspector General's Southeast Region. "The DOJ OIG will continue working with its law enforcement partners to ensure that anyone participating in this type of behavior is brought to justice."On Tuesday, a federal judge sentenced the Atlanta man to one year and six months in prison to be followed by one year of supervised release.

title: Bell Gardens HS student arrested for allegedly bringing gun on campus, causing school lockdown
description: A Bell Gardens High School student was arrested on Wednesday after they allegedly brought a gun on campus, causing an hours-long investigation and campus lockdown.
content: A Bell Gardens High School student was arrested on Wednesday after they allegedly brought a gun on campus, causing an hours-long investigation and campus lockdown. Police were called to the school on Agra Street just before 9:30 a.m. after learning that a student had a handgun, according to a news release from the Bell Gardens Police Department. Arriving officers detained and arrested a student whom they found in possession of the firearm, the release said. "Officers confirmed there was no active shooter situation, no shots had been fired on campus, and no students or staff were injured," the release said. "This is an isolated incident, and there are no further known threats to the school or our community."According to Montebello Unified School District officials, the school was placed on lockdown around the same time police were called. "The measure was taken out of an abundance of caution," the MUSD statement said, noting that all students were released from campus early on Wednesday at noon. "The safety and wellbeing of our students, staff, and our school community will always be our highest priority," Bell Gardens HS Principal Hector Velasquez said.The name of the student who was arrested was not immediately identified by police as their investigation continued. Anyone with more information was urged to contact Detective Sergeant E. Roberts at 562-806-7694 or eroberts@bgpd.org. Anonymous tips can be submitted online at https://www.lacrimestoppers.org or by calling LA Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477.

title: 2 suspects in Merced County shooting arrested in Turlock
description: Two suspects in a shooting that happened in Merced County this week were arrested just over the border into Stanislaus County, officials said Wednesday.
content: Two suspects in a shooting that happened in Merced County this week were arrested just over the border into Stanislaus County, officials said Wednesday.The Merced County Sheriff's Office said the shooting happened Tuesday afternoon along Shaffer Road in Winton. Deputies arrived to find a victim with a single gunshot wound. That victim was taken to an area hospital, but investigators could not provide information on the person's condition.Investigators said they were later able to identify two people of interest â 25-year-old Joanna Mendoza and 44-year-old Samuel Rojas â and notified surrounding law enforcement agencies to be on the lookout.The Merced County Sheriff's Office said that by 11 p.m., Turlock police officers had found and detained both suspects. Mendoza and Rojas have since been transported back to Merced County.Rojas was booked into the Merced County Jail on suspicion of attempted murder, while Mendoza was booked on suspicion of being an accessory to attempted murder, the sheriff's office said.Turlock is located in Stanislaus County, roughly 15 miles northwest of Winston.

title: San Francisco reports first fatal overdose from synthetic opioid sold in gas stations, smoke shops
description: A San Francisco resident has died after ingesting a semi-synthetic opioid sold in gas stations and smoke shops, the first such case in the city involving dihydro-7-hydroxymirtragynine, also known as MGM-15, health officials said.
content: A San Francisco resident has died after ingesting a semi-synthetic opioid sold in gas stations and smoke shops, the first such case in the city involving dihydro-7-hydroxymirtragynine, also known as MGM-15, health officials said. The kratom-derived opioid, estimated to be up to 50 times more potent than morphine, is not approved for any medical use and was recently designated as a Schedule 1 drug by the U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency. The San Francisco Department of Public Health issued an alert to the public and health care providers on Wednesday about MGM-15, and said the person who ingested it died late last month.Despite it being illegal for sale, MGM-15 has been found in products marketed as "uncaria tomentosa" or "cat's claw," and SFDPH said MGM-15 has also been identified in overdoses in Utah and Washington. The "Script botanicals x Maui labs" tablets the San Francisco decedent consumed do not list kratom or 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH) in the packaging, SFDPH said, although the medical examiner's office found MGM-15 in both the decedent and the product packaging.It was the second time this year that San Francisco's health department issued a public warning about a synthetic opioid. In April, SFDPH alerted about the drug cychlorphine following the overdose death of a 16-year-old boy. San Francisco police said cychlorphine, estimated to be 10 times estimated more powerful than fentanyl, can be found in counterfeit pills designed to look like Xanax, Adderall and Oxycontin. Health officials recommend administering naloxone to anyone who appears to be overdosing and calling 911.

title: Is Texas running out of water? What most people get wrong about the state's growing water crisis
description: In the next 50 years, water use is expected to increase by 6%, but water supplies are projected to decline 10%.
content: In water management, there's this thing known as "day zero." It refers to the point where a city or region's water supply reaches critically low levels, six months away from demand exceeding supply. Just this year, one Texas city was projected to become the first in the U.S. to reach that point: Corpus Christi.The crisis is not only the result of drought and high heat. Corpus Christi is just one extreme example of a problem decades in the making. Water shortages do not often get attention from state lawmakers, and fights over resources can pit rural landowners against cities.All of it has left a lot of Texans asking how close the state is to running out of water, and is there any way to stop it?Where does our water come from?Currently, most of the water we use comes primarily from reservoirs or aquifers. And even though water planners do want to diversify the portfolio, reservoirs are going to be important to Texas's future for a long time. Reservoirs are among the cheapest ways to acquire additional water supply because you essentially dig a big hole and the rain fills it up," said Sarah Kirkle with the Texas Water Association. Water planners are looking to increasingly rely on methods such as desalination, which is a strategy under consideration in Corpus. And water re-use, like the George W. Shannon wetlands near Corsicana. Still, in 2080, surface water sources like reservoirs are projected to make up the biggest share of our state's water supply.But you can't just build a reservoir anywhere. You have to build one by an existing water source, and this is where things can get ugly. Water is not naturally distributed evenly across our state. The piney woods of East Texas are naturally wetter than the southern and western regions."At some point, it becomes a challenge that within your own region, you may not have available water supplies to meet those needs. And so then you end up having to look elsewhere in other parts of the state. And some of those areas are concerned about their own future needs," Kirkle said.Inter-regional conflictsDisagreements over the future of water in Texas are already playing out. Take, for instance, the fight over the Marvin Nichols Reservoir. First introduced in the state's water plan in 1968 as the Naples Reservoir, the project would flood 66,000 acres of the Sulfur River basin in northeast Texas, with the majority of the reservoir supply going to DFW. Building it would require taking private property from landowners, some who have been on their land for generations.Water planners say this project is deeply important for the state's future. But the affected landowners say they aren't willing to give up their land without a fight, regardless of what the state is willing to pay for it."There's not a price for this land ... I can't put a price on seven generations," said cattle rancher Eddie Belcher, who inherited the property from his mother."The land would lose everything. The community would be gone forever. And all of this wonder we see out here in nature would literally be drowned. And that's what devastates us," said cattle rancher Jim Marshall.The Marvin Nichols Reservoir isn't the only interregional water fight the state has had. In another recent headline-grabbing example, a Dallas millionaire plans to export groundwater from under his property in East Texas to the Metroplex. It's prompted outrage and a legal battle.These problems will likely only get worse over the next few decades, with thirsty parts of the state increasingly wanting to supply their regions with water from areas with more supply."Balancing out the needs of the basin that needs the water, the basin that has the water, and understanding what their needs are going to be in the future is a really big challenge, and we're having a lot of conversation on the policy and legislative cycle about that," Kirkle said.Water planners are constantly assessing these sometimes competing needs, and have been since the 1950s. That's when Texas started formal water planning after its worst drought in recorded history. That drought spanned six years and ended in 1957, with heavy rain that flooded every major river and tributary in Texas. It is still considered the statewide drought of record, and it's used to plan for future droughts.How does water planning work in Texas?The state is broken up into 16 planning groups. Every five years, each group develops a regional plan for water supply needs over a 50-year period. These plans look at things like future population growth and how much water Texas could have during a drought, and they recommend ways to develop new water supplies and prevent shortages before they happen.Once they're finalized, all 16 regional water plans are sent to the Texas Water Development Board. The board then looks at all of the plans and creates one statewide water plan."It's a national model because it means that the local interests are invested in solving their problems. They understand their water situation much better than anyone else, and they have the responsibility at the local level for securing their additional supplies," Kirkle said.Why the shortage? At this point, lawmakers have been talking about water shortages in Texas for decades, but in more recent years, there has seemingly been increased urgency to these warnings."The water issues in Texas are basic supply and demand. So we've got escalating demand that has to do with a large increase of population, as well as the economic development that goes along with that," Kirkle explained. "And then we've got supplies that are decreasing for a number of factors, including drought."The amount of water Texas needs in the future is a moving target, which is why the state releases a new plan every five years. According to the draft of the latest plan, released in April of 2026, in the next 50 years, the state's population is expected to increase more than 50% to 52 million people.Despite all those new people, water use is expected to only increase by 6%, but we are going to have a lot less water to go around. Texas's existing water supplies are projected to decline 10%, mainly because of aquifer depletion.Water planners measure water in acre foot units. An acre foot is enough to cover an entire football field with one foot of water. According to the state's most recent water plan, if no additional water sources are brought online, the state could be short 3.6 million acre feet by 2030 and 5.8 million in 2080.To meet these needs, the State Water Board's plan has recommended more than 3,000 projects by 2080, costing an estimated $174 billion, 50% more than the dollar amount presented state's last water plan five years ago. A number that big can be hard for most people to conceptualize. It's billions more than it costs to fund all public schools in the state every year. By some estimates, it's enough to house every person experiencing homelessness in the U.S. for at least five years.And as big as the $174 billion price tag is, it does not even account for future inflation or the cost to fix the state's aging water infrastructure.Potential impact of water shortagesCities will likely never literally run out of water, as restrictions would be put in place before it happens. But even shortages can devastate a region economically. By the Texas Water Development Board's estimates, a severe drought could cause an estimated $91 billion in economic damages in 2030 and $177 billion a year by 2080 if the state does not implement its strategies.We can also look to what has happened during water shortages around the world. From 1996 to 2012, Australia experienced a drought dubbed the "Big Dry," which shrank its GDP by 1.6%. When Cape Town, South Africa nearly ran out of water in 2018, 3.4% of the region's GDP was lost.In Texas, a fight over water had a major impact on the economy in the Rio Grande Valley when the state's last sugar cane mill shut down due to the lack of enough water to keep the crops alive. A group of investors has since partnered to reopen the mill. But the Texas agriculture commissioner said the closure's temporary economic and cultural issues were profound.Lessons from Corpus ChristiIn Corpus Christi, recent floods have delayed the city's water emergency until 2028, buying leaders there some time. But experts say there's a lot to can take away from their emergency."It can be really sexy to have a park or a library or these things that people can see more immediately that you don't see in water, because water and wastewater pipes, they're kind of an invisible problem ... As long as the toilets are flushing and the and the taps are turning on, people don't realize that we have a water crisis that's looming," Kirkle said.Because Corpus Christi water issues are about more than just drought. They are also about a lack of planning and delaying major projects, and they highlight the importance of having a long term lens when addressing community needs.

title: FBI offering $20,000 reward in search for suspect in downtown Atlanta ICE building arson attack
description: The FBI is now offering a reward of up to $20,000 for information about an arson attack that officials say targeted the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement building in downtown Atlanta.
content: The FBI is now offering a reward of up to $20,000 for information about an arson attack that officials say targeted the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement building in downtown Atlanta.The incident was reported around 9:30 p.m. Oct. 20, according to FBI Atlanta. The agency said personnel and evidence technicians were at the site collecting evidence."There is no known threat to public safety at this time," the FBI said in a statement.Atlanta police confirmed officers responded to reports of an object being thrown at 180 Ted Turner Drive SW. No injuries or active fire were reported, police said.On Wednesday afternoon, investigators shared surveillance footage of a man the FBI said a suspect in the incident. Investigators believe the man fled southbound on Ted Turner Drive after allegedly throwing the device.In a statement, Georgia Attorney General Chris Carr called the attack "unacceptable and will not be tolerated.""Those responsible must be prosecuted, and we stand ready to assist our federal partners with whatever they need," Carr said,Authorities are asking anyone with information about the case to call the FBI's Toll-Free tipline at 1-800-225-5324) or their local FBI office.CBS News Atlanta has reached out to ICE for more information. We will update this story when we hear back.

title: Western Wisconsin man sentenced to life in prison in wife's shooting death
description: A western Wisconsin man who was accused of killing his wife after she was found dead in their basement in 2024 was sentenced Wednesday to life in prison.
content: A western Wisconsin man who was accused of killing his wife after she was found dead in their basement in 2024 was sentenced Wednesday to life in prison.Jared Ler'che was charged with first-degree intentional homicide in his wife, Margaret Ler'che's, death. He pleaded no contest in July, meaning he did not admit guilt but accepted the conviction and penalty.Officers found Margaret Ler'che after her father requested a welfare check for her after he spent the afternoon helping her pack her belongings at her Osceola, Wisconsin, home. According to documents, her father told officers that Margaret Ler'che and her two children had been living with Jared Ler'che in Iowa for the last three months. The couple was having marital issues, he said.Roughly 10 minutes after Margaret Ler'che's father contacted authorities, St. Paul dispatch called Polk County, Wisconsin, law enforcement, saying that Jared Ler'che had contacted a crisis line. He said he was driving around with his two children and having thoughts of suicide, the criminal complaint said.Officers went to the Ler'che home and found Margaret Ler'che dead in the basement, under a blanket. There was a .22 rifle on the ground next to her and she had been shot in the back of the head, according to documents.Ler'che will be eligible for parole after 33 years.For anonymous, confidential help, people can call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233 or 1-800-787-3224.If you or someone you know is in emotional distress, get help from the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988. Trained crisis counselors are available 24 hours a day to talk about anything.In addition, help is available from the National Alliance on Mental Illness, or NAMI. Call the NAMI Helpline at 800-950-6264 or text "HelpLine" to 62640. There are more than 600 local NAMI organizations and affiliates across the country, many of which offer free support and education programs.

title: School bus driver in Huntley, Illinois, arrested for possession of child sexual abuse materials
description: A school bus driver in northwest suburban Huntley has been arrested on charges of possessing child sex abuse materials.
content: A school bus driver in northwest suburban Huntley has been arrested on charges of possessing child sex abuse materials.Huntley police said the Internet Crimes Against Children Task force provided them with information that a phone number in Huntley tried to upload potential child sex abuse materials to a cloud-based online storage service, and police were able to trace the phone back to 43-year-old Jon Roth.On Tuesday, police and investigators from the Illinois Attorney General's office executed a search warrant at Roth's home and seized several electronic devices. Roth agreed to come in for questioning and after investigators completed an analysis of the electronic devices, he was arrested on 10 counts of possession of child sexual abuse materials involving a victim under 13 years of age.Roth was taken to the McHenry County Jail to await a detention hearing. Court records show he is due to appear in court on Tuesday.In a letter to staff and families, Huntley Community School District 158 confirmed Roth works as a school bus driver for the district.Roth has been removed from all duties and placed on leave. District 158 officials said the school bus aide assigned to Roth's bus never reported any concerning conduct, and officials have no reason to believe the child sexual abuse materials found on the devices at Roth's home involve any students."We understand that this news may be deeply concerning to families. As always, the safety and well-being of our students is our highest priority. We will continue to support law enforcement's investigation while maintaining our commitment to student safety," Superintendent Jessica Lombard wrote in the letter.Police asked anyone with information on the case to contact the Huntley Police Department at 847-515-5311. Anonymous tips can be submitted by calling the Huntley Police Tip Line at 847-515-5333.

title: Gov. DeSantis approves execution for man convicted of killing pregnant woman and her husband in Florida Keys
description: Thomas Overton, 70, was sentenced to death in 1999 for killing Michael and Missy MacIvor, who was eight months pregnant, and the state executed William Reaves a day earlier.
content: Gov. Ron DeSantis signed a death warrant Wednesday for Thomas Mitchell Overton, who in 1992 killed a Florida Keys couple whose unborn child did not survive the attack.With another execution set for Nov. 5, the planned Nov. 19 execution of Overton, 70, would become the 20th conducted by the state this year, the most for a year since the death penalty was reinstated by the U.S. Supreme Court in 1976.DeSantis signed the warrant a day after the state executed William Reaves for killing Indian River County Sheriff's Deputy Richard Raczkowski four decades ago.DeSantis' warrant for Overton sets the execution for 6 p.m. Nov. 18 at Florida State Prison in Starke.Overton was arrested in 1997 for the 1992 rape and murder of Missy MacIvor, 29, and the murder of Michael MacIvor, 30. At the time, Missy MacIvor was eight months pregnant.According to court records, Overton knew the MacIvors because he worked as a service-station clerk in Tavernier --- part of Key Largo --- before breaking into their home in August 1992.Michael MacIvor was hit in the back of the head with a blunt object and kicked in the midsection before being strangled. Missy MacIvor was then strangled after being bound and raped.James Zientek, who was incarcerated with Overton at the Monroe County Detention Center, testified that Overton said he had broken into the MacIvor's residence to rape Susan MacIvor and had killed the couple to muddle the crime scene, according to the sentencing order."The evidence found at the crime scene was consistent with the testimony of Mr. Zientek and shows beyond a reasonable doubt that a fundamental part of the Defendant's criminal plot was a carefully conceived plan to avoid detection and arrest," the sentencing order stated.Despite his efforts to confuse the crime scene, Overton's DNA was found in separate tests conducted in 1996 and 1998, matching a bedding sample from the MacIvors' home.Overton was sentenced to death in 1999 for the murders and given life sentences for sexual battery on Missy MacIvor and for burglary of a dwelling, and 15 years for the death of an unborn child.Before Overton's execution, Jesse Guardado, 64, is to be put to death Nov. 5 at Florida State Prison for the murder of Jackie Malone, 75, in 2004. The Walton County woman had helped Guardado find a place to stay and a job after he was released from prison.

title: Yorkville banquet hall owner charged with possessing child sexual abuse material
description: Yorkville police said they learned of the alleged images involving minors here after being contacted by Montgomery police, who were investigating Silva in a separate case.
content: Yorkville police are asking for the public's help as they investigate a case where a banquet hall owner is accused of possessing child sexual abuse material.According to police, Eleno Silva, 57, of Oswego and owner of Martini Banquet Hall in Yorkville, was charged with six counts of child pornography and three counts of child sexual abuse material after they said he copied surveillance video from designated changing areas at the business where underage girls were in various stages of undress and put those images on his cellphone.The banquet hall is known to host events like weddings, bridal showers, quinceñeras or traditional celebrations in Hispanic culture to mark a girl's 15th birthday.Police said they learned of the alleged images involving minors here after being contacted by Montgomery police who were investigating Silva in a separate case.CBS News Chicago learned Silva was charged earlier this year with three counts of unauthorized video recording in a case police say happened at a restaurant he owns called Riverside Diner in Montgomery.Court documents allege Silva video-recorded a female employee in a restroom multiple times between 2025 and 2026.In the Yorkville case, police are asking for information from anyone who attended, worked or hosted an event at Martini Banquet Hall in 2023."It's not uncommon anymore for police to discover a crime on these video cameras and not know who the victim is," said retired Chicago police first deputy superintendent Anthony Riccio. "It's a far stronger case if they could identify who these victims are, have the victims provide a statement that they were not aware that there were video cameras capturing them undressing and it builds a stronger case and a better prosecutable case."Silva turned himself in to Kendall County Jail on Monday after police got a warrant for his arrest and is out on bond.His next court appearance is scheduled for Tuesday, Nov. 10. CBS News Chicago reached out to him but has not heard back.

title: Top Justice Department official asks Minnesota judges to step aside from immigration cases
description: A top official at the Justice Department is attempting to disqualify two Minnesota federal judges from a pair of cases related to immigration.
content: Washington — A top official at the Justice Department is attempting to disqualify two Minnesota federal judges from a pair of cases, claiming comments they made to the New York Times about the Trump administration's handling of immigration cases in the state call their impartiality into question.The motions, filed against Judges Patrick Schiltz and John Tunheim, are an escalation of the Justice Department's ongoing campaign against judges who it claims have treated the Trump administration unfairly. Both of the requests were made by Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward, the third-highest-ranking official at the Justice Department.Woodward also moved over the weekend to disqualify U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes, who sits on the trial court in Washington, D.C., from overseeing a case involving President Trump's efforts to overhaul a historic public golf course in the nation's capital. Reyes rejected the Justice Department's effort Sunday and accused the Justice Department of weaponizing "selective quotations to bring a baseless recusal motion."The requests seeking the recusals of Schiltz and Tunheim came in two separate immigration cases and were each filed by Woodward on Tuesday. In the case overseen by Schiltz, the Trump administration is seeking to strip a Minnesota man of his U.S. citizenship. In the second case, assigned to Tunheim, a South African national faces two charges of illegally voting in the 2024 election. She has pleaded not guilty.Schiltz has scheduled a hearing on the motion against him for Nov. 23. Under ethics rules, judges cannot publicly discuss cases pending before them.At the center of both requests are comments Tunheim and Schiltz made to the New York Times for an article published last month. The judges each raised concerns about the Trump administration's handling of cases stemming from its immigration crackdown in Minnesota earlier this year, called Operation Metro Surge.Woodward claimed in each of the filings that the judges' comments raised questions about their ability to remain impartial in the cases. "A judge who has publicly taken sides on the political issue of immigration enforcement cannot then preside over a case concerning one of the Justice Department's key immigration initiatives: pursuing the largest denaturalization effort in Department history to restore trust and integrity in U.S. citizenship," he wrote in the motion to disqualify Schiltz. "Absent recusal, the American people will reasonably question whether Judge Schiltz can be impartial regarding this important matter defending the integrity of American citizenship."Woodward separately claimed that Tunheim's remarks to the Times suggest that he may view the charges against the South African national as unwarranted. "To Judge Tunheim, the 'rule of law' apparently means ignoring the law when it comes to illegal aliens who have broken the law," he wrote.The associate attorney general said Schiltz and Tunheim's statements and participation in the Times article "give rise to the appearance of bias in immigration-related cases," warranting their recusals. Woodward is the only government lawyer who signed the motions.What comes nextExperts on judicial ethics expect the Trump administration will likely fail in its efforts to sideline Schiltz and Tunheim from the cases. Still, these motions to disqualify are rare, and yet even more rare when they are made by the government."They're looking to essentially antagonize the judges and to square off against them in some manner," said Charles Geyh, a law professor at Indiana University Bloomington who focuses on ethics and judicial conduct.In the rare instances where the Justice Department believes a judge should step aside from a case, government lawyers might write to the judge privately and lay out the reasons why they think recusal is warranted, said Stephen Gillers, a law professor at New York University who has written on judicial ethics. But with the efforts involving Schiltz and Tunheim, not only did the Justice Department file their motions on the public dockets, it also promoted them on social media."It's obvious DOJ has decided that its game plan is to challenge the fairness of the judges as a way of undermining judicial authority in the eyes of the public," Gillers said.He called the filings "performative" and said the Justice Department "wants to publicize them to discourage public confidence in what the courts are doing when they rule against the administration."The disqualification motions are the latest in a line of actions taken by the Trump administration that target judges who have ruled against it. The Justice Department filed a judicial misconduct complaint against all but one of the federal judges in Minnesota, including Schiltz and Tunheim, last month because of the Times article. It also submitted ethics complaints against Reyes and U.S. District Judge James Boasberg, the latter of which was dismissed.The Justice Department sued all 15 of the federal judges in Maryland over a standing order that temporarily blocks the immediate removal of immigrants challenging their deportations. A judge in Virginia dismissed the lawsuit, and the Justice Department has appealed that decision. Mr. Trump and senior members of his administration have also publicly insulted judges, including Supreme Court justices, by name and called for their impeachments."This is just a perpetuation of the project," Geyh said. "It's part of the network of efforts to delegitimize the judges involved, make them look partisan, make them look biased as a way to quiet them and diminish the check from the judiciary."Amid rising tensions between the federal judiciary and Trump administration, Schiltz and Tunheim are not the only federal judges who have raised concerns about what they say is the government's disregard of court orders. Others have pushed back against the harsh rhetoric from the president and top administration officials.The Judicial Conference, the policy-making body for the federal courts, issued an advisory opinion in February stating that ethics principles "permit judges to speak or write about the independence of the judiciary, or advocate for the rule of law in general, including why both values are crucial to our system of government."Additionally, the Judicial Conference said its Committee on Codes of Conduct believes there is "room, in at least some circumstances, for the measured defense of judicial colleagues from illegitimate forms of criticism and attacks that risk undermining judicial independence or the rule of law, whether or not they rise to the level of persecution.""If you're talking generally about the concerns with the rule of law as a consequence of the general pattern of conduct the Department of Justice is exhibiting, it's the opposite of bias," Geyh said. "It is them really doing what they need to do to protect the rule of law."

title: New Mexico attorney general accuses Epstein's lawyer, accountant of concealing crimes
description: New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez filed a lawsuit Wednesday against two of Jeffrey Epstein's closest confidants, attorney Darren Indyke and accountant Richard Kahn.
content: The New Mexico attorney general filed a lawsuit Wednesday against two of Jeffrey Epstein's closest confidants, seeking to stop them from receiving payments for serving as executors of his estate.The lawsuit claims attorney Darren Indyke and accountant Richard Kahn "facilitated and concealed" sex trafficking by Epstein at his Zorro Ranch, outside Santa Fe.New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said in a statement announcing the suit that "Jeffrey Epstein did not operate alone, and his death does not end the pursuit of accountability for the people who helped make his crimes possible." "The allegations in this lawsuit describe a network of people and financial arrangements that helped sustain and conceal the abuse of vulnerable girls and young women, including here in New Mexico," Torrez said. "Those who allegedly enabled this exploitation should not be allowed to profit from it while survivors continue to live with its consequences."Indyke and Kahn said in March testimonies before Congress that they were unaware of Epstein's crimes, beyond a 2008 guilty plea on prostitution charges. Lawyers for the men said Wednesday that they "emphatically reject the New Mexico Attorney General's allegations that they were complicit in or in any way knowingly facilitated Mr. Epstein's sexual abuse or trafficking – conduct that by all accounts occurred behind closed doors, in secluded locations, and at times when neither Mr. Indyke nor Mr. Kahn was present.""Neither the New Mexico Attorney General nor anyone from his office asked to speak with Mr. Indyke or Mr. Kahn to seek relevant information from them before filing this baseless lawsuit, raising serious questions about the thoroughness of the Attorney General's investigation and the motivations for his lawsuit," they said.Indyke worked closely with Epstein for decades, and Kahn for more than 10 years, before Epstein's 2019 death in a federal jail, where he was being held on charges of sex trafficking minors. The medical examiner determined his death was suicide.The lawsuit claims Indyke and Kahn were central to "an informal network of associates bound together by a single purpose: knowingly facilitating and concealing his decades-long criminal conduct to preserve and grow Epstein's fortunes and influence."Survivors of Epstein's abuse have claimed Indyke and Kahn were key figures in the management of dozens of interconnected companies used to make payments on Epstein's behalf. The men recently settled a lawsuit in which they were accused of facilitating sham marriages in which foreign-born victims married Americans whom Epstein abused, for immigration purposes.Six survivors lauded the New Mexico lawsuit in a statement Wednesday."Those who argue that [Epstein] could not have acted alone are right. His operation depended on the appearance of legitimacy and access to money carefully structured to avoid exposing his crimes," said Marina Lacerda, Anouska De Georgiou, Julia Molchanova, Courtney Wild, Jena Lisa Jones and Chauntae Davies. "This lawsuit is aimed at the two men most responsible for that appearance and structure."Epstein purchased Zorro Ranch in 1993, building a mansion, airstrip and helipad on the property. He was under investigation in the state at the time of his death and Torrez reopened the investigation this year.

title: Family physicians ask administrative court to halt Florida's plan to end 4 school vaccines
description: The Florida Academy of Family Physicians says the Department of Health failed to follow proper rulemaking procedures, and the Surgeon General says the change would strengthen parents' role.
content: A group of physicians is asking an administrative court to halt Florida's push to end the requirement that children get four vaccines to attend school.The Florida Academy of Family Physicians filed a petition with the Division of Administrative Hearings on Friday. It alleges the Department of Health failed to follow proper procedures in moving to roll back the requirements for hepatitis B, varicella (chickenpox), Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) and pneumococcal conjugate vaccines.The other petitioners are Dr. Danielle Carter of Jacksonville, a 70-year-old with chronic myelomonocytic leukemia who is vulnerable to viruses and is identified as T.K. in court documents; and a school nurse identified as K.O. Both are anonymous.The petition says the "philosophical beliefs" of Surgeon General Joseph Ladapo, who helped lead the push for the repeal, do not override the department's statutory mandate "to prevent the spread of communicable diseases by supervising and securing the vaccination of all children in Florida against vaccine-preventable diseases."The requirements are an agency rule, not state law, so the department can repeal them without legislative approval.The petition says the Department of Health "did nothing" to advance the rulemaking for 225 days, while the limit is 180 days. When rulemaking is delayed, state law requires an agency to submit a "concise statement that identifies the reasons for the delay in rulemaking" every quarter. The department sent letters to the Joint Administrative Procedures Committee on Feb. 26 and June 30 but did not give reasons for the delay, the petition argues."There were no legitimate reasons identified for the delay in rulemaking and the Department did not indicate that it would proceed with the issuance of a notice of proposed rule in its June 30 correspondence," the petition states.The department held its first public meeting on the issue Dec. 12, 2025, in Panama City. On Aug. 24, it proposed a rule that followed the earlier vaccine rule almost word for word. On Sept. 30, it dropped an effort to expand exemptions from the immunization requirements and announced an Oct. 8 public meeting in Lake Mary on the change.The academy is asking for an administrative hearing and a determination that the department acted outside its authority.Ladapo said removing the four vaccines from state requirements would improve parents' rights and benefit the state's overall health."A public health system where parents are actively making decisions and choices about their health, about the health of their children, rather than just going along with something because they don't feel like they have a choice, leads to a much stronger public health system," Ladapo said.The academy disagrees. It says the proposal is not based on "new medical or scientific evidence or data calling into question the necessity, safety, or efficacy of these vaccines." Instead, it says the move abandons "longstanding public health protections without conforming to recognized standards of medical practice, without corresponding medical or scientific justification, and in direct violation of the Department's statutory duty."Gov. Ron DeSantis, First Lady Casey DeSantis, and Ladapo first pushed to remove all vaccine mandates more than a year ago. No legislator filed a bill in any of the 2026 legislative sessions to remove all requirements. Efforts to pass a "Medical Freedom" bill that would have expanded vaccine exemptions and required doctors to provide an alternate vaccine schedule passed the Senate but failed in the House.

title: North Hollywood pedestrian killed by alleged hit-and-run driver, LAPD says
description: The crash happened at around 2:20 a.m. near the intersection of Sherman Way and Lankershim Boulevard, police said.
content: Police are searching for a hit-and-run driver who allegedly struck and killed a pedestrian in North Hollywood early Monday morning. The crash happened at around 2:20 a.m. near the intersection of Sherman Way and Lankershim Boulevard, where Los Angeles Police Department officers said they were called after learning that a light-colored SUV, possibly a yellow Jeep Wrangler, crashed into a pedestrian who was crossing the street. Police said the driver fled eastbound on Sherman Way without stopping to help the pedestrian. Los Angeles Fire Department paramedics pronounced the victim dead at the scene. The victim has not yet been identified pending notification of next of kin. On Wednesaday, LAPD investigators shared a video of the vehicle they believe was involved in the incident. It can be found on LAPD's YouTube channel. A standing reward of up to $50,000 is offered to anyone with information leading to the identification, arrest and conviction of the hit-and-run driver through Los Angeles' Administrative Code Hit-and-Run Reward Program Trust Fund. Anyone who was in the area or who believes they know more was urged to contact LAPD Valley Traffic Division Officer Lozon at 818-644-8117 or Officer Reyes at 818-644-8114.

title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion to New Mexico for misleading consumers about data privacy
description: A jury found that the social media company had deceived consumers for years about its data privacy policies.
content: Meta has been ordered by a judge in New Mexico to pay $25 billion to the state after a jury found that the social media company deceived consumers for years about its data privacy policies. Judge Francis Mathew handed down the amount, which New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez described as "one of the largest, if not the single largest state verdict against a company in American history." "This judgment should be a signal, an unambiguous message, to Silicon Valley," Torrez said in a news conference.In September, jury members found that Facebook had made false or misleading statements by telling consumers that they controlled how their information was shared. The social media giant also misled consumers by claiming it didn't sell or share personal information with advertisers, the jury concluded.The jury found that the company's "most senior leadership," including Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and former chief operating officer Sheryl Sandberg, made misrepresentations about the service's data privacy policies, the judge ruled."These communications were part of a coherent strategy designed to mislead the public," Mathew wrote.The case stemmed from allegations that Facebook deceived users about a data breach stemming from a third-party personality quiz that harvested data from roughly 87 million profiles and sold it to a political consulting firm, Cambridge Analytica, to generate targeted ads. In a statement on Wednesday, Torrez said that the case "has always been about more than one company or one scandal."He added, "It is about whether corporations can mislead consumers about what happens to their personal information without facing meaningful consequences." C.J. Mahoney, Meta's Chief Legal Officer, said in a statement that the company is confident it will "prevail on appeal.""This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online."Where the $25 billion could goUnder the New Mexico Constitution, fines for violations of consumer protection laws are funneled toward state education spending."We may have paid for the construction of schools for the next 100 years," Torrez said, while noting that the money would be tied up if Meta appeals the decision, as expected.Forty-eight other states settled with Facebook in a nationwide case, but New Mexico chose to take the social media company to court on its own. Attorneys for New Mexico had sought $35 billion to $40 billion, arguing that the company would only change its ways with a sum large enough to affect its stock price.Lawyers for Meta said the company should pay no more than $3.4 billion, arguing that a much larger award would violate due process, be unconstitutional and not hold up on appeal.In 2019, the Federal Trade Commission hit Facebook, then called Meta, with a $5 billion fine over its role in allowing Cambridge Analytica to collect users' data without their consent.Meta argued that New Mexico failed to prove that the tech giant's executives made misleading statements about privacy and that its content moderation practices harmed state residents.Shares of Meta rose $13.56, or 2%, to $707.81 in Wednesday afternoon trading.

title: Childcare costs are rising faster than rent, straining U.S. family budgets
description: A growing share of American families are having to shell out more than $2,000 a month for childcare services, new data shows.
content: The rising cost of childcare in the U.S. is vying with food prices and healthcare expenses in straining household budgets.Nearly 8% of families are spending more than $2,000 per month on childcare services, including daycare, nanny services and other programs. That's more than double the share of households that spent that much just three years ago, according to new research from the Bank of America Institute. In September, the cost of daycare and school-related fees rose faster than other essential expenses, such as rent and medical care, compared to the same period a year ago, according to federal labor data. Families nationwide spent an average of 8% of their monthly incomes on childcare services in September, BofA found. Under federal guidelines, childcare is considered affordable when it consumes no more than 7% of household income. Assuming a family spends $24,000 annually on childcare, it would need to earn roughly $343,000 to remain below the 7% threshold. In 2025, median household income was $87,460, according to Census Bureau data. Lower- and middle-income families spend nearly 9% of their annual incomes on childcare payments, while higher-income households spend 7.3%, according to BofA. Along with facing rising childcare costs, workers have also seen slowing wage growth, heightening the financial pressure on many families, Economic Policy Institute economist Elise Gould told CBS News.Separate research from AARP shows that families are turning to grandparents, who provide $172 billion per year in direct financial assistance. Where are childcare costs growing fastest? In some parts of the U.S., childcare fees are rising even faster, according to BofA. In September, median childcare costs rose fastest in Nashville, Tennessee, followed by Jacksonville, Florida, and Phoenix, Arizona, compared to the same period a year ago, according to BofA's analysis."There's been an increase in domestic migration to these areas," BofA Institute economist Taylor Bowley told CBS News, noting that an increase in demand for childcare services is putting pressure on prices. A shortage of childcare workers also appears to be driving up childcare expenses. Employment in the sector fell 0.7% in September compared to one year earlier, making it harder for providers to deliver such services."You see job growth falling and price pressures creeping in, leading to a bit of an availability problem," BofA Institute senior economist David Tinsley told CBS News. A lack of affordable childcare disproportionately affects women's employment opportunities, according to the researchers. Women are more likely than men to take on childcare responsibilities, according to data from the American Time Use Survey."Beyond childcare being a household expense, it's a form of economic enablement," Bowley said.

title: LAPD searching for semi-truck involved in deadly San Pedro hit-and-run crash
description: LAPD detectives asked for help finding a semi-truck driver involved in a deadly hit-and-run crash in San Pedro.
content: The Los Angeles Police Department asked for help finding a semi-truck driver involved in a deadly hit-and-run crash in San Pedro. Detectives said the fatal collision happened around 1:30 a.m. on Oct. 21 near the intersection of Channel Street and Gaffey Street. The tractor-trailer driver allegedly turned left onto Gaffey Street and struck a 47-year-old woman with the truck's right rear tires. Officers said the driver did not stop and continued driving. Los Angeles Fire Department paramedics responded to the scene and pronounced the pedestrian dead. "Drivers are reminded that if they become involved in a collision, they should pull over and stop as soon as it is safe to do so, notify emergency services, and remain at the scene to identify themselves," LAPD wrote in a statement.A standing reward of up to $50,000 has been offered for information leading to the identification, arrest and conviction of the hit-and-run driver, police said. The reward is part of the Los Angeles Administrative Code's Hit-and-Run Reward Program Trust Fund. Investigators urged anyone with information on the collision to contact Detective Elizarraraz and Detective Kolke of the South Traffic Division at (323) 421-2577. Anyone wishing to remain anonymous can call LA Crime Stoppers at 1(800) 222-8477 or go directly to their website at lacrimestoppers.org.

title: Pappas crab cakes in Baltimore sold to technology firm, 1 year after founder died
description: Pappas Seafood Co. -- a longtime Baltimore restaurant popular for its crab cakes that has even been endorsed by celebrities including Oprah -- has a new owner.
content: Pappas Seafood Co. -- a longtime Baltimore restaurant popular for its crab cakes that has even been endorsed by celebrities including Oprah -- has a new owner.The restaurant was recently sold to a financial technology firm called Teamshares, the general manager of Pappas, Justin Windle, confirmed to CBS News Baltimore in an email. The opportunity came about about a year ago at a time when employees started to think about retirement benefits after the passing of former owner, Mark Pappas, Windle said. "The idea is to take the business from the retiring owner to turn it over to the employees who work hard for the company," he added. The purchase will merge the management for all locations and employees will now receive health benefits and a 401k plan that were not possible under "a small, family-owned business," Windle said. Who bought Pappas?Teamshares is a publicly-traded firm headquartered in New York City that buys small businesses with the goal to shifting ownership to employees, according to our media partner, The Baltimore Banner. Founded seven years ago, the Teamshares business model involves the purchase companies to give employees in the company a 10% stake, the company's chief operating officer, Madhuri Kommareddi, told the Banner. "The profits of the business basically buy down the Teamshares stock and increase the employee stock," said Kommareddi.The firm hopes every business it acquires will be 80% employee-owned within 20 years, but it depends on the specific company and its profitability, Kommareddi added.It was the first business venture for Teamshares in the Baltimore area, according to the Banner. Why Pappas? The seafood company sold nearly one year after Pappas founder Mark Pappas passed away. Mark Pappas started his first restaurant in Parkville in 1972 and for 50 years, the seafood company has expanded to include five different locations. The company is currently run by Steve Pappas, Mark Pappas's son, who wants to find someone to run the company when he retires, since his own children have shown no interest in continuing the restaurant. "I didn't want them to be in the restaurant business anyway," Pappas told the Banner. "You need a strong financial backing to survive the ups and downs."What's next for the Baltimore staple?Teamshares says it will place a new president in charge at the restaurant and look for ways to grow profits. The firm hopes to improve consistency for all five restaurant locations."They have different French fries in each restaurant," said Eric Braunstein, the industry lead for food and beverage.The restaurant also hopes that Teamshares can expand their business on third-party food platforms such as UberEats.Pappas wants their customers to know that they will not notice a difference when they walk in the door. "People need to know that nothing is changing at all," he said.Except the crab cakes. The price of the crab cakes can get higher due to market conditions, Pappas said.

title: Eagan City Council approves $500M plan for Ecolab campus expansion
description: Eagan, Minnesota, officials on Tuesday approved a plan for Ecolab to expand its footprint in the city.
content: Eagan, Minnesota, officials on Tuesday approved a plan for Ecolab to expand its footprint in the city.The $500 million investment would add approximately 105,000 square feet to the existing facility at 655 Lone Oak Dr. Construction is planned from 2027 through 2030.According to the Eagan City Council, the campus will feature enhanced labs, customer experience areas and more employee amenities. "Ecolab's continued investment is a clear sign of the confidence businesses have in Eagan and its future," said Eagan Mayor Mike Maguire. "Projects like this strengthen our tax base and support economic opportunity. It's this kind of investment that continues to make Eagan a successful city and a strong community."The 89-acre campus was developed in 1989 as the headquarters for Cray Research and was acquired by Ecolab in 2004.

title: Suspect arrested for San Leandro CVS robbery, assault of store worker
description: A man suspected in a robbery last month at a San Leandro CVS store along with an assault against a store worker was arrested over the weekend, police said Wednesday.
content: A man suspected in a robbery last month at a San Leandro CVS store along with an assault against a store worker was arrested over the weekend, police said Wednesday.The incident happened on Sept. 10 at the CVS at the San Leandro Plaza on Washington Avenue. The San Leandro Police Department said in a press release that the suspect, identified as 38-year-old San Leandro resident Chyance Anderson, gathered merchandise from the store and attempted to leave without paying. Police said that as Anderson was leaving, he struck a 69-year-old female employee with his shoulder, knocking her into a refrigerator and leaving her with significant injuries.After reviewing surveillance footage, interviewing witnesses, and looking at additional evidence, detectives were able to identify Anderson as the suspect, police said. On Saturday, officers arrested Anderson in San Leandro on charges of second-degree robbery, assault likely to produce great bodily injury, and elder abuse. Police said the charges presented to the District Attorney's Office also include allegations of great bodily injury involving an elderly victim and aggravating circumstances."This was a violent incident that left an elderly victim with significant injuries," said police spokesperson Lt. Jeff Walton. "I'm proud of the work our detectives did to identify the suspect and bring this case to a successful resolution."

title: Peggy Flanagan says she is a Phi Beta Kappa member, despite "false reporting"
description: U.S. Senate hopeful and current Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan is disputing reporting that she lied about her status as a member of the Phi Beta Kappa honors society.
content: U.S. Senate hopeful and current Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan is disputing reporting that she lied about her status as a member of the Phi Beta Kappa honors society. On Wednesday, her campaign released a statement from Phi Beta Kappa that contradicts Wall Street Journal reporting that she inflated her academic record. "I can verify that Lt. Governor Peggy Flanagan is a member of Phi Beta Kappa, having been inducted in 2002 at the University of Minnesota," said Amber Cox, Associate Secretary and Chief Operating Officer of Phi Beta Kappa.Flanagan's campaign says she was unable to afford the membership fee as a student. "According to Phi Beta Kappa, universities or donors often cover fees for students with unmet financial need, sometimes at the last minute, so students may not know their fee was paid on their behalf," her campaign said. Flanagan graduated from the University of Minnesota in 2002. Flanagan, the DFL nominee for U.S. Senate, has been Minnesota's lieutenant governor since 2019. She is running against Michele Tafoya, the Republican nominee for U.S. Senate, a former NBC sideline reporter and four-time Emmy winner who is now a conservative commentator.

title: Mystery transgender mailers sent to Texas students traced to newly formed Wyoming company
description: As early voting gets underway in Texas, the CBS News Texas I-Team uncovers business records linking mysterious LGBTQ+ student mailers to a Wyoming-registered company just weeks before the election.
content: A flyer addressed to Texas students and sent by what appears to be a fictitious transgender organization can be traced to a newly formed company registered in Wyoming.The mailer, which presents itself as a resource guide for LGBTQ+ students, began showing up in mailboxes across Texas as early voting got underway for the Nov. 3 election.The return address lists the Texas Transgender Student Union, an organization that appears to have no website, social media presence, or any other online footprint.However, business records reviewed by the CBS News Texas I-Team show a company registered under that name in Wyoming.According to state filings, Texas Transgender Student Union LLC was formed Sept. 2, 2026, using an address at 30 N. Gould St. in Sheridan, Wyoming.So why Wyoming?The state has become one of the nation's most popular destinations for forming limited liability companies. Wyoming is home to roughly 900,000 active business entities, according to the Wyoming Secretary of State, despite having a population of only about 590,000 people.Many of those companies are created by people who do not live in Wyoming.By using a registered agent with a physical Wyoming address, businesses can take advantage of the state's business-friendly laws without being physically present there.One of Wyoming's biggest draws is privacy. State law does not require LLC owners or members to be publicly listed in business filings. In many cases, a public search reveals only the company name and registered agent, not the individuals who control the business.That is the case with the filing for Texas Transgender Student Union LLC.Online speculation about who may be behind the flyers has grown rapidly.CBS News Texas contacted the campaigns of Ken Paxton and James Talarico. Both said they had no involvement with the mailer.Much of the information in the flyer appears to have been taken from the Transgender Education Network of Texas (TENT).But TENT says it had no involvement in the mailing.In a statement posted on its website, the organization said the flyer was not authored, approved, or distributed by the group.

title: Baltimore makes list of best places in the world to visit in 2027. Here's why it was chosen.
description: Baltimore joins the ranks of 24 other locations on National Geographic's list of "The Best Places in the World to Travel to in 2027."
content: Marylanders know Baltimore is a world-class destination, and now Charm City has made a coveted list of the best places in the world to visit in 2027. Baltimore joins the ranks of 24 other locations on National Geographic's list of "The Best Places in the World to Travel to in 2027.""A compact city of vibrant neighborhoods and a gateway to the Chesapeake Bay, Baltimore also proudly wears its outsize role in U.S. history," National Geographic's Brooke Sabin writes.The list includes three other destinations in the continental U.S. – Madison in Wisconsin, the Pacific Coast Highway in California, and the Southern Ozarks in Missouri and Arkansas – along with Puerto Rico and others around the world. Here's a closer look at why Baltimore was chosen.Birthplace, and bicentennial, of the American railroadCharm City chartered the nation's first commercial railroad, the Baltimore and Ohio (B&O), in 1827. Next year, the National Museum of Railroad History & Innovation, formerly known as the B&O Railroad Museum, will celebrate the bicentennial of American railroading with a $38 million upgrade.The upgrade will turn "a niche repository for train buffs" into "a broader and livelier exploration of how railroads have transformed American life," Sabin writes. The museum currently features a 22-sided roundhouse, a collection of vintage equipment and an exhibit on the B&O's role in the Underground Railroad. It's also set to open an outdoor amphitheater this December, along with a new Innovation Hall next January."In what was once the country's oldest continuously operating railroad repair facility, the museum is unveiling archival treasures, such as letters from President Lincoln, and immersive exhibits on current and future railroad technology," writes Sabin. Rich history, and present, along the waterfrontThe National Geographic list also notes "Baltimore's deep sense of community and ties to the water."One example is Lexington Market, which dates back to 1782 and underwent a major redevelopment in 2023. The market includes dozens of local merchants, like the 140-year-old family-owned Faidley's Seafood.Inner Harbor is another historic example that still plays a large role in the city today. It's home to the National Aquarium and the USS Constellation warship, as well as newly developed parks, restaurants and retail spaces."Also along the waterfront, the gradual redevelopment of the Baltimore Peninsula neighborhood, anchored by Sagamore Spirit whiskey distillery, has brought green spaces and restaurants like Nick's Fish House (home to the city's best steamed crabs) to a former industrial area," Sabin writes. "Meanwhile, the Baltimore Blueway has launched a network of kayaking trails—an active, eco-friendly way to explore waterfront landmarks across 20 miles."Sabin also suggests visiting Fort McHenry for panoramic views of the city. That's where Francis Scott Key was inspired to write "The Star-Spangled Banner."

title: Illegal dumping calls in San Joaquin County down 40% over last two years
description: Calls for service regarding illegal dumping in San Joaquin County are down by 40% since 2023-2024.
content: Calls for service regarding illegal dumping in San Joaquin County are down by 40% since 2023-2024, the county board of supervisors said on Oct. 21.The county says the numbers were in a report presented to the board of supervisors on Tuesday by the Illegal Dumping Task Force. The report said that 612 calls had been recorded in 2025-2026, a 21% decrease from the previous fiscal year according to the county."Illegal dumping damages our communities, threatens our environment and costs taxpayers money every time crews are sent to clean up," San Joaquin County Board of Supervisors Chair and Third District Supervisor Sonny Dhaliwal said. "These results show that our coordinated efforts are making a difference, and we're committed to building on that progress." The county approved $2 million in ARPA funding in 2022 that was used to establish the task force, which developed what it refers to as the "Three E's plan," standing for Education, Enforcement, and Eradication. The plan includes awareness campaigns, deployment of Flock Safety Flex cameras in areas known for illegal dumping, as well as numerous community cleanup events. The ARPA funding that the plan relies on is it set to expire Dec. 31, 2026. The county says initiatives will continue by using existing funding in departmental budgets.

title: Man killed in road rage shooting on George Washington Bridge, police sources say
description: A Rockland County man died in a road rage shooting on the George Washington Bridge, police sources said.
content: A Rockland County man was killed in a road rage shooting on the George Washington Bridge on Tuesday night, police sources said. The Port Authority Police Department, which is heading up the investigation, said it had received reports of a single-vehicle crash mid-span just after 7 p.m. When officers arrived, they found the driver, Koran Irvine, with a gunshot wound. Irvine, 46, was taken to Englewood Medical Center in critical condition, but later died, the NYPD said.Utility company Con Edison said Irvine was an employee."We are heartbroken by the tragic loss of a member of the Con Edison family in this senseless act of violence. Our deepest condolences go out to his family, friends, colleagues, and everyone who knew and loved him," a statement read.The NYPD said Irvine was shot in the shoulder, but Port Authority Police said he was shot in the head. No arrests have been made, according to the NYPD. All lanes on the upper level's westbound side were closed for several hours after the shooting, creating a major traffic problem for people trying to get out of New York City. Chopper 2's Dan Rice said one factor that complicated the situation is commercial vehicles only being permitted to use the upper level of the bridge.The closure caused a massive backup across the Bronx to the Major Deegan Expressway, Rice reported.The New York City Emergency Management Department said the westbound side on the upper level of the bridge reopened early Wednesday morning.Prior to then, traffic was seen crawling on the eastbound side of the bridge heading into the city.Anyone with any information is asked to call the NYPD's Crime Stoppers hotline at 1-800-577-TIPS (8477), or for Spanish, 1-888-57-PISTA (74782). You can also submit a tip via the Crime Stoppers website or via DM on X, @NYPDTips. All calls are kept confidential.

title: Massive sinkhole opens in parking lot of Pittsburgh-area Dunkin', leaving customers concerned
description: The Dunkin' on Rodi Road in Penn Hills has been the home to a massive sinkhole since early September.
content: Dunkin' Donuts, or...dunking tires? That's the question in Penn Hills, where a growing sinkhole is raising concerns at the busy coffee shop. For so many, missing their morning coffee puts a hole in the day, and it's being taken to the next level at the Penn Hills Dunkin' Donuts on Rodi Road. The sinkhole has been growing for more than a month now. "It's big, it's growing, and it looks like something is going to crawl out of there," said Angel Jackson, a customer who was at Dunkin' on Wednesday morning. The sinkhole is deep enough that it has exposed old storm drainage under the parking lot. Jackson said she noticed the sinkhole back in September, and since then, it has doubled in size. "I think something needs to happen before somebody's car falls in it, because it's huge," she said. "The hole continues to grow," added customer Nick Buckshaw. "Just very dangerous as cars pull out of the drive-thru; it's really hard to see sometimes, especially in the mornings." Heartland Restaurant Group owns the Dunkin', and they said the issue isn't new; it's actually the third sinkhole due to the piping underneath. Now, they're looking to the municipality and state for help. "We want to make sure this is a long-term solution," said Mike Zappone of Heartland Restaurant Group. "We've had some other issues on this same pipe over the years that have been at our expense, now well over $100,000 in repairs." That bill is only getting larger — not unlike the sinkhole. "We do have some additional safety measures that are coming in [on Wednesday]," he said. "We certainly feel their frustration; we have the same frustration. We just want to get that area as safe as possible for people while we work through this with the authorities and try to come up with a solution." Zappone said they have heard PennDOT is planning to do a study, and they are hopeful they can work together toward a more permanent solution.

title: 78-year-old priest carried out of Colorado ICE facility by fellow detainees after judge orders release
description: A 78-year-old Ugandan priest who spent more than a year in immigration detention was released from an Aurora facility Tuesday.
content: A 78-year-old Ugandan priest, who spent more than a year in immigration detention, was released from an Aurora facility Tuesday, but he was unable to walk out on his own.CBS Colorado cameras captured two fellow detainees carrying Edward Nalwamba from the GEO-operated ICE detention facility to his ride after staff reportedly refused to allow him to use a wheelchair beyond the facility's gate.Nalwamba, who has lived in Colorado for more than two decades, was released after a federal judge granted his petition challenging his continued detention and ordered immigration officials to free him by Tuesday.His release comes after 13 months in ICE custody, during which his attorney says his health deteriorated dramatically."I was walking. I was exercising. I was playing ping pong," Nalwamba said shortly after his release, describing his physical condition before he was detained in September 2025.Now, he says he cannot walk without assistance. Nalwamba told CBS Colorado that staff initially brought him toward the facility's exit in a wheelchair, but would not allow him to take it the rest of the way to his transportation."They get me outside and say we can't go beyond this," Nalwamba explained. "And I'm asking, 'Can't the car come here?' They say, 'No.' I say, 'So how am I going to get the car?'"Nalwamba said two other detainees stepped in and offered to carry him. He knew one of the men from his housing unit but said he did not know the other."Those friends offered to carry me, and, I mean, I'm so grateful to them," he said.The circumstances of his release have drawn criticism from Colorado U.S. Sen. John Hickenlooper.In a social media post Tuesday, Hickenlooper said members of his staff visited the detention center earlier in the day and specifically requested that GEO staff allow Nalwamba to call his caretakers before his release and provide a wheelchair to take him to his ride home.The senator said GEO staff assured his office that both requests would be honored."They failed to deliver on either," Hickenlooper wrote. "No phone call. No wheelchair. No human decency."Hickenlooper called the incident an act of cruelty and pledged to continue holding those responsible accountable.CBS Colorado has reached out to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security seeking an explanation for the wheelchair restrictions, the circumstances surrounding Nalwamba's release and allegations concerning his medical treatment. DHS responded to CBS Colorado with this statement, "On September 18, 2025, ICE arrested Edward Nkugwa Kironde Nalwamba, an illegal alien from Uganda, in Lakewood, Colorado. Nalwamba legally entered the country on January 1, 2002, but chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation's laws. He was granted voluntary departure by an immigration judge on March 2, 2007, and still refused to depart. On June 2, 2009, the Board Immigration Appeals dismissed his appeal and on April 8, 2010, following a dismissal of his appeal in the 10th Circuit, he was issued a final order of removal. On October 20, ICE was forced to release Nalwamba after an activist judge ordered his release. He remains in the country illegally."Nalwamba's attorney, Joy Athanasiou, says her client entered into ICE custody in good health but has experienced serious medical problems while detained."When he came to the detention center a year ago, he was extremely healthy. He was very fit. He exercised regularly. He could do 15 to 20 push-ups. Now, he is wheelchair-bound. He is extremely weak," Athanasiou said.Athanasiou said Nalwamba was diagnosed with pneumonia in January, lost more than 30 pounds and collapsed while detained. She also says he has suffered from an ongoing respiratory illness since June, and accuses ICE of failing to provide adequate testing and treatment.Nalwamba described experiencing chest pain, coughing, dizziness and weakness in his legs.His attorney says his supporters are working to arrange a medical appointment and hope he can begin physical therapy and rehabilitation.In a statement provided to CBS Colorado in June, the Department of Homeland Security defended the medical care available to people in ICE custody."It is a longstanding practice to provide comprehensive medical care from the moment an alien enters ICE custody," a DHS spokesperson said. According to the agency, that includes access to medical appointments and 24-hour emergency care.Nalwamba previously served as a priest at Resurrection Anglican Fellowship in Greenwood Village for approximately 15 years.
