He arrived in the United States from Uganda in 2002 and remained in the country after his tourist visa expired.Nalwamba and his supporters have said he fears returning to Uganda because of persecution connected to his pro-democracy political activities.In its June statement, DHS said Nalwamba had overstayed his visa, was granted voluntary departure in 2007 and received a final order of removal in 2010. ICE detained him on Sept. 18, 2025.Before that arrest, Nalwamba says he had been living under an immigration order of supervision.His attorneys challenged his prolonged detention through a federal habeas corpus petition, arguing the government could not continue holding him indefinitely.Athanasiou says she is concerned that ICE could attempt to detain Nalwamba again.On Monday, a judge granted the petition and ordered Nalwamba released no later than Oct. 20. Despite that ruling, his underlying immigration case remains unresolved."I am back to where I was when they first arrested me," Nalwamba said. "So I was asking myself, 'Why did they arrest me in the first place?'"

title: Colorado movie theater reopens after health inspectors find dead mice, droppings
description: An AMC movie theater in Westminster is back open after health inspectors found dead mice and droppings in a kitchen area.
content: An AMC movie theater in Westminster is back open after health inspectors found dead mice and droppings in a kitchen area, prompting an immediate closure last week.The closure came after months of complaints from moviegoers, who said they saw mice inside the theater. Some customers said the theater's response felt delayed.Mice are not exactly part of the moviegoing experience. So, when Ed Rose spotted one during a showing this month, he pulled out his phone and started recording."I felt something on my leg, and legit (shudders)" Rose told CBS Colorado.When asked if he then stayed for the rest of the film, Rose said, "Yeah, I did. Like, my feet were up."Rose is a regular at the theater and said he's seen mice more than once. Online reviews show similar complaints dating back months, with customers describing mice inside the theater."It is a little obnoxious that it's like, you know, we've seen them," Rose said. "So, when you tell them, it's just kind of," he shrugged.Jefferson County Public Health said customers raised concerns in May, June and again last week. During an inspection Thursday, health officials reported finding dead mice and droppings in the kitchen area. The health department then ordered the theater to close over immediate health concerns. The theater remained closed for four days."I was gonna go see (a film) yesterday and it was closed, and I didn't realize that. So I showed up and I was like, 'Oh, dang it! I forgot my mouse trap!'" Rose joked.AMC made efforts over the weekend to clean the theater, sharing a statement, "The theatre is open and welcoming guests following a temporary closure. AMC takes this matter very seriously and has been working closely with a professional third-party pest control vendor to address evidence of pest activity at the theatre. Over the weekend, extensive cleaning and pest remediation were completed. The theatre has reopened following completion of that work and clearance from the Health Department."The county health department took another look at the theater Monday and cleared it to open. Business appeared to continue as usual Tuesday, as some moviegoers said they were willing to give the theater another chance following the cleanup."It's the closest theater to me, so it's like, if they say they got it under control, I'll probably still go," one customer said.CBS Colorado contacted Jefferson County Public Health for clarification about the findings in the kitchen area and how they compare to concerns about mice elsewhere in screening rooms. According to the county health department, AMC Westminster typically receives its routine health inspection in December.JCPH responded to CBS Colorado with this statement, "Food safety regulations divide retail food establishments into food preparation and dining areas. The movie theater auditoriums are considered dining areas, while routine inspections primarily focus on food preparation areas. During our visit last week, staff found evidence of mice in both areas and required the theater to temporarily close while the issue was addressed. Our inspection and cleanup requirements included the auditoriums, seating areas and concession areas."

title: Sen. Warnock's new report highlights Georgia election readiness, concerns about mail and threats
description: Election officials interviewed across 10 Georgia counties say they are ready for the November midterms, but mail delays, threats against workers and funding needs remain concerns, according to a new report​ from U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock's office​.
content: Election officials interviewed across 10 Georgia counties say they are ready for the November midterms, but mail delays, threats against workers and funding needs remain concerns, according to a new report from U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock's office.All 10 administrators expressed confidence in their preparations, rating their readiness an average of 8.8 out of 10. The interviews included counties with Democratic, Republican and nonpartisan leadership.Election officials report strong staffing, concerns about threatsMost administrators reported success recruiting and training poll workers. One said applications numbered in the thousands, exceeding available positions. Another said the county had enough workers to share with neighboring counties.But six of the 10 administrators said their workers had reported threatening calls, bomb threats or other intimidation.According to the report, counties have responded with additional security and training on defusing confrontations, along with coordination with local law enforcement. Officials also described emergency plans for power outages, severe weather and disruptions at polling places.Mail ballot delays remain a concernSix administrators identified mail-in voting as a potential challenge, citing ballots arriving late or getting lost. Three said mail from their counties goes out of state for processing.Several officials said they planned to collect ballots from local post offices rather than wait for delivery. The report described one administrator who traveled to Florida during a previous election cycle to retrieve ballots.Some administrators said Georgia's 2021 election law, SB 202, had shortened the time available for voters to receive and return absentee ballots.Warnock calls for more election fundingAdministrators said additional federal funding could help hire seasonal workers, upgrade equipment, improve polling-place accessibility and strengthen emergency preparations.Warnock, a Georgia Democrat, is urging Congress to increase election security funding and pass the John Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act and the Freedom to Vote Act."It is now up to Congress to implement meaningful safeguards that maintain election integrity by protecting and supporting those on the frontlines," Warnock said in a statement.

title: Hal Steinbrenner blames Yankees players for coming up short, defends Aaron Boone and Brian Cashman
description: The Yankees have gone 17 seasons without a World Series title. That matches their  longest drought since winning their first championship in 1923.
content: Yankees owner Hal Steinbrenner defended manager Aaron Boone and general manager Brian Cashman following New York's failure to win the World Series and blamed the players for the lack of success."I thought Boone managed a good season, especially with the pitching staff," Steinbrenner said Wednesday. "The bottom line is the players didn't live up to their end of the bargain in the playoffs."New York has gone 17 seasons without a World Series title. That matches the Yankees' longest drought since winning their first championship in 1923, a gap between titles in 1978 and '96."If we don't win a championship while I'm here, I'm sure that will be a frontline story of it all and how people think of me and how a fanbase reacts," Boone said. "I understand that."Steinbrenner spoke alongside Cashman during a joint Zoom news conference from team's spring training ballpark in Tampa, Florida, and Boone followed with a video news conference from Yankee Stadium.New York went 93-68 and finished second in the AL East to Tampa Bay. After sweeping Boston 2-0 in an AL Wild Card Series, the Yankees were swept 3-0 by the Rays in a Division Series.Boone finished his ninth season as manager and has one season left on a two-year contract extension agreed to in February 2025. The 53-year-old former third baseman has led New York to a 790-565 regular-season record and three first-place finishes in the AL East but a 27-30 postseason mark."At the end of the day, we haven't won a championship with me at the helm," he said. "Ultimately that's what has to happen to satisfy certainly myself - that's why I'm doing this - but to answer those questions ultimately."Boone defended not calling out players publicly for mistakes."There is probably a time and place for that, but generally speaking to me that's not leadership," he said. "That's me giving red meat to people that want to be upset with somebody."Cashman, who turns 60 in July, said he and the team have agreed to a new contract and are working on minor details. He became general manager in February 1998 and is the most senior head of baseball operations in the major leagues - San Diego's A.J. Preller, hired in August 2014, is second.When Cashman took over from Bob Watson in 1998, it was the 15th change at GM since George Steinbrenner bought the Yankees in January 1973. Cashman has been the only GM under Hal Steinbrenner, who succeeded his father as controlling owner in November 2008.

title: Domestic violence suspect arrested in Livermore after standoff with police
description: A person was arrested on Wednesday following a domestic violence incident and a standoff with police at a business in Livermore, authorities said.
content: A person was arrested on Wednesday following a domestic violence incident and a standoff with police at a business in Livermore, authorities said.The Livermore Police Department said the suspect who was possibly armed had barricaded themselves inside a business near Fourth Street and South Livermore Avenue in downtown Livermore.Police were seen using an armored vehicle and a remote-operated camera at the scene, and the department said officers are attempting to contact the suspect and negotiate a peaceful resolution.At about 12:30 p.m., police said the suspect had been taken into custody. A department spokesperson said that further details of the incident were forthcoming.

title: Record-breaking 36-pound channel catfish caught in Allegheny River: "That just doesn't happen"
description: A 36-pound channel catfish was caught in the Allegheny River, setting a new state record.
content: A 36-pound channel catfish was caught in the Allegheny River, setting a new state record.The Pennsylvania Fish and Boat Commission said the giant fish was caught by 44-year-old David Taylor Jr. of Munhall on the evening of Oct. 3. Taylor and his friend Alex Atkinson of Sewickley Township were fishing in the Tri-State Hawg Hunters tournament on the Allegheny River and had just set their lines below the Highland Park Lock and Dam near Sixmile Island around 8 p.m. when Atkinson told Taylor there was something tugging on his line. Taylor said he initially thought his catch was a blue catfish, and it wasn't until Sunday morning when the pair returned to the tournament weigh-in at the Southside Public Boat Launch that another angler suggested that his catch might actually be a very large channel catfish.Taylor suspected he had a record-breaker on his hands, so he took it to a certified scale at Reddi Bait and Tackle in Bridgewater, where the fish weighed in at 36 pounds and 2 ounces. But since the scale couldn't produce a printout of the official weight, which is required for breaking a record in Pennsylvania, Taylor had to get the fish weighed somewhere else.The Fish and Boat Commission said he arranged to meet Waterways Conservation Officer Abigail Luteri in Ford City, where a certified scale was also available. Though the fish seemed to be doing fine in the livewell, Taylor was concerned about it making the trip. "I told her that my biggest concern was the health of the fish, and if I felt I had to, I would pull over and release the fish, even if it cost me a chance at the state record," Taylor said in a press release from the Fish and Boat Commission. Fortunately, he said he had caught a tough fish, and it made it to Goodman's Bait and Tackle, where it once again weighed in at 36 pounds and 2 ounces, beating the previous state record set in Northampton County in 1991 by 9 ounces. While only weight is considered for record certification in Pennsylvania, the fish also measured 42 inches long with a girth of 26 inches.After the weigh-in and in-person fish inspection, Taylor and Luteri went to a nearby access point on the Allegheny River and released the channel fish in good health. "Everything worked out in the end, and it feels incredible," Taylor said. "I want to thank my friend, Alex, the bait shops, and Officer Luteri for their help. Honestly, I've always dreamed of catching a state record, but I thought it would be a Flathead Catfish because we catch so many big ones out here in Pittsburgh. So, to catch a Channel Catfish that size? That just doesn't happen. It just goes to show, you never know what's on the other side of that hook. It could be just another fish, or it could be life changing. My advice to other anglers is to pay attention to your tackle and have confidence in your gear. Always make sure your line is strong and hooks are sharp for a moment like this."

title: Man arrested after road rage incident, shots fired outside school in Aurora identified
description: The man who was arrested in Aurora on Tuesday after police said he fired a weapon in the parking lot of a high school has been identified as Luis Melendez.
content: The man who was arrested in Aurora on Tuesday after police said he fired a weapon in the parking lot of a high school has been identified as Luis Melendez.According to the Aurora Police Department, Melendez, 35, and another man were at Rangeview High School to pick up students when an argument broke out between them over a road rage incident. The argument turned physical, and investigators said Melendez fired a weapon before leaving the scene.No one was injured in the shooting.Melendez was arrested shortly after the shooting and investigators said officers recovered a firearm during the arrest.

title: Illinois First Lady MK Pritzker donates $500K to Amy Acton's Ohio governor campaign after Ramaswamy attack ads
description: Illinois First Lady MK Pritzker donated $500,000 to Amy Acton's campaign to become Ohio governor in the wake of Republican Vivek Ramaswamy releasing attack ads featuring her estranged mother.
content: Illinois First Lady MK Pritzker donated $500,000 to Amy Acton's campaign to become Ohio governor in the wake of Republican Vivek Ramaswamy releasing attack ads featuring her estranged mother. The ads feature Donna Arthur, who has been estranged from Acton since the 1970s and whose husband was accused of raping Acton when she was a child, calling the candidate a "liar." Acton's campaign and her brother denounced the ad as a "despicable low."Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker posted a statement from his wife on her donation to Acton in response to the ads. "Bad men gain power when we don't fight back," MK Pritzker's statement reads. "Vivek Ramaswamy represents everything that is wrong with our politics today: arrogance, cruelty, dishonesty, and the belief that it's acceptable to say and do anything for power. I refuse to sit quietly while men like Vivek Ramaswamy exploit a highly qualified woman's pain for political gain.""There comes a time when simply condemning someone's actions isn't enough – we have to put it all on the line to defeat these MAGA men," the statement continues. "This race is about standing up to bullies, confronting extremism, and making damn sure that men who thrive on cruelty and division don't get a free pass to govern. Ohio deserves better, Ohio deserves Amy Acton as their Governor, and I'm willing to fight for her."Pritzker echoed her statement in his post and added simply, "I'm proud that my wife, MK, is supporting Dr. Amy Acton today."Ramaswamy's ad was criticized by both Democrats and Republicans when it exploded into public view Tuesday. "I would not have run that ad," Republican Sen. Jon Husted said in a statement to The Associated Press. Husted is in a tough fight with former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, who on Tuesday called the spot "disgusting."Husted appeared with Vice President JD Vance and Ramaswamy at a Wednesday night rally in Ohio for GOP candidates. Vance said during that stop he was "disgusted" by Republican pushback against Ramaswamy's ad. Husted did not raise the issue during his appearance.Nikki Haley, who sparred with Ramaswamy during the 2024 Republican presidential primary over the personal nature of his attacks, called him "a bad guy" in a social media post Tuesday. "It's a shame he continues to get away with it," she wrote.Ramaswamy said he will spend $4 million to promote it despite the backlash from some members of his own party. Acton, Ohio's former health director, has made no secret of facing homelessness and abuse as a child.Arthur lost custody of her children after their stepfather was indicted for raping Acton. Police and court records show Cledith Arthur was arrested and charged with the rape of his stepdaughter, then 12, in July 1978, after Acton's biological father reported him to authorities. The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978.

title: School bus manufacturer announces $300 million investment in Georgia's Peach County, hiring hundreds
description: One of the largest bus manufacturers in the United States is planning to invest around $300 million in a new manufacturing facility in Georgia and will hire over 300 new employees over the next few years.
content: One of the largest bus manufacturers in the United States is planning to invest around $300 million in a new manufacturing facility in Georgia's Peach County.The Blue Bird Corporation and Gov. Brian Kemp said that it plans to convert a former manufacturing site for diesel-powered motorhomes in Fort Valley into a 1-million-square-foot manufacturing facility to produce various types of school buses.As part of the expansion, the company will open 375 new jobs over the next three years, officials said."For nearly 100 years, Blue Bird has been an incredible part of Georgia's story, and now that story will continue to be written for years to come," Kemp said in a statement. "We are proud when our long-time partners can grow and adapt to changing markets right here in the Peach State, and this expansion is the latest example that our pro-business environment is fostering sustained success for our business partners. I want to congratulate Blue Bird, Fort Valley, and Peach County on this announcement and their continued prosperity."Currently, the company supports more than 1,900 employees across the state."Georgia is where Blue Bird was born, and it has been our home for nearly 100 years. Every bus that rolls out of our plant carries the pride of the people across Middle Georgia who build it," Blue Bird Corporation President and CEO John Wyskiel said. "Our new facility in Fort Valley is our way of investing back into the community where we will continue to build more of the safe, dependable buses that school districts rely on, so we can keep getting children to school safely for the next hundred years."Construction is expected to begin in Q1 2027 with new job openings in manufacturing, operations, and technician roles. Anyone interested in applying for a job at the facility can learn more on Blue Bird's career site.

title: Federal agents knock on doors to track down possible noncitizen voters ahead of midterms
description: Armed and in uniform, agents from the Department of Homeland Security have been knocking on doors to ask residents about their immigration status whether they're registered to vote.
content: Armed and in uniform, federal agents from the Department of Homeland Security have been knocking on doors in several states to ask residents about their immigration status — and to inquire if they have registered to vote or cast votes in past elections, a CBS News Investigation has found. The operation is part of an effort to root out potential noncitizen voters ahead of the midterms. DHS has alleged that there could be as many as 250,000 citizens illegally registered to vote, although election experts have disputed the accuracy of this figure. Just 156 people have been charged with voting-fraud related offenses since the beginning of the Trump administration, according to the Department of Justice. There are 227 million registered voters in the U.S.Critics say that sending armed federal agents to the doors of U.S. residents could be intimidating for legal voters. "What we're seeing now is the federal government is inserting itself into the state process for verifying their voter roles in an unprecedented way," said Jessica Marsden, a lawyer for Protect Democracy, a left-leaning advocacy group that is suing the federal agency over the door-knocking campaign. "And they are doing it in a way that seems maximally designed to scare lawful voters from participating."The home visits ramped up in September, in the thick of the midterm campaign season, and continued over the past weekend. The Justice Department announced Monday that Homeland Security agents in California arrested more than 20 people, all of them green card holders, on allegations they had illegally registered or cast a vote. As part of that roundup, dozens of federal agents descended on the residence of a 72-year-old man from Belize, who was taken from his home in his pajamas and arrested on charges he allegedly voted illegally in the past four elections. "HSI is actively rooting out and investigating election fraud wherever it can be found," said a DHS spokesperson. "Under President Trump, HSI is committed to restoring integrity to our election systems and ensuring that American citizens and only American citizens are electing American leaders."Eric Balliet, a former Homeland Security Investigations agent, said the door-knocking operation is a significant departure from traditional law enforcement activities. "In my 23 years with HSI, I never engaged in or was aware of any incident or initiative that sent Special Agents to private residences to verify the eligibility of voters," Balliet said, who served in the federal government under multiple administrations.In June, the DHS directed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, to assist in deportations of alleged noncitizen voters. Homeland Security Investigations, the agency conducting the at-home visits, is one of the enforcement arms of ICE and typically focuses on criminal cross border investigations like child exploitation, drug smuggling and money laundering. Months later after the announcement, hundreds of agents were pulled off their cases and assigned to track down alleged noncitizen voters as part of a "surge" initiative, according to internal documents reviewed by CBS News. The directive, first reported by CNN, describes a "Criminal Voter Fraud " initiative that includes "field reviews" in at least six states including California, Georgia, Missouri, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin. Photos and videos posted on X show agents from Homeland Security Investigations, some of whom are carrying firearms, approaching houses and knocking on doors, under captions like, "AMERICAN ELECTIONS ARE FOR AMERICANS." One photo from Kansas City HSI's account shows four agents at the door of a woman standing on her porch holding a child's hand. The woman is identified in a Department of Justice press release as Mariana Alexandra Dewey, a Peruvian national who was charged with four counts of voter-fraud related crimes including illegally casting a ballot in the 2024 election. Her case has not yet been heard. Her lawyer declined to respond to CBS News' request for comment. Hours after this article was published, Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson, the ranking member of the Homeland Security Committee, wrote to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin to demand the that DHS immediately cease "law enforcement activity aimed at intimidating the public as the 2026 midterm elections are underway." He said the DHS operations "reflect an anti-democratic departure from the mission Congress set for the Department, and serve only President Trump's voter suppression agenda, not a legitimate enforcement objective."For civil rights advocates, the show of force has sparked concerns about the chilling effect it could have on legal voters."It is sending the signal to a much broader community, do not show up at the polls. Do not vote," said Dr. Carol Anderson, a professor of African American Studies at Emory University."And so if you are somebody who has registered to vote and you're a naturalized citizen, what you see in that community is that — because this is not a regime that makes those discernments — that you're gonna stay away from the voting booth."A DHS spokesperson said, "DHS and DOJ are laser focused on prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and preventing the dilution of the votes of U.S. citizens… Those who are here legally and are not breaking other laws have nothing to fear.""Target List"In one video, agents are filmed holding a document that says, "Target List."That list can be far reaching, said a HSI agent familiar with the initiative who asked to speak anonymously. DHS pulls from internal databases, voter rolls, and other datasets. Then employees attempt to match names against citizenship data provided by the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, or USCIS. In September, a USCIS whistleblower said that employees were asked to review the voter information of tens of thousands of individuals across the country, including citizens. Employees were given quotas to investigate 40 subjects a day, which is a rate of roughly 12 minutes per subject.DHS has defended the data matching program and the work USCIS has done to identify potential noncitizen voters. "Far from being rushed or untrained, these investigative efforts are conducted diligently and professionally," said a DHS spokesperson. "There is no quota on criminality. DHS will pursue each and every illegal voter to the fullest extent of the law .""There's every reason to expect that there are many, many more false positives in these lists," said Marsden. She noted that Homeland Security officials initially said they had identified nearly 16,000 noncitizens on Nevada's voter rolls, but ultimately they were unable to provide evidence of a single illegally registered voter.

title: Musk chose to restrict Ukraine's access to SpaceX satellite network, sources say
description: A decision by Elon Musk led to restrictions on Ukraine's use of SpaceX's satellite communications network, people familiar with the matter told CBS News.
content: A decision by Elon Musk led to restrictions on Ukraine's use of SpaceX's satellite communications network, people familiar with the matter told CBS News.The satellite service, which is used for drone operations, hitting certain targets and protecting sites in Ukraine, was slowed significantly last week.Musk held multiple conversations with administration officials leading up to the order, the sources said. He wanted clarity on the president's thinking on the matter. Musk has expressed distaste with his company being seen as profiting from the continued war between Russia and Ukraine.It's not clear how Musk's order to curtail service was executed. Musk licenses SpaceX's Starshield technology to the U.S. government. He said last week the U.S. controls who can access the technology and what level of service those users receive. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Musk, the world's richest person, wrote on X.Musk did not reply to a request for comment. CBS News has reached out to the White House and the Pentagon for comment.The Wall Street Journal was first to report on Musk's order.The temporary restrictions came as a surprise to some officials inside the administration, who said neither Mr. Trump nor the Pentagon specifically ordered any limits meant to deliberately disrupt drone operations and battlefield communications.Mr. Trump said Monday he was seeking details on who ordered the slowdown."I don't know who it was, but I'd like to find out," he said.Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Tuesday the Pentagon has not manipulated the service."We haven't pulled anything back. There are terms of service that ultimately need to be complied to. And that's where Starlink has the option to make those decisions, but nothing's changed from our view. We haven't made any directives or anything like that," Hegseth told reporters, adding that "we wish the Ukrainians, obviously, success."Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's office told CBS News on Wednesday that Ukraine's use of the system was still throttled.What is Starshield?Starshield is a military-grade satellite network made by SpaceX for the U.S. government and its partners. It runs on similar technology to its civilian sister, Starlink.The U.S. government pays to use Starshield and controls who can access the technology. Its use has been limited to Ukraine and occupied territories. It is not available in Russia.Starshield is essential to Ukraine's armed forces as it allows personnel to communicate and carry out strikes, including by maintaining contact with drones across long distances.There is no working alternative to Starlink, which has put a massive constellation of low-earth satellites into orbit, and no direct competitor comes close.What happened in Ukraine?Ukrainian officials and soldiers told CBS News the country's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment late Tuesday, including a throttling effect that made it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones. Sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defense said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions.Regular Starlink terminals have a 70 km/hr speed cap, that is, the speed at which internet can be used in a vehicle in motion. At rates faster than the cap, the internet degrades and is no longer usable. Starshield has no artificial speed cap and is known to work at speeds of at least 160 km/hr. Strike drones equipped with Starshield cruise at 160 km/h or higher, and they're the backbone of Ukrainian mid-range strikes. Ukrainian units reported link drops at speeds as low as 90 km/hr, making those drones inoperable. The degradation of Starshield is estimated to have cost Ukraine tens of millions of dollars in losses, according to an analysis by Dimko Zhluktenko, a drone pilot and analyst in the Armed Forces of Ukraine.Zelensky said Saturday the speed limits had prevented Ukraine from using Starshield to shoot down Shahed attack drones.The Ukrainian leader wrote on X last week that "the Russians are trying to take advantage of the problems with Starlink in Ukraine, as our interceptor drones depend on this connection among other things."Zelenskyy has suggested there are still some restrictions. He told NBC News over the weekend the maximum speed was 161 km/hr, and he said Tuesday that he'd spoken with Secretary of State Marco Rubio about "the situation with Starlink/Starshield, which needs to be restored." The apparent restrictions drew swift pushback from U.S. lawmakers, with a bipartisan group of senators asking the Defense Department's internal watchdog to investigate last week."There needs to be an investigation, we need to find out who these people are because lives are at risk and lives are lost over these things," Republican Rep. Mike Turner of Ohio said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" over the weekend.Why have Trump and Zelenskyy clashed?Beyond the Starshield disruptions, Zelenskyy has said in recent days that Russia struck Ukraine without warning from the U.S., and deliveries of key interceptor missiles to Ukraine have slowed down.A senior Pentagon official told CBS News on Monday there had been "no change to Department of War policy regarding intelligence sharing or any capabilities we are enabling Europeans to provide to Ukraine."Mr. Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with Zelenskyy in recent weeks, accusing him of not doing enough to seek an end to the Russia-Ukraine war.The U.S. president argues the war is responsible for high energy prices. His administration waived restrictions on buying Russian diesel earlier this month in an effort to ease pressure on the price of the commodity, a move Zelenskyy argued could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin. Mr. Trump also waived sanctions on Russia last week.Mr. Trump said earlier this month that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop striking each other's energy infrastructure — announcing an "energy ceasefire." Zelenskyy initially said Ukraine was willing to abide by such an agreement, but that Russia's strikes never ceased, and several days later he told the Financial Times his country would no longer hold off on striking Russian refineries because Russia was still attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.The Russian government never confirmed that it had agreed to a ceasefire.In a Newsmax interview late Thursday, Mr. Trump called Zelenskyy "not a good guy for us to deal with," and argued Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries would be a "disgrace," as he urged both sides to make a deal while adding that the Ukrainian leader is harder to deal with than Putin."I'm not a big fan of Zelenskyy," Mr. Trump said.

title: Two charged with illegal gold mining in Sierra County enter no contest pleas; "This is not 1849"
description: Two men charged with illegal gold mining in the Sierra along with felony vandalism of public land and private property entered no contest pleas, prosecutors announced Wednesday.
content: Two men charged with illegal gold mining in the Sierra along with felony vandalism of public land and private property entered no contest pleas, prosecutors announced Wednesday.Gregory Arnoldi Jr. and his father Gregory Arnoldi Sr. were also charged with felony conspiracy along with misdemeanor charges of water pollution, altering a stream without notifying state authorities, mining without a permit or reclamation plan, and grading without a permit. The Sierra County District Attorney's Office said both men pleaded no contest on Oct. 8 to the felony vandalism and misdemeanor water pollution and stream alteration charges. In a post on the Sierra County Sheriff's Office Facebook page, the DA's office said the defendants used heavy equipment to modify a historic carriage route to carry their truck and mining equipment, and their work resulted in rock and soil passing into Keystone Creek which flows into the North Fork of the Yuba River near Loganville.District Attorney Sandra Groven said the men were originally charged on in May after an investigation that sprung from a tip by a concerned citizen.Both defendants were sentenced to 30 days in county jail along with a $8,135 fine each, and ordered to implement and pay for a restoration plan for the damaged public and private properties, the DA's Office said. They were also placed on felony probation for three years and banned from performing any mining work during that time."This was a serious illegal mining case submitted to our office by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife," District Attorney Sandra Groven said in a prepared statement. "While Sierra County is proud of its mining history and heritage that continues to this day, we take the laws that govern mining seriously. In this case, the defendants' illegal mining scheme vandalized private and public property and caused significant damage to those properties and to the natural resources that make Sierra County a desirable place to live and visit, including damage to mining artifacts. This is not 1849." In addition, the DA's Office said the defendants were given an Aug. 1, 2027 deadline to complete the restoration work, or face an additional eight months in jail and over $30,000 in additional fines.Groven told CBS News Sacramento that prosecuting illegal mining operations can be a challenge in the county."We are a small county with a lot of public lands which are remote so enforcement can be difficult," Groven said in an email. "We prosecute the cases which are reported and substantiated by sufficient evidence. In this case, damage done to the environment was extensive."Groven said the sentence would be served sometime in early 2027 and a remand date would be scheduled in January.

title: Georgia Instagram personality Shawty Dred indicted on $4 million SNAP card fraud scheme, DA says
description: Shawty Dred would show off private jets, luxury cars, and stacks of money on social media. Prosecutors say his lifestyle was fueled on money meant to help poor Georgia families.
content: An Atlanta social media personality has been arrested on federal charges for allegedly stealing millions of dollars in Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits by using fraudulent accounts, prosecutors say.Mercedes Reshard New, who goes by "Shawty Dred" on social media is accused of taking more than $4 million meant to feed poor Georgia families to fund his lavish lifestyle.According to investigators with the U.S. District Attorney's Office of Northern Georgia, New allegedly controlled more than 350 SNAP accounts created using false identities between 2020 and 2026, having the electronic benefit transfer debit cards mailed to multiple addresses around metro Atlanta. New also allegedly applied for his company, Shawty Dred LLC, to become an authorized SNAP retailer, allowing him to use the cards for purchases. The USDA revoked Shawty Dred LLC's authorization in 2025, and local police arrested New shortly afterward for allegedly selling SNAP benefits, prosecutors say. The officers seized 14 EBT debit cards, which he promptly requested replacements for.In all, federal prosecutors say that New tricked the Georgia Division of Family & Children Services into giving him around $4.6 million in SNAP benefits, which he was able to siphon $4 million from accounts. All the while, prosecutors say he had flaunted flying on private jets, posing with luxury vehicles, and calling other people "broke motherf****s" on social media. "New allegedly stole over $4 million meant for poor families who need help putting food on the table," said U.S. Attorney Theodore S. Hertzberg. "My office is fully committed to rooting out abuses of the SNAP program and holding accountable criminal con artists and scammers who appallingly seek to profit by stealing taxpayer money meant to feed vulnerable Americans."Earlier in October, a federal grand jury indicted New on 46 counts of mail fraud, 15 counts of aggravated identity theft, and one count each of SNAP fraud and illegal transactions with access devices.New was arrested on Oct. 13 and placed in the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service.

title: Saudi Arabia spends billions on its military. Why can't it stop deadly attacks by Iran's Houthi allies?
description: Experts tell CBS News geography, interceptor shortages and evolving Houthi tactics are helping the Iranian proxy menace Saudi Arabia, and global energy supplies.
content: Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent weeks have inflicted severe losses on the kingdom, with missiles hitting energy infrastructure and civilian airports, killing at least 20 people.The Iranian proxy group has struck the headquarters of Saudi Aramco, the world's largest oil company, and is fighting Saudi-backed government forces for control of Yemen's coastline on the Red Sea, a vital waterway for global energy supplies. The fighting has put further upward pressure on oil and gas prices as Iran and the U.S. fight over the nearby Strait of Hormuz.Saudi Arabia, despite its size, wealth and a substantial military, has appeared to be on the back foot as it faces the Yemeni rebels. The kingdom's opaque government releases regular statements about Houthi ballistic missiles and drones being intercepted, including five it said were destroyed Wednesday. But many have got through, including an Oct. 10 strike that killed 13 people at Riyadh's King Khalid Airport, including a U.S. citizen."No country can ever have a 100% interception rating, that just doesn't really exist," Elizabeth Dent, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, told CBS News, but that "was a hell of a one to miss."Saudi Arabia spent $83 billion on defense last year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute — far more than any other country in the Middle East, including Israel.So why has the kingdom struggled to stop the Houthi barrage?GeographySaudi Arabia is vast and, analysts say, geographically vulnerable. Its east, home to the kingdom's oil fields, is bordered by the Persian Gulf — all that separates Saudi Arabia from longtime foe Iran. Early in the war, Iran launched strikes targeting bases used by the U.S. in Saudi Arabia in retaliation for U.S. attacks.To the north, across Saudi Arabia's long border with Iraq, are Iran-backed militia groups that the Saudis — along with the U.S. — struck in July in response to dozens of attempted drone attacks on the kingdom's infrastructure and on U.S. installations in the region.To the south, Saudi Arabia shares a more-than-800-mile border with Yemen. A vast portion of the war-wracked nation is controlled by the Houthis. To Saudi Arabia's west, the Houthis have also been battling for control of the Red Sea's vital shipping lanes."Over the last eight months, they have been facing threats from every direction," said Dent."There is a lot of critical infrastructure: multiple airports, many pipelines, as well as extensive oil production and export infrastructure, military bases, government buildings, royal palaces, and so on," said Thomas Juneau, associate fellow at the Chatham House think tank's Middle East and North Africa Program. "It is simply extremely difficult to provide air defenses for all these sites over such a large area." "If the Houthis are able to hit Saudi infrastructure with only a minority of their attempted drone or missile attacks, it counts as a success for them and an embarrassment and a loss for Saudi Arabia," Juneau told CBS News.Neither Saudi nor Houthi authorities responded to CBS News' request for comment on this story.The interceptor shortageThe ongoing wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have caused a global supply shortage of the interceptors used to shoot down ballistic missiles and other weapons, including the U.S.-made Patriot system used by Saudi Arabia and other American allies.U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, asked about Ukraine's longstanding request for Patriot interceptors, said Tuesday that "every other country in the world" also wants them. "I also talked to Saudi Arabia today. They'd like interceptors. Israel would like interceptors. We would like interceptors. Every country in the world would like interceptors," Rubio said, calling it "probably the most in-demand product right now in the defense field." "Demand coming from the international [market] is stronger than ever," Tim Cahill, president of missiles and fire control at Lockheed Martin, the world's biggest weapons manufacturer and maker of the Patriot interceptors, told CBS News last week when asked about the short supply.Saudi Arabia is secretive about its weapons systems and stockpiles, but CBS News reported in March that Gulf countries were seeking emergency resupplies of interceptors, while the Wall Street Journal and Associated Press have reported that the kingdom has sought air defense systems from Japan, South Korea, France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt.Patriot interceptors are expensive, costing as much as $4 million per unit."If there's fear over utilizing or drawing down your resources," said Dent, "are you more reticent to pull the trigger?"Evolving Houthi tacticsSaudi Arabia has purchased 730 Patriot interceptors from Washington since 2020, according to U.S. military data, but even if it does have enough, the pricey missiles aren't ideal for combating everything in the Houthi arsenal.Patriots were designed to intercept ballistic missiles, and the Houthis have launched those at Saudi Arabia. But the rebels also have an array of relatively cheap drones, including weapons supplied by Iran, and locally made copies of Iranian attack drones.These inexpensive weapons have been a key element in the Houthis' tactics, analysts say. They can be launched in swarms, Allison Minor, a senior fellow in the Middle East Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told CBS News. The Houthis "combine an overwhelming number of relatively cheap systems, namely drones, to distract and disrupt and exhaust, and then amid that, also weave in these more catastrophic missile attacks," she said.The Saudis' multi-layered air defense system is sophisticated, but Houthi drones and cruise missiles can change their trajectory, making them harder to track, said Dent, "so if one aspect of that layered defense system breaks down, it can create a gap in coverage, like what may have occurred for the airport attack.""This is a whole new ballgame," said Dent. "It's a tactic that requires some adjustments."One possible solution could be Ukrainian-developed drone interceptors, which cost in the thousands of dollars to manufacture and are produced in the tens of thousands annually, unlike Patriots, which are produced in the hundreds.Saudi Arabia and some of its neighbors have already made deals with Ukraine to acquire such systems, but Dent said they won't be a quick fix as "a lot of what the Ukrainians have been implementing is very hands-on." The systems require skilled operators, in other words, and they require training. A military with a narrow focusAnother issue is the Saudi personnel available to receive that training. Analysts do not rate the kingdom's military among the world's best, despite its huge defense budget.Saudi Arabia's armed forces have a reputation for being "structured and run according to the interests of its royal leadership, with an emphasis on regime security," said CBS News national security analyst Aaron MacLean."You can spend all the money you want on your military and your missile defenses, but you also have to have a culture of readiness and excellence among the troops responsible," he said. "If that's lacking, again, the problem is inherently a hard one: fighting intelligent people who really are trying to kill you and are willing to be quite creative in their pursuit of that goal," he said. "Some shots are going to get through."When patchwork support "is too patchy"Faced with Houthi successes and dwindling Patriots, the Saudis have been "aggressively seeking out air defense support from a variety of partners," said Minor, at CSIS.The kingdom has invoked a mutual defense pact signed last year with Pakistan and Turkey, under which an attack on one country is considered an attack on all three, much like the NATO alliance's Article 5. Pakistan has already confirmed a troop deployment to the kingdom, and Turkey is also working toward sending forces.France recently agreed to send "military means" to help protect the crucial Yanbu oil terminal on the Red Sea, and announced a separate agreement to help protect other Saudi oil facilities, without offering details. The U.K. government said Tuesday that it would "fly defensive counter air missions" to protect Saudi cities and critical infrastructure from Houthi attacks, but that the aircraft would not take part in strikes against the group in Yemen. Egypt announced Sunday that it was prepared to provide military assistance to Saudi Arabia. Greece has operated a Patriot battery in Yanbu since 2021 and Italy, which has troops in Saudi Arabia and provided the Saudis with radar and anti-missile batteries before the war broke out in February, said in October that it could be willing to bolster the European Union mission protecting Red Sea shipping if other EU nations also step up.There have also been reports of Saudi Arabia attempting to recruit foreign fighters, and using less reliable Chinese interceptors.But this many-pronged approach to national defense could be problematic."Do you eventually get to a point where that patchwork is too patchy?" asked Minor. "The interoperability of different troops and aircraft and radar and interception systems — does that become too much to manage at some point?"The key question, she said, is the extent of the Houthis' own weapons stockpiles."The Houthis have maintained a very steady pace of attacks over the past few weeks," she said. "It's not clear to me if the Houthis are able to sustain that for the long term — if they're gearing up for another years-long confrontation, or if this is an intense shorter-term salvo to try to get back to the negotiating table on better terms."

title: California state workers stage one-day strike over healthcare, pay, remote work
description: Tens of thousands of California state workers are walking off the job Wednesday in a one-day strike, as they are seeking a new contract.
content: Tens of thousands of California state workers are walking off the job Wednesday in a one-day strike, as they are seeking a new contract.The workers, who are represented by Service Employees International Union Local 1000, are protesting what they are describing as unfair labor practices and bad-faith bargaining by Gov. Gavin Newsom's administration. About 100,000 workers across several state agencies are part of the union, including cooks, custodians, nurses and office staff.Earlier this month, more than 96% of workers voted to authorize the strike. The walkout is the first strike in the history of the union."We are going on strike because we know the Newsom administration can and must do better. They must return to the table and bargain in good faith toward a contract that allows state workers to afford groceries, child care, rent and other necessities," SEIU Local 1000 president Anica Walls said in a statement. "Striking is not an action we take lightly. It's an action we are taking because state workers have no other choice."Walkouts are being held across the state, including Oakland, Los Angeles, San Bernardino and Sacramento, where workers rallied outside the California Department of Human Resources (CalHR), before marching towards lawmakers' offices near the State Capitol. "We hope that today prompts the state to do the right thing and come back to the table and bargain with us fairly," union chair Susan Rodriguez told CBS News Bay Area at a rally in Oakland.In a new contract, SEIU is calling for a 20% raise over three years, saying that the Newsom administration had previously deferred raises for state workers. Workers are also seeking increased state contributions toward healthcare costs, along with what they describe as "transparent telework policies based on operational needs."An executive order by Newsom requiring state workers to be in the office four days a week as of July 1 has faced resistance from employees. Last month, Newsom vetoed a bipartisan bill that would have allowed each state agency to make its own telework policy.CalHR, which represents the state in labor negotiations, told CBS News Bay Area, "Departments also maintain regularly updated contingency plans that can be activated as needed to address any potential disruptions in government operations...The department remains focused on achieving a fair and responsible agreement and continues to be available at the bargaining table."About 5,000 union workers deemed "essential" by the Public Employment Relations Board will not be striking. The essential workers include employees at the Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation, Correctional Health Care Services, Department of Veterans Affairs and Caltrans.

title: Sterling Heights man convicted of stabbing death of pregnant girlfriend
description: A Sterling Heights man was convicted of the fatal stabbing death of his pregnant girlfriend​, which resulted in the death of her unborn child.
content: A Sterling Heights man was convicted of the fatal stabbing death of his pregnant girlfriend, which resulted in the death of her unborn child. On Oct. 16, a Macomb County jury found 33-year-old Damarion Winston Goler guilty of second-degree homicide, homicide causing the death of an unborn fetus and tampering with evidence where a homicide is charged, prosecutors said. In March 2024, Macomb County prosecutors say Goler allegedly stabbed his girlfriend, 31-year-old Talic Mersina, near the door of their Sterling Heights apartment. Authorities found Goler and Mersina in the victim's car in the parking lot of his mother's apartment building in Clinton Township. Mersina and her unborn child were both killed. "I hope this conviction brings some measure of closure to the victims' family. The defendant has been held accountable for his actions, but no verdict can undo the tragic loss or erase the pain this family has endured," said Macomb County Prosecutor Peter Lucido in a statement. Goler has been held without bond at the Macomb County Jail since his arraignment in March 2024. He is scheduled to be sentenced on Dec. 3.

title: Arson suspect in custody after 1 rescued, 1 injured in large apartment fire in Plano, officials say
description: According to Plano Fire Rescue, just before 12:10 a.m., firefighters responded to a large blaze at a complex in the 600 block of Legacy Drive.
content: One person was rescued, and another was injured after an early morning fire at a Plano apartment that, officials say, was possibly set intentionally. One suspect is in custody. According to Plano Fire Rescue, just before 12:10 a.m., firefighters responded to a large blaze at a complex in the 600 block of Legacy Drive. When they arrived, heavy flames were visible coming from a balcony, prompting a second alarm to dispatch additional crews. One resident said he had to jump from his patio. "As I was jumping, they had to get the ladder," resident Timothy Howard told CBS News Texas. "There was an older man on top of me, and he was like, 'Help, help,' so they got the ladder. And thank God for these firefighters out here." Plano Fire Rescue said following his rescue, another person was transported to the hospital in an unknown condition, but they were treated and released late Wednesday morning. Officials said that several apartment units were damaged in the fire. "We're estimating approximately 10 units are affected right now, not sure the total amount of residents," Plano Fire Rescue spokesperson Allison Smith said. "We are actively working with building management. They've been very cooperative to get them into a safe place tonight. I know it's cold; l I know it's not ideal conditions early in the morning… So, we're working hard with them and the Red Cross."Authorities told CBS News Texas that the incident is being investigated as arson and that a suspect has been taken into custody. Later in the morning, Plano Police confirmed the suspect's identity as 27-year-old Travon Tamar Andrews. She faces two arson charges: arson causing bodily injury or death, and arson intended to damage a habitat or place of worship.

title: Pedestrian killed in El Dorado County hit-and-run crash identified by officials
description: The woman struck and killed by a hit-and-run driver Oct. 19 on Lotus Road has been identified as 28-year-old Donna Elizabeth Saghebi, the El Dorado County Sheriff's Office Coroner Division said Wednesday.
content: The woman struck and killed by a hit-and-run driver Oct. 19 on Lotus Road has been identified as 28-year-old Donna Elizabeth Saghebi, the El Dorado County Sheriff's Office Coroner Division said Wednesday.CHP Placerville said they were notified of the crash just before 3:30 a.m. on Oct. 19. Lotus Road was closed in the area of Highway 49 and Henningson Park for hours as officers investigated the incident.No suspect vehicle information has been shared by officials.

title: NFL commissioner welcomes review of how Philadelphia Eagles handled Jalen Hurts' blood clots
description: Roger Goodell says the league welcomes an investigation into the Eagles' handling of Jalen Hurts' blood clots after the players' union asked for one.
content: NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said that the league welcomes an investigation into the Philadelphia Eagles' handling of Jalen Hurts' blood clots after the players' union asked for one.Goodell said in his news conference Wednesday at the end of the NFL's annual fall meeting that Dr. Allen Sills, the league's chief medical officer, has gone through the steps that were followed and added that the union had a right to call for a review."Obviously, there was a medical evaluation, and I think our protocols were incredibly good there," Goodell said. "The protocols were followed. Our process is to make sure that's the case, and our chief medical officer has gone through that, so we're comfortable that what we've seen in the protocols have happened."Sills on Tuesday offered a passionate defense of the Eagles medical staff. The NFL said officials were in touch with team doctors and trainers, as well as the Cleveland Clinic in London.Executive vice president Jeff Miller said officials had a good sense of the course of events. He disputed a report that Hurts was awake for more than 30 hours before playing against Jacksonville on Oct. 11, saying that the QB returned to the hotel and slept for roughly seven or eight hours.Hurts is on injured reserve and expected to miss the rest of the season after a blood clot in his left calf traveled to his lungs. The Eagles and agent Nicole Lynn said Monday that Hurts has deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary embolisms.Goodell downplayed the role that international travel may have had in the situation."The most important thing here is Jalen's health, ultimately, and the future of him," Goodell said. "He's a wonderful young man: not just a great player, but he's someone we all care deeply about. I'm more worried about his health, ultimately, but the protocols were followed."

title: Electricity bills force 1 in 5 Americans to cut back on food, Consumer Reports finds
description: Americans living on a fixed income are particularly vulnerable when electricity costs surge, a Consumer Reports expert says.
content: About one in five Americans say they have had to cut back on groceries to afford their electricity bills, while roughly a quarter of consumers are turning down their heating or air conditioning to uncomfortable levels to lower their energy costs, according to a new survey from Consumer Reports. About 80% of people who have lived in the same home for at least three years say their electricity bills have increased over that time, according to a national survey of more than 2,000 adults by the nonprofit advocacy group. The largest share, 28%, said their bills had surged between 20% and 49% over that period. Electricity prices across major U.S. cities have jumped 14% over the last three years, according to federal data.Rising utility costs are worsening the affordability crunch facing millions of American families, who are facing sharply higher gasoline and diesel prices amid higher oil costs due to the war in Iran. The survey found that consumers are cutting back where they can, such as switching to less expensive foods or spending less on discretionary items, to cope with rising electricity bills."We're hearing a lot of folks who don't know what they can possibly do to afford rising [electricity] rates," Sara Enright, senior director of safety and energy at Consumer Reports, told CBS News. "Vulnerable populations like students and retirees who live on a fixed income don't have a lot of flex in their budgets, and so when they get a surprise bill in the heat of the summer, it can be frightening."Consumers often prioritize paying their utility bills because they need to keep their lights on and their refrigerators running, she added. "People are cutting back on food" to pay their utility bills, Enright said. "They're definitely cutting back on non-essentials like vacations and eating out."Other polls show that energy costs are weighing on voters ahead of next month's midterm elections, along with other cost-of-living issues. The cost of food is the top concern for voters in battleground states, followed by gas prices and utility bills, according to an October survey from Climate Power, a clean energy advocacy group."Increasingly distrustful"Consumer Reports found that Americans blame their higher electric bills on utility companies seeking to maximize profits and on the rapid buildout of data centers. Electricity demand is forecast to increase 16% by 2029, mainly due to the proliferation of data centers across the U.S., according to energy management company Schneider Electric.The price of natural gas, ongoing electrification of buildings and vehicles, and other factors are also contributing to rising power costs. Meanwhile, a majority of respondents said they don't believe state utility regulators are protecting their interests, Consumer Reports found. "The public is becoming increasingly distrustful that government is looking out for them, and this is true across party lines," Enright told CBS News. "Everyday people, as the cost of living is rising, are concerned that their needs and interests are not being centered by the politicians and legislators that are supposed to represent them."As electricity prices spike, more middle-income households are applying for government energy assistance despite their incomes being too high to qualify, Mark Wolfe, executive director of the National Energy Assistance Directors Association, told CBS News. The federal Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program is limited to people who earn less than 60% of their state's median income. "People are dealing with high food bills, high gasoline bills, and they've just gone through high summer cooling bills," he said. "If you're living on a tight budget, from paycheck to paycheck, then the cost of driving goes up by $100, $150 a month, that might be the whole surplus in your budget."Consumers "feel the government's not standing behind them, and they can't control these prices," Wolfe added. Help decoding your energy billConsumer Reports said it's launching a new initiative called Power Smarter to help households reduce their energy costs. The effort includes a service called the CR Bill Decoder, where consumers can submit their electric bills. Consumer Reports, which will anonymize the bill data, will use the information to analyze trends and map prices across the U.S.Bill Decoder "is intended to be a simple first step for anybody who wants to learn more about their energy bill and how they can take more power over their bill," Enright said. "We anonymize it and aggregate the data that we collect from it, and we'll be doing national-level and state-level evaluations of what's driving energy costs, and using that information to advocate for the American consumer to keep energy costs affordable."

title: Lime deploys foot patrols to fix badly parked scooters in Chicago
description: Lime deploys foot patrols to fix badly parked scooters in Chicago
content: Lime, Divvy's rival in Chicago's electric scooter and e-bike market, said this week that it is working to clean up Chicago's streets.The company pushed hard against a contract extension with the city by Lyft, the rideshare company that has operated Divvy since 2019. Lime said the contract extension would create a monopoly for Lyft.Nearly two weeks ago, the Chicago City Council Committee on Traffic and Pedestrian Safety deferred consideration of the city's proposed extension of its contract with Lyft.Now, Lime says it is deploying foot patrol teams that will go out and fix poorly parked scooters manually. This is combined with investments by Lime in AI-powered high-tech parking solutions and rider education, the company said.Foot patrol teams will start out in the 40th Ward on the city's North Side, which includes parts of Lincoln Square, Bowmanville, Edgewater, Andersonville, Arcadia Terrace, and West Rogers Park or West Ridge.Ald. Andre Vasquez (40th) recently emphasized the need for scooter parking improvements in the ward, according to Lime.Lime plans by the end of the year to deploy its foot patrols throughout Chicago â especially in high-ridership neighborhoods such as Lincoln Park and Lakeview, in the areas of busy Chicago Transit Authority 'L' stops, and along South and West Side commercial corridors such as 79th Street on the south.

title: Minneapolis police investigate triple shooting on West Broadway
description: Minneapolis police say they are searching for the shooter who injured three men Tuesday night in a busy north side business district.
content: Minneapolis police say they are searching for the shooter who injured three men Tuesday night in a busy north side business district.Officers were called to West Broadway between North Dupont and Bryant avenues after the city's ShotSpotter system and several 911 callers reported gunfire around 8:37 p.m.Police say about 15 minutes later, three men arrived at North Memorial Health hospital in neighboring Robbinsdale with gunshot wounds, all not deemed to be life-threatening."Firearm Assault Shoot Team (FAST) investigators are working to determine the sequence of events that led to the shooting," police said.No arrests have been made.

title: Russia says Ukraine must make "necessary decisions" to end war as Witkoff meets Putin
description: U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, meeting with Vladimir Putin in Russia, voiced hope for new trilateral talks involving Ukraine, and Moscow indicated the talks could resume in November.
content: Progress toward a negotiated resolution to Russia's war on Ukraine is "theoretically possible," Kremlin officials said Wednesday as U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg, but any headway will require Ukraine's leaders to make "necessary decisions," according to Russian state media.If Ukraine fails to make those decisions, the situation for the country "will be worse," the officials said, according to Russian state news agency TASS.Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was quoted by Russian news agencies as saying Moscow would study proposals on the Ukraine war brought to St. Petersburg by Witkoff, but that the talks would take a long time.During Witkoff's meeting with Putin, he and the Russian leader confirmed that Stephen Hubbard, a U.S. citizen jailed in Russia for more than four years, had been released from custody. President Trump said Putin agreed to free the American with "no 'swap' necessary," but he also said it wouldn't have happened had the U.S. not prevented new sanctions against Moscow from taking effect last week. Witkoff told Putin he was a "humanitarian" for releasing Hubbard, sparking backlash in the U.S. State media said Russian officials told Witkoff on Wednesday that a meeting between Mr. Trump, Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping was "possible," referring to an idea the White House has also floated, but Ukrainian officials have balked at as it would sideline them from talks on their own country's fate. After Putin and Witkoff's meeting, a U.S. official told CBS News that the Russians and Ukrainians had agreed to the resumption of trilateral talks with the U.S. at the technical level.According to a Kremlin transcript, Putin's senior foreign policy aide Yury Ushakov said that the Russian leader told Witkoff that Moscow was prepared, in principle, to resume the talks in early November. Ushakov also said the talks would involve building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the war.But Ushakov also said that the proposals brought to St. Petersburg by Witkoff, which he attributed to Ukraine and the European Union, "contained little that was useful in the context of resolving the Ukrainian crisis."Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Fox News on Wednesday that he believed trilateral talks between himself, Mr. Trump and Putin were the best way to resolve the conflict, and that he would not accept any resolution crafted by China, Russia and the U.S., saying: "Don't talk about us without us." Zelenskyy also said any negotiated end to the war would need to be approved by Ukraine's Parliament.Secretary of State Marco Rubio told journalists on a separate trip Wednesday that Witkoff held "positive" talks with Zelenskyy on Tuesday in Oslo before traveling to Russia, and that he would share ideas discussed with Zelenskyy with the Russian side in an attempt to "make some progress."After that meeting with Witkoff in Oslo, Zelenskyy thanked Washington for restoring U.S. intelligence sharing on Russian strikes, after saying this week that his country had stopped receiving advance warnings of imminent Russian missile strikes."We are thankful that intelligence works," Zelenskyy told reporters in Oslo. He said the early warnings for ballistic missiles were "very, very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians."Zelenskyy told Fox on Wednesday, however, that access to data from the Starshield satellite network, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink system, remained "limited" in Ukraine, but that Rubio was working on it and expected full access to be restored.Witkoff planned to return to Oslo for more consultations with European officials following his visit to Russia, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said."I think we may have entered a phase now where the Russians are also looking for opportunities for diplomacy," Støre told Norwegian broadcaster NRK on Wednesday morning.Zelenskyy was still in Oslo on Wednesday, where he said "a lot depends on whether the American side manages to hear something new from Russia today."The diplomacy comes after weeks of friction between Kyiv and Washington, with Mr. Trump criticizing Zelenskyy for Ukraine's continued response to relentless, deadly Russian strikes on energy and civilian infrastructure with Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil infrastructure.Mr. Trump announced an "energy ceasefire" earlier in the month, claiming both sides had agreed to halt strikes on each other's energy infrastructure, but within hours Russia launched new missile attacks on Ukrainian refineries and other sites, and neither Ukraine nor Russia ever confirmed agreeing to a truce of any kind.The U.S. president also announced a deal with Moscow on Oct. 10 for Russia to release millions of tons of diesel fuel over the next several months, which Zelenskyy labeled a sign of "weakness."Russian state media said the first shipment of diesel had been dispatched for the U.S. on Wednesday.

title: Georgia business owner, Florida attorney charged in $2-million Ponzi schemes, prosecutors say
description: Investigators say the metro Atlanta business owner and former prosecutor living in Florida stole around $2 million from investors between 2018 and 2022.
content: Federal prosecutors have indicted a Duluth business owner and a former prosecutor living in Florida accused of running two multi-million-dollar Ponzi schemes for years.Investigators say 70-year-old Roosevelt Tobias "Toby" Bailey and 48-year-old Alvin Jones allegedly stole around $2 million from investors between 2018 and 2022.Prosecutors with the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Georgia say that Bailey operated the schemes through his company, Borg Global. According to the indictment, Bailey promised investors that the company would pool investment funds to buy precious stones and metals outside the country and then resell them inside the United States, doubling their investment. Prosecutors say he also claimed that his company would lease or monitRoosevelt Tobias "Toby" Bailey, a Duluth, Georgia resident, and Alvin Jones, a former prosecutor and current practicing attorney, have been indicted, arrested, and arraigned in federal court on charges arising from two alleged multi-year, multi-million-dollar Ponzi schemes. According to U.S. Attorney Hertzberg, the indictment, and information provided in court: From approximately October 2018 through October 2022, Bailey allegedly operated two fraudulent investment schemes through his company, Borg Global. The first schemeâcalled the Micro-Cap programâpromised investors that Borg Global would pool investor funds to purchase precious stones and metals from outside the United States and then resell them for a higher price within the United States, effectively doubling the initial investments. He also claimed that the company would lease or monetize specific legal guarantees known as Standby Letter of Credit from banks, telling investors that he would take some of the proceeds of those leases to pay investors, prosecutors said. Instead of paying his victims back, investigators say Bailey funneled the money to himself for his own personal expenses, hiding his use of the funds by having his investors send the money to Jones' special lawyer accounts. Jones then kept a portion for himself and sent another part to previous investors to continue the scheme, prosecutors alleged.Bailey received nearly $2 million in investor funds before he cut off communication with his victims in October 2022, officials said."Bailey allegedly lured investors based on promises of massive returns and false assurances that their investments would be held in Jones's trust accounts. But instead of safeguarding that money, Jones allegedly funneled it to Bailey, keeping a piece for himself, while investors lost their savings," U.S. Attorney Theodore S. Hertzberg said.In September, a federal grand jury charged Bailey with seven counts of wire fraud, one count of money laundering conspiracy, and three counts of money laundering. Jones was charged with one count of money laundering conspiracy and three counts of money laundering.Bailey was arrested on Oct. 16. Jones was arrested on Tuesday.

title: St. Paul school board delays vote on English learner teacher cuts after contentious, 5-hour meeting
description: After about five hours and chants of "let them speak," the board put off a decision until the end of the month. District officials say they're losing nearly $5 million because of lower enrollment.
content: The St. Paul school board put off a vote on cutting about 18 English learner teachers until the end of the month, deciding at 10:30 p.m. Tuesday after a meeting that lasted about five hours.District officials laid out the cuts at the meeting, saying St. Paul Public Schools is losing nearly $5 million because of lower enrollment.Based on January figures, the district projected 8,787 English learner students would enroll. As of Oct. 1, actual enrollment was 8,245, a drop of 542 students. The district blames the decline on Operation Metro Surge, the federal immigration enforcement operation in the Twin Cities that happened in early 2026.The St. Paul Federation of Educators, the union representing district educators, has said the cuts would affect at least two dozen schools. Union President Carrie Kyung has alleged the plan was made in secret and rushed through.Superintendent Stacie Stanley rejected that, saying the plan was not something she did in secret or "on a whim." She said she has to make sure the children who are in the district can continue to have the experiences she, board members and the leadership team want for them.Stanley said she "certainly could not have imagined" being in a situation that was not created by the board, her leadership team or herself, but by the effect of Operation Metro Surge. She acknowledged the situation is complex and said it brings "no easy answer."The district said students who need English learner services will still have access, but acknowledged many will experience a disruption.Public comment ended after 45 minutes, and families and teachers in the crowded room began chanting "let them speak." Two people took a megaphone and spoke against the cuts before the board voted to allow more people to share their thoughts. One woman told the board the plan "will decimate our EL program."Board members said they were weighing competing needs. Board member Yusef Carrillo said the board has to bridge a divide between students' needs, especially English learners, whose needs have been "doubly affected," and the district's long-term future. Board member Chauntyll Allen said the board has to make "very difficult decisions" now because avoiding them affects the future.Educators, union members and families rallied outside district headquarters before the meeting. Kristine Ranweiler, an English language teacher, told WCCO that students need support in language, and that when they don't get it, families leave for other districts and schools."We love our students, and we want them to stay in St. Paul," she said.When it approved its budget for the 2025-26 school year, the district said it faced a $51.5 million deficit.

title: Supreme Court rejects Trump bid to restrict some medical treatments for transgender inmates
description: In an unsigned order, the Supreme Court rejected an emergency appeal seeking to revive a policy ending certain medical treatments for transgender inmates.
content: Washington — The Supreme Court on Wednesday left intact a lower court decision that blocked the Trump administration from enforcing a new Bureau of Prisons policy that would end certain medical interventions for transgender inmates.In an unsigned, one-line order, the high court rejected an emergency appeal from the Justice Department asking it to freeze the district court order and revive the new rules. The policy would cut off surgical and hormone therapy treatments, as well as social accommodations, for inmates who have been or will be diagnosed with gender dysphoria. Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas said they would have allowed the Trump administration to enforce the change.The Trump administration sought the Supreme Court's intervention in the dispute last month and argued that the new policy for transgender inmates is needed to "maintain institutional security." But lawyers for a transgender woman and two transgender men in federal prisons who challenged the rules said the Bureau of Prisons has provided hormone treatment to people with gender dysphoria since 1992. They said that the new policy required the end of treatment for nearly 1,000 inmates in the bureau's custody.Li Nowlin-Sohl, a lawyer with the American Civil Liberties Union who represented the inmates, said the Supreme Court's decision is critical for transgender people who are incarcerated in the federal system."The denial of medically necessary health care, including gender-affirming health care, to people in prison is a violation of their fundamental constitutional rights," Nowlin-Sohl said in a statement. "We will continue to defend the rights of our clients and all incarcerated people."
