Incoming chief of staff Reince Priebus told NBC News the administration had discussed holding news conferences in the Eisenhower Executive Office Building, which is adjacent to the West Wing.Mr. Trump ultimately did not follow through with the plans, telling Fox News two days before his 2017 inauguration: "The press went crazy, so I said, 'Let's not move it.'"The idea has appeared to reemerge after more than a year of disputes between the Trump administration and journalists over access to the White House.Last month, Mr. Trump attempted to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House complex, accusing them of unfair coverage. Journalists from all three outlets were briefly unable to access the building, but a federal judge reinstated their press credentials, finding the ban likely violated the First Amendment and the news outlets' right to due process.The Trump administration has continued to periodically block CNN from participating in the television press pool, a group of five networks that cover the president's travel and events on a rotating basis and provide video to other news organizations.(CNN and CBS News are both part of Skydance, the parent company formed by the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery.)More than a year ago, the White House prevented the Associated Press from accessing the Oval Office and some other spaces because the wire service declined to refer to the Gulf of Mexico by Mr. Trump's preferred term, the Gulf of America. The Pentagon has also clamped down on press access. Last year, the military required reporters to sign onto a set of restrictions — including a promise not to "solicit" sensitive information — in order to maintain daily access to the Pentagon. Most news organizations declined to sign the new rules and vacated the building.After a judge struck down the Pentagon's press restrictions earlier this year, the military announced it would stop allowing reporters to enter the building unescorted altogether.Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said a "new and improved press workspace will be established in an annex facility outside the Pentagon, but still on Pentagon grounds."

title: AI-generated political ads have appeared in Pennsylvania. Are these kind of ads allowed?
description: The Stacy Garrity campaign recently released an AI-generated attack ad in Pennsylvania
content: With less than two weeks before Election Day, the Pennsylvania governor's race has taken an artificial intelligence turn. An AI-generated ad by Stacy Garrity's campaign has joined a handful of others around the country in major races, and the use of AI has raised eyebrows. The ad uses an AI-generated likeness of Governor Josh Shapiro and makes references to a sexual harassment complaint that was made against an aide to the governor, not Shapiro himself. It's leading to the question, "Should this be allowed?" Robert Morris University communications professor Dr. Anthony Moretti said no one should be surprised. "It's really well done," he said. "In an environment where, basically, AI is allowed to roam free, why can't a political campaign do this?" Dr. Moretti pointed out that in an age of limited attention spans, the ad doesn't admit to being AI-generated until 45 seconds in. "By 40 or 45 seconds, the message is pretty well-delivered: that 'I, Josh Shapiro, am a bad guy,' but obviously, that's not Josh Shapiro," he said.Obvious if you're paying attention. The Garrity ad joins similar uses of AI-generated attack ads in high-profile races in Michigan, Georgia, New York, Texas, and Kentucky. Garrity told KDKA-TV that she stands by the ad, while the Shapiro campaign told Axios it's "cheap, dishonest, AI BS." "We've got to ask ourselves: Do we want AI manipulating our thoughts leading up to political elections?" Dr. Moretti asked. "As a society, if that answer is yes, I don't know what the ramifications are. If the answer is no, then I think this ad will be discredited pretty quickly." Dr. Moretti added that if restraints are going to be put on AI in our political races, it's going to have to happen fast, because if this can happen in the midterms, one can only imagine what might come in the presidential election in two years. However, deepfake content is not new, and while there have been limited and unsuccessful legislative efforts at the federal level, states like Minnesota, California, and Texas have prohibitions on deepfake impersonations in ads close to Election Day. About two dozen other states require a disclaimer in the ad. Here in Pennsylvania, a deepfake prohibition bill has passed the House, but needs Senate approval before it can go, ironically, to Governor Shapiro.

title: Self-proclaimed Pittsburgh influencer sentenced to nearly 4 years in prison for stalking 11 women
description: The 31-year-old Michael Dadig was sentenced to 46 months in prison and thee years of supervised release after pleading guilty to stalking multiple women.
content: A self-proclaimed influencer from Pittsburgh will spend nearly four years in prison after being convicted on charges of cyberstalking and threats. The Department of Justice announced on Wednesday that 31-year-old Michael Dadig was sentenced to 46 months in prison, followed by three years of supervised release. "Using the Pittsburgh area as a home base, this defendant moved from city to city, brazenly and aggressively stalking, harassing, and intimidating different women in each location," said U.S. Attorney Troy Rivetti. "He sought to terrorize these women in person as well as through hate-filled social media posts, text messages, phone calls, and podcasts, and, at times, in violation of Protection from Abuse orders."Dadig pleaded guilty earlier this year after he was accused of stalking 11 women across multiple states, including Pennsylvania, Ohio, Florida, Iowa, and New York. He was accused of harassing, threatening, and intimidating the women in person, through social media, and on his podcast. "Stalking is not a harmless fixation or a strictly online behavior - it is a pattern that can leave victims fearing for their safety in their homes and workplaces. This defendant did this across multiple communities in different states, taking his conduct from the internet to the real world, and this sentencing holds him accountable for his actions," said FBI Pittsburgh Acting Special Agent in Charge Christopher Giordano. According to the original indictment, Dadig took advice from AI chatbots, including ChatGPT, which led him to claim that the chatbots told him God's plan was for him to build a platform and stand out. He would then show up at victims' homes or places of business unannounced and take pictures of them and post them online without their consent. "Dadig's comments included references to breaking victims' jaws and fingers, dead bodies, burning down gyms, and his victims suffering 'judgment day,'" the news release said in March.

title: Should you trust personal AI agents with your money and data? Here's what experts say.
description: The more access you give personal AI agents, the more capable they can be. But should you trust them?
content: Cybersecurity expert Hed Kovetz would love to have a personal AI agent handle some of his administrative tasks and lighten his workload. But he doesn't trust any of the commercially available agents, like Meta's Muse or OpenAI's Dots, with access to his email accounts, banking details, health records and other sensitive information."It's tempting to use a personal AI assistant. They access your email, order stuff and pay your bills. I would love to get that kind of help," he told CBS News. "But they could be taken advantage of or decide to go beyond the scope of what they are told to do." While Kovetz sees tremendous commercial value in such products, he believes leading technology firms rushed them to market without sufficient security measures. For that reason, he advises consumers to be discreet about what they share with personal AI agents. Yet other AI security experts advise that consumers can use the tools as long as they rely on safeguards and are aware of the risks of providing personal data to an AI agent. "I would be careful about giving full access to some of these commercial AI agents," Kovetz said. "I am aware of the fact that their security and privacy are far from being ready. Some consumers say, 'I don't care, I don't have anything to hide.' But that's not true; they still have medical records, bank accounts." Such agents are already tremendously popular among consumers. When Meta's Muse first became available last month, it quickly became the most downloaded product in Apple's App Store. But while AI agents promise to save consumers time and even money by reading private correspondence and spending money on a user's behalf, they could also take actions that a user never explicitly authorized, leaving the user with limited recourse. For example, it may be hard to know whether your AI agent is working for you or a retailer, Lindsay Owens, a consumer protection expert, told CBS News. She noted that Walmart's shopping agent, named Sparky, boosted average consumer basket sizes by almost 40% compared to shoppers who browse normally. Such data suggests that some AI agents could be trying to upcharge their users, she said.Here's what security experts say they would and wouldn't let an AI agent do for them.Should you let an AI agent shop for you?Lynette Owens, a consumer education expert at TrendLife, an organization formed to protect households in the age of artificial intelligence by informing them about its capabilities and risks, also warned consumers against entrusting personal AI agents with too much access and information about them. When it comes to online shopping, she believes AI agents can be extremely useful for researching products and comparing deals, but she cautions against letting them spend money. "If you want to offload something like comparing deals, that's OK, but I'm not ready to hand off agency around a purchase, especially a high-ticket one. I wouldn't let it use my credentials like a credit card," she said. One reason why she doesn't trust any commercially available AI agent to roam the internet with her credit card in hand is that criminals could trick it. Using what's called a "prompt injection," cybercriminals can trick an AI agent into ignoring its original instructions, such as "Don't spend more than $25." Unlike traditional cyberattacks, prompt injection doesn't necessarily require hackers to break into an account or install malicious software. Instead, an attacker can plant instructions in a webpage, email or document that an AI agent encounters while carrying out a legitimate task.If the agent mistakes those instructions for commands it should follow, it could be manipulated into revealing private information or taking actions its user never intended."We've seen an increase in incidents of prompt injections, and criminals are getting more clever about how they're hiding malicious code on websites," Owens said. "We're so excited about these new capabilities, but with any new technology, the security piece always lags."Media and technology attorney Douglas J. Wood said consumers are liable if they authorize an AI bot to shop on their behalf, and it misinterprets instructions or overspends. "If you give an AI agent, e.g., Muse, credit card information, you are making the bot an authorized user with the power to act on it," he told CBS News. "If it exceeds your instructions and spends your money, the card issuer will argue you authorized the purchasing tool."Under federal law, such an individual would not be entitled to loss protection, Wood explained. "Since you can't pursue the AI bot for improper use (it is not an entity that can be sued), your only remedy is to cut it off," he said, adding that by then the harm will have already been done. His advice to consumers is: "Don't be lazy.""Shop the old-fashioned way with the card in your hands. Authorizing an AI agent to use your card is like giving a bank robber the vault combination and telling him to steal only $100," he said.How much data are you sharing?New York-based entrepreneur Chris Franco, founder of marketing firm Woodridge Growth, has taken the opposite tack. He said tech companies have been collecting consumers' personal data for decades for various uses, such as selling it to advertisers, who use it to better market their goods and services."We've been giving out personal data to ad platforms for the last 20 years, and all we got back was better ad targeting," he told CBS News. "With these agents, you're sharing information, but the benefits are greater. It's a trade-off, but it's a much better deal."To be sure, he wouldn't feel comfortable giving a Muse, Dots or Instinct AI agent full rein over his life, and believes it necessary to give it strict instructions while also monitoring its behavior and activity. He likened giving an AI agent his credit card details to a parent handing off an exclusive credit card for high-net-worth individuals to a teenager without parameters. Both would be unwise, according to Franco. Franco also allows his personal AI agents, including Muse and Grok Bot, to comb through his Gmail inbox. He's tasked them with organizing his receipts into a spreadsheet so that he can manage — and cancel — subscriptions. It's a task he'd estimate would take him hours to do manually, if he ever got around to it at all. "In 10 minutes, it had found a few I wasn't using. I would have canceled them anyway, but this did it way sooner," Franco said. He acknowledges that it has insight into his personal life, including sensitive family matters, but at the end of the day, believes that the benefits of giving AI agents great access to his life outweigh the risks. "The upside and pros of giving it context, in my view, are so much greater than whatever sci-fi-like scenarios there are of it going rogue," he said. "I am comfortable with it having that knowledge about me, because it can help me meet my goals faster." Ask how it worksMatt Fredrikson, a computer engineering expert at Carnegie Mellon and founder of Gray Swan AI, an AI security company, said he gives his AI agents a fair bit of autonomy but also closely monitors their activity, using tools his company builds. "The consumer-facing agents meant for normal people aren't immediately transparent about what they're doing with your data," he said. "But you can ask for that info if you probe them."Simply ask your agent for a plain-language summary of how it went about completing the tasks it handled for you.He also likened outsourcing administrative tasks to an AI agent to hiring a human personal assistant, which comes with a similar set of risks. "If you have a human assistant, you've built a relationship with them, and there's a reason why you hired them in the first place. You trust them with a certain level of authority and autonomy," he said. Simultaneously, when working with a human personal assistant, you're engaging in conversation with them and asking them to explain their thought processes. "You have to do that with these agents as well," he said. Columbia Business School psychology and computer science expert Sandra Matz also drew parallels between working with a human assistant and an AI agent. "If you wouldn't trust another person to deal with your personal information and process it safely, I wouldn't trust an agent," she said. She highlighted one distinct difference between AI and humans, though. "What prevents humans from sharing things they know about you is that they might feel guilty or ashamed, or have a negative emotional response to breaking the trust you've built with them," she said. "You can train an agent not to violate your trust, but they may violate it because they don't have guilt."

title: Memphis fails to pass 1-year data center moratorium, instead opting for a shorter-term ban
description: Memphis has become a hotspot for data centers driven by Elon Musk's SpaceXAI.
content: In a heated city council meeting on Tuesday, leaders in Memphis, Tennessee, voted against a moratorium that would have paused data center development for a year in the city, which has become a hotspot for the facilities driven by Elon Musk's SpaceXAI.Instead, city council members passed a substitute ordinance — which some said they received on short notice and did not have time to review — that would halt construction of data centers for 135 days.Residents and activists have pushed back against data center development in the region for years, starting with the construction of SpaceXAI's Colossus 1 data center in 2024. The company has also built two other data centers and has two under construction in Memphis and the surrounding region, including across the state border in Southaven, Mississippi. Also in Southaven, a plant powering the company's data centers is using methane gas turbines, which prompted a lawsuit from the NAACP and other organizations over alleged pollution.SpaceXAI did not reply to a request for comment. The Trump administration moved to dismiss the case, but earlier Tuesday, a Mississippi federal judge blocked that bid. Supporters of data centers argue they are needed to support the growth of artificial intelligence technology. Advocates also say they will create much-needed jobs, although experts counter many of those jobs are in the construction industry and therefore temporary.The moratorium would have paused the construction of new data centers for a year, allowing the city to adopt permanent zoning and development regulations as well as establish disclosure requirements for data center applicants. It also would have provided the opportunity to study impacts on air quality, electrical infrastructure, water protection and noise. The moratorium would not have halted existing data center operations.The language of the ordinance that was passed Tuesday states that it is intended to complement Memphis Mayor Paul Young's executive order to establish a 90-day period to study the impacts of data center development. Many attendees in the chambers appeared shocked and confused at the proposal for the new ordinance. A few members of the crowd remained in the chambers following the vote where they sang, chanted and vocalized their frustrations. The city council's move comes after a postponement of the vote earlier this month spurred protests in the chambers and resulted in an early end to an Oct. 6 meeting. Community members' opposition to data center development in Memphis is reflective of the broader attitude across America in recent months. According to a recent Pew Research Center survey, over half of Americans say they're not comfortable with a new data center operating in their area — a sentiment that's spilling over into city council meetings and town halls across the country.Ahead of the vote, KeShaun Pearson, the executive director of the Memphis Community Against Pollution, said that community members were concerned about what they feel has been a lack of transparency from local government officials and data centers' environmental impact. "It's as if the people who have been elected to protect us and to stand up to corporations and be that representative have just completely abdicated that responsibility, and left us to fend for ourselves," he said. Pearson and his brother, Tennessee Rep. Justin Pearson, were among a handful of people barred from city council meetings following the protests at city hall earlier this month. A federal judge lifted the ban and the two were present during the vote. Pearson and the group have sued the city council over the ban.

title: Tow truck carrying forklift crashes into Hubbard's Cave; southbound I-90 lanes partially closed
description: Two of the southbound lanes of the Kennedy Expressway are closed at Hubbard Street after a crash involving a tow truck carrying a forklift at Hubbard's Cave.
content: Two of the southbound lanes of the Kennedy Expressway are closed at Hubbard Street after a crash involving a tow truck carrying a forklift at Hubbard's Cave.Illinois State Police said they were called just after 8 a.m. after a forklift fell off a tow truck and hit the bridge at Hubbard's Cave. As a result of the crash, battery acid leaked onto the roadway, but state police said no hazmat response was necessary.The middle and right lanes of I-90/94 southbound are closed for crash cleanup. How long the lanes will remain closed was not immediately known. No injuries were reported. State police did not offer any information about possible citations.

title: WNBA Finals return to Atlanta: Dream tickets sold out for Games 3
description: The Atlanta Dream are back home for Game 3 of the WNBA Finals on Wednesday night after winning Monday in San Francisco.
content: The Atlanta Dream are back home for Game 3 of the WNBA Finals on Wednesday night after winning Monday in San Francisco.Game 3 was moved up to Wednesday because of a concert scheduled at State Farm Arena on Thursday. The scheduling conflict could have sent the Dream to Gateway Center Arena, which holds 3,500 fans. State Farm Arena, the Dream's new home next season, can hold more than 16,000 fans."We are expecting sell outs of both games," a team spokesperson said.Fans who don't want to buy a ticket but still want to join the excitement can attend the Dream's newly announced All for Atlanta WNBA Finals watch parties. The free events will take place at bars, restaurants and gathering spaces across metro Atlanta for both home and away games, according to the team.Atlanta Dream WNBA Finals watch party locationsParticipating venues include:Jolene JoleneThe BeverlyStats Brew PubTom, Dick, and Hank in College ParkPark Tavern — select datesHudson Grille MidtownHudson Grille Downtown — select datesSweetWater Brewing CompanyMcCray's Tavern BeltlineDuke's HideawayHudson Grille TuckerHudson Grille Sandy SpringsHudson Grille KennesawJR Crickets CascadeThe Dream said more locations are expected to be added. Fans should confirm participation for their preferred game with the venue, particularly those hosting on select dates.CBS News Atlanta spoke with Jolene Jolene's general manager about what fans can expect."Watching the games here with the fans, watching the energy come into the building the way they cheer, it's almost as good as being at the game, so we've been having a lot of fun this year cheering for the Dream," said Kelsey Numun.Game 4 of the best-of-seven series is also at State Farm Arena, with tipoff scheduled for 1 p.m. Saturday.

title: Who is running for Michigan governor? Meet the candidates running for the state's top job
description: In August, Michigan voters chose the Democratic and Republican candidates for governor. Candidates from five parties will be on the November ballot.
content: With Michigan's Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer term-limited from running again after her second four-year term, Michigan will see a new face in the state's top job in January.In August, Michigan voters chose the Democratic and Republican candidates for governor. Candidates from five parties will be on the November ballot.Who are the candidates running for Michigan governor in 2026?Jocelyn Benson, Democratic PartyDemocratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson announced in January 2025 that she would be running for governor. Similar to the governor's two-term limit, Benson is nearing the end of her two-term limit as secretary of state, which began in 2018.Winnie Brinks is running for lieutenant governor for the Democratic Party alongside Benson. Benson says her achievements in her current role as secretary of state include upgrades to online services, cutting average wait times of in-person visits and creating self-service stations at branch offices and grocery stores. Benson's campaign promises to make Michigan more affordable, take public schools to the top 10 in the nation and make the government work for Michiganders.John James, Republican Party U.S. Rep. John James, who was reelected to Congress in 2024, announced in April 2025 that he was running for governor. The Republican lawmaker represents Michigan's 10th congressional district. Jay DeBoyer is running with James for lieutenant governor alongside James. James served as an aviation officer in the U.S. Army for eight years and was president of a supply chain and logistics solutions group. He lost U.S. Senate races in 2018 and 2020 to Debbie Stabenow and Gary Peters. He faced Democrat Carl Marlinga twice in the 2022 and 2024 elections, winning in both. James says his plans include supporting small businesses and skilled careers, elevating academic excellence and building safe communities.Anthony Hudson, Libertarian PartyIn March 2025, Anthony Hudson joined the list of gubernatorial candidates, describing himself as a "hardworking Michigan conservative." He worked as a truck driver for 20 years and moved to Michigan in 2012.Hudson ran in the 2024 Republican primary for a U.S. House seat, but lost to Paul Junge. Democrat Kristen McDonald Rivet eventually won the seat. Hudson, of Grand Blanc Township, initially didn't state his party affiliation for this race, but it was later revealed that he is running as a Libertarian Party candidate for governor, with Beau Parmenter for lieutenant governor. This was until the Michigan Libertarian Party disavowed Hudson in a resolution on its website following an emergency meeting on Sept. 27. The party says that the decision was due to "public statements that the Party determined ran counter to Libertarian principles, including statements opposing the freedoms of speech and religion protected by the First Amendment." Details on Hudson's statements were not revealed, but Hudson went live on social media nearly two weeks prior, saying "F*** the Libertarian Party" and accusing members of trying to censure him over comments regarding the LGBTQ community.Hudson says his plans include eliminating property and state income taxes, stopping "the data center and solar panel invasion of our state" to protect farmland and returning power to local communities.Donna Brandenburg, U.S. Taxpayers Party of MichiganDonna Brandenburg is the 2026 U.S. Taxpayers Party of Michigan candidate for governor, running with Robert Donald Cowper II for lieutenant governor. Brandenburg ran for governor in 2022 as a Republican, but was kept off the Republican primary ballot after the state elections bureau found thousands of fraudulent signatures on petitions. However, there was no evidence that the candidates at the time were aware of the fraud.According to the U.S. Taxpayers Party, Brandenburg is an entrepreneur and constitutional conservative who has built businesses across energy, real estate, farming and technology.Brandenburg says her plans include eliminating property taxes and the state income tax, implementing a true Department of Government Efficiency "to slash waste and bureaucracy," and returning government to serve the people.Douglas Campbell, Green PartyDouglas Campbell is running for Michigan governor as the Green Party candidate, and Bobbie Clay is running for lieutenant governor.Campbell ran for U.S. House in 2024, 2012, 2010 and 2008, and for governor in 2006 and 2002, but was not elected in any of the races.In a speech at a recent Green Party event, Campbell said he recommends indexing the hourly federal minimum wage to one-ten-thousandth of the total compensation of the highest-paid member of Congress.Campbell says that if elected, he will focus on affordability, energy, civil rights and public safety.

title: Upload a selfie, find out your "biological age." New FaceAge AI tool available for anyone to use.
description: The FaceAge AI tool from Mass General Brigham lets users upload selfies to find out their biological age.
content: Boston researchers have developed a new AI tool, now available to the public, that lets users upload a selfie in order to find out their "biological age."It's called FaceAge and it's part of a study by Mass General Brigham. Anyone can go to faceage.bwh.harvard.edu, fill out a brief survey and upload three to 10 photos for AI to analyze.Mass General says the whole process takes less than 10 minutes. The AI model has been trained using more than 40 million facial images to give an estimation of biological age."Biological age reflects your body's physiological condition and aging process rather than your actual chronological age," the website explains.Why is biological age important? The researchers say people who look older than their age have higher health risks. They're also studying an AI model that predicts survival rates among cancer patients using just a photograph."As the population ages, physicians need better ways to estimate physical reserve and frailty before recommending intensive treatments such as radiation, surgery or systemic therapy," study author Dr. Raymond Mak said in a statement. "Our goal is to make face photograph-based health assessment more quantitative, consistent and scalable so it can support personalized treatment decisions rather than replace physician judgment."Lifestyle factors like heavy drinking, drug use and smoking can cause someone to look biologically older, researchers said. Users can upload multiple photos over a period of time to see how their biological age changes. FaceAge users have to fill out a consent form before using the AI. Mass General says the photos will only be used for research purposes.

title: Man accused of threatening Mall of America and schools is released; police found no explosives
description: A court document says the suspect said he wanted payback for George Floyd's killing and planned to travel to Washington, D.C., to assassinate the president. Officers found no explosives at his home.
content: A Minneapolis man called 911 and said he had built multiple bombs at home and planned to attack the Mall of America in Bloomington and schools in Minneapolis the next day, but officers who searched his home found no explosives, according to a court document.Minneapolis police responded Oct. 11 to the bomb threat. The caller, a 26-year-old man, said he wanted payback for the killing of George Floyd and belonged to a group that would carry out the attacks the next morning, the document says. He also said he would travel to Washington, D.C., to assassinate the president. He claimed he was part of a terrorist group in Ethiopia as a child and said the United States has been his enemy since then. Officers spoke with the man by phone. He told them he wasn't home and said, "You will not find us," then hung up and could not be reached again. Officers called his sister, who indicated he was inside the home.He eventually came outside and was detained. Asked about the threats, he told officers a friend had told him to call 911 and make them, the document says. He said he is in a GroupMe group chat with people who are planning terrorist attacks at the Mall of America, and that demons are telling him to do things.Officers got a search warrant for his home and found digital electronics, but no explosives.The man was released Oct. 13 and is out of custody. Citing the severity of the threats and public safety, the document asks for a warrant. It does not say what charges he faces, if any.Court records list a hearing on Nov. 17 and an omnibus hearing on Nov. 30.

title: Harriton High School's football future not over, as district announces merger with Lower Merion
description: Harriton High School canceled its 2026 football season after opening with a 53-0 loss to Pottstown.
content: Harriton High School's football future is not over, after the Lower Merion School District on Tuesday announced it would merge the football programs of the district's two high schools next season.In 2027, students from Lower Merion High School and Harriton will be eligible for the new team after the PIAA approved the district's merger application at its October meeting.The logistics of the merger will have to be worked out in meetings with the schools' principals, athletic directors and coaches, Superintendent Dr. Frank Ranelli wrote in a letter to the district community. There's no immediate word on what the team will be called or how the schools' cheer teams and pep bands will be affected."While thoughtfully implementing this change to our high school football programs will require a lot of work, the goal is to create a sustainable program that prioritizes the safety of our student athletes while preserving their opportunities to participate," Ranelli wrote.Harriton canceled its football season in September after opening with a 53-0 loss to Pottstown. The school's principal and athletic director cited player safety and low participation as the reasons for the decision. The Harriton team hadn't won a conference game in the past 10 seasons.Last year, over 300 people signed a petition asking the Lower Merion School District to merge the two high school football programs.

title: Bright sun glare prompts I-70 closures in Colorado's mountains, from sunrise to mid-morning
description: The Colorado Department of Transportation said that starting Wednesday morning, drivers traveling along I-70 through the Floyd Hill area will notice eastbound highway closures between sunrise and 8:30 a.m. due to sun glare.
content: As the days get shorter with winter approaching, drivers in Colorado traveling on I-70 will start running into a new issue: sun glare while they are driving.The Colorado Department of Transportation said starting Wednesday morning, drivers traveling through the Floyd Hill area will notice eastbound highway closures between sunrise and 8:30 a.m. These closures will go through Mile Points 244 to 248.CDOT said the preparatory traffic holds are needed to keep drivers safe, especially when you cannot see the highway or really anything in front of you during that time. CDOT says this hold of traffic is needed for at least an hour to make sure your visibility is not impacted.CDOT said the steep grades and sharp turns reduce visibility and stopping sight distance during sun glare. CDOT also said sudden obstacles such as wildlife become unforeseen hazards because of the sun's glare.Drivers should expect this morning closure every single day, starting officially in November and lasting through February. Drivers who need to reroute can take eastbound I-70 at the bottom of Floyd Hill, continue east on US 6 through Clear Creek Canyon, or take the eastbound Frontage Road to re-enter I-70 at Beaver Brook.

title: Polymarket removes bets on outcome of Cornell sexual assault case
description: The market had amassed $450,000 in wagers by the time it was pulled from the international platform.
content: The online predictions market platform Polymarket has removed a contract that allowed users to bet on whether any of the seven men accused of sexually assaulting or exploiting a Cornell student in 2024 will be charged with a felony sex crime.More than $450,000 had been wagered on this question before it was taken off Polymarket's platform. It had been available since Sept. 30 and was slated to close on Jan. 31. The company's U.S. exchange is regulated by the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which bans trading related to "activity that is unlawful under Federal or State law.""Our primary goal at Polymarket is to bring objective, data-driven insight to the most important questions of our time," a Polymarket spokesperson said Tuesday. "This market addressed whether the government would take action — a process that deserves scrutiny, particularly in a case of such serious concern. That said, we believe in the wisdom of crowds, have heard them loud and clear, and removed the market."Some of the recent outcry over the Polymarket contract has been aimed at its celebrity promoters. Philadelphia 76ers star LeBron James has an endorsement deal with the platform, and he recently appeared in a star-studded commercial that also included cameos by Derek Jeter, Eli Manning, Sue Bird and several others.A spokesman for Spike Lee, who also appeared in the Polymarket commercial with James, told the Associated Press the director had no comment.Polymarket also has partnership agreements with the NHL, Major League Baseball, Major League Soccer, the UFC and ATP Tour. A woman identified in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit last month alleging that seven fraternity members sexually assaulted or exploited her in October 2024 and that Cornell mishandled her complaint. All of those men have denied her allegations, saying either that their interactions were consensual or that they weren't involved. They have not been charged with a crime.Online critics characterized the Polymarket contract as degrading and questioned why celebrity ambassadors would associate themselves with the company. An online petition launched by UltraViolet, a women-led national advocacy organization, singled out James, Manning, Daddario and model Emily Ratajkowski while calling on other famous endorsers to cut ties with the company.

title: Evan Bouchard's OT goal lifts Oilers over Wild, 4-3
description: Evan Bouchard scored on a power play at 3:32 of overtime to give the Edmonton Oilers a 4-3 victory over the Minnesota Wild on Tuesday night.
content: Evan Bouchard scored on a power play at 3:32 of overtime to give the Edmonton Oilers a 4-3 victory over the Minnesota Wild on Tuesday night.Connor McDavid set up Bouchard's goal for his third assist of the game, pushing his NHL-leading points total to 26 and extending his season-opening points streak to nine games.Leon Draisaitl scored twice, Mathieu Joseph also connected and Devon Levi made 27 saves. The Oilers (7-1-1) have won two in a row and seven of eight. Joel Eriksson Ek, Kirill Kaprizov and Ryan Hartman scored for Minnesota (6-2-2), and Jesper Wallstedt stopped 28 shots. Kaprizov leads the NHL with 11 goals.Kaprizov and Hartman scored in the third period as Minnesota overcame a 3-1 deficit to force overtime.Wild: At Calgary on Thursday night.Oilers: Host Carolina on Thursday night.

title: SEPTA bus crash on westbound I-76 injures 5, snarls morning commute in Philadelphia
description: A SEPTA driver and four passengers suffered minor injuries in a crash near the Montgomery Drive on-ramp Wednesday morning.
content: A SEPTA driver and four passengers were hurt when the bus they were on was involved in a crash on westbound Interstate 76 in Philadelphia, blocking several lanes during the morning rush hour.The crash happened shortly before 8 a.m. Wednesday near the on-ramp from Montgomery Drive, just south of the Strawberry Mansion Bridge.Crews could be seen removing the bus's windshield as it was being hooked up to a tow truck.The bus driver sustained a cut to the face, and four passengers were transported to a hospital with minor injuries, a SEPTA spokesperson said.We're working to determine what caused this crash and when the road will be cleared.One lane is getting through.

title: Cartel-linked woman wanted in brutal 1997 murder of her child in Arizona is captured in Mexico
description: Anna Marlene Somoza is now awaiting extradition to the United States, where she will face first-degree murder charges, officials said.
content: A woman linked to drug cartels and accused of torturing and murdering her daughter in Arizona in 1997 has been captured in Mexico nearly 30 years after the crime, officials said Wednesday. Anna Marlene Somoza was connected to a "major transnational drug trafficking network" along the Arizona border through the 1980s and 1990s, the U.S. Marshals Service said in a news release. She was arrested for selling and transporting marijuana in 1993, and agreed to act as a confidential informant for Arizona law enforcement. In November 1993, Somoza had a daughter, Crystal Reyes. The child was born in Nogales, Mexico. Her father was Darren Stockwell, a law enforcement officer and U.S. citizen, the U.S. Marshals said. Somoza and Crystal then moved to Ahwatukee, Arizona, to live with her boyfriend, narcotics detective Avelino Tamala. The U.S. Marshals Service said that Somoza and Tamala began an "improper romantic relationship" while she was a law enforcement source. While living with Somoza and Tamala, Crystal was allegedly subject to "severe physical abuse," including being bound and gagged in a small dog kennel for weeks at a time, the U.S. Marshals said. The abuse "escalated fatally" on January 30, 1997, when Crystal suffocated inside a sealed cardboard box, the agency said. Nearly a year later, in November 1998, human bone fragments were found in Mobile, Arizona. The bones could not be identified. In 1999, Somoza and Tamala were arrested on drug and weapon offenses. DNA was collected. When compared to the bones, the analysis "could not eliminate Somoza as the maternal source," the U.S. Marshals said. But without a paternal DNA source, an identification could not be made. In 2008, Somoza was released from prison.The case went cold until 2014, when Stockwell was located and interviewed by cold case detectives. A sample of his DNA was collected and analyzed, allowing investigators to identify the bone fragments as Crystal's. Somoza and Tamala were indicted on charges of first-degree murder on December 12, 2014. Arrest warrants were issued. Tamala was arrested that day by the U.S. Marshals and Arizona's WANTED Violent Offender Task Force. The task force quickly determined that Somoza had fled to Mexico. They began collaborating with the U.S. Marshal Service Mexico Foreign Field Office, but Somoza could not be found. In 2016, Tamala was sentenced to life in prison. Federal, state and local officials continued to investigate the case for the next 12 years, the U.S. Marshals said. "Extensive investigative efforts" were taken to locate Somoza, but law enforcement found that she "had taken deliberate and extensive measures to evade detection by law enforcement." The long search was also "affected by her close connections with cartels," officials said. In September 2026, members of a U.S. Marshals task force became aware that Somoza was in Cernavaca, Mexico. On Sunday, Mexican police and Interpol officers were able to arrest Somoza in Xochitepec, Mexico. Efforts to extradite Somoza are underway. She will face charges in Arizona, the U.S. Marshals said. Attorney Juan Rocha, who teaches at Arizona State University, told CBS affiliate KPHO-TV that Mexico often seeks assurance the death penalty will not be pursued. Prosecutors have not publicly said whether they will seek the death penalty against Somoza. "No one can hide from American justice forever," said Timothy Courchaine, U.S. Attorney for the District of Arizona, in the news release. "The United States Attorney's office stands in partnership with both our federal and critically our state partners to ensure defendants have their day in court. We look forward to now working alongside our Mexican partners to bring this fugitive back to Arizona."

title: South Fulton horseman's fight over seized horses reaches federal appeals court
description: Nearly a decade after Fulton County seized his horses over allegations of animal mistreatment, a South Fulton horseman's fight to receive just compensation for his property has become a potentially precedent-setting constitutional case.
content: Nearly a decade after Fulton County seized his horses over allegations of animal mistreatment, a South Fulton horseman's fight to receive just compensation for his property has become a potentially precedent-setting constitutional case.Brandon Fulton, whose seven horses were seized in 2017, appeared Tuesday outside the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in downtown Atlanta, where judges heard arguments in his long-running lawsuit against Fulton County.Fulton was never indicted, and the allegations against him were dismissed in 2018. But by the time he sought the return of his horses, the animals had been sold or transferred by rescue organizations entrusted with their care.Fulton sued the county, arguing that its failure to return the animals or compensate him violated the Fifth Amendment's Takings Clause, which protects private property from being taken by the government for public use without just compensation.A three-judge federal appeals panel previously sided with Fulton on his right to pursue a constitutional claim, prompting further review by the full appeals court. Tuesday, during more than an hour of arguments, judges focused on whether Fulton should have pursued other legal remedies under Georgia law before bringing his constitutional claim in federal court.His attorney, Brian Williams, argued that the Fifth Amendment itself provides a legal avenue for seeking compensation, regardless of other remedies that may have been available."He chose to bring a federal claim, which was his right," Williams told CBS News Atlanta.Williams acknowledged the legal complexities but said the underlying principle is straightforward."The merits of the claim are clear to a layperson," he said. "Where it gets tricky is the legal technicalities about how you bring a claim in court."Fulton maintains that rescue organizations sold his horses before the criminal case against him was resolved, despite agreements he says required the animals to be held until its conclusion."The final disposition wasn't until 2018," Fulton said. "So how are all the horses being sold prior to 2018?"Speaking outside the courthouse while sitting on horseback, Fulton said the dispute has become about more than the animals themselves."This is my livelihood," he said. "This is my life."He also questioned the county's treatment of him throughout the ordeal."They don't treat me equal under the Constitution and value what I stand for," Fulton said. "And there's many more out there like me."If the appeals court upholds the earlier panel's ruling, Fulton could continue pursuing financial compensation from the county. The case could also eventually reach the U.S. Supreme Court.A written ruling is expected in the coming months.As for the horses, nearly 10 years after they were seized, Fulton still does not know where they are, and suspects he may never see them again.

title: Waukegan police officer charged with misconduct for misusing license plate readers, law enforcement databases
description: A Waukegan police officer is facing five felony charges for allegedly misusing the city's automated license place readers, like Flock cameras, and law enforcement databases.
content: A Waukegan police officer is facing five felony charges for allegedly misusing the city's automated license place readers, like Flock cameras, and law enforcement databases.Waukegan police and the Lake County State's Attorney announced Tuesday that Oscar Magpali is facing five counts of official misconduct.Magpali has been a department employee for 11 years, officials said. Officials said they first identified "numerous" searches of vehicles registered to Waukegan Police Department Employees and people associated with those employees. As they investigated those searches, WPD said an administrative and a criminal investigation were launched separately. Their investigation of electronic and departmental records, as well as witness interviews, led them to examine activity in the Illinois Law Enforcement Agencies Data System, or LEADS, and the National Crime Information Center. As a result of that investigation, five official misconduct charges were filed against Magpali.Police said a department-wide administrative investigation and audit into officers' use of law enforcement databases remains ongoing. Magpali was placed on administrative leave after the initial allegations, and remains on leave at this time, police said. Police also said their administrative investigation is ongoing and remains separate from the criminal investigation.Magpali is due in court on Nov. 3.

title: 2 Michigan cities and 15 villages have no one running to lead them as mayor this election cycle
description: A Bridge Michigan analysis found that close to 1 in 10 of the more than 5,400 local elected positions on the ballot could be left vacant. Rural communities are hit hardest, and school boards make up close to a third of the gaps.
content: As a real estate agent, Tish Mallory is used to crisscrossing the country roads of Seville Township in mid-Michigan's Gratiot County looking to match homes with buyers.But this summer, she drove those same roads looking for something more elusive: someone, anyone, willing to run for township clerk, a job that pays $12,960 a year and often comes with a fair amount of abuse from residents."I asked several people who said 'no,'" before the deadline to get names on the November ballot, said Mallory, the rural township's supervisor."We have an appointed clerk now who I had to beg," Mallory said. "'Please, I need a clerk!'"A Bridge Michigan analysis of ballots in communities across Michigan found at least 478 elected races with no candidate or too few candidates running, threatening to leave close to 1 in 10 offices vacant out of the more than 5,400 local elected positions on the ballot across Michigan on Nov. 3.Those unwanted jobs range from library boards that decide what books to purchase and put on shelves to school boards that help set education policy to village presidents to township supervisors. The openings are spread across the state but hit rural communities particularly hard. Local school board positions are by far the office most frequently going unfilled, making up close to a third of the positions lacking candidates.City, township and village boards can appoint individuals to vacant positions after the election if there were no candidates. If boards are unable to fill those positions, the vacancies return to the ballot in the next regularly scheduled election.It's not just a Michigan problem. One study found 10,000 open seats in which there were no candidates across the country in 2024.Experts say it's a growing but little-recognized problem. While top-of-the-ticket races such as governor and U.S. senator get lots of attention and candidates, Michigan's local communities struggle to find people willing to shoulder the typically part-time, low-paid jobs that keep water flowing and roads repaved.Three out of four townships and villages report having more difficulty filling mandatory elected positions, according to a recent University of Michigan survey of community leaders. Animosity toward national politics has seeped into town halls, where trust in government is making public service jobs less attractive, said Stephanie Leiser, director of U-M's Center for Local, State and Urban Policy, which conducted the survey."Who wants to sign up for a low-paying job where you're officially working 12 hours (a week) but it's more like a full-time job," Leiser said. "And by the way your neighbors may hate you."Those vacancies matter, because many of the positions directly impact daily quality of life, from collecting taxes to running elections, Leiser said."We want smart, motivated people in these jobs," she said. "If you're just begging people to take positions, you're probably not going to get the most qualified person."There are at least 14,500 elected local government positions in Michigan townships, villages, cities and school boards. The majority are part-time, with those in small, rural areas often paid less than $10,000 a year.Trustees in smaller townships can make as little as $50 a meeting. Many school and library boards are unpaid.Bridge Michigan collected online samples of ballots in every community across the state to compile a list of races in which no one is running. The list includes races in which there are not enough candidates to fill multiple available positions, for example, if only two candidates are running for three open school board posts.The analysis found 145 school board posts without candidates, 151 village board posts and 29 library board positions.Many openings are critical to the operations of local communities. The city of Laingsburg in Shiawassee County has no one running for mayor. Neither does Arenac County's city of Omer, which also has no candidates for two city council seats.Fifteen of Michigan's 252 villages have no candidates for village president, including New Lothrop Village in Shiawassee County."What are we going to do?" asked Karen Maksimchuck, who has been the clerk of New Lothrop for 39 years. The village of 565 people also has a board post for which no one is running. By law, the president and board members must be residents of the village."Our previous mayor moved Up North. My husband is filling in (as village president), but he's already done his two years."Maksimchuck said the village board will "advertise in the local paper after the election" to solicit applications for the post so the board can appoint someone.No one is going to do it for the $1,800 annual salary, the clerk said."I don't think (the trouble finding candidates) has anything to do with the pay," Maksimchuck said. "I think some people don't want to get involved."There are 10 township clerk openings on Michigan ballots for which no one is running. One vacancy is in 745-resident Bridgehampton Township in Sanilac County.Township clerks manage elections, but it's become harder to recruit and retain township clerks since changes to the state constitution mandated additional days of voting, said Bridgehampton Township Supervisor Leo Sonck."It's a lot more work (than in the past)," Sonck said. The clerk post pays $11,000 a year. "Even if we wanted to add extra compensation, we can't."There's been a heavy turnover of clerks in the last four years, because of the extra work," Sonck said. "There were a lot of veteran clerks who said, 'I'm done.'"Ingallston Township, near the Wisconsin border in Menominee County, is one of four townships with no one running for treasurer, a position responsible for tax collection and banking."We've been looking for a treasurer since I started two years ago," said Ingallston Supervisor Dan Bartell. "It's a really good position for somebody that's retired and can be part-time, work from home, earn a few extra bucks. But generally, people don't like to deal with the public. There's a lot of demanding people out there who expect things to happen yesterday."Michael Siegrist, clerk of Canton Charter Township, the second-most populous township in the state with about 99,000 residents, said he believes the struggles to find candidates for local offices can be traced to a general decline in public service."Volunteerism is down everywhere, from Elks Clubs, Rotary, Kiwanis," said Siegrist, who serves as president of the Michigan Municipal Clerk Association. "There's some fraying of community ties."For example, the Jaycees, which bills itself as a leadership training and civic organization, has suffered membership declines of more than 10% annually across the country in recent years. Those organizations used to serve as feeder systems for public service, Siegrist said."Civics as a value has been more challenged," Siegrist said. "And institutions don't have the same value or respect as they used to."Several bills that could make it easier to fill local government jobs are getting little traction in Lansing.One set of bills would appropriate $3.5 million to provide "back office" help with finance, human resources and information technology, easing the strain on clerks and treasurers. Another would allow townships to hire someone who is certified to run elections from outside the township if the clerk position is vacant."Most of these positions are over and above the employment that people have," Siegrist said. "The load on our individuals in our society has gotten heavier, and that makes it more difficult."Faced with candidate shortages, some townships are working around the law to appoint deputy clerks and treasurers who aren't required to be community residents. Without the same residential requirement, many villages have switched from elected to employee clerks and treasurers, and shrinking councils to the legal minimum of five members.Meanwhile, Mallory is already looking for someone who'd be willing to run for township clerk in 2028."It's hard," she said. "Somebody's gotta do it."

title: Multiple armed carjackings involving ride-hailing service drivers lead to arrest of Baltimore man
description: A man has been arrested and charged in connection with multiple carjackings last month that involved ride-hailing service drivers in Baltimore.
content: A man has been arrested and charged in connection with multiple carjackings last month that involved ride-hailing service drivers in Baltimore.Twenty-three-year-old Caron Davis is accused of committing three armed carjackings in different neighborhoods, the Baltimore Police Department (BPD) said in a statement posted to X. The incidents occurred in the 1500 block of Montpelier Street, the 2600 block of Tyler Street and the 200 block of Waldorf Avenue.Davis -- who is known to police due to several prior arrests -- was taken into custody Oct. 8 as part of a sweep conducted by the city's Warrant Apprehension Task Force (WATF). Davis has been charged with three counts of armed carjacking and multiple firearm violations. He is also facing theft and assault charges.The first carjackingCharging documents obtained by CBS News Baltimore state that on Sept. 19, an employee for Baltimore Sedan Services called police and said that he had been carjacked. Police met the victim, who explained that he was sent to the 1500 block of Montpelier Street to pick up a rider. Once at the location, the driver told police that a man entered his vehicle and immediately held him at gunpoint. The man told the driver "not to touch anything and get out," according to the charging documents. The suspect then climbed into the front seat and drove off. The victim told police he didn't get a good look at the suspect, but did see that he was a Black male, young, wearing dark clothing and carrying a light-colored bag.Police contacted the car service and received the phone number and address of the caller who requested the ride. Police discovered that the suspect used a cellular service that could only be used when connected to Wi-Fi.Investigators used data from Apple, ComcastPolice then issued a warrant to the cellular service, hoping to identify the user of the cellphone. Investigators later received the username and email address of the account holder, the charging documents said. Police also served a search warrant to iPhone maker Apple Inc. for the account email address, as well as to Comcast Cable Communications for the IP addresses associated with the phone.Police said they were able to obtain the suspect's address, in the 1500 block of Montpelier Street, but were unable to take the person into custody at that time. The next carjackingsWhile that investigation was unfolding, there were two more reports of rideshare drivers being carjacked at gunpoint. A report on Sept. 20 came from the 2800 block of Waldorf Avenue, while another came on Sept. 22 from the 2600 block of Tyler Avenue. That address is one block away from the Montpelier incident, Baltimore police investigators said.The same company, Baltimore Sedan Services, was contacted for a ride in both incidents. When the drivers arrived, they were held at gunpoint until the suspect drove off in their vehicles.How police caught their suspectA 911 call for a domestic dispute ended up leading to Caron Davis's arrest in the carjackings. On Oct. 2 a woman called police to the 1500 block of Montpelier Street. That caller was later identified as Davis's girlfriend. During their investigation, police noticed that Davis matched the description of their carjacking suspect. They also observed him using an iPhone to provide someone the same address police had visited for one of the armed carjackings.Police learned that Davis was on probation at the time and the email address he used to register his phone was the same email received from the cellular texting service, Apple Inc. and Comcast Cable Communications during their carjacking investigation.

title: We bought and tested what was sold as an experimental weight loss drug. The lab results were "pretty terrifying."
description: CBS News tested what was marketed as an experimental weight loss drug bought from several sources to find out what's actually in the vials.
content: A drug that's not FDA approved and still in clinical trials is being advertised all over the internet. Buying it turned out to be alarmingly easy.First, CBS News national correspondent Adam Yamaguchi placed an online order through the website for Reset Wellness, a clinic started by a nurse practitioner, for 20 milligrams of retatrutide. The weight-loss medication, known as Reta, is an experimental peptide drug that Eli Lilly is studying as a next-generation obesity treatment. At checkout, he was promised a health evaluation, but the product arrived a week later without ever having to speak to a health professional. Next, he purchased Reta from the website for Bodystreet Jupiter, a gym in Florida, after confirming he met its Body Mass Index, or BMI, requirement. The site said a doctor would review his intake form. The product arrived two days later without a consultation.He even found a poster advertising the product for sale over the counter, at a bodega in Brooklyn.Yamaguchi was able to buy a vial labeled "Retatrutide" at the corner store for $90. It came with a warning on the label that read "Research use only, not for human consumption."Dr. Reshma Ramachandran, a Yale physician who has studied the growing use of peptides and weight loss medications, said it's "astounding" how easily accessible these drugs are. She said people who try products labeled as retatrutide are essentially acting as guinea pigs, because the drug is still in clinical trials and has not been certified as safe and effective.She said prescribing a drug should involve a conversation about a patient's medical history, the risks and whether the treatment is appropriate.What's actually in the vials?University of Iowa research scientist Jason Galpin analyzed the samples for CBS News.Both samples Yamaguchi bought online were consistent with a basic standard Galpin created for retatrutide, which isn't the same as the drug being studied in Eli Lilly's clinical trials. But the bodega sample didn't appear to even contain a peptide at all."It does not look anything like a peptide," Galpin said of the sample Yamaguchi bought at a Brooklyn corner store, which was labeled as Reta.Instead, Galpin found a compound called phenylacetic acid, which he described as a filler. It's commonly found in fragrances and lip balms.Further testing by Carl Ross, director of development at the University of Iowa's Center for Biocatalysis and Bioprocessing, found 13 colonies of bacteria in the sample. He warned that injecting material contaminated with bacteria could cause an infection. "As kids, we're all taught to wash out cuts if we get cut, but in this case … we're injecting bacteria under the skin where it could multiply," Ross said. "It's pretty terrifying."Ramachandran shared the concern."What's frightening to hear is that someone who's buying this, who's spending money on this, is going to potentially get themselves very sick," she said.Ramachandran said she hopes regulators can find ways to oversee these platforms as access to unapproved drugs continues to grow."I am trying to be hopeful that there might be ways to regulate these platforms… like the horse is out of the barn and so we're going to be trying to catch up to what's our current reality of really easy access"CBS News has reached out to INDR Labs, Reset, Bodystreet for comment. They have not yet responded.A spokesperson for Eli Lilly sent CBS News the following statement:"Regulated manufacturers must demonstrate quality and consistency, dose after dose. Black-market sellers do not. A single test is a snapshot, not a guarantee that the dose will be sterile or stable in two weeks, let alone that the next vial will be safe. Giving consumers false confidence in unregulated products based on limited testing risks putting more people in harm's way. Every day FDA, DOJ and other authorities fail to act against the growing black market is another day unsuspecting consumers are put at risk. Third-party testing of a single sample with unknown ingredients and origin does not make an illegal product safe. Neither does taking a previous dose without apparent harm. Consumers are gambling with their health, with no way of knowing when a dangerous vial may arrive at their door. CBS itself recently reported on two deaths associated with black-market retatrutide, while media outlets in the UK, Ireland, an Australia have reported serious injuries and at least one death associated with similar illicit products. Just this week, Bloomberg reported that two manufacturers formerly on FDA's Green List had been laundering product from other sources, had been contaminated with black mold and bugs, and had been destroying records."

title: 3 injured in violent Davie crash involving van, recycling truck, police say
description: Davie police said the crash is under investigation, but it doesn't appear to be criminal in nature at this time.
content: Drivers in Davie are being asked to seek an alternate route after a violent crash early Wednesday morning forced officials to shut down several lanes of S. State Road 7, according to police.According to Davie police, officers responded to the 4000 block of S. State Road 7 to investigate reports of a traffic crash in the area.Video from the scene showed that the crash appeared to involve a van and a large recycling truck.Police said three adult passengers in the van were rushed to a hospital with serious injuries. The driver of the other vehicle remained at the scene and was not transported to the hospital.Police are asking drivers to seek an alternate route because all three northbound lanes on S. State Road 7 are shut down from Orange Drive (Southwest 45th Street) to Oakes Road (Southwest 36th Street).Police said that Traffic Homicide Detectives also responded to the scene and continue to actively investigate the incident.However, police added, the crash did not appear to be criminal in nature.No other details were available.

title: 30 residents of Hopkinton, Massachusetts assisted living facility sent to hospital since woman's death
description: The health director in Hopkinton, Massachusetts is demanding answers after a series of new problems at the Golden Pond Assisted Living Facility.
content: The health director in Hopkinton, Massachusetts is demanding answers after a series of new problems at the Golden Pond Assisted Living Facility.Last month, an 86-year-old woman died in a unit there where the temperature reached 99 degrees. Now, 30 other residents have been taken to the hospital in the last three weeks, according to health director Shaun McAuliffe."I don't have access to why all the residents were transported. I do know that there were four complaining of heat-related issues," McAuliffe told WBZ-TV Tuesday.The transports happened as the town and multiple authorities work to determine how the woman died on Wednesday, Sept. 30. A police report said her "apartment was extremely hot with the thermostat indicating that the room temperature was 99 degrees Fahrenheit."According to the report, a facilities manager told police that the heat had been turned on a day prior.According to a timeline provided to WBZ by McAuliffe, Hopkinton's Health, Building, and Fire Department staff found the temperature of the building to be above the legal threshold of 78 degrees Fahrenheit on Oct. 1. The dead woman's room was at 81 degrees and heating returns ranged from 85 to 104 degrees, McAuliffe wrote.Golden Pond's HVAC contractor turned the heating system off on Oct. 1, but McAuliffe says the town continued to receive calls stating that the facility was dealing with temperature issues. The heating system remained off until Oct. 15.The town also conducted a food safety inspection of the facility on Oct. 14 and found multiple issues including rodent droppings in a cookware storage room and cockroaches crawling along the wall in the food prep area of the kitchen.McAuliffe said he's now seeking immediate action from the facility. He wrote a letter to Golden Pond's director and the Massachusetts Executive Office of Aging and Independence (EOAI) seeking an explanation for the facility's HVAC issues by Wednesday, Oct. 21."The Board of Health will take action if Golden Pond fails to comply with orders," the letter states.The EOAI told the health director it had four inspectors on site Tuesday completing a full compliance audit.Douglas Noble, director of operations at The Communities at Golden Pond, did not respond to a request for comment on this story.He sent WBZ this statement after the resident's death:"The Communities at Golden Pond, an assisted living residence, is closely cooperating with its regulatory agencies regarding the death of a resident last week," Noble said. "Our HVAC system is professionally maintained by a licensed contractor on both a seasonal and as-needed basis and was working properly at the time of this incident. Each apartment in our community has an individual thermostat that residents can operate directly, although we encourage our residents to push their call button for staff assistance with it."McAuliffe said he has the power shut down Golden Pond, but noted it's a solution that might not work."I can't do that here because we have residents with various memory care issues and other needs, so there needs to be a plan in place," he told WBZ.

title: Twin Cities man charged with killing father with hammer
description: A 29-year-old North St. Paul, Minnesota, man is accused of fatally striking his father with a hammer last weekend.
content: A 29-year-old North St. Paul, Minnesota, man is accused of fatally striking his father with a hammer last weekend. The man, who was charged Tuesday, faces two counts of second-degree murder in connection to the incident on Saturday. According to the charging documents, officers were dispatched at approximately 1:30 p.m. to the 2700 block of Chippewa Avenue on an assault call. The 911 caller told police that their schizophrenic son had struck her 69-year-old husband on the head with a hammer. When officers arrived, they found the victim suffering from a significant head wound. He died the next morning at Regions Hospital. The victim's wife said her son was diagnosed with schizophrenia five years ago and recently changed medications, which changed his behavior. She said he was more stressed, stayed up for days and stopped eating. She told police that he had never been aggressive or violent in the past and loved his father, the charges said. He recently had a seizure and moved into the home the day before the incident. The victim's wife said the son hit the father twice in the head with the ball-peen hammer "without any warning or prior argument." He then fled the home. With the help of the alleged attacker's brother, he was found and arrested. When talking with police, the son admitted to hitting his father and said that "he was holding me for hostage," the criminal complaint said. He faces up to 40 years in prison. If you or someone you know is in emotional distress, get help from the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988. Trained crisis counselors are available 24 hours a day to talk about anything. In addition, help is available from the National Alliance on Mental Illness, or NAMI. Call the NAMI Helpline at 800-950-6264 or text "HelpLine" to 62640. There are more than 600 local NAMI organizations and affiliates across the country, many of which offer free support and education programs.

title: USPS reviews security clearance concerns at Golden Post Office as ballots show up in mail
description: As Jefferson County ballots enter the mail, the U.S. Postal Service says it is reviewing concerns about whether some people handling mail at the Golden Post Office had completed required background screening and security clearances.
content: As Jefferson County ballots enter the mail, the U.S. Postal Service says it is reviewing concerns about whether some people handling mail at the Golden Post Office had completed required background screening and security clearances.Austin Wolf, who has worked for the Postal Service in various capacities over the past five years, said his concerns about security at the facility began about two years ago when a shortage of mail carriers was followed by an influx of people he did not recognize working inside the post office.Wolf said he understood the importance of postal security requirements after leaving a Postal Service job and later returning as a contractor."I have been a postal employee. I quit and began contracting, and I was under the impression that my clearance still existed."Wolf said he was informed that his clearance became invalid when he resigned and that he could not return to work inside the building until completing the screening process again."It was a very rigorous process, fingerprints, background check," he added. Wolf said he became concerned after observing individuals working in restricted areas and handling mail. He said it appeared some people were sharing badges and questioned management about who was being allowed access to secure areas.He later reported his concerns to the Postal Service's Office of Inspector General but believed they were not receiving sufficient attention.Despite his concerns, Wolf said he has not witnessed any ballots being improperly handled."Just to be clear, I have not seen anything happen to a ballot that shouldn't have happened."A job posting for the Golden Post Office states that a criminal background investigation includes a 10-year review of locations where an individual has lived, worked, or attended school in the United States or its territories. It states that anything less would be considered incomplete.On Oct. 4, CBS Colorado asked USPS whether contractors working at the Golden facility had completed the required clearances.The following day, a USPS spokesperson thanked CBS Colorado for bringing the concerns to the agency's attention and said officials would coordinate internally to gather the facts.CBS Colorado later learned a staff meeting was held at the Golden Post Office that same day. "They started collecting all the information from the contractors that were there that didn't have clearance. They asked them to leave and said they would expedite their processing," Wolf said. "We got answers back, and there were quite a few that weren't cleared and still can't be cleared."After the meeting, USPS provided CBS Colorado with an updated statement saying postal officials were reviewing the concerns and emphasizing that only properly authorized individuals are permitted to handle mail and access postal facilities.The agency said any contractor who has not completed required screening will not be authorized to perform mail-handling duties until those requirements are met.USPS said Jefferson County ballots will be handled under established election mail procedures and security protocols.The agency declined to provide detailed figures on how many contractors work at the Golden Post Office or how many, if any, were working without the required clearances. Instead, USPS directed CBS Colorado to submit a federal records request, a process that could take several weeks. CBS Colorado has submitted that request.Voters who want to track their ballot this election can follow its path online.

title: University of Pittsburgh student charged after bomb threat prompts evacuation
description: Eden Schwartz, a University of Pittsburgh student, was charged after allegedly making a bomb threat against Wesley W. Posvar Hall.
content: A University of Pittsburgh student has been charged after allegedly making a bomb threat against Wesley W. Posvar Hall on Tuesday, authorities said. Eden Schwartz, a 19-year-old Pitt student, has been charged with terroristic threats and threats to use weapons of mass destruction, according to the criminal complaint. She is accused of posting an Instagram story that was captioned, "On my way! to bomb the statistics department." The criminal complaint said Schwartz is enrolled in a statistics class located within Posvar Hall. According to an alert from the university's Emergency Notification Service that went out at 3:57 p.m. on Tuesday, the University of Pittsburgh Police Department was investigating threats made toward a department inside Posvar Hall. The building at South Bouquet and Roberto Clemente Drive was then evacuated. In a 5:45 p.m. update, the university said officers cleared the hall, which was reopened, and normal activities resumed. A university spokesperson said K-9s searched and cleared the building. "Because this is an active criminal case, the University will have no further comment," the spokesperson added. The incident prompted a large police presence that impacted traffic, and people were asked to avoid the area. The university's police department, along with the Pittsburgh Bureau of Police, learned of the alleged bomb threat from the Federal Bureau of Investigation. "It's almost like we've gotten used to it in this day and age," Pitt student Logan Krock told KDKA-TV. "It's crazy, but it's not that odd of a scenario. It happens all the time." Posvar Hall houses the College of General Studies, the Office of Veterans Services, the Osher Lifelong Learning Institute, the School of Education, the Graduate School of Public and International Affairs, the University Center for International Studies, plus the social sciences departments of the Dietrich School of Arts and Sciences, according to Pitt's website. It is the largest academic-use-only building on campus and sits on the former site of Forbes Field.

title: Mistrial in trial of man accused of setting fire that killed 3 Baltimore firefighters
description: A judge declared a mistrial after a jury failed to reach a verdict in the trial of James Barnett, charged in a 2022 fire that killed three Baltimore firefighters.
content: A judge declared a mistrial after a jury failed to reach a verdict in the trial of James Barnett, who was charged in a 2022 fire that killed three Baltimore firefighters on Stricker Street.After nearly a week of deliberations, jurors were dismissed Tuesday without reaching a verdict.Barnett was charged with second-degree arson, involuntary manslaughter and reckless endangerment in connection with the Jan. 24, 2022, fire.Baltimore Fire Lt. Kelsey Sadler, Lt. Paul Butrim and Firefighter/EMT Kenny Lacayo died while battling the blaze."Today's outcome is deeply disappointing for the families of Lt. Paul Butrim, Lt. Kelsey Sadler, and EMT/Firefighter Kenny Lacayo, whose lives were tragically cut short in the Stricker Street fire in 2022," Baltimore State's Attorney Ivan Bates said. "After hearing the evidence, the jury was unable to reach a unanimous verdict. While this is not the outcome we sought, our commitment to these families and to pursuing justice has not changed."Bates added that "justice delayed is justice denied."We recognize that not every case results in a conviction on the first attempt, and not every path to accountability is easy," Bates said. "But a case's difficulty will never diminish our responsibility to pursue justice for the victims and their loved ones.
