Three members of the Baltimore City Fire Department family lost their lives in this devastating fire, and EMT/Firefighter John McMaster was injured. The pain and loss experienced by their families, friends, and colleagues remain immeasurable."A juror told CBS News Baltimore off-camera that the jury was split 6 to 6. The juror said deliberations were extremely frustrating because some didn't want to listen to the evidence. The juror added that every piece of information from prosecutors proved Barnett guilty beyond a reasonable doubt, saying their heart goes out to the family because they should have gotten a guilty verdict.Jurors began deliberating Wednesday afternoon and continued Thursday and Friday before breaking for the weekend. They resumed deliberations Monday and continued through Tuesday but were unable to reach a unanimous verdict.Last week, the judge dismissed the murder charges against Barnett, leaving the charges of second-degree arson, involuntary manslaughter and reckless endangerment.Prosecutors argued that video showed Barnett creating at least four flashes of light inside the vacant rowhome, which they believe were flames. They also pointed to what they described as conflicting statements Barnett made during a police interview.Barnett's attorney argued that prosecutors could not prove the person shown in the video was Barnett.The three-week trial included hours of video evidence and testimony from multiple witnesses and experts, including a medical examiner who discussed the injuries that killed the three firefighters.The state has a chance to retry the case. The judge told prosecutors if they do, schedule the case as soon as possible."Some people actually saw the evidence for what it was and didn't think outside of the box or anywhere else," said Brandon Sadler, Lt, Kelsey Sadler's husband. "They saw the evidence and they stuck with just the evidence, and others decided not to."

title: Lakers to open post-LeBron era at home against Steph Curry, Warriors
description: Luka Doncic and the Lakers are looking to build on a second-round appearance last season.
content: For several decades, it's almost been a prerequisite for the NBA's best players to don the Purple and Gold at some point in their careers. Luka Doncic has done that for parts of two seasons now, after the shocking trade that sent him to Los Angeles in February 2025, but he spent that time in the shadow of the legendary LeBron James.But now that James has taken his talents to southeastern Pennsylvania to play for the Philadelphia 76ers after eight seasons in LA, there's no giant on the Lakers for Doncic to stand on the shoulders of. It's the 27-year-old's team now.Doncic and the new-look Lakers open the post-LeBron era at 7 p.m. Wednesday night at Crypto.com Arena as the Western Conference's predominant member of the old guard steps into the fray in the form of Stephen Curry and the Golden State Warriors.Off the heels of an impressive first-round playoff victory over the Houston Rockets, expectations for the Lakers remain firmly in the playoff picture. The team was swept in the second round by the Oklahoma City Thunder, however, firmly highlighting the gap between LA and the top of the conference.Coming in to help Doncic and Austin Reaves is 7-foot-2 center Walker Kessler, acquired in a trade from the Utah Jazz over the offseason. LA is hoping Kessler can protect the paint and offer some defensive stability, which has been a weakness in recent history, particularly at the center position.

title: Australian politician who was intentionally hit by car loses both her legs
description: Australian lawmaker Helen Haines, who was intentionally hit by a car in an apparent political attack, has lost both of her legs, her husband said.
content: Australian lawmaker Helen Haines has had both legs amputated after being hit by a car, her husband said on Wednesday, hailing her as a "fighter" despite critical injuries sustained in what police described as a targeted attack.Haines, 65, is now in a stable condition at a Melbourne hospital days after being struck by a car on Monday near her office in the town of Wangaratta, which is just over 200 kilometers, or 120 miles, northeast of the Victoria state capital.The incident has prompted soul-searching in a country where political violence is rare but where police have documented a steady rise in threats and abuse toward elected officials in recent years.Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has led tributes to Haines, an independent member of parliament and a passionate campaigner for transparency and against corruption. He has also acknowledged the need for Australians to turn down the temperature and embrace respectful disagreement over polarization.Speaking at the hospital on Wednesday, Haines' husband of almost 40 years, Phil, said that after days in intensive care, surgeons had been forced to amputate both her legs."But the good news in all this is Helen is alive and she's stable. That is the most important thing for our family," he said, adding, "The two most important parts of Helen for us as a family are her heart and her mind."Haines' husband went on to describe her as "a very compassionate, caring, loving person" with a "huge" heart. "Helen's road to recovery will be long and difficult, but we know she is a fighter," he said."Extremist views"The man alleged to have wounded Haines in what police have called a "targeted" attack faced court for the first time earlier on Wednesday.Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury and intentionally causing serious injury, as well as the federal crime of harming a public official, which carries a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison. He has also been charged with cultivating a cannabis plant and possession of the drug, according to court documents shared with AFP.Nugent's initial hearing took place at a courthouse in Wangaratta, according to an AFP journalist at the scene. He didn't speak in court or apply for bail, and his next hearing is scheduled for Feb. 4.In court, Nugent's lawyer Chirag Patel told Magistrate Allison Vaughan that his suffered from idiopathic transverse myelitis, a neurological condition, as well as a concussion. The lawyer didn't explain how Nugent had become concussed. Patel also said his client was suffering from potential mental health issues but had never been diagnosed with any mental health problem.According to the Cleveland Clinic, idiopathic transverse myelitis is a rare condition that damages the spinal cord's protective myelin sheath and disrupts nerve signals between the brain and body, leading to rapid muscle weakness, sensory loss, pain, and bladder and bowel dysfunction.The motive for the attack remains unknown, and authorities will not speculate while the investigation is ongoing. But police said Wednesday they were examining all possible leads, including that Nugent may have held radical anti-government views."We're examining social media associations, talking to witnesses, friends and colleagues," Victoria police commissioner Mike Bush told reporters. He said, however, that authorities had no intelligence on the suspect and hadn't seen anything to suggest he posed an immediate threat.Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett pointed to a growing and concerning level of "extremist views" online, saying the incident was "what many had been dreading for some time."World "more dangerous"Helen Haines entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife, becoming known for stances such as supporting stronger climate action.The independent lawmaker was standing near the trunk of her car when she was struck by a Toyota Land Cruiser on Monday afternoon. Witnesses told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation that they saw her pinned between the two vehicles.Threats against Australian lawmakers and electorate offices doubled between 2021 and 2025, with 1,067 incidents reported to police last year.Governor-General Sam Mostyn — King Charles III's official representative in Australia — said the nation was crying out for "decency" in the wake of the attack on Haines."Australians are yearning for kindness and care, and they're asking us why we've lost the great skill of disagreeing well," Mostyn said, speaking alongside Phil Haines.Highlighting the tense climate, police in Western Australia charged a man late on Wednesday after he made threats and swung nunchucks at the office of state lawmaker Hannah Beazley, media said.The incident has drawn comparisons to other acts of violence against elected officials elsewhere, most notably the killing of British lawmaker Jo Cox outside her office in 2016."It's a reminder that the world is a more dangerous and divided place than it was a generation ago," Prime Minister Albanese told ABC Melbourne radio.

title: Groundbreaking set for Foundry Park development along Chicago River's North Branch
description: Groundbreaking set for Foundry Park on Chicago River's North Branch
content: Groundbreaking was set for Wednesday for a major new development along the North Branch of the Chicago River.The $3 billion Foundry Park development seeks to transform the former A. Finkl & Sons steel mill site in the Clybourn Corridor into a new neighborhood with more than 3,700 homes and 970,000 square feet of office, retail, and hotel space.Plans for the development also include public parks and an extension of The 606 Trail, which now ends at Ashland Avenue on the other side of the river.Last month, the Chicago City Council approved $201.6 million in funds collected from Tax Increment Financing districts to develop public infrastructure for Foundry Park, spokespeople said.Developers expected the completed Foundry Park project to generate more than 2,500 permanent jobs.Foundry Park supersedes Lincoln Yards, developer Sterling Bay's controversial $6 billion redevelopment plan for the same area. Opponents complained of a lack of affordable housing in the proposed Lincoln Yards development, while Ald. Brian Hopkins (2nd) plans for a soccer stadium and an entertainment district run by Live Nation as part of the project.The Live Nation proposal in particular drew concerns and opposition from independent venues such as The Hideout, located on the other side of the river at 1354 W. Wabansia Ave.Lincoln Yards did not end up being built.Finkl Steel moved from its 22-acre property near Southport Avenue and Cortland Street in 2014, relocating to the city's South Side. The other major industrial holdout in the old Clybourn Corridor area, General Iron at 1909 N. Clifton Ave., closed its plant in 2021.At one time, both plants were major components of the Clybourn Corridor Planned Manufacturing District, which was established in 1988 with zoning to prohibit residential development and place restrictions on commercial uses in an effort to protect the manufacturing economy in the area. The planned manufacturing district was eliminated in July 2017 with a zoning change that imposed fewer restrictions.The groundbreaking for Foundry Park is set for 2:30 p.m. Wednesday. Mayor Brandon Johnson, Ald. Scott Waguespack (32nd), JDL development founder and chief executive officer Jim Letchinger, Kayne Anderson Real Estate chief investment officer David Selznick, and Chicago Department of Planning and Development Commissioner Ciere Boatright were expected to attend.

title: 2 Colorado cities pass temporary bans on new data center applications
description: A total of four municipalities in Colorado took action on data centers this week.
content: A total of four municipalities in Colorado took action on data centers this week. On Tuesday night, both Brighton and Lafayette passed temporary bans on new applications. Brighton's temporary ban will be in place for one year, and the moratorium in Lafayette is for 18 months. Littleton and Fort Collins held the first readings for their own six-month moratoriums at the latest city council meetings this week. Both will require another vote and public hearings before the moratoriums will take effect. Those cities are the latest in Colorado to pause data center construction while community members consider the potential risks and advantages of having those businesses near homes and schools. In Aurora, Mayor Mike Coffman delayed a vote set for earlier this week on an indefinite data center moratorium to Oct. 26 after he called for a "Special Council Meeting for Vote on Indefinite Data Center Moratorium." Denver created a working group on data centers with the goal of creating policy recommendations for the city. It is diverse, composed of community members and experts in a multitude of industries, and was created after the city council approved a moratorium to pause the construction of data centers in Denver.Fort Collins and Littleton are considering a first reading of a six-month moratorium on data center construction. The pause in Fort Collins would apply to 10-megawatt or larger data centers if passed.

title: Up to 20% of MS diagnoses are wrong, like Christina Applegate's. Here's what doctors say patients should know.
description: A multiple sclerosis expert answers questions about MS misdiagnosis after Christina Applegate said she doesn't have the chronic condition after all.
content: Actor Christina Applegate announced Tuesday that she had been misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis after years of believing she had the condition — and experts say her experience is more common than many people realize.Applegate shared the news on her podcast, MeSsy, where she and actor Jamie-Lynn Sigler discuss life with MS. In a follow-up episode, Dr. Marwa Kaisey, an associate professor at the Cedars-Sinai Medical Center department of neurology, said that almost 1 in 5 people who are told they have multiple sclerosis "didn't actually have it." There is no single test to confirm MS, a disease where the body's immune system attacks the central nervous system. Symptoms vary from person to person and it can progress in different ways, according to the National Multiple Sclerosis Society. How can an MS misdiagnosis be discovered?CBS News spoke with Dr. Robert Bermel, the director of the Mellen Center for MS at Cleveland Clinic, a multidisciplinary center that cares for more than 11,000 patients with multiple sclerosis, about the risk of an MS misdiagnosis and what patients need to know. He said a misdiagnosis is most often found when a person seeks out a second opinion because their symptoms aren't getting better. This doesn't always mean the diagnosis is wrong, but can be an indicator for more advanced tests. (Bermel said most MS treatments, especially the ones most commonly used, are "very safe" and wouldn't put a person's health in danger.) When a misdiagnosis happens, the root cause is typically that abnormalities on brain scans were misinterpreted, Bermel said. Lesions on the brain are considered a hallmark of MS, but they can also be caused by other medical issues such as high blood pressure, smoking or migraines. More advanced MRI sequences can help differentiate between MS lesions and those caused by other conditions, Bermel said. When concerns about a potential misdiagnosis arise, the next steps typically involve running specialized tests. Those can include advanced MRI sequences to study the lesions more closely, a spinal MRI, or spinal fluid analysis that can identify specific abnormal immune proteins, Bermel said. How common is an MS misdiagnosis? On MeSsy, Kaisey described MS misdiagnoses as "fairly common." Bermel said that the largest studies looking at the risk of misdiagnosis have shown that between 15% and 20% of patients diagnosed with MS are found to not actually have the condition. Dr. Josef Gutman, the director of NYU Langone's Long Island Comprehensive MS Care Center, told CBS News that the wide spectrum of symptoms that can be attributed to multiple sclerosis makes the condition difficult to diagnosis. "It's important to keep in mind that those symptoms are not necessarily specific in a lot of ways. It's sort of the story, combined with MRI imaging, combined with other markers like spinal fluid, that help us make the MS diagnosis," Gutman said. "It's not like diabetes, where there's one blood test and if it's above this number, it's diabetes, if it's below this number, it isn't. There's a lot of things going into the diagnosis." New multiple sclerosis diagnostic criteria, developed by an international panel of experts in the field, were published in 2025 to try to reduce this risk. These criteria are more specific than before, according to Bermel, especially when it comes to interpreting brain lesions. "We really place a high premium on getting the diagnosis correct from the start, so that then we can move very confidently into highly effective therapy for MS," Bermel said. What happens after an MS misdiagnosis? If a patient's multiple sclerosis misdiagnosis is identified, doctors will then start looking at other potential causes for their symptoms, Bermel said. They may be suffering from an autoimmune condition, which can cause joint pain, swelling and system-wide inflammation. Fibromyalgia is a "commonly identified diagnosis that mimics MS," Bermel said. Migraines are also a possible diagnosis, because migraine can cause lesions and other neurological symptoms. Chronic pain or fatigue syndromes can also "masquerade as MS," Bermel said. Sometimes, a person may not have one disorder but several, Bermel said, noting that an incorrect diagnosis "really sidetracks things.""MS can sometimes be a gratifying solution to a patient with many symptoms because it's thought of as kind of a single, solitary root cause of things," he said, adding that he has seen patients whose fatigue is caused by a sleep or thyroid disorder, while rheumatoid conditions or fibromyalgia cause pain and swelling. On her podcast, Applegate said learning she had the wrong diagnosis has made things harder for now, since there's still no explanation for the debilitating symptoms that affect her daily life and mobility. "You don't get misdiagnosed and then all of the sudden I'm better," Applegate said. "If anything, I've gotten worse. So I'm back at square one where I don't know what's going on with me. And that's going to be an online investigation that my doctors are going to be getting into just to find out what has been going on since 2021, why did this happen?"When to seek out a second opinion While only a minority of patients are misdiagnosed, anyone concerned about their diagnosis should always feel comfortable seeking a second opinion, Bermel said. Even when the original diagnosis is correct, a second opinion can help a patient find other resources, he noted."MS is a life-changing diagnosis, and anytime somebody is facing something like that, I always think a second opinion is potentially in order," Bermel said. Patients can also seek out a multiple sclerosis expert, Bermel said. The National Multiple Sclerosis Society maintains an online registry and map of care centers and MS specialists nationwide. Bermel called that list a "really good starting point to identify" nearby resources. MS specialists are likely to be up to date on diagnostic criteria, Gutman said. They are also more likely to be familiar with conditions that mimic multiple sclerosis, and have access to the more specific tests that can help confirm a diagnosis.

title: Sterling Heights City Council votes to renew Flock contract
description: A divided Sterling Heights City Council voted to renew its contract to use Flock cameras in the early morning hours of Wednesday.
content: A divided Sterling Heights City Council voted to renew its contract to use Flock cameras in the early morning hours of Wednesday.On Tuesday night, the city council was slated to vote on whether to renew its contract with the surveillance camera system, a topic of nationwide controversy.While Sterling Heights Police Chief Andrew Satterfield acknowledged the misuse that has happened nationwide, he also mentioned the misinformation being spread about the camera system.The chief presented to the public and the council the measures that would be implemented if their contract with Flock were renewed.Satterfield says the camera system does not take photographs of people, record audio or measure speed.He shared that system usage will be reviewed every 30 days rather than every year to prevent misuse.The chief also shared the successes the department has had with the system and that Sterling Heights Police Department has no history of misuse of the camera system.However, residents in the audience were divided over Flock."Right now there is no trust," said a man during public comment."I don't want to live in this type of surveillance state, and I don't want my children to."Some who spoke during public comment wondered whether the footage would be stored securely and whether they could trust that the data would not be shared.While others were for the tool for police."This department is fully transparent, and they deserve this tool to keep us safe," said one man who spoke from the audience.A former captain for the Sterling Heights Police Department spoke during public comment.She reiterated that the Flock cameras are on public roads, capturing images that anyone can take in public.However, after hours of deliberation by the community and a recess, the Sterling Heights City Council voted to renew the contract. Before the meeting, CBS News Detroit caught up with Councilman Michael Radke, who has voted against Flock.While he acknowledged the system is effective, he is not for a surveillance state. He voted no.He proposed the city make it a local misdemeanor if an officer misuses the data.The majority of the council objected to the idea, with the Chief mentioning that laws are already in place.

title: Scariest part of Halloween this year might be the cost: "Everyone is suffering from it"
description: The most frightening thing about Halloween this year might be the cost.
content: The most frightening thing about Halloween this year might be the cost.Higher prices for candy, costumes, and decorations are forcing people to get creative."Every year things get a little bit pricier, and at the same time the quality is getting a little worse," said Billy Gridley, a Waltham, Massachusetts, homeowner with a well-known Halloween house in town.He has been building the mammoth display in his yard for 13 years, and it is crammed with creep."I added a zombie, a jumping scarecrow and the alien," said Gridley. "Prices are expensive. I try to take advantage of coupon deals and discounted items from years prior that aren't selling."Even his family gets in on the savings."My family and I, we all get our flu shots at a grocery store, and they give you coupons. So, we save all of our coupons and I use those specifically just for Halloween candy," said Gridley.To save money on a costume, he's simply becoming one of his broken animatronics."I might be able to hide out here during Halloween, and they might not know it's me," said Gridley.MIT economist Jonathan Gruber said gas is behind the growing price for ghouls and ghosts. He calls it a byproduct of tariffs and the war in Iran."The hit to diesel has been much bigger and that matters because diesel is what is used by the trucks that deliver all of the things including the candy," he told WBZ-TV. "Everyone is suffering from it, so your neighbors aren't going to be mad at you if you don't have the fanciest and most candy."Jonny Woodard is a big Halloween fan. WBZ caught up with him after he grabbed a spooky snack."This simple Twix skulls, share size. So, you're supposed to break it and share it with someone else. This was $2.89 before tax," said Woodard holding the candy. "That's for a little candy bar that used to be $1.30 years ago.""Prices go up, that is the thing, I think we had a very long stretch of low inflation, and we got used to it," said Gruber.Now, there is nothing fun about paying for fun size.

title: Thanksgiving travelers may pay more if they wait to book flights, experts say
description: Americans planning to fly for the holidays may want to book sooner rather than later.
content: Americans planning to fly for the holidays may want to book sooner rather than later.Travel experts say holiday airfare is already higher than it was this time last year, and waiting for a last-minute deal could cost you even more.According to travel booking platform Hopper, average domestic airfare for Thanksgiving is around $400, up 30% compared to last year. Christmas fares are averaging about $450, a 23% increase. Industry data from Kayak suggests travelers who wait until the final two weeks before departure could pay up to 20% more for their tickets.Last-minute deals are harder to findFor years, travelers often counted on last-minute airfare discounts. But that strategy has become increasingly risky as airlines rely on dynamic pricing models that adjust fares based on demand.On the latest episode of the In Your Corner podcast, AAA spokesperson Jana Tidwell said travelers who find flights within their budget should consider booking sooner rather than waiting for prices to fall."The days of waiting until the last minute and finding an incredible travel deal are mostly behind us," Tidwell said.Flexibility can lead to savingsTidwell said flexibility remains one of the best ways to reduce travel costs during busy holiday periods.Thanksgiving travel is often most expensive for passengers looking to depart the Wednesday before the holiday and return the Sunday afterward.Shifting travel plans by even a day can make a difference."If you're searching for Wednesday and returning on Sunday, so is everybody else," Tidwell said.For Christmas, experts say avoid flying Dec. 18 through Dec. 20 and Dec. 27, which are expected to be among the busiest and most expensive travel days.Travelers willing to consider alternate airports or less popular flight times may also find lower fares.The cheapest day to fly may surprise youKayak data suggests the cheapest day to fly during the holiday period is often the holiday itself.While many travelers prefer to arrive before the holiday, experts say flying on Thanksgiving Day or Christmas Day can mean lower demand and lower ticket prices.You can find the full conversation on the CBS Philadelphia YouTube channel or wherever you get your podcasts.Looking for help with a consumer issue? Click here to submit your complaint to In Your Corner.

title: Girl shot in Burnsville, leading to brief shelter-in-place alert, police say
description: Police say a girl is recovering after she was shot Tuesday evening in Burnsville, Minnesota, leader to a brief shelter-in-place alert.
content: Police say a girl is recovering after she was shot Tuesday evening in Burnsville, Minnesota, leader to a brief shelter-in-place alert.The shooting happened around 7 p.m. on McAndrews Road West, just north of County Road 42 and east of County Road 5. Officials issued the shelter-in-place alert around 8 p.m. and asked the public to avoid the area while police investigate. The order was lifted around 11 p.m.The victim, whose exact age hasn't been release, suffered minor injuries and was treated at an area hospital, police say.It's unclear if any arrests were made or if police have a suspect in this case.

title: Dream's first draft pick Ty Young shares lessons with girls at clinic during Atlanta's WNBA Finals run
description: While the Dream are chasing a historic championship, girls ages 7 to 17 got to fall in love with the game on Tuesday, chasing their own dreams on the court.
content: The Atlanta Dream are making huge moves on the court, sailing through the WNBA Finals. It's no wonder so many young girls want to play like Angel Reese or Rhyne Howard. While the Dream are chasing a historic championship, girls ages 7 to 17 got to fall in love with the game on Tuesday, chasing their own dreams on the court. "Basketball takes you everywhere," said Embry, who's been dribbling the ball since she was four years old. She's teaming with Bailey Edwards, who's all about the girls around her. "It's wonderful because I get to compete, and I also get to make friends. We get to fellowship over the game and have fun and grow and get better together," said Edwards as she learns from the players' journeys. "The love that they have and why they choose to stay in it after all this time. It's really beautiful to hear from them so I can be inspired to continue on my journey playing sports," she said. It's not Bailey's first Dream clinic. Much like the team's game itself, the Dream say what happens here goes beyond the score. Ty Young played for the franchise in its first season and was its first draft pick. She sees herself in these girls."It helps build character. It helps show teamwork. It helps build confidence. So it's more than just about basketball and the score for these young ladies," said Young. The message to every girl in the gym: you belong here.Young told CBS News Atlanta what she would tell herself at that age: "To seize t he moment, to enjoy the moment that I have right now… Go dream."It's exactly what Edwards is doing herself. "The energy is amazing in the arena. So really excited for the game, and we're going to get that championship this year," she said.The Dream plays Wednesday at 8 p.m. in Atlanta, hoping to break their tied-up series against the Golden State Valkyries in their quest for the Championship.

title: BGE asks state regulator to "protect" utility customers outside Baltimore City from conduit fee increase
description: Baltimore Gas and Electric has filed a request with Maryland's Public Service Commission to "protect" its customers in surrounding counties from additional costs resulting from Baltimore City's decision to increase utility conduit fees.
content: Baltimore Gas and Electric (BGE) said Tuesday it had filed a request with Maryland's Public Service Commission (PSC) to "protect" its customers in surrounding counties from additional costs resulting from Baltimore City's decision to increase utility conduit fees.Baltimore has collected nearly $375 million since 2016 and is planning to raise its new conduit fees by 84%, said a news release issued by BGE. Baltimore officials have "not been transparent about where that money went, how customers benefited, and why an increase is justified," the utility provided added.Baltimore's planned conduit increases will serve as "a customer-funded city infrastructure tax" that would eventually be recovered through electric bills, BGE said. This would result in "burdening all BGE electric customers with nearly $50 million in new costs next year alone."Agreement calls for $120 million in improvements over four yearsBaltimore City's century-old network of underground conduits -- which houses electrical, telecommunications and fiber-optic cables -- is set to be solely updated by the city beginning at the end of 2026. The city's conduit agreement with BGE calls for $120 million of capital improvements over the course of four years. BGE says the proposal it is submitting to the PSC would shield customers outside of Baltimore City from paying costs associated with the Baltimore-owned conduit system. An estimated surcharge of around $9 per month would be added to the bills of Baltimore City electric customers beginning January 1, 2027. "With no direct connection to the customer-driven reliability needs, infrastructure priorities, or operational requirements of the electric distribution system, the city's conduit fee increase ought not be paid by BGE customers outside Baltimore City," said the BGE statement. City responds to BGEThe following joint statement was issued on Tuesday by Baltimore Brandon M. Scott, Council President Zeke Cohen, and Comptroller Bill Henry: "News of BGE's attempt to avoid paying its fair share of the cost to maintain the city's underground conduit system is disappointing but unsurprising. Worse, they are asking the Public Service Commission to approve an unprecedented surcharge that would apply to only Baltimore City residents. Notably, BGE claimed at the Board of Estimates in August that Public Service Commission staff suggested such a surcharge, but the council president's letter requesting evidence to support this assertion received no response. The mayor, council president, comptroller, and members of the city council demand that the commission reject this illegal and unprecedented request from BGE and fulfill their responsibility to the people of Baltimore City, to protect them from corporate overreach."Baltimore owns the underground conduit system it is raising fees on, making the city responsible for managing, maintaining, inspecting and improving it. "City law requires underground electric facilities in Baltimore to be placed in the city-owned conduit system, leaving BGE with no alternative but to use the infrastructure," BGE said. "This is a matter of doing what's equitable for our customers. BGE cannot support requiring families and businesses outside the city to pay for a revenue increase imposed by Baltimore City," said Tamla Olivier, president and CEO of BGE. "Customers across central Maryland are already concerned about affordability, and our filing ensures that those costs remain where the city's decision was made."

title: 10 years ago I was diagnosed with melanoma. Here's what my dermatologist wants you to know.
description: More people are diagnosed with skin cancer each year in the U.S. than all other cancers combined.
content: Ten years ago, I was at a routine dermatologist appointment when my doctor found two concerning spots on my back. Soon after, Dr. Elizabeth Hale told me my biopsy revealed I had melanoma, the deadliest form of skin cancer.Thankfully, Hale caught it early and removed it before the cancer spread. It was a wake-up call.Now, when I spend time in the sun, I seek out the shade, wear UV protective clothing, and consistently reapply broad spectrum sunscreen. Growing up in Texas, I spent a lot of time outdoors and got sunburned. One of my biggest regrets was going to tanning salons. Around 20% of Americans will be diagnosed with skin cancer. According to the Skin Cancer Foundation, where Hale is the senior vice president, more people are diagnosed with skin cancer each year in the U.S. than all other cancers combined.But Hale wants people to know that skin cancer is also "the most preventable," and "it's almost always curable."Hale is a board-certified dermatologist. We went to her practice, CompleteSkinMD, in New York City to discuss what we should all know about skin cancer.Melanoma in young womenThere's been an increase in incidences of melanoma among women in their 20s and 30s. "It is directly related to exposure to tanning beds and to sunburns," Hale said.Melanoma is one of the most common cancers in young women. In fact, before age 50, melanoma is more common in women than in men. Hale said melanoma can be found anywhere on the body, but for women, it commonly occurs on lower legs and places like the buttocks. "[Places that] never sees the sun, except for when you're undressed in a tanning bed," Hale said. "We have to keep our kids out of tanning beds and get them to practice good sun protection."The Skin Cancer Foundation reports that "exposure to tanning beds before the age of 35 … increases your chance for melanoma, which is the most serious type of skin cancer, by 75%."Another future impact of these harmful tanning habits and sun exposure is seen in how skin ages and how fast.To Hale, the science is clear: "Up to 90% of skin cancers are caused by overexposure to the sun, but also up to 99% of the signs of premature skin aging."The "tanmaxxing" social media trend is a problemTanning trends have been going viral across social media platforms with young women exposing themselves to harmful UV rays without any protection for hours on end. From bathing in direct sunlight to frequent trips to tanning salons, "people are bragging about the sunburn they're getting," Hale noted.Long hours under the sun may be popular, but it puts people at risk. According to the FDA, any kind of tan greatly increases someone's risk of getting skin cancer."There really is no such thing as … a safe, healthy tan," Hale said. While a tan might look nice, the reality behind why your skin gets darker is more troubling. The tan is actually "representing DNA damage" that can manifest as cancer later. The types of skin cancerThere are three main types of skin cancer. Basal cell carcinoma is not only the most common skin cancer but also "the most common cancer diagnosed in the United States overall," as it accounts for 80% of new skin cancer diagnoses.Basal cell carcinoma also doesn't metastasize into deadlier forms of skin cancer but dermatologists will still recommend the tumor or mole be removed, as "they can start eating away through the skin into the underlying structure" if left unattended. Hale assures patients the procedures are "little nothings" and leave minimal scarring.Squamous cell carcinoma is the second most common, but unlike basal cell, this skin cancer can spread if untreated. This carcinoma is also the "most correlated with chronic sun exposure." The scalp, neck, and backs of hands are the most common at-risk areas.Melanoma is the third most common and the most dangerous of the three main skin cancers. The statistics are striking. "Even though it only accounts for 5% of new cases of skin cancer, it's responsible for more than 75% of skin cancer-related deaths," Hale said."There have been major advances in melanoma treatment, but it's still really best to get your skin checked because when melanoma is caught early it has greater than a 99% five-year survival. But once it spreads, that survival rate goes down precipitously," she said.Be familiar with your skin and get it checked regularlySkin cancer, when detected early, is "almost always curable," Hale said. However, if people neglect to care for their skin and have it checked by a physician, benign moles can develop into cancer and metastasize.Hale says people should have their skin checked annually starting at 18 years old. Those with a family history of skin cancer or others who are at high risk should talk with their dermatologist to see if they would benefit from more frequent visits to identify early any signs of skin cancer.Sunscreen every day — multiple times a dayWhat kind of sunscreen is best? The bottom line, according to Hale, is "the best sunscreen is the one you'll actually use" — but not all sunscreens are created equal. A broad spectrum product with SPF 30 or greater should be a part of your daily skincare regimen.Look for ingredients like zinc oxide or titanium dioxide in your sunscreen, which keep both UVB and the more dangerous UVA rays at bay. For days at the beach or when you expect to sweat, choose a chemical sunscreen with avobenzone. The FDA recently approved bimotrizinol (BEMT), an ingredient that has been used in Europe and Asia for decades. Hale believes it can provide broad spectrum protection while also being water and sweat resistant.When spending the entire day outside, Hale recommends reapplying sunscreen every two hours to maintain optimal skin protection.

title: Suspect arrested after 2 shot near Weatherford, sheriff's office says
description: The Parker County Sheriff's Office said deputies are trying to locate 22-year-old Ozzy Fierros in connection with the incident.
content: The Parker County Sheriff's Office said after an hours-long search, the suspect wanted in connection with a shooting that left two injured was taken into custody in Weatherford on Tuesday. The sheriff's office said that at about 3:05 p.m., deputies located 22-year-old Ozzy Fierros and arrested him without incident. The shooting happened Tuesday morning in the 4500 block of Arrowhead Drive, just south of Weatherford.Authorities said two people, who haven't been identified, were injured and transported to a Fort Worth hospital in unknown conditions. Fierros was initially wanted for questioning, but the sheriff's office confirmed he is the sole suspect in the case. The investigation is ongoing.

title: Repairs begin on NYC building deemed unstable over the summer
description: Crews will begin repairing the Manhattan building that became unstable in July when columns buckled and floors started to sag.
content: Operations to repair a building on Manhattan's East Side that became unstable over the summer will begin Tuesday.Crews will begin lifting the damaged floors of the former Pfizer headquarters on East 42nd Street to get it ready for permanent repairs. Issues began in July when firefighters responded to reports of falling bricks. But the bigger concern was inside, where two steel columns had buckled on the 21st floor, causing floors above to sag. There were numerous evacuations nearby, including a school, and several blocks of Midtown were shut down while crews worked to stabilize the building. At the time, developer Metro Loft was turning the old office building into apartments, with plans to add another 16 stories.Three months later, crews are scheduled to begin lifting the damaged floors about six inches in a process called jacking.Crews will use powerful hydraulic equipment to slowly raise part of the structure. They will lift the floors just one-sixty-fourth of an inch, which is about the thickness of a business card. The Department of Buildings said the repair plan went through extensive reviews by its senior engineers and an independent engineering firm.The construction is not expected to impact anyone who lives or works in Midtown.

title: Miami jury recommends death penalty for Alberto Sierra for killing estranged wife, her young daughters
description: Emotions ran high inside the courtroom when the verdict was read, with the victim's surviving son breaking down in tears.
content: A Miami jury has recommended the death penalty for Alberto Sierra, the man who pleaded guilty to killing his estranged wife and her two daughters in 2012.Emotions ran high inside the courtroom late Tuesday afternoon when the verdict was read, with the victim's surviving son breaking down in tears.For the killing of Gladys Machado, the jury voted 11-1 to recommend the death penalty, while the jury voted 12-0 in favor of the death penalty for 6-year-old Julia Padron, and 8-4 for the killing of 3-year-old Daniela Padron.Jurors deliberated for about six hours on Tuesday before the decision was announced late Tuesday afternoon.However, while the jury recommended the death penalty, the judge will have the final say as to what punishment to impose.The judge is expected to make that decision next month.Emotional death penalty trial lasted for weeksProsecutors had argued that Sierra initially tried to cover up the crimes but was ultimately linked to them through DNA evidence."Gladys and her little girls never came home again, all because of that person – right over there. He decided that that day would be their last," the prosecutor said when the death penalty trial began.Among witnesses who took the stand was the neighbor who discovered the bodies of Machado and her daughters, as well as the Miami-Dade Fire Rescue first responders who were first at the scene.Jurors heard emotional testimony from the victims' family members, including Machado's son, Michael Padrino Jr., who was 5 years old at the time and survived because he didn't want to go shopping that day. He instead wanted to stay home and watch a TV show."You took them," he said. "You know you did."He was then escorted out of the courtroom as he wept uncontrollably. The defense began arguing its case by calling a doctor to the stand, and he brought up Sierra's medical history.He discussed how Sierra had been previously hit by a car and was diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes. The defense also said he has antisocial and borderline personality disorders. It asked jurors to consider life in prison without parole."He had a chance to have a family, but I think there were things going on in his brain that I want you to consider as to why he destroyed it," defense attorney Khurrum Wahid told jurors.But the prosecutor then argued that the doctor hadn't treated Sierra and had never met him until the trial. Family members of Sierra also took the stand to defend him in the hopes that he would be spared from being sentenced to death.Sierra himself did not take the stand in his death penalty trial."Ask yourself — is this the case — is this the defendant who should get my grace? I would submit to you that it is not," prosecutor Abbe Rifkin said.Closing arguments were held Monday, and the jury began deliberating on Tuesday.What happened to Gladys Machado and her daughters in 2012?The killings happened in November 2012 after Sierra, Machado, and her daughters went to the Mall of the Americas on West Flagler Street, according to investigators.Police said Sierra and Machado argued during the visit, and Sierra stabbed her. He then drove Machado and the girls to the family's home on Northwest 4th Street in west Miami-Dade.Investigators said Sierra forced the family inside the home and locked the girls in a bedroom before taking Machado into the master bedroom and suffocating her with a plastic bag. Police said he then suffocated the two girls.Investigators also accused Sierra of sexually assaulting Machado and one of the girls after their deaths."It was deliberate; it was cold. It was calculated, and it showed a heightened level of premeditation," the prosecutor said.A third child, Machado's son, now 19-year-old Michael Padrino Jr., was with his grandmother at the time and was not harmed.The bodies of Machado and her daughters were discovered days later after a neighbor noticed a foul odor coming from the home.Police said Sierra confessed to the killings during questioning.Witnesses during the trial included Sierra's mother, Mercedes Pedraza; Michael Padrino Sr., the girls' father; and Padrino Jr.

title: Pittsburgh's stretch of sunny and seasonable fall weather lasts through the weekend
description: It will be another cool morning that turns into a comfortable afternoon with plenty of sunshine.
content: The calm weather pattern is set to continue through the weekend and beyond, with the biggest forecast challenge being how aggressive to go with high temperatures, with sunny skies and low humidity levels most days. The temperature forecast will remain challenging over the next couple of days, with slight changes in the overall air mass's temperatures. While on the surface every day looks the same, 850mb temperatures show a difference of around 4°C from yesterday through Friday. The 850 mb temperature is modeled to be at 9°C today during the afternoon. Model data says that is good for highs in just the low 60s. Modeling data on both Monday and Tuesday also showed similar forecast highs in just the low 60s. Both days saw highs well over that, with a high of 67° on Monday and 68° on Tuesday. I am going to keep the 68° forecast high that I had yesterday for today's high. Morning lows will dip to near 40 degrees. I have noon temperatures in the low 60s with winds out of the northeast this afternoon between 5 - 10mph. Particular focus should be paid to Thursday morning, with modeling showing conditions perfect for thick fog development. I expect some fog advisories to go into effect for Thursday morning with widespread dense fog development. Parts of Ohio are under a dense fog advisory this morning. I have morning lows on Thursday dipping to the mid to upper 30s. Thursday highs should hit the mid-60s, with another sunny afternoon expected. What we call a 'backdoor' cold front will roll in on Friday morning, briefly bringing temperatures down to the mid-to-low 60s for highs. We will see partly cloudy skies on Friday with the thickest clouds rolling through just before noon. Friday lows will stay in the 40s.The weekend will be dry with highs in the mid to upper 60s on both Saturday and Sunday. Morning lows on both days will dip to the mid-30s.

title: Former mayoral candidate faces court after Sandy Springs "No Kings" rally
description: A "No Kings" rally organizer who has run for Sandy Springs mayor twice is heading to court after police cited him on Saturday for violating his public assembly permit.
content: A "No Kings" rally organizer who has run for Sandy Springs mayor twice is heading to court after police cited him on Saturday for violating his public assembly permit."One of the lieutenants walked up to us telling us we didn't have permission to be where we were," said Dontaye Carter, an organizer of the "No Kings" rally who lives in Sandy Springs.Carter said the rally encouraged people to vote. A city record provided to CBS News Atlanta shows the city issued Carter a public assembly permit. A city letter sent with the permit stated the rally had to stay in a designated area shown in an attached Exhibit A. Carter's attorney said the group did not get that attachment."They sent all the documentation for the permit, and the appendix was not sent to the organizers," said Gerald A. Griggs, Carter's attorney and a well-known civil rights lawyer.The citation said the permit covered the south parking lot near City Hall. It said about 125 people gathered instead on a public sidewalk area at two corners. One was the northwest corner of Roswell and Johnson Ferry roads. The other was the southwest corner of Roswell Road and Mount Vernon Highway.Video shared with CBS News Atlanta captured the exchange between Carter and police."This is not saying that you can protest or anything like that, just that it was in violation of the city," said an officer in the video.The footage also shows the group on the corner.Carter said the citation reminds him of one written for his ancestor in 1828 for unlawful assemblage."And on mine it says that I was cited for violation of public assembly, very similar," said Carter.Sandy Springs city code sets rules for public gatherings, including a ban on blocking access to public or private buildings. The citation said officers asked the group to move to the permitted area, but the group did not move.CBS News Atlanta asked Emory Law professor John Acevedo to review the citation, the permit paperwork Carter received and video of the encounter."In the video we've seen, it appears police make a lawful request to move the protesters. That said, the protesters were clearly peaceful and clearly on was normally a public forum area, the sidewalk," said John Acevedo, a professor at Emory Law.Acevedo said the city could argue Carter should have asked for Exhibit A."Constitutional rights say you have the right to protest. But there is something called time, place and manner restrictions that allow a city to place reasonable content neutral. So they have to apply to everyone, regardless of the subject of your speech. Those can be placed on protests," Acevedo said.So, do you need a permit to protest?"It's not absolutely necessary. Actually, anyone has the right to assemble and to protest," Acevedo said.Acevedo said a large crowd most likely needs a permit. He said anyone planning a protest should ask their city or police early.Carter is due in Sandy Springs Municipal Court on Dec. 16.CBS News Atlanta reached out to the City of Sandy Springs and the Sandy Springs Police Department multiple times about the permit and citation but has not received a response as of this publication.

title: University of Arizona sorority member alleges she was sexually assaulted by 2 men at fraternity house
description: The sexual assault allegations surfaced two weeks after the university had suspended activities for its 21 fraternities amid reports of misconduct.
content: A sorority member at the University of Arizona has alleged she was sexually assaulted by two men at a fraternity house during a night of drinking in late August. The student told the university's police department that she consensually kissed one of the men at one point while at the Sigma Phi Epsilon house on Aug. 26 but doesn't remember agreeing to sex, according to search warrant records posted Monday night by CBS affiliate KOLD-TV in Tucson. The sexual assault allegations surfaced two weeks after the university had suspended activities for its 21 fraternities amid reports of misconduct, including assault, hazing and drug- and alcohol-related behavior. Suspensions on all but five fraternities have since been lifted after they had mandatory meetings with the dean of students. In speaking with an investigator, the sorority member recalled consuming tequila, including sharing a cup of the beverage with friends; witnessing two men sexually assaulting her, even feeling one man's breath on her face; awakening the next morning without pants and underwear on; and noticing a difficulty in swallowing, a possible sign of strangulation, according to the records. Later that day, she reported the allegations to police and underwent a forensic exam at a hospital. In a recorded call with the sorority member two days after the encounter, one of the men acknowledged he had sex with her, but he said she had agreed to it and denied that another man had sex with her. He said he had been drunk and "fuzzy" on what happened. He said people took video of the sorority member and him kissing in a bathroom, according to the records. The Associated Press left email and phone messages with the university Tuesday seeking comment. Its police department said the investigation is ongoing and declined to say if any arrests had been made. The Pima County Attorney's Office said the case hasn't been referred to it for prosecution. The university had put Sigma Phi Epsilon on probation from July until May of next year after a hazing complaint. Sigma Phi Epsilon isn't among the five fraternities that are currently listed as suspended. The national fraternity organization said they ordered members of the Arizona chapter to comply with any investigation. "The Fraternity has suspended those involved while the investigation proceeds. Any member found responsible will be expelled from Sigma Phi Epsilon, and we will cooperate fully with law enforcement as it seeks accountability under the law," read a statement from Brian Warren, chief executive officer of Sigma Phi Epsilon. Retaliation against the alleged victim or any witnesses would also not be tolerated, Warren said.Other cases of alleged sexual assault at fraternities Meanwhile, at Cornell University, a former student alleged that multiple Chi Phi fraternity members sexually assaulted her in October 2024. The allegations have sparked campus protests, renewed scrutiny of the Ivy League school's disciplinary system and a state investigation into the alleged assault. Several of the men have denied that they engaged in any nonconsensual sex or denied they touched the woman at all. Jane Doe sent a letter to the school saying she "felt unsupported and disbelieved" by the university's president.This week, a woman sued Alpha Delta Phi and its Chicago chapter, alleging she was raped in February by a member of the fraternity at the University of Chicago. The woman, identified in the lawsuit as Jane Doe, claimed she was sexually assaulted during a party at an on-campus residence and that she reported the assault to city police the next day. When asked about the case, Chicago police did not name the fraternity or provide an exact address, but said they are investigating a report of a sexual assault that happened on the same block early on Feb. 8. The University of Chicago and Alpha Delta Phi did not respond to emails in time for publication. Chicago police are also investigating after a woman reported being sexually assaulted during a party at another fraternity earlier this month. The University of Chicago said in a statement last week that a woman reported being sexually assaulted at the Alpha Epsilon Pi fraternity house. The fraternity said none of its members took part in the alleged attack.The University of Chicago was set to hold a public safety meeting on Wednesday.

title: Widespread rain expected to drench parts of Southern California as storm moves into region
description: CBS LA climatologist Marina Jurica says the rain will start in Ventura County by mid-morning and move through Los Angeles County through the rest of the day.
content: A low-pressure system from the Pacific Northwest is moving south and it is expected to bring widespread rain to Southern California on Wednesday afternoon. The rain will continue through the night and into Thursday with a chance of thunderstorms. Forecasters are saying this system will be the biggest storm of the season so far. CBS LA climatologist Marina Jurica says the rain will start in Ventura County by mid-morning and move through Los Angeles County through the rest of the day. "Heaviest rain looks to move in late Wednesday through Thursday morning," Jurica said. Rainfall totals for this storm will be between 1 and 1.5 inches, with some areas in the coastal foothills and slopes getting up to 3 inches. There is concern for some minor flooding and debris flows in recent burn scar areas. Areas near the Santa Ynez and Santa Mountains will likely get 3 inches of rain. A National Weather Service flood watch is expected to go into effect for those communities later on Wednesday. The low-pressure system will also bring cooler conditions. Temperatures will be in the high 60s to low 70s across most of the region.

title: Detective in James Craig murder case punished for speech criticizing Aurora police
description: The Aurora police detective who led the investigation into dentist James Craig, convicted of poisoning and killing his wife, was targeted for an unpaid suspension by her own police chief after criticizing her department during a speech to law enforcement officials.
content: The Aurora police detective who led the investigation into dentist James Craig, convicted of poisoning and killing his wife, was targeted for an unpaid suspension by her own police chief after criticizing her department during a speech to law enforcement officials.But Aurora's Civil Service Commission recently concluded that the proposed 10-hour suspension was "excessive" and inconsistent with discipline imposed in comparable cases. The commission reduced the punishment for Agent Bobbi Jo Olson to a written reprimand.The disciplinary action stemmed from a speech Olson delivered in April at the Minnesota Chiefs of Police Association Law Enforcement Expo. Olson was on duty and being paid by the Aurora Police Department at the time.According to disciplinary documents obtained by CBS Colorado, Olson used profanity and made derogatory comments about fellow officers, department command staff, and the department generally while discussing the Craig investigation.Aurora Police Chief Todd Chamberlain concluded that Olson violated two department directives, including rules governing conduct unbecoming an officer and conduct toward fellow employees."It is expected that every department member act with professionalism and integrity when representing APD in any capacity," the chief's office said this week in response to questions from CBS Colorado.The controversy began after one Minnesota police chief contacted Aurora police to complain that he was "offended" by Olson's language and criticism during her presentation.None of the other 107 law enforcement personnel attending the presentation complained, according to Aurora's internal affairs investigation. The investigation also noted that Olson's presentation was not recorded. The complaint nevertheless triggered a full internal investigation into Olson, who had not previously been disciplined during her 13 years with the Aurora Police Department.Olson did not dispute using profanity and expressed remorse, according to the investigative findings. But she said she did not believe such language would be considered inappropriate among a group of experienced law enforcement officers.The disciplinary documents say Olson used profanity and criticism to convey her frustration with what she viewed as a lack of understanding and support from some department members while she was dealing with the Craig murder investigation and threats against her life.She said her presentation was intended to educate other officers about how to support law enforcement personnel experiencing similar stress.Craig was convicted in 2025 of murdering his wife, Angela, whom prosecutors said he poisoned. The jury also found him guilty of solicitation-related offenses stemming from efforts to arrange killings and obtain false testimony, including a murder plot targeting Olson, according to trial proceedings.Olson appealed the proposed suspension to Aurora's Civil Service Commission, which found the punishment "excessive" and out of line with discipline in comparable cases. The commission overturned the suspension last month and reduced the penalty to a written reprimand.An attorney for Olson, Kodie Clinton, declined to comment.In a written statement, the chief's office defended its handling of the complaint."One complaint from anyone, anywhere, is met with the same level of propriety as if a member of the public were bringing forward a concern," the spokesperson said.The chief's office added that it respected the Civil Service Commission's decision.

title: Westboro, Massachusetts approves new bylaw to restrict Amazon drone deliveries: "Like David and Goliath"
description: Residents in Westboro, Massachusetts, are pushing back against Amazon's plans to launch drone deliveries in their community.
content: Residents in Westboro, Massachusetts, are pushing back against Amazon's plans to launch drone deliveries in their community, overwhelmingly approving a new bylaw aimed at restricting the service.At a special town meeting Monday, residents voted 510-13 in favor of the bylaw, which would regulate noise, nuisance and privacy issues associated with commercial drone deliveries and impose fines for violations. The bylaw has to be reviewed and allowed by the state attorney general before it can take effect.It comes as Amazon has made plans to begin delivering packages by drone in Westboro and surrounding communities by the end of the year.The company is already operating drone delivery flights in about a dozen metro areas, with plans to expand the service to several hundred cities and towns across the U.S. by the end of 2026.Amazon Prime Air uses autonomous drones measuring about 5 feet by 5 feet to deliver packages directly to customers' properties, within an hour of an order being placed."Westboro, Mass. has been exactly that type of beacon of innovation that we're looking for," said Amazon's Tareq Wafaie during an August Select Board meeting about the proposal, pointing to the company's already large footprint in Westboro, which includes a fulfillment center and robotics facility.But some residents say the convenience of faster deliveries isn't worth the potential impact on their neighborhoods."We're very passionate about this issue. It might feel like David and Goliath, but I like how that story ends," said Stephanie Stuchlik, who is part of the growing opposition to Amazon's plans."I spend a lot of time outdoors with my kids. I have two little girls, so I am disturbed by the thought of having this quality time outside with them, reading books and hearing and seeing these drones flying overhead all day long. It feels like not what I want my kids to grow up into," she added.While the Federal Aviation Administration largely controls the use of airspace and has green-lit drone deliveries, residents are attempting to regulate the operation of commercial drone deliveries at the ground level."Public nuisance, public safety issue. For what gain? To save 20 or 30 minutes to get your toothpaste or a bottle of Thousand Island dressing? It doesn't make sense," said Rod Jané."I think it's a really, really bad idea for the town, and I think we're doing the right thing in opposing it," Jané added.The opposition in Westboro has also caught the attention of state and federal lawmakers.In a letter, State Sen. Michael Moore and other area lawmakers are requesting Gov. Maura Healey's administration establish a task force to review commercial drone deliveries and consider potential policy changes."Do we want our quality of life impacted by this?" Moore questioned.Moore said the outcome in Westboro could have implications beyond the town."Whatever happens here will be the precedent for obviously Massachusetts and maybe New England. That's why it's so important that we try to get this right," he said."Most of us are Prime customers," said resident Christine Farmer. "But if drone delivery services operate, that opens the gateway for any other retailer. So that's the reason why the townspeople are saying, 'no thank you.'""It's really a disruption to the peace and the quality of life that we would have here to have something just show up and make a delivery stopping 13 feet from your window," Farmer added.In a statement, Amazon acknowledged the town's vote, but indicated it is continuing to evaluate its plans."We are aware of the bylaw recently passed in Westborough regarding commercial drone delivery. We remain committed to engaging with local officials and community members as we continue to assess our plans for the area," the company said.Amazon also defended its Prime Air program, which already operates in several states and metropolitan areas, describing the service as safe and reliable."Each Prime Air site creates new jobs spanning operations, engineering, safety, and more, with employees earning competitive wages and full benefits from day one," the company said.Meanwhile, residents are preparing for another challenge through the local zoning board.Opponents argue that Amazon should not be allowed to use its existing Westboro facility to launch drone deliveries and plan to appeal to the board as part of their ongoing efforts."We need to stop, we need to pause, we need to do everything in our power to preserve our skies and also our quality of life," Farmer added.

title: Why are there so many ballot questions in Massachusetts?
description: Why are there so many ballot questions in Massachusetts and what do the state's most powerful lawmakers have against them?
content: Massachusetts voters will be asked to vote on nine ballot questions in the 2026 election. It's the most since 1992. These questions affect candidates, cannabis, voter registration and nature conservation. In theory, you get to make or change nine laws and every lawmaker on Beacon Hill wants to change the system."Why do you think there's an issue with how we do ballot questions?" WBZ-TV's David Wade asked Sal DiDomenico, assistant majority leader of the Massachusetts State Senate. "There's a lot of folks behind those questions and we want to know who they are," he said. Ballot question transparencySen. DiDomenico (D) was the lead sponsor of Senate legislation to force the groups behind the ballot questions to be more transparent about where they're getting their money. The Senate passed his legislation, 38 to 0. Then the House passed a similar version, 149 to 0.Both sides want to put an end to what they call the "dark period." Right now, for eight months, starting in January, ballot campaigns don't have to report who's giving them money until 60 days before the election. Yet, individuals running for office have to file those reports every month.DiDomenico explained the unanimous Senate vote. "So, you have all these TV commercials, you have all this advertisement, you have all the things that people are watching to try and influence them, so we're just trying to say, 'you know, if you want to spend money on the campaign, it's your right to do that, but the public should know who is spending and how much is coming in,'" he said.Senate President Karen Spilka (D) and House Speaker Ron Mariano (D) both say deep-pocketed special interest groups have taken over. WBZ went to Spilka's office, tried calling her and sent emails, but did not receive a response. Speaker Mariano sent WBZ a statement saying, "The current process is fundamentally broken ... allowing ballot question campaigns to operate in the dark."What do lawmakers have against ballot questions?But is there a hidden motivation? Perhaps there's resentment that so much power has shifted to the voters.Reporter Mike Deehan of Axios Boston has covered the Massachusetts State House for 18 years. He thinks lawmakers have real concerns about so-called "dark money," but he also describes sort of a turf war."Of course, they don't like it when so many issues are going before voters and not through them," Deehan said. "They want to be the arbiters of what becomes law. They are lawmakers in Massachusetts."The man in charge of the state's elections, Secretary of State William Galvin, says the reason there are this many ballot questions is because of lawmakers and their inaction. A special legislative committee reviewed the questions and chose not to get involved."Remember, any ballot question that makes it to the ballot has been sent to the Legislature first, to vote on it, or to take some action on it and they failed to do that," explained Galvin.Republican Senator Peter Durant voted "yes" to making the process more transparent. "I think it's safe that we can trust the voters, but we do have to give them information, and that's the real crux of the problem," he told WBZ."Lot of inaction up here" But Durant was also pretty honest when asked if there's a lot of inaction at the State House."Yeah, I tend to think there's a lot of inaction up here and it's kind of odd for a legislator to say this, but yeah, we need to, we need to take up the issues that are important to the people that we represent, get them done in a timely manner," Durant said. The House version of this ballot question transparency legislation would also set up a special review board to make recommendations by the end of 2027 if there should be a constitutional amendment to change the way Massachusetts handles ballot questions. Ironically, any type of constitutional amendment would have to be approved by voters, as a ballot question.The House and Senate will now have to come together for a compromise to turn their respective legislation into law, but it's obvious, that change is coming.If you have a question you'd like us to look into, please email questioneverything@cbsboston.com.

title: IHSA calls reported hateful comments at Evanston-New Trier football game "sad and unfortunate"
description: The Illinois High School Association is responding as an investigation continues into hateful comments against Evanston Township High School students who were part of marching band during a football game at the new Ryan Field last week.
content: The Illinois High School Association is responding as an investigation continues into hateful comments against Evanston Township High School students who were part of marching band during a football game at the new Ryan Field last week.Evanston Township was taking on New Trier Township High School on Friday, Oct. 16, in a massive rivalry matchup with more than 27,000 tickets sold.In a joint statement Evanston Township High School District 202 and New Trier Township High School District 203 said on the sidelines, the Evanston marching band was subjected to racist and homophobic comments along with other offensive behavior by New Trier fans during the game.ETHS color guard members Kevin Watts and Kiro Tabor said they were just moments away from performing with their high school color guard and marching band when they noticed aggressive chants from the opposing student section for NTHS.They say it started with people shouting 'f- you,' but things escalated."Somebody was pointing Kevin out, called Kevin the f-slur and then a group of boys had looked at me, called me the N-word a couple of times," Watts said.In a statement released Tuesday, IHSA executive director Craig Anderson said the IHSA has been in contact with the administrations of both schools. "It is sad and unfortunate that such a historic night celebrating the power of community and high school sports was marred by the despicable actions of a few," Anderson said in the statement. "Both schools are taking these allegations very seriously and working together to identify those involved, including to verify if they are current high school students, and if they attend either of the participating schools."Anderson said IHSA will continue to work closely with both schools and determine what will happen next.

title: Massachusetts lawmakers scrap Gov. Healey's plan to suspend gas tax
description: Massachusetts state lawmakers stripped Gov. Healey's gas tax suspension out of their $2.3 billion supplemental budget, killing the proposal before it had a chance for a full vote.
content: On Tuesday, Massachusetts state lawmakers stripped Gov. Maura Healey's gas tax suspension out of their $2.3 billion supplemental budget, killing the proposal before it had a chance for a full vote.Last month, Healey announced her proposal to temporarily suspend the state's gas tax for two months. The governor said the estimated $120 million in consumer savings would have been covered by excess revenue from the state's so-called "millionaire's tax," but the House Ways & Means Committee pulled it from the supplemental budget they are currently debating."I am disappointed and I am going to keep fighting for it," Governor Healey told WBZ-TV Tuesday night. "Because this is about providing relief to people. Donald Trump got us in this war, it's raising the price of everything, including the price at the pump. People can't afford it."Healey doubled down and said the state has the money to pull this off. The chair of the House Ways & Means Committee suggested he didn't see a way to keep gas stations from raising prices to offset the 24 cents.Mike Minogue, the Republican candidate for governor, grilled Healey for not getting her own proposal across the finish line. "She said there's only so much a governor can do, well then push back on the legislature," Minogue said. "She did not push back on the audit. She's not pushing back on the gas tax. She said she had the money for it and the legislature is blowing her off. We have a one-party system; they do whatever they want. We need balance."Minogue, who has his own proposal for eliminating the gas tax, said he would have funded it with dollars from exposing "waste, fraud and abuse" within state government.WBZ met Mike Ballas filling up his tank. He said gas prices have caused his family to change how they go about their day and even forced them to change their car."My wife got a hybrid car," Ballas said. "So we save now almost two tanks of gas a month. [We take] less trips, carpooling, kids almost exclusively carpool to soccer now. There is no single driver trips anymore."Sharon Bracket drives from Boylston to Boston four times a week for work and has to fill up twice a week. "This car takes premium, so almost $6 a gallon," she said. "I am not happy. It's not just gas prices. It's the price of everything."Bracket is unconvinced the alleged 24 cents in savings per gallon would make a real difference, citing the staggering cost of living. "I think it's a wash. I think it's a last-ditch effort to try to turn around some voting," she said. "They are thinking people are taking hard hits here and feeling it, but I think people are feeling it everywhere."

title: Macklin Celebrini's OT power play goal lifts Sharks past Canadiens
description: Macklin Celebrini scored his second goal of the game on a power play at 2:13 of overtime to give the San Jose Sharks a 4-3 victory over the Montreal Canadiens on Tuesday night.
content: Macklin Celebrini scored his second goal of the game on a power play at 2:13 of overtime to give the San Jose Sharks a 4-3 victory over the Montreal Canadiens on Tuesday night.Celebrini fired a one-timer into the top-left corner after goalie Jakub Dobes was called for interference on Colin Graf.Celebrini added an assist and Tyler Toffoli and Michael Misa also scored to help San Jose (5-4-1) rebound from a 3-1 loss to Toronto on Monday night.Sharks goalie Alex Nedeljkovic stopped 31 shots.Juraj Slafkovsky, Cole Caufield and Nick Suzuki had a goal and an assist each as Montreal (4-3-2) surrendered a two-goal advantage for the fourth time this season. Dobes made 26 saves.Misa, who hit the post earlier in the period, cut into the Canadiens' lead at 5:36 in the third, finishing a feed from Kiefer Sherwood after Montreal defenseman Lane Hutson turned the puck over.Toffoli tied it with 8:51 remaining in regulation when he buried Celebrini's pass on the power play with Arber Xhekaj in the penalty box for unsportsmanlike conduct.Up nextSharks: At Ottawa on Thursday night.Canadiens: At Chicago on Friday night.

title: LeBron James talks smack with New York Knicks fans, drops 14 points in victorious Philadelphia 76ers debut
description: Knicks fans enjoyed giving LeBron James a hard time in his 76ers debut.
content: LeBron James got the business from Knicks fans still gloating and riding an emotional high from an NBA championship banner celebration.As he stepped to the free-throw line for the Philadelphia 76ers early in Tuesday night's season opener, Knicks fans erupted toward James with chants of "We don't want you! We don't want you!"Such a rude reception from New Yorkers to one of the city's newest residents.The shouts of rejection came in part because there was a plausible scenario under which James would have opened the season at Madison Square Garden in a Knicks uniform.James and his agent, Rich Paul, had said the Knicks would have been James' first choice in free agency had New York not won its first NBA championship since 1973 last season.Knicks fans said, we're good.The 41-year-old James got the final word as the Sixers won 106-100.James talked smack with fans in the lower level. Yes, that was Spike Lee trying to play peacemaker.James finished with 14 points and nine rebounds and had plenty of help in getting the W from new Sixers and holdovers. Tyrese Maxey scored 28 points, Jaylen Brown had 19, Joel Embiid had 13 points and 11 rebounds, and the Sixers ruined the Knicks' championship party.A good night in New York totally spoiled? Not quite, according to James."I wouldn't say that," James said. "It was a great night for New York fans. Fifty-plus years. I was a part of that at one point where we hadn't won a major championship in Cleveland in over 50 years. The fans will never forget this moment."James' first basket for the Sixers was not nearly as memorable. He took a feed from Embiid in the paint and went up strong for an uncontested right-handed layup.Just two points. Just one bucket of what the Sixers expect to be many, many more over the next two seasons as the NBA's career scoring leader opened his record 24th season.Embiid appeared to wonder during the national anthem where the Knicks' championship banner was hanging in the rafters as James sat nearby on the bench with his head bowed and hands clasped. The banner was indeed raised in a pregame ceremony.It's the same kind of celebration the 76ers expect James, Embiid and the rest of a stout starting lineup to deliver on opening night next season.It's the thrill of the chase, to end a championship drought — much like he did to break that drought in Cleveland — that in part drives James to keep playing after racking up a list of accomplishments unrivaled by his peers.The Sixers got a first look at the potent lineup they put together this summer in hopes of winning their first title since 1983.
