No meaningful disciplinary consequences followed," attorneys wrote in the lawsuit.The family pulled their son out of Oaks Christian School following the allegations."He's doing better because he's out of that environment," Glassman said. "The psychological harm that was done to him while at Oaks Christian, being routinely and repeatedly subject to racism in such an ugly way, like turning his last name into a racial slur, just horrible, despicable things."

title: The roof fell, but faith never did: North Texas church builds a bigger future
description: After months of storm damage, flooding and uncertainty, Kingdom Culture Dallas is planning a larger sanctuary and a new space dedicated to serving children with special needs.
content: The roof is gone. The walls are coming down. But the faith that built Kingdom Culture Dallas is standing.Demolition crews moved in Tuesday to tear down the sanctuary that an estimated 50,000 pounds of ice had crushed during a January winter storm.It was a painful but promising moment for a congregation that had endured flooding, destructive winds, and insurance battles.For Apostle Sherman Dumas, the rubble represents more than ruin."Knocking down what once was so that we can reveal the thing that God wants it to be on the other side of a chaotic situation," Dumas said.The congregation's troubles began Jan. 27, when a church leader called Dumas and his wife, Dr. Jaquet Dumas, about the collapsed roof.The destruction was devastating for a congregation that relied on donations from around the world to secure its four-acre property."So many people sowed into it," Dumas said. "We call it our miracle property ... because people gave in to it all over the world. And to see it destroyed was just like, whoa."The ice was only the beginning.Rainwater flooded the exposed sanctuary. Winds reaching 80 mph knocked down an exterior wall and disrupted power. The church was displaced, and the damage kept mounting."And we had those moments when we wanted to find something we can control," Dumas said. "But incident after incident let us know that we were not in control."Help arrived from Transformation Church in Tulsa, Oklahoma, which contributed $100,000. Dumas said the gift helped restore electricity and allowed the congregation to return to part of its property.From demolition to a bigger missionThe church now plans to build a sanctuary twice the size of the original, with room to expand its community outreach.Dumas said the vision includes three tiny-home villages behind the church, one of which is dedicated to serving children with special needs.The demolition brought mixed emotions."So part of it was a little bit of grief," Dumas said. "And then at the same time, joy because, oh, this is making way for the new thing to come into place."For months, people have recognized Kingdom Culture Dallas by its destruction."I meet people all the time. They say the church with the roof!" Dumas said. "I don't mind it because the church with the roof has become a sign and the symbol of hope to people."The church hopes to move into its new building by May.Dumas sees the broken stones as reminders of what the congregation survived and what it believes is ahead."It's like, okay, this becomes a stepping stone to the next thing that God wants to do through us," he said.For Kingdom Culture Dallas, the storm is no longer the story.What rises from the rubble is.The demolition came days from the church's second anniversary. Typically, services would be held in their cafe-turned-sanctuary. It remains intact.He said the celebration is at 10 am at the Ruthe Jackson Center in Grand Prairie.

title: Long Beach protesters demand leaders do more after U.S. citizen injured during ICE operation
description: Protesters gathered outside of Long Beach City Hall on Tuesday, days after video captured the moments a local man's arm was broken during an encounter with immigration agents​ over the weekend, to demand more action from city leaders.
content: Protesters gathered outside of Long Beach City Hall on Tuesday, days after video captured the moments a local man's arm was broken during an encounter with immigration agents over the weekend, to demand more action from city leaders. "They broke someone's arm; we're lucky it didn't escalate further," one resident said during Tuesday's city council meeting, during which the protesters continued to voice their concerns and demands for ICE to get out of Long Beach. "Immigrant communities deserve to be here, they helped build this country, and it's absolutely upsetting that this can happen in a state like California," said Ernesto Huerta, a labor organizer. Video from Saturday's encounter, captured via one onlooker's cellphone, shows ICE agents on top of Ricardo Gonzalez, a former city worker and U.S. citizen, as he screams in pain and tries to tell them that his arm is broken. In a statement on Tuesday, Department of Homeland Security officials said that Gonzalez was arrested after he allegedly smashed the mirror of a government vehicle as "anti-ICE agitators" threatened officers and "attempted to impede" their attempts to arrest an "at-large criminal illegal alien.""I think it's awful. I mean, it's clear from the video that he was riding his bike down the street, and these guys were speeding down a one-way street," said Long Beach resident Stacie Straw. "He broke their mirror because they ran over him. They collided with him."DHS officials say they are investigating charges against Gonzalez for the damage to their SUV. Meanwhile, Long Beach city leaders have taken to social media to speak out against the encounter. "Another terrible abuse of power by ICE in our streets," said a statement from Senator Adam Schiff. "How many more citizens will suffer abuse or die from ICE actions before Republicans in Congress can be convinced to help rein in this out-of-control agency?"Long Beach Mayor Rex Richardson has also filed a formal complaint against DHS, demanding accountability and an independent investigation. Some residents say they need more from leaders. "The situations that we're put in nowadays, it could be any of us. It doesn't matter if you're documented, undocumented," said Viviana Aguilera. A GoFundMe for Gonzalez, organized by his daughter, says he's still being treated for serious injuries.

title: After a baby was found dead in a Fort Worth dumpster, officials promote "safe haven" baby boxes
description: In Ennis, a newborn was safely surrendered through one of these boxes earlier this year, showing how they can help save lives.
content: Twenty-three-year-old Avia Cantrell is now charged with capital murder, while a man believed to be her boyfriend, 26-year-old Camron Baker, is charged with abuse of a corpse.According to court documents, Cantrell admitted to leaving her newborn daughter face down in bathwater for about 30 minutes.The newborn was found dead near a dumpster outside a Fort Worth motel late Sunday night. "It's unfortunate that the circumstances of that event happened," McLendon-Chisholm Fire Chief Eddie Stough said. Years ago, he responded to a similar incident. "It's almost surreal... and police, fire and EMS, we tend to disassociate in order to keep our mental clarity," he said. "It's very difficult to do that when a child is involved... and the circumstances with the children that I have dealt with in the past, it was atrocious." Installing Rockwall County's first Safe Haven Baby Box at the McLendon-Chisholm Fire Department was a priority for Stough. It's been here since January, giving parents a way to anonymously surrender a newborn."We would much rather see that than us responding to a circumstance like what just happened," he said. After a baby is surrendered, a parent has 60 seconds to leave before an alarm sounds. There are no cameras outside, allowing them to remain anonymous."It notifies the fire department staff, EMS staff, which is Rockwall EMS," Stough said. "It also notifies CPS. At no point does it notify law enforcement." Under Texas' Baby Moses Law, parents can safely surrender an unharmed baby 60 days old or younger to staff at designated locations, including hospitals and fire stations. Baby boxes are another option. "Anybody who feels like they're in a position that they need to surrender their child, please give us the opportunity to assist you," Stough said. He said interest in baby boxes is growing across North Texas, with Rowlett installing one this past summer. In Ennis, a newborn was safely surrendered through one of these boxes earlier this year, showing how they can help save lives.

title: Declan Chisholm's goal, Jake Allen's 31 saves lead Devils over Avalanche
description: Declan Chisholm scored the go-ahead goal midway through the second period and Jake Allen made 31 saves as the Devils beat the Avalanche 4-3 on Tuesday night.
content: Declan Chisholm scored the go-ahead goal midway through the second period and Jake Allen made 31 saves as the New Jersey Devils beat the Colorado Avalanche 4-3 on Tuesday night.Chisholm scored his first goal for the Devils at 12:33 on a power play, putting New Jersey in front to stay after the teams traded goals in the first.Luke Evangelista, Arseny Gritsyuk and Jesper Boqvist also scored for the Devils, who recovered from a 4-2 loss at Washington in their previous game.The 34-year-old Allen, honored before puck drop for playing his 500th career game earlier this month, improved to 4-2-0.Gabriel Landeskog scored and Artturi Lehkonen added two late goals for the Avalanche, who lost for the third time in four games. Colorado was beaten 3-2 at Philadelphia on Monday.Colorado goalie Scott Wedgewood made 37 saves against his former team. He entered 5-0-0 with a 1.52 goals-against average versus the Devils.Evangelista opened the scoring at 6:40 of the first with his third goal.Landeskog tied it at 14:32 with his fourth of the season. The Avalanche captain missed more than three seasons following major right knee surgery. He returned to score 14 goals in 60 games last season.Gritsyuk's fourth goal came at 4:39 of the third. Boqvist scored an empty-netter at 16:05 to make it 4-1.Lehkonen scored at 16:46, then added his team-leading eighth goal with 3.5 seconds left.New Jersey won for the fourth time in six home games.Avalanche defenseman Brent Burns played his 1,015th consecutive game. The 41-year-old is 49 games from tying Phil Kessel for the NHL ironman record. Burns has played 1,589 career games.Up nextAvalanche: Host the Tampa Bay Lightning on Friday.Devils: Host the Anaheim Ducks on Thursday.

title: Michigan officials detect chronic wasting disease in farmed cervid in Hillsdale County
description: Michigan officials say a fatal neurological disease has been detected in a farmed cervid in Hillsdale County.
content: Michigan officials say a fatal neurological disease has been detected in a farmed cervid in Hillsdale County.According to the Michigan Department of Agriculture and Rural Development, officials detected a case of chronic wasting disease (CWD) through the CWD surveillance program. Officials say other cases have previously been detected in Calhoun, Kent, Lake, Mackinac, Mecosta, Montcalm, Newaygo and Osceola counties. MDARD is also working to rule out any additional exposures to other farmed cervids as part of its response.MDARD says there are no human cases reported."While regular surveillance leads to early detection and is a fundamental piece of the response effort, MDARD's ongoing collaboration with herd owners, their veterinarians, and our federal partners is crucial to managing the disease for the long-term," said State Veterinarian Dr. Nora Wineland. "Ensuring the health of Michigan's farmed cervid population has been and continues to be a team effort." According to MDARD, CWD is a progressive disease that affects various cervid species, such as white-tailed deer, mule deer and moose. It can be transmitted from one animal to another and indirectly through the environment. Infected animals will eventually show signs of abnormal behavior, weight loss and physical debilitation in later stages of the disease.The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that infected animals not be consumed as food by humans or domestic animals.

title: Islanders score 3 first-period goals, hold on to defeat Ducks
description: Ondrej Palat, Viktor Eklund and Simon Holmstrom scored first-period goals and the Islanders beat the Ducks 3-2 on Tuesday night for their second straight victory.
content: Ondrej Palat, Viktor Eklund and Simon Holmstrom scored first-period goals and the New York Islanders beat the Anaheim Ducks 3-2 on Tuesday night for their second straight victory.Ilya Sorokin made 15 saves to help the Islanders improve to 3-0-1 in their last four games.Frank Vatrano and Alex Killorn scored for Anaheim, which lost its fourth straight game. Lukas Dostal finished with 22 saves.Palat opened the scoring with 6:21 left in the first period. Jean-Gabriel Pageau found Palat streaking toward the net, and the forward fired a wrist shot past Dostal.Eklund doubled the lead less than three minutes later. Emil Heineman floated a wrist shot from the blue line, and Eklund corralled the loose puck and buried it for his second goal of the season.Vatrano pulled the Ducks within a goal 49 seconds later, lifting a backhander past Sorokin off a feed from A.J. Greer.Holmstrom restored New York's two-goal advantage with a power-play goal with 1:18 left in the first, deflecting Mathew Schaefer's shot from the point past Dostal.Killorn pulled Anaheim within a goal with 2:40 remaining in the third.Up nextDucks: At New Jersey Thursday night.Islanders: Host Los Angeles on Thursday night.

title: Mayor Bass pledges relief for LADWP customers amid sky-high bills
description: Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said LADWP customers "can just pay what they can afford now" as she urges the board to pause shutoffs amid skyrocketing bills.
content: With just two weeks to go until Election Night, sky-high utility bills have become a major issue in the Los Angeles mayor's race, with both incumbent Mayor Karen Bass and Nithya Raman promising action. Bass addressed the concerns about the mounting costs in a statement on Tuesday, promising relief for Los Angeles Department of Water and Power customers. "First, LADWP customers can just pay what they can afford now," she said. "Second, I have asked the LADWP Board to pause shutoffs through the end of the year for customers facing higher bills after the record heat."Bass added that customers who can't pay their residential bill will have their electricity or water shut off. The announcement comes after a San Fernando Valley man called for an independent audit into LADWP after receiving a $3,300 utility bill over the summer, $600 more than his bill for last summer."This is insane," San Fernando Valley resident Micah Reed said in a social media video. "All I did during August is keep my thermostat at 74 degrees so my family wouldn't melt."Reed quickly learned that he wasn't alone, prompting an investigation by LA City Controller Kenneth Mejia. Following the announcement, said he's glad his video spurred some action. "I wasn't expecting to lead the charge, but I'm happy to be a part of it," he said. He added that he's not focused on the potential political fallout surrounding LADWP's billing, just looking for a solution."I'm not accusing anybody of any nefarious action, however, there is a big question mark, and there is a lot of concern around LADWP," Reed said. "This is something I've been listening to for years."Raman also seized on the issue, calling for transparency and justification. "The public deserves transparency about the costs that they are experiencing," she said. "They deserve public justification of these enormous costs."

title: Family remembers motorcyclist killed by 12-year-old driving stolen car in Baltimore
description: Friends and loved ones packed Morning Star Baptist Church in Woodlawn Tuesday morning to pay tribute to Barry Wright Sr., a 69-year-old motorcyclist struck and killed by a 12-year-old boy driving a stolen car in West Baltimore late last month.
content: Friends and loved ones packed Morning Star Baptist Church in Woodlawn Tuesday morning to pay tribute to Barry Wright Sr., a 69-year-old motorcyclist struck and killed by a 12-year-old boy driving a stolen car in West Baltimore late last month. Wright's funeral comes as police apprehended another 12-year-old behind the wheel of a stolen car that crashed in the same neighborhood near Coppin State University over the weekend.Stolen on SundayIt was around 2 a.m. Sunday when police said a 12-year-old boy stole a Hyundai Sonata from the 1200 block of North Gay Street in East Baltimore. The owner of the car declined an interview, but his girlfriend said he was able to track the Hyundai online and showed pictures of severe damage to the front end when it crashed into a home more than four miles away in the 2800-block of West North Avenue. Baltimore police said the juvenile had prior contact with law enforcement, and they released him to a parent and made what is called a Child In Need of Supervision referral to the Department of Juvenile Services or DJS.Fatal impact Just three weeks earlier, in almost the same area of North Avenue, another 12-year-old boy driving a stolen Kia slammed into a motorcycle.Police said the impact killed 69-year-old Barry Wright Sr.That 12-year-old was also a repeat offender.Baltimore City State's Attorney Ivan Bates said he was under DJS supervision at the time but will never face criminal charges because of juvenile justice reform legislation passed in the General Assembly in 2022 that will not allow those under 13 to face certain charges. At 10:30 a.m. on Tuesday, Wright's loved ones said their final goodbyes and remembered the beloved father, husband and grandfather at his funeral."From the bottom of my heart, we're going to miss Barry," one friend said at the service, which included a montage of Wright on the motorcycle he loved to ride. The pastor spoke of Wright's dependability, how he was always there for his friends and family."May Barry's life speak for him," he told the crowd of mourners.Just 12 days earlier, state's attorney Bates read a statement the family's behalf, outraged at the lack of charges under the law and the "cruel injustice of this system."Wright's son said in that statement, "Annapolis seems to glance at the tragedy, shrugging its shoulders as if life didn't matter at all so long as the perpetrator is under the age of 13. The boy who stole my father's life is a mere 12 years of age and is walking free."The son's statement referred to "gut-wrenching injustice that [the 12-year-old] has more rights than his innocent victims."Speaking to the state's attorney Bates, who slammed the inability to get justice for the family, also addressed juvenile accountability in his new Beyond the Status Quo podcast with DJS Secretary Betsy Fox Tolentino."I think my role is to always make sure we're going to do things better, so we don't have these incidents, but when we do, they are incredibly heartbreaking. My heart goes out to the victims," the secretary said. Fox Tolentino told Bates mandated confidentiality often makes it harder to show what is being done behind the scenes to rehabilitate troubled juveniles."That's something that could be really challenging for the community outside the system to understand because they want to know what's happening in the system," the DJS secretary said. "They want to know the system is working the way they think it should be, and when you can't see, it's hard to trust that it's working the way they want it to work."You can watch more of their conversation here.

title: Florida executes man who killed deputy after fighting for gun, marking the state's 18th execution this year
description: Florida carried out its 18th execution this year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis' aggressive use of the death penalty.
content: Florida carried out its 18th execution of the year on Tuesday under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis' aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term. William Reaves, 77, was pronounced dead at 6:12 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison near Starke. He was convicted of first-degree murder for the 1986 shooting of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkowski.The injection began immediately after that. About 30 seconds later, Reaves took several big breaths and then stopped moving. After a few minutes, the team warden shook Reaves by the shoulders and yelled his name, but there was no response.A medic was called into the chamber a short time later to check for a heartbeat or any other signs of life, and Reaves was pronounced dead about a minute later.Reaves was the eighth Florida prisoner over age 70 put to death this year, highlighting the nation's aging death-row population as Florida continues to far outpace the rest of the country in total executions.Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year. Another execution is scheduled for November, which would tie that mark if both are carried out as planned.DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said previously that his goal is to bring justice to victims' families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out.Reaves fought with deputy after dropping gunAccording to court records, Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986. Reaves acknowledged that he had placed the call at a payphone outside the store. While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves' shorts, officials said. The men struggled over the firearm and Reaves eventually regained control over it. Investigators said the deputy attempted to run away before Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds.Reaves was initially convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. The Florida Supreme Court reversed the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death a second time in 1992, and subsequent appeals have been unsuccessful.The Florida Supreme Court rejected Reaves' final appeals last week. One issue raised by his attorneys was Florida's method of execution. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. It differs from the single-drug injection used by states like Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike was rushed to the hospital last month after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital.Defense attorneys also argued that the jurors who recommended the death penalty for Reaves were never told that the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs rated Reaves, an Army veteran, as 100% disabled by post-traumatic stress disorder, which was caused by his service in the Vietnam War. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter on Monday asking him to stop the execution.Final appeals for Reaves were still pending before the U.S. Supreme Court.Florida close to matching last year's record-setting number of executionsA total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. in 2025. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half the 31 total executions in the U.S. so far this year. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so.Jesse Guardado, 64, is next scheduled to die by injection in Florida on Nov. 5. He was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.

title: "Operation Mincemeat" brings bizarre World War II mission to stage in Boston
description: The Tony Award-winning musical inspired by the wild scheme that helped defeat Adolf Hitler during World War II is now playing in Boston.
content: The Tony Award-winning musical inspired by the wild scheme that helped defeat Adolf Hitler during World War II is now playing in Boston. "Operation Mincemeat" tells the true story of how MI5 agents came up with the ruse that led to the end of the war. "It's about World War II, and it's a comedy. And also, it's incredibly moving at times," said Katie Kleiger, who portrays Ewen Montagu, one of the plan's real-life masterminds. "He's such a galvanizer which I think is such a cool thing to be like he's like, 'let's do it, let's like act. Let's not think or talk, let's do the thing,'" Kleiger told WBZ-TV. "And I think that's like a really awesome trait to have." In 1953, Montagu wrote "The Man Who Never Was," a book detailing the operation. The mission involved faking a plane crash and planting documents on a dead body, convincing Hitler to move thousands of troops. "It facilitated the invasion of Sicily and if that hadn't happened D-Day probably could never have happened or wouldn't have happened in the same way," Sarah Montagu, Ewen's granddaughter, told WBZ-TV. "He always used to say that he really enjoyed fooling Hitler." Saul Montagu, a great-grandchild of Ewen's, and Sarah are both big fans of the show. "It's such an unlikely subject for a musical that it's, I said we were all surprised but you know, everybody thought it was great," Sarah said. "I got to know him more after the actual musical had come out," Saul told WBZ-TV. "So the show itself kind of drove me to actually, you know, I never got to meet him but got kind of closer to who he was in the past." Kleiger said that the research she did before taking the role allowed her to more intricately understand the type of person Ewen Montagu was. "This is life or death for so many people and the reality of what that time was for the world," Kleiger said. "They did an incredible thing. And I think, I hope that the descendants of these people are proud to see their family members on stage portrayed in that way." Sarah Montagu told WBZ-TV that her grandfather spent time in the United States after the war, including a semester at Harvard University in Cambridge. You can see "Operation Mincemeat" at the Emerson Colonial Theatre in Boston through Sunday, Oct. 25.

title: San Francisco leaders call for more immigration legal aid funding after apparent ICE detention
description: Surveillance video shows a man being detained by masked U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers in San Francisco's South of Market neighborhood on Monday.
content: Surveillance video shows a man being detained by masked U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers in San Francisco's South of Market neighborhood on Monday.The video has prompted renewed calls from city leaders and immigration legal defense advocates for additional funding."Stop touching me! Stop touching me! You are violating my rights as a U.S. citizen!" the man can be heard shouting in the footage.The encounter was cited by a coalition of San Francisco supervisors and immigration legal defense groups as they called for emergency funding to expand legal services and support the city's Rapid-Response Network, a coalition that responds to immigration enforcement activity in the city and confirmed the detention involved ICE officers. Speaking on the steps of City Hall on Tuesday, Supervisor Jackie Fielder said the city must continue to oppose federal immigration enforcement efforts."We are here to say once more, ICE, you are not welcome here to terrorize the citizens of San Francisco," Fielder said.Fielder also emphasized the need for the city to back its sanctuary policies with additional resources."We will defend our sanctuary city not just in words but in action," she said.Supervisor Bilal Mahmood also raised concerns about the federal government's intentions."Because make no mistake, the intention of our federal government is to intimidate," Mahmood said.The coalition pointed to Monday's encounter as an example of why they believe the city needs to act quickly. They warn that without adequate funding, people affected by immigration enforcement could struggle to find legal representation, understand their rights or determine where to turn for help.The circumstances surrounding Monday's detention remain unclear, and the man has not been publicly identified. The surveillance footage captures the confrontation but does not establish what led to the encounter.In the video, the man can be heard responding to the individuals surrounding him."You ran," one person says."No, I didn't run," the man responds, repeatedly shouting, "I'm a U.S. citizen!"The coalition says its message to city leaders is that preparation cannot wait until another incident occurs.The San Francisco Rapid Response Network said it has connected the man with a public defender and has provided other means of support.CBS News Bay Area has reached out to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement for comment on this story but has not immediately heard back.

title: Iran lauds ties with Russia, contradicting Trump's claim of little Russian support for Tehran
description: Iran says its ties with Russia are stronger than ever after a visit by Putin's top envoy, challenging Trump's assertion that Moscow isn't helping Iran in the war.
content:
Follow updates on the war in the Middle East for Wednesday, Oct. 21, here . See earlier developments below.
King Charles III praised Oman's peacemaking attempts in the Middle East Tuesday as Sultan Haitham bin Tariq began the first state visit by an Omani ruler to the U.K. in nearly half a century.
Hailing longstanding diplomatic, military and royal ties at a Windsor Castle banquet, the British monarch paid tribute to Muscat's "noble efforts" to help reopen the choked Strait of Hormuz.
"I would especially like to recognize, at a time when conflict has returned so painfully to the region, Oman's enduring commitment as a trusted interlocutor to all parties," Charles told around 160 guests at the lavish dinner.
"Oman's role across the Gulf and her 'constructive neutrality' — as you put it — matters far beyond Hormuz, and is worthy of our utmost respect," Britain's king added in a toast to the Omani sultan.
The first state visit to Britain by a sultan of Oman for 44 years comes amid severe turbulence in the Middle East prompted by the U.S.-Iran war.
Oman, a key U.K. military ally which borders the vital Hormuz waterway, has acted as a mediator in talks between the U.S. and Iran since the conflict flared in late February.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth confirmed Tuesday that he visited Israel on Monday and met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, saying he "was there visiting our troops" and "had a chance to talk to the prime minister."
The unannounced visit came just over a week before Netanyahu's party faces elections. It also comes after President Trump floated resuming military operations against Iran following next month's U.S. midterm elections.
"Of course, the nature of our conversations is not something I would talk about but they've been good partners and I appreciate that," Hegseth said of his meeting with Netanyahu.
U.S. diplomatic missions across the Middle East have issued a new round of security warnings to Americans amid escalating attacks by Iran-backed Houthi militants against Saudi Arabia, including an Oct. 10 strike on Riyadh's international airport that killed an American citizen.
The alerts, issued Sunday by U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and several other countries, warned that hostilities could rapidly and without warning spread beyond areas already affected by the fighting. The advisories urged Americans to exercise vigilance and prepare for possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and other travel disruptions.
"We are actively warning U.S. citizens about the very real threat the Houthis pose and urging them to heed official guidance," Edgar Vasquez, the State Department's deputy assistant secretary for press, told CBS News.
"These alerts are part of a proactive effort by the Trump administration to ensure Americans are aware of potential risks," Vasquez said, adding that the safety and security of American citizens remain the department's "top priority."
President Trump said the U.S. is "doing very well with Iran" and he's just deciding how he wants to win the war.
"As you know, we're doing very well with Iran," Mr. Trump said as he took questions from reporters in the Oval Office at an unrelated executive order signing. "We just have to make a final decision of which way do we want to win? Do we want to win the nice way or the not nice way? But we're doing very well."
The war, which Mr. Trump said would take only a few weeks in March, has now dragged on for almost eight months with no apparent end in sight. Iran said on Tuesday it would not return to the negotiating table unless the U.S. drops its sanctions, threats and pressure campaign — an unlikely demand.
The president also discussed Europe not helping the U.S. with the war with Iran, saying, "We don't need any help. But I was testing them."
"I just called individual presidents and prime ministers to ask, would they like to help us? And they said, 'No,'" Mr. Trump said. "I said, 'Well, that's not nice.' You know, we spend hundreds of billions a year on NATO. And they said no."
Iran is taking a hard-line stance on negotiations with the U.S. to end the war, with President Masoud Pezeshkian saying Tuesday there will be no return to talks without a halt to the pressure campaign by the U.S.
Pezeshkian met with representatives from Pakistan, including army chief Asim Munir, on Tuesday. Pakistan has played an integral role as a mediator in peace talks between the U.S. and Iran, including the brief success of the Islamabad Memorandum in June.
"(Pezeshkian) told Pakistan's Field Marshal Asim Munir that US warmongering lies behind regional tensions, including disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz," according to a readout of the meeting from the official Iranian government account on X . "He said Washington must lift its pressures, threats and sanctions before any negotiations."
Those conditions are unlikely to be agreed upon by the U.S., which has stepped up its sanctions , dubbed Operation Economic Outcast, over the past month. President Trump has said the economic pressure campaign has become the main strategy for ending the war.
Pezeshkian also met with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in Tehran on Tuesday. Iran and Russia have become powerful allies.
Naval mines have halted three tankers attempting to travel the Strait of Hormuz via routes considered illegal by Tehran, Iranian Revolutionary Guards said on Tuesday.
"Two violating oil tankers were set ablaze and halted due to the explosion of mines planted by the brave sailors of the IRGC Navy at an illegal crossing point in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz," the Guards said in an earlier statement on their official Sepah News website.
The Guards later said in a statement carried by state TV that a third oil tanker "exploded and caught fire after striking a naval mine south of the Strait of Hormuz."
The tanker "carrying over 2 million barrels of crude oil, had deactivated all of its radar and navigation systems," the statement added.
Iranian forces have, since the outbreak of the Middle East war, repeatedly targeted ships attempting to pass through Hormuz via a southern, U.S.-approved route close to the Omani coast.
President Trump has said on several occasions that the Strait of Hormuz has been cleared of all mines.
Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, on Tuesday told visiting Pakistani army chief Asim Munir that Tehran will not allow nuclear material to leave the country, according to state TV.
"Not even a tiny bit of enriched nuclear material will leave Iran. Such materials constitute a major asset and national wealth for the Iranian people, intended for use within the country," said Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council.
"There will be no negotiations until America takes steps to build trust — a process that must begin with the fulfillment of Iran's conditions."
President Trump has made preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon the administration's top priority.
"They can't have a nuclear weapon," Mr. Trump said Monday night at a rally in Kansas. "OK, and they won't. By the way, somebody said you could leave right now. It's true. We can leave right now. They're not going to have a nuclear weapon."
Iran's envoy to the U.N., Gholamhossein Darzi, sent a letter to United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Tuesday detailing concerns over the potential use of the so-called "Mother of All Bombs" by the United States if the war with Iran restarts after the midterms, according to state-run ISNA news.
"I wish to draw your immediate attention, as well as that of the members of the Security Council, to the recent brazen existential threats made by the President of the United States regarding the possible use of the GBU-43/B bomb, officially known as the Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB), also referred to as the "Mother of All Bombs," against Iran, as well as the renewed threats by the Israeli regime of military aggression and its declared intention to target all of Iran's energy infrastructure," Darzi wrote in his letter, according to state-owned media.
The letter from Darzi asks for Guterres and the head of the U.N. Security Council to convene a meeting and highlights four demands from the 15-country group, which permanently includes the U.S., China, Russia, France and the U.K.
Iran asks for the security council to call upon the U.S. and Israel to end their "unlawful threats" toward Iran; explicitly and unequivocally condemn threats to attack Iran; address threats to regional peace; and ensure accountability and reparations for damage from "wrongful acts committed by the United States and the Israeli regime against Iran."
"Threatening to use the 'MOAB' bomb (the Mother of All Bombs) against Iran's civilian infrastructure and to target all of the country's energy infrastructure constitutes, among other things, a flagrant violation of international law," Darzi wrote.
The Israeli army has no plans to leave southern Lebanon anytime soon and may in fact take over more territory, according to Defense Minister Israel Katz.
"The IDF will not move out of the security zone as long as Hezbollah has not been disarmed throughout Lebanon — and the threat to the residents of the north has not been removed," Katz said on social media.
Katz also threatened to bomb part of Beirut every time an attack drone or missile was launched toward Israeli cities or kibbutzim in the north.
"We are pursuing a determined policy stipulating that any shooting or launch of drones and UAVs toward Israeli cities, moshavim, or kibbutzim will be met with a powerful response against the Dahiyeh district in Beirut," Katz said.
While Katz did say the army was willing to take more than the 700 square kilometers already below the Israeli-designated Yellow Line, it said the army would only do so if there was a coordinated attack from Iran.
"If Hezbollah joins an Iranian attack on Israel, it will be dealt a severe blow, and the IDF is prepared to carry out a ground maneuver into additional areas around Nabatieh and the Litani River," Katz said. "The territory that is captured will be evacuated of its residents, dealt with in the same manner, and permanently made part of Israel's security zone in Lebanon."
Qatar and Pakistan have presented Washington and Tehran with a compromise proposal aimed at preventing renewed escalation and bringing the two sides back to the negotiating table, Qatari outlet Al-Araby Al-Jadeed reported, citing informed sources.
The initiative was met with U.S. approval and a positive response from Iran, the outlet reported.
The proposal was conveyed to Iranian officials by Pakistan's army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, who arrived in Tehran on Tuesday at the head of a delegation of Pakistani officials, according to the report.
The suggested arrangement includes a partial response to Iran's demand for the release of frozen assets. Under the initiative, Iran would receive interest generated by $6 billion in Iranian funds frozen in Qatari banks, the sources said.
In return, Tehran has reportedly agreed to an undisclosed visit by the International Atomic Energy Agency to Iranian nuclear sites, addressing a key U.S. demand concerning Iran's nuclear program.
The sources said a potential breakthrough could be announced this week.
An Iranian military official said Tuesday that Tehran is pursuing legal action over the U.S. torpedo attack on the IRIS Dena warship, arguing the vessel was not a legitimate military target.
In early March, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said a torpedo launched from a U.S. Navy submarine had sunk an Iranian warship in the Indian Ocean "that thought it was safe in international waters."
"Instead it was sunk by a torpedo — quiet death," Hegseth said. It was the first time a U.S. Navy submarine had used a torpedo to sink a warship since 1945.
The strike killed more than 80 Iranian service members.
In an interview with Iranian state TV on Tuesday, Brig. Gen. Moslem Yaghoubi, the Iranian army deputy for legal affairs, said the vessel was an unarmed training ship carrying trainees and that it was hit about 1,200 miles from the battlefield.
"Just this one point is enough to establish that striking it was militarily unnecessary," he said.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in June that Iran was collating documents related to the incident for what state media described as "legal follow-up," but Tehran has not specified a court in which it intends to file its legal action.
Saudi Arabia said Tuesday it had intercepted a drone targeting Riyadh, as well as a missile it previously said was taken down.
Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen, said on X that a drone had also been intercepted and destroyed, without specifying who was believed to have launched it.
The bulletin came after the country's Civil Defense said earlier that people in the Riyadh area should "avoid crowds or going to dangerous areas, and refrain from taking photos" in a post on X , before saying the danger had passed .
Shortly after, Al-Maliki said a ballistic missile launched by the Iran-backed Houthis at Riyadh had been " intercepted and destroyed ."
French President Emmanuel Macron has secured the delivery of an additional 200,000 tons of diesel per month from the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain during a tour of the Persian Gulf, the French presidency said Tuesday.
He obtained commitments for around 100,000 tons per month from the UAE, and an additional 100,000 tons from Bahrain, the French Elysee presidential palace said, according to the AFP news agency.
With the addition of deliveries from Saudi Arabia, France has commitments for 295,000 tons per month, representing just over 10% of its consumption, the statement added.
Macron is undertaking a tour of key energy suppliers in the Gulf in an effort to secure oil and diesel and bring down prices in France after a weekend of violent protests over soaring living costs and other social issues.
The G7 countries, chaired this year by France, agreed in early October to release up to 100 million barrels of oil from their strategic reserves to ease pressure on global fuel supplies amid the U.S.-Iran war.
The shipments for France will be sent overland via Oman, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz, the French presidency said. Experts have questioned whether the deliveries will have an impact on prices in France, however, given the risk of renewed fighting in the region.
Iran's Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces warned Tuesday that Tehran would not wait for the U.S. midterm elections before retaliating to any new U.S. attack.
Maj. Gen. Abdollahi said Iran "has not waited, nor will it wait, for the results of the U.S. congressional elections" to respond to any new attack.
He blamed regional insecurity on the presence of U.S. forces and warned countries hosting American troops to remain vigilant.
"Countries hosting the United States in the region should also know that the main cause of insecurity in the region is the presence of the terrorist U.S. military," he said.
The U.K. government announced Tuesday that it is expanding military support for Saudi Arabia as it faces ongoing attacks by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, including "defensive" air patrols by British Royal Air Force jets over the kingdom.
Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said Royal Air Force Typhoon jets would "conduct defensive counter-air operations over Saudi Arabia, helping to protect Saudi cities, civilian populations and critical national infrastructure from Houthi attack."
He said British planes would not strike Houthi targets in Yemen.
The U.K. will also send a military transport plane and an unspecified number of military advisers to Saudi Arabia, Streeting said.
The announcement follows Britain's decision last month to offer in-air refueling of Saudi planes operating against the Iran-backed rebels. That mission is being extended by another 90 days, Streeting said.
The death toll from a Houthi missile strike on a government military camp in southern Yemen rose to 73 people Tuesday, making it the deadliest strike since fighting in the country began escalating three months ago, a senior Yemeni government official said Tuesday.
The recruits were all aged between 18 and 20, and some were still missing a day after the Iran-backed Houthis hit the al-Alam camp in the southern province of Shabwa with ballistic missiles, according to provincial governor Awad Ibn al-Wazir.
Negotiations between Iran and the United States are ongoing despite rising tension and repeated statements from President Trump that the U.S. could resume major strikes on Iran next month, Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed al-Ansari said Tuesday.
"The negotiation is ongoing. We are seeing engagement from the parties," al-Ansari, who also serves as an adviser to Qatar's prime minister, said at the Global Security Forum in Doha on Tuesday.
Al-Ansari did not offer any further information on the negotiations, including whether there have been any recent direct contacts between Iranian and U.S. officials or if the talks are being conducted entirely via mediators.
He said discussions were continuing with regional partners and expressed hope that diplomatic efforts would eventually lead to an agreement, while cautioning that conditions on the ground were becoming increasingly difficult.
"Escalation left unchecked will mean that we are spiraling towards a regional war that will expand beyond the borders of our region," he warned.
Iran's military said Tuesday morning that it had destroyed another U.S. MQ-9 Reaper drone and attacked two more tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, causing fires on the unnamed ships.
In a statement, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed to have struck and destroyed an MQ-9 drone over the Strait of Hormuz.
At least 24 American MQ-9 Reapers, two MQ-1 drones and an MQ-4C Triton have been lost since the U.S. began its war with Iran, representing a loss of more than $800 million, according to a report released by the Congressional Budget Office in September.
The IRGC also claimed two oil tankers trying to transit the Strait of Hormuz without Iran's permission, using a southern route endorsed by the Trump administration but not recognized by Tehran, were hit by sea mines laid by the IRGC, forcing them to halt due to fires on board.
Iran has routinely targeted vessels in and near the strait for months, challenging Trump administration assertions that the vital shipping lanes are open to commercial traffic and that the U.S. military has complete control of the waterway.
At the end of August, President Trump himself declared the strait mine-free , saying U.S. forces had "totally cleared the strait of mines … Any boat goes through with a mine, we take it out."
The U.S. Navy has also struck vessels in the region as part of its own blockade of Iranian ports and associated vessels.
Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir, a central figure in the country's efforts to mediate between Iran and the U.S., was expected to return for a new visit to Tehran on Tuesday, but Iran played down any hope for new wider peace talks.
Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said talks with Munir "relate to issues concerning the negotiations, but they are mainly focused on bilateral relations and strengthening interactions and cooperation."
The visit comes a day after Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov made his first visit to Tehran since the U.S. launched its war with Iran.
Lavrov said his visit was "aimed at preventing the return of a large-scale war," and he called the U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran illegal.
Saudi forces intercepted a ballistic missile that was targeting the kingdom's capital, a military spokesman said Tuesday, after authorities issued a warning for people in Riyadh to take shelter.
The kingdom "intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh," Turki Al-Malki said in a post on X.
Riyadh has been targeted repeatedly by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen for weeks. Attacks on two major airports, most of them directed at Riyadh's King Khalid International, killed 20 people in one week earlier this month.
The Israeli military accused the Lebanese army on Tuesday of working with the Iran-backed Hezbollah militant group in the country's south.
In a statement, the Israel Defense Forces said the Lebanese army "assisted efforts to prevent, delay, or thwart enforcement operations and enabled Hezbollah to prepare in advance to remove and transfer weapons from the area."
The Israeli military cited a weapons storage "asset" in Kfarra, in southern Lebanon, which it said was identified in December 2025 and flagged to Lebanese forces. The IDF said several months later, Hezbollah was still operating at the site, despite the Lebanese army claiming to have "addressed" it.
The IDF cited a 2024 ceasefire agreement between Israel and Lebanon that called for the Lebanese army to act "against the presence of weapons and military infrastructure belonging to the Hezbollah terrorist organization in southern Lebanon."
Under that agreement, Israel was to begin transferring control of "pilot zones" in the south to Lebanese state forces in July.
The plan faced early issues, with Lebanon accusing Israeli forces of firing at its troops, while Israel said it only fired warning shots.
After a shaky start in late July , President Trump's senior Middle East adviser, Massad Boulos, told reporters "things are progressing" with the pilot zone plan, which he called a "brilliant concept."
There has been little indication of meaningful progress on the transfer of territory occupied by Israeli troops in southern Lebanon - in a "security zone" that stretches about six miles into Lebanese territory - back to Lebanese forces since the summer.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tuesday that Russia and Iran have never worked so closely, as Moscow seeks to present itself as a possible mediator in the Middle East war.
Araghchi hosted his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov in Iran on Monday — the veteran Russian diplomat's first visit to Iran since the U.S. and Israel launched joint strikes on the Islamic republic at the end of February, sparking the war.
"We covered everything from Europe to West Asia, including Lebanon, Palestine, Ukraine and Yemen. Also focused on expansion of economic and nuclear cooperation," Araghchi wrote on X. "Never in our history have Iran and Russia worked as closely as now."
Lavrov said ahead of his visit that Moscow's efforts were "aimed at preventing the return of a large-scale war," with talks stalled between the United States and Iran.
On Sunday, President Trump said in a Truth Social post that "Russia is doing very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran."
Mr. Trump has in recent weeks controversially eased U.S. sanctions against Russia , imposed over Moscow's ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine, in a bid to bring down fuel prices for Americans.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth quietly visited Israel on Monday and met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, according to a senior U.S. military official who spoke to CBS News under condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
The unannounced visit came just over a week before Netanyahu's party faces elections. It also comes as President Trump floats resuming military operations against Iran after next month's U.S. midterm elections.
Hegseth confirmed in an X post that he was in U.S. Central Command's area of responsibility on Monday, sharing a photo of himself addressing American service members who he said were "on a historic mission." He did not specify his location or mention Israel.
The Pentagon declined to comment on the visit.
Axios was first to report Hegseth's visit.
Iran's top security official called for stronger cooperation with Russia to bolster regional security after meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in Tehran on Monday, Iran's state-run IRNA news agency said.
Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said that cooperation could include joint economic projects, such as the completion of transportation corridors. Lavrov, meanwhile, condemned the U.S.-Israeli military attacks on Iran as illegal during his first visit to Iran since the U.S. launched its war with Iran almost eight months ago.
Also in Tehran on Monday, Iran summoned Germany's ambassador over what it called baseless accusations, the Iranian Foreign Ministry said. Germany had summoned Iran's ambassador in Berlin the same day after a court sentenced two men with ties to Iran's intelligence service for plotting to kill the leader of a Jewish organization in Germany.
President Masoud Pezeshkian also said Iran is willing to resolve tensions through dialogue, blaming U.S. interference for divisions in the region, state-run IRNA reported.
Pezeshkian made the remarks during Monday's meeting with Lavrov, saying the presence of U.S. military bases in neighboring countries had only increased tensions, instability and insecurity.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu released a video on Monday of a phone call between him and President Trump, in which the two leaders traded praises and suggested they may again attack Iran together.
Netanyahu shared the call one day after Mr. Trump endorsed his reelection bid. In it, the U.S. president could be heard telling the prime minister on speakerphone: "I think you're going to have a tremendous victory, actually."
"You're the man I want by my side, Bibi," Mr. Trump said, referring to Netanyahu by his nickname.
Netanyahu hailed Mr. Trump for joining Israel in attacking Iran in late February.
"Donald, we have a job to finish," a beaming Netanyahu said. "We'll finish it together. We'll finish it, and no one else will do it."
Netanyahu did not elaborate but again described Iran's clerical state, which remains in power nearly eight months after the joint attack, as "the greatest danger."
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a statement Monday that the group had carried out six military operations in Saudi Arabia over the previous 48 hours, amid a sharp escalation in hostilities between the Iran-backed group and the kingdom.
Saree said the attacks targeted military sites, airports and oil infrastructure, including King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Aramco facilities in Yanbu on the Red Sea coast, and the Shaybah oil field near the border with the United Arab Emirates.
Other strikes hit Abha International Airport, radar installations, Khamis Mushait air base in southwestern Saudi Arabia, a Saudi naval force camp, and a separate radar site in Bir Askar in the kingdom's south, according to Saree.
He described the attacks as retaliation for more than 200 Saudi strikes and missile attacks on Houthi-held areas over the previous 48 hours, saying the Houthis would pursue a policy of "escalation for escalation" until attacks on Yemen cease.
On Sunday, the Houthi-run Health Ministry blamed Saudi-led forces for airstrikes that killed or wounded more than 30 people in Yemen's rebel-held territory over the weekend, including one in the northern province of Saada that left at least nine dead. Five children and two women were among those killed, according to the rebel group.
At least 53 soldiers were killed and another 200 recruits were injured at a military camp on Monday, when Houthi rebels struck Yemeni forces with ballistic missiles, Yemeni military officials said. The targeted camp is in the southern province of Shabwa. The provincial government there also acknowledged the strike, as did the Iran-backed rebel group.
The attack was one of the deadliest since fighting resurged between the Houthis and Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces this summer, as a widening front in the Iran war that began in February.
The provincial government in Shabwa said the death toll from Monday's attack could rise.
"This bloody, treacherous attack targeted new recruits in the training and preparation phase and is considered an extremely critical military escalation and a blatant aggression on the security and stability of Shabwa province," the provincial government said in a statement, which also called on Yemen's president, the Saudi-led coalition and the government to expedite air defense and early warning systems to reinforce Shabwa's capabilities.
The head of Yemen's ruling Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, promised a "firm response" and said the attack reflects the Houthis' "approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter."
One Yemeni military official said the missiles struck while recruits were lining up in formation for a training session. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to the media.
Residents of Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's capital city, received alert messages from authorities on Monday that warned of "a hostile aerial threat." AFP journalists received the alerts, too, which were sent to their phones, according to the outlet.
"A warning has been issued by the National Early Warning Platform in Riyadh City to alert of a potential danger," Saudi Arabia's civil defense agency said in a statement on X. The agency also reported that the same warning had been issued for the nearby Kharj area.
A woman in her thirties living in northern Riyadh said she heard the sound of explosions, telling AFP: "we got used to this."
The warning, which often signals incoming Houthi attacks, was lifted shortly after the defense agency's announcement. But it came as attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis have intensified in Saudi Arabia. Hours later, the Houthis claimed a series of missile and drone attacks on Riyadh's international airport and other targets across the kingdom over the past two days.
A major Saudi investment conference has been postponed to next year, its chief executive officer said on Monday, as the kingdom comes under repeated attacks from Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis.
Maha Al Saud, the CEO of the annual Future Investment Initiative (FII) Institute, said the event, which was scheduled to take place in Riyadh from Oct. 26 to 29, would instead happen in 2027 in a statement posted on X . She said organizers wanted to ensure the gathering's 10th anniversary edition delivered the "full scale" and "extraordinary quality" participants expected.
"This decision comes from a deep commitment to our partners, members, speakers and delegates," her statement said, adding: "A decade of partnership and shared vision deserves nothing less than our absolute best."
New conference dates will be announced soon, while current registrations and partnerships will remain valid, according to the statement.
For nearly a decade, the conference has served as a showcase for Saudi Arabia's efforts to attract global investors, business leaders and heads of state. The postponement dealt a blow to the kingdom's ambitions to draw foreign capital, diversify its oil-reliant economy and push its reform agenda.
Three sources familiar with the matter had earlier told AFP the conference would be postponed.
Egypt's parliament on Monday postponed its debate on President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi's request to authorize military support to Saudi Arabia, which has faced mounting attacks from Yemen's Houthis, Egyptian state media reported. The debate has been delayed until next week, according to the report.
"House Speaker Hisham Badawi has adjourned the second parliamentary session dedicated to discussing authorization for taking necessary measures to support and assist the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, with discussions set to resume on October 26," Egypt's state-run Al-Akhbar newspaper reported.
The postponement concluded a second day of parliamentary sessions in which Egyptian lawmakers weighed Sisi's request to approve support for Saudi Arabia, if requested by the kingdom. An emergency session on Sunday also ended without a decision.
Two lawmakers told AFP on Sunday that most parliamentarians supported the proposal, and a decision wasn't reached during that first session in order to "give all lawmakers the opportunity to speak and express their views."
The Egyptian Social Democratic Party, an opposition party with nearly a dozen seats in parliament, said it had instructed its parliamentary bloc to abstain from voting.
Although it described its solidarity with Saudi Arabia as "firm," the party said any deployment of Egyptian forces abroad should be guided by "specific objectives, clear information" and "an accurate assessment of the potential risks to the lives of our soldiers."
Yemen's Saudi-backed government claimed Monday to have killed 558 Houthi fighters over the past 24 hours. In a post on X , Col. Majed Al-Nazili said Yemeni forces had carried out 1,164 operations against the Iran-backed rebels.
"The operations resulted in neutralizing (558) militia elements, including field commanders," he wrote.
A major Saudi investment conference is set to be postponed, three sources briefed on the matter told the French news agency AFP on Monday, amid repeated attacks on the kingdom by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels .
One source said the event "won't happen on time" and that organizers "won't announce a new date soon." A second source, who confirmed the event would be postponed, told AFP: "Who would be willing to risk flying to Riyadh these days?"
Saudi Arabia's Future Investment Initiative (FII) Institute hosts an annual forum often referred to as "Davos in the desert." The event typically draws foreign leaders and business titans, and this year it is scheduled to be held in Riyadh from Oct. 26 to 29.
The Wall Street Journal reported that the conference would either be held online or postponed.
Iran's top diplomat on Monday accused the United States of being responsible for the insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz that has left the nearly-eight month conflict sparked by joint U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran unresolved, despite the cessation of major military operations.
"The war imposed by the United States and the Zionist regime [Israel], combined with the economic blockade [on Iran's ports], constitutes the principal source of insecurity in our region," said Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, echoing many similar statements by himself and other senior Iranian figures.
He made the remark Monday during a joint news conference with his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov, who arrived in Tehran earlier Monday for his first visit since the outbreak of the war, as Russia tries to frame itself as a potential mediator despite close ties with the Iranian regime.
Lavrov was also scheduled to meet Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian during his visit, according to Russia's foreign ministry. The veteran Russian diplomat said Moscow's efforts were "aimed at preventing the return of a large-scale war," with talks between Tehran and Washington at a standstill.
Iran's Acting Oil Minister Hamid Bovard met Qatar's Minister of State for Energy Affairs, Saad Sherida al-Kaabi, in Doha on Monday to discuss energy relations and cooperation between the two countries.
According to Iran's official news agency IRNA , al-Kaabi confirmed the meeting, which focused on bilateral energy ties and opportunities for cooperation.
The death toll from a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's government-controlled Shabwa province rose to 50 on Monday, a government official told the French news agency AFP, after military sources earlier put the toll at more than 30.
The Iran-backed rebels fired ballistic missiles at the al-Alam military camp in the southern province of Shabwa.
"The death toll has risen to at least 50, with more than 100 people injured, some of them in critical condition," said Fahad al-Khalifi, deputy governor of Shabwa.
He added that hospitals in the province were overwhelmed and had been forced to transfer the most seriously wounded to facilities in neighboring Hadramout and Aden.
Iran-backed Houthi rebels struck a military camp for government forces in southern Yemen on Monday, killing at least 20 soldiers, two Yemeni military officials said.
The rebels fired ballistic missiles at the al-Alam military camp in the southern province of Shabwa in an attack that left at least two dozen more troops wounded, the officials said.
The military officials with the internationally recognized government of Yemen spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to brief the media.
Yemen's decade-long civil war has intensified and become intertwined with the wider regional conflict sparked by the U.S. war with Iran over the last few months, as the Houthis, considered one of Iran's most potent proxy forces, attack the government's Saudi backers on their home turf.
Houthi strikes on Saudi infrastructure, including civilian airports, have killed more than 20 people in recent weeks, and President Trump has said he's considering joining Saudi operations against the rebels. The Houthis have warned that if the U.S. does intervene, it would prompt a "swift and painful" retaliation against U.S. personnel and interests across the region.
Oil prices were down early Monday, with Brent crude, the international standard, falling 2.5% to $107.16 per barrel and benchmark U.S. crude dropping 2.2% to $96.84 per barrel.
The prices fell after President Trump late Friday signed an executive order to put new U.S. sanctions against Russia on hold just days before they were to come into effect, drawing disappointment from Ukraine , with the move likely resulting in more energy exports from Russia.
Mr. Trump's decision came not long after he said earlier this month he had reached a diesel deal with Russia in an attempt to bring down elevated U.S. fuel prices ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
But despite Mr. Trump's controversial efforts to ease energy costs for Americans, oil prices have remained much higher compared to before the Iran war, due in large part to the ongoing risks to the supply chain caused by the crisis in the Middle East .
On Friday the price of Brent crude hit nearly $110 a barrel, its highest level since mid-May.
A tugboat traveling near the Strait of Hormuz was struck by two unknown projectiles, a British maritime monitoring agency said Sunday .
The U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center (UKMTO) said in a statement that a tugboat traveling southbound off the coast of the United Arab Emirates "reported being struck by two unknown projectiles."
"The tug has sustained damage but is continuing on its route," the agency said, "one minor casualty has been reported."
Last week saw 10 attacks on commercial vessels in and near the strait, according to the UKMTO, which said October has already become the worst month for attacks on shipping in the strait since the early days of the war in March.
The U.S. issued a security alert on Monday urging Americans in the Middle East to "exercise heightened vigilance."
"Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," the statement said.
It added that hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly and that groups backed by Iran may target U.S. interests overseas "or at locations associated with the United States and Americans throughout the world."
At least 20 people, including one American, were killed in one week in October when Houthi rebels attacked Saudi airports.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov was expected to pay his first visit to Iran on Monday since the U.S. and Israel sparked the ongoing war with the Islamic Republic by launching joint strikes on Feb. 28.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said Sunday that the two sides would discuss "regional and international developments," while Lavrov said his visit was "aimed at preventing the return of a large-scale war."
Russian President Vladimir Putin told his Iranian counterpart in early October that Moscow was prepared to contribute to mediation efforts.
Iran presented a seven-day ceasefire proposal in late September that called for an end to the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and a return to direct negotiations on Tehran's nuclear program. President Trump rejected the proposal, which Iran says remains on the table.
Conflict raged between the Houthis and the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Iran-backed rebel group on Sunday, as both sides traded strikes.
In Riyadh, where intensifying violence has disrupted life for residents, the landmark Kingdom Centre skyscraper ordered "mandatory" remote working for office tenants until further notice. Although a reason for the order wasn't provided, it followed a security alert and two drone interceptions around the capital city, in addition to a number of attacks by Houthis on Saudi targets in recent weeks.
Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition, which backs the internationally-recognized government in war-wracked Yemen, has launched repeated air raids on regions of the country that Houthis control. One alleged Saudi airstrike in northern Yemen killed at least nine people and wounded 16 others on Sunday, the Houthis' Saba news agency reported.
The coalition said Sunday that two pilots were killed when their helicopter crashed in Najran, near the Yemen border, blaming a "technical malfunction" for the incident. The Houthis said they "downed an Apache helicopter belonging to the Saudi enemy" in the same area.
Iran's foreign minister said Sunday that Tehran's conditions to reopen the Strait of Hormuz have not changed, but that its proposal for a limited ceasefire with the U.S. to reopen the vital waterway remains on the table.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Iran's semi-official Tasnim news agency on Sunday that Tehran is still reviewing "comments" from the U.S. on the Iranian proposal for a seven-day ceasefire that was first presented in September, but rejected by President Trump .
"If they comply with our conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will reopen on the sixth day, and negotiations will begin on the seventh day," Araghchi said, referring to the timeline proposed by Iran, which calls for the U.S. to lift its naval blockade on Iranian ports and to ease sanctions on the country, among other concessions.
"Our conditions are fair, and if the United States is willing to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, it can meet them within a few days," Araghchi said.

title: The AI doom scenario you've never heard of may be the hardest to stop
description: The time to prepare for "gradual disempowerment" is now, according to researchers. One calls it "a civilization-scale problem."
content: It seems that almost daily, a big tech company releases a new AI-driven digital assistant. Muse by Meta, Gemini by Google, dots by OpenAI. By the time this article is published, a new one from [insert tech company here] will probably have a press release touting its ability to manage your work and life — to take things off your plate, automate your processes, speed up your tedious tasks. It sounds helpful and, to lower the bar, harmless. But some researchers say this is the beginning of a treacherous path for humankind, one where bots take more and more off our plate until all that's left is an empty vessel, and we human users become nothing more than thoughtless "approvers." It's not just a threat to jobs. They warn that allowing our skills and knowledge to deteriorate, and surrendering our critical thinking to AI, poses an existential danger to humanity.One term for this path is "gradual disempowerment" — a scenario where AI displaces human labor in the economy, replaces human decision-making in all key societal concerns, erodes human creativity, and degrades human cognition along the way. And though the word "gradual" is in the name, that does not mean the problem is something to worry about far in the future, according to experts. "I put gradual disempowerment on the very top of my list," said Jay Chooi, the founder and CEO of Robocurve, a company that tracks and measures AI-driven robotics capabilities. Chooi believes gradual disempowerment is just as worrisome as the threat of engineered pandemics and more destructive cyberattacks, which could be accelerated by capable AI."It's a civilization-scale problem," Chooi said of gradual disempowerment. "A lot of people feel very powerless, because it requires a lot of effort and a whole-of-society approach to solve it."What is "gradual disempowerment" and how could AI cause it?The term "gradual disempowerment" stems from a paper published in early 2025.At the heart of the gradual disempowerment scenario is AI technology continuing to advance in capabilities, as it has rapidly since the launch of ChatGPT in 2022. AI models may soon be better at nearly all cognitive tasks than humans — solving frontier math problems, doing hard science, coding, writing and creating art and music, to name a few of the areas where AI increasingly excels. At the same time, advances in robotics could lead to AI-powered robots performing better than humans at physical labor like packing boxes, constructing homes, building cars, painting murals, mining for rare minerals, and even building IKEA furniture. We like to think that in an ideal world, the best applicant generally gets the job, and they are paid based on the level of demand for their skills. But imagine if a human is never the best person for the job. That's a world that some AI prognosticators and whistleblowers expect.It's a world where an AI agent or AI-enabled robot is better at every task and sub-task that it takes to do my job and your job. They move faster than us, think deeper, have more patience and stamina. They more cordially answer phones, do more thorough research, and more dexterously wield a scalpel or a nail file. Plus, they never need to sleep or take sick days, they never show up hungover or moody, and they never threaten to leave for a better job. To picture gradual disempowerment more clearly, here's a scenario: Let's say you run Hammer Co., a company that manufactures hammers. You have line workers who shape the steel heads and wooden handles and then fit them together, and managers who keep the factory running smoothly. You have people who maintain your supply chain and teams to handle marketing, sales, accounting, and all the other functions that help your business thrive.But then a tech company comes out with AI-powered Hammer Bots. The robot workers can make hammers far faster than your human workers, while AI agents can run the business side with little oversight. They'll work all night, never make mistakes, and cost far less than your happy, well-paid staff. You don't want to fire your human workers. You see them around town and have known their families for years, after all. But your competitor gets the Hammer Bots. Most customers just want the cheapest hammers — they don't care who or what makes them. As CEO of Hammer Co. you either compete or die. So you fire all your humans and get Hammer Bots to replace them. Now, try to envision this is the case for every company, and every job. With normal free-market incentives, the company that stays loyal to its human employees will be outcompeted by the company that gets AI to do the work instead. Here's where gradual disempowerment comes into play.The fewer humans that participate in labor, and the more work that's outsourced to AI agents, the more humanity becomes dependent on AI for decision-making and the more human skills deteriorate. How long until the finer points of hammer-making will be forgotten?With AI making all our complex decisions for us, humans become less capable of understanding and overseeing those decisions or of pushing back against them. "If people aren't actually practicing the skills that the agents are doing for them, they lose the ability to have that skill, and so now you become reliant," said Margaret Mitchell, an AI research scientist at Hugging Face and co-author of another recent paper on the importance of keeping humans in the loop in an AI world. "What happens when something goes wrong? There's no human you can point to who can fix it. So now you've become fully dependent on these systems to fix themselves, and what if that's not possible?"A risk to democratic governanceIt's not just economics and labor at risk. Take the military, for example. All or most decisions in war involve humans today, even if AI contributes to the process, but the balance is likely to shift as the technology becomes more capable. If the United States uses AI to make decisions in battle, its enemies across the field will be pressured to do the same. The side that leans more heavily on humans will be slower and less efficient. Human soldiers need food and rest. Robot soldiers will not. Human decision-makers are limited in the scenarios they can conceive and plan for; AIs can take into account all of human knowledge. "The states need citizens. They need us because we pay taxes and we fight for the states in the military," said Jan Kulveit, a co-author of the gradual disempowerment paper and co-founder of ACS Research Group. States also use people to enforce laws. But what if law enforcement is all automated in the future? "If, or when, existing states don't need their citizens, they're less likely to be democratic," said Kulveit. Kulveit compares theoretical future countries that are mostly run by AI to oil states today. He said the oil states tend to be authoritarian because they don't rely on most of their citizens to pay taxes and don't need citizens' votes to rule. States that rely on AI to run the economy and military could have similar outcomes, said Kulveit. If that is the case, and citizens no longer are the backbone of labor or warfare in a world of gradual disempowerment, then humans lose perhaps their greatest leverage against those in power.
