"A lot of people are talking about rogue AI hacking into data centers and taking over the world, but it is not in the mainstream consciousness that like AI could literally take over the world just by continuing to do what it's supposed to do, which is automating everything," said Jay Chooi of Robocurve."Organizations are all going to have a very strong economic pressure, and political pressure, to phase out humans and move work more and more into robots or AI."How does humanity avoid gradual disempowerment?Humans ceding control to AI, say the gradual disempowerment authors, is almost a natural transition once very advanced AI is here. Gradual disempowerment "does not need to emerge from a deliberate scheme or powergrab by AI systems," wrote Kulveit and his colleagues. "In the short-term, it is being incentivized by the perceived value that AI systems can bring to economic, cultural and state functions.""We can't be in the situation where we are competing with the machines," said Kulveit. "Because if we are just competing with the machines, we will probably lose."The gradual disempowerment authors believe stopping our disempowerment may be a heavy lift for humanity, since it involves complex systems that feed into each other — government, culture, and the economy. "This may be a bigger challenge than merely preventing AI systems from pursuing overtly harmful goals," they write. One first step in slowing disempowerment is keeping indicators of how much work is being ceded to AI, and of what kind of specific jobs AI systems are capable of handling. If thousands of workers are being displaced by AI in, say, call center jobs, it helps to know that in granular detail. But measurement isn't enough without action, Mitchell said. She argues that removing humans from the loop in AI processes both worsens oversight and degrades the skills of the human overseer. Therefore, companies and leadership in all fields must take proactive steps to keep humans engaged. "This general practice within tech is we want our systems to be frictionless," said Mitchell, referring to the idea that everything should move fast and without obstacles. "There's this sense that the less friction the better, but there's been a push within the more ethical AI community that strategic friction can be good because it can draw people's attention to critical issues that otherwise they might overlook."Mitchell argues that strategic friction — keeping humans in the work loop at predetermined steps — can be done both by developers of AI, companies like OpenAI and Anthropic and Google, and by companies and organizations that deploy AI. Thoughtful and purposeful design of AI can benefit society as a whole, and the individuals who use it. Kulveit agrees that AI should be thoughtfully designed to add value to humans, not necessarily replace our every task. "You want to carve out places where we agree that we will not allow competitive pressures to remove humans from the loop," he said. "It would be nice if the companies train the AIs to be more complementary to humans. Currently, the AIs are implicitly trained to be a replacement for humans. But you can imagine training the AIs so they are better at explaining to us what's happening." Kulveit is describing AI that doesn't just spew out the answers to whatever question you ask it, at the very least in sectors where it is critical to include human expertise and decision-making, like war. Quick and easy answers can be helpful, but they can also make you dependent and credulous, believing anything the chatbot tells you, whether right or wrong. But AI can be more than that. It can help you not just by doing the work for you, but by educating you along the way. That way the human worker continues to learn while using AI as a partner, not a substitute. "There has been such a singular focus on capability or functionality of these systems to the detriment of people, to the detriment of users," said Mitchell. "If your only goal is to get a high score on a benchmark, then you are not going to be taking into account cognitive support design. But if your goal is to make a system that works really well for people — like if the race is for a utility as opposed to benchmark score — then you end up designing fundamentally different systems."If gradual disempowerment really is a large-scale risk, compared to more talked-about doom scenarios — like AI helping to design bioweapons or chemical weapons — it may suffer from a relative lack of vividness. "We know what it means for a robot to take over the world. We know what it means for countries to nuke each other," said Chooi. "AI taking over the world is very legible in the human consciousness. But gradual disempowerment? No one has made a movie about gradual disempowerment."But to Chooi, gradual disempowerment is very easy to picture. "All the organizations have the incentives to adopt it and phase out humans," he said. "This is a very logical conclusion. It's not very hard to see it."

title: Michigan umpire accused of possessing, distributing child pornography
description: A Waterford man who worked as a local umpire for youth sports is accused of possessing and distributing child pornography, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office.
content: A Waterford man who worked as a local umpire for youth sports is accused of possessing and distributing child pornography, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office.Kevin Cathcart, 57, appeared in federal court on Monday under a criminal complaint. A judge ordered for Cathcart to be detained. Federal prosecutors say Cathcart was an umpire, including at Little League baseball games organized through the Waterford Coaches Association, and volunteered for youth hockey. Officials are unaware of allegations of misconduct connected to Cathcart's positions in Little League or youth hockey.Cathcart is due back in court for a preliminary examination on Oct. 29.Anyone with information

title: Ambulance response times in NYC before city council: "A huge crisis in EMS," union says
description: Lawmakers on Tuesday heard from FDNY members, health officials and residents regarding concerns over ambulance response times across New York City.
content: A New York City Council hearing on Tuesday focused on ambulance response times in the five boroughs as concerns about delays grow.The Committee on Fire and Emergency Management and the Committee on Hospitals held the joint oversight hearing.Lawmakers looked at disparities in borough-specific response times. They also got information from the FDNY about allocation of EMS resources for ambulance availability and paramedic staffing. Representatives from the FDNY, NYC Health + Hospitals Emergency Management and members of the public testified. Many say delays in ambulances are due to staff shortages, closures of hospitals and a growing number of patients with complex needs.Michael Greco, the president of a union representing EMTs, paramedics and fire inspectors, said there has been an "insane jump in response times over the past 10 years.""Currently, we're responding to cardiac arrests north of 14 minutes, so it's a huge crisis in EMS," he said. "If we had a system that responded to every 911 call in a seven or eight-minute response time, we would be saving hundreds of lives a year, and that's what we're trying to make people understand." Vincent Variale, the president of the Uniformed EMS Officers Union, also weighed in."We need support and funding from the mayor's office and city council to provide the funding needed to get the people on the job to get the staffing that's needed," Variale said.During the hearing, city officials also considered legislation about emergency notifications. If passed, it would require the city's emergency management to issue notifications each time FDNY-EMS has more than 25 pending ambulance dispatches.

title: Knicks look to defend championship title as season begins with MSG banner-raising ceremony
description: The Knicks will mark their season opener as NBA champions on Tuesday night at Madison Square Garden with a banner-raising ceremony before their matchup against the 76ers.
content: The New York Knicks will mark their season opener as NBA champions on Tuesday night at Madison Square Garden with a banner-raising ceremony before their matchup against the Philadelphia 76ers.The banner will go up to the rafters before the tipoff at 7 p.m.Last season's historic playoff run culminated with the Knicks defeating the San Antonio Spurs in Game 5 of the NBA Finals, clinching their first championship in 53 years. The team then spent the summer celebrating.This season, starting five Jalen Brunson, Karl-Anthony Towns, Josh Hart, Mikal Bridges and OG Anunoby will be looking to build on the chemistry that helped the team capture the Larry O'Brien Trophy. "People say we're defending the title, I mean, that's one way to look at it, but it's something we've won. We've put it in our past, and now we're just trying to attack another," Brunson said.But first, they have to get through revamped Philadelphia.The Knicks swept the 76ers out of the playoffs in June. On Tuesday night, they will look for another win against the team that has added LeBron James to the picture.The 76ers handled the Knicks in the preseason 120-97, and they did it without some key players, including James, who signed with Philly as a free agent over the summer."Wherever Bron went [in] the East, I figured that would probably be our opening night," Hart said. "Getting the ring, hanging the banner, that would be dope, but also excited to kind of move on from it.""The energy in the city the last few days even has picked up. Everybody I run into has been talking about it. The excitement from everybody will be palpable," Landry Shamet said.Hart said he knows the banner is about last season, and the Knicks have to show they can do it again."Obviously, 53 years. Multiple generations of fans are gonna be there to witness this. We want them to have as much fun as physically and humanly possible," Hart said.Demand is high for the opener considering the banner-raising, the first game of the new season at the Garden, and the star power on the 76ers. Ticket prices were going for more than $2,000 per seat on Tuesday afternoon, CBS News New York's Otis Livingston reported."I mean, it's hard, because they're human, and there's a part of you that wants to keep celebrating, but you know, you've got to turn it off," Knicks coach Mike Brown said.There will also be a series of commemorative elements at MSG honoring the Knicks and fans who witnessed it.In addition to the banner-raising, the Knicks players will get their championship rings, but so will some others. Team owner James Dolan promised rings to the players' significant others as well, highlighting that the support and sacrifices of the players' partners during last season's playoffs were vital to securing the title."It's really cool that Jim did that. They make huge sacrifices, too. Not just during the playoffs, but the whole year," Hart said, adding with a laugh, "As long as my ring is bigger than hers."A Defining Moments exhibit will be on the sixth-floor concourse in sections 103-104. It will have game-worn jerseys, game-used items, newspaper clippings, and pieces from the championship parade, among other things.Two moments will also be added to the "Garden 366" display, including the team's 22-point fourth-quarter comeback to defeat the Cleveland Cavaliers in overtime during Game 1 of the Eastern Conference finals. The other moment is Anunoby's game-winning tip-in against the Spurs during Game 4 of the Finals."Even though our team lived it on the court, the city was just as much a part of this as we were. Being able to put these pieces in front of the fans is one way of saying thank you," Brunson said in a statement. "The Championship belongs to them as well, and we are excited to play for them at The Garden this season."Fans will also have the opportunity to see and take pictures of the Larry O'Brien Trophy, which will be in Chase Square starting Wednesday, and the Empire State building will be lit up in orange and blue to commemorate the opener.Fans were pumped up for the banner-raising."It's always going to be an honor and privilege to see and watch them play because the Knicks got so much rich history," one person said."Tonight, they finally get their rings and the banner goes up into the rest. It's about time. Should have been up there, but it's never too late," another fan said.

title: University of Miami football player shares racist, threatening messages made by Florida Bar employee
description: The Florida Bar says the messages violate its social media policy, and Wilson's teammates said they are standing by him.
content: A University of Miami football victory was overshadowed after defensive lineman Damon Wilson shared racist, homophobic, and threatening direct messages he received on social media following Saturday's double-overtime win over rival Florida State.Wilson posted the messages under the caption "Glimpse into the life of a black student-athlete," revealing a rant that included racial slurs, gay slurs, and violent threats.The sender was identified as a Florida State graduate working in the technology department for the Florida Bar. The organization subsequently placed the employee on administrative leave."The messages are not only ethically and morally reprehensible but violate our internal social media policy," the Florida Bar said in a statement. "…we are committed to enforcing our policies and procedures while making sure due process rights are protected."Wilson's teammates rallied to his support during a session with reporters."He's my brother, so anything he needs, we will be there for him," said tight end Elijah Lofton.Teammate Chase Smith added, "We gotta keep focused. Block out noise, whether bad or good."

title: ICE interaction with North Bergen, N.J. teenager unnerves elected officials, residents
description: A New Jersey community is demanding answers after a high school student was questioned by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents on his way to school.
content: A New Jersey community is demanding answers after a high school student was questioned by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents on his way to school.Department of Homeland Security officials say he was an adult and was being questioned during an investigation.A young woman walking her dog recording video of ICE agents surrounding North Bergen High School student George Castillo on Monday morning as he sat and waited for a friend to walk to school."I was like so confused as to what was going on because this is probably the second time this happened to me," Castillo said.Castillo, who says he's 19, spoke CBS News New York about his encounter."I was like just act normal and try not to talk too much, and they they came to me and asked me if I was American," Castillo said.Gloria Estrada, the university student capturing the moment, said she pushed record because Castillo is her neighbor."I was scared, but I knew what was right and what is wrong," Estrada said. "They stereotyped him for being, looking Hispanic, and it wasn't right what they're doing."DHS said agents briefly spoke to Castillo, who is an adult, during a targeted operation that resulted in the arrest of "nine illegal aliens with criminal histories, including assault and abuse of a child."DHS also blasted initial reports Castillo was a minor, adding, "Allegations that ICE questioned minors or targeted schools are false."Democratic state Assemblymember Gabriel Rodriguez said minor or not, he wants ICE out of this community."The image of three masked agents approaching a child who is going to school, making him sit down or having him sit down, surrounding him, sets a tone of fear in our community," Rodriguez said.North Bergen officials have been holding seminars and passing out fliers to let residents know about their rights if they're stopped by ICE, including the right to remain silent."Everybody is scared about this and we're all concerned about it," North Bergen Commissioner Hugo Cabrera said.One mother said she worries about her son, who looks older."You always have your ID. You don't need to speak to a weird person. Just call. 'I need to talk to my mom,'" Bernice Escobar said."I say that people shouldn't be afraid of these people because they are just people trying to scare you," Castillo added.DHS also said agents will not abide by what it calls unconstitutional mask mandates in New Jersey, and will continue to wear face coverings to protect themselves against threats and agitators.

title: What to know about Jalen Hurts' condition after blood clots found in Eagles star's lungs, leg
description: Jalen Hurts' agent and the Eagles said in a statement Monday his "prognosis is very good, and we anticipate a full recovery."
content: Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts, a Super Bowl champion and one of the NFL's top stars, is now facing a long absence because of blood clots in his lungs — and his team is facing serious questions over his medical treatment.Hurts' agent, Nicole Lynn, and the Eagles said in a statement Monday his "prognosis is very good, and we anticipate a full recovery."The condition can be life-threatening, and the Eagles say Hurts could miss the rest of the season. However, Hurts was cleared to play a week ago in London after a blood clot was found in his leg. He threw for 222 yards and a touchdown, but the Eagles lost to the Jacksonville Jaguars, 19-17. Just one day earlier, he was diagnosed with a superficial blood clot in his left calf and ordered by doctors to stay awake overnight, according to NFL insiders, who report the quarterback did not sleep for roughly 36 hours. After being released from the hospital, he was reportedly given some time to rest before taking the field against the Jaguars.The NFL in a statement Tuesday disputed that reporting, calling it "misinformation" that Hurts did not sleep for 36 hours before the Oct. 11 game. "That was not true and no one told him not to sleep because of his situation," NFL spokesman Brian McCarthy said. "The club told all players, coaches and personnel to try to stay awake as long as they could on Saturday as the team was returning back home after the game in London. The team did not have a bye week and like other NFL teams that travel to London and back, they were trying maintain as much of a normal routine as possible."Since then, the diagnosis has worsened. The star quarterback is now facing deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli with blood clots in his left leg and both lungs, the team and his agent said.Deep vein thrombosis, also known as DVT, refers to a condition when a blood clot develops in the deep veins, usually in the lower extremities, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. A pulmonary embolism, or PE, is the term for when the clot breaks off and travels to the lungs, which can be life-threatening, the CDC says."You have a clot in your leg. The problem is it can travel up the veins and go to your heart, and from there, go to your lungs, and block the blood vessels in your lungs. And you get things called pulmonary emboli. That's very serious," CBS News chief medical correspondent Dr. Jon LaPook, who is not treating Hurts, told "CBS Mornings."Whether it could be career-ending, LaPook said, it's "too soon to know.""Normally what you do is you would treat this with blood thinners for three months and then sort of see what happens," he continued. "Now, they're going to follow him closely. It may be more than that, and then after that, you take them off the blood thinners."LaPook said Hurts' doctors would then likely test his blood to see if there is an issue that increases the risk of clotting.The revelation of the diagnosis is sparking backlash against the Eagles and its medical staff.Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni did not answer Monday why the quarterback was allowed to play in London or fly back with the team to the U.S. after the game."I'm not a medical expert. I lean on our guys in all those situations, right? I'm a football coach," he said. "I lean on our medical experts in every situation. I have full trust and full faith in them."McCarthy in his statement Tuesday said that the NFL has "been in contact throughout the process with the Eagles medical personnel, and the Cleveland Clinic in London where the tests were conducted."The National Football League Players Association, the union which represents the players, is demanding the league conduct a "full investigation into what occurred." An NFLPA spokesperson told CBS News in a statement Tuesday night that it was "not aware of any NFL investigation into the medical care provided to Jalen Hurts," adding that the league had "previously informed the union that it did not plan to review the care he received."Flying could be a concern, doctor saysA main question from fans is whether flying to London, or flying back, could have exacerbated the injury. LaPook said it's possible it could be an issue."In flying, you can get dehydrated, you're not moving around a lot," so your blood doesn't return to your heart as well, LaPook said. "When he got there (to London), they did a test, and they found this superficial thrombophlebitis, so a little clot, and they ... clear him to play. He ended up playing, and then right after the game, he flew back."The fact Hurts did not sleep much was not as big a concern as the flying, LaPook said."Well, the bigger point to me is not the not sleeping, it's the fact that he had a flight there, a flight back within a few days," he said. "That increases the risk of blood clot in the first place. We tell people when they're on flights to walk around, maybe wear compression stockings."The CDC makes similar warnings about flying."Extended periods of limited mobility are inherent to long-distance travel and can increase a traveler's risk for VTE," according to the agency. "An association between VTE and air travel was first reported in the early 1950s; since then, long-distance air travel has become more common, leading to increased concerns about travel-associated VTE."Different organizations offer different guidance on how soon someone with DVT should fly, but they are significantly longer than the time it took for Hurts to fly back to the U.S.The International Air Transport Association says if a person is stable, they should wait at least five days before a flight, while the British Thoracic Society advises someone with DVT or PE should wait two weeks before flying."Over the last few days, Jalen Hurts has received comprehensive medical evaluations by physician experts," the Eagles and Hurts' agent said in the statement announcing his long-term absence.For now, the Eagles will wait three months to see how the condition is improving with blood thinners."We anticipate that he will have the opportunity to resume contact football activities when off the blood thinners," the statement said. "In the meantime, he will remain active around the team and continue to condition. More importantly, we anticipate that he will have no long-term effects. "We are thinking of Jalen and looking forward to a strong recovery."

title: Delaware County voters to decide on $120 million open space borrowing proposal
description: Delaware County voters will decide whether to allow the county to borrow up to $120 million for land conservation projects.
content: Voters in Delaware County, Pennsylvania, will decide Nov. 3 whether to allow the county to borrow up to $120 million for land conservation projects.The referendum has drawn support from environmental advocates who believe it would protect natural resources and curb development, and opposition from those concerned about the cost and potential impact on housing.County officials said conservation projects could protect drinking water sources, improve water quality in rivers and creeks, preserve wildlife habitats, conserve trees and wetlands, create greenways and parks and safeguard natural areas from development.Jaclyn Rhoads, president of the Darby Creek Valley Association, supports the referendum. Rhoads said open space benefits communities in multiple ways."It maintains the community character and protects our drinking water," Rhoads said. "Not only that, it increases property values. It prevents pollution that we would have had to pay for later with increased wastewater bills."Delaware County has already invested in open space. In 2021, County Council purchased a 213-acre wooded property at the former Don Guanella School in Marple Township. The county plans to transform the site into Delco Woods, a park with paved hiking paths, mountain bike trails and a dog park.Council member Elaine Schaefer said last year that the project would cost $50 million. The county plans to seek grants to cover the cost, but it remains unclear whether any money from the proposed borrowing could go toward Delco Woods."Our natural resources are not just pretty things to look at and enjoy," Schaefer said. "They perform really important environmental services that keep quality of life in our communities high."The Delaware County Republican Party opposes the referendum, citing concerns about a potential property tax increase. The county estimates that borrowing the full $120 million would cost the average household about $24 a year."We give an inch and they take a mile," Michael Straw, chairman of the Media Borough Republican Committee, said. "I don't think it's appropriate to necessarily shoulder the burden of acquiring green space on the entire county, when there are specific areas within this county that don't have green space left to preserve."The home-building industry has also raised concerns, arguing that preserving additional land could leave less room for new single-family homes, townhouses, condos and apartments."When you conserve a piece of property, supply and demand don't suspend themselves," Joseph Viscuso, a spokesperson for the Home Builders Association of Chester and Delaware Counties, said. "We have a shortage of about 5 million affordable homes. And when I say affordable, I'm talking about nurses, teachers, police officers. Affordable housing is a crisis in the U.S. today."Some of the money would be distributed through the Green Ways Grants Program, which invests in parks and trails throughout the county. The referendum could shape the county's landscape for years to come.

title: Pennsylvania man stole more than $118,000 from relative, officials say
description: Ronald Palicka is accused of stealing more than $100,000 from a relative.
content: A man from Westmoreland County is accused of stealing more than $110,000 from a relative's financial accounts. Ronald Palicka is facing theft, access device fraud, and receiving stolen property charges in connection with the incident, according to a news release from the Westmoreland County District Attorney's Office. According to the news release, police said Palicka moved money from the victim's account into his own personal accounts to pay various bills and subscriptions, including Chewy, cable TV, Apple, Omaha Steaks, and Advanced Auto. The district attorney's office said the man from Jeannette stole more than $118,000 from the victim's accounts. The district attorney's office said the investigation began after the North Huntingdon Township Police Department was contacted by the victim's grandson, who reported that a relative had been taking money from the victim's bank account for years. Police obtained documentation and bank statements detailing transactions dating back to December 2023, and investigators also learned that Palicka was assigned power of attorney for the victim in 2011, the district attorney's office said. The news release said investigators were provided a check made out to Palicka for $12,000 from the victim's account in 2021, though police believe the thefts began as early as July 2020. Online court records show Palicka is due back in court later this month for his preliminary hearing. He was taken to the Westmoreland County Jail, but later posted his $125,000 bail, according to online court records.

title: One critically injured after Texas DPS pursuit ends in crash on I-30 in Fort Worth, authorities say
description: The crash happened Tuesday evening along westbound Interstate 30 near Las Vegas Trail.
content: A pursuit involving the Texas Department of Public Safety ended in a crash Tuesday evening on westbound Interstate 30 near Las Vegas Trail in Fort Worth, leaving one person critically injured, officials said.The crash happened around 6:40 p.m., according to authorities.Fort Worth police referred questions about the incident to DPS. A DPS spokesperson said details about the pursuit and crash were not immediately available, but the agency was working to gather additional information.Fort Worth Fire EMS confirmed that one person was taken to a local hospital in critical condition.Authorities have not released details about what prompted the pursuit, how many vehicles were involved in the crash, or the identity of the injured person.CBS News Texas will provide updates as more information becomes available.

title: Cornell responds to Jane Doe's letter saying she felt disbelieved, unsupported by school president
description: Cornell has denied claims made in a letter from a former student, known as Jane Doe, about a remark by the school's president.
content: The former Cornell student known as Jane Doe has sent a letter to the school saying she "felt unsupported and disbelieved" by the university's president, Michael Kotlikoff, after she accused multiple men of sexually assaulting her at a fraternity house in 2024. In a statement Tuesday, Cornell disputed her account of Kotlikoff's comments. The letter, obtained by CBS News, was sent earlier this month to Cornell's Faculty Senate as it considers a no-confidence vote in Kotlikoff's administration. In the letter, Jane Doe describes what she calls "a second-hand account" of a conversation between Kotlikoff and the then-president of Cornell's Tri Delta sorority chapter."After the conversation she shared with me, with concern, that President Kotlikoff's initial response was along the lines of, 'Why did she wait so long to report it?'" wrote Jane Doe in the letter. "She interpreted his question as an expression of doubt in the veracity of my story." Jane Doe reported the alleged assault to campus police on Nov. 8, 2024, about three weeks after she said it took place at the Chi Phi fraternity house.The university said in its statement Tuesday that her description of Kotlikoff's comment in the letter is "incorrect, based on a documented first-hand account.""The question 'why did it take so long for the assault to be reported' was directed at bystanders who did not use Cornell's anonymous tip line, despite ongoing social media activity about the incident in October 2024," Cornell said. "He was not questioning Jane Doe's reporting." In her one-page letter, Jane Doe wrote that hearing of the comment "diminished my confidence in the administration's ability to approach my experience with the understanding, sensitivity, and fairness I had hoped for and expected from what had been my dream school."She added, "I am sharing this account now because, to my knowledge, only a few individuals are aware of the conversation; I do not know if you or other members of the Faculty Senate are among them."In a statement provided to CBS News on Tuesday regarding the letter, Jane Doe's attorney said, "Jane Doe, through counsel, provided a statement to the Dean of Faculty and Speaker of the Faculty Senate regarding her understanding of comments made by President Kotlikoff in the presence of one of her sorority sisters and one or more faculty members. The letter was sent for informational purposes only. Jane Doe thought it important that the faculty senate have this information as it deliberates and considers the resolutions or motions before it. Jane Doe would ask the faculty senate to give her letter whatever weight or credibility it deems appropriate." How Cornell and its leadership handled Jane Doe's original report of the alleged assaults is one of the issues raised in the civil lawsuit she filed last month against the university, the Chi Phi fraternity and seven of its then-members, and others including her sorority at the time, Delta Delta Delta.CBS News has reached out to the seven former fraternity members. All have denied wrongdoing. None of them has been charged with a crime.In a court filing Tuesday, a former president of the Chi Phi fraternity was dropped from her lawsuit. His attorney, Eric Bernstein, told CBS News in a statement that his client wasn't serving as president of the fraternity at the time of the alleged assault."We're not validating or commenting on the charges or the allegations themselves but they had the wrong guy here. We're happy with the outcome," Bernstein said in the statement.

title: Parents charged with child endangerment in Garden Grove teen electric motorcycle death
description: Vu Thanh Nguyen of Santa Ana has been charged with one felony count of child endangerment and one misdemeanor count of contributing to the delinquency of a minor for buying his son the powerful electric motorcycle.
content: The parents of a 13-year-old boy who died after he lost control while riding his electric motorcycle in Garden Grove earlier this year have both been charged with child endangerment, the Office of the District Attorney of Orange County announced.Benson Nguyen was riding his electric motorcycle at speeds over 40 mph when he crashed into a concrete light pole on May 7. According to the DA's Office, Nguyen was seen speeding, running red lights and doing wheelies on the street shortly before he lost control. He was transported to a local hospital, where he died.The 13-year-old "was repeatedly injured while riding a different electric vehicle, including breaking his leg just six months before he died," the DA's Office said. His father, Vu Thanh Nguyen of Santa Ana, has been charged with one felony count of child endangerment and one misdemeanor count of contributing to the delinquency of a minor for buying his son the powerful electric motorcycle.Prosecutors said Vu Thanh Nguyen had been warned multiple times about his son's reckless riding.The boy's mother, Hong Cuc Thi Nguyen, 49, of Santa Ana, has been charged with one misdemeanor count of child endangerment."When parents refuse to hold their children accountable and that refusal to parent results in unspeakable tragedy, then I have no choice but to hold parents accountable," OC DA Todd Spitzer said in a news release.According to prosecutors, Benson posted videos of himself doing leg switches and wheelies on his electric motorcycle to social media. The E-Ride Pro SS 2.0 E-Moto ridden by Benson was classified as a motor-driven cycle under CVC section 405 or a motorcycle under CVC section 400. Both classifications require a valid motorcycle license for street operation, as well as DMV registration, license plate, insurance and full motorcycle equipment.California law distinguishes between e-bikes and e-moto based on three main features: the power limit of its motor, its maximum speed limit, and whether it is equipped with operable pedals.In May, Spitzer announced the creation of a new e-bike/e-moto unit to review potential criminal charges against juveniles and adults, including parents who knowingly allow their children to ride e-motos and e-bikes illegally.This followed a spike in deaths attributed to the electric bicycles and motorcycles, including a 15-year-old boy who was riding on an e-moto with a friend in La Habra, a 21-year-old who died five days after crashing an e-bike in Huntington Beach, and an 81-year-old man who was hit and killed by a 14-year-old illegally riding an e-moto.Vu Nguyen faces a maximum sentence of six years in state prison if convicted on all charges and Hong Nguyen faces a maximum sentence of one year in county jail if convicted.

title: Minnesota governor's race ads fact check: Demuth, Klobuchar at odds on ICE surge, fraud
description: A DFL Party ad on the ICE surge doesn't mention that Demuth also blamed "high-level local decisions" for inflaming the situation. WCCO checks that ad and another in the governor's race.
content: A DFL Party ad attacking Republican House Speaker Lisa Demuth leaves out part of what she said about the deaths of two Minnesota residents during the ICE surge. It's one of two ads in Minnesota's governor's race that WCCO looked at for facts and context, with about two weeks until Election Day.The ad says Demuth praised President Trump and Kristi Noem on the ICE surge, and that the deaths of two Minnesota residents were "the cost of it."What the ad doesn't mention is that Demuth said in the Star Tribune: "But it was local decisions, high-level local decisions that inflamed the entire situation."Republican analyst Amy Frederiksen said the ad is "completely unfair" because it makes it sound as if Demuth is shrugging off the deaths as the cost of doing business. "It's not believable," she added.The same ad says Demuth said Mr. Trump's health care cuts were good for Minnesota, even as they drive up costs and put nursing homes at risk. Demuth did say that. She agrees with Republican arguments that the cuts are important to reduce waste, curb fraud and make sure taxpayer aid goes to qualified applicants.But federal cuts have increased costs for states, and Medicaid reimbursements no longer cover what they used to, contributing to some nursing facilities closing.A second ad claims Sen. Amy Klobuchar has no plan on fraud. That's not true, according to Andy Luger, a Klobuchar supporter and former U.S. attorney. Asked whether Klobuchar has a plan to address fraud, Luger said, "I think she's got the plan." Her plan is also featured on her website. Prior WCCO reporting said it includes an audit of state agencies starting "on day one," blocking payments to anyone convicted of fraud and stronger criminal penalties.Luger also disputes the ad's claim that Klobuchar did nothing on fraud. He said she delivered on getting more prosecutors after Feeding Our Future, the pandemic-era scheme prosecutors have described as a $250 million fraud, and that his office ended up with the largest award of any U.S. attorney's office in the country.Political ads average 30 seconds, which isn't much time to make a point. That's why they can skim over context and history. The ads will keep coming, but only until Election Day.

title: Judge keeps $150,000 bond for driver accused of 100 mph Deerfield Beach crash that killed wife
description: Prosecutors say surveillance video shows Jean Claude Saint Cyr driving 98 to 102 mph in a 30 mph zone before the May crash that killed his wife and injured two others.
content: A driver accused of traveling at more than triple the speed limit in a May crash that killed his wife and injured two others appeared in front of a judge on Tuesday.Jean Claude Saint Cyr was behind the wheel during the violent crash in a Deerfield Beach neighborhood.Prosecutor Ross Weiner said surveillance video captured before the collision showed Saint Cyr traveling an average of 98 to 102 mph in a 30 mph zone.The state requested bond be set at $190,000. Defense attorney Shlomi Presser argued for a lower amount Saint Cyr's family could afford, noting that his client voluntarily surrendered as promised on the 19th after charges were filed."Clearly my client is not a flight risk," Presser said, arguing the surrender proved Saint Cyr would appear at future hearings.When it became clear the family intended to raise funds to post bond, Judge Allison Gilman addressed Saint Cyr's son, attempting to persuade him to leave his father in jail to save their money. Gilman noted that even if she cut the bond in half, $7,000 would go to a bondsman."Respectfully, I think to be frank, I think the family, regardless of the amount, is going to sell everything they own to get dad out," Presser told the court.Gilman then turned directly to the defendant: "Mr. Cyr, would you like them to mortgage their homes in order to get you out of jail?"Saint Cyr answered, "Yes.""Okay," Gilman said. "I'm leaving the bonds as they are."His bond was set at $150,000.

title: Denver Public Schools piloting new gym class, brings together students with and without disabilities
description: Denver Public Schools is piloting a new gym class called Peer-to-Peer PE that brings together students with and without disabilities.
content: Denver Public Schools is piloting a new gym class called Peer-to-Peer PE that brings together students with and without disabilities.In class at East High School, kids are free to be kids, to play and to laugh unapologetically. "So, I've had kids in the past that are now education majors, now special education majors, now PT (physical therapy) majors, or occupational therapist majors," said CarolAnn Skeats, who created the program. "It's been great seeing them want to go above and beyond just being in the class for the classroom; they want to do it, you know, for a career."The year-long pilot course includes honors students and athletes learning to lead in an inclusive environment. "Their need to do something and adapt something for a kiddo without even a second thought is the most heartwarming thing we can leave for society," said Skeats. "And our community is going to be better because we are introducing this at such a young age and allowing them to experience that it's okay for growth and failure, and to succeed."Fifteen-year-old Dodge tells us in sign language that this is his favorite class."By having this class, we get to build relationships with people with special needs and disabilities that might not get those connections without it," said Ryan Vanskoit, a senior at East High."The kids are doing the skills and drills; the kids are making up the lessons," said Meghan Ireland, a physical education teacher who runs the class. The kids are the ones that are, you know, trying to form and adapt everything to work for the entire class."Naturally, everyone leaves having gained something. "I learned to be encouraged by other people," said Jakole Martin, a 12th-grade athlete in the class. The plan is to pilot the program in more schools next year. Those behind the program's launch hope it stays and grows so more students can experience it. "It is probably my proudest thing in DPS," said Skeats.

title: Broward man accused of trying to kidnap 13-year-old from Miramar gas station, police say
description: The incident took place at a Shell gas station on S. State Road 7 in Miramar, according to police.
content: A 32-year-old Broward man has been arrested after police said he tried to kidnap a 13-year-old from a gas station on Monday.According to information provided by the Miramar Police Department, officers were called to the Shell gas station at 2840 S. State Road 7 in Miramar to investigate reports of a possible attempted kidnapping.Miramar Police Chief Delrish Moss said the girl was walking to her home when the incident happened. He said, "This guy walks next to the child and suddenly puts his arm around the child and puts the kid in a headlock, and that child starts screaming, and she broke free and ran into one of our business locations where help was available."Police said that the suspect, who has since been identified as Michael Polanco, of Davie, tried to kidnap the teenager and then fled west away from the gas station."This suspect is from Davie, and why he was in Miramar I don't know, but the message is if you do the crime, one, you shouldn't do it and two, don't come to our city if you are doing it because we are going to catch you," Police Chief Moss said. As police officers were responding to the location, they received information that a man matching Polanco's description had been spotted in the area, causing another disturbance.Police officers then diverted to that area, found the suspect, and detained him to investigate. That suspect was then positively identified by both the teenager and a witness who saw the incident unfolding."It was very smart of this kid to fight and to break free and to draw attention to the situation and make sure help is available. One thing here is that if they take you from one location to the next location, you don't know what dastardly things can happen, so you have to run, and you have to fight and draw attention to yourself so you will not be taken away," Chief Moss said. Polanco was then arrested and transported to the Broward Sheriff's Office. He is charged with battery causing bodily harm and kidnapping and inflicting bodily harm upon or terrorizing a victim."We do know he has an extensive criminal history and one of the things that was disturbing is that he had a previous history of indecent exposure or exposing himself to someone, so that kind of gives us an idea of the motivation, but we may never be sure," Moss said. Police said Polanco has been charged in the past with felony battery, burglary, and possession of illegal narcotics.CBS News Miami stopped by his home in Davie, but no one answered the door when we knocked.Chief Moss said the victim's family did not want to say anything about this case.

title: Christina Applegate reveals she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis: "Not happy at all"
description: Christina Applegate said on her MeSsy podcast that her doctor recently revealed she did not have multiple sclerosis.
content: Christina Applegate announced Tuesday that she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis, more than five years after announcing she had been told she had the chronic condition. Applegate, 54, shared the news in a double episode of her podcast MeSsy, where she and co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler discuss life with multiple sclerosis. Applegate had taken a break from the podcast in recent weeks. She said Tuesday she had taken that time to process the new information. Applegate said that "all of a sudden, a few years ago," her doctor wanted to take her off an infusion treatment and see how her B cells reacted. The cell count didn't increase or decrease after the treatment stopped, which began "kind of a study into my diagnosis," Applegate said. Eventually, her doctor had surprising news: Applegate had never had multiple sclerosis at all. "She came into my room and said, 'Congratulations, you don't have MS,' " Applegate said. "I was, like, not happy at all. Everybody else was so happy."Multiple sclerosis, or MS, is a disease where the body's immune system attacks the central nervous system. Symptoms vary from person to person, according to the National Multiple Sclerosis Society, and there are multiple types of the disease. The condition has no known cause, and its progression is impossible to predict. Dr. Marwa Kaisey, an associate professor at the Cedars-Sinai Medical Center department of neurology, said on the podcast that almost one in five people who have been told they have multiple sclerosis "didn't actually have it." Misdiagnoses with the condition are "fairly common," she said, because there is no one test for it. Applegate said at the time of her initial diagnosis, she underwent tests including a spinal tap and MRIs. Scans showed lesions on her brain, she said. Applegate said that she continues to have debilitating symptoms that affect her daily life and mobility. "You don't get misdiagnosed and then all of the sudden I'm better," Applegate said. "If anything, I've gotten worse. So I'm back at square one where I don't know what's going on with me. And that's going to be an online investigation that my doctors are going to be getting into just to find out what has been going on since 2021, why did this happen?"The investigation will begin next week, she said. Applegate has previously described living with symptoms including numbness, an off-balance feeling, and a tingling sensation in the limbs. She said in a 2022 interview with The New York Times that she "can't walk without a cane." In the same interview, she said she used a wheelchair during filming of the Netflix hit "Dead To Me," and the show's script was adjusted to accommodate her symptoms. In 2023, Applegate said her symptoms might lead to her giving up acting on camera. She said Tuesday that she has physical therapy three times a week. After she was officially diagnosed with the disease, she became an outspoken advocate for MS. On Tuesday, she said the misdiagnosis made her feel "like I let everybody down." "It's very unnerving and it's really confusing for me," Applegate said.

title: Cornell faculty member alleges "silencing of Jane Doe's voice," says her letter was not shared with Faculty Senate before crucial meeting
description: Some Cornell faculty members say a letter from Jane Doe in which she said she "felt unsupported and disbelieved" by university president Michael Kotlikoff was not shared with them.
content: Some Cornell faculty members say a letter from Jane Doe in which she said she "felt unsupported and disbelieved" by university president Michael Kotlikoff was not shared with them. One faculty member called that a "silencing of Jane Doe's voice." Doe has filed a lawsuit alleging gang rape at a 2024 fraternity party. The allegations have started a firestorm of controversy and prompted a criminal investigation as well as an independent review at Cornell over how it handled her allegations. The letter from Doe was dated Oct. 14 and sent to Cornell faculty leaders. That's the same day members of the Faculty Senate began debating a possible no-confidence vote in Kotlikoff's administration. In the letter, Doe says she felt "disbelieved" by Kotlikoff. The letter also asks the faculty be made aware of its contents. Doe says she's not trying to tell the faculty how to vote, she just wants them to have this information before they vote. However, three Cornell faculty sources tell CBS News New York's Mahsa Saeidi they never received the letter from university administration. "I think what's the most important at this point is that the Faculty Senate did not receive that letter from Jane Doe," Cornell Faculty Senate member Risa Lieberwitz said. Lieberwitz said because the Faculty Senate didn't receive the letter from Doe, they may have missed the opportunity to question Kotlikoff directly about it. "What we have is the silencing of Jane Doe's voice to the Faculty Senate when we were meeting and when we had the opportunity to ask about it," Lieberwitz said. The university says the dean of faculty sent the letter to general counsel for verification and then shared it with the independent review. "Now we have an administrator responding through a spokesperson who is saying this is what I recorded in my notes. And I think that there's a real question, once again, of transparency," Lieberwitz said. CBS News New York obtained a copy of the letter through another university source. It describes a conversation that Doe says was relayed to her by her former sorority president who claimed Kotlikoff questioned why Doe didn't come forward with her allegations sooner. The letter goes on to say that, as a result, Doe "felt unsupported and disbelieved by President Kotlikoff." Cornell disputes the secondhand account the letter references, saying Kotlikoff was questioning why bystanders didn't report the incident sooner, not Doe. "Jane Doe, through counsel, provided a statement to the Dean of Faculty and Speaker of the Faculty Senate regarding her understanding of comments made by President Kotlikoff in the presence of one of her sorority sisters and one or more faculty members. The letter was sent for informational purposes only. Jane Doe thought it important that the faculty senate have this information as it deliberates and considers the resolutions or motions before it. Jane Doe would ask the faculty senate to give her letter whatever weight or credibility it deems appropriate," Doe's attorney Thomas Giuffra said in a statement. Multiple faculty members told CBS News New York the letter should have been shared with them. Lieberwitz said it was fortunate they received the letter before the second meeting to discuss a no-confidence vote on Oct. 24. As of right now, Kotlikoff is not scheduled to be present at that meeting, members of the Faculty Senate told CBS News New York. Associate Professor David Bateman of the American Association of University Professors supports a vote of no-confidence. "Why I've come out in favor of a no-confidence vote, is simply that I was not persuaded after that meeting that the university administration is actually going to change its structures to listen to students and to faculty in a serious, deliberative way," Bateman said. Tuesday, former Acting U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates, who has been appointed by Cornell to lead a review of the university's handling of sexual assault allegations, sent an email which CBS News New York obtained from a member of the Cornell community who received it. In the email, Yates promises to review the university's response to Doe's allegations and Cornell's sexual harassment and assault policies as well as make recommendations from its findings. All seven men accused of wrongdoing in Doe's lawsuit deny the allegations. Do you have a story that needs investigating? Let us know.Editor's note 10/21/26: This story has been updated to include a statement from Doe's attorney.

title: New York governor's race heats up as Kathy Hochul and Bruce Blakeman clash over high energy costs
description: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman butted heads on the campaign trail Tuesday over energy policy and the increasingly high cost of utility bills.
content: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman butted heads on the campaign trail Tuesday over energy policy and the increasingly high cost of utility bills.Hochul took off the gloves, apparently fed up with the constant attacks from the Nassau County executive, including him blaming her for high energy costs. She blamed President Trump and the war in Iran and challenged Blakeman to use his close friendship with the president to do something about it."Now, if he's got such a close relationship, you ought to call him up and say, 'Mr. President, this is really killing my chances to ever have higher office because of what's going on here,'" Hochul said.And there it was laid bare, Hochul playing the MAGA card to express her frustration with the constant attacks from Blakeman about high utility bills."I have acknowledged that our new prices are high," Hochul said. "He is blaming me for everything, including the fact that the sunrise is now at 7:12 in the morning, instead of earlier. I mean, he is blaming me for everything," Hochul said.Blakeman escalated his attacks Tuesday, appearing in Washington Heights with former Gov. George Pataki to claim that energy costs are three times more than when Pataki was in office -- 11.1 cents per kilowatt hour in 1995 compared to 29.4 cents per kilowatt hour today.One target was the All-Electric Buildings Act of 2023, which bans the use of fossil fuels for heating, hot water and cooking in all new construction."Natural gas is the cheapest effective way that people can heat their homes or generate electricity, and we're not being allowed to do that," Pataki said."Kathy Hochul's own state energy research board has said that her policies will increase our utility bills by $4,000 in the next five years," Blakeman said.Hochul put the ball back in Blakeman's court."You know what would be a lot better for driving down energy costs in the state of New York? Stopping the war with Iran. I have yet to hear Bruce Blakeman give any blame to the Trump administration on why our costs have gone [up]," Hochul said. "We want to know what the main cost of energy is. It is the war with Iran. Everything is more expensive. The cost of gas, the cost of diesel that powers many of our plants," Hochul said.Energy policy is complicated, and the two have punched and counter punched. Hochul says President Trump's opposition to wind power has hurt the state. Blakeman says her opposition to fracking is particularly to blame. "We're sitting on one of the largest natural gas reserves in the world here in New York state. Yet, Kathy Hochul won't let us extract that natural gas," Blakeman said. "In Pennsylvania, with a Democrat governor, Josh Shapiro, their utility bills are half ours because he allows for the extraction of natural gas."Over the last few weeks, New Yorkers have started receiving energy rebate checks of up to $200 to help offset the pain.

title: MS misdiagnoses raise concerns, Colorado doctors warn of unnecessary treatment risks
description: A recent revelation by actress Christina Applegate that she does not have multiple sclerosis has sparked conversations about the frequency with which misdiagnoses occur. Colorado doctors say pinpointing the disease can be complicated, and misdiagnosis rates are high.
content: A recent revelation by actress Christina Applegate that she does not have multiple sclerosis has sparked conversations about the frequency with which misdiagnoses occur. Colorado doctors say pinpointing the disease can be complicated, and misdiagnosis rates are high.Colorado has one of the nation's higher rates of multiple sclerosis, or MS, and specialists at the Rocky Mountain MS Center at the University of Colorado are working to better understand the disease and improve diagnostic accuracy.For Marissa Poppens, living with MS means never knowing what each day will bring."From the moment I wake up, I never know if it's going to be a good day or a bad day," Poppens said.Her life changed in April 2015 when, at 30 years old, she woke up paralyzed from the waist down."Once they did an MRI, they found a bunch of lesions on my brain and spine that was affecting my mobility," Poppens said.She was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis, a chronic disease in which the immune system attacks the central nervous system, disrupting communication between the brain and the rest of the body. Today, Poppens relies on a cane and walker to get around. She said managing her symptoms often requires multiple medications."MS is so unpredictable," Poppens said. "Sometimes I'm doing fine with my five medications, and sometimes it's eight or more."Even after receiving her diagnosis, Poppens said getting treatment was difficult. Insurance issues left her without treatment for a year, and she eventually lost her job and much of her independence."I was scared at first, and then concerned," she said. "Like, what is my future going to hold? How am I going to navigate life now that I have this diagnosis?"That is why Dr. Anna Shah, a neurologist at UCHealth University of Colorado Hospital, says it is important to get a second look to confirm the diagnosis. She adds that diagnosing MS can be challenging because symptoms such as fatigue, numbness and vision problems can overlap with other medical conditions."It's not as simple as something like a diagnosis of diabetes, where you do a singular blood test and then you get your answer of whether you have it or not," Shah said.Shah said that, in her experience, about 10% to 15% of new patients she evaluates may have been misdiagnosed previously.Unlike some other conditions, doctors cannot confirm MS with a single test. Specialists must evaluate a patient's symptoms, medical history, neurological examinations and imaging results to determine whether the disease is present."With MS, we kind of think about these complexities that come into play, which is looking at clinical symptoms that someone may have, as well as looking at more evidence of MS," Shah said.The risks of an incorrect diagnosis are real and, in some cases, deadly. Shah warned that an incorrect MS diagnosis can have serious consequences, particularly for patients who are prescribed medications that alter the immune system.Many MS treatments work by modifying or suppressing immune activity to reduce attacks on the central nervous system. However, some of those medications can increase the risk of infections and other complications."In MS, the issue is the immune system is doing all the wrong things, and so most of our medications are primarily focusing on changing how the immune system functions," Shah said.She emphasized that patients who do not have MS could face unnecessary health risks from those treatments."So when we think about it in that context, it can be really quite dangerous if that's not the diagnosis you have," Shah said.For Poppens, who has spent more than a decade navigating the challenges of MS, the possibility of an incorrect diagnosis underscores the importance of getting answers before beginning long-term treatment.Specialists recommend seeking a second opinion from a neurologist who specializes in MS when a diagnosis is uncertain, particularly before starting medications that affect the immune system.For patients like Poppens, an accurate diagnosis is about more than finding the right treatment. It is about understanding what the future may hold while managing a disease that can change from one day to the next.

title: Lack of debates in 1st Congressional District race on Long Island exposes new political reality
description: There appears to be a disturbing trend in both local and national politics. Analysts say candidates no longer want to debate​, perhaps because they are afraid of getting caught in "gotcha" moments.
content: There appears to be a disturbing trend in both local and national politics. Analysts say candidates no longer want to debate, perhaps because they are afraid of getting caught in "gotcha" moments. The 1st Congressional District race on Long Island is now in the spotlight."Debate ... allows voters to kick the tires of their politicians" Chris Gallant, an openly gay military pilot and firefighter, has seen a surge in fundraising since acknowledging explicit sexual photos taken years ago were of him. He has since rolled out a new theme: "Make politics sexy again.""I am not ashamed or shy of who I am," Gallant said. "I was in the military prior to 'Don't Ask, Don't Tell.'"Gallant is facing incumbent Nick LaLota in the 1st Congressional District, which is the largest in the state, spreading throughout Suffolk County.LaLota is challenging Gallant to a debate."Debate is important. It allows voters to kick the tires of their politicians. You wouldn't buy a car without test-driving it. I think we should be held to a similar standard," LaLota said.Gallant says too few watch debates."The numbers are very low or nonexistent," he said.Instead, Gallant is holding candidate forums."Talking to voters and listening to voters is what we need at this moment," Gallant said."Democracy isn't a spectator sport"Barbara Epstein of the League of Women Voters usually sponsors multiple debates, but said this year requests were denied or candidates pulled out at the last minute."Democracy isn't a spectator sport," Epstein said. "We are very upset that the candidates choose not to debate."The only debate scheduled on Long Island, and one of the few in the New York area, is Rep. Tom Suozzi and challenger Mike LiPetri in the 3rd Congressional District on Tuesday night.Political and legal debates date back to ancient Rome and have been a key part of our nation, beginning with Lincoln-Douglas, yet experts say, sadly, are no longer perceived as necessary."They're really like a job interview. I think really nothing prepares candidates better for office and gives insights to the public more than these debates, which are unscripted and you never know what's going to happen," said Aaron Kall, a professor and the director of debates at the University of Michigan.Had there been a debate, LaLota and Gallant acknowledge major issues that could have been discussed have shifted from crime to the economy."When you get down to Washington, you have to debate these issues so that candidates can explain what their views are," LaLota said."Putting my heart and soul into the job mission is everything, and so this is me changing the uniform and attempting to serve my country in a different way," Gallant said.

title: Adrian Kempe scores 2 goals and Kings beat Capitals 5-2 for first win of season
description: Adrian Kempe scored twice and the Los Angeles Kings got their first win of the season, rallying from an early deficit to beat the Washington Capitals 5-2.
content: Adrian Kempe scored twice and the Los Angeles Kings got their first win of the season, rallying from an early deficit to beat the Washington Capitals 5-2 on Tuesday night.Artemi Panarin, Erik Gustafsson and Scott Laughton also scored for Los Angeles (1-4-2), and former Capitals goalie Darcy Kuemper made 30 saves.Ryan Leonard and Cole Hutson scored for the Capitals, who took a 2-0 lead in the first period but were held scoreless for the final 41:25. Washington's Logan Thompson stopped 21 shots.The Kings, who came in having scored just four goals over their previous four games and 12 goals through six games, lost second-line center Quinton Byfield to an upper-body injury in the first period. He played just 2:44.Hutson put the Capitals ahead 2-0 on the power play with 1:25 left in the first, but Kempe found the net less than a minute later and Panarin scored 2 seconds before the intermission.Gustafsson put the Kings ahead at 7:28 of the third on the power play. Kempe scored his second goal midway through the third, and Laughton added an empty-netter that gave the Kings their highest-scoring game of the season.Absent the injured Pierre Luc-Dubois and Justin Sourdif down the middle of their forward ranks, the Capitals were unable to beat Kuemper, who played for Washington from 2022-24.Up nextKings: Visit the New York Islanders on Thursday night.Capitals: Host Buffalo on Saturday night.

title: Riverside County deputies investigating man's suspicious death near Perris
description: Deputies said the 42-year-old man was found dead in the unincorporated community of Good Hope, and upon further investigation, they noted "unusual circumstances."
content: Riverside County deputies are investigating a man's death near Perris on Monday. In a news release shared by the Riverside County Sheriff's Office, deputies said they were called to the area near Read Street and Olive Avenue, in the unincorporated community of Good Hope, at around 5:40 p.m. for a possible deceased person. "Upon arrival, deputies located a deceased adult male at the scene," the release said. "Perris Sheriff's Station investigators responded and, after noting unusual circumstances, notified investigators with the Riverside County Sheriff's Central Homicide Unit."Investigators identified the victim as 42-year-old Riverside resident Lonn Lucas. The circumstances surrounding his death remain under investigation. No suspects have been identified and no arrests have been reported. Anyone with more information was urged to contact Central Homicide Investigator Chua at 951-955-2777 or Perris Station Investigator Hadeen at 951-210-1000.

title: Teacher charged with public drunkenness after 2 vehicles damaged on Pittsburgh's North Shore
description: An Upper St. Clair teacher has been arrested by Pittsburgh police for allegedly damaging two vehicles on the North Shore.
content: An Upper St. Clair High School teacher was arrested for public drunkenness after police said he damaged two vehicles on the North Shore last week. Police charged Ronald Sivillo with two misdemeanor counts of criminal mischief and disorderly conduct and a summary charge of public drunkenness. He is out on an unsecured $5,000 bond. An Upper St. Clair spokesperson confirmed that Sivillo has been a teacher at Upper St. Clair for over 20 years. According to the police paperwork, the two victims were working at Tom's Watch Bar. One said she has $11,000 in damage to her vehicle and that she found Sivillo inside her Volkswagen. Police said Sivillo left behind a shattered rear window, two detached mirrors, a partially ripped-out center console and a damaged screen on Friday. According to police paperwork, a woman who works at Tom's Watch Bar on the North Shore came face to face with Sivillo. She told him to get out of her car, and later, she said she found a pair of black shoes, a blue hoodie and a black satchel in her trunk.Police questioned Sivillo and said he admitted to drinking five IPAs and attempting to break into the Volkswagen, thinking it was his vehicle and that the items in the trunk belonged to him. A coworker of the victim discovered damage to her car, which was parked at a nearby garage. Her driver's side mirror was broken off. A third person flagged down officers claiming that a man was attempting to slash the tires on a white Bronco parked on West General Robinson Boulevard. The Bronco had no damage. The Upper St. Clair spokesperson added that Sivillo "has been out on paid administrative leave since Sept. 23, 2026." It was not immediately clear why he was placed on leave last month.

title: Railroad crossing reopens after passenger train catches fire in Watauga, officials say
description: Passengers were aboard the train when the locomotive caught fire near Highway 377.
content: A railroad crossing in Watauga reopened Tuesday evening after a Union Pacific passenger train caught fire and became disabled near Highway 377, city officials said.The fire was reported shortly before 4 p.m. near Hightower Drive and Basswood Boulevard. The flames were confined to the locomotive's engine compartment and were extinguished by Watauga firefighters, according to a city spokesperson.Passengers were aboard the train, which had approximately eight to 10 cars attached, but no injuries were reported, authorities said.Highway 377 was temporarily closed for approximately 30 minutes while firefighters placed a water supply line across the roadway. Watauga police redirected motorists around the area.Northbound and southbound traffic on Highway 377 resumed, and the railroad crossing at Highway 377, Basswood Boulevard and Hightower Drive reopened by 6 p.m., allowing eastbound and westbound traffic to resume, officials said. Railroad crossings at Watauga Road and North Tarrant were not affected and remained open throughout the incident.Officials said the fire did not spread beyond the locomotive.Union Pacific representatives arrived and are investigating the incident.CBS News Texas will provide updates as more information becomes available.

title: Northern Colorado nursery prepares to grow millions of seedlings to help forests recover from wildfires
description: A newly remodeled and expanded nursery in Northern Colorado is preparing to grow millions of tree seedlings that could help reforest areas damaged by wildfires and support conservation efforts across the state.
content: A newly remodeled and expanded nursery in Northern Colorado is preparing to grow millions of tree seedlings that could help reforest areas damaged by wildfires and support conservation efforts across the state.The Colorado State Forest Service recently completed renovations at its nursery in northwest Fort Collins, where the first seedlings are already growing inside the facility's greenhouses."What we're doing here is a major part of the reforestation pipeline," said Laura Miller, nursery manager for the Colorado State Forest Service.The project was made possible by $10.3 million in state funding and $5.3 million from the U.S. Forest Service."Today is a culmination of three years of hard work," said Kristin Garrison, associate director of forest planning and implementation for the Colorado State Forest Service.The nursery is designed to produce low-cost seedlings for conservation, with some trees available for purchase and others used to restore forests affected by wildfires."The Colorado State Forest Service is the leader in producing low-cost seedlings for conservation," Miller said.Inside the greenhouses, staff are growing a variety of tree species, including ponderosa pine. Each species is tracked to help ensure seedlings are planted in environments where they have the best chance of surviving.Miller said the seedlings typically grow for about a year and are only sent for planting in regions in which specific species thrive. "With our new facility, we're able to give the seedling exactly what it needs in terms of temperature, relative humidity, and with irrigation," Miller said. "So the whole goal is to have a high-quality seedling that will survive when it is out planted."The nursery could eventually hold up to two million seedlings at a time when operating at full capacity.The trees will be available for orders in the spring, with customers expected to pick up their seedlings in late spring or early summer.After years of planning and construction, Miller said the completed facility will help the Colorado State Forest Service expand its work supporting forests and conservation throughout the state."It's just exciting to see the facility come to life and be able to support our mission here at Colorado State Forest Service," Miller said.

title: Two weeks before election day, here's what Minnesota voters say are their top issues
description: Just two weeks from the midterm election, many Minnesotans aren't waiting for Nov. 3, but are casting their votes early.
content: Just two weeks from the midterm election, many Minnesotans aren't waiting for Nov. 3, but are casting their votes early.In less than three days, more than 1,500 people have voted early in Eagan, including Kathy McMonagle, who has one thing on her mind: fraud."We need to not just clean up and prosecute and collect, try to get money back that's been used in the wrong way but put it to use in the right way," she said.It was also an issue for others.In Hastings, it's far from the only issue voters say are pushing them to the polls.Affordability and gas prices were also issues that several voters mentioned. Lori Goetz said her vote would go towards anyone who pledges to lower prices."I have seen things go off the rails, and affordability of course. Everyone's not happy about that," she said. "Gas. Gas is the worst. I've noticed that my heat and electric bills have gone up. Food. Food has gotten pretty terrible."Early voters say the only wrong answer is not being informed, or not voting at all.WCCO has an election guide that helps you meet candidates for office, check your registration and find your polling place.

title: Some Steelers fans reconsidering travel to Paris amid riots: "Roll of the dice"
description: While many people are moving forward with trips to Paris to see the Steelers play the Saints, there are some reconsidering amid civil unrest.
content: While many people are moving forward with trips to Paris to see the Steelers play the Saints, there are some fans reconsidering amid civil unrest. Chris Slagle travels from Canonsburg for every Steelers game as a season ticket holder, and when the Paris ones were released, he quickly bought them for him and his girlfriend."The Steeler game for us was certainly a big bonus, but it wasn't the only thing we wanted to do," Slagle said.He said they were looking forward to exploring the city and all it has to offer."Neither of us have been to Europe before, anywhere in Europe, so it's something that at this point in our lives we want to start doing more of," Slagle said.They were planning to fly out Thursday, but then they started thinking hard about changing their plans as they followed the news and saw protests turning violent across France."For the amount of money that we're going to spend to go over there and stay, it's kind of a roll of the dice in my opinion," Slagle said. Slagle said it wasn't a gamble worth taking, so they decided to contact their travel agent and switch their trip to Madrid and Barcelona, still wanting to enjoy their time off.They're not the only ones. Ian Petrulli with Holiday Travel International said a few have canceled their trips through his office, but he's encouraging others to hold off, as demonstrations largely have been a distance from the arena."Just be aware of your surroundings and check the State Department's website," Petrulli said. "Things like this do happen in Europe quite often, so at least you know once or twice a year it's happening somewhere in Europe, so it's not all that of a surprise for something like this to be going on."For those who want to adjust their plans, you may have options. Airline-only tickets are easy to change, but accommodations have their own terms, with many non-refundable. Travelers' insurance also may not help."Fear of the unknown usually isn't an excuse for travel insurance," Petrulli said.If you want to go somewhere else, that could be possible, depending on your airline.As for Slagle, it's been a challenge to sell his tickets, but he knows pivoting was the right decision for him and he's wishing the best for all in Paris."I honest to god hope I'm wrong, and that everything goes off without a hitch, and everybody going over there has a blast," Slagle said.

title: WBZ's Lisa Hughes and David Wade to be inducted into New England Emmy's Silver Circle
description: The New England Emmy's are inducting WBZ-TV's Lisa Hughes and David Wade into the Silver Circle.
content: The New England chapter of the National Academy of Television Arts & Sciences is honoring longtime WBZ-TV News anchors Lisa Hughes and David Wade with a prestigious award.The pair will be inducted into the 2026 Silver Circle later this year along with other leaders in the television industry.The Silver Circle "celebrates television professionals with 25 or more years of distinguished service whose work, leadership, and mentorship have made a meaningful and lasting impact.""The Boston/New England Chapter has inducted more than 180 television professionals into the Gold and Silver Circle, recognizing individuals whose achievements have advanced the art and science of television, strengthened their communities, and inspired those pursuing careers in the industry," the chapter said. It's the first time in a decade that two members of the same team have been honored at the same time - the last were Boston Celtics broadcasters Mike Gorman and Tommy Heinsohn. Hughes joined WBZ in 2000 and Wade has been reporting in Boston since 1998. Together the award-winning journalists anchor the WBZ-TV News at 5, 6 and 11 p.m.This year's honorees will be formally inducted on Dec. 10 at a ceremony in Quincy.

title: Driver charged in Newton road-rage stabbing says 60-year-old approached him "aggressively out of nowhere"
description: A driver accused of stabbing a 60-year-old man in a road rage incident in Newton, Massachusetts said he was defending himself.
content: A driver accused of stabbing a 60-year-old man in a road rage incident in Newton, Massachusetts said he was defending himself.Albeldy Manuel Pinales-Villar, 28, was arraigned in Newton District Court Tuesday, a day after the violent confrontation. He pleaded not guilty to assault and battery with a dangerous weapon.
