Bail was set at $5,000 with the condition that he have no contact with the alleged victim in the case.Police said Pinales-Villar bumped into the man's car while the 60-year-old was leaving his home around 2 p.m. Monday on Drumlin Road in Newton.Investigators said the unidentified man tried to get Pinales-Villar to stop to exchange information, but Pinales-Villar allegedly passed him and blocked his car in.According to the prosecution, the 60-year-old man got out of his car, approached Pinales-Villar to get his information, and was stabbed in the ribs before Pinales-Villar left the scene.The man was taken to Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston with non-life-threatening injuries and was later released. Police were able to use Pinales-Villar's license plate to find him at his home and arrest him."The fact that this was such a violent crime against a stranger due to a minor incident of road rage is very concerning to the Commonwealth," the prosecutor said while unsuccessfully arguing for higher bail. "We have strong concerns for public safety, and that is why we are asking for the condition for the defendant not drive and that he be on home confinement and possess no dangerous weapons."Pinales-Villar's defense attorney Christine Breslin argued there was no contact between the two cars. Breslin said there are two videos that show the 60-year-old man approaching Pinales-Villar's car and telling him to get out.The attorney said Pinales-Villar took one of the videos, which she told the judge shows the entire incident. "So essentially, what we have is an incident that's very unclear," Breslin said, adding that Pinales-Villar was protecting himself from a stranger who was coming at him "aggressively out of nowhere."Pinales-Villar is due back in court on Nov. 10."This is definitely a bizarre place for there to be a road-rage incident. It's really all neighborhood people driving down the street, so it's incredible shocking and weird," said Deena Baker, who lives in the neighborhood.

title: Union employees locked out of New Jersey oil refinery after contracts expire
description: Union-represented employees have been locked out of the Phillips 66 Bayway Refinery and Linden Terminal in New Jersey.
content: Hundreds of workers have been locked out of the largest oil refinery on the East Coast. Some 400 union employees were kept out of New Jersey's Phillips 66 Bayway Refinery and the Linden Terminal after contract negotiations failed. Dozens of Teamsters Local 877 were out on the picket line outside the Bayway Refinery and Linden Terminal on Tuesday. They even blocked trucks from going in at times. The union says it is asking for a better and safer contract. So far, the two sides have not come up with a deal. Passing cars honked their horns in support of the locked-out labor. "I would much rather be working. But the company refuses to give us a fair and safe contract," Teamsters Local 877 member David Zaccardi said. Phillips 66 said the company locked those workers out in the absence of a further contract extension, and to meet its commitment to safe and reliable operations. The Teamsters say they're just asking for better benefits and safety protections. Employees say that includes reinstating sick days that have been cut by the company. "People are coming to work sick, OK? And when you come to work sick, sometimes you have an accident, make a mistake. And that can be devastating in a place like this," Teamsters Local 877's Ed Goldmann said. Phillips 66 officials say the facilities are still operating and are now staffed by supervisors and engineers. "To me, running this refinery with a skeleton crew is a huge safety risk. The company maintains that they can do it. I hope they can," Teamsters Local 877 President Jeff Sanford said. Bayway Refinery is the largest of its kind on the East Coast. It processes gasoline and diesel fuel, and it provides jet fuel to Newark Liberty International Airport. Employees say there are reserves, but if the lockout drags on, it could impact fuel prices in the region. Both sides returned to the negotiating table Tuesday afternoon. A Teamsters representative expressed cautious optimism that a deal could be done soon.

title: Rep. Mike Kelly faces challenge from Justin Wagner in Pennsylvania's 16th Congressional District
description: Democrat Justin Wagner is looking to unseat Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Kelly in Pennsylvania's 16th Congressional District.
content: Democrat Justin Wagner is looking to unseat Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Kelly in Pennsylvania's 16th Congressional District.Kelly, who has coasted to victory in the last eight elections, is touting his experience and accomplishments for the district against Wagner, all amid an unpopular war and rising gas and grocery prices. However, Wagner believes this might be the year to end that streak given Kelly's close alignment with President Trump. "In a way, yes, it is a referendum on the president's policies, and folks like Kelly who just go along instead of standing up for the people in the district," Wagner told KDKA-TV in an interview. "I am running against a guy that has absolutely no background," Kelly told KDKA-TV in an interview. "That's not a slight of him, by the way. It's just the truth."While Wagner is an engineer and an Iraq War veteran, he has limited government experience as a councilman in Mercer. Kelly, on the other hand, has become a power broker on Capitol Hill over the past 15 years. While conceding that midterms are sometimes a referendum on the sitting president, Kelly stands on his individual record of delivering for his district. "If you check my record, you'd have a hard time finding somebody who's done a better job in Congress than I have," Kelly said. "Why would I say that? Well, look at it from 2011 until this year, I have been elected time after time after time by voters. Not just by Republicans, but also Democrats."If affordability is the main issue in this campaign, Kelly said inflation skyrocketed under former President Joe Biden but is stabilizing under Trump. He also pointed to his own work to reduce expenses for everyday Americans. "If you were to take a look at the biggest change in the last two years, it's the Working Families Tax Cuts and Jobs Act," Kelly said.As the senior member of the House Ways and Means Committee, he helped craft the Working Families Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, otherwise known as the Big Beautiful Bill, which he said will amount to $191 billion in net tax relief, including no taxes on tips and overtime. "We saved the average person 22 percent in taxes when they were going to go up," Kelly said.Though Wagner argues the act actually hurts struggling families."Cut to Medicaid, cuts to SNAP benefits, cuts to everything that helps everyday working-class Americans," Wagner said. Despite unfavorable polling on the war, tariffs and immigration enforcement, support for Mr. Trump remains high in the 16th District, which runs from Butler County up to Erie. But Wagner sees cracks and a potential opportunity with those who supported the president in the past. "I hope that they see what's happening now is the direct result of the policies of this administration," Wagner said. "And they can take a look and say, 'Hey, we got this new guy. Maybe he has some good ideas. Let's give him a chance and see if he can help us out.'" Over his eight terms in Congress, Kelly has attained power and influence in Washington, D.C., and has enjoyed the overwhelming support of his constituents. If Wagner prevails, it would be one of the biggest upsets in the country.

title: Feds investigate multiple adult daycare centers across NYC, officials say
description: Federal agents were out across New York City Tuesday investigating multiple adult daycare centers. The White House and Gov. Kathy Hochul say it's part of a joint investigation into healthcare fraud.
content: Federal agents were out across New York City Tuesday investigating multiple adult daycare centers. The White House and Gov. Kathy Hochul say it's part of a joint investigation into healthcare fraud. Tuesday morning, federal agents carried boxes outside of an adult daycare center on Eighth Avenue in Sunset Park, Brooklyn. Federal law enforcement sources confirmed the massive presence was related to ongoing investigations into healthcare fraud. Agents also took enforcement action at an adult daycare center on Fort Hamilton Parkway in Borough Park, and in Flushing. The FBI said centers on Staten Island were part of the searches, too. "We're targeting providers who we believe engaged in illegal activity, ranging from money laundering, to kickbacks, to improper billing," Hochul said. Hochul said it was a monthslong investigation and that she went to Washington, D.C. herself to meet with the feds about Medicaid fraud. Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator of the U.S. Center for Medicare and Medicaid, said he visited the locations earlier in the year. "It was the largest enforcement action of its kind. You'll hear more about it later in the week," Oz said. A person who answered the phone at the Borough Park location said he had no comment. Calls to the other two locations named by law enforcement sources were not returned. "It's usually an enterprise involving several individuals," said David Shapiro of John Jay College of Criminal Justice. "You want to get the gist of the method of the operation, you know, who's involved, the vendors, the providers, the patients, real or bogus.""It is what we used to call paper-intensive," he added. Over the summer, a CBS News data analysis found Medicaid paid adult daycare providers $3.35 billion nationwide in 2024, and 17% of that money went to New York state facilities - more than any other state. Tuesday afternoon, the FBI released a video message on social media indicating an audit found that between 2019 and 2024, Medicaid spent more per enrollee in New York than the national average, with costs 40% to 60% higher. The FBI wants the public to send in tips of suspected fraud.

title: Stockton grandmother's car lit on fire by suspected arsonist, officials say
description: A car fire is under investigation in Stockton after a homeowner captured a masked person on a bicycle lighting her car on fire this week.
content: A car fire is under investigation in Stockton after a homeowner captured a masked person on a bicycle lighting her car on fire this week. The car, parked along Hammer Lane outside of her home near Cesar Chavez High School and Panella Park, was lit up in broad daylight. Mary Guillen, the owner, said she was at home that afternoon when she heard a "boom" outside. "I opened the gate, I saw my car on fire... is that my car burning? The first thing I could think was getting the water hose," said Guillen. She said she attempted to fight the fire, calling for help from any neighbors until one arrived. They called the fire department and Guillen said she was in a state of shock. "I always call it my little blue car, the first car I ever owned in my name. I've almost paid for it." said Guillen. Video from her security cameras shows a masked person on a bicycle ride up next to her car. Moments later, smoke is seen coming from the gas tank side of the vehicle. The person seen on camera was gone by the time the fire department arrived. Stockton police told CBS News Sacramento they cannot provide any specifics as the case is under investigation. They have not confirmed a suspect's identity or whether the person in the video is a serial arsonist.

title: El Dorado County supervisors unanimously appoint next sheriff amid dispute
description: The El Dorado County Board of Supervisors unanimously voted Tuesday to appoint Undersheriff Eric Palmberg as the county's next sheriff, amid a public dispute involving current Sheriff Jeff Leikauf and former Sheriff John D'Agostini.
content: The El Dorado County Board of Supervisors unanimously voted Tuesday to appoint Undersheriff Eric Palmberg as the county's next sheriff, amid a public dispute involving current Sheriff Jeff Leikauf and former Sheriff John D'Agostini.The appointment comes after Leikauf announced he would retire at the end of the year. D'Agostini, who previously served as sheriff, has publicly criticized Leikauf's leadership and management in local media and on social media while seeking to return to the position.Both men addressed supervisors during Tuesday's meeting, acknowledging the controversy surrounding the sheriff's office."The first thing I would like to do is apologize to you all for having to go through what you have gone through the past several weeks," Leikauf said.D'Agostini said he wanted to return to the position to address what he believes went wrong after he chose Leikauf as his successor."My sole purpose in seeking this appointment is to right a wrong, that's it," D'Agostini said. "I made it abundantly clear that I'm pursuing this appointment to return to the seat I left to repair what I broke by choosing my successor."Leikauf also spoke about the impact the controversy has had on his family."For all the challenges that have been hurled at our family for the past year and a half, we are beginning the next chapter even closer together," Leikauf said.Several supervisors expressed concern about the public conflict and its effect on the community.Supervisor Brooke Laine said the divide between the two has left the community reeling."It's very unfortunate," Laine said. "It's two families that have been in the community a very long time."Supervisor Greg Ferrero said the decision should focus on the needs of the sheriff's office rather than personal rivalries."This is a stressful situation. There is a lot to unpack," Ferrero said. "This is not a popularity contest for one person or the other."Supervisor Lori Parlin also urged those involved to stop escalating the dispute publicly."We need to stop this nonsense, stop stirring things up, get off social media," Parkin said. "Please, it is the worst thing on the planet."Palmberg is scheduled to take over as sheriff the day after Christmas.

title: Electric rates to rise this winter in Pennsylvania as power demand outpaces supply, experts say
description: Be prepared to pay more for your electricity this winter.
content: Be prepared to pay more for your electricity this winter. Rates in Pennsylvania will once again increase on Dec. 1.Electric companies said bills should only increase by a few dollars per month, but at a time when people are trying to stretch a paycheck as far as it can go, it presents another challenge.The major suppliers in the Pittsburgh area, Duquesne Light, Penn Power and West Penn Power, will all see an increase. West Penn goes from 12.08 to 12.39 cents per kilowatt-hour. Penn Power will go up from 13.48 to 13.89 cents per kilowatt-hour. Duquesne Light will go from 14.14 to 14.56 cents per kilowatt-hour."This is the part of the bill that we do not control as a utility. It's a part of the bill that we do not profit from as a utility. This is purely a carry-through," said Matt Neistein, Duquesne Light's director of communication and brand.This charge is the price for generating electricity. It's a problem of supply and demand. According to economic experts, AI data centers are one of the biggest drivers of demand."They are huge consumers of power, and so that certainly has impacted our rates," said Dr. Dorene Ciletti, Point Park University's director of the sales and marketing program.Duquesne Light says this is some of the highest demand it has seen in years, and it only gets bigger as supply lags."Supply is simply not keeping up. We are not, as a society, as a state, generating enough power to meet that demand," Neistein said.There is the availability to shop around for a power provider, but experts strongly advise doing research before entering into a contract. What can feel like a deal may end up costing you more."There is a lot to it in terms of reading the fine print and making sure that if you are making a change in your supplier, you understand what you're getting into short term and long term," Ciletti said. It's recommended that residents continue to utilize whatever energy-saving measures they take this time of year.

title: Boxing gym, bar brings new life to former Schmidt Brewery site in St. Paul
description: A historic building that once housed part of the Schmidt Brewery and later became a popular marketplace is getting a new purpose, with help from a former Minnesota Vikings player.
content: A historic building that once housed part of the Schmidt Brewery and later became a popular marketplace is getting a new purpose, with help from a former Minnesota Vikings player.The former Keg and Case Market building is being transformed into Keg House Commons, a fitness and entertainment destination featuring a boxing gym, sports lounge, juice and coffee bars, and an event center that can accommodate up to 500 people.The project is led by Dalton Outlaw, who has operated Element Boxing and Fitness in St. Paul, Minneosta, for 15 years, former Vikings wide receiver Michael Floyd and local developer Sean Divine. Outlaw said Floyd's wife, Sydney, is also part of the ownership team."We are excited that we now get to rewrite the chapter, the next chapter for what this building exists as," Outlaw said.The ownership group purchased the property after it went into foreclosure and has spent the past year renovating the building. Outlaw said the work has largely focused on dividing the interior into different spaces while preserving much of its original character.The building previously served as Keg and Case Market, a gathering place for local food vendors, small businesses and community events.Outlaw said the goal is to continue that community connection while introducing new opportunities for fitness, recreation and entertainment."We're going all in on social wellness," Outlaw said.The new facility will house Element Boxing and Fitness, offering a space for workouts and boxing training. The owners also envision hosting amateur boxing events and fight nights.Other amenities include a juice bar featuring St. Paul-based, Black-owned business Life Juice and a coffee shop. Floyd said he is also exploring the possibility of adding a sauna and cold plunge area.Former Viking joins the projectFor Floyd, the investment is an opportunity to give back to a community he knows well. Floyd said he has known Outlaw and his family since he was about 12 or 13 years old and has watched their involvement in community initiatives over the years.The former NFL receiver, who attended Cretin-Derham Hall High School in St. Paul, said the project's location made the opportunity especially meaningful."I've been so blessed in my life to fulfill my dreams of playing in the NFL that what I like to do now is to give back, but also to give back to certain individuals, especially like kids," Floyd said.He hopes the facility will become a welcoming destination for people of different ages and backgrounds, whether they are interested in fitness or simply looking for a place to connect.Sports lounge planned for private and public gatheringsOne of the building's main attractions is the Keg House Lounge, a sports viewing and social space featuring 12 televisions, including a 150-inch video wall, and seating for more than 75 people.The lounge also includes an upstairs private area that can be rented for corporate gatherings and other functions.The owners envision hosting watch parties for Vikings, Timberwolves, Wild and Twins games, along with other sporting events. However, the lounge's public access is still being developed.Floyd said some gatherings may initially be private or invitation-only, but the ownership group wants to work toward making the space accessible to the general public."I envision hosting both private, invite only gatherings and events that are open to the public. Building relationships and connecting with people is important to me. I want to get to know the community, meet new people, and create an environment where everyone feels welcome," Floyd told WCCO.The owners have not announced a finalized schedule for regular public access to the lounge.Outlaw said the larger vision includes creating opportunities for community members to gather for sporting events, live music, art crawls, vendor markets and other activities.The building also features an event center planned for weddings, celebrations and corporate functions, along with outdoor patios and green space.Grand opening weekend begins FridayKeg House Commons is preparing to welcome visitors during a series of grand opening events beginning Friday, Oct. 23.An open house is scheduled from 4 p.m. to 7 p.m. Friday, with plans to show the Timberwolves game in the sports lounge. An amateur boxing event is planned for Saturday, followed by a workout and Vikings game viewing event Sunday.The owners say additional programming and rental opportunities will be announced as the facility continues to develop.Outlaw hopes the new destination will attract both longtime neighborhood residents familiar with the former marketplace and people visiting the building for the first time."Come on in, come and check us, come say hello. Even if you stop by just to say hello, that's great for us," Outlaw said.

title: Sheetz is the 3rd best retail workplace in the country, Fortune says
description: Sheetz is the third best retail workplace in the country, according to a new ranking from Fortune.
content: Sheetz is the third best retail workplace in the country, according to a new ranking from Fortune. Fortune's Best Workplaces in Retail list places Sheetz only below Wegmans and Target. Sheetz says it's its 11th straight year on the list. According to the survey, Sheetz employees say they're encouraged to challenge the status quo and to try new things. The mentality of caring for others is "embodied from the top down," Fortune says. "Being recognized among the nation's leading companies for creating a positive workplace culture for more than a decade is an honor we don't take lightly," said Sheetz President and CEO Travis Sheetz in a press release. "Our employees are at the heart of everything we do, representing our brand and making a difference in the communities we serve every day. We're committed to creating an environment where our people feel valued, respected and empowered to build meaningful careers while living out our shared commitment to caring for others."Sheetz is based in Altoona but employs more than 30,000 people at over 850 stores in multiple states, including Michigan, West Virginia, Maryland, Ohio and North Carolina. Sheetz says it offers a benefits package to all employees, including medical and dental insurance, a 401(k), quarterly bonuses and vacation time. DICK'S Sporting Goods, which is based in Coraopolis, also made the list, coming in at No. 7. Great Place to Work has been surveying employees for 30 years, and in the last year, it surveyed 7.3 million people in the U.S. Out of the 1.3 million responses, nearly 76,000 were received from employees who were eligible for the Best Workplaces in Retail List.

title: Vegetation fire breaks out above UC Berkeley campus, 35 years after Oakland Hills firestorm
description: Fire crews stopped the forward progress of a fire that broke out in the hills above the UC Berkeley campus Tuesday morning.
content: Fire crews stopped the forward progress of a fire that broke out in the hills above the UC Berkeley campus Tuesday morning.According to the Berkeley Fire Department, the fire was reported on the 800 block of Panoramic Way around 11:40 a.m. At least 2 to 3 acres of vegetation were burned. Shortly after 2 p.m., Oakland Fire said crews were mopping up hot spots.Firefighters from Berkeley and Oakland, along with crews from Cal Fire and the Alameda County Fire Department, responded to the scene Tuesday afternoon. Firefighters say one structure had been damaged, but there were no immediate reports of injuries.A grim reminder 35 years to the dayWhile the fire didn't cause any tragedy, it did cause some trauma. Exactly 35 years ago to the day, the Oakland Hills firestorm destroyed thousands of homes and killed 25 people.Some of those who perished were Ronna Kabatznick's neighbors."My house burnt to the ground 35 years ago today. It's kind of in my blood. It just feels like I would know this day any time," she said.While she feels lucky to have survived that fire, she said seeing the smoke on Tuesday, on this of all days, triggered what she described as PTSD."It's kind of always with you. Everything we have is dated from that day on because everything burned, so I don't have a life before I was 40," she said. "That life burned."Most of Joe Garret's block also burned 35 years ago, but what he remembers most is the feeling of terror."Back then, the word went out that they were making the last stand at the Claremont Hotel. The fire chief said if the Claremont burned, there was so much wood in the air and embers that it would burn to the bay. Imagine how scary that was."

title: French government extends curfews after riots sweep across the country
description: French authorities are extending curfews and increasing the police presence in public spaces as President Emmanuel Macron's government tries to regain control after rioters torched buildings and looted thousands of businesses this weekend.
content: French authorities are extending curfews and increasing the police presence in public spaces as President Emmanuel Macron's government tries to regain control after rioters torched buildings and looted thousands of businesses this weekend. But addressing the problems that have brought students and workers to the streets for the last five weeks will be a tougher proposition. Protesters are demanding better schools and relief from rising living costs, while the government faces mounting debt and a fractured parliament that makes even passing a budget difficult.More police and curfewsPrime Minister Sébastien Lecornu promised a "massive" police deployment Tuesday ahead of the next demonstrations scheduled for Oct. 24. The announcement followed Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez's acknowledgment that authorities had underestimated the unrest and lost control in some cities during Saturday's protests. More than 2,500 people had been taken into police custody by Monday evening, Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said, after violence that included the burning of a historic town hall in Limoges, a city in central France. Overnight curfews have been imposed around Paris' Place de la République and Les Halles shopping district, with restrictions also introduced in Lyon and other cities. Paris and Lyon reported no major incidents Monday night, and authorities are extending the measures.In an address Sunday, Macron distinguished between the peaceful protests for better schools and working conditions and the rioters who he said hijacked those protests, saying that the government would both listen to the protesters' demands and punish rioters. He blamed "radical far-left groups" and "criminals" for the violence and said that "those who sought to bring down the republic will be held accountable."Political gridlock and financial pressureThe protests began in mid-September when high school students and teachers in the suburbs of Paris called for changes to overcrowded classrooms, deteriorating buildings and teacher shortages. They have since drawn in trade unions and Yellow Vest activists, a French grassroots organizing group, becoming a broader movement against high living costs and declining public services.The government has offered some concessions. On Oct. 8, the Ministry of National Education announced plans to deploy more than 3,000 substitute teachers to high schools most in need, and authorized several hundred additional hires. But worsening financial pressure and political gridlock make more comprehensive changes more difficult. France's public debt stood at nearly 3.6 trillion euros at the end of June, equivalent to 119% of its annual economic output, according to the national statistics agency.The government expects this year's deficit to reach 5.4% of economic output and is trying to reduce it to 5% in 2027. Interest payments alone are projected to rise by 12 billion euros next year, to 91.2 billion euros, further squeezing the money available for public services.Macron's allies also lack a majority in the French parliament. This year's budget was adopted only in February, after the government pushed it through without a final vote on the bill, which survived two no-confidence motions.An Ipsos poll conducted Oct. 7-8 put Macron's approval rating at just 15%. A September Ipsos poll put Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally party, well ahead of the field, with 33% to 35% support in different first-round matchups. Former Prime Minister Édouard Philippe and Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the far-left party La France Insoumise, were among those vying for second place.In April, France will hold presidential elections to choose a successor to Macron, who cannot run for a third term.

title: North Central College changing name to North Central University Naperville in July 2027
description: A private college in Chicago's western suburbs is getting a new name. Starting in July, North Central College will change its name to North Central University Naperville.
content: A private college in Chicago's western suburbs is getting a new name.Starting in July, North Central College will change its name to North Central University Naperville.The school's board of trustees approved the name change on Thursday. The renaming is the 165-year-old university's attempt to rebrand.In a statement, North Central President AbiÃ³dÃºn "G-P" GÃ²kÃ¨-ParÃ­olÃ¡ said the "university" designation better reflects the school's academic profile. Naperville was also added because the suburb where North Central is located is "one of the nation's most respected communities.""In many ways, the institution has already become what the new name reflects. The name is simply catching up to the reality of who we are and the opportunities we provide our students," GÃ²kÃ¨-ParÃ­olÃ¡ wrote in a letter to students and staff.The school has changed its name twice before. It was founded as Plainfield College in 1971, changed its name to North-Western College in 1864, and then to North Central College in 1926.The school plans to develop an updated logo and other marketing materials in the coming months to accompany the launch of its new name.

title: University of Illinois Chicago report puts $1 billion price tag on recidivism in North Lawndale neighborhood
description: A new report finds repeat incarceration in one Chicago neighborhood has cost Illinois taxpayers more than $1 billion, but researchers say there's an easy way to break that cycle.
content: A new report finds repeat incarceration in one Chicago neighborhood has cost Illinois taxpayers more than $1 billion, but researchers say there's an easy way to break that cycle. A new report from the University of Illinois Chicago is putting a billion-dollar price tag on recidivism, or the cost of people returning to prison after they've been released, in the North Lawndale community. "They've made a mistake, they've served their time, they've re-entered back into society, but they can't find work," said Brenda Palms, president and CEO of the North Lawndale Employment Network. "It's not that people don't want to work, but they actually have significant challenges to employment."Palms said the North Lawndale Employment Network has had the pleasure of training more than 20,000 job seekers returning from incarceration through their "Sweet Beginnings" program over the last 25 years. "Growth takes time, but we are making progress," she said.Palms is no stranger to the barriers uncovered by UIC's Great Cities Institute, which examined more than two decades of data on employment, incarceration and economic conditions in North Lawndale.Researchers found that between 2005 and 2024, recidivism among North Lawndale residents cost Illinois taxpayers at least $1 billion.The recidivism rate in North Lawndale during that time was at 92 percent, one of the highest for any Chicago community area.The average cost of incarceration was about $45,000 per person per year."I think don't we necessarily realize what has been the fiscal impact of incarceration," said Great Cities Institute director Teresa CÃ³rdova.She helped present the researchers' findings at the City Club of Chicago on Tuesday, with a focus on how investments in community-based employment, social enterprise, and re-entry supports can generate outsized returns. "Our primary goal is how can we be of use?" she said.For example, the Sweet Beginnings program shows significantly lower recidivism ratesâbelow 10% for participants. Researchers also found, for every $1 invested in these kinds of programs, an estimated $5.60 in social and economic value is generated."That will save us as taxpayers money in the long run. So, money is better spent when it's reinvested in communities," CÃ³rdova said.The report's authors said nearly 40% of people released from Illinois state prisons return to Chicago â many to already disinvested West and South Sides of the city.

title: The NFL says it's "confident" with security plans for the Steelers-Saints game in Paris
description: Peter O'Reilly, who oversees international events for the NFL, said the league is being "very vigilant" in its approach to this weekend's game.
content: The National Football League said it is confident with its security plans for the upcoming game between the Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints that's being played in Paris this weekend, amid ongoing unrest and violence throughout the French capital. "All of our plans for the Paris game this weekend are moving forward as planned," said Peter O'Reilly, executive vice president of club business, international and league events for the NFL, in a briefing Tuesday. O'Reilly said that the NFL's operational and security personnel have been in Paris for around 10 days and are working closely with the French authorities, as well as the U.S. Department of State."Obviously taking, being very vigilant in everything we do and all of our planning," O'Reilly said, adding that the league is monitoring things on an hour-by-hour basis and communicating with the teams.The New Orleans Saints have already arrived in Paris, while the Steelers are due to travel to the French capital later this week."We've got confidence in the plans, both from an ops and a security standpoint," O'Reilly said, noting that other major events are being held in Paris this week, such as a UEFA Champions League soccer match between Paris Saint-Germain and Barcelona on Tuesday evening.At least 1,800 people were arrested this past weekend after violent groups clashed with law enforcement during nationwide protests over rising living costs and poor school conditions. Paris police said Sunday that 855 people were arrested in the French capital region alone.Looting and damage were reported around the Place de la République square, which is located around 5 miles south of the Stade de France, the site of Sunday's game. In a press conference on Monday, Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy said he's "obviously very aware" of the unrest in Paris and has been in contact with the league. "We feel like we have a really good plan, we're aware of the situations over there and have a lot of confidence in our plan," McCarthy said. Sunday's game will be the first-ever NFL game played in France.

title: Penn-North Metro Station closed for hours after shooting leaves man injured
description: Baltimore's Penn-North Metro Station was closed for several hours Tuesday after a man was injured in a nearby shooting, according to Maryland Transit Police.
content: Baltimore's Penn-North Metro Station was closed for several hours Tuesday after a man was injured in a nearby shooting, according to Maryland Transit Police.Officers responded around 1:10 p.m. to a report of a shooting near the station, where they found a man suffering from a gunshot wound.Police said the man was conscious and alert when he was taken to a nearby hospital. He is expected to survive.Investigators are reviewing surveillance video and interviewing witnesses to determine what led to the shooting.The Penn-North station reopened around 4 p.m. While it was closed, subway trains bypassed the station.

title: "Forever chemicals" detected at all 20 Georgia water testing sites in new report
description: The Environment Georgia Research & Policy Center presented findings from a recent report examining PFAS contamination in Georgia's waterways.
content: The Environment Georgia Research & Policy Center presented findings from a recent report examining PFAS contamination in Georgia's waterways.The report, produced with Frontier Group, draws on testing data collected from 2022 through 2024 through the Environmental Protection Agency's Water Quality Portal and local riverkeepers. Environmental advocates said the findings underscore the need for more research, resources and legislative action, including the PFAS Transparency Act.PFAS were detected at all 20 Georgia testing locations included in the report. As many as 17 different PFAS compounds were detected at one or more sites, according to the groups.The report, titled "PFAS in America's Rivers and Lakes," covers 40 states. Its findings do not include all available PFAS testing data, and many waterways have not been tested, the groups said.PFAS, often called "forever chemicals," are used in products such as nonstick cookware, food packaging and waterproof clothing. According to the report, they can enter waterways through industrial and sewage treatment plant discharges, firefighting foam and contaminated sewage sludge spread on farmland.During Tuesday's news conference, Environment Georgia Research & Policy Center State Director Jennette Gayer said contamination is widespread."PFAS has been linked to a wide range of health impacts including decreased fertility, developmental delays in children, compromised immunity and some types of cancer," Gayer said.The groups said people can be exposed by consuming contaminated water or fish."Standing in the middle of a Georgia river or stream and trying to hook a fish with nothing but a rod, reel and fly is a challenge that Georgia's anglers treasure," said Mike Greenman, president of the Atlanta Fly Fishing Club.Greenman said PFAS contamination threatens fishing, future generations and the recreation spending anglers bring to Georgia.Jason Ulseth, riverkeeper and executive director of Chattahoochee Riverkeeper, said recent sampling found contamination in the Chattahoochee River."There is no denying that PFAS contamination is a national crisis," Ulseth said. "Our latest sampling confirms that it is in the Chattahoochee and I know our fellow Riverkeepers have found similar problems in other rivers around the state."Microplastics in Georgia's waterways were also raised as a concern during the news conference.The groups are calling for potential polluters to notify treatment facilities about PFAS in their discharges, a phaseout of PFAS use, and restrictions on industrial discharges into rivers and sewage treatment plants. They also want an end to spreading PFAS-contaminated sewage sludge on farmland.

title: Teen arrested after homeless woman stabbed to death in Roseville, police say
description: A 15-year-old boy has been arrested after a woman was stabbed to death in Roseville this week, officials said Friday.
content: A 15-year-old boy was arrested last week after a woman was stabbed to death in Roseville, officials said.According to the Placer County District Attorney's Office, upon our request, the suspect was identified as 15-year-old James "Jimmy" Wong, whom they say has since made his first appearance in juvenile court and is charged with first-degree murder.The Roseville Police Department said officers were called around 1 a.m. on Oct. 14 to the area of Atlantic Street and South Grant Street after receiving a report that someone had been stabbed.Officers arrived to find a woman dead at the scene. The Placer County Sheriff's Office has identified the woman as 57-year-old Cherie Dodge, who was homeless.Dodge was a mother of five, with 10 grandchildren and one great-grandchild. She was fatally stabbed while sleeping on a bench near Atlantic and South Grant streets.That bench is now a heart-breaking tribute to a woman family members say "was more than just a homeless person.""She was a person. She was a human being, you know? She didn't deserve anything like that," granddaughter Laila Brandt said.Roseville police said detectives gathered a variety of evidence and leads that helped identify a person of interest. Detectives obtained and then served a search warrant at the teen suspect's home on Buckley Court early Friday morning.The teen was then taken into custody and has been booked into Placer County Juvenile Hall.Family members now want justice and action to protect others living on the street."I'm coming at Placer County. I'm coming at the city police department. I'm coming at anyone who can make a difference in this case right now because this means everything to our family," son Charles Rodriguez said. "It's something no one should have to think about."Roseville police said there are no outstanding suspects in the case and noted that there doesn't appear to be any known connection between Dodge and her suspected killer.

title: Porto's Bakery announces first ever Inland Empire location
description: The Inland Empire will soon be home to one of Southern California's most iconic bakeries after Porto's Bakery & Cafe announced plans to open in Ontario as soon as 2028.
content: The Inland Empire will soon be home to one of Southern California's most iconic bakeries after Porto's Bakery & Cafe announced plans to open in Ontario as soon as 2028. In a press release shared hours after teasing the IE shop on Instagram, Porto's Bakery officials said the location would open at the southwest corner of Archibald Avenue and Inland Empire Boulevard, where a new commercial development is slated for construction. "The City of Ontario has been working to bring Porto's to our community for nearly a decade, and we're proud they chose Ontario for their first Inland Empire location," said a statement from Ontario City Manager Scott Ochoa. "Porto's has a strong regional following. As Ontario grows as a destination, businesses like this give residents and visitors more reasons to spend time here, supporting our local economy and the broader community."Porto's was founded in 1960 by Rosa Porto and quickly became a Southern California staple thanks to baked delicacies, including pastries and cakes, as well as coffee and meals for breakfast, lunch and dinner. After serving the area for more than six decades and now operating multiple locations, the bakery still relies on its Cuban roots and classics like the Cheese Roll and Potato Ball to draw crowds daily. "For our family, this is a meaningful moment," said a statement from Beatriz "Betty" Porto, the owner and Vice President of Community Affairs. "For years, we've met families from across the Inland Empire who have made the trip to visit our bakeries and shared how much they hoped we would one day be closer to home. We're grateful for the support we've received and excited to become part of Ontario."Porto's currently operates locations in Glendale, Burbank, Downey, Buena Park and Northridge. Along with the new Ontario location, the company is also developing a store in the Downtown Downey District. "For years, we've welcomed guests from across the Inland Empire who have traveled to visit our bakeries, and we're excited to finally have a home here," said Raul Porto, Porto's CEO, in a statement. "Porto's has a strong regional following. As Ontario grows as a destination, businesses like this give residents and visitors more reasons to spend time here, supporting our local economy and the broader community."The new Porto's location will be part of the new 8.6-acre commercial development at the corner of Archibald and Inland Empire Ave., near the Capital City Entertainment District, which will also include 50,000 feet of commercial space designated for restaurant, cafe and retail uses, according to Ontario city officials. Construction on the project is slated to begin in 2027, with the bakery projected to open as soon as 2028.

title: South Los Angeles hit-and-run driver arrested for killing 83-year-old community icon
description: Los Angeles police have arrested a hit-and-run driver who allegedly fatally struck an 83-year-old South Los Angeles community icon in September.
content: Los Angeles police have arrested a hit-and-run driver who allegedly fatally struck an 83-year-old South Los Angeles community icon in September. In a news release shared Tuesday, October 20, LAPD detectives said that 29-year-old John Anthony Cardenas was arrested near his place of work in Carson following an investigation that spanned nearly a month after the deadly crash on September 30. Police were called to the intersection of 69th Street and South Central Avenue at around 8:45 p.m. that day upon learning of a crash involving a pedestrian. Upon arrival, they learned that 83-year-old Akil Saud Batani-Khalfani, known by loved ones as Bird, was walking across the street when he was allegedly struck by a dark blue four-door sedan driving through the intersection. Los Angeles Fire Department paramedics pronounced him dead at the scene. Instead of stopping to help Batani-Khalfani, police alleged that Cardenas continued driving, fleeing the scene of the hit-and-run crash. After Cardenas was arrested, LAPD Central Traffic Division detectives executed a search warrant at his home, where they located and impounded the vehicle that was allegedly involved in the deadly crash. He was booked on suspicion of hit-and-run resulting in death and was held in lieu of $1 million bail, police said. In the days following Batani-Khalfani's death, community members held a vigil to honor the man who had lived in the area since the 1940s. "For him to be taken from, you know, what he wanted; he wanted to die in his home, and that would've been okay with me," said D'ixara Batani-Khalfani, Bird's daughter and one of 15 children he left behind. "But for him to be taken from out on these streets? That's not okay. Not okay with me at all."Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass also shared a statement after his death, calling him a community leader, historian, author and neighborhood advocate. "His loss is felt deeply by his family and the many people whose lives he touched. My heart is with his children, grandchildren, and loved ones as they mourn this devastating loss," Bass' statement said. "My office has been in communication with Bird's family and has connected them with services."As LAPD detectives continue investigating the crash, anyone with more information was urged to contact Central Traffic Division Investigator A. Leon at 213-833-3713.

title: Runway at Midway Airport temporarily closed for safety repairs, CDA says
description: Runway 22L is now closed to arrivals and departures for repairs to a runway safety system.
author_name: Jeramie  Bizzle, Victor  Jacobo, Asal  Rezaei
content: A runway at Midway International Airport has been temporarily closed for safety repairs, the Chicago Department of Aviation announced this week.Runway 22L is now closed to arrivals and departures for repairs to a runway safety system that helps stop airplanes from going off the runway.According to the department, the Engineered Materials Arresting System (EMAS) at the departure end of the runway was damaged by recent aircraft activity, including jet blast.The safety system on which crews must make repairs was installed after an accident in 2005, which claimed the life of a 6-year-old boy named Joshua Woods. A jetliner, Southwest Airlines Flight 1248, was trying to land in heavy snow when it slid off the runway and onto a busy street."Safety is the top priority at Chicago's airports, and we are working to complete these repairs safely and promptly," said CDA Commissioner Michael McMurray. "We're coordinating closely with our partners at the FAA and the airlines to reduce disruptions for travelers and return the airfield to normal operating conditions as quickly and safely as possible."Transportation expert Joe Schwieterman with DePaul University said no other airport in the U.S. relies on the system more than Midway. He added that, with Midway being located in a densely populated area, it elevates the importance of a working EMAS."You have the relatively short runway, high-intensity flight operations, residential neighborhoods right next to the airport so having that crumbling surface that can bring an airplane to a stop ... really important," he said.The CDA says the closure could cause flight delays and cancellations, with the extent varying based on airline schedules and weather conditions â particularly wind directions.CBS News Chicago Travel Editor Peter Greenberg says it's not going to be possible delays, but probable delays. "Unless the airlines voluntarily and proactively change their schedules, you better build an hour to an hour and a half delay on every flight and that's being mild," he said.Travelers are being advised to continue monitoring their flight status and check with their airline before heading to the airport. Those impacted should work directly with their air carrier about rebooking or other changes."You throw in some bad weather, the heavy traffic of Thanksgiving, where flight activity picks up and you are going to have some pain points there. Let's hope it's manageable. It's pretty unclear now just how this is going to play out," Schwieterman said.The department said it will coordinate closely with the Federal Aviation Administration and airlines operating at Midway to minimize operational impacts whenever possible and keep partners informed throughout the repair process.The repairs are expected to be complete by mid-November.

title: Trump says U.S. will compensate fraud whistleblowers, and he'll decide who gets paid: "I will be very generous"
description: President Trump said successful whistleblowers will get 1% of any fraud they report, although there may be limits.
content: Washington — President Trump on Tuesday announced the federal government will compensate whistleblowers who report people defrauding the U.S. government and taxpayers, but said he will decide who gets paid. "I will be the arbitrator of all of these decisions," the president said during his Oval Office announcement with Vice President JD Vance, who heads up the administration's fraud task force, beside him. "In other words, I'll determine whether or not the person is deserving and I'll determine — and I will be very generous, believe me." Through the Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program, Mr. Trump said whistleblowers, who can be ordinary citizens, will be eligible to receive 1% of the amount of fraud they report, even if the reported fraud is $100 billion. America.gov/fraud, however, says successful whistleblowers will be paid up to $30,000, dependent upon the report resulting in criminal charges. Asked by CBS News for clarification, Mr. Trump said there is no limit to whistleblower compensation, and criminal charges aren't necessary. "That's the answer. I quit while I'm ahead," Vance joked. The president promised to be "fair" in his decisions. "You'll get your money immediately, but I'll make the determination," he continued. "So if two people are fighting over it, maybe they'll split it or maybe whatever, but I'll make that determination."The America.gov/fraud website says reports are encrypted and will go directly to the Treasury Department. It's not immediately clear who reviews reports, although the Department of Justice will administer the program. The first person to benefit from the program is Nick Shirley, a 20-something YouTuber who published a video alleging fraud at childcare centers in Minnesota. He stood alongside Mr. Trump in the Oval Office Tuesday and was presented with a $10,000 check.Some whistleblowers can already receive compensation from the False Claims Act, which allows some whistleblowers to be entitled to up to 25% to 30% of proceeds recovered. But the requirements are stringent. Vance said "99%" of the fraud they're finding isn't covered by the False Claims Act.Naomi Seligman, president of nonprofit Whistleblower Aid, was skeptical of Mr. Trump's announcement, saying the president "is more interested in hunting down whistleblowers.""If the president is truly interested in rooting out wrongdoing, Whistleblower Aid invites him to start by examining the violations perpetrated by his own administration, including senior officials," she said in a statement. "We would happily work with him on this vital accountability effort to help save our democracy."

title: NBA season tips off with Pistons rallying to beat Celtics 121-113
description: Javonte Green scored 19 points after not playing in the first half and Cade Cunningham finished with 22 points and eight assists, helping the Detroit Pistons come back and beat the Boston Celtics 121-113.
content: Javonte Green scored 19 points after not playing in the first half and Cade Cunningham finished with 22 points and eight assists, helping the Detroit Pistons come back and beat the Boston Celtics 121-113 on Tuesday.The NBA picked the matinee matchup to tip off the season and it delivered plenty of entertainment.Paul George scored 38 points, the most by a Celtic in his debut. The nine-time All-Star, in his 17th season, showed he's still got it in his first game with Boston since it acquired him from Philadelphia in exchange for 2024 NBA Finals MVP Jaylen Brown.Jayson Tatum, though, was off his game.He missed 17 of 23 shots had 13 points and 11 assists. His lack of hustle on defense allowed Green to take his time for a fifth 3-pointer that gave the Pistons a 13-point lead with 3:33 left.Tatum, a six-time All-Star, is set to play his first full season since tearing his Achilles tendon in May 2025.Boston took its biggest lead early in the third quarter at 72-50 after George made three 3-pointers in less than a minute.Detroit cut its deficit to six points after three quarters and surged ahead in the fourth. Green made a go-ahead 3, Duren added a three-point play and Robinson connected on a 3 to put the Pistons ahead 107-99 with 5:10 to go.Jalen Duren had 22 points and nine rebounds, Duncan Robinson scored 21 points â making 5 of 9 3-pointers â and Ausar Thompson added 11 points and 11 rebounds for the Pistons.Boston's Derrick White and Payton Pritchard scored 17 points apiece.Celtics: Host the New York Knicks on Friday.Pistons: At Miami on Friday.___See AP's full NBA coverage here

title: Steve Hilton says California is ready for change as Election Day approaches
description: During a brief stop at one of the most iconic San Francisco viewpoints, the Marin Headlands, gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton was glad to meet some of his supporters and introduce himself to some visiting the Golden State.
content: During a brief stop at one of the most iconic San Francisco viewpoints, the Marin Headlands, gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton was glad to meet some of his supporters and introduce himself to some visiting the Golden State."See, when I'm governor, lots more people will be coming here," he said. "Including all the people who moved out, because it'll be easier to live here. Lower taxes, cheaper gas â that's what's going to be happening. California will be the place to be."Hilton is looking to be the first Republican elected to statewide office since 2006."Enough is enough," he said. "Sixteen years of doing it one way, I think it's time to try something different."He says that as governor, he would bring practical solutions to the state's problems, from lowering energy bills to making California more business-friendly."I think we've been putting out very simple, positive, practical plans that are solutions to our problems â $3 gas, your first $150,000 tax-free, capping vehicle registration at $73 for your car or your truck, eliminating mass homelessness by the end of my first year, and we have plans to deliver all of that," Hilton said. Hilton said that those are not ideological or divisive, but rather partisan ideas."They're just practical solutions that everybody can get behind," he said. "I'm very much looking forward to working with anyone who wants to work with me. I'm not an ideologue, I'm not going to take orders from the White House, I'm not going to take orders from Sacramento, I'm an outsider who wants to shake up the system that is obviously not working."With two weeks until the election, Hilton is in the home stretch of an uphill battle. His challenger, Democrat Xavier Becerra, has a 25.6-point advantage among likely voters, per a recent poll from Activote."That's a completely made-up poll. That's an online survey of 400 people where you have to download the app, so that you shouldn't take seriously at all," Hilton said. "More seriously, you've got the establishment polls in California, like PPIC and the Institute of Government at Berkeley, and, you're right, they show the same kind of gap that we've had for 20 years in California. But, they have a particular model of the electorate of who is going to show up and vote that, frankly, I don't think captures the energy of this moment."Other polls show similar outlooks, with expected support for each candidate along party lines."If you're going to win statewide in California as a Republican, you've got to do two big things: lock down your base, number one, and then persuade enough Independents and yes even some Democrats, to come to your side," said Gary Dietrich, senior political analyst for CBS News Sacramento. "Is he able to pull more voters above that Republican base number?"That answer will come on Election Day, which will produce revealing results, says Dietrich."Hilton is right when he says, voters agree with him on many key issues. It's just that they aren't ready to put the stamp of approval on a Republican candidate," Dietrich said. "I think people are going to be watching these numbers very carefully for a trend line in California. Is California beginning to trend more purple when it's been thought of as deep blue?"Hilton is endorsed by President Trump. When asked if he believes the endorsement was beneficial or detrimental to his candidacy?"Remember, I didn't ask for his endorsement. It was a great surprise to receive it, but yeah, I'm honored to have it. I'm a new American citizen. To be endorsed by the President of the United States, on a personal level, I think everyone would treat that as something that they would be proud to have, whoever the president is, as an immigrant," Hilton said. "But I think the question about President Trump, It's interesting. I only really ever get asked it by people in the media. It's never once come up in any of the hundreds of town halls that we've done up and down the state."Caroline Heldman, a professor of politics at Occidental College, believes the gap between Hilton and Becerra is too big to close."Steve Hilton, in a different time, may have been a much better candidate. But in the era of Trump, Californians are just absolutely not going to elect a Republican in the highest seat," she said. "His only path to winning was with independents, but the split with independents in California also favors Becerra about 2-1."Regarding his opponent, Becerra, Hilton said, "He's taking this election for granted. He's not putting out any solutions to anything. He's going to be four more years of the same," Hilton said. "I want everyone to really understand that we can change things. We don't have to put up with what we've got. We can aim for something better."The last Republican to be elected governor in California was Arnold Schwarzenegger back in 2006. He won re-election by a margin of about 1.5 million votes.

title: Tarrant County Jail faces scrutiny after 7th inmate death; sheriff says he's a victim of transparency
description: It has a county commissioner calling for an investigation, but the sheriff says none of the inmate deaths this year have been attributed to abuse or neglect.
content: For the third time since August and the seventh time this year, a Tarrant County Jail inmate has died while in custody. It has a county commissioner calling for an investigation, but the sheriff says none of the inmate deaths this year have been attributed to abuse or neglect. Video from inside the Tarrant County Jail shows guards removing 46-year-old inmate Mack Greer from his cell back in June and transporting him on a gurney to JPS hospital, where he would later die. Greer, who had been arrested for theft, acted erratically in the days before, according to Tarrant County Sheriff Bill Waybourn. "After he was in general population for a little bit, he banged his head," said Waybourn. "He intentionally banged his head a little bit, didn't hurt himself.""While in that custody, he suffered fatal head injuries," Tarrant County Commissioner Alisa Simmons said in a statement days after Greer's death.Simmons'comments infuriated Waybourn, who said they improperly suggested that Greer died from abuse. Tuesday, the sheriff announced an autopsy found that Greer actually died from an undiagnosed medical condition. "There's a lot of times that somebody walks into the jail, they're horribly sick," Waybourn said. Waybourn is defending his operation of the jail after the death on Sunday of 41-year-old Broshundrick McNeal. She was incarcerated after being arrested earlier this month for aggravated assault. McNeal is the seventh Tarrant County Jail inmate to die in custody this year. The cause of her death and that of two others remains undetermined, and there are renewed calls for an outside investigation. Waybourn says Tarrant County believes the scrutiny he is facing over in-custody deaths is unfair. He says other county jails in Texas, such as Harris, Bexar and Dallas, have had more jail deaths since he took office in 2017. Texas jail deaths by county since 2017:Harris: 149Bexar: 115Dallas: 85Tarrant: 79"Well, I think one of the appearances is because we're one of the very few major counties that sends out a press release when we have a death in custody, and we've been doing that for several years," said Waybourn.Waybourn accuses his critics of politicizing a problem that all jails face, and that he's a victim of being more transparent than other sheriffs.

title: Bank scam in Anne Arundel County has victims withdraw funds, then pick the money up at homes, police say
description: Anne Arundel County police have warned residents about a phone scheme in which scammers persuade people to withdraw money from their bank accounts.
content: Anne Arundel County police are warning residents about a phone scam in which callers posing as bank employees convince victims to withdraw money from their accounts before arranging for a rideshare driver to pick up the cash from their homes.The scammers often claim to work in a bank's fraud department and use high-pressure tactics to convince victims their money is at risk, according to the Anne Arundel County Police Department.Victims are told someone has tried to access their debit card or bank accounts and that they must withdraw their money immediately to protect it.Some victims told police the phone number displayed on their caller ID matched the number printed on their debit cards, making the calls appear legitimate.Once the victims withdraw their money, the scammers arrange for a rideshare driver to collect the cash from their homes."They'll say, 'Hey, we're with the fraud department, your debit card is being used or accessed, and in addition to your debit card, people are trying to gain access to your savings account,'" Anne Arundel County police spokesperson Justin Mulcahy said."They keep them on the phone and then they're even using rideshares to come to the house to get the money," Mulcahy said.How to avoid scamsPolice say there are a few steps community members can take to avoid phone scams. Follow the Golden Rule. Bank institutions will never ask for immediate payment over the phone or in-person. They will also never ask you to move money to another account to protect it. Demands for immediate paymentPolice warn that a demand for urgency in payment could be a red flag, especially through untraceable methods such as gift cards, cryptocurrency, or wire transfers.High preassure threatsScammers may threaten victims with immediate arrest if they hang up. SecrecyScammers will tell victims not to talk to family, friends, or even their bank.The "stay on the line" tacticVictims are kept on the phone for long periods of time so they can't hang up and call for help.Stop. Breathe. Don't Panic Scammers want victims to act emotionally. Taking 10 seconds to pause before reacting can make a difference.Resist the PressureIf it is legitimate, it will rarely if ever require a fast decision. Take notes and hang upWrite down the caller's name and why they claimed to call. Then, end the call.Get helpCall someone you trust to get the answers you need.Keep your information privateNever give out your social security number, bank information, or passwords to anyone over the phone.Report the incidentIf you are a victim of a scam or an attempted scam, report it promptly to the police and your bank. "What they are preying on is your vulnerability, your emotions, your stress, your anxiety," Mulcahy said. "So we ask people to kind of slow it down at that point and the best thing to do is document and call your bank."Senior citizens are often targeted by scammers, but police warn that anyone can become a victim."It's high-pressure, it's immediate payment requests," Mulcahy said. "Those are your immediate red flags, when someone is pressuring you to withdraw money right away."

title: After grieving her father, this estate lawyer went through death doula training to better serve clients
description: A Minnesota estate lawyer is taking a different approach to her practice, hiring a death doula grief specialist to train her team to be better prepared for having tough conversations.
content: A Minnesota estate lawyer is taking a different approach to her practice, hiring a death doula grief specialist to train her team to be better prepared for having tough conversations.In law school, Rachel Schromen said she was trained to "get the facts" and "weed out the emotion." But as an attorney, she got a new perspective when she became a client."That was a huge eye-opener because sitting in that grief, that was really personal to me. I wasn't an estate planning attorney; I was a grieving daughter," she said.Schromen lost her father in 2019 on his 70th birthday. She described him as a "cowboy boot-wearing Harley rider" who was also "really sensitive" and sentimental. With new loss and new perspective, Schromen made a decision that her law firm would not avoid her clients' emotions, and instead, they would acknowledge them. She hired a death doula grief specialist to make sure her team was educated in sensitivity. She flipped the script on estate planning and loss."I think we just take our time a little more with conversations. When I'm meeting with clients, I feel like I'm just more aware emotionally, visually, energetically," she said. "We try to open it with that so they feel comfortable and also feel safe to let emotions and things come up during the meeting naturally and organically. And they feel seen and heard in their pain."Schromen Law has also started offering clients sessions with a grief consultant to help them navigate the days ahead.

title: Atlanta bridge closed after vehicle damages water line, causes supporting structure to collapse
description: The Moores Mill Road bridge over Peachtree Creek will remain closed through at least Oct. 26 after an overnight water valve failure caused a supporting wall to collapse and damaged the bridge
content: A heavy vehicle struck the Moores Mill Road bridge over Peachtree Creek, damaging a water line and causing part of the bridge's supporting structure to collapse, Atlanta officials said in an update.The bridge remains closed while crews assess the damage and determine what repairs are needed, according to the Atlanta Department of Watershed Management. The department did not provide a reopening date.The latest account differs from an earlier explanation by Atlanta City Councilmember Dustin Hillis, who said an overnight water valve failure caused a supporting wall to collapse. Hillis had said the bridge would remain closed through at least Oct. 26.Watershed Management and Atlanta Department of Transportation crews are on-site assessing the structural and water line damage and investigating the circumstances.Moores Mill Road bridge detoursOfficials provided the following routes:Eastbound: Turn left onto Ridgewood Road NW, right onto West Wesley Road NW and left onto Moores Mill Road NW.Westbound: Turn right onto West Wesley Road NW, left onto Ridgewood Road NW and right onto Moores Mill Road NW.Drivers should allow extra travel time and follow posted signs and new traffic patterns while the bridge is closed.The bridge is more than 100 years old, according to Hillis. He previously said replacement remains a priority for Districts 9 and 8, even if the bridge can reopen or be repaired.

title: Baltimore County man pleads guilty to vandalizing Jewish cemetery with antisemitic symbols
description: A Baltimore County man pleaded guilty to federal charges for vandalizing a Jewish cemetery in 2023.
content: A Baltimore County man pleaded guilty to federal charges after vandalizing a Jewish cemetery in Dundalk in 2023, federal prosecutors said.George Horn, 36, of Dundalk, admitted to spray-painting swastikas and other symbols on multiple headstones at Ohr Knesseth Israel Anshe Sfard Cemetery in July 2023.According to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Maryland, Horn said he targeted the cemetery "because it is a Jewish cemetery."Horn was arrested and charged with religious vandalism.According to his guilty plea, Horn used black spray paint to deface 12 gravestones. Court records also documented his antisemitic animus toward Jewish people.Investigators found antisemitic messages and other items in Horn's car and storage unit, including a journal containing references to Nazism and white supremacy. Authorities also found a nine-second video on his phone showing Horn spray-painting two gravestones, along with a translated copy of Adolf Hitler's autobiographical manifesto, Mein Kampf.Federal officials said the cemetery, located in Dundalk, was established in the late 19th century.Horn is scheduled to be sentenced on Thursday, Jan. 14, 2027. He faces a maximum sentence of three years in prison for damaging religious property.

title: Diners pack Sign of the Beefcarver ahead of restaurant's closing
description: A long line of customers wraps around the red brick building on Woodward Avenue on Tuesday, for one more chance to dine at Sign of the Beefcarver.
content: After nearly 70 years, an iconic Metro Detroit restaurant is closing its doors.The owners of Sign of the Beefcarver in Royal Oak made that announcement over the weekend.At its height, there were 23 locations, including some in Chicago, but now the final and original location is shutting down operations at the end of the week.A long line of customers wraps around the red brick building on Woodward Avenue on Tuesday, for one more chance to dine at Sign of the Beefcarver.Restaurant vice president Joseph Joliet greets guests at the door.He promises they won't run out of roast beef."We have ordered extra all week, and we're going to do our best to make sure that everybody has a very fond final memory of us," Joseph Joliet said.Joliet's father, Jay Joliet, the company's CEO, checks in with staff and patrons at the register.He explains what inspired his father to open the restaurant in 1957."He was trying to find a restaurant that was different than every other short-order restaurant. We fell onto the idea of a cafeteria style, but not a cafeteria, a beef buffet, and that's where this all started," Jay Joliet said.While the restaurant has maintained the model and level of service over the years, "These are the original recipes from 57 years ago. Some have evolved. Some are, but the roast beef is roast beef, and it's been slow roasted since day one," Jay Joliet said.The owners say attracting new consumers has been challenging."We tried to increase our social media marketing and presence. We tried to incorporate DoorDash delivery. We were cutting some of our costs and updating some of our expenses and that sort of thing, and we made a big improvement, but it just wasn't enough," Joseph Joliet said.Joseph Joliet says since the COVID-19 shutdown, it's been hard to keep their head above water."We've never recovered to our customer turnout that we did before 2020, and every single cost on our balance sheet went up significantly since then," Joseph Joliet said.He says the extreme financial pressure from rising food costs, including the historically high price of roast beef, has made the business unsustainable."We get updates from our suppliers multiple times a week, saying what the cost per pound is, and each of our roast beef rounds starts at 60 to 70 pounds. So, that is a very big, significant part of our food costs. But also, the milk is more expensive, the cheese is more expensive, the bread is more expensive. It is, it is all the things," Joseph Joliet said.Since the announcement, there's been an overwhelming amount of support from the community."I wish that they would have started coming five years ago, but at the same time, some of the comments about people that worked here, people that their first job, they've been coming here since they were a child, and now they're in their 70s. It's absolutely heartwarming," Jay Joliet said.And while Joseph Joliet is disappointed, he won't be able to pass along the business to his children."We used to eat at the Bloomfield location every Sunday after church growing up, and they won't have that tradition, and that's tough. But we have pictures and memories, and that's what we're going to be holding on to going forward," Joseph Joliet said.A 70-year history is something they can all be proud of."It's very unusual for any business to last 70 years, let alone a restaurant. I think the lifespan of a restaurant is usually about three or four years," Jay Joliet said. A final message from the owner."Thank you, thank you to every customer, every employee, everybody's ever worked for us. I can't tell them how much I appreciate it," Jay Joliet said. Based on this turnout, the Metro Detroit area appreciates the Sign of the Beefcarver.The Sign of the Beefcarver's final day is Sunday, Oct. 25.

title: Voters in this Pennsylvania swing region could hold key to U.S. House control
description: Lehigh Valley residents are no strangers to the spotlight during election season. President Trump won the district in 2016 and 2024, while voters opted for Joe Biden in 2020.
content: Driving on Leithsville Road in Hellertown, Northampton County, it's campaign sign after campaign sign lining the street. These Lehigh Valley residents are no strangers to the spotlight during election season, though."Doesn't surprise me," Vince Murante said. "You never know which way it's gonna go."This region in Pennsylvania has long been one of the swingiest regions in the swingiest of states. President Trump won the district in 2016 and 2024, while voters opted for Joe Biden in 2020. Just two years ago, Republicans flipped the 7th Congressional District, but only by a little over 4,000 votes. And its purple hue isn't just recent history. West Chester University political science professor John Kennedy said this House seat has swung back and forth since the 1950s."It's had different configurations, of course," Kennedy said. "But generally, this Lehigh Valley seat has been controlled in the House by each party an equal number of times."So it's no surprise national eyes are watching the Lehigh Valley once again. Not only is the region home to some key races for the state legislature, but its 7th Congressional District seat is one of four in the state currently held by Republicans that could decide which party controls the U.S. House.Republican Ryan Mackenzie will look to defend his seat against Democratic challenger Bob Brooks. It's a race that has gotten personal and chippy in this homestretch, something voters in this region have noticed."One is calling the other one a liar, and they're all lying. You know? You can't trust any of them," Janice Zavacky of Hellertown said. "I have gotten to the point now that when I see the ads come on the TV, I turn the television down.""The bashing of the candidates is bad," Murante said.It's not the biggest concern for these voters. Some cited the war with Iran. Others pointed to healthcare. But far and away the top issue was the cost of just about everything."The cost of everything has really risen and we need to get better on the job market," Jim Fisher of Easton said."Gas prices. Fuel prices. Grocery prices," Jonathan DeRaymond of Bethlehem said."I was only planning on spending about $40 on groceries. I spent almost $100," Iyonia Burns of Hellertown said.Republicans have controlled Congress for the last two years, but face headwinds coming into the 2026 elections. Generally, the party in power loses seats in the midterms. A Quinnipiac poll earlier this month showed 54% of Pennsylvania voters favored Democratic candidates on a generic ballot. That same poll showed Mr. Trump's approval rating in the state sat at 37%.All of these are challenges that Mackenzie will have to overcome to keep his seat, Kennedy said."You're going to have to convince a significant number of voters who may not approve of the current administration to bear with us for another two years," Kennedy said. "And that's a tough sell."On the other side, Kennedy said he'll look to see if Brooks, a longtime firefighter, can win back a key demographic in the region that broke with Democrats two years ago."Democrats have struggled in recent years, particularly in 2024. We saw this among blue-collar voters," Kennedy said.

title: Baltimore mayor calls police meeting after 5 killed in shootings in less than 48 hours
description: In less than 48 hours, five people were killed, and as many as 10 others were injured in multiple shootings across Baltimore, prompting Mayor Brandon Scott to call a meeting with police command staff to discuss efforts to stop retaliatory violence.
