Police emphasized that payment alone does not restore driving privileges; all applicable requirements must be completed and processed.Boosie received a speeding citation and warnings for not wearing a seat belt and using a cellphone, the department said."Lucky I ran across some cool officers ... South Fulton," Boosie says in a video recording the encounter. In a Facebook post, police explained that officers can consider the circumstances when deciding whether warnings, citations or other enforcement are appropriate within the law and department policy."Taking a few extra minutes to listen, explain, and help somebody understand what needs correcting is part of the job, too," the department wrote.Police did not say whether Boosie's license has since been reinstated.

title: Atwater Village coyote who attacked child was euthanized, officials confirm
description: The 16-month-old was treated and subsequently released from a local hospital, officials said.
content: DNA testing has confirmed that the coyote captured in Atwater Village and euthanized last week is the same animal that attacked a young child, the California Department of Fish and Wildlife said.The department said the coyote was involved in an incident with a 16-month-old near the 3300 block of Glenhurst Avenue on Friday. Later that evening, it was located and killed.The child was treated and subsequently released from a local hospital, officials said.In August, a coyote nicknamed "Wiley" roamed around Atwater Village and was sometimes seen chasing children. Neighbors raised concern over the animal's behavior, and it was speculated that someone in the area could've been feeding it."We've run into the coyote maybe a few times a week. Every time we go walking," said Libby Stankaitis, who lives in the neighborhood.CDFW said it's illegal to feed wildlife and urged residents to secure spaces and remove items that could attract coyotes.Other residents say they wish there was a more humane way to take care of the wildlife in the area. "I think coyotes are doing great in the urban area, and I think it's sad that we're putting them down," said Jacob Wollner. It's not yet clear if the coyote that was euthanized was Wiley.

title: Egypt moves toward sending troops to Saudi Arabia to help defend against attacks by Iran-backed Houthis
description: Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels have intensified their attacks on Saudi Arabia, targeting airports and oil infrastructure.
content: Cairo - Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi has asked the country's Parliament to authorize the military to help defend Saudi Arabia after Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels intensified their attacks on the kingdom, targeting airports and oil infrastructure.Al-Sisi stressed that it would be a defensive mission and only if the kingdom requests assistance."Egypt will take any measures requested by Saudi Arabia to protect and defend it," al-Sisi said Saturday during a military graduation ceremony.Under Egypt's Constitution, the president must consult the National Defense Council and obtain approval from two-thirds of Parliament before deploying the armed forces on a combat mission abroad.On Sunday, al-Sisi chaired a meeting of the National Defense Council, which reviewed what the Egyptian presidency described as the "grave escalations unfolding in the region" and the "unacceptable attacks" against Saudi Arabia.The council pledged to provide "all necessary and possible forms of support to the sisterly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to defend its security and stability, and to safeguard its resources, territorial integrity, and Islamic holy sites."Egypt has managed, so far, to stay out of all the recent military conflicts in the region and has tried to de-escalate and find political solutions. For some, this is one of al-Sisi's greatest achievements.But Samir Ragheb, a retired army brigadier and political and strategic analyst, told CBS News that it was time for Egypt to make good on commitments it had made to helping secure the region."Egypt has repeatedly pledged to support the security of the Gulf states and has issued numerous statements reaffirming this commitment," Ragheb said. "However, this is a time of war, not politics and statements. If Egypt fails to deliver on these promises, they will lose their meaning and amount to nothing more than empty threats.""The Gulf states have invested billions of dollars in Egypt. Morally, it's Egypt's turn to return the favor," he said.Parliament convened an emergency session on Sunday and was expected to approve the resolution on Tuesday, but the vote was postponed until next Monday.The Egyptian Social Democratic Party instructed its parliamentary bloc to abstain from voting on the resolution, saying in a statement it had not received sufficient information about "the mission's scope, costs, and risks, as well as the arrangements in place to protect Egyptian forces."Ragheb is certain the region is heading toward a more severe escalation."Egypt is not going to defend the kingdom against the Houthis," he said. "The threat is much bigger than the Houthis. This includes Iran, Iraqi militias and sleeper cells within the kingdom itself."However, he also believes Egypt will lose much of its influence in the region if it doesn't intervene."If you want to be a regional player, you must play a role," he said. "Otherwise, you will lose your seat at the table."Ragheb argued that the United States' refusal to attack the Houthis in support of Saudi Arabia created a vacuum that must be filled by others. He said Egypt should take on the Arab share of that role.Other regional powers are also trying to fill the vacuum. In August, Saudi Arabia signed a joint defense agreement with Turkey and Pakistan known as the Mecca Accords."Even before Saudi Arabia asked for Egyptian support, the Mecca Accords was a death certificate for the idea of relying on America for any form of defense," Ragheb said.

title: Parents lobby Pennsylvania State Senate to vote on revised school phone ban before session ends
description: The proposed bill would enforce a bell-to-bell ban on student cellphones and mobile devices.
content: A parent-led advocacy group is urging the Pennsylvania State Senate to act on legislation banning students from using cellphones and other mobile devices during the school day. The proposed Phone-Free Schools bill would enforce a bell-to-bell ban on student cellphones and mobile devices. Supporters say the measure is intended to protect students and help them focus on learning.The legislation has received widespread bipartisan support, but PA Unplugged, a parent-led movement advocating for phone-free schools, says it is concerned the bill may not make it across the finish line."We are not positive that the Senate is actually going to revote on a bill that they already passed 46-1," said PA Unplugged co-lead Kristen Beddard.The Pennsylvania House passed the bill Monday. But because the House passed a revised version, the Senate must vote on the legislation again before it can be sent to the governor's desk for a final vote."We need to protect our children's education. We need to protect those buildings and spaces so those children can learn in the classroom and those social, emotional opportunities outside of the classroom," said PA Unplugged co-lead Kelly Marsh.Marsh said the group is calling on Senate leadership to bring the measure up for a vote as time is running out for the end of the legislative session."We are just asking that the Senate do that," said Marsh. "In Pennsylvania, our Senate is Republican-controlled, so it's really the Republican Senate leadership that we're imploring they move this bill and get us to the finish line."PA Unplugged says it has not seen the legislation listed on an upcoming voting agenda. With only four scheduled voting days remaining, the group is concerned the bill could die if the Senate does not act.Beddard said she wants an explanation for why the legislation has not moved forward."Honestly, I would love a phone call from somebody in the Senate to say this is why it's not happening. I think, ultimately, what we're asking is that the Senate chooses kids over politics," said Beddard.If the legislation fails to advance, Beddard said the organization will continue its efforts."We will keep working on it, but again, be really disappointed that a year and a half of taxpayer dollars and legislative time has been wasted on something that is considered an easy win everywhere else," Beddard said.KDKA-TV reached out to Senate Majority Leader Joe Pittman and Senate President Pro Tempore Kim Ward for comment or an explanation but has not received a response.

title: Timberwolves, Jaden McDaniels agree to 1-year, $40M contract extension
description: The Minnesota Timberwolves and forward Jaden McDaniels have agreed to a one-year, $40 million contract extension through the 2029-30 season.
content: The Minnesota Timberwolves and forward Jaden McDaniels have agreed on a one-year, $40 million contract extension through the 2029-30 season, furthering their commitment to keeping the two-way standout as part of their long-term core.McDaniels has three seasons left on a five-year, $136 million contract he signed right before the 2023-24 season. This extension, which was first reported by ESPN on Monday night, was confirmed to The Associated Press by one of McDaniels' agents, Nima Namakian.The deal gives the Timberwolves another year of cost certainty in managing future salary caps around the next maximum contracts anticipated for star guards Anthony Edwards and LaMelo Ball. The extension also makes McDaniels eligible for another one in two years at a higher rate, thanks to the hefty raise he'll get from about $29.8 million in 2028-29 to the $40 million in 2029-30.The 6-foot-9 McDaniels had a career-best season in 2025-26, with an average of 14.8 points per game and 41.2% shooting from 3-point range, and the Timberwolves are confident the arrival of Ball and his keen passing ability can help unlock even more offensive potential. McDaniels, who was drafted with the 28th pick in 2020 out of Washington, has long been the team's best perimeter defender, as well. He was an NBA All-Defensive second-team selection in 2023-24.

title: Apna Ghar, Chicago nonprofit, releases cookbook collected from gender-based violence survivors
description: The Chicago-based nonprofit Apna Ghar announced Tuesday that it has released a cookbook of 29 multicultural recipes collected from survivors of gender-based violence.
content: The Chicago-based nonprofit Apna Ghar announced Tuesday that it has released a cookbook of 29 multicultural recipes collected from survivors of gender-based violence.Apna Ghar, based in the Uptown neighborhood, works against gender-based violence through outreach and advocacy across communities, including immigrants, refugees, and marginalized groups.The new cookbook, "Recipes from Our Home," is composed of recipes that were collected over several years by gender-based violence survivors who used Apna Ghar's emergency housing and joined its cooking groups. The cookbook includes everything from breakfast crepes to stews and curries, and represents the strength of both the people who submitted them and their cultures, Apna Ghar said."This book leaves me in awe of the incredible courage and resilience of the survivors Apna Ghar serves," Neha Gill, executive director and chief executive officer of Apna Ghar, said in a news release. "'Recipes from Our Home' demonstrates how survivors find more than safety at Apna Ghar. They also find community, healing, and empowerment."The cookbook also features commentary from survivors about their experiences.Apna Ghar serves gender-based violence survivors from 50 countries, and 75% of participants are immigrants and refugees. Food allows for a connection between participants even if they don't speak the same language, Apna Ghar said."Our cooking groups are powerful moments for survivors to share traditions with one another and create new, empowering memories," Tegest Enyew, program coordinator at Apna Ghar and a recipe collector and tester for the book, said in the release. "It is so wonderful that everyone who reads 'Recipes from Our Home' will have a chance to share that connection and continue to pass it along among their own communities.""Recipes from Our Home" also features artwork, copywriting, and designs from artists from South Africa, India, and Singapore, Apna Ghar said.The book is available through the Apna Ghar website as an eBook and on paper, and will be in bookstores in the winter. title: Atlanta City Council authorizes $68 million detention center sale to Fulton County
description: The Atlanta City Council has authorized the $68 million sale of the city's downtown jail to Fulton County, but the governments still need to work out the details before the deal can move forward.
content: The Atlanta City Council has authorized the $68 million sale of the city's downtown jail to Fulton County, but the governments still need to work out the details before the deal can move forward.The council approved the measure Monday, Oct. 19, allowing the sale of the Atlanta City Detention Center and a transition of operations to the county, according to the council's meeting summary.The transaction remains contingent on an agreement between the governments outlining its terms. The legislation also calls for Atlanta and the Fulton County sheriff to negotiate a separate agreement covering how space and services will be shared, including housing people detained on municipal charges.The measure was sent immediately to Mayor Andre Dickens' office, the council said.The proposed purchase would give Fulton County about 1,300 additional detention beds.Dickens proposed the $68 million price in an Aug. 31 counteroffer after the county offered approximately $56.5 million. Atlanta initially sought $80 million.Earlier discussions included allowing the Atlanta Department of Corrections to retain one floor and administrative space to oversee municipal detainees. The Fulton County Sheriff's Office also said it would welcome city corrections employees who want to continue their careers with the agency.Officials are working toward a Dec. 8 deadline, when Fulton County's current lease for space at the detention center expires.

title: Wayne County unveils new program for survivors of domestic and sexual violence
description: Survivors of domestic and sexual violence who later become involved in the criminal justice system may soon have a new path forward in Wayne County.
content: Survivors of domestic and sexual violence who later become involved in the criminal justice system may soon have a new path forward in Wayne County.On Tuesday, Kym Worthy announced the launch of Survivors FIRST, a new diversion program designed to connect eligible survivors of gender-based violence with trauma-informed services rather than immediately moving forward with prosecution.FIRST stands for Facilitating Interventions and Resources for Survivors of Trauma.The program is a partnership between the Wayne County Prosecutor's Office and First Step, a nonprofit that supports survivors of domestic violence and sexual assault."This is a survivor-centered diversion program that we're announcing today that's designed to assist individuals charged with crimes, who have a history of gender-based violence victimization," Worthy said.According to Worthy, Wayne County receives roughly 10,000 domestic violence cases each year from law enforcement agencies across the county.She said research shows a significant number of women who end up incarcerated have previously experienced abuse."Research and this is important, has consistently found that 75 to 90% of incarcerated women are themselves survivors of abuse," Worthy said. "Often, the abuse suffered by the survivors is a direct contributing factor to the subsequent involvement in the criminal justice system."The program is intended for people who have experienced gender-based violence, have no prior felony record, and are currently facing misdemeanor or qualifying felony charges prosecuted by Wayne County.Eligible participants will have their cases put on hold for 180 days while they work with First Step and participate in services tailored to their individual needs.Those services may include counseling, housing assistance, safety planning, employment support, legal aid and other resources.Worthy said the goal is to address the impact of past trauma and help prevent survivors from becoming further involved in the criminal justice system."These are not traditional defendants, because they've been previously recognized as victims of our system," Worthy said. "This program is designed to help break this cycle and support these survivors in every way by connecting them with trauma and trauma-informed resources."The Survivors FIRST program will begin accepting applications on Nov. 2, 2026. In the coming weeks, prosecutors plan to educate defense attorneys and judges about how the program will operate.

title: Inkster tables data center request, company drops development in response
description: A company that planned to house a data center in Inkster said it would choose another location for its facility.
content: A company that planned to house a data center in Inkster, Michigan, said it will instead change plans and choose another location for its facility. The Inkster City Council met Monday night, during which it tabled an agenda item and declined to approve the proposed data center, at least for now. The matter was highly contentious in the community, with residents arriving at Inkster City Hall 90 minutes before the council meeting began and waiting outside to speak during public comment. The residents shared concerns about noise, water use, lighting and potential environmental impact should a vacant warehouse building be converted into a data center. "No motion was brought forward, and the project was never put to a vote," company representative Robert Kato said in a statement issued on Tuesday. "We respect the Council's process and the concerns of the residents it represents. The project will now proceed in a neighboring municipality." Kato did not say where the company would be seeking to relocate, but added, "We look forward to working with a community prepared to embrace that future." Background on Inkster data center plans The Inkster city council's agenda for Monday night included documentation of an offer from Klever Technology Center of Madison Heights to Sage Fidelis of Inkster for the purchase of property at 27181 Southern St., which is south of US. 12. The purchase offer was $1.1 million for the land and an existing warehouse. The plans were to convert the currently vacant building into a "micro-data center," according to a report made to the council for the meeting. The Inkster Planning Department reviewed the special land use application for a proposed data center, which is a permitted use under the existing zoning. The planners told council members that the project would require a public hearing, special land use application approval by the City Council, and then a final site plan to proceed. The company told city officials this would result in about $75 million investment in private capital and around 90 to 100 jobs in technical, maintenance and security workforces. The city's planning commission held a special meeting on Oct. 12, during which it recommended a conditional approval of the data center.

title: Ukraine's military evacuates wounded soldier with aerial drone in apparent world-first
description: Ukraine's military says a soldier reportedly trapped by Russian fire on the front line for more than a year was evacuated by an aerial drone.
content: Ukraine's military says it carried out a front-line medical evacuation by aerial drone — an apparent world-first for the drone-savvy nation — as Russia's full-scale invasion nears the five-year mark. The Ukrainian Ground Forces' 92nd Assault Brigade said Monday that it had evacuated a wounded soldier from the front line using a heavy-lift aerial drone. For almost 500 days, soldier Konstantyn Vlasenko of the 30th Separate Brigade was stuck in a position out of reach for Ukrainian ground forces or robots due to dense mining and heavy Russian drone activity, according to Ukrainian news outlets, including some linked with the military. The reports said Vlasenko was wounded by a Russian drone earlier this year while trapped, forcing him to carry out partial self-amputations of both of his legs as he hoped for a rescue.A Ukrainian-made Gurzuf Defence heavy hexacopter, originally configured as an attack drone to drop bombs on Russian positions, was used for the rescue operation — provided to the military free of charge, according to the statement from the 92nd Brigade. Specialists worked with the company to modify the unmanned aircraft to carry a person without flipping or swinging them, and the new configuration was tested before the rescue was planned. Four different Ukrainian brigades were involved in the complex operation, which took seven days to prepare, though the actual rescue only took about an hour and 15 minutes. In that time, the drone flew almost 40 miles, with Ukrainian units using other drones to distract the Russian military, the brigade said.Gurzuf Defence co-founder Pavlo Feldbloom told CBS News the company "never set out to create a platform designed exclusively for evacuation; instead, we developed a heavy-duty, modular, multi-mission platform."He said the company understood, however, that a drone capable of carrying such a payload should also be capable of carrying out rescue missions. "At the same time, we do not believe that aerial evacuation will become a routine, large-scale practice," he said, as the "risks to a wounded person in the air are simply too high." "Aerial transport is the last resort — an option to be used only when there is no other way to save a person's life," Feldbloom said.Before the aerial evacuation, there was an attempt to rescue Konstantyn using a ground drone, another technique pioneered by Ukrainian forces during the war, but it was destroyed on its way to him, according to the Ukrainian Armed Forces 2nd Mechanized Battalion.When Vlasenko landed, he described his evacuation flight as calm and said he was relieved to be back on friendly ground.

title: Georgia father educates teen drivers about tire safety after son's death
description: It's National Teen Driver Safety Week, and a Marietta father is working to make cars safer for young drivers after losing his son in a crash.
content: It's National Teen Driver Safety Week, and a Marietta father is working to make cars safer for young drivers after losing his son in a crash.The Road Ready Foundation encourages drivers to check tire tread and pressure and inspect their tires for damage.Founder Alex Bebiak lost his son Jackson in 2023. Jackson was a passenger in a car that hydroplaned and hit an 18-wheeler. Bebiak said the crash was caused by insufficient tire tread."We learned that the crash was due to lack of tire tread on the tires," Bebiak said.The loss led his family to learn more about tire safety and identify an opportunity to educate teen drivers.Bebiak now speaks at schools and driver's education programs across the country, encouraging young drivers to check their tires."We found that three out of ten teen drivers are actually driving on unsafe tires through programs we've done at local high schools by checking their tires," Bebiak said.He said the foundation also found that 43% of teen drivers had never checked their tires or tread for safety. Three in 10 did not know what the tire pressure monitoring system warning light meant.Tire Discounters is partnering with Road Ready to offer free tire checks for teens during National Teen Driver Safety Week.

title: Eagles QB Jalen Hurts out for season after blood clots discovered in lungs, league sources say
description: Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts is expected to make a full recovery after being diagnosed with blood clots in his lungs.
author_name: Joe  Brandt, Stephanie  Stahl, Tom  Ignudo
content: Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts is on blood thinners after additional testing revealed a deep vein thrombosis and blood clots in his lungs, his agent, Nicole Lynn, said in a joint statement with the team Monday.Hurts missed Sunday's game against the Carolina Panthers and was placed on injured reserve after what was initially described as a "superficial" blood clot in his left calf. League sources told CBS News Philadelphia that Hurts is expected to miss the rest of the season.Further testing Monday revealed Hurts was diagnosed with a deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli — lung blood clots, according to the joint statement.Hurts is clinically stable and has no significant functional limitations. He was placed on anticoagulants, also known as blood thinners, and won't be participating in football while on this medication."Jalen's prognosis is very good, and we expect a full recovery. We anticipate that he will have the opportunity to resume contact football activities when off the blood thinners," the statement said.Hurts will stay active around the team and keep in shape."We anticipate that he will have no long-term effects. We are thinking of Jalen and looking forward to a strong recovery," the statement reads.Nick Sirianni addresses Jalen Hurts' blood clot diagnosis in press conferenceEagles head coach Nick Sirianni was grilled by reporters Monday in his first news conference since Hurts' new diagnosis. Sirianni declined to go into detail about the team's decision to have Hurts play the Jacksonville Jaguars in London in Week 6, saying the Eagles care "deeply" about the players and that the medical staff made the decision. "Guys, I'm not a medical expert," Sirianni said. "I lean on our guys in all those situations. I'm a football coach. I lean on our medical experts in every situation. I have full faith and trust in them. It's not just me that has major care for our players; it's them as well. So, we are all there, and I'm glad to be part of an organization that cares about the guys the way our guys do."According to numerous reports from NFL insiders Monday, Hurts was awake for more than 30 hours and didn't sleep as a precaution before the Week 5 game in London. Following up on his initial report, The Ringer's Tom Pelissero says he spoke to Lynn, who clarified that while Hurts was up until early Sunday morning at the hospital, he was able to sleep upon rejoining the team.The Eagles reportedly had a room set aside for him at the stadium before kickoff."That reporter [who] put that out came out with another report," Sirianni said. "I know you guys saw that. The health of our players is always at the forefront of our mind. We leave that up to the medical experts, but we always, always care deeply about our players."When you are completely focused on together and connection, you're always thinking about the well-being of your guys. That's where we were in that situation."What is a pulmonary embolism?Dr. Parth Rali, the director of the pulmonary embolism response team at Temple Health, said the standard treatment for Hurts is blood thinners, which can help dissolve the clots. A pulmonary embolism is a blood clot in the lung that can interfere with blood flow. For Hurts, it's in both lungs, which is not unusual."Ideally, minimum blood thinners has to be for three months," Rali said. "You cannot have any contact sports because on blood thinners … you have chances of bleeding."Hurts had initially been diagnosed before the game in London with a superficial blood clot in his calf.Doctors said there's a risk the superficial blood clot can turn into a deep vein thrombosis, which is a more serious blood clot that can travel to the lungs.However, doctors cleared Hurts to play in London and fly back home to Philadelphia. Did the flights make Hurts' blood clot worse? "It can happen even with the best of care, so I'm not sure that we can really say that anything that he did or the way he was treated was necessarily causative," said Dr. William Gray, who specializes in cardiology, heart and vascular care at Main Line Health. Gray said that the report that Hurts was advised to not sleep while he was at the hospital before the London game "doesn't really make a lot of sense.""A superficial blood clot is 90% of the case is benign, managed with conservative therapy, like compression, heat and generally goes away," Gray said. Doctors said once the blood clots are resolved, Hurts should be able to completely recover and resume playing football.Timeline of Jalen Hurts' blood clots diagnosisHurts' injury first came to light Oct. 8 when he requested treatment on his calf, saying he had been cleated during the Rams game on Oct. 4. A small blood clot was revealed by an ultrasound performed after the team's flight to London to face the Jaguars. Specialists in London at that time diagnosed Hurts with a superficial blood clot.Hurts played in the London game, a heartbreaking, last-second loss to the Jaguars.Hurts was placed on injured reserve before the Week 6 game against the Panthers on Oct. 17. Further testing diagnosed him with a deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli, according to a joint statement by the Eagles and Lynn on Oct. 19.

title: Democrat Ro Khanna to campaign in Nebraska with independent Senate candidate Dan Osborn
description: Dan Osborn, who says he won't caucus with Republicans or Democrats if he wins, is campaigning with Democratic Rep. Ro Khanna Saturday.
content: Dan Osborn, an independent who has vowed not to caucus with Republicans or Democrats if elected to serve as Nebraska's next senator, will hit the campaign trail Saturday with progressive Democratic Rep. Ro Khanna.Khanna is the first elected official to campaign with Osborn, who is trying to unseat incumbent Sen. Pete Ricketts, a former Nebraska governor. There are no Democrats in the state's congressional delegation, making it the most heavily Republican state where the California congressman has campaigned for any 2026 candidate. Khanna has campaigned for Democrats in a growing list of battleground races, including Iowa and Michigan. He says he's happy to help in any way and indicated he is sensitive to the message his appearance might send to conservative and independent voters."I tell these folks, do you really want an Indian American of Hindu faith who's a proud progressive coming out?" Khanna told CBS News. "I'm happy to not come out and raise the money for you or send an email, but they said, 'No, we want you to come out.'"Khanna will be participating in a town hall for Osborn alongside former Montana Gov. and RNC Chair Marc Racicot and former Illinois Congressman Joe Walsh. Both are critics of President Trump: Racicot was rebuked and censured by the Montana GOP after opposing Mr. Trump and other GOP candidates. Walsh, who supported Mr. Trump in 2016, briefly ran against him in 2020 and later left the Republican Party and registered as a Democrat in 2025.Osborn said the Jeffrey Epstein case brought the panel together. "We all have very different backgrounds, and we're not going to agree on everything—no party has a monopoly on good ideas," Osborn wrote in a statement to CBS News. "But we all share the core belief that D.C. is broken because Epstein Class billionaires like Pete Ricketts are putting profit over everyday people."Osborn met with survivors when the Epstein Bookmobile came to Omaha in September, and his campaign frequently describes his campaign as a "vision of a Nebraska built for everyday people, not Epstein-class billionaires."Khanna is one of the key voices on the Epstein files, advocating the passage of the Epstein Files Transparency Act with Republican Thomas Massie and continuing to push for a full release of the files. He says the accountability concerns are why he's heading to states where "I never would have told you that I would be invited."Khanna suggested that the Trump administration's handling of the Epstein files speaks more generally to a broader sense of betrayal for many voters."In terms of the swing, the slice of voters who feel betrayed by Trump and who could swing to us, the polling shows that this is its single biggest issue," Khanna said. "It gets to the sense of the rigged economy and the corruption."On Monday, the five-term congressman was in Michigan campaigning with William Lawrence, who is attempting to unseat GOP Rep. Tom Barrett in Michigan's 7th Congressional District. He also campaigned with Democratic Senate candidates Josh Turek in Iowa and Chris Pappas in New Hampshire. Sabato's Crystal Ball rates Lawrence and Turek's races as toss-ups. With less than three weeks to go before Election Day, it shifted New Hampshire in Pappas' favor from Lean Democratic to Likely Democratic and Nebraska in Osborn's favor, from Likely Republican to Leans Republican.

title: Bird flu confirmed in Barron County, Wisconsin, commercial poultry flock
description: State officials say the commercial flock in Barron County was quarantined and the birds depopulated to stop the disease from spreading. The U.S. Department of Agriculture is helping with the response.
content: Wisconsin agriculture officials have confirmed highly pathogenic avian influenza, commonly called bird flu, in a commercial poultry flock in Barron County, in the northwestern part of the state.The Wisconsin Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection announced the case Monday. The department's announcement did not say what kind of birds were in the flock, how many there were or when the virus was detected.The property has been quarantined to restrict the movement of poultry and poultry products, and the birds there were depopulated to prevent the disease from spreading. The state says birds from the flock will not enter the food system. The department and the U.S. Department of Agriculture are working together on the response.When bird flu is found in a Wisconsin flock, the state sets up a control area within 10 kilometers, or about 6 miles, of the infected property. The area restricts movement on or off any premises with poultry. Owners can check whether their birds are inside a control area using the department's mapping tool.The department is urging livestock owners to wash their hands, disinfect equipment, limit access to animals and separate new additions to a flock or herd for at least 30 days. Poultry owners are asked to keep their birds indoors when possible. Owners who see increased deaths or signs of illness among domestic birds are asked to report it to the department.The virus has circulated among wild and domestic birds in North America since December 2021.Minnesota is the nation's top turkey producer. In September 2025, bird flu was found at turkey farms in Le Sueur, Blue Earth and Stearns counties, weeks after the state's first detection since April in a Redwood County flock.

title: Inside the hive: How metro Atlanta beekeepers help honeybees prepare for colder months
description: Beekeepers Mark Schwartz and Deborah DeWitt offer a close-up look inside a honeybee colony, from workers storing honey to the search for its queen.
content: Before opening a beehive, master beekeeper Debra DeWitt looks for clues.At a teaching apiary in College Park, bees returning to the hive with tiny granules of pollen on their legs tell her something about what is happening inside."You can see little granules of pollen on their legs," DeWitt said. "And so that tells me that they're raising brood inside."DeWitt, president of the Tara Beekeepers Association, and Vice President Mark Schwartz help care for colonies at the association's apiary at Metro Atlanta Urban Farm.For Schwartz, who has kept bees for about 15 years, preparing to inspect a hive starts with protective gear and a smoker. The smoke helps calm the bees and allows beekeepers to work inside the hive with less disturbance.Once the lid comes off, an entire community is revealed.Worker bees are female and perform much of the work inside the colony. Male bees, known as drones, have a much different role."They really just kind of hang out and eat," DeWitt said. "Their sisters feed them."One of the most important things beekeepers look for heading into colder weather is whether a colony has enough food.During the inspection, DeWitt pulled out a frame packed with capped honey."This is a beautiful frame of honey right here," she said.While some honey could be harvested for people, Schwartz said the beekeepers are leaving it with the colony."This is honey that we could harvest and use for human consumption, but we're going to leave it for the bees," Schwartz said.That stored honey becomes especially important as temperatures fall and fewer food sources are available outside the hive.During cold weather, honeybees cluster together inside the hive. They generate and conserve heat while using stored honey for the energy they need to survive the colder months.Food is only part of what DeWitt looks for during an inspection. She also searches for the queen."I'm always looking for the queen," DeWitt said while scanning a frame. "She could be on a frame like this, but I don't see her here."Frame by frame, the search continued until DeWitt spotted her."Here's the queen," she said.The queen was marked with a small white dot, making her easier to identify among thousands of bees. DeWitt said the queen is noticeably larger than the workers and is responsible for laying the eggs that sustain the colony.The bees also communicate in ways that can be easy to miss. DeWitt pointed to workers touching antennae around the queen. The queen produces a pheromone that is passed among bees, signaling her presence throughout the colony.For DeWitt, those small details are part of what has kept her interested in beekeeping for eight years."I love bees," she said. "To me, working a hive, it's like a walking meditation."The work happening inside a hive also reaches far beyond it."They pollinate so many crops that we consume," Schwartz said. "They're so beneficial to the environment."The Tara Beekeepers Association uses its College Park apiary as a teaching space, giving new beekeepers an opportunity to learn how to inspect, manage and care for honeybee colonies.

title: Dallas ISD agrees to $1 million settlement tied to ex-teacher charged in Forney case, officials say
description: U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould said Michael Roell was under four investigations at DISD at one point.
content: The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Texas says Dallas ISD has agreed to a $1 million settlement and major changes to how it handles reports of educator misconduct and abuse after the office said it didn't properly handle investigations into Michael Roell, the same teacher facing a grand jury indictment on charges he and a Forney ISD principal tried to circumvent hiring safeguards.U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould hosted a press conference on Tuesday, announcing a settlement to resolve federal civil claims tied to reporting laws related to a special education grant running from 2022 through 2024. Raybould said Roell had taught special education at DISD before he was hired at Forney ISD, but that Roell faced four separate investigations involving misconduct or the abuse of minors. However, Raybould said DISD never reported anything to state officials and that Roell left DISD with no public record of misconduct that could be shared with other school districts.Raybould did note that DISD accepted responsibility for this and agreed to make changes to how investigations are handled and to reporting, saying some information lived in different silos within the district administration.What was Roell reported for?Raybould briefly discussed one of the four DISD investigations into Roell during the press conference. According to Raybould, a boy came to school in September 2023 and reported that Roell had sexually abused him at a Boy Scout camp in Athens, located in East Texas. The boy said Roell had picked him because Roell thought he wouldn't report him, and that Roell had touched other boys while serving as a scout leader.Raybould said DISD, rather than reporting the four cases to law enforcement, gave Roell a choice: resign or face termination. Raybould said resignation meant that Roell's name was relegated only to an internal do-not-hire list within DISD, while a termination would've required the involvement of the board of trustees and a public review.Raybould said Roell then moved on to work at Forney ISD. Raybould also noted Roell was fired by Garland ISD prior to his time at DISD, specifically accused of touching a student and observing students in the restroom, but that DISD still hired him despite knowing this.What changes will DISD need to make?Raybould said Dallas ISD will require all employees, contract workers and volunteers to disclose any finding against them, civil or otherwise. Background checks must now encompass any pending or settled civil cases. Raybould also said the district withheld key information about Roell from his principal and assistant principal during the investigation in 2023; that now ends, he says, and DISD is now required to dismantle internal information silos.Further, Raybould said DISD is now required to involve outside law enforcement in any investigations involving educator misconduct. Raybould said the allegations against Roell were referred to DISD's own police department, allowing them to be rerouted internally. DISD will also need to undergo mandatory training and coordination to change its own culture.Are other school districts facing similar investigations?Raybould said other North Texas school districts are facing investigations, many of which don't know those investigations are underway. He has urged district superintendents to come forward about past failures, claiming most investigations have been spurred by parents and teachers making reports.What is Project Safe Schools?Project Safe Schools is a new initiative announced in August by U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould. It was launched after a series of high-profile child sex abuse allegations involving North Texas educators. During a press conference announcing the initiative, Raybould said "the problem is clear and urgent", saying educator misconduct was happening too often."Some districts have even engaged in what is referred to as 'passing the trash', quietly moving educators with known misconduct issues to new campuses or new districts, where they hurt other children," he said. "That practice puts children at risk, it violates federal grant conditions, and it ends today."The initiative is a partnership involving the Texas Education Agency and local, state, and federal law enforcement agencies. Raybould said the TEA has opened more than 9,700 educator misconduct investigations in the last two years, leading to more than 590 disciplinary actions and the placement of more than 480 educators on a registry to prevent their hire elsewhere.Levi Fuller, the TEA's first inspector general for educator misconduct, previously told CBS News Texas that the goal is to move investigations more quickly and keep educators accused of serious misconduct out of classrooms while cases are reviewed."We're expanding our capability," Fuller said.Fuller is nearly six months into the new position, created as Texas faces growing scrutiny over how school districts handle allegations involving teachers, coaches, and other school employees.The TEA has received more than 16,000 educator misconduct reports this year, Fuller said. About 9,000 investigations are currently active.Under changes implemented by his office, about 7,100 of those cases can now go through a temporary suspension process, which Fuller said has helped speed up investigations.More details about the TEA's efforts and how to report educator misconduct, abuse, or neglect can be found online.Have North Texas educators been recently arrested?Yes. The August announcement for Project Safe Schools happened weeks after Paul Campbell, a longtime Plano ISD elementary school teacher, was arrested on accusations that he sexually abused second-grade girls in his class as recently as the 2025-26 school year.Another former teacher and coach, Caleb Elliott, faces numerous federal and state charges for allegedly taking secret recordings of dozens of middle school boys inside a Celina ISD locker room.Other recent cases alleging sexual misconduct in schools have involved a McKinney ISD athletic trainer, a teacher at a Little Elm charter school, and a Crowley ISD high school teacher.

title: Suspect in custody after gunfire outside Kluczynski Federal Building in Chicago
description: Suspect in custody after gunfire outside Kluczynski Federal Building
content: A suspect was in custody Tuesday morning after shots were fired near the John C. Kluczynski Federal Building in downtown Chicago.The U.S. Department of Homeland Security said early Tuesday morning, a Federal Protective Service officer reported an "active shooter" near the federal office building, at 230 S. Dearborn St. Chicago police said a man was seen outside firing a gun. The initial call came in around 4:40 a.m.The DHS said there was minor damage to federal property.A bullet hole was also seen in the window of the Central Standard Building, which spans the square block from Clark Street west to LaSalle Street and from Quincy Street south to Jackson Boulevard and houses Wintrust financial offices. Its Clark Street frontage, lined with Ionic columns, is right across from Federal Plaza.It was unclear how many directions the shooter was firing in, and what exactly his target was. It was also unclear what led up to the shooting.No one was struck by gunfire or injured, authorities said.Chicago police arrested the suspect, the DHS said. A gun was recovered, police said.Dozens of DHS and Chicago police officers were out in force along Clark Street at the western edge of Federal Plaza early Tuesday. Investigators were seen collecting shell casings and bullet fragments from the scene, and numerous evidence markers were set down. Dispatch audio indicated about 15 shell casings at the scene. Police have not confirmed how many shots they believe were fired.The Kluczynski Federal Building houses offices for several federal agencies, including the Department of Labor, the DHS, and the IRS. It also houses the offices of U.S. Sens. Dick Durbin and Tammy Duckworth, both Illinois Democrats.The Kluczynski Building is located on Federal Plaza across Dearborn Street from the Dirksen Federal Courthouse.The Trump administration announced plans to sell the Kluczynski Building and 10 other Chicago buildings owned by the federal government in March 2025, but no sale of the Kluczynski Building has gone ahead.Charges were pending against the man who was arrested Tuesday morning as Belmont Area CPD detectives continued to investigate.The DHS also said the investigation remained active, and that additional information will be limited for now.

title: Data centers are expanding rapidly. What does that mean for local communities?
description: What's paranoia and what's real when it comes to community concerns about data centers?
content: The term data center stirs emotions in many people. Communities are standing up and saying, "not in my backyard," as they come with a long list of concerns.But what's paranoia, and what's real?If you think this boom in data centers is driven by artificial intelligence, you are absolutely right. But slowing AI is usually way down on the list of concerns.First, realize you already use data centers daily."We need them for everything from cloud computing, storing all of our photos and files in the cloud, to online purchases to sports betting. All data centers support all of those digital activities," said Hannah Wiseman, a professor of law at Penn State focusing on all the elements of law surrounding data centers.But the catalyst for the current boom is new and clear."It's the expansion of artificial intelligence," Wiseman said.And what really stokes the opposition comes from people's wallets."There's been evidence of higher bills as a result of data centers," Wiseman said.Professor Wiseman says that concern is real because data centers use a lot of power and water."Anyone in that utility's service territory can see higher bills if the utility has to spend money to build and operate new infrastructure for the data center. Those costs can be spread among all of the customers," Wiseman explained, adding that a data center's humming noise can be an issue."The noise is something like 90 decibels, which is somewhere between heavy city traffic and a jackhammer."Noise control remains a key issue developers face. And there's the intangible conflict."You have a well-resourced, wealthy developer, typically not from the community, coming in and saying, 'We want to build something. We want to build it fast.' And the communities are saying, 'Wait a minute. We don't know you. We don't necessarily trust you. We want more time.'"Wiseman says pressing pause to see if the issues can be resolved makes sense because trust will come only through conversations, negotiations and commitments. The data center boom appears to be moving faster than politicians can act to regulate it, as often happens with new technology. That is why Dr. Wiseman says policies like the one introduced by Gov. Josh Shapiro to ensure data centers pay their own way are important, advisable and part of a growing national trend.

title: Sacramento man convicted of child sex assaults sentenced to 650 years
description: A California judge has sentenced a man convicted of sexually abusing two girls to more than 600 years in state prison, prosecutors said.
content: A California judge has sentenced a man convicted of sexually abusing two girls to more than 600 years in state prison, prosecutors said.The Sacramento County District Attorney's Office announced Monday that 43-year-old Michael Jones received a sentence of 650 years to life. On Sept. 17, a jury convicted Jones of 16 counts of child sexual assault, with aggravating factors of substantial sexual conduct and multiple victims.According to prosecutors, Jones committed hundreds of sexual acts against the first victim, who was between 11 and 13 at the time."Jones initially began by grooming the victim and quickly progressed his conduct," prosecutors said in a statement.After the victim revealed the abuse, prosecutors said Jones evaded law enforcement for seven years and began sexually assaulting another girl when she was 9 years old.According to the DA's office, Assembly Bill 2727, a newly approved state law has lengthened the time before Jones is eligible for a parole hearing. Under AB2727, Jones will not be eligible for an elder parole hearing until he turns 65 and has served at least 25 years in prison.Previously, Jones was eligible for an elder parole hearing once he turned 50 and served 20 years, according to prosecutors.The DA's office said Jones would also be evaluated to determine if he is a Sexually Violent Predator (SVP). If officials determine if Jones is an SVP, he would face an "indeterminate civil commitment" at a secure state hospital facility.

title: Police investigating fatal shooting in Southfield, suspect in custody
description: Southfield police were called to Dorset Avenue on Monday afternoon on a report of shots fired. The victim was pronounced dead at the scene.
content: Police are asking the public for information as they investigate a fatal shooting that happened in Southfield, Michigan. The Southfield Police Department said they received a report of shots fired at about 3:02 p.m. on Monday in the 17000 block of Dorset Avenue, which is west of M-10. When officers arrived, they found a man with gunshot wounds. He was pronounced dead at the scene, police said. The suspect is a 21-year-old man from Southfield who is a family member of the victim, police said. He was taken into custody. "At this time, there appears to be no additional threat to the public," police said. The investigation is continuing. Police ask that anyone who has information that can assist officers contact the Southfield Police Department at 248-796-5500 or Crime Stoppers of Michigan at 800-SPEAK-UP.

title: How to talk to your parents about end-of-life planning
description: End-of-life planning can be difficult to discuss, but the right approach can make the conversation easier.
content: There are some financial conversations families can put off without much consequence, but a discussion about end-of-life plans with aging family members isn't necessarily one of them. Without a clear understanding of what an aging parent wants, adult children may eventually have to make difficult financial, medical and logistical decisions with little guidance — and could end up doing so during an already stressful time.Still, bringing up the subject can be uncomfortable. Talking about wills, medical wishes, funeral arrangements or who will handle the finances if a parent becomes incapacitated can feel intrusive, particularly when a parent is still healthy and independent. Parents may also be reluctant to discuss their finances with their children or may view the conversation as unnecessary.But end-of-life planning involves more than just determining what happens to someone's assets after they die. It can also affect how bills are paid, how medical decisions are handled and how family members navigate an emergency. So, while there may never be a perfect time to start the discussion, the way adult children approach it can make a significant difference. How exactly should you do that, though? That's what we'll consider below.Learn more about your life insurance options with USAA here.How to talk to your parents about end-of-life planningEnd-of-life planning can cover a lot of ground, and trying to address everything in one conversation can quickly become overwhelming. A more manageable approach may be to start with the most important questions and build from there. Here's how to best approach it:Choose the right momentA conversation about end-of-life planning is unlikely to go well if it comes without context or when everyone is distracted. Look for a natural opening instead, such as when a parent is updating a retirement plan, reviewing insurance coverage or after the family has dealt with an aging relative's estate.The goal doesn't have to be to complete an entire checklist in one sitting. The first conversation may simply be about whether plans exist and where important documents are kept. Starting there can make it easier to return to more detailed issues later.Find out what life insurance coverage options you have today.Make it about their wishesHow the subject is framed matters, too. Asking parents what they want in terms of end-of-life planning can feel very different from telling them what they need to do to prepare for it. That keeps the focus on preserving the parent's control over future decisions rather than shifting that control to their adult children.For example, the discussion might center on who they would want making medical or financial decisions if they could no longer make those decisions themselves. It could also cover whether they have preferences for long-term care, funeral arrangements or how certain assets should be handled.Cover the essential legal and financial documentsOnce parents are comfortable discussing their plans, it can help to determine which documents are already in place. That may include a will, durable financial power of attorney, health care power of attorney or proxy and an advance health care directive.It's also worth discussing beneficiary designations on retirement accounts, life insurance policies and other financial accounts. Those designations can play an important role in determining where certain assets go, so they should generally be reviewed periodically and after major life changes.Parents may also want to consult an estate planning attorney or financial professional to determine which documents and strategies make sense for their circumstances.Talk about the financial details that could matter in an emergencyAdult children don't necessarily need a detailed accounting of every dollar their parents have. That said, they may need enough information to know where to turn if something happens. That could mean knowing where important documents are stored, which banks or financial institutions hold accounts, whether a parent has life insurance or long-term care coverage and how to contact their attorney, financial advisor or insurance agent. It may also be useful to understand how recurring household expenses are paid.Digital information can matter as well. Parents may have online financial accounts, subscriptions and other digital assets that someone will eventually need to manage. Creating a secure plan for accessing that information now can prevent unnecessary complications in the future.Don't assume one conversation will settle everythingEnd-of-life plans can change, meaning a parent's finances, health, family circumstances or preferences may look very different five or 10 years from now. As a result, this discussion may work better as an ongoing family conversation rather than a one-time event. Plans can be revisited after major events such as retirement, the death of a spouse, a move, a significant health change or a major change in assets.And if a parent isn't ready to discuss the issue the first time it comes up, pushing for immediate answers could make future conversations more difficult. It may ultimately be more productive to explain why the information matters and revisit the subject later.The bottom lineTalking to parents about end-of-life planning can be uncomfortable, but avoiding the subject can leave families with far more difficult decisions later. The objective isn't to take control of a parent's finances or dictate what their plans should look like. It's to understand what they want and make sure the right documents and information are accessible if they're ever needed. Starting with a few basic questions can make the process less daunting. From there, families can gradually address the legal, financial and medical details — and revisit those plans as circumstances change.

title: In-laws plead not guilty in deadly California shooting of son-in-law, New York Times exec
description: An elderly California couple has pleaded not guilty to murder charges in connection with the deadly shooting of their son-in-law, a New York Times executive, attorneys said.
content: An elderly California couple has pleaded not guilty to murder charges in connection with the deadly shooting of their son-in-law, a New York Times executive, attorneys said.According to the Alameda County Public Defender's office, 77-year-old Shouyong Zhang and his wife, 77-year-old Shili Chen, entered their pleas on Monday. In addition to murder charges, Zhang and Chen were charged with personal use of a firearm causing death, and lying in wait, a special circumstance that carries the possibility of a life sentence without parole.The pair are accused of fatally shooting 40-year-old Jonathan McKinsey in the parking lot of the Dublin Sports Grounds on the afternoon of Sept. 26. Dublin is located about 35 miles east of San Francisco.McKinsey, who was head of engineering at New York Times Games, was pronounced dead at the scene. Chen and Zhang were arrested near the Dublin police station minutes later.Dublin Police Services said Zhang admitted to shooting McKinsey, and that Chen has refused to talk after their arrest. A second gun was found during the search of the couple's car, according to police.The shooting followed years of documented family strife involving McKinsey, his wife - identified as Candice Jang, their three children, and his in-laws. In Oct. 2025, McKinsey was charged with child endangerment involving their 2-year-old, and corporal injury involving their 6-year-old, following accusations from Jang. McKinsey pleaded not guilty to both charges.Days later, Jang filed for a restraining order against McKinsey to keep him away from both her and the children, which was followed by McKinsey filing his own restraining order against Jang in December 2025. McKinsey also filed for divorce days later.Court documents indicate that McKinsey alleged his in-laws had long abused him for being a transgender man and alleged that Jang had physically and emotionally harmed him and their children for years and allowed her parents to do the same. McKinsey also alleged that Zhang had punched him in the chest while he was recovering from a double mastectomy, and alleged that Chan struck her grandson after he wanted to wear his sister's dresses, and called him derogatory names.Police have not elaborated on the motive for the shooting and have not addressed the previous charges against McKinsey or subsequent court actions.In a statement to CBS News Bay Area, the public defender's office said Tuesday that they plan to ask a judge for Zhang's release or to set bail, saying he had not been in trouble with the law previously, is physically frail and is showing signs of dementia."We are very concerned about his health and well-being if he remains in custody and are exploring all options to ensure he receives appropriate medical care and accommodations given his age," the public defender's office said. "We are also examining how these illnesses may have contributed to this tragedy."Jail records show both Zhang and Chen are scheduled to appear for a bail hearing on Nov. 4.

title: Eight-year-old boy dies in ATV crash in Georgia, sheriff's office says
description: An 8-year-old boy died in an ATV crash in Newnan on Monday afternoon, according to the Coweta County Sheriff's Office.
content: An 8-year-old boy died in an ATV crash in Newnan on Monday afternoon, according to the Coweta County Sheriff's Office.Deputies responded to the 100 block of Pate Road around 4:15 p.m. and immediately began trying to save the child's life.They continued until emergency medical personnel arrived and took over his care. The boy was pronounced dead shortly afterward, the sheriff's office said.The Georgia State Patrol is investigating the crash. The sheriff's office did not release the child's name or details about what led to the accident."The Coweta County Sheriff's Office extends its deepest condolences to the child's family and loved ones during this tragic time," the agency said.

title: Shooting in Baltimore Monday night kills 1, injures 2
description: A shooting in Baltimore on Monday night killed one person and injured two others, according to the Baltimore Police Department (BPD).
content: A shooting in Baltimore on Monday night killed one person and injured two others, according to the Baltimore Police Department (BPD).An officer was conducting a business check in the 3200 block of Belair Road around 11 p.m. when he heard multiple gunshots and sent outside the business to investigate, said a statement issued Tuesday by the BPD.The officer found a 39-year-old man suffering from life-threatening gunshot wounds. Additional officers then arrived on the scene and discovered a 21-year-old man also suffering from gunshot injuries, the statement said.A third victim from the incident -- also a 21-year-old man -- walked into a hospital to be treated for gunshot wounds, the BPD said.EMS workers responded to the scene and transported the two wounded individuals to the hospital. The 39-year-old died of his injuries. The injuries of the other two wounded men were not considered life-threatening, the statement said. BPD homicide detectives are urging anyone with information to contact them at 410-396-2100 or reach out to Metro Crime Stoppers at 1-866-7Lockup.The incident on Belair Road was the latest in a wave of recent shootings across the city.

title: Conyers TikTok star trades health care career for auto repair and helps train new mechanics
description: Desiree White says she never thought she would become a mechanic. But when she left her health care career in 2019, she had been exploring the trade for a few months, buying, selling and gradually learning to repair cars on the side with her children.
content: Desiree White says she never thought she would become a mechanic. But when she left her health care career in 2019, she had been exploring the trade for a few months, buying, selling and gradually learning to repair cars on the side with her children."We started doing big, big jobs just to test ourselves and learn and really found that it was just so much drive and completing something and starting it back up. And it's not explainable," White said. "The feeling that you get as a person being able to accomplish something like that, especially without formal training."In 2021, White bet on herself, earned her certification and launched her mobile mechanic business, Crown's Corner Mechanics. She repaired cars across metro Atlanta before a customer encouraged her to open a shop and lent her the money to move into the building.White has since gained more than 160,000 followers on TikTok while documenting her journey."At first, you know, you think that you're going to get so much backlash because you're a female doing a man's job, and that's not the norm even still in this day and age. And to see that everybody was like, ra ra ra, let's go. Let's see what else you can do. I mean, it's been pretty amazing," White said.Her son, Dakota Curry, said his mother's venture has boosted his confidence."With how different the world is now compared to 20 years ago when our parents were working and getting their jobs and going to college, there's a lot more opportunities for trades. I mean, mechanics, they're not going to go anywhere. We're going to have cars all the time," Curry said.To help develop the next generation of skilled workers, White launched the Pro-Tech Pathway Foundation, a nonprofit offering hands-on workforce training for people interested in the automotive industry.Jeremiah Durden was working at Chipotle when White took him under her wing."And then I made the jump and probably like one of my best decisions of my life. I love my job," Durden said.As a mechanic, Durden said, he is constantly learning something new.Though it took White five years to get into the building, she said this is only the beginning."We have to own it. We have to expand and we have to bring in more businesses," White said.She envisions bringing together businesses to offer customers a one-stop shop and create more opportunities for people pursuing careers in the trades.

title: Walmart introduces discounted joint membership with Sam's Club
description: Amid stubbornly high inflation, the retailer is offering a combined Walmart+ and Sam's Club Plus membership for $120 a year.
content: Walmart on Tuesday debuted a discounted joint membership with Sam's Club, the retailer's warehouse club, in a bid to attract inflation-weary customers. Walmart said it's offering a combined Walmart+ and Sam's Club Plus membership for $120 a year, saving shoppers who buy them individually about $100 annually, according to the company. The joint membership gives customers access to members-only discounted prices at Sam's Club, free delivery on goods from both retailers, a Peacock or Paramount+ subscription plan, 10 cents off on gas at 17,000 stations across the U.S. and rewards on eligible purchases (Paramount+ is owned by Skydance, which also owns CBS News)."For $120 a year, we're raising expectations for what a membership can deliver: more money in their pockets and more time to call their own," Walmart CEO John Furner said in a statement. Existing members can also upgrade their plans. Walmart+ members can switch to the dual membership for $22 more per year, while Club members can upgrade to Sam's Club Plus for $60 more per year, which includes Walmart+. Walmart is betting that low prices and discounts will draw cash-strapped Americans into its stores. In August, Chief Financial Officer John Rainey announced price cuts across a range of products, including food. "We're investing heavily in price because customers need us to and because we believe it drives market share gains over time," Rainey said at the time. Walmart's efforts to ease prices come as consumers continue to grapple with elevated inflation, with the Consumer Price Index rising at an annual rate of 3.7% in September.After five years of elevated inflation, nine in 10 Americans say prices are the most important factor shaping their economic outlook, according to a recent CBS News poll.

title: How to find your Georgia sample ballot and key races in the 2026 midterm elections
description: Planning to vote in the Georgia midterm elections? Here's what you need to know before you walk into your polling place.
content: Early voting is underway in Georgia, and more than half a million people have already cast their ballots.Several key races are on the statewide ballot, including the governor and lieutenant governor's seats, both of which are open without incumbents running. Georgia's Senate race has drawn considerable national attention, with incumbent Sen. Jon Ossoff as the only Democrat running for reelection in a state that President Trump won two years ago. The senator is facing Republican Rep. Mike Collins in what has been a fiery few months of debates and rallies.How to see your county's sample ballot for the Georgia midtermsSo how do you know what races will be on your ballot before you head to your local polling place? There are a few ways you can check.One way is to use the Georgia Secretary of State's My Voter Page. Once logged in with your name, county, and date of birth, you can click a link to see your sample ballot and update your voter information. You can also see where you can cast your vote and your voter registration info.You can also check your county election department, which will have links to see the sample ballot.Statewide races will be on every voter's ballot, like the primaries for governor, lieutenant governor, and U.S. senator. Most other races are dependent on the county or legislative district.What races are on Georgia ballots?While local contests will very, most Georgians will see several statewide races that include:U.S. Senate: Mike Collins vs. Jon OssoffGovernor: Rick Jackson vs. Keisha Lance BottomsLieutenant Governor: Greg Dolezal vs. Josh McLaurinSecretary of State: Tim Fleming vs. Penny Brown ReynoldsAttorney General: Brian Strickland vs. Tanya MillerCommissioner of Agriculture: Incumbent Tyler Harper vs. Katherine E. Juhan-ArnoldCommissioner of Insurance: Incumbent John King vs. Keisha Sean WaitesState School Superintendent: Incumbent Richard Woods vs. Lydia PowellCommissioner of Labor: Incumbent Barbara Rivera Holmes vs. Nikki PorcherPublic Service Commissioner District 3: Fitz Johnson vs. Incumbent Peter HubbardPublic Service Commissioner District 5: Josh Tolbert vs. Sheila EdwardsResolutions on the Georgia midterm election ballotAlong with the state and local races on the ballot, Georgians will get the chance to vote on three constitutional amendments. To be ratified, the amendments need to only receive a majority of votes.Resolution 1: Tax exemption for farmland and timberlandVoters can decide whether the state will double the amount of farmland and timberland that can be counted as "bona fide conservation use property" from 2,000 to 4,000 acres.That land is taxed at 40% of its value with the requirement that it remains only for agricultural use, rather than for residential or commercial purposes.Resolution 2: Nonpartisan elections for some judgesVoters will decide on whether to amend Georgia's constitution to require all the state's probate court judges be elected on a nonpartisan basis.Currently, those judges in some parts of the state have a party affiliation, though most counties have made their probate court elections nonpartisan through local laws. The state's constitution already requires almost all of the state's judges, including Georgia Supreme Court justices, to be elected in nonpartisan races.Resolution 3: Creating a statewide Next Generation 911 FundThe third amendment would allow Georgia lawmakers to dedicate some tax revenue the state already receives to a new nonlapsing fund known as the Georgia Next Generation 911 Fund.That fund would be used exclusively to expland, maintain and operate 911 systems across the state.

title: Oakland County investigating vehicle crash, subsequent shooting, in Pontiac
description: The Oakland County Sheriff's Office is investigating a crash in the 700 block of East Beverly Avenue, with shots fired afterward.
content: Deputies are seeking information from the public about a shooting and vehicle crash in Pontiac, Michigan. The Oakland County Sheriff's Office said it received a report at about 1:37 a.m. on Sunday about a crash in the 700 block of East Beverly Avenue, with shots fired afterward. Witnesses told deputies that a tan sedan rear-ended a white sedan near the intersection of East Beverly Avenue and Arlene Street, which is near Pontiac High School. After the crash, a man got out of the white car, approached the driver's side of the tan car, and fired multiple gunshots into the ground while standing outside of the vehicles. Both cars then sped off westbound on East Beverly Avenue toward Joslyn Avenue. Deputies responding to the scene found 10 spent 9 mm shell casings and one live round of ammunition. Vehicle debris was also located on the roadway. Investigators were also able to obtain security footage that showed part of the incident. The circumstances surrounding the shooting remain under investigation. Deputies ask that anyone with information about the crash and shooting, including the identities of those involved or the location of either vehicle, contact the Oakland County Sheriff's Office at 248-858-4950.

title: Trump signs executive order creating women's health division within NIH
description: "Who the hell wouldn't have a women's health division?" President Trump said Monday.
content: Washington — President Trump on Monday signed an executive order creating a women's health division within the National Institutes of Health and a White House Women's Health Task Force.First lady Melania Trump joined him for a signing ceremony in the Rose Garden and said the executive order will make progress on five objectives: Directing research funding to find cures that disproportionately affect women.Using artificial intelligence to speed up medical discoveries.Accelerating new therapeutics for women.Delivering medical breakthroughs for women at an affordable price.Making conversations about women's health less taboo. "This is a transformative moment for women in America," the first lady said. "Beginning today, we will change the reality of women's health. Previous generations fought for women's rights. Our generation will fight to discover the cures that will ensure a woman can live her life in health and to the fullest."Mr. Trump credited the first lady with conceiving the idea for a women's health division within NIH. The first lady added her signature to the executive order after the president did, although her signature has no legal weight. "Think of it, a women's health division," Mr. Trump said. "Who the hell wouldn't have a women's health division? Melania said, 'They don't have it.'"The president said Americans will soon hear about "incredible things that we're doing" to get women the care they need, although he didn't offer specifics. It's not yet clear how much funding will be directed toward research funding, accelerating therapeutics, or making medical breakthroughs more affordable for women.During an interview on "CBS Mornings" Tuesday, NIH Director Dr. Jay Bhattacharya said the amount of funding for the new project was still undetermined."The first lady made it very clear that she wants to focus on topics in women's health that have been just neglected, you know, endometriosis, menopause, a whole host of topics that, you know, frankly, we've underinvested in, learned less about than we should have over the years," Bhattacharya said. "And so it's very, very exciting, and, yes, some new money will very likely be devoted to this, although that's still to be determined exactly how much."Bhattacharya was joined on "CBS Mornings" by the director of the government's Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, Alicia Jackson. She said Mr. Trump's executive order directs agencies to use funding on critical issues in women's health."We're going to have several announcements over the course of this year where we are putting — and our agency has the liberty and the luxury of doing this — but $100 million, $200 million towards massive efforts that impact women, to drive solutions as quickly as possible," Jackson said.The women's health announcement comes on the heels of White House chief of staff Susie Wiles' battle with breast cancer. She continued in the job after her March diagnosis, and in September announced she is cancer-free.Mr. Trump gave a shout-out to Wiles during Monday's announcement, calling her "fantastic.""I don't know if Susie wants this brought up, but as many of you know, Susie recently won her battle against a very tough opponent, breast cancer," the president said. "It wasn't easy. We went through it, we got her through it, and she got through it, and she's tough. But she's a tremendous fighter and much like our first lady, she cares deeply about improving the health of American women." White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said the White House task force "will work to close critical research gaps and strengthen care for women across all stages of life, targeting some of the most widespread health conditions affecting them."

title: After decades in prison, Georgia man helps others navigate life after release
description: A Clayton County commissioner spent Monday night listening to formerly incarcerated people talk about what is keeping them from a fresh start.
content: A Clayton County commissioner spent Monday night listening to formerly incarcerated people talk about what is keeping them from a fresh start."We're coming home and doing the right thing," said Genesis Asiatic, who works with The Life Unit Prison Help & Support Services.Commissioner Tashé Allen partnered with Barred Business for a volunteer membership meeting and listening session Monday night in Jonesboro. Organizers invited formerly incarcerated people, their families and community advocates to share their experiences, challenges and ideas.Barred Business is a membership-based organization that helps formerly incarcerated people. The group said probation, fines, fees and job restrictions hold many people back after they return home.The group also runs STABLE, a program that helps formerly incarcerated Black women with housing, leadership and financial stability. More than 213 women have completed the program, according to Barred Business.Asiatic said he spent more than two decades in a Virginia prison. He entered at age 23, unable to read, and went on to earn his GED and become a tutor.He said he grew up with his mother and grandmother and was looking for a male role model."But unfortunately, the ones I saw … actually in the streets and a lot of times I think that's what young men are looking for," Asiatic said.One moment in prison still stays with him.
