Asiatic said he shared a cell with a young man who was headed in the wrong direction but chose not to speak up."But that individual went home and took the life of somebody that I knew," he said.Asiatic now works with The Life Unit Prison Help & Support Services, which he said attends community events and helps people find jobs and resources to stay out of prison.He said he did not know how to look for a job online when he returned home. People leaving prison need to be patient with themselves, he said.Asked what he would tell his younger self, Asiatic did not hesitate."Don't do it," he said.He encouraged young people to consider how their choices will affect their lives, their families and those around them.People interested in joining Barred Business or volunteering can sign up through the group's website.

title: Shark kills woman swimming off popular beach in South Africa
description: Local media reported the woman was a regular swimmer and had been swimming with a group when the attack occurred.
content: A woman died after being mauled by a shark while swimming off a popular beach on South Africa's southeastern coast on Tuesday, witnesses and authorities said.Fatal shark attacks are uncommon worldwide but South Africa has a history of deadly encounters along its long coastline.Tuesday's attack was at Orient Beach in KuGompo City, previously known as East London. Police said they were called to the scene at around 7:00 am local time, where they found the body of a 65-year-old woman with "open wounds."Local media reported the woman was a regular swimmer and had been swimming with a group when the attack occurred. A local community group said other swimmers had spotted a shark's tail and fin. The group said the woman sustained "severe injuries to the right side of her arm and leg." "We all realized she'd been bitten by a shark, and she was in a very bad way," a witness told public broadcaster SABC. "The bites were very severe, but there were only two, one on her thigh and one on her upper arm." After the attack, the municipality closed nearby beaches and urged the public to stay out of the water."It has been confirmed that a shark attack occurred at Orient Beach this morning, and this resulted in a tragic incident," the local municipality said in a statement.The incident comes about one month after a man was killed by a shark in front of beachgoers as he swam off a Western Australian city shore.There were 65 unprovoked shark bites worldwide in 2025, up from 47 the previous year, including nine fatalities, according to the University of Florida's International Shark Attack File. There was one unprovoked attack in South Africa last year, which was fatal. By contrast, there were 25 unprovoked attacks in the U.S. (one fatal) and 21 unprovoked attacks in Australia (five fatal).In 2022, there were two fatal shark attacks in South Africa, including a 39-year-old woman who was on vacation with her husband and young child when she was killed. Researchers say encounters can be influenced by a range of factors, including growing coastal populations, increased use of marine waters, environmental changes and shifts in the distribution of sharks and their prey.

title: How new and refurbished arenas and stadiums are shutting out loyal sports fans
description: The cost of attending live sports has shot up 123% since 2000 — a staggering increase that cannot solely be blamed on inflation​.
content: PHILADELPHIA — A few months before basketball superstar LeBron James made his decision to join the 76ers, season ticket holder Aaron Selkow was also staring down a crossroad: does he renew for a 59th season or has the buzzer sounded on the family's longtime investment?"I'd been thinking about it forever," Selkow, 56, recalled to CBS News. "Those seats are us. I went from being a baby sitting on my parents' lap to being next to my dad at games. The Sixers are more than a basketball team."Don Selkow, Aaron's father, first purchased season tickets in 1968. The two seats were located only a few rows back of the visitor bench at a cost of $6.50 each. "It's like watching the ballet," Don quipped. "They're right in front of us. We love the sport. We love each other. What could be better?"For decades, the Selkows would see all the greats, from George McGinnis to Julius Erving, Charles Barkley to Allen Iverson.By 2026, however, each ticket to each game ran more than $600."It wasn't even just the finances," Aaron said. "It just didn't make common sense. We have a daughter in college who wanted to and now is going to graduate school. And we had wanted to, you know, do some fun things in our life."After nearly 60 years, it was game over — a decision so agonizing that instead of calling his father, Aaron wrote all his thoughts in a letter to his dad. Aaron's letter was also published in an op-ed in the Philadelphia Inquirer — a choice that would resonate with other sports fans across the region and even around the country."It was Eagles tickets or it was New York Giants tickets or it was Detroit Pistons tickets," Aaron added. "The world has changed and the rate of the increase in prices is going faster than the rate of inflation. The Sixers want someone who will pay the price and that's their product."From family experiences to exclusive offeringsThe cost of attending live sports has shot up 123% since 2000, according to the Consumer Price Index — a staggering increase that cannot solely be blamed on inflation. When the Selkows first became season ticket holders, the 76ers played their games at the Spectrum, a modest arena built in the 1960s in the same style as the Boston Garden, Chicago Stadium and Los Angeles' Great Western Forum. The 76ers moved to the since-renamed Xfinity Mobile Arena across the street in 1996, a sprawling multi-level arena that slightly increased capacity but also made the seats plusher with suites, clubs and restaurants. The arena has since completed a $400 million renovation last year.So while the number of seats for fans might have gone up, the actual number of seats for sale to the average fan have actually gone down — a trend that is on a roll across the country in all major sports.The CBS News Data Team analyzed all stadiums and arenas in America's biggest sports cities like Philadelphia with professional teams in the four major sports: the NFL, MLB, NBA and NHL. According to CBS News analysis, new stadiums and arenas built since 2000 have actually lowered overall capacity by nearly 90,000 seats, while those venues have been running up the score on the percentage of those seats reserved for clubs, boxes and suites.In NFL stadiums, that's especially true in Buffalo, where the new Highmark Stadium is now the smallest among 32 teams, with a capacity of roughly 60,000 — down 16% from Bills Stadium's capacity of more than 71,000. The stadium also features two suite levels, while the team sold more than 3,600 club suite licenses for $65 million.Globe Life Field, the new home of baseball's Texas Rangers, also shrank by more than 16% compared to The Ballpark at Arlington. Globe Life Field also added more than 130 suites and more than 3,000 club seats.Rebuilds and renovations remove seats too. Angels Stadium in Anaheim's 1998 conversion cut 19,076 seats, while Miami's Hard Rock Stadium cut 10,692 in its remodel in 2015–16. Soldier Field, the current home of the Chicago Bears, cut 5,444 in its renovation in 2003.Several franchises, including the Bears, Kansas City Chiefs, Dallas Stars, Washington Commanders and Philadelphia 76ers, among others, are planning new arenas and stadiums in the next five years."Everything is getting more expensive"While the cost to attend a game has gone up, so have the costs of running a sports franchise, especially one that fields a winning roster.Mike Vorkunov, a sports business writer for The Athletic and The New York Times, says owners are trying to maximize revenues through premium seating and exclusive offerings."Everything is getting more expensive," he told CBS News. "Player costs are going up, the cost of coaches are going up, the cost of general managers and front office members are going up, the cost of travel is going up, the cost of sending your scouts across the world and across the country are going up, the cost of [research and development] and tech. There's a lot of costs ... outside of just paying for the players and salaries that I think a lot of people don't know about."Vorkunov added that new owners are especially looking to cash in after paying billions to purchase a franchise."I think for a lot of years, people thought of sports as something fun, something that was like a mom-and-pop organization, they could run a small deficit and be OK with it," he said. "I think now how much it costs to buy a team, the get-in price for a team is so much higher. The amount of losses that you can incur are so much higher because there's so much more money in play. The entire sports ecosystem is that they're being incentivized to treat it like a business to try to make a profit every year."As for loyal fans like the Selkows, Vorkunov says owners are increasingly recognizing the need to appeal to those kinds of returning customers that at one time might have been the bread-and-butter of the business."That's something that everyone has to kind of wrestle with, where it doesn't feel like sports at every level is something that's unattainable anymore," he said.The Selkows themselves may not be in their seats anymore as the 76ers pursue their first championship since 1983. But if LeBron James helps bring them to the NBA Finals, Aaron and Don will no doubt be watching together."Everybody that knows us knows that the Selkows and the Sixers do sort of go together," Aaron said.

title: FBI investigates "suspicious" letters containing "unknown substance" sent to at least 4 Colorado lawmakers
description: The FBI is investigating after multiple Colorado politicians were sent letters packed with an unknown white powder, and Colorado isn't the only place targeted.
content: The FBI is investigating after multiple Colorado politicians were sent letters packed with an unknown white powder, and Colorado isn't the only place targeted.Similar letters were sent to politicians in more than a dozen other states last week. They were addressed to U.S. senators, representatives and secretaries of state offices.At least four Democratic Colorado lawmakers reported receiving suspicious letters to their Colorado offices Monday. Luckily, those lawmakers say their staff is safe.A suspicious letter containing white powder was delivered Monday to Congressman Joe Neguse's Boulder County office.The Democratic representative shared the following statement:I take seriously the safety of my staff and the community I represent, and I'd like to extend my gratitude to the local and federal law enforcement officials who acted swiftly to respond to reports of a threatening letter with suspicious substances being sent to our district office in Boulder County. Because of them, there is no continued threat to public safety in the area.The nature of this mailing, and others like it being received by elected officials across the country, whether to cause physical harm or provoke unease among public servants, will not prevent me and my team from working day in and day out to serve the people of Colorado's 2nd District.It's clear that there has been a real, palpable sense of fear percolating in communities across the country lately. And while we know that fear can be contagious, I firmly believe that so is hope. I'll continue to do everything in my power to choose hope — and to stand up for the people of Colorado.— Congressman Joe Neguse, D-ColoradoThe same day, suspicious letters arrived at U.S. Rep. Jason Crow's Aurora office, U.S. Rep. Brittany Pettersen's Lakewood office, and U.S. Rep. Diana DeGette's Office.They shared the following statements:Earlier today, my congressional office in Aurora received a letter with a suspicious substance. This appears to be one of many unfortunate instances across the country where congressional offices have received mail containing unknown, suspicious substances.My staff is safe, and our district office remains open for those who need assistance. Attempts to intimidate me or my team will not stop our work on behalf of Coloradans.I want to thank the FBI, U.S. Capitol Police, Aurora Police Department, and other law enforcement for swiftly working to investigate this matter and keeping everyone safe.— Congressman Jason Crow, D-ColoradoThis is a deeply disturbing effort to intimidate sitting Members of Congress. I'm grateful for the safety of my staff — who are hardworking public servants, and should not have to fear for their lives while doing their jobs. I'm also grateful to the Colorado FBI for their quick action to protect us. This will be fully investigated and the people responsible must be held accountable.— Congresswoman Brittany Pettersen, D-ColoradoEarlier today, my office received a letter containing a suspicious substance. My staff is safe and unharmed, and I thank local law enforcement for their rapid response, investigation, and commitment to public safety. I remain focused on serving my constituents to the best of my ability, and I reject this shameful act of intimidation targeting me and my fellow colleagues.— Congresswoman Diana DeGette, D-ColoradoIt's not just Colorado's representatives. Postal investigators intercepted a suspicious letter addressed to Sen. John Hickenlooper's Denver office.A Hickenlooper spokesperson shared this statement:"Our office has been notified that postal investigators intercepted a suspicious letter addressed to our Denver office. We're grateful to federal authorities for their work to protect our staff and others who have been targeted. Violence and intimidation have no place in our politics. Not now, not ever."The FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating the suspicious mailings, which the FBI says are being sent to secretaries of state, congressional and election offices across the country.While so far only Democratic lawmakers in Colorado have reported receiving the suspicious letters, nationwide, at least three Senate Republicans have received one, as well as several Democratic House and Senate members from other states.Many of those officials have reported the letters contained white powdery substances, though none have been confirmed to be harmful.It's not clear what, if anything, the letters said.CBS Colorado did not find evidence of any hazardous materials response to the reported letters in Colorado, with workers in the shared office buildings of Pettersen's and Hickenlooper's offices telling CBS Colorado they were never evacuated and didn't see any first responders or commotion Monday.In a statement, the FBI said it's working to identify the person or persons responsible and pledged to safeguard the public and American elections."The FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices, and Congressional offices. Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident. We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters. This FBI and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service will continue to safeguard the public and secure elections for American citizens."-FBI DenverSen. Michael Bennet's Denver office tells CBS Colorado they have not received one of these letters.Gov. Jared Polis's office did not receive a suspicious letter and released this statement, "Reports of suspicious mail being sent to congressional offices across the country are very scary, and I hope that staff and members whose offices have been targeted are safe. These incidents must be thoroughly investigated, and I hope to see those responsible held accountable to the full extent of the law." CBS Colorado reached out to other state leaders, including Secretary of State Jena Griswold, Attorney General Phil Weiser, Rep. Lauren Boebert and Rep. Gabe Evans, and have not heard back about whether their offices received anything suspicious.

title: How to find your Florida sample ballot and key races in the 2026 midterm elections
description: Florida voters can review their sample ballots ahead of the midterms, including personalized ballots for Miami-Dade, Broward, Palm Beach and Monroe counties.
content: Florida voters can preview exactly what will appear on their ballots ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, with races ranging from governor and U.S. Senate to congressional seats, state offices and local ballot questions.With early voting already underway across South Florida, sample ballots allow voters to see the candidates, constitutional amendments and local measures they will be asked to decide. They can also help voters research unfamiliar races and make informed decisions before casting their ballots.Because some contests vary by congressional district, municipality and precinct, voters should review their personalized sample ballot rather than relying solely on a countywide version.How to find your Florida sample ballotEvery Florida county has a Supervisor of Elections office that provides sample ballots and other voting information ahead of Election Day.Voters can generally find their personalized ballots by visiting their county elections website and using the voter information lookup tool.Here's where to find sample ballots in South Florida:Miami-Dade CountyMiami-Dade voters can access their personalized sample ballots through the county's ⁠Voter Information Lookup tool.The website allows registered voters to review their voting districts, polling locations, registration information and the specific contests that will appear on their ballots.The county has also published its ⁠official 2026 general election sample ballot, which includes candidates and ballot questions.Broward CountyBroward voters can view their personalized sample ballots through the ⁠Broward County Supervisor of Elections website.The homepage includes a "View Your Sample Ballot" section that directs voters to their ballot information.The website also provides information about polling locations, voter registration and other election resources.Palm Beach CountyPalm Beach County voters can find their sample ballots through the ⁠Palm Beach County Supervisor of Elections website.The county has published sample ballots for all precincts participating in the Nov. 3 general election, along with a comprehensive ballot showing all contests and proposed constitutional amendments.Voters can also use the county's voter information tools to review their personalized ballot and find their assigned Election Day polling place.Monroe CountyMonroe County voters, including those living in the Florida Keys, can access sample ballots through the ⁠Monroe County Supervisor of Elections website.The county has published separate sample ballots for several jurisdictions, including Key West, Key Colony Beach, Islamorada and other areas. Sample ballots are available in English and Spanish.Voters should select the ballot corresponding to their jurisdiction to review the races and questions they will be eligible to vote on.Residents of other Florida counties can find their local elections office through the ⁠Florida Division of Elections' statewide directory.What are some of the key races on Florida's 2026 midterm ballots?Florida voters will decide several major statewide races on Nov. 3, along with congressional contests that could help determine control of the U.S. House and Senate.Some of the key elections include:Florida governor and lieutenant governor: Voters will elect the state's next governor and lieutenant governor.U.S. Senate: Florida voters will choose a U.S. senator to represent the state in Washington.U.S. House of Representatives: All of Florida's congressional districts are up for election, including several closely watched races in South Florida.Florida attorney general: Voters will choose the state's chief legal officer.Florida chief financial officer: The position oversees several aspects of the state's financial operations.Florida agriculture commissioner: Voters will select the official who leads the state's Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services.Florida Legislature: State House seats and applicable state Senate seats are on the ballot.Judicial retention elections: Voters will decide whether certain Florida Supreme Court justices and district court of appeal judges should remain in office.Constitutional amendments and local measures: Voters will also weigh in on proposed changes to the Florida Constitution and local ballot questions.Depending on where they live, voters may also see contests for county commission seats, school board positions and other local offices.Not every race or ballot question will appear on every voter's ballot.Why should you review your sample ballot before voting?Reviewing a sample ballot gives voters an opportunity to research candidates and understand ballot questions before arriving at a polling location.This can be particularly helpful for lengthy ballots containing judicial retention questions, constitutional amendments and local measures that may be less familiar to voters.Voters can also use their sample ballots to identify races they want to research further and prepare their selections ahead of time.It is important to note that a sample ballot is for reference and cannot be printed and submitted as an official vote.When is Election Day in Florida?Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, with polls open statewide from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.Early voting began Oct. 19 in Miami-Dade, Broward, Palm Beach and Monroe counties.In Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach counties, early voting runs through Nov. 1. In Monroe County, early voting ends Oct. 31.During early voting, registered voters can cast their ballots at any designated early voting location within their county of registration.On Election Day, however, voters must cast their ballots at their assigned precinct polling location.Voters can confirm their polling place, review registration information and access other election resources through their county Supervisor of Elections website.

title: Early voting is underway in Texas. Here's how to find your polling place in North Texas
description: Early voting in Texas runs Oct. 19-30 ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Here's what North Texas voters need to know about polling locations, hours and requirements.
content: Early voting in Texas began this Monday, Oct. 19, and runs through Friday, Oct. 30, ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms.Long lines, voting machine problems or other issues at the polls? CBS News Texas wants to hear from you, click here. The Nov. 3 ballot includes races for the U.S. Senate, governor, lieutenant governor, attorney general, comptroller, land commissioner, agriculture commissioner, railroad commission, congressional and state legislative seats, state board of education, and judicial offices. County and local races vary by location.Here's what North Texas voters need to know about voting dates, hours, identification requirements, and polling locations.When is Election Day in Texas?Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3, with polls open statewide from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.Registered, eligible voters can cast their ballots early in person without needing a special reason.Am I registered to vote?The deadline to register for the Nov. 3 election was Monday, Oct. 5.Voters can check their registration status through the Texas Secretary of State's Am I Registered? website.What are the early voting hours in Texas?Early voting hours may vary by county and location, but state law establishes minimum hours for main early voting polling places:Oct. 19-23: At least nine hours each weekday. Saturday, Oct. 24: At least 12 consecutive hours. Sunday, Oct. 25: At least six consecutive hours. Oct. 26-30: At least 12 consecutive hours each weekday.These are minimum requirements for main polling locations, not uniform statewide schedules. Voters should check their county's election website for specific hours.Where can you vote early in North Texas?Registered voters can cast their ballots at any designated early voting location in their county of registration.Voters can find polling locations through the Texas Secretary of State's Find Your Polling Place website.The state's voter lookup system allows voters to search using their name, county, date of birth, and ZIP code. Early voting locations are scheduled to appear in the system on Saturday, Oct. 17.Polling locations and hours are also available through county election offices:Dallas County: Dallas County Elections Tarrant County: Tarrant County Elections Collin County: Collin County polling locations Denton County: Denton County ElectionsOn Election Day, voters in counties participating in the countywide polling place program may vote at any designated countywide location. Other counties require voters to use their assigned precinct polling places.What do I need to bring to the polls?Texas voters are generally required to present one of seven acceptable forms of photo identification:Texas Driver License issued by the Texas Department of Public Safety (DPS) Texas Election Identification Certificate issued by DPS Texas Personal Identification Card issued by DPS Texas Handgun License issued by DPS U.S. Military Identification Card containing a photograph U.S. Citizenship Certificate containing a photograph U.S. Passport (book or card)For voters ages 18 to 69, photo identification must be current or expired no more than four years. Voters 70 and older may use an otherwise valid ID that has expired for any length of time. U.S. Citizenship Certificates do not expire.Voters who cannot reasonably obtain an acceptable photo ID may present an approved supporting document, such as a current utility bill, bank statement, or voter registration certificate, and complete a Reasonable Impediment Declaration at the polls.For more information, including identification exemptions, visit the state's voter ID requirements website.For additional information, visit VoteTexas.gov.

title: Australian man charged in "targeted" attack on lawmaker Helen Haines, who reportedly lost leg
description: Australian police charged a man on Tuesday over what they alleged was a "targeted" attack with a vehicle on independent lawmaker Helen Haines.
content: Australian police charged a man on Tuesday over what they alleged was a "targeted" attack with a vehicle on independent lawmaker Helen Haines.Haines has reportedly lost one of her legs in the aftermath of the incident on Monday afternoon, in which a car rammed into her multiple times as she stood near the trunk of her own parked vehicle in the southeastern city of Wangaratta, according to the Australian Broadcasting Corporation.Authorities said the 65-year-old was getting something from the back of her car when her alleged attacker drove past in a Toyota Land Cruiser. He allegedly turned the car around before veering into Haines, pinning her against her own vehicle and then reversing before ramming into her again, according to local authorities and Australian Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke. Brendan Nugent, from nearby Tarrawingee, was charged with intentionally causing serious injury, dangerous driving causing serious injury and causing harm to a federal official, police said in a statement on Tuesday. Police have said little about the suspect's potential motive, but they have characterized the incident as a "deliberate" act of violence. Political violence is historically uncommon across Australia, though data show threats have grown in recent years.Suspect to face court on WednesdayNugent has been in police custody since shortly after Haines was injured and a crowd of bystanders subdued him. He will appear in a Wangaratta court on Wednesday, when he could potentially be released on bail.His father, Rod Nugent, released a statement Tuesday describing Haines as a "deeply respected, valued and much-loved member of our local community." "Helen has been our friend for more than 20 years and what happened to her yesterday is devastating and unfathomable," the father said, adding that he would cooperate with police."Absolutely devastated"Wangaratta Mayor Irene Grant said a somber mood had settled over the town of about 30,000 people, a regional hub about 250 kilometers, or 155 miles, northeast of state capital Melbourne."Helen was well-respected. She was diligent and hard working," Grant told AFP. "What has happened to Helen has caused the community to step back in utter disbelief. We can't believe it, people are horrified by what has happened."Locals, meanwhile, are struggling to comprehend why anyone would wish harm on the well-liked Haines.Florist Jess Woodrow said Haines was a friendly face who would pop into the store when she was not tied up in the capital Canberra."We are absolutely devastated to hear what has happened. Helen was a beautiful person. She didn't have a bad bone in her body," Woodrow told AFP. "It's the last thing you would think would happen here."Haines entered parliament as an independent lawmaker in 2019, representing the sprawling seat of Indi. Her popularity led to her holding the seat in the 2025 election, with a hefty margin of more than 18,000 votes.Haines was a vocal champion for greater climate action, better rural healthcare, and help for struggling small businesses, while the First Peoples' Assembly of Victoria said Haines was a "staunch supporter" of Indigenous rights as well. But it was her work to hold politicians to account that perhaps earned Haines the most respect both inside and outside parliament."Helen Haines is characterized by her kindness, her compassion, her diligence, her intelligence," Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said. "She's someone who is such a strong advocate and is widely respected right across the political spectrum because the way that she advocates is very respectful."

title: Boston Pops celebrate Day of the Dead with concert and Disney's "Coco"
description: The sounds of Mexican music will soon fill Boston's Symphony Hall for the third annual Dia de Muertos concert.
content: The sounds of Mexican music will soon fill Boston's Symphony Hall for the third annual Dia de Muertos concert. The Day of the Dead is a multi-day celebration, traditionally taking place on Nov. 1 and 2. Conductor Keith Lockhart and the Boston Pops are bringing in some incredible musicians to Symphony Hall to mark the holiday. "To be able to bring not only the Mexican, but the entire Latino community into Symphony Hall, celebrating a shared cultural moment is really, really important. And plus, it's a lot of fun," Lockhart told WBZ-TV. The concert's lineup features several Mexican music acts, namely indie rock band Enjambre, singer-songwriter Silvana Estrada and mariachi singer Veronica Robles. "I think it's beautiful. There's a bunch of Latino community in Boston," Estrada said. Robles, who is based in New England, is returning for her third Day of the Dead concert with the Boston Pops."We are bringing something different to the audiences of Massachusetts. And the orchestral lovers have the opportunity to see beautiful culture through music," Robles said. The Boston Pops' Day of the Dead celebration will also feature "Disney and Pixar's Coco in Concert Live to Film." "It's a beautiful story. It's a universal story," Lockhart said. "And it's entirely about the Day of the Dead, what we leave behind and who we remember." "You don't need to speak the language to understand the feeling of the composer and the feeling of the arrangement and the feeling of the lyrics," Robles said. "Because it's something that you can embrace it without understanding the words." The Boston Pops' Day of the Dead concert at Symphony Hall is set for Oct. 29. "Disney and Pixar's Coco in Concert Live to Film" will play at Symphony Hall on Oct. 30 and 31.

title: Ukraine's Zelenskyy says if Trump "cannot rein Putin in," at least clear interceptor missile shipment
description: Ukraine's leader calls on Trump to allow delivery of interceptor missiles already purchased by European allies if the U.S. "cannot rein Putin in."
content: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an interview published Tuesday that if President Trump "cannot rein Putin in," he should provide long-requested interceptor missiles so Ukraine can defend itself, as the war of words between the two leaders continues to escalate."If you cannot rein Putin in, then give us interceptor missiles so I can protect our energy infrastructure," Zelenskyy told the Italian newspaper Corriere Della Sera, referring to Russia's autocratic President Vladimir Putin. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said later Tuesday that Mr. Trump has been "frustrated" by what he described as false accusations that "he is doing things to deliberately harm Ukraine." He insisted that nothing had been "deliberately denied to Ukraine," but added: "It's simply, it's a balance between our obligations to other partners and frankly our own ... requirements for our own facilities as well." The exchange came as Zelenskyy prepared to meet U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff in Norway on Tuesday, with his fellow envoy, Mr. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, expected to join remotely.Zelenskyy has accused the Trump administration this week of delaying shipments of interceptor missiles to Ukraine, as well as constraining Starlink satellite data that is vital to Ukrainian forces' ability to intercept incoming Russian attack drones.Ukraine has nearly run out of the U.S.-made Patriot air defense interceptors used to take down Russian ballistic missiles, and Zelenskyy has long pleaded for more. This week he said the U.S. was delaying delivery of Patriots already purchased by European nations for Ukraine.Rubio, on a visit to India, said "every other country in the world" also wanted Patriots. "I also talked to Saudi Arabia today. They'd like interceptors. Israel would like interceptors. We would like interceptors. Every country in the world would like interceptors," he said. "It's probably the most in-demand product right now in the defense field. So, when a country doesn't get interceptors from the United States, it's not because we're denying." The meeting comes as daily Russian drone and missile attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities continue claiming civilian lives, and as relations between Kyiv and Washington appear more strained than they have been since Zelenskyy's tumultuous February 2025 meeting in the Oval Office.The Ukrainian president said Monday that his country had suffered another night of Russian strikes, "and again there was no warning from partners." At least four people were killed in the capital in the latest attacks, Kyiv officials said Tuesday.Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said Finnish President Alexander Stubb would also join the talks in Oslo, with "the aim to put diplomatic efforts on a more constructive path," according to a statement from the prime minister's office.Starshield and PatriotsMr. Trump on Friday waived some sanctions against Russia, reducing penalties for its energy sales in a bid to ease rising U.S. gas prices caused by the ongoing war with Iran — a policy Zelenskyy says could embolden Moscow to step up its four-and-a-half-year invasion of Ukraine.Mr. Trump has criticized Zelenskyy for saying he would resume strikes on Russian refineries in retaliation for the latest Russian onslaught.Zelenskyy said Saturday that Ukraine was still unable to use Starshield — the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite network — to intercept Russian drones.The Trump administration has denied ordering Starshield restrictions. A senior Pentagon official told CBS News Monday that there had been "no change to Department of War policy regarding intelligence sharing or any capabilities we are enabling Europeans to provide to Ukraine."In recent days, Mr. Trump has intensified his public criticism of Zelenskyy, saying in a Truth Social post that the Ukrainian leader "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did," and telling reporters, "maybe it's time for Zelenskyy to get somebody else to negotiate."Mr. Trump has never publicly acknowledged that Russia started the war against its neighbor, which initially began in 2014, and has at times blamed Zelenskyy for the full-scale invasion ordered by Putin on Feb. 24, 2022.Ahead of his Tuesday meeting with Mr. Trump's envoys, Zelenskyy said he had a "substantive conversation" with Rubio the previous day in which he stressed that Starshield "needs to be restored" and ballistic missile interceptors "are needed to protect lives."Zelenskyy told a bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers via video call on Monday that "the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles" already paid for by European countries. He said Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth hadn't signed off on the shipment.Multiple European countries were waiting for U.S. approval to transfer their own Patriot interceptors, he added, saying he believed "some political decision has been made to slow down ... support for us."Rubio said Tuesday that it ⁠could be accurate that a batch ‌of interceptors purchased for Ukraine ⁠had not been delivered, but he told reporters: "I think the important takeaway for ⁠you is that there has not been some ‌deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine."Rubio also said Mr. Trump was "frustrated because, first of all, he doesn't like to be blamed for things that aren't true, including accusations that somehow he had ordered intelligence sharing to be cut off. And that's not true. He's said that repeatedly.""I think the president, more than anything, is responding to the insinuation that somehow he is doing things to deliberately harm Ukraine — which is not fair and not true," he added.In his interview with the Italian newspaper, published hours earlier, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had built its relationship with Washington "on honesty, fairness, and, most importantly, transparency.""When you lie while your people are at war, it is very painful. That is why I have always wanted to hide nothing and never lie to the President of the United States," Zelenskyy told the paper, adding: "We would like to continue having the same open, honest, and pragmatic relations with America that we have today.""The Russians are striking. America cannot stop them," he said. "Let's believe that America really wants to, but cannot. Then, as a partner, I am willing to meet President Trump halfway: if they strike us and we cannot strike back — that is neither honest nor fair — but if this is what you need, if you cannot rein Putin in, then give us interceptor missiles so I can protect our energy infrastructure."Trump-Xi-Putin summit on Ukraine?U.S.-led efforts to end the nearly five-year conflict have stalled in recent months, with Washington more focused on its war with Iran.Mr. Trump recently said he was ready to meet with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in China next month for talks that could include discussion of the Ukraine war.Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has confirmed that "the topic of such a hypothetical has indeed been mentioned."Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said this week that any such meeting on his country's fate, without Ukraine at the table, would "only encourage Putin to continue this war."

title: Massachusetts couple discovers surprising series of connections while wedding planning: "What are the odds of that?"
description: A newlywed couple in Franklin, Massachusetts, recently discovered that their connection goes back to their baptism.
content: Sometimes the best love stories come with a surprise that you never saw coming.A newlywed couple in Franklin, Massachusetts, recently discovered that their connection goes all the way back to their baptism."It was junior year of college and he did tell me that we were going to get married the day that he met me," recalled Jessica McGinty, laughing.It was love at first sight for Ryan McGinty, when then-Jessica Connolly came to visit her friends at his college campus. Quite the meet-cute for these now newlyweds, who grew up in neighboring Westwood and Walpole. "Seven minutes away from each other our whole life and didn't know each other," she said.Complete strangers, but both belonged to St. Timothy Catholic Church in Norwood. "My dad's still a lector here," said Ryan McGinty. "We still come here. This is probably the best place to be because this is where we've been our whole lives."They grew up in different towns, had different friends, and went to different colleges. But when planning the details of their wedding day, God's divine direction in their lives was clear - he makes everything beautiful in its time. "Our moms both knew it was a day in February, and it was freezing cold, it was our baptism," Jessica explained, of piecing it all together."I was looking at the registry books and sure enough they were baptized together," said pastoral associate Michelle Gallo. "I decided to look at the other sacraments, sure enough, first communion, confirmation, and now wedding. What are the odds of that? To think that you were together to receive all those graces four times? That's pretty special."And as they look ahead to their future, the couple feels so blessed to build on this strong foundation, with supportive families, a parish that feels like home, and a real respect and admiration for each other. "Even when I'm having a bad day, come home from work and I'm maybe in a bad mood, I still feel Ryan's love all the time," Jessica said. "You would have a really hard time with all the people that know her, to find one person that had a bad thing to say about her," her husband added.

title: Trump won Iowa by 13 points, but Republicans are on defense heading into November
description: Trump will return to Iowa twice before the Nov. 3 election. Democrats are running spirited campaigns for governor, Senate and several U.S. House seats in a state Trump carried by 13 percentage points two years ago.
content: Standing in the doorway of his home near the corn and soybean fields that blanket this stretch of northeast Iowa, Dave Roethler doesn't know what happened to the man he supported during President Trump's first term.Mr. Trump did a "heck of a good job" back then, the 70-year-old school custodian said. But now Roethler laments an economy in which "it's the middle-class families that are taking the big hit" while Mr. Trump is "going to come out way ahead." He scoffs at the Republican president's effort to win accolades such as the Nobel Peace Prize or a spot on Mount Rushmore."I think he has delusions of grandeur," said Roethler, who plans to support Democrats in November in a state that has become a midterm battleground after Mr. Trump carried it by 13 percentage points in 2024. The president will return to Iowa twice before the election to rally supporters.Democrats face a steep challenge in winning rural communities like this one in Chickasaw County, a one-time party stronghold that swung sharply to the right in the Trump era as a broader realignment swept through much of the agricultural Midwest. But by simply narrowing their losses with appeals to voters such as Roethler, Democrats hope to become newly competitive from Iowa and Kansas to Nebraska and Ohio.Josh Turek, the Democrat running for a U.S. Senate seat in Iowa, said his party has "looked at this math problem incorrectly.""You've got to go out there in these rural counties and trim the margins," he said in an interview.Republicans know they are on defense in these states. Mr. Trump recently held a rally in Nebraska to boost U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts and will do the same for U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas on Monday. Republicans are pumping money into both states before the Nov. 3 election.Few places represent the party's challenge like Iowa, where Democrats are mounting spirited campaigns for governor, U.S. Senate and several U.S. House seats, including the 2nd Congressional District, which encompasses much of the state's northeast and was considered reliably Republican until recently.Tariffs are disrupting the agricultural economy, and the war in Iran is driving up gas prices. Diesel tops $6 a gallon in Iowa. House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, swung through the district to ask voters to keep his fragile majority in place."This state is so important to us," Johnson said in Cedar Falls.The Republican erosion was evident about 45 miles north in New Hampton. A few houses away from Roethler, 69-year-old Bill Stonecypher voted for Mr. Trump in 2016, expecting him to apply his business acumen to governing. Now Stonecypher plans to vote for every Democrat on the ballot for the first time in his life."I just know it's a mess and it's going to take years to fix," he said.Another neighbor, 70-year-old Deb Thorne, backed Mr. Trump in 2024 but said he hasn't followed through on his pledge to lower costs."He lied to us," she said. "I'm looking more at Democrats for everything."Democrats in Iowa are buoyed by Rob Sand, the state auditor whose campaign for governor is built on explicit overtures to independents and disaffected Republicans.A few dozen people gathered recently in an American Legion hall in St. Ansgar, a square-mile town near the Minnesota border. Sand opened by describing a "pretty standard upbringing" centered on hunting, fishing and church.He distanced himself from the fighting over cultural issues that has bogged down the national party. A few heads in the room nodded as he spoke of opposition to transgender girls playing on female sports teams."All that stuff was stuff that nobody was talking about back when we were in high school," said Sand, whose opponent is Republican Zach Lahn, a political newcomer.The only reason he was a Democrat at all, Sand said, was that he had to pick a party to participate in primaries and he thought Democrats were stronger on issues like clean water and protecting public land.Jim Wherry, a Republican member of the Mitchell County Board of Supervisors, attended the event and said Sand "has a pretty good chance.""My big thing is sometimes things get focused on urban areas," he said. "So I like that he's actually incorporating rural Iowa."Sand, who has won two statewide elections as state auditor, said he's received support from voters who also backed Mr. Trump."One of the things that people who vote for both of us find in common is that we say what we think and we're dissatisfied with the political system," he said.Democrats are stepping up their rural investments. The Democratic Governors Association has directed $10 million each to campaigns in Iowa, Georgia, Ohio and Wisconsin and could spend elsewhere ahead of the election."What I see is a map that has grown and grown and grown and that is good for Democrats," Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who leads the group, said in an interview.The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, which is focused on retaking the House, launched a rural engagement program for the first time this election cycle, including polling, paid media and staff. The group has made a six-figure investment in television advertising in Iowa's 2nd Congressional District alone.Democratic candidate Lindsay James, a chaplain who often speaks of her faith to connect with voters, could see a boost because the district includes Sand's hometown of Decorah. She's competing against Republican Joe Mitchell, a former state representative who worked in the Trump administration.In an interview, James said she was "committed to showing up everywhere." When asked why Democrats lost rural voters in previous elections, she was blunt in her assessment."Democrats in Washington have left the Midwest behind," she said.The economic headwinds in Iowa could give James and other Democrats an opening.A poll conducted in August by The Associated Press, in partnership with KFF, found that rural voters in the United States are economically frustrated with Mr. Trump. About half of rural voters believe the national economy is "worse off" than when Mr. Trump returned to office in January 2025. The survey found about 6 in 10 rural voters disapprove of Mr. Trump's handling of the war with Iran.Still, the survey found that rural voters were unlikely to support Democrats on a large scale in November.Mark DeVries, a 64-year-old farmer in Franklin County, Iowa, said he does not agree with everything Mr. Trump does and acknowledged the president's tariffs have hurt his business. But he said he was sticking with Mr. Trump and Republicans."He's doing stuff that needs to get done," DeVries said of Mr. Trump.Campaigning with Mitchell, Johnson drew on that loyalty to Mr. Trump to warn of the consequences of Democrats regaining control of Congress. An impeachment of Mr. Trump, he said, "is the first thing that would happen."But the Democrats hoping to go to Congress avoided being drawn into that fight.Turek said he had "no interest" in impeachment and that Democrats "need to look forward, not back."James, who has made fighting corruption a campaign theme, said she's "not interested in political theater.""I'm certainly interested in accountability," she said. "But I'm singularly focused on policies that are going to provide, immediately, relief for families."

title: California state testing data breach may impact millions of students, officials say
description: Information involving millions of students across California may be compromised following a data breach that involved a testing company, state education officials said.
content: Information involving millions of students across California may be compromised following a data breach that involved a testing company, state education officials said.The California Department of Education (CDE) on Friday disclosed the breach involving the Educational Testing Service (ETS), which is under contract to provide state and federally required testing to all students enrolled in the state's public schools. ETS provides support for the state's assessment programs, including the California Assessment of Student Performance and Progress and the English Language Proficiency Assessments for California.On Sept. 25, ETS found unauthorized activity involving a secure file transfer protocol site used to exchange California statewide assessment information with the California Department of Education. After taking the site offline, ETS launched an investigation with the help of outside cybersecurity experts.Investigators determined that hackers used a compromised login credential to access the site and copy files containing California student information between May 22 and Sept. 18.Officials said student information "including but not limited to all students enrolled in the three previous school years" had been accessed and copied. The CDE reports that more than 5.7 million students were enrolled in California public schools in the 2025-26 school year."The information that was accessed and copied contained student demographic, program participation, and assessment data that ETS maintains in connection with California's statewide assessment programs," officials said.While the information accessed and copied varies by student, officials said data may include name, date of birth, address, school district and grade level, along with gender, race or ethnicity, primary language, country of origin and English learner status.Additional data that may be compromised include Disability and Section 504 status, eligibility for certain programs and English language proficiency information statewide assessment registration, participation and results.Officials said Social Security numbers, drivers license numbers, financial account information or account passwords were not compromised. The incident did not involve personal information involving parents or guardians.After discovering the breach, officials said ETS has built a new secure file transfer site and taken other steps to reduce the risk of data being made accessible to the public. So far, ETS has not found evidence of the data being made public.In addition, CDE and the State Board of Education said they are working with state cybersecurity experts to assess the impact of the breach on students and families. Officials said notices to families were sent out beginning on Oct. 16 and are expected to be sent through early November.ETS is providing complimentary identity protection services through Experian IdentityWorks for two years. Additional information about the services can be found on the California Department of Education Website.
