But we can honor those we've lost through the care we show those who are grieving, the questions we are willing to ask, and the changes we make moving forward," said Devlin. "We are here with you, and we will keep doing the work to make Erie a place where every family is seen, supported, and safe."

title: Prominent Sikh separatist Pannun says FBI told him of new "imminent threat" against his life
description: Gurpatwant Singh Pannun told CBS News that the FBI visited his home to warn him about what he said was an "imminent threat to my life."
content: Sikh separatist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, who was the target of a foiled 2023 assassination plot allegedly directed by an ex-Indian intelligence official, is facing new threats to his life that are being investigated by the FBI, Pannun told CBS News on Thursday.Pannun, a vocal critic of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, said that FBI agents paid a visit to his New York City home earlier in the day to warn him about what he called an "imminent threat to my life."On Oct. 18, his organization, Sikhs for Justice, plans to hold a non-binding referendum in Edmonton, Canada, on whether the northern Indian province of Punjab should be declared independent and re-named "Khalistan." Sikhs have been invited to vote on the measure.Pannun said in a statement that the question is not whether he "survives another assassination plot." Instead, it's whether the right of Sikh people to self-determination "can be stopped through assassination threats."It cannot," he said.FBI agents told Pannun they are investigating leads and said the threat is connected to potential travel to Canada to participate in the referendum but did not provide him with any further information. The FBI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Federal prosecutors in Manhattan previously charged Indian national Nikhil Gupta and former Indian intelligence officer Vikash Yadav with plotting to assassinate Pannun, a dual American and Canadian citizen.Gupta, who in February pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering, is set to be sentenced in November, and Pannun is expected to speak at the sentencing.The alleged plot targeting Pannun unfolded at the same time that Hardeep Singh Nijjar, another prominent Sikh separatist and friend of Pannun, was gunned down and killed in June 2023 by assassins outside his gurdwara in Surrey, British Columbia.In September 2023, Canadian officials said they had evidence linking his killing to Indian government agents, in violation of Canada's sovereignty.India has previously denied involvement in Nijjar's killing and the attempt on Pannun's life. It has labeled Sikh separatists as "terrorists" and claims they represent threats to India's security.This is not the first time American or Canadian law enforcement officials have warned Pannun of possible credible threats this year. Pannun said that in August and September, he was contacted by both the FBI and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police about other separate threats.He said the warnings by law enforcement started not long after federal prosecutors in Los Angeles in July announced criminal charges against the prominent leader and eight associates of the Indian organized criminal group known as "Bishnoi," tying them to Nijjar's 2023 assassination.Bishnoi was arrested by Indian authorities in 2015. Despite this, the indictment says he continued to run a global crime syndicate from his prison cell.Bishnoi's childhood friend, Satinderjit Singh Brar, allegedly directed the group's North American operations and is also accused in the indictment of ordering the assassination, the indictment said.

title: Port Authority Bus Terminal construction will cause major traffic disruptions for years in Midtown
description: Port Authority is changing bus routes starting Thursday as part of the ongoing construction of a new Midtown Bus Terminal.
content: The Port Authority changed bus routes starting on Thursday as part of the ongoing construction of a new Midtown bus terminal.Transportation officials warned that customers may experience delays, particularly during weekday evening rush periods, as a result.Buses coming from the Lincoln Tunnel and Dyer Avenue were diverted onto West 39th Street before reentering the terminal's ramp system near 10th Avenue.The exclusive bus lane through the tunnel wasn't affected, but the Port Authority still warned about possible delays once the buses arrived in Manhattan."We hope that it actually goes extraordinarily smoothly, but, as you know, we committed when we said we were going to rebuild the bus terminal, that we would do it all on our own property. And so, in order to do that, we have to take down some of the current ramps and move the buses to another ramp to get in so that we can actually do the building," Port Authority Executive Director Kathryn Garcia said.Regular drivers may also feel the impact of the $11 billion project to replace the aging bus terminal, which has been a fixture for more than 75 years.Port Authority officials said it's the busiest bus terminal in the world, with more than 7,200 buses moving through it and an estimated 260,000 passenger trips on a busy weekday. The terminal is aging, overcrowded and struggling to keep up with modern commuting demands. New ramps will be built along with dedicated areas where buses can wait between trips, instead of contributing to congestion on nearby streets. A larger, more modern facility will take its place, with the goal of getting buses to move more efficiently, reducing traffic bottlenecks and making the commute more reliable. "It's not well organized," one commuter said about the current terminal. "During the peak hours, it's very bad."Port Authority officials said traffic agents will be at all corners to make sure things go smoothly.The first phase of the project is expected to wrap up by the end of 2030, with the entire project targeted for completion in 2035.Residents near the terminal say they are already feeling the impacts of the construction. One man said his apartment was vibrating Wednesday night as crews worked nearby. "I went to bed around 11:15 last night and right when I laid down, everything started shaking, so it felt like an earthquake," Cooper Arnold said. Judine Somerville, a commuter, said she's willing to be patient for the changes."You want the ride to be safe, you want it to feel right. Although it's going to be really painful because there's going to be a lot of changes, and so I think it's a great idea," she said."It's crazy, insane. I come in a few times, a few times a month. [My] daughter lives here. I think I'll be avoiding it," Peggy Letsche said. "It was tough coming in where it stops coming through the tunnel. Now we are trying to get out early.""We'll probably do what we always do here, which is to hold our nose, hope that the new development is going to be a good thing," Midtown resident Alex Joseph added.

title: Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams feels ready to test injured hamstring against Atlanta Falcons
description: Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams feels ready to play against the Atlanta Falcons, although coach Ben Johnson hasn't made a final decision on whether to start him.
content: Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams feels physically ready to start against the Atlanta Falcons on Sunday after missing three games with a right hamstring injury.Williams is awaiting the final go-ahead from the coaching staff and trainers after going through his first full practice Thursday since he was injured in a 9-3 loss to Minnesota in Week 2."I mean, I can move, I can run," Williams said. "I hit a top speed the other day, one of my high speeds I've ever hit and so I can move, I can run, I've got strength."It's like I said, just going through the stress test because obviously fibers and things like that in your hamstrings and things like that in your hamstrings and muscles have to connect back together to be able to go out there and play a 60-minute game."On Sunday, it will be four full weeks since the injury. Tyson Bagent and Case Keenum both saw time at quarterback as the Bears went 2-1 without Williams.The third-year QB said even if he plays, his hamstring will not be fully healed."A hamstring of any person doesn't fully heal after three weeks, four weeks, five months," he said. "It takes a while, but there are certain parameters that allow you to go out there and play. There are certain parameters that clear you to go and lower the risk of reinjuring, and obviously just being smart with it throughout the week. And then obviously in game it's game and you got to go play, you got to go make plays for the team."He couldn't put a percentage on how steady he feels when he puts pressure on the hamstring."We'll see with this week," he said. "This week is a big week. Obviously I go through all the cutting and planting and things like that throughout the weeks, or the past couple weeks, and it's felt good."I mean, y'all (reporters) have been able to see me on Friday moving a little bit and then obviously before the Packers game, being able to get out there and move. So, it's felt good, but it's different when you got to go through a whole week of practice and then you got to prepare for a game and all of that, the stress of the mind, body and spirit. And so yeah, I think we'll see how it goes this week."Williams injured the hamstring making a cut at the Vikings 6-yard line and went down in obvious pain. The expression on his face and reaction afterward led to ridicule, as some around the league suggested he was overreacting to the injury."Yeah, I'm always going to show emotion, especially when I can't be out there with the guys when something like that happens," Williams said. "When I went through the draft process, I went to two places and the two places was here and popped over to the Vikings for a visit, as we all know. And they asked me what's the difference between you and everyone else? It's because I care about the team, about the organization, winning, being out there, my teammates, all of that."Williams said the criticism didn't necessarily bother him as much as fuel his comeback."My character has been attacked since, for a while," he said. "It's just another motivating factor when I get out there and get going again."Williams is 36 of 55 for 407 yards with two touchdowns, an interception and a 92.0 passer rating. He also has 107 yards rushing and seven first downs, key numbers that kept the chains moving for the Bears.Offensive coordinator Press Taylor said the team seemed recharged to have Williams back after last week's 31-7 loss to Green Bay."You certainly feel his energy when he's around," Taylor said. "He's got a big personality to begin with. People respond to him, people look to him just as a leader of our team, as a captain, so you sense that from him."The Bears are 3-2 and tied with the Lions and Packers, two games behind the unbeaten Vikings in the NFC North. "I want to be out there and so, you know, it's frustrating, but I mean we went 2-1 in the time that I was out and we'll see how this week goes," he said.

title: Deputies searching for allegedly naked driver after incident on Upson County highway
description: Authorities in Upson County are looking for a driver accused of hitting the road without any clothes in the middle of the day.
content: Authorities in Upson County are looking for a driver accused of hitting the road without any clothes in the middle of the day.Officials with the Upson County Sheriff's Office say deputies were called to Yatesville Highway around 3 p.m. on Tuesday after receiving a public decency complaint.An employee working traffic control as a company did utility work by the road said they spotted a man who appeared to be shirtless driving a Toyota.The man approached the vehicle and called out to the worker about the construction, police say. When she got closer to the Toyota, the woman said he realized the man was naked."He inquired about how to get a job with the construction company saying that he was 'tired of warehouse work,'" Upson County Sheriff Dan Kilgore wrote on Facebook.The man was described as a white male with a buzz haircut and thick lens glasses who "resembles the cartoon character Bobbie Hill from the 'King of the Hill' series," officials said. He was believed to be driving a dark gray Toyota Scion with a 1776 Georgia tag.If you have any other information about the case, call Upson County Sheriff's Office at 706-646-7936.

title: Pittsburgh-area funeral home director accused of pet cremation fraud agrees to plead guilty
description: Patrick Vereb, a former funeral home director accused of pet cremation fraud over a number of years, intends to plead guilty.
content: A former funeral home director accused of pet cremation fraud has reached an agreement to plead guilty to all charges.The Pennsylvania Attorney General's Office tells KDKA-TV that in court, Patrick Vereb indicated he will plead guilty to all charges, with no agreement on what his sentence would be. Vereb, of Vereb Funeral Homes and Eternity Pet Memorial, was charged with eight counts of deceptive or fraudulent business practices and other felonies after he was accused of defrauding thousands of pet owners over several years. A whistleblower alleged in 2025 that Vereb took payments to give people's pets dignified burials or cremations, but then would dump the bodies and give back ashes belonging to something else. According to investigators, Vereb promised nearly 6,500 pets a proper burial, but the bodies were dumped in landfills or left in leaking garbage bags. While Vereb is expected to plead guilty, that means he will also skip a jury trial. However, that trial is exactly what his alleged victims were looking forward to."It's kind of like a slap in the face. To just be like, no, you're not going to have it now. No one is ever going to hear your story or what you have to say about it," said Tiffany Mantzouridis, Vereb's former intern-turned-whistleblower.Vereb's defense offered no comment to KDKA-TV."I feel like whatever happens, nothing could be a harsh enough sentence for what he did and the amount of people he affected and instilled mental anguish," Mantzouridis said."He took our animals, and he threw two of my dogs in the landfill to rot with trash," pet parent Pamela Terry said.Terry plans to attend the sentencing in person.Victims are encouraged to submit victim impact statements to the AG's office if they haven't already. Officials say they have already received 10,000 impact statements.Now, the judge will work to find a courtroom and overflow space big enough to fit all the victims."I don't understand why this didn't go to trial. He needed to face the people he victimized," Terry said.The judge will determine the sentence and will consider everything, including the sentencing guidelines. The AG's office says Vereb's sentence could range from house arrest up to more than a year in jail. Vereb could also be looking at upwards of $ 600,000 in restitution to be paid back to the victims.Vereb is now expected to plead guilty to all criminal charges before a judge next Thursday. Funeral home director named in class-action lawsuitIn May 2025, a class-action lawsuit was filed against Vereb, and accused him of throwing thousands of pets in the trash after he received payments from the owners to cremate them. "These families were deceived. ... They care for their animals greatly, as you can see from the photographs that are here today," attorney Rob Peirce said at the time. According to the Pennsylvania Attorney General's Office, from 2021 to 2024, Vereb took more than $600,000 in payments from pet owners for cremation services, but ultimately dumped the bodies in a landfill. He then allegedly gave the owners the ashes of other animals. "What we know to date is that there are approximately 6,500 pets who were improperly either cremated or disposed of. And even worse, multiple families in western Pennsylvania have had their hearts broken," Peirce said.Pittsburgh pet owners learn if they were victims of fraudNot long after charges had been filed against Vereb, the Pennsylvania Attorney General's Office began contacting alleged victims to let them know if their pets had been involved. One of those owners, Kristin Lakin, had a plastic bag that was supposed to contain what remained of her Yorkie, Logano, but she was unsure. "Logano was dropped off on Tuesday morning, and then the news broke on Thursday, and that's when everything went silent," she told KDKA-TV. "Seeing people were not being charged on the last day to come pick up their pets after I was just charged $300 the day before, and I don't know if I truly got my dog is gut-wrenching." Another pet owner, Rosemary Sabol, was woken up by heartbreaking news. "I got my confirmation email that my Ringo, my baby, was part of this, and to be honest, it's been a really hard day," she said at the time. Vereb tells a pet parent it was the fault of the investigators Text messages from a cell phone that belonged to Vereb showed him blaming investigators for the situation. "The AG office is instantly sending out the same form letter to everyone. They are inciting this riot to make it more sensational so someone can get more fame with a nationwide outcome," the text read. At the time KDKA-TV was alerted to the text messages, we reached out to his attorney to confirm if that was his stance on the case. The office told KDKA-TV that they do not comment on active cases.

title: 2 women file federal lawsuit against ex-Florida Rep. Matt Gaetz alleging violation of anti-trafficking law
description: The women say they met Gaetz in 2017 through Joel Greenberg, and Gaetz says much of the alleged conduct is false.
content: Two women filed a lawsuit Thursday against former U.S. Rep. Matt Gaetz, saying they were sexually exploited by him and other men in violation of a federal anti-trafficking law.The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Orlando, comes nearly two years after the House Ethics Committee said the Florida Republican had regularly paid for sex, including once with a 17-year-old girl, purchased and used illicit drugs, and violated state laws while a member of Congress.Gaetz had left office by the time the report was released and denied wrongdoing. But the report helped to tank his nomination to become attorney general in President Donald Trump's second administration.Two women said they were in their early 20s in 2017 when they met Gaetz through Joel Greenberg, who was a tax official in Seminole County and is now in prison for a raft of crimes, including a sex crime. Gaetz provided drugs and paid the women for sex, out-of-state travel, lodging, and other expenses, according to the lawsuit."Much of the conduct alleged against me is false," Gaetz said in response."The lawsuit relies almost exclusively on a Congressional Committee report that didn't allow me to confront my accusers. Now I will finally have that chance," he said in a statement.Gaetz also appeared to mock the women on the social platform X, sharing a 2018 photo of the backs of three women in bathing suits looking out at the ocean in the Bahamas."I'm shocked nobody responded to their repeated cries for help, posted to Instagram," he said Thursday. The lawsuit also names Greenberg, another man, and businesses tied to Greenberg's family."Every part of this venture ran on an exploitative power imbalance," the women's attorney, Spencer Kuvin, said in the lawsuit. "On one side stood a sitting congressman, an elected tax collector, and a former state legislator, men with public office, private homes, and money to spend. On the other stood young, financially vulnerable women in their early twenties."Gaetz hosts a political talk show on One America News Network. He was recently appointed to the board of Triumph Gulf Coast, which oversees how Florida spends money recovered for damage from the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill.

title: Baltimore's "padlock" bill cracking down on illegal smoke shop activity signed into law by mayor
description: Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott officially signed the city's "padlock" bill into law on Thursday.
content: Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott officially signed the city's "padlock" bill into law on Thursday.Scott was joined by City Council President Zeke Cohen and other officials during a signing ceremony held at City Hall. The law authorizes police to shut down smoke shops that repeatedly violate current regulations by selling unlicensed cannabis or controlled dangerous substances. Baltimore's City Council approved the measure late last month. "To be clear, Baltimore is home to legal, regulated cannabis sales," Scott told reporters before signing the law. "This bill is not about businesses that are following the law. This about addressing those that are breaking the law, and is based on experience and study.""Every Baltimore neighborhood deserves a fair, reliable response to repeated illegal activity. That also protects the rights of businesses operating lawfully in our city," Scott added.President Cohen: "do not sell poison to our kids""Let's just be clear, Baltimore is open for business," said Cohen. "But do not sell poison to our kids and our communities. We have seen far too often young people walking, unabated, into smoke shops, buying products, and then getting sick off of what they buy."Cohen added, "We know, like the mayor said, we have in the state of Maryland, a legalized cannabis dispensary system where cannabis purveyors can get the license, their product is heavily regulated, it is safe to buy, and they are very clear that they do not sell to children."Under the bill, the Baltimore Police Department can seek an abatement order from the Office of Administrative Hearings for any business that receives two citations for illegally selling cannabis or a controlled dangerous substance.After an administrative hearing, the office can issue a proposed abatement order that could include padlocking the business as a nuisance. BPD would then have 15 days to abate the nuisance. City estimates at least 1,400 licensed smoke shops existCity officials said approximately 1,400 smoke shops in Baltimore City are licensed by the state to sell tobacco.The law followed testimony from city officials and residents who said some smoke shops sell untested, unregulated and dangerous products, including to children.Last summer, Scott signed a similar measure into law requiring smoke shops in the city to be at least 750 feet away from schools, parks and recreation centers.

title: Affordability is top of mind for many New Yorkers ahead of 2026 midterm elections
description: Many New Yorkers say affordability will be the number one issue on their minds when they head to the polls in a few weeks.
content: Many New Yorkers say affordability will be the number one issue on their minds when they head to the polls in a few weeks.A new poll by the Pew Research Center finds many Americans are struggling to afford basic necessities.The survey found:60% say they do not currently have enough income to lead the kind of life they want53% say they do not have emergency funds that would cover their expenses for three months27% cannot pay some of their monthly bills or can only make partial payments32% say they worry every day or almost every day about the cost of healthcare and the amount of debt they have70% of U.S. adults say they have cut back on spending for extras, such as eating out, streaming services and entertainmentIn New York, many say the pain is felt at the grocery checkout counter."Sometimes I can't even afford a bread or milk, just the basics, or juice. I'm a diabetic," one woman said."I don't even have milk in my house right now. I don't have a gallon of milk in the house right now," one man said. "I have a cat. I don't even have food for my cat. I have to borrow money to buy food for cat.""A hundred dollars is getting smaller and smaller, and I shop only for sales," another woman said. "I don't buy anything that I want. I buy only what I need."A dog walker who spoke to CBS News New York said she can't afford to take the subway to her job."Now I have to walk, you know. I can't afford to pay a $3 for a ride every day," she said.New Yorkers say it's affecting how they're voting."Trump and all his team are crooks, and they are not qualified," one woman said. "They're the reason why we're in this. What are we doing fighting a war?"Candidates who are on the ballot are bringing up affordability as they continue to campaign."I have been laser-focused on affordability," Gov. Kathy Hochul said during a debate with Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman on Tuesday."Everywhere I go, people are telling me how they're struggling," Blakeman said during the debate."New York is paying 60% more for electricity than the rest of the country," Rep. Nicole Malliotakis said at a press conference Thursday.Republicans and Democrats are now playing the blame game.Staten Island Republicans say Hochul's policies have raised utility rates."This is nothing more than a cynical political ploy to divert attention from the failure of Washington Republicans to address Trump's affordability crisis," a spokesperson for Hochul said.

title: Boston police officers befriend and empower older adults in Roxbury neighborhood
description: For several hours every Friday morning, older adults in Roxbury convene on the Melnea Cass Recreation Complex to reconnect with one another and with police officers.
content: In the Boston Police Department's B-2 Precinct, Friday isn't just special because it's the end of the work week. For several hours every Friday morning, older adults from several surrounding buildings convene on the Melnea Cass Recreation Complex in Roxbury to reconnect with one another and with police officers. A host of activities - walking, games, dancing, and even pickleball - engage the seniors in a convenient place where they can socialize at no cost. At a time when loneliness and isolation affect up to a third of older adults, BPD's Walk the Beat program addresses a real concern. There is a Walk the Beat Program in every BPD district. The Boston Police Foundation funds the activities.The officers who welcome the older adults in Roxbury are also a draw. "They're very positive," former retired BPD officer Yma Arrington says. Officers Carina Shepard and Joey Key are 20 and 23-year veterans of the department respectively. The seniors say the officers' personal investment makes all the difference. Another retired BPD officer, Susan Reed, who attends the Friday morning gatherings, offers an example. "They call you. 'How are you doing? What are you doing? Get yourself out here. Come on out!' You know. 'How are you feeling?' It's not just on these days. In general, they just care about you," Reed said. The affection is mutual. "We didn't just meet these seniors yesterday," Officer Shepard explains. "They've been coming here for some time. And now they come here looking for us." She lights up describing how it feels to see so many older adults, many of whom come from surrounding residential buildings on Friday mornings. "Once they come through the doors, they're special to us," Shepard said. "We get to know their names. We know where they live. We know their neighborhoods. And we just make ourselves available. If you ever have a problem, you can reach out to us." Seniors regularly take them up on that offer. Officer Key cites the duo's relationships with nonprofit organizations as a plus when an older adult needs help. "If we have somebody in need," he says, "we've built those partnerships … They're likely to help us. Nobody's really turned us down." Looking around the room at the seniors walking, laughing, and playing games, the officers know their efforts are paying off. "To see them all get together and interacting with each other, I think that's a huge success for us," Officer Key says. Officer Shepard nods, adding, "We love to be a resource for all the elderlies in our community." The officers visit individual buildings in the neighborhood to check on older adults. They arrange Bingo games and community nights. They host holiday gatherings and serve festive meals. And they provide seniors with information to protect themselves - particularly against fraud. Levance Fergus, who recently joined the Friday walking group, is grateful for the chance to get to know the officers one-on-one. "I think they're doing a good job. They're very friendly," he says, pausing on the track. "We enjoy them too because we like to have their protection. If there's anything going on, we can call the police officer for safety." It's how Officer Key wants the seniors to feel. "We, as officers, would love for the community to see a different side of us," Key said. The department's programs and events are successful, he says, because the seniors attend them. They know about events throughout the year and make a point to be there. "They're looking forward to hanging out with us and they're looking forward to attending those events," Key said. Asked how that makes him feel, Officer Key smiles. "It feels awesome!" Before a truck of fresh produce arrives for the seniors from the nonprofit organization Spoonfuls, Officer Shepard walks around the track with Stephanie Thomas, a Roxbury resident who doesn't miss a Friday gathering. "They welcome you with a lot of compassion," she says of the officers. How does it feel to see so many seniors moving around the track and enjoying one another? Officer Shepard says simply, "Mission accomplished."

title: Man arrested after fatal stabbing, standoff in West Philadelphia
description: Police arrested a man accused of a fatal stabbing Thursday morning in West Philadelphia.
author_name: Andrew  Krietz, Nate  Sylves, Ross  DiMattei
content: A man accused of stabbing another person to death before barricading himself inside a home Thursday morning in West Philadelphia was arrested.Firefighters responded around 9 a.m. to the home in the area of Arch and Edgewood streets for a report of someone who was stabbed, Philadelphia Police Department Deputy Commissioner Frank Vanore said.Once inside, they found a 60- to 70-year-old man who was dead, according to police. Two other women were also inside the home with the suspect, Vanore said."[Police] declared it a barricade, and in a very short period of time, they safely removed the two females and took that male into custody," Vanore said.The suspect's identity is not known at this time.It's also unclear what led up to the fatal stabbing.The barricade came days after two Philadelphia police officers were shot, one fatally, in West Philadelphia. The wave of violence is raising questions about mental health resources and community safety."We shouldn't be having individuals being murdered because of mental illness," Pennsylvania state Rep. Amen Brown said. "Mental health is real. Mental health don't have age. It don't have gender. It don't have any of that. It don't have a race."Brown said preventing tragedies like this starts with investing in mental health services and reaching people before a crisis."We got to figure this out. We have to invest more into mental health services," Brown said. "As politicians and local community leaders, we got to get into these homes."At nearby Marvin's Unisex Barbershop and Salon, owner Atif Olberton said financial pressures can make an already difficult time of year even harder, especially in this economy."Every time it get close to Halloween and the holidays, people ain't got no money," Olberton said. "Things get strange, get dark quick."For parents in the neighborhood, the repeated violence is another source of fear."It's scary because we have to walk our children to school every day, and they need to be safe," Tanisha Myers said.Community leaders said accessible, culturally relevant mental health support could make a difference."I think that what we need is more mental health resources in our neighborhoods that are culturally relevant, that people feel like they can connect to," Councilmember Jamie Gauthier said.

title: Man sentenced to life in prison for 2025 "rejection killing" of Richfield woman
description: Jose Luis Lopez Xique, 27, was convicted at trial of first-degree premeditated murder in Kayli Arseth's death. The Hennepin County Attorney's Office calls it a "rejection killing," a form of gender-based violence.
content: Jose Luis Lopez Xique, 27, was sentenced Thursday to life in prison without the possibility of parole for the 2025 murder of Kayli Arseth in Richfield, according to the Hennepin County Attorney's Office.Arseth, who was 22, was found dead in her Richfield apartment on June 17, 2025, after a welfare check. Police said at the time that she had been shot.Prosecutors charged Lopez Xique in July 2025. Charges said that in the days before her death, he had been asking Arseth for a romantic relationship and she told him she was only interested in friendship, according to earlier reporting on the criminal complaint.Arseth met Lopez Xique on a dating app, family said. Three-and-a-half weeks later, they said he took her life. Lopez Xique had been stalking not only Arseth, but also her parents and siblings, according to family members. "The right evidence was there, so a monster could be put behind bars," said Kayli Arseth's sister, Heather Arseth. "Kayli should still be with us, enjoying music, art, and restoring her motorcycle," Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said. "These 'rejection killings' are deeply rooted in misogyny and are part of a broader pattern of gender-based violence targeting women."Lopez Xique was convicted at trial of first-degree premeditated murder, second-degree intentional murder and harassment with aggravated violations using a dangerous weapon. Moriarty's office said rejection killings are a form of femicide in which women are targeted for asserting autonomy over their bodies. The office said they are distinct from domestic violence and intimate partner violence, but because they are often counted alongside those crimes, it's unclear how common they are.Meggie Royer, Senior Communications Manager for Violence Free Minnesota, said rejection killings like this one are not uncommon."It's really rooted in misogyny and gender based violence," said Royer.They're also not well documented."There's no national tracking system for these kinds of homicides, so no comprehensive data on it," said Royer. "There have been kind of some more informal efforts by women to track that information."Royer said it's about engaging men and boys, having conversations about misogyny, and respecting women and girls.Heather Arseth said she wants those who commit rejection killings to see stiffer sentences, like longer prison time. "Let Kayli be a memory and an example, so that we can set new precedences, new laws and make changes, so that this type of crime does not happen again," said Arseth.A first-degree murder conviction triggers a mandatory sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole, Moriarty's office said.Standpoint, a Minnesota organization, provides free, over-the-phone legal advice and advocacy for victims of stalking, harassment, sexual and domestic violence, and trafficking in Minnesota. Its action line can be called toll-free at 800-313-2666 or 612-343-9842.If you or someone you know needs help, you can contact the National Domestic Violence Helpline at 1-800-799-SAFE or Minnesota Day One at 1-866-223-1111.

title: Minnesota man dies after routine dental cleaning in Hopkins, police investigating
description: A family wants to know why their loved one died while undergoing a routine dental cleaning.
content: A Minnesota family wants to know why their loved one died while undergoing a routine dental cleaning.Edan Cherrill was 25 years old and loved adventures with his family."They loved him tremendously, " said Attorney Rashanda Bruce. "They spent a lot of time together and they loved music and swimming and going on road trips with his family."Cherill's mother took him to Gendler Dental Center in Hopkins, Minnesota, on Sept. 23."Edan was autistic and so due to sensory issues they needed the sedation for him, but it was a procedure he had done a routine cleaning multiple time before," said Bruce.But this time, Bruce says things were different."During that cleaning he went into cardiac arrest and later died," said Bruce.Cherill was taken to the hospital where he was placed on life support. He died days later."We understand that there is an investigation at this time that the family hopes will give them the answers that they are seeking," said Bruce.According to police records, another patient, two weeks earlier, was taken to the hospital after going into cardiac arrest during a similar procedure.Police would only confirm that there is an active investigation into Gendler Dental Center."Edan was someone who was loved tremendously. He was one who was full of life that he enjoyed spending time with his family and making memories and they hope that his organs will help save the lives of others," said Bruce.Cherill loved superheroes and his family says he is now a true superhero. His organ donations saved four lives and skin and tissue donations helped more than 75 people.In their grief, his family celebrates the gift of life he gave to others.WCCO reached out to Gendler Dental Center, but they said they do not have a comment at this time.

title: Cook County Clerk hosts "Love Purse" drive for domestic violence survivors
description: Hundreds of donated purses will soon be in the hands of domestic violence survivors across Cook County.
content: Hundreds of donated purses will soon be in the hands of domestic violence survivors across Cook County.The purses are essentially care packages collected by staff at the Cook County Clerk's Office for the annual "Love Purse" drive.Beside the pile of purses and heap of handbags, there's a lot of love in the room."It just feels overwhelmingly great," said Maria Castro, CEO and founder of the nonprofit #LovePurse. "These little notes go on the outside, and they're our tagline. It says, 'Putting love on the shoulders of women in need, one Love Purse at a time.'"#LovePurse collects new purses and fills them with toiletries and other necessities for women who need them most."Hundreds of women who have been unfortunately, either in a shelter â homeless or domestic violence shelters," Castro said.The purses piled up at the Cook County Clerk's Office on Thursday were collected by employees from for Domestic Violence Awareness Month."Together, we're showing that even a simple act of kindness can have a lasting impact," Clerk Monica Gordon said. "There's a lot of love out there. People want to help each other, and that's what community is about â helping each other."Every single purse is packed with essentials, including important words every survivor needs to hear."Every time a woman opens one of these cards, they know that that somebody took the time to write it," Castro said.They're messages a woman can carry with her for a lifetime."This is from somebody who loves you, and you will never meet me, but I have met you where you are. Love you. Maria," Castro said, reading from one of the cards.

title: Truck driver caught in viral video trying to run Pittsburgh-area motorcyclists off the road
description: A motorcyclist said she and two other bikers were almost run off the road by a pickup truck in an apparent road rage incident that has since gone viral.
content: A motorcyclist said she and two other bikers were almost run off the road by a Pittsburgh-area contractor's pickup truck in an apparent road rage incident that was caught on camera and has since gone viral. New Sewickley Township police said an investigation is underway after video appears to show a truck driver trying to run over several motorcyclists in Beaver County."I was like, 'I'm going in the grass. I'm gone,'" said Sarah Miller, one of the motorcyclists.Miller said she and two other bikers were taking their last joy ride of the season on Tuesday when the incident happened."We're out enjoying our ride, it was probably going to be the last ride of the season, given that the weather's turning. There were two lanes; we were in the left lane, the truck's in the right lane. He had already been driving pretty aggressive at that point. He tried to cut us off and kind of break up our group so that some would be ahead, some would be behind, and he could kind of get in the middle and I guess control whatever traffic he wanted to," Miller said.Miller's video, taken on an Insta 360 camera, shows the white truck approaching behind her before the driver cuts off another motorcyclist."Truck cut him off, and we go and merge, and then he gets behind us, and I get ran off road, my buddy gets ran off the road," Miller said.In the video, you can see CE Little Contracting on the side of the truck before Miller speeds ahead to get away from the truck.As the video continues, you can see the white truck cross into the opposite lane of traffic to catch up to Miller when she began pointing at her camera."As soon as I pointed to that camera, it looks like he kind of backs off and slows down a little bit. Maybe he didn't realize I was recording," Miller said.KDKA-TV asked Miller what led up to the encounter."No idea. We weren't really doing anything you shouldn't be doing. Just out trying to enjoy the last ride, and he came out of nowhere on that side lane or whatever, and tried to get in front of us. He couldn't," Miller said.She said nothing like this has ever happened to her on the road before and believes it could have ended a lot differently."I'm only 115 pounds. My bike's probably 450 pounds. Truck's at least 10,000 pounds, if not. I mean, a slight bump, it really could have been a different kind of story," Miller said.Since Miller posted the video on social media, it's gone viral. KDKA-TV asked her what she wanted to see happen to the driver involved."I didn't post the video to get anybody in trouble. I just posted it to bring attention to bad drivers in Pittsburgh. We have a lot of those," Miller said. "It was very dangerous what he did. Hopefully, he can learn from this."She said she plans to take extra precautions moving forward and will always have the camera rolling."We just want to get point A to point B safely, just as cars do. We're never looking for any trouble. We just want to enjoy the ride, the wind, the sun," Miller said.KDKA-TV reached out to CE Little Contracting several times for comment. We never heard back.New Sewickley Township police said they are investigating the incident and are asking all of those involved to give them a call at 724-774-2473.

title: Metro Atlanta wedding and event venue helps people make memories while saving lives of animals
description: Nestled in the heart of Cumming, Georgia, is a place where human memories are made, and the lives of animals are saved as a direct result.
content: Nestled in the heart of Cumming, Georgia, is a place where human memories are made, and the lives of animals are saved as a direct result.Shiloh Gardens is a nonprofit wedding and event venue that hosts hundreds of weddings, parties, meetings, fundraisers, and other celebrations yearly. The money made from the venue goes directly to Furkids Animal Rescue and Shelters, according to CEO and f/ounder Samantha Shelton."There is still a significant problem – too many animals, not enough homes," Shelton said. "We love saving animals, and we love bringing people and animals together so people can experience that loving, healing bond that we share with animals."Furkids has shelters across metro Atlanta, but the roughly 9-acre property has become its headquarters. The site used to be the home of Wakoola Water Gardens before it went out of business. Shelton said the property was purchased in 2018 and was overgrown and neglected after sitting for years. The site was cleaned, revamped, its water features fully restored, and opened to the public in 2019. "We restored the grounds," Shelton said. "We restored the main building. Then we moved our headquarters here after being in Atlanta for 15 years."Since 2019, Shelton said the ability to save more animals by way of Shiloh Gardens being a division of Furkids has been immense."There's no wedding venue or event facility in the state of Georgia that is like what we have here at Shiloh Gardens," Shelton said. "It is peaceful. It is tranquil, and it is first of its kind. We saw it as an opportunity to raise money for our cause, our mission, which is saving homeless animals, providing their medical care in this nurturing environment, and helping to find their forever homes."Shelton said the venue raises over half a million dollars a year towards saving the lives of homeless animals. In the last 25 years, she says, Furkids, a no-kill shelter system, has saved 85,000 animals in our communities.On site at the property are a new dog shelter, a new cat shelter, and a new medical center, in addition to the venue area that comprises Shiloh Gardens. The property can house up to 250 animals, some of which may require specialized care or may have illnesses or specific diseases that would, in most cases, cause them to be euthanized or turned away.The medical center is where small and large surgeries are performed: X-rays, dental work, and more."We are doing all of their intake vetting here, their surgeries, and preparing them for adoption," Shelton said.Shelton said knowing that people are creating life-changing memories and marking major life milestones while also fully benefiting Furkids' mission of saving the lives of homeless animals is what makes Shiloh Gardens so impactful on the people and the animals.Pets are welcomed at all ceremonies hosted at Shiloh Gardens, something Shelton said is an added touch. Many renovations and plans for expansion are underway, including the launch of a community clinic in 2027 to give pet owners more affordable options for vaccines and spay and neuter services.More information about the venue and Furkids can be found here and here.

title: 80-year-old NYC high school soccer coach has been mentoring and inspiring his players for decades
description: Martin Jacobson, known as Coach Jake, has been a hero to kids at Martin Luther King Jr. High School in Manhattan for more than 40 years.
content: Martin Jacobson, known as Coach Jake, has been a hero to kids at Martin Luther King Jr. High School in Manhattan for more than 40 years. Jacobson, 80, and his boys' soccer team have won 21 public school city titles, which is more than any other school in New York City. Since the mid-1990s, the coach has been helping his kids not just succeed on the pitch but off it, too. "I'm kind of a person who believes in helping others, whether we do it through the vehicle of sport, and I am also involved with my foundation," he said. Jacobson founded The Coach Jake Foundation, which is a nonprofit that provides legal, educational, immigration and social-service support to students. The work has been an ongoing mission for Jacobson, and his players have gone on to play in college and even professionally. The school has also benefited, as his players have a graduation rate of at least 95%. Goalie Luke Rodriguez said Jacobson is like family to him"He's watched me change all four years of my high school," he said. "I met him the summer of freshman year. When I first met him, he was one of the nicest coaches I've ever met. He's family to me." For Jacobson, winning is important, especially as his team goes for its 22nd city title, but he says the real victory is helping others. "I think you gotta kick it forward. Help others, learn, just go out there; I don't need anything from you. As long as I have my health, I am happy. But you go ahead and help others," he said.

title: Horses tie the knot at special wedding on Georgia farm: "They just really fell in love"
description: The couple did not exchange rings, but there was a symbolic exchange of horseshoes.
content: It was a wedding fit for a fairy tale with a few unexpected twists.One couple's big day at Fortitude Farm in Milton had guests cheering, plenty of reasons to smile, and a bride and groom who were a little distracted.This was no ordinary wedding.Eddie is the groom. His full name is Eddie Manhattan Project, and he is a former big-time racehorse.Annie, the bride, is a beautiful brown and white mare described as a small-town country girl.Their love story began at a horse rehab in Cobb County.Grania Holman owns Sunnybrook Stables, once the home of her nonprofit Red Heart Horse Retirement, Rehab, & Rescue. "We had Eddie first. We didn't have a pair for him. He was really missing having a special relationship. We had an uneven number of horses at the time, so he was alone in his paddock, and then we got Annie," Holman said.At Red Heart, horses are paired up as they recover and work through their individual needs. Annie and Eddie's bond went a little further."They just really fell in love, and during camp last year, the kids said we should do a horse wedding," Holman said.The kids got their wish in the fall of 2026, complete with wedding attire, an officiant, and vows.Holman read Eddie's vows."Annie, I found you forever at Fortitude Farms. You taught me I didn't have to spend the rest of my life trying to prove what I could do. You are my dream girl, my small-town country girl who I didn't need to keep chasing," Eddie told his bride through Holman.Annie's caretaker then read her vows to Eddie."Now I known something I didn't know before. Sometimes home isn't a place, but a heart standing beside yours. Eddie, I'm choosing your story," according to the bride.While the sentiments were read, the bride and groom were a little busy eating the landscaping.The couple did not exchange rings, but there was a symbolic exchange of horseshoes. There were no objections from the happy couple, although neither had much to say.Debora Selinger, an ordained minister and horse owner, was the big day's officiant."The horses do love each other," Selinger said. "People come in, they brush their horse, hook it up, ride it, bring it back, and put it back in their stall, but people don't realize horses are incredibly empathetic."When it was time to make things official, Selinger pronounced the couple gelding and mare. Their official newlywed name is Annie and Eddie Manhattan Project. From the racetrack to the wedding aisle, Eddie finally found his "mane" squeeze.There's no word on a honeymoon, but for Eddie, Annie, and their loved ones, it was a wedding to remember.The pair will continue their happily ever after at Fortitude Farms in Milton, Red Heart's new home. The nonprofit provides lifelong care for aging, retired, rescued, and rehabilitating horses, while also offering volunteer opportunities and summer camps to teach kids about horse care.

title: Gunman sentenced to 25 years for Baltimore mass shooting that killed 16-year-old Deanta Dorsey
description: The gunman convicted of killing Baltimore teen Deanta Dorsey in a 2023 mass shooting at Edmondson Village has been sentenced to 25 years in prison.
content: The gunman convicted of killing Baltimore teen Deanta Dorsey in a 2023 mass shooting has been sentenced to 25 years in prison. Bryan Johnson, 20, pleaded guilty to murder, attempted murder and gun charges in the shooting that killed 16-year-old Dorsey and injured four other teens. Johnson, who was 16 at the time, and the victims were all students at Edmondson-Westside High School. The shooting took place around lunchtime on Jan. 4, 2023 outside a Popeye's restaurant at the Edmondson Village Shopping Center, which sits across the street from the school. Dorsey was shot more than a dozen times. His family said he was the oldest boy of 11 children, a "loving, quiet child who loved to play basketball and video games."The other victims were identified as two 17-year-olds and two 18-year-olds. Dorsey's family was in court Thursday, hoping for justice. His stepmother, Juatrinia Crowder, said his birthday is coming up next month, but they will have to celebrate standing over his grave. His aunt said the 25-year sentence was not enough, but it's a win and they will take what they can get. The family also thanked prosecutors and victim advocates. Johnson's family and friends were in court as well, but had no comment. A second suspect in the case, Daaon Spears, was acquitted of the charges against him after two separate trials. The shooting also sparked criticism of the shopping center, with Mayor Brandon Scott calling out the Popeye's for serving the students during school hours, which is a finable offense in the city.

title: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore issues directive to strengthen policies against campus sexual assault
description: Maryland Governor Wes Moore has signed a directive instructing the state's higher education agency to recommend actions to improve campus sexual assault policies across the state.
content: Maryland Governor Wes Moore has signed a directive instructing the state's higher education agency to recommend actions to improve campus sexual assault policies across the state.In the directive, signed by Moore Wednesday, the governor references recent "deeply troubling accounts" of students in other states coming forward to report sexual assault. Media attention in recent weeks has focused on allegations of sexual assault on the campus of New York's Cornell University. A woman alleges that she was drugged and sexually assaulted by multiple men at a fraternity house at Cornell in 2024. While Cornell did conduct an internal investigation, and expelled or suspended several of the men, no criminal charges were brought against the accused at the time. In addition, Moore notes in his directive that the U.S. Department of Education issued a Title IX rule "that rolled back protections for victims of sexual assault.""This is a call to action. In Maryland, we will continue to identify opportunities to enhance the safety of our college campuses and to ensure accountability when these efforts fail," Moore said.The directive requests the secretary of higher education "to issue comprehensive, actionable recommendations for improving campus sexual assault policies" within 90 days."These shall include recommendations for strengthening sexual misconduct policies, reporting frameworks, and disciplinary standards across the state's institutions of higher education," the directive states.The measure calls for close coordination between Maryland's Higher Education Commission and the Office of the Attorney General in developing the new policies.

title: Terry Bradshaw reflects on life, health struggles in new memoir
description: Terry Bradshaw has shared more stories from his lengthy career as a former NFL player and analyst in a new book.
content: Terry Bradshaw has told many stories in his life, many of them on the football field. But the four-time Super Bowl champion quarterback and Pro Football Hall of Famer has shared more in his new, 272-page book, "Looking for Terry: A Memoir," now available in stores.Bradshaw, 78, discussed the process of writing the book and the concept behind it during a recent interview with CNN, while also sharing details about the adversity he's overcome, including beating two different types of cancer and going through three divorces."It felt good," said Bradshaw. "I know if it sells five copies or 50 â who knows â this book is going to help people that are struggling with any of those issues."One of those issues he described was finally seeking professional help after battling depression for years."If I could describe it, it's the sickest you've ever been times 10," he said. "It's a horrible feeling, and you can't get away from it, and you have to face the fact that something's wrong."Bradshaw said his current wife, Tammy, whom he married in 2014, even gave a name to his depression."Tammy calls him 'Roy,'" he said. "When Roy starts to show up, when it creeps in, what happens is I become isolated, and I know it. But she sees it two or three days before I feel it."He credits his wife, visiting multiple doctors and his support group for helping him find his path to treatment.Bradshaw also discussed his future in broadcasting, having worked as an NFL analyst for 43 years. He's currently under contract with FOX for their Sunday game-day studio show."I haven't said I'm going to retire, but I'm pretty sure they're going to want me to retire," said Bradshaw. "I'm never going to announce it. I'm just not going to show up. But I'll be 80 by the end of my contract."Bradshaw said the opportunity to tell this collection of stories wasn't easy, and finding the right publisher took longer than he expected until HarperCollins Publishers â the world's second-largest consumer book publisher â finally agreed."It was a hard sell," he said. "Everybody said, 'We don't want a football book. We're tired of football.' And I kept saying, 'I'm a football player, but it's not a football book.'"

title: Stoughton police chief testifies during Matthew Farwell's trial in death of Sandra Birchmore
description: Jurors in the federal trial of former Stoughton, Massachusetts, police officer Matthew Farwell heard from five witnesses on Thursday.
content: Jurors in the federal trial of former Stoughton, Massachusetts, police officer Matthew Farwell heard from five witnesses on Thursday as testimony continued for a third day Thursday in a South Boston courthouse. Witnesses included the Stoughton police chief, a friend of Birchmore's and testimony about cellphone evidence.Farwell is accused of killing the 23-year-old Sandra Birchmore and her unborn baby in her Canton apartment in February 2021. Initially, her death was ruled a suicide, but in 2024 Farwell was charged with a federal count of killing a witness or victim. In 2025, he was also charged with causing the death of an unborn child.The former Stoughton police officer faces a mandatory sentence of life in prison if convicted. He has pleaded not guilty to both charges.Former Stoughton deputy chief testifiesBrian Holmes, the police chief for the Kingston Police Department, was the final witness to take the stand on Thursday. Court ended for the day with Holmes still on the stand. He will continue cross-examination on Friday.Holmes was previously the deputy police chief in Stoughton. He was responsible for conducting the internal investigation following Birchmore's death.Like several other witnesses so far in the trial, Holmes testified that Farwell was critical of COVID pandemic precautions, including masks. Prosecutors have confirmed through several witnesses that it was out of place for Farwell to be wearing a mask when he entered Birchmore's apartment the day she died.Sandra Birchmore's cellphone dataNicholas Guarino, an investigator from the Norfolk District Attorney's office who also testified in Karen Read's high-profile trials, testified for several hours about Birchmore's cellphone data.Guarino was previously a Massachusetts State Police trooper assigned to the Norfolk District Attorney's office, but is now a civilian digital forensic examiner.He was a trooper for more than a decade.During Read's second trial, it was Guarino who was tasked with reading text messages between Read and John O'Keefe for the jury.Guarino said that in Farwell's case, he extracted cellphone data. There were five total devices he examined, including Birchmore's phone.According to Guarino, the password to Birchmore's laptop was Mfarwell1, and the password to the DoorDash account on her phone was mfarwell1.Guarino said he searched Farwell's phone. He put in Birchmore's phone number, but it did not show up. The phone was returned to Farwell.On cross-examination, the defense asked Guarino about files that were deleted."Is it protocol to delete anything in a criminal investigation?" the defense asked. "So again, it would depend. Originally this came to me as a suicide. That's what I had marked it as," Guarino responded, adding that redundant data was removed to conserve space on the server.Guarino said investigators also lost files when an external hard drive died."There's no evidence I'm withholding. I did not purposefully come in and say 'I'm not going to write a report,'" Guarino told the defense attorney.On re-direct questioning, Guarino was asked if he destroyed the hard drive. He said he did not.Guarino completed his time on the witness stand around 3:20 p.m.Stoughton Police Chief Donna McNamara on standDonna McNamara, the Stoughton police chief who is currently on leave, testified as the third witness of the day.McNamara was police chief in 2021 when Farwell was one of about 60 sworn officers in Stoughton.Reading Farwell's resume in court, McNamara said he was in the police explorers program himself from 1998-2010. Farwell went to Stoughton High School but did not graduate. He completed 11th grade and then got his GED.In March of 2012, Farwell was hired as a patrol officer.McNamara was asked if Stoughton police investigated Birchmore's death. She said they did not because it was not in the department's jurisdiction.She said the Stoughton Police Department did start an internal affairs investigation. In 2022, McNamara announced that the investigation determined that Farwell, his twin brother William Farwell, and former Stoughton deputy police chief Robert Devine had an inappropriate relationship with Birchmore.The report determined that all three men "should never have the privilege of serving any community as a police officer."On cross-examination, McNamara said that the police explorers program was disbanded in September 2022.McNamara told the defense attorney that John Fanning from Massachusetts State Police kept her updated on the investigation into Birchmore's death "on occasion, at the beginning." She said the first time she saw video surveillance footage of Farwell in the lobby of Birchmore's apartment building was when it was published online.The police chief concluded her testimony around 12:40 p.m.Sandra Birchmore's friend called as witnessLesley Davis, who was friends with Birchmore, took the stand Thursday morning.Davis is 30 years old and met Birchmore in middle school at a gym in Stoughton.Prosecutor Torey Cummings asked if at some point Birchmore told her about Farwell. Davis said Birchmore told her about Farwell "almost immediately" when she was 15 years old."She said that he was someone who would always help her with her homework and he paid a lot of attention to her, like he would always text her and wonder where she is," Davis said.Cummings asked Davis if she would talk about sexual relationships with Birchmore."When I would talk about mine, she would talk about hers with Matthew Farwell," Davis said. "She would have sex with him in his police vehicle as well as his personal truck."Davis said that as she got older, Birchmore talked about wanting to be a mom "almost every time I talked to her."Birchmore told her in 2020 that she was pregnant and asked Davis to be the godmother. "She was so happy, maybe the happiest time in her life, she was very excited for the baby," she said.Davis said there was one time when Farwell pushed Birchmore to the ground, and she kicked him out of her apartment.The night of Birchmore's death, Davis and Birchmore spoke on the phone for about 25 minutes just before 8:30 p.m. The prosecutor asked Davis if she would remember the call if Birchmore had said she wanted to kill herself."I would have 100% remembered, yes," Davis said. Davis said when she learned Birchmore died, she drove to the Canton Police Department with her mother and brother to tell them about Farwell. She spoke with two men at the department, but said they did not take any notes. She later received a phone call from a law enforcement officer about the case, and testified that she told them they should investigate Farwell.On cross-examination, the defense tried to show that Davis and Birchmore had an "up and down" friendship.The defense also noted that Birchmore had increased her dose of antidepressant medication and had written a suicide note in 2017.Davis completed her testimony after about an hour.Stoughton police officer testifiesStoughton Police Sgt. Robert Kuhn was on the stand when court ended for the day on Wednesday. He completed his testimony earlier Thursday morning. Kuhn testified that he was friends with Farwell outside of work. He also met Birchmore when she was in the youth explorers program, and knew her from his job as the resource officer at Stoughton High School. Kuhn said he attended a homicide conference that was put on by Massachusetts State Police in October 2019, and Farwell attended as well.After, he continued spending time with Farwell at work and sometimes socially.The prosecutor asked Kuhn what behavior he noticed from Farwell in 2021. Kuhn said he was taking a lot of phone calls, was stressed and was drinking more. Kuhn described Farwell as taking "more frequent phone calls than usual."During the trial, prosecutors have shown surveillance video from the lobby of Birchmore's apartment building on the day of her death. Farwell can be seen wearing a hood and medical mask and leaving about a half-hour later. Kuhn was asked if Farwell said anything about mask requirements during the COVID pandemic."He despised them," Kuhn said. "For him to be wearing a mask was very odd to me, yes," he added. Kuhn later said he never saw Farwell wearing a mask when he was off duty. On cross-examination, the defense tried to show that Farwell regularly wore jeans, boots and hooded sweatshirts similar to what he was wearing in the video.Farwell's attorney attempted to ask Kuhn several times if Farwell received his COVID vaccine, but the prosecution objected each time and the judge sustained those objections. On re-direct questioning, Kuhn was asked when her friendship with Farwell ended."I would say the minute the allegation was made," he said. Kuhn completed his testimony around 10 a.m.Testimony in Matthew Farwell trialOn Wednesday, testimony focused on the police investigation that prosecutors say was insufficient.Massachusetts State Police Trooper Matthew Dunne completed a second day of testimony after about five hours on the witness stand. Dunne initially investigated Birchmore's death and ruled it a suicide.Dunne testified that there was no suicide note found in Birchmore's apartment.He also said he did not record or take notes when interviewing Birchmore's coworkers at the school where she worked. Dunne also said he did not record or take notes during either of the two times he interviewed Farwell.On cross-examination, Farwell's attorney highlighted that Dunne did not see any signs of a struggle in Birchmore's apartment.Investigators have said Farwell started sexually abusing Birchmore when she was 15 and he was 27 years old. Prosecutors said Birchmore learned she was pregnant in December 2020 and told Farwell he was the father. The defense said DNA testing confirmed Farwell was not the father.

title: Atlanta career fair offers hope to job seekers looking to rebuild their lives
description: As Georgia reports record employment, thousands of people across the state are still searching for work. An Atlanta career fair is hoping to help by bringing job seekers face-to-face with employers looking to hire.
content: As Georgia reports record employment, thousands of people across the state are still searching for work.On Thursday, a career fair in southwest Atlanta brought job seekers face-to-face with employers looking to hire.For Emmanuel Dixon, finding a new job means more than collecting a paycheck. It's another step toward rebuilding the life he once had.On Thursday, Dixon arrived at Pittsburgh Yards with resumes in hand, hoping to connect with employers at the Southside Works Career Fair.Before entering the event, he stopped at a Goodwill bus to print copies of his resume. Inside, he moved from table to table, introducing himself to recruiters and exploring employment opportunities.Each conversation represented another chance at a fresh start."It's been rough," Dixon said. "It's been a very challenging year."Dixon says he previously worked as a field organizer for Kamala Harris' 2024 presidential campaign through CADC LLC. That position ended after the election, and he began driving for Lyft.When that work fell through, Dixon faced financial difficulties that eventually left him without stable housing.His younger sister initially gave him a place to stay for several days before helping him connect with Atlanta Mission, where he spent about two months.He later moved to the Gateway Center, a decision he credits with helping turn his situation around. Through the Gateway Center, Dixon connected with the Atlanta Center for Self-Sufficiency, a nonprofit workforce development organization that provides career coaching, employment training, and connections to employers.Dixon completed the organization's job-readiness boot camp and began receiving weekly job leads. His career coach also encouraged him to attend Thursday's fair.The free event focused on connecting South Atlanta residents with employers actively seeking workers. Participants could explore current job openings, meet recruiters from multiple industries, and learn about no-cost training opportunities, including programs in technology and logistics.The fair was organized through a partnership involving Southside Works, the Atlanta Center for Self-Sufficiency, Emmaus House, Per Scholas, STRIVE Atlanta and Gangstas to Growers.Dana Inman, president and CEO of the Atlanta Center for Self-Sufficiency, said the event was designed to remove some obstacles people face when applying for jobs."They're applying for a lot of jobs every day, and they're getting no response back from employers," Inman said.She explained that online applicant tracking systems can leave job seekers uncertain about whether employers have even reviewed their applications.Meeting recruiters in person offers a different opportunity."We make sure they have actual job openings," Inman said. "We make sure that they understand who our clients are, our residents are."According to Inman, some participating employers had immediate openings and were prepared to conduct interviews or potentially extend job offers during the event.The organization also works to address barriers that can prevent people from accepting or keeping jobs, including transportation and child care.Inman said staff can provide MARTA assistance, gas cards, and connections to other community resources.The Atlanta Center for Self-Sufficiency works with approximately 1,500 people annually across the city. Its 2026 goal is to help 600 people secure employment.Inman said the organization continues supporting participants for at least a year after they are hired, helping them to retain their jobs and pursue career advancement."We want to really focus on a career pathway," she said.The challenges facing job seekers come as Georgia continues reporting strong overall employment figures.According to September 2026 figures attributed to the Georgia Department of Labor, the state's unemployment rate stood at 3.3%, with approximately 178,884 Georgians unemployed, an increase of about 3,400 from August.Inman said some workers also face changing employment demands as automation and artificial intelligence reshape certain administrative, human resources and technology jobs.Her organization helps participants identify new career paths and obtain training for positions that match their skills and interests.For Dixon, who has been searching for work since spring, the assistance has already helped him achieve a major milestone.After months of housing instability, he moved into his own apartment in Decatur about a month ago."Even now, even like things are starting to look up, I have my own place," Dixon said. "So I'm starting to feel like myself again."He acknowledged that staying motivated during his struggles has been difficult, particularly while dealing with depression and uncertainty about his future.But he said he has tried not to allow those circumstances to stop him from moving forward."I know this is just a temporary situation and that's what I'm focusing on," Dixon said. "So I'm taking the steps to better myself and to get back to where I was."Although Dixon had not secured a job at the time of his interview, he remained optimistic about the opportunities ahead."I feel like I'm still like a work in progress," he said. "God isn't through with me yet."For Dixon, Thursday's career fair was another step forward and another reason to believe his next chapter is still being written. For details about future job fairs, click here.

title: New training center planned near East Palestine, Ohio, after 2023 train derailment
description: More than three years after the Norfolk Southern train derailment, first responders will soon have a permanent training facility.
content: More than three years after the Norfolk Southern train derailment in East Palestine, Ohio, first responders across the region and nationwide will soon have a permanent training facility.Leaders have yet to decide on the exact location, but it will be in the East Palestine area.It is a night that remains ingrained in Brian Rutledge's memory: Feb. 3, 2023, when a Norfolk Southern train derailed, bursting into flames and releasing toxic chemicals into the air at the Ohio-Pennsylvania border."Initially came in as a train fire. We were the first engine arriving and knew immediately that it was more than that," Rutledge said.The East Palestine fire battalion chief, who is also the Columbiana County Emergency Management deputy director, and his colleagues across various neighboring agencies quickly realized the magnitude of the event."Our bottom-line training was protecting life and safety, and so that's what we did at the time," Rutledge said.Now, they can revisit the lessons they've learned since that night and share them with others at a multifaceted training facility in the region. It's a partnership between the village, Ohio, Youngstown State University and Norfolk Southern.On Thursday, leaders revealed a new conceptual drawing that gives an idea of what it may look like, with structures for hands-on training, real freight cars and even an airplane."Our determination is that they will have every tool in their kit, every arrow in their quiver that they need to respond to these kinds of disasters," said Bill Johnson, Youngstown State University's president.The railway company is investing $20 million in the construction and operation of the facility and also donating four full-size freight cars."If a first responder is called to a rail emergency, it's not the first time that they're seeing that equipment, that they're putting their hands on it," said John Fleps, the railroad's chief safety officer.Dr. Jennifer Adams, Youngstown State University's provost and vice president of academic affairs, said plans include indoor simulation, outdoor response training, drone operations, rail and hazardous material scenarios, and a space to honor what happened in the village. They expect to build it in phases.She and others said it will benefit volunteer firefighters who face more challenges traveling to specialized training centers, and who are more likely to experience potential incidents in rural areas. However, leaders also feel the space will bring in first responders from across the country and help the local economy."My prediction is other people will see this and say we need this in our part of the country," Ohio Governor Mike DeWine said."East Palestine went through something no community ever wants to experience, but through this project, East Palestine can also help teach others how to be better prepared, better coordinated, and more resilient," Adams said.The hope is they can make a difference after tragedy."You're not going to get that in training itself, but all the pieces added up together, you know, would make things a whole lot better," Rutledge said.As for when the center is set to open, that's unclear, but the village manager said they expect to break ground in 12 to 18 months.

title: George Washington Bridge's pedestrian South Walk reopening
description: Pedestrians crossing the George Washington Bridge will once again have a path of their own.
content: Pedestrians crossing the George Washington Bridge once again have a path of their own.The bridge's South Walk reopened Thursday following a major renovation that included wider sections of walkway, new lighting, security upgrades and viewing platforms overlooking the Hudson River.The project is part of the Port Authority's $2 billion "Restoring the George" program."It makes it so that it is even more of an amenity, connecting the region," Port Authority Executive Director Kathryn Garcia said during an exclusive tour before the reopening.The South Walk closed in 2023 for construction. During the closure, pedestrians and cyclists shared the bridge's North Walk.Beginning Friday, pedestrians will return to the South Walk, while cyclists will use the North Walk, restoring the separation of traffic that officials and users say improves safety."So it really is much better for the world to separate the two of us," cyclist Roger Cox of the Upper West Side said. "Everybody will be happier about it, and safer."The 1.5-mile crossing includes several new features designed to improve both safety and the experience for users. The walkway has been widened in certain locations and now includes upgraded lighting, security cameras, crisis phones, new signage and viewing platforms. Officials also installed 11-foot-high security fencing aimed at preventing people from climbing over the bridge's edge."We want you to enjoy it. We want you to be protected. We want you to come home safely," Garcia said.The George Washington Bridge walkways are used by commuters and recreational users alike. Last year, more than 637,000 trips were recorded across the bridge's pedestrian and bicycle paths, according to the Port Authority.The reopening comes as the George Washington Bridge prepares to mark its 95th anniversary later this month.Nearly a century after opening, the iconic span is welcoming pedestrians back to a newly renovated South Walk and a familiar view of the Manhattan skyline.

title: Skyler Gill-Howard talks rookie season with Detroit Lions: "I belong in this league"
description: Lions sixth-round pick Skyler Gill-Howard beat the odds with a resilience and perseverance that match the city that drafted him.
content: Every young football player has dreams of making it to the NFL, but very few see that dream become a reality. Lions sixth-round pick Skyler Gill-Howard beat those odds with a resilience and perseverance that match the city that drafted him."It's been awesome, you know, just being out there with the guys, being able to make an immediate impact has been awesome," said Gill-Howard. "The coaches trust me. I knew I could play in this league, and I belong in this league."Gill-Howard has one sack and eight tackles through his first five games of his NFL career. His belief in himself never wavered."[It's been] a super long journey," said Gill-Howard. "My only offer out of high school was D2. I walked on to Upper Iowa University. I didn't even visit, but when I got up there, I was like, this is going to be rough. I was working my tail off, but I didn't get the opportunity.
