That semester was rough because you're in the middle of nowhere. The closest Walmart was an hour and 45 minutes away. Just straight isolation, so it was just me and the weight room."With no offers coming out of the transfer portal in 2022, Gill-Howard continued to train and even picked up a job, working the early morning shift at FedEx to make ends meet â hoping for one chance."I was working that whole spring, and that second wave in the portal is when NIU offered me a walk-on, but the catch was I had to play D-line," said Gill-Howard.That meant gaining about 60 pounds and learning a new position. Gill-Howard made the most of his chance, turning his time at Northern Illinois into a scholarship offer from Texas Tech, where he was a leader for the Red Raiders before an ankle injury ended his senior season early. Then came the call from the Lions in the sixth round of the 2026 NFL Draft."It was crazy because I knew I was going to fall just because of my injury," said Gill-Howard. "So, I'm just like, whenever I get my name called, I'm going to make the most of it. When they first called, I saw the 313, I'm like, 'I don't know anybody from Michigan,' but I answered, and 'Hey, this is Brad Holmes,' and I'm like, 'Oh my God.' When you hear that, it was super exciting because it fits the type of team that I want to be a part of. My whole career has been grit, been getting it out of the mud, been working for what you think you deserve.""For a rookie, he's very urgent," Lions head coach Dan Campbell said. "You hear me say that a lot, right? Do it with urgency. He's an urgent player. He's an urgent practice player. When you tell him something, he's going to do it, and he's going to do it all out, and he's going to do it just right."Gill-Howard has always led by example. He's the oldest of nine siblings, and this journey to the NFL is about much more than just himself. Four years ago, one of Gill-Howard's younger brothers, Prestin Gill, was killed by gun violence in his hometown of Milwaukee. Gill-Howard held a picture of his brother by his side on draft night."My main reason why I started playing this game and why I started taking it serious is because I knew I had a future in it, but I also knew that whatever my future was in it, I could help my siblings because that's been my main goal trying to get them out of that situation," said Gill-Howard. "Getting the call, it was emotional, but at the same time, I'm doing everything that we talked about. I'm doing everything that I told him I would. He's smiling up there that I'm doing everything I said I would. He's playing with me every game. He's taking care of my every game, watching over me, and I talk to him every game, just letting him know we're here."Gill-Howard earned his spot in the NFL, and now that he's arrived, he's going to use that incredible work ethic to make sure he stays for a long time."I come in here knowing that nothing can be taken for granted," said Gill-Howard. "Every time I step on that field or walk into a meeting, I'm super grateful to be there because you never know when it could be done, especially in this league; people are gone every day. So, I just come in with a grateful attitude, and this is all I got, so why not give it everything I got this day, and we'll worry about tomorrow when it comes."

title: A Minnesota Bishop keeps his faith during his lung cancer diagnosis
description: In early 2026, Bishop Kevin Kenney of the Archdiocese of St. Paul and Minneapolis knew something was wrong. He had developed a cough and a cold. While the cold symptoms went away, the cough lingered for months.
content: In early 2026, Bishop Kevin Kenney of the Archdiocese of St. Paul and Minneapolis knew something was wrong. He had developed a cough and a cold. While the cold symptoms went away, the cough lingered for months.Kenney decided to have it checked. The results were shocking. He had stage 4 lung cancer."Cancer is a word that you don't want to hear, but with God's grace, I'm like, okay, well, at least I have to accept it if that's what it is," Kenney said.Despite the diagnosis, his faith remains steadfast.I always was positive about it. I never really felt upset about it and just thought, well, the outcome will be good, whatever that is.Kenney was worried about his friends and family, unsure how to break the news to them. He eventually decided to release a video through the archdiocese. The outpouring of prayers was immediate."I was surprised by how quickly and how viral that video went," Kenney said."The support of people has been incredible."One of the supporters is Pope Francis. Kenney recently visited Rome, met the Pope, and asked for his blessing."I just greeted him and thanked him for his ministry, what he was doing, and told him who I was. And then I said, I just want to alert you that I was diagnosed with stage four lung cancer back in July," Kenney recounted.Pope Francis assured Kenney he would pray for him and that everything would work out.It was just a few days later that Pope Francis revealed his own lung cancer diagnosis. Bishop Kenney could hardly believe the news."It was a shock, I mean I almost fell over, I was like 'what? What did he just say?' It was just surreal," Kenney said.Despite having the same diagnosis, Kenney finds comfort in knowing he is not alone."I just thought what a blessing it was that I can journey with him in that way," Kenney said."He gave me a blessing, now I can continue to pray and ask everyone to pray for him as well."Bishop Kenney says his prayers are with everyone who is struggling with their health while he finds a new outlook on his own."It really has made me more aware that each day is a gift," Kenney said."I don't know what the experience is or what it will be, but the sense is that it will continue to bring joy and peace and continue to be good and hopefully will help others in their lives as well."

title: Nicolás Maduro, wife plead not guilty to new torture charges
description: Ousted former president of Venezuela Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores de Maduro, pleaded not guilty Thursday to new charges of torture.
content: Ousted former president of Venezuela Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores de Maduro, pleaded not guilty to new torture charges Thursday.Maduro, 63, entered the courtroom with his feet shackled, waving to the gallery, saying "good morning" in Spanish, shaking his attorneys' hands and nodding to the press. His wife entered next.When asked to enter a plea to the fifth superseding indictment, which includes allegations of torturing three United States citizens, Maduro started rambling, saying in part, "I reject this document in its entirety of false accusations."The judge had to interrupt and say a plea of not guilty would be entered on Maduro's behalf.Flores de Maduro said, "I am completely innocent. I am not guilty."The two are accused of conspiracy to commit torture in an effort to silence political opposition. The methods alleged include starvation, electric shock, asphyxiation and beatings.The couple is also facing narcoterrorism and weapons charges.Defense attorneys argue their clients are innocent and the U.S. case should be tossed based on sovereign immunity. When Maduro left the courtroom, he waved to the judge.The trial was pushed back two weeks to June 14.A small group of anti-Maduro demonstrators gathered outside the courthouse.Earlier this week, President Donald Trump was asked about the new charges."It's going to go through court, but he did some very bad things," Mr. Trump said.Their next pre-trial court date is in December.

title: Denver police, DEA make 107 arrests, seize 223 pounds of illegal drugs in "Operation Overdose Intercept"
description: The Denver Police Department and the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration Rocky Mountain Division teamed up to make more than 100 arrests and seize more than 223 pounds of illegal drugs, including fentanyl, meth, and cocaine, in Operation Overdose Intercept.
content: The Denver Police Department and the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration Rocky Mountain Division teamed up to make more than 100 arrests and seize more than 223 pounds of illegal drugs, including fentanyl, meth, and cocaine, in Operation Overdose Intercept. The coordinated effort was designed to reduce overdoses and overdose deaths in Denver by arresting dealers and seizing potentially deadly illicit fentanyl. According to the DEA, the enforcement included more than 112 operations over 10 weeks, resulting in 107 arrests, drug seizures totalling 223.16 pounds, including fentanyl, methamphetamine, cocaine, MDMA, heroin, with 23 firearms recovered and cash seized totalling around $200,000."Every overdose and overdose death is a heartbreak that ripples through our community, and each loss reminds us of the importance of protecting those upon whom drug dealers prey," said Denver Police Chief Ron Thomas in a statement. "By leveraging our law enforcement partnerships and doubling down on the great work done every day by our officers, we can help protect the vulnerable, disrupt the distribution of deadly drugs, and save lives together." According to the Denver Department of Public Health and Environment, 137 deaths in Denver for the first five months of the year have been confirmed to involve fentanyl. In 2025, 563 people in the Denver community were lost to drug-related deaths. "Our goal at DEA is a Fentanyl Free America. We appreciate the partnership with the Denver Police Department and look forward to getting fentanyl and criminals off our streets," said Drug Enforcement Administration Rocky Mountain Field Division acting Special Agent in Charge Miguel Chino in a statement.Additional Information from the Denver Police Department:The community can assist with these enforcement operations by providing information about individuals or networks selling drugs in Denver. Tipsters can provide information through Metro Denver Crime Stoppers at 720-913-STOP (7867), and tipsters can remain anonymous.

title: Long Island homeowner says serial vandal is trying to kill his lawn
description: A Nassau County homeowner says a mystery vandal has repeatedly targeted his North Massapequa home, pouring an unknown liquid on his lawn in the middle of the night and leaving behind dead patches of grass.
content: A Nassau County homeowner says a mystery vandal has repeatedly targeted his North Massapequa home, pouring an unknown liquid on his lawn in the middle of the night and leaving behind dead patches of grass. John Giurco said surveillance cameras captured the same man trespassing on his Linden Street property on three separate occasions in recent months, each time around 4 a.m. The suspect is seen pouring a liquid across the lawn and even over a backyard fence.Giurco and his neighbors believe the damage appears to be intentional."Strange brown lines. Fungus doesn't grow like that," neighbor Peter Ekstrom said.Giurco believes he knows who is responsible. He said the dispute began months ago when he confronted a man walking dogs across his front lawn and near a flower bed where he was working."He walks his dogs right on the front lawn, right up to the flower bed where I was working," Giurco said. "I got a little startled, like, what are you doing on my front lawn? And he took very large offense to this."Neighbors described Giurco and his wife as friendly residents and said the vandalism appears to be personal."When someone does damage to personal property, there is a vendetta," neighbor Laura Millard said. "It's not like someone said, 'I don't like that lawn.'"Giurco said the incidents have left him and his wife unsettled and considering moving."She can't stand it anymore. We are about to sell," he said.Nassau County police are searching for the suspect, who is described as a man in his 60s, about 5-foot-8 with gray hair. Giurco said the man was frequently seen with two large dogs but has since disappeared.Crime Stoppers is now offering a reward for information leading to the identification of the suspected serial vandal.Anyone with information is urged to contact Nassau County Crime Stoppers at 1-800-244-8477 or by submitting an anonymous tip here.

title: Palatine mass shooting plot suspect targeted Hindu temple attended by Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, he says
description: A Palatine teen arrested for an alleged mass shooting plot targeting a Hindu Temple was working alone, police said. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi said he targeted the temple he and his family attend, and they were there at the time.
author_name: Lauren  Victory, Sabrina  Franza, Sara  Tenenbaum
content: A Palatine, Illinois teen arrested for an alleged mass shooting plot targeting a Hindu temple was working alone, police said Thursday. CBS News Chicago spoke exclusively to a close friend of his, who did not want appear on camera, but said they are completely blindsided by this news, describing Alexandros Paporakis as a "really nice, quiet, shy kid."Thursday morning, police from Palatine and Mount Prospect, along with the Chicago FBI, said the 19-year-old had apparently been planning the attack for some time, but as far as they can tell he was only working by himself.Paporakis is charged with one count of making a terrorist threat and one count of unlawful possession of a weapon for possessing a rifle with a barrel less than 16 inches long, both felonies. Palatine police thanked Mount Prospect police several times for contacting them immediately when a good Samaritan called them to report the plot on Sunday. According to prosecutors, the good Samaritan was one of Paporakis' coworkers, who he texted on Sunday and told him he had gone to carry out his plan to attack a Hindu temple but his gun jammed.After an extended Signal conversation in which Paporakis allegedly sent photos of an AR-style rifle and himself in a tactical vest, the coworker called Mount Prospect police, who immediately contacted Palatine police.Palatine police said surveillance video showed Paporakis' car entering the parking lot of a "known large Hindu temple" in Aurora at 12:25 p.m. Sunday, then leaving at 12:38 p.m. Police also said they do not plan to release the specific name of Hindu temple he targeted, but U.S. Rep. Raja Krisnmamoorthi (D-IL 2nd) said he and his family are worshippers at that temple, and were there at the time of the planned attack."It was a very special day, it was the start of one of the high holidays for the Hindu religion, if you will, which is called Navaratri, and so huge crowds visited that temple that day," Krishnamoorthi told CBS News Chicago.He was shocked by the news of the arrest and said no one at the temple had any idea of what was transpiring outside."We have to do everything we can to stop this," he said.Police said Paporakis then returned to Palatine. They said video showed Paporakis driving and alone in the car.Police believed Paporakis would again try to execute his violent plan, so they arrested him outside his Palatine home Sunday afternoon.While searching his home, police said they found a rifle, multiple loaded rifle magazines, hundreds of additional rounds of rifle ammunition, tactical equipment, a tactical vest containing body armor, and a patch with imagery associated with white supremacist extremism. Officers also found an eight-page manifesto, containing both text and photos. Police said Thursday the manifesto indicated Paporakis was planning this attack "for some time." It is apparently filled with hateful thoughts toward non-white people, especially those who are Indian. In it, Paparokis allegedly self-identifies as a white supremacist and neo-Nazi. Law enforcement said he wrote about being "an ordinary white kid going to college and working. Underneath that façade was a sociopathic white supremacist neo-Nazi filled with hatred, fantasizing about mass murder nearly every day."Police said Thursday they will not comment any further on the manifesto's content.Police said Thursday that Paporakis had lived in Palatine with his mother for approximately a year. He did not have prior contact with either Palatine or Mount Prospect police. Palatine police said they have questioned his mother, but she is not cooperating with the investigation.While federal charges have not yet been filed, the FBI said they are not off the table. Authorities are still sorting through the manifesto and considering any additional charges. Court documents say Paporakis suffered from mental and emotional health issues and had been without prescribed medication. He was ordered detained while awaiting trial.

title: Dawson-Boyd High School community mourning deaths of 3 current, former students within a week
description: A small school in Dawson, Minnesota, is mourning the loss of three current and former students in just the last five days.
content: A small school in Dawson, Minnesota, is mourning the loss of three current and former students in just the last five days. Dawson-Boyd High School sent out a message this week, informing students and parents of the deaths."It just hurts that we see people losing loved ones," said Principal Ryan Stotesbery. On Saturday, 18-year-old Carter Monaghan, a senior football player, died in a car crash near town. "He's just a really good kid," said Stotesbery. He said that Monaghan was a hard worker who planned to attend technical college next year. He was also known for helping younger students. "He drove one of our 7th graders to football practices on the other side of town. He gave him a ride every single day to football practice," said Stotesbery. At Wednesday night's football game against Lakeview, students from both schools wore "Play for Carter" T-shirts. "I don't even know how many shirts were bought. A lot of people from Lakeview bought the shirts and wore them last night, which was really cool," said Stotesbery. On Monday, Katherine Frank, a 2018 Dawson-Boyd graduate died. She was a sheriff's deputy in South Dakota who was shot in the line of duty. "That one hit home for me a lot as well," said Stotesbery. He said Frank made a lot of friends during her high school years."Great personality. Got along with all types of other students," said Stotesbery. "It's the type of student, and Carter is the same way, it's the type of student we want to graduate from here and send out into the world."A GoFundMe page, which has raised more than $90,000 for funeral costs, describes Frank as someone who was more than her badge. Another graduate, Aaron Gebur, whose mom was a paraprofessional at the school, died on Sunday. "It's really difficult, anytime you lose a young person, I think it's hard for the whole community. Because we see them all the time. We are at activities all the time," said Stotesbery. He said a team of counselors came to Dawson-Boyd High School to helps students cope with their grief.

title: Who is running for the U.S. House in the Chicago area during the 2026 midterm elections?
description: With five Democratic incumbent members of Congress in Illinois giving up their seats at the end of their terms, voters will elect a handful of new members of the U.S. House of Representatives in the 2026 midterm elections.
content: With five Democratic incumbent members of Congress in Illinois giving up their seats at the end of their terms, voters will elect a handful of new members of the U.S. House of Representatives in the 2026 midterm elections.Here's who is on the ballot for the House in the Chicago area in the general election on Nov. 3:Who is running in the 1st Congressional District?Jonathan JacksonJackson, the Democratic incumbent, has represented the 1st District in Illinois since 2023. He is a husband and the father of three adult children.Jackson also previously served as national spokesman for the Rainbow/PUSH Coalition, founded by his late father, Rev. Jesse Jackson. He also was a part owner of a Chicago beer distributor for more than a decade alongside his brother, Yusef, but as of 2011, no longer had a stake in that company, which his brother later sold in 2013.Campaign website: jacksonforcongress.comChristian MaxwellMaxwell won the Republican primary for the 1st District in March with 64.5% of the vote over Marcus Lewis, and faces an uphill battle to defeat Jackson. The 1st District seat has been held by a Democrat since 1935. A businesswoman and mother of four, Maxwell has never run for public office before. She said she voted for Donald Trump for president in 2024 but not in 2020 or 2016.Campaign website: christianmaxwellforcongress.comWho is running in the 2nd Congressional District?Donna MillerAfter Democratic incumbent Robin Kelly opted to run for the U.S. Senate rather than seek re-election to the House, Cook County Commissioner Donna Miller defeated nine other candidates to win the Democratic primary in March, with 40.4% of the vote.A longtime political ally of Kelly's, Miller has served on the Cook County Board of Commissioners since 2018, representing a district that covers several southern suburbs, including parts or all of Alsip, Bridgeview, Chicago Heights, Crestwood, Matteson, Oak Forest, Orland Park, Park Forest, Sauk Village, Steger, Tinley Park, and Worth.Campaign website: donnaforcongress.comMike NoackNoack ran unopposed in the Republican primary in March. It's his first bid for public office.A truck driver from Kankakee County, Noack faces long odds at winning the general election. The 2nd District has not elected a Republican to Congress since the 1950s. Campaign website: noack4congress.comWho is running in the 3rd Congressional District?Delia RamirezRamirez, the Democratic incumbent, has been in office since 2023. She is the first Latina elected to Congress from the Midwest.An outspoken opponent of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown known as Operation Midway Blitz, she was previously an Illinois state representative from December 2018 until December 2022.Campaign website: deliaforcongress.comAngel OakleyOakley ran unoposed in the Republican primary in March. She also ran as an independent write-in candidate for the 2nd District in 2024.A former Winfield village trustee, Oakley is the owner of a marketing and communications firm, and a mother of three. She faces a difficult challenge to win election in a district that Democrats have held since 1975.Campaign website: libertyangel.usWho is running in the 4th Congressional District?Patty GarciaGarcia is the chief of staff to incumbent Democratic U.S. Rep. Jesus "Chuy" Garcia (no relation), who is stepping down at the end of his term. Chuy Garcia faced intense criticism from fellow Democrats for his last-minute decision not to run for re-election, clearing the path for Patty Garcia to be the only Democrat on the ballot for the March 17 primary.A longtime aide to the incumbent congressman, to whom she is not related, Garcia is a longtime Democratic political operative and advocate for immigrant rights.Campaign website: pattyforillinois.comChris GettyGetty has been the mayor of southwest suburban Lyons since 2009. He joined the race as an independent candidate after Chuy Garcia decided not to run for re-election.Born and raised in Lyons, Getty also runs a family-owned insurance agency in Lyons, and is the elected township supervisor for Lyons Township. Campaign website: chrisgettyforgongress.comLupe CastilloCastillo ran unopposed in the Republican primary in March. She also ran for the seat in 2024, losing to Chuy Garcia.A wife and mother, Castillo is also a former 22nd Ward Republican Committeewoman, a party official who help with voter outreach, party endorsements, and choosing replacement candidates when a local or state legislative office becomes vacant.Campaign website: castillolupe.comEd HersheyHershey ran unopposed in the Working Class Party primary in March. He also ran for the seat in 2022 and 2024, losing to Chuy Garcia. He also ran for alderman of the 25th Ward in Chicago in 2015, finishing in fourth place, losing to Daniel Solis.A science teacher at Lindblom High School in Chicago, he's also a Chicago Teachers Union representative.The 4th District has elected a Democrat to the seat in every election since 1988.Campaign website: Workingclassfight.comWho is running in the 5th Congressional District?Mike QuigleyQuigley, the Democratic incumbent, has represented the 5th District since 2009. He's also a former Cook County Commissioner, having spent three terms on the Cook County Board of Commissioners.A member of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, Quigley also is running for mayor of Chicago in 2027.Campaign website: quigleyforcongress.comTommy HansonHanson won the Republican primary in March over two other candidates, winning 72% of the vote.Hanson runs a commercial real estate firm and has run for the seat four other times, losing to Quigley each time in the general election between 2018 and 2024. He faces long odds to win election to the 5th District, which has elected a Republican only one time since 1906.Campaign website: votetommyhanson.comWho is running in the 6th Congressional District?Sean CastenCasten, the Democratic incumbent, ran unopposed in the March primary election. He has held the seat since 2019.A scientist from Downers Grove, Casten is also a former clean energy entrepreneur and fuel chain analyst.Campaign website: castenforcongress.comNiki ConfortiConforti defeated Skylar Duensing in the Republican primary in March. She has run for the seat twice before, losing to Casten in the general election in 2024, and losing in the Republican primary in 2022.An energy consultant and single mother, Conforti also previously worked in healthcare administration, and ran her own staffing business.Campaign website: conforti4congress.comWho is running in the 7th Congressional District?La Shawn FordFord defeated 12 other Democrats in the March primary race for the seat held by longtime incumbent Danny Davis, who is retiring at the end of his term.Ford has been an Illinois state representative since 2007, representing a district that includes parts of the West Side of Chicago and suburbs like Oak Park, Forest Park, Brookfield, and Western Springs. He also ran for mayor of Chicago in 2019, failing to make the runoff election that pitted Lori Lightfoot against Toni Preckwinkle.Campaign website: fordforcongress.comChad KoppieKoppie defeated Patricia Easley in the Republican primary in March. He has run for the seat twice before in 2022 and 2024.A farmer from Kane County and a perennial candidate, Koppie also ran unsuccessfully for U.S. Senate in 2008, 2014, 2016, and 2020. In all but one of those elections, he was removed from the ballot for failing to gather enough signatures on his nominating petitions as a third-party candidate. In 2018, he unsuccessfully ran for lieutenant governor as a Constitution Party Candidate.A Republican hasn't won in the 7th District since 1946.Campaign website: chadkoppie.comWho is running in the 8th Congressional District?Melissa BeanBean defeated seven other candidates in the Democratic primary in March in the race to replace Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, who instead ran for U.S. Senate. Bean, a wife and mother of two, previously represented the 8th District for three terms from 2005 to 2011, losing re-election in 2010 to Tea Party Republican Joe Walsh. The 2026 race for the seat is Bean's first foray back into politics since she lost the seat. Since losing re-election in 2010, she once served as CEO of the Executives' Club of Chicago, a local business forum, and as an executive for JP Morgan Chase.Campaign website: melissabeanforcongress.comJennifer DavisDavis defeated three other candidates in the Republican primary in March. This is her first campaign for elected office.A wife and mother of 10 kids, Davis and her husband own a software company headquartered in West Dundee.A Republican has won in the 8th District only one time since 2004.Campaign website: votejenniferdavis.com Who is running in the 9th Congressional District?Daniel BissAfter incumbent U.S. Rep. Jan Schakowsky announced she would be retiring at the end of this term, Biss defeated 14 other candidates in the Democratic primary in March, with 29.4% of the vote.Biss has been the mayor of north suburban Evanston since 2021. Before that, he was an Illinois state lawmaker, spending six years in the Illinois Senate from 2013 to 2019, and two years in the Illinois House from 2011 to 2013. In 2018, he ran for governor, finishing second in the Democratic primary to eventual Gov. JB Pritzker. Before his career in politics, he was a math professor at the University of Chicago.Campaign website: danielbiss.comJohn EllesonElleson defeated three other Republicans in the March primary election, winning 48.9% of the vote.Pastor of Lakewood Chapel in Arlington Heights, Elleson also ran for the 9th District seat in 2018 and 2022. In 2018, he lost to Schakowsky by a wide margin, getting only 26.5% of the vote. In 2022, he was removed from the ballot for failing to collect enough valid signatures on his nominating petitions.A Republican hasn't won election in the 9th Congressional District since 1946.Campaign website: johnelleson.comWho is running in the 10th Congressional District?Brad SchneiderSchneider easily defeated Democratic challenger Morgan Coghill in the March primary, winning 78.8% of the vote.A former insurance company manager and business advisor, Schneider was first elected to Congress in 2012, defeating Republican incumbent Bob Dold. In 2014, Dold won the seat back, and then Schneider defeated him again in 2016, and has held the seat ever since.Campaign website: schneiderforcongress.comCarl LambrechtLambrecht ran unopposed in the Republican primary in March. An optical engineer and owner of a Highland Park optical instrument manufacturer, Lambrecht also previously ran for the Illinois House of Representatives in 2024, losing to incumbent Rep. Bob Morgan in the 58th District.Lambrecht does not have an active campaign website.Who is running in the 11th Congressional District?Bill FosterFoster ran unopposed in the Democratic primary in March. A former high-energy physicist and particle accelerator designer at Fermilab, Foster was first elected to Congress in 2008, winning a special election in the 14th District to replace former Speaker Dennis Hastert, who resigned over a sex abuse scandal. Foster served two terms in the 14th District before losing re-election to Republican Randy Hultgren in 2010. After moving to Naperville in 2011, he ran for the 11th District seat in 2012, defeating Republican incumbent Judy Biggert, and has held the seat ever since.Campaign website: billfoster.comJeffrey WalterWalter defeated three other candidates in the Republican primary in March, winning 42.6% of the vote.A U.S. Navy veteran, Walter has been mayor of the village of Elburn since 2017, and before that was a village trustee since 2009. He also has experience as a business consultant.Campaign website: jeffwalterforcongress.comWho is running in the 14th Congressional District?Lauren UnderwoodUnderwood ran unopposed in the Democratic primary in March.A nurse from Naperville and a former senior advisor at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Underwood was first elected to Congress in 2018, defeating Republican incumbent Randy Hultgren, and has held the seat ever since.Campaign website: underwoodforcongress.comJames MarterMarter defeated three other candidates in the Republican primary in March, winning 74.9% of the vote.A former information technology developer, Marter owns a software consulting company based in Oswego. He also ran against Underwood in 2024, losing by a 10-point margin.Campaign website: marter4congress.usWho is running in the 16th Congressional District?Darin LaHoodLaHood ran unopposed in the Republican primary in March.The son of former U.S. Rep. Ray LaHood, who served the 18th District from 1995 until 2009, Darin LaHood has served in Congress since 2015. From 2015 to 2023, LaHood represented the 18th congressional district, but following the decennial redistricting process, he was drawn into the 16th District before the 2022 election.Before his election to Congress, Darin LaHood was an Illinois state senator from 2011 to 2015. He's also a former Tazewell County prosecutor and private practice attorney.Campaign website: lahoodforcongress.comPaul NolleyNolley ran unopposed in the Democratic primary in March.The executive director of Project First Rate, a nonprofit that works with union contractors and building tradespeople, is running for elected office for the first time. He also has worked as a cook, cashier, cleaner, and farmhand.Nolley faces long odds at winning the general election, as the 16th District has not elected a Democrat since 1990.Campaign website: nolleyforcongress.com

title: Plaza Hotel in NYC closing for 4-year renovation starting in 2027
description: The Plaza Hotel in Midtown Manhattan is closing in January for repair and restoration work on its facade.
content: New York City's Plaza Hotel is closing for at least four years for repair and restoration work on its facade.The iconic Fifth Avenue hotel will shut its doors starting in January, officials announced Wednesday. The Plaza has been a landmark in Manhattan for more than 100 years. It first opened in 1907 and has been recognized for its "architectural character, exceptional craftsmanship, and enduring presence.""Understanding the unique place in New York City's architectural heritage and cultural history it holds, The Plaza Hotel is advancing plans for repair and restoration works to its landmark-protected façade," the announcement stated. "The undertaking reflects the complexity of maintaining a property of such architectural and historical significance, with careful consideration given to preservation requirements and the building's long-term care, as well as the safety of our guests, employees, and the wider community."No details about how much the makeover will cost or specific renovations were released.The announcement said the plans require detailed planning and coordination with stakeholders and adherence to historic preservation requirements.The Department of Buildings said its most recent inspection of The Plaza found that its facade is unsafe, which is why it's required to have a sidewalk shed around it. However, the DOB told CBS News New York there's nothing on the city's end that would prevent hotel from staying open while repairs are made.There are residents who live in the hotel full-time, but it's unclear if they will be impacted.The last time the hotel closed was during the coronavirus pandemic in 2020, when it shut its doors for more than a year. It also closed from 2005 to 2008 for a $450 million lobby-to-roof restoration."Home Alone 2," "Bride Wars," and "The Great Gatsby" are just a few movies that were filmed at the hotel. Meanwhile, the classic children's books "Eloise at the Plaza and Eloise at Christmastime" are about a young girl living at the top of the hotel.

title: Terrorism threat levels are down in Minnesota compared to 10 years ago, but threat remains, former U.S. Attorney says
description: Just last week, an 18-year-old Twin Cities man was arrested for allegedly planning to kill people at Mall of America. He's also accused of supporting ISIS, a terrorist organization.
content: Just last week, an 18-year-old Twin Cities man was arrested for allegedly planning to kill people at Mall of America. He's also accused of supporting ISIS, a terrorist organization. In 2016, there was a wave of young men from Minnesota who pledged allegiance to ISIS. Some were tried and convicted. One was killed in Syria while fighting for the terror group. The prosecutor for the case was former U.S. Attorney Andy Luger, who served from 2014 to 2017, and again from 2022 to 2025.Luger says ISIS is still recruiting in Minnesota, though not as aggressively as it was 10 years ago."That doesn't mean it isn't a threat, and it doesn't mean we shouldn't be alarmed," Luger told WCCO's Esme Murphy.His comments come after the recent arrest of 18-year-old Sheikhdoon Mohamud of the Twin Cities, who is accused of planning to kill people at Mall of America and of supporting ISIS. Federal prosecutors say he had talked online for months about joining the group and plotting an attack, but wasn't arrested until he bought an AK-47 from an undercover agent. An FBI informant first began talking to him when he was 16 years old, according to FBI reports."You need something more than just talk," Luger said. Luger said authorities constantly monitor online chat rooms and discussion rooms, a practice he saw in both of his stints as U.S. attorney. They watch for ISIS-related terrorism, he said, but also for "all sorts of violence."Luger also finds recent violence that law enforcement officials are tying to Somali gangs alarming. But he doesn't see it as a path to terrorism."I don't think it's a bridge to terrorism so much as there's disaffection in a lot of ethnic and other groups," Luger said.Luger pioneered the use of RICO statutes against gangs in North Minneapolis, and he sees an opening to use those racketeering laws again."The gang culture is the gang culture," Luger said. "It's very localized."He described a largely online fight in which a perceived slight leads to shootings and then retaliation.

title: State Fair of Texas' oldest Black-owned concessionaire celebrates 50 years in business
description: Brothers Juan and Brent Reaves are carrying on their father's legacy at Smokey John's, serving up barbecue, family recipes, and traditions that have brought people together for generations.
content: You've probably smelled the aroma of savory barbecue and turkey legs walking by Smokey John's at the State Fair of Texas. The oldest Black-owned concessionaire is celebrating half a century in business.The year was 1976, and "Smokey" John Reaves founded one of the most iconic barbecue restaurants in North Texas."I was about five years old, and I'm looking at this building with a support beam in the middle, and I couldn't believe that that was going to be our restaurant," Juan Reaves said.Juan Reaves remembers working with his dad at the original restaurant on the corner of Lemmon and Mockingbird in Dallas."My dad was larger than life. Dad had never met a stranger and was everyone's best friend," Juan Reaves said.Now, 50 years after its founding, Smokey John's son, Brent, continues building relationships with customers."It feels really good to impact on people's through food because it's so funny, the food creates emotions," Brent Reaves said.The brothers get to bring people together as the oldest Black-owned concessionaire at the State Fair of Texas."The State Fair is an opportunity to do what we love and bring good food to people across the metroplex," Juan Reaves said.The brothers hope to bring the warmth of family traditions to their customers. Their grandma's banana pudding recipe has been in the family for more than 100 years."We're as much in the people in business as we are in the food service industry, and I think we realized on that food is a way of connecting. We all have to eat. We all enjoy eating," Juan Reaves said.The brothers carry on their father's legacy while making their own mark by creating new recipes, such as the Twinkle Twinkle Brisket Star."It's remarkable for us to be able to keep his legacy going, keep his name going and push it forward, and maybe so the third generation if possible," Brent Reaves said.Juan and Brent plan to continue serving customers food made from the heart and hope the business grows for another 50 years.

title: Former U.S. Rep. Melissa Bean seeks return to Congress in race vs. Republican Jennifer Davis
description: With U.S. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-Illinois) stepping down at the end of his term following a failed bid for the Senate, former U.S. Rep. Melissa Bean is looking to return to the seat she once held for six years.
content: With U.S. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-Illinois) stepping down at the end of his term following a failed bid for the Senate, former U.S. Rep. Melissa Bean is looking to return to the seat she once held for six years.The 8th District includes multiple north and northwest suburbs, including Schaumburg, Elgin, Des Plaines, Hoffman Estates, St. Charles, and West Dundee.Krishnamoorthi has represented the district since 2017, but gave up his seat to run for the U.S. Senate. Bean represented the district from 2005 to 2011, after losing the 2010 election to Tea Party Republican Joe Walsh, who served one term before losing re-election to future Sen. Tammy Duckworth in 2012.After years working as as CEO of the Executives' Club of Chicago, a local business forum, and as an executive for JP Morgan Chase, Bean is trying to win back the seat in November. She's facing off against Republican Jennifer Davis, a mother of 10 and tech entrepreneur who said she's ready to bring artificial intelligence expertise to Congress."When you don't have experts, then expertise gets bought, and I think that's really bad for the voters," Davis said.Both candidates said they're focused on the key issue of affordability."There's no response from Congress to look out for affordability and, you know, affordable health care, affordable housing, affordable groceries. And [voters] just feel like, who's representing me? And that's a concern that I think people are very worried about the direction of the country on," Bean said."It's the affordability, it's being able to have high quality, affordable healthcare, and it's a very entrepreneurial district. So it is all of the issues that impact small businesses. We have so much red tape that really makes it impossible to be an entrepreneur in this area," Davis said.Asked if she would support an attempt to impeach President Trump if Democrats take control of the House, Bean said, "I think we'd have to look at what offenses are we looking at.""He's been impeached before. He's clearly committed impeachable offenses," she said.CBS News Chicago asked Davis if the Trump administration's immigration crackdown last year, dubbed Operation Midway Blitz, was a success or a failure. "These are people doing jobs, and so I think we have to look at two elements to it. We have to look at do individuals make mistakes? Certainly there was mistakes that could have been done. Do we need to have strong law enforcement and strong borders and strong communities? Absolutely," she said.Bean said she agrees that the United States needs to secure its borders, but criticized the Trump administration's handling of Operation Midway Blitz and other immigration enforcement efforts in across the U.S."What we've seen on our streets of people being murdered, you know, people disappearing from their communities, is just out of hand," she said. "We really need to cut back this excess funding of ICE and make sure that they are properly trained and held accountable when they go rogue."Asked if the government needs better guardrails in place to prevent elected officials from enriching themselves while they're in office, Davis said, "I would love that, and that's something that's really important to me.""I don't agree with it, regardless of what side of the fence it's on," she said.Asked if she believes the president has enriched himself beyond a reasonable amount of money while in office, Davis said, "I don't know that.""I mean, that's not something that I've researched or paid that much attention to," she said.Bean and Davis sharply differ on abortion. Davis supports the overturning of Roe v. Wade, which returned abortion regulation to states. Bean said protecting abortion rights is not negotiable, calling for Roe v. Wade's protections to be written into federal law.

title: Illinois Rep. Ramirez introduces bill to abolish DHS one day after feds raid Omar's home in D.C.
description: Rep. Delia Ramirez said that if federal agents are "willing and able" to search Omar's home, "they can do it to anyone." She said the raid pushed her to file a bill to abolish DHS.
content: Weeks before the Nov. 3 midterms, Illinois Rep. Delia Ramirez has made an accelerated effort to put immigration reform at the forefront of the conversation. She says the federal raid on Rep. Ilhan Omar's home should worry everyone.At 4:30 a.m. Monday, Homeland Security Investigations searched Omar's Washington home as part of what the Justice Department called a "federal criminal investigation" into decades-old paperwork. Agents took her phone, two sources told CBS News, and her relatives have been issued subpoenas.In a statement on social media, Omar called it an "outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies." Her office has said she has "done nothing wrong." President Trump told reporters he "had nothing to do with" the raid.Ramirez told CBS News Chicago that the early-morning raid pressured her to file the "Reimagining Safety Act" this week, a bill that would abolish the Department of Homeland Security and transform it into a cabinet-level Department of Community Safety. Ramirez first announced the bill at a Sept. 23 news conference in Chicago, CBS Chicago reported. According to that report, it would also abolish U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE."What happened to my colleague and my sister, Congresswoman Ilhan Omar, is bone-chilling," she said, calling it an abuse of power against "political enemies" of the president.Ramirez is worried about the broader implications and the precedent this sets for her constituents and everyone living in the U.S."It should scare everyone, because if they're willing and able to do that to Ilhan Omar, they can do it to anyone," she said."They're not stopping. We need to stop them," Ramirez said.Ramirez, 43, who is the child of two Guatemalan immigrants, shared her own fears."I'm human, and it's actually why this work is so personal to me and why I am so persistent," she said. "But it doesn't mean I don't worry."Ramirez has been an outspoken critic of Mr. Trump. She said she is sometimes nervous about what an administration "obsessed with targeting people with whom they disagree" could try to do to her, and that it is why she continues to raise the alarm about her colleagues.Ramirez also stood alongside local and national immigration and civil rights groups at a press conference to introduce the "People's Vision for Immigration Reform," a platform to preserve and expand pathways to citizenship.The resolution has 19 congressional co-sponsors and the backing of 54 civil and immigration rights organizations. The press conference, held at the Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights office, was packed with representatives from local and national advocacy groups."We've seen the consequences of the inability of Congress to prioritize legislation and the overreach of the Trump administration that has taken a sledgehammer to refugee admissions, temporary protected status, healthcare, food access, and due process," said Lawrence Benito, the coalition's executive director.He said the coalition was formed 40 years ago, in direct response to the last time Congress, under then-President Ronald Reagan, enacted major immigration reform legislation. It has helped hundreds of thousands of people prepare applications and gain access to citizenship, and has helped pass numerous pro-immigrant state-level laws.The Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986 was the last sweeping, multifaceted overhaul of U.S. immigration laws. It created a pathway to citizenship for more than 2.7 million people and strengthened border protection.Representation was broad, from Korean to African organizations, as well as the ACLU of Illinois."Immigration policy can be based on a commitment to family unification, fairness, and due process, and recognize the dignity and worth of people from other countries," said Ed Yohnka, director of communications for the ACLU of Illinois.The 71-page bill proposes how and where to redistribute DHS's funds and responsibilities across other departments, including the creation of the Department of Community Safety.The bill would preserve FEMA and cybersecurity functions within the new Department of Community Safety, while moving immigration enforcement back to the Department of Justice, which initially oversaw it before the Sept. 11 attacks. Customs functions would move to the Department of the Treasury, and the TSA and Coast Guard to the Department of Transportation.The bill would also redirect DHS funds into Medicare for All, housing and education. It would also limit government surveillance, rein in what Ramirez called "unlawful abuses of data," and curb militarized enforcement.The bill has fewer than seven co-sponsors and faces long odds in a Republican-controlled Congress that is out of session until after the Nov. 3 midterms.The National Republican Congressional Committee called the legislation "utterly insane.""The radical socialist agenda for the Democrat Party is on full display, and it's utterly insane," committee spokesman Mike Marinella said. "Democrats are rolling out the welcome mat for criminals and cartels, and expecting Americans to go along."Some moderate Democrats, such as Rahm Emanuel, also think abolishing ICE goes too far. Ramirez said border work would continue."I'm not saying that there's no work in the border," she said to CBS News Chicago. "The work of the border needs to be done by the Department of Treasury, as we know that at ports of entry, we are handling and managing imports and exports all the time," she said, referencing drugs and guns.Abolishing ICE has become a campaign issue for many candidates, most notably Juliana Stratton, who won her primary running on it, compared to her competitor Raja Krishnamoorthi's call to "abolish Trump's ICE." A January Economist/YouGov poll found 46% of Americans support abolishing ICE, compared to 43% who oppose it."What is radical about calling out and dismantling an agency that is less than 23 years old? An agency that has proven to us for the last 23 years that it cannot be trusted with our tax dollars to protect people. That is now the biggest threat to the homeland," she said. Both Ramirez and the community groups emphasized that this issue did not start or end with Mr. Trump, and called on Congress to be more courageous and reassert its power."The fact that Ronald Reagan, in November of 1986, passed the bill that established some form of immigration reform, and that neither Democrats nor Republicans have been able to do anything since then, tells us that the only permanent safety for people in this country is actually a roadmap," Ramirez said."But really it's the bills that we have to actually pass in Congress that actually get to legal pathways, so people don't have to go through a border, or experience what they've experienced," she said.Even with that push, Ramirez said it all comes down to people's advocacy."The community is ready," she said. "And it's the community that's going to lead the charge — whether it's to dismantle DHS, or to actually get this Congress to give a damn and actually do something about immigration reform."

title: 'Partial win for customers': Illinois Commerce Commission approves $82 million rate hike for Nicor Gas
description: The Illinois Commerce Commission approved an $82 million rate hike on Thursday. The amount was negotiated between Nicor Gas and the attorney general's office as part of a settlement that reduced the company's original request by nearly two-thirds.
content: The Illinois Commerce Commission approved an $82 million rate hike on Thursday. The amount was negotiated between Nicor Gas and the attorney general's office as part of a settlement that reduced the company's original request by nearly two-thirds.The rate increase is expected to add around $2 a month to residential customers' bills beginning in November."A settlement is a compromise, so we're not thrilled about every element, but we are pleased the Commission approved it," Illinois PIRG Director Abe Scarr said in a statement. "We are excited that the settlement sets a lower, $15, monthly fixed charge. Lower fixed charges reward energy efficiency and conservation and give customers more control over their bill."The prior fixed fee was $21 per month, regardless of the volume of gas used.The lower monthly charge gives consumers more control over their bills and protects low-income customers who often use less gas than high-income customers, according to Environmental Law and Policy Center senior attorney Rob Kelter."The larger users cause there to be more investment in the system," Kelter said. "It's fair to ask them to pay more."Kelter said he'd like to see that charge go down to $12 a month or lower. He thinks Nicor is moving in the right direction and has shown a willingness to do better.But consumer advocates say the decision is only a "partial win for customers," in that it still raises rates, building on other past rate hikes from the utility, and allows a higher profit rate than they hoped to see.The settlement allows for a 9.48% return on equity for shareholders, which is between the 8.95% that Illinois PIRG and Legal Action Chicago had sought and the 10.35% rate that Nicor originally requested. Utility watchdog groups had characterized that request as "outrageous" and "exorbitant."Nicor serves a large swath of northern Illinois, excluding the city of Chicago.Labor agreementThe settlement negotiated by Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul's office included a side deal on union labor that drew criticism from consumer advocates and was lambasted by the Chicago Tribune's editorial board as a "nonsensical jobs deal."That deal committed Nicor to maintaining this year's union staffing levels through the end of 2027 and continuing its capital investment levels.But like at all public utilities, spending on infrastructure is how Nicor makes its profit. Consumer advocates fear that the agreement could give Nicor fuel for a future rate case, in that it could say the commission already blessed the spending by signing off on the labor side deal. The consumer and environmental advocates who were party to the primary settlement declined to be party to the secondary labor deal.While the commission accepted the agreement as "consistent" with its rate-making decisions, it also emphasized its own authority to scrutinize future rate cases without being held to conditions agreed to between Nicor and the attorney general's office."The commission is not bound by any of the terms of this settlement in any future matter, and the commission retains the authority to make rate-making determinations regarding the prudence, justness, and reasonableness of any future expenditures and resulting rates," Commission Chairman Doug Scott said of the labor agreement.That is, if the company were to spend at a higher-than-justified level to meet the terms of its agreement with Raoul's office, whether that spending can be passed on to ratepayers will still be subject to the commission's scrutiny.Scott added that it is outside the scope of the commission's role to dictate who should perform any work for the utility."The commission's role with respect to workforce commitments and who performs work is limited to determining whether any expense is reasonable," Scott said.Pattern of rate casesConsumer advocates say Nicor has already indicated that it believes more investment is needed in its system, so they expect the company to file another rate case in January.Nicor did not respond to questions about future rate case plans.Scarr of Illinois PIRG described the rate hikes as part of a pattern of 'excessive spending.'"This is Nicor's sixth rate hike in a decade," Scarr said. "These rapid and significant rate hikes are driven by wasteful spending on unnecessary fossil fuel infrastructure, which threatens to lock northern Illinois into paying for polluting infrastructure for generations to come."But environmental law center attorney Kelter said it's also a symptom of a regulatory body that's doing its job."The Illinois Commerce Commission has shown that it is going to scrutinize every penny that utilities ask for in rate cases, and when you have a really strong commission that doesn't rubber stamp rate hikes, you're going to have utilities coming in more often for rate cases," Kelter said."And so, while nobody likes to see utilities coming in for rate cases, that's the product of having such a strong commission that's protecting consumers in Illinois."Capitol News Illinois is a nonprofit, nonpartisan news service that distributes state government coverage to hundreds of news outlets statewide. It is funded primarily by the Illinois Press Foundation and the Robert R. McCormick Foundation.

title: Georgia midterm election turnout surpasses 500,000 on 3rd day of early voting, data shows
description: Polling places across Georgia are seeing record-breaking crowds as early voting in the state's important midterm election continues for its third day.
content: Early voting continues across Georgia, and the state is seeing high traffic at its polling places.According to the Secretary of State's Office, more than half a million Georgians have already cast their vote as of 5 p.m. on Thursday. That's around 6.9% of all of the state's over 7.5 million active voters.Most of the voters cast their ballots in-person, with about 21,700 mail-in ballots already accepted.The counties with the highest percentage of turnout so far during the early voter period included Towns, Greene, Union, Putnam, and, Fayette. Of those that have cast their votes, around 54% were women, 45.9% were men. The state had already set a record for first-day early voting in a midterm election with an increase of around 40% compared to the first day of the 2022 midterms."This record-breaking turnout proves that voters have confidence in the integrity of our elections," said Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger. "It's a testament to our strong election system overseen by 159 of the best county election officials in the country."Early voting continues through Oct. 30, and voters can cast their ballot at any polling place in their county of residence.You can learn more about how to vote early in the midterms here and how to vote by mail here.

title: Reading man sent disturbing messages to friends after allegedly killing mother, prosecutors say
description: A not guilty plea was entered on behalf of Ryan Hanafin, 22, on a first-degree murder charge in the death of his mother, 49-year-old Andria Hanafin.
content: The young man accused of killing his mother in Reading, Massachusetts appeared in Woburn District Court for the first time since his arrest. A not guilty plea was entered on behalf of Ryan Hanafin, 22, on a first-degree murder charge in the death of his mother, 49-year-old Andria Hanafin. Ryan is also facing additional charges for improperly storing firearms near a minor and receiving an untraceable firearm. He is being held without bail for the murder charge. For the additional firearms charges, he is being held on a $5,000 cash bail. Police said Ryan Hanafin shot his mother in their home on Center Ave. in Reading on Oct. 7 and then drove to Vermont, where he was arrested the next day. Investigators said Matthew Hanafin, Ryan's father, called 911 after arriving home from work around 12:30 a.m. on Oct. 8 and found his wife's body in the kitchen of their home on Center Avenue. Their 13-year-old son was also inside the home, unharmed. An autopsy later found that Andria was shot in the head. During Ryan's arraignment Thursday, prosecutors said Matthew and Andria last spoke during a phone call at around 6:51 p.m. on Wednesday, Oct. 7. Prosecutors said Andria told Matthew she had been arguing with Ryan and said that she wanted him to move out of the house. According to prosecutors, on the day of her death, Andria said to a friend that Ryan told her "he had ruined her life." Prosecutors said Andria and Ryan had an ongoing dispute over the number of cats in the home. Andria Hanafin was known to foster cats. Eighty-four cats were found in the home after her death and are now with the Massachusetts Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (MSPCA). Prosecutors added that Andria had expressed to another friend that she was afraid of her son and feared retaliation from him because he had access to firearms. Ryan Hanafin had a license to carry a firearm and had 10 registered firearms, according to prosecutors. Investigators say they found 19 firearms in Ryan Hanafin's room at the family's home in Reading, including a ghost gun, leading to the untraceable firearm charge. A 3D printer was also found in his room. Investigators found text messages shared between Ryan Hanafin and relatives during what prosecutors believe to be the hour of Andria's death. In one of the messages, prosecutors said Ryan Hanafin told a cousin that he "blew madre to pieces." Investigators found that Ryan Hanafin called his mother "madre." Prosecutors said Ryan Hanafin wrote in another message to a cousin that he "blew her s--- smooth off." Ryan Hanafin is next scheduled to appear in court on Nov. 10. Hundreds of people went to Memorial Park in Reading Wednesday night to pay their respects to Andria Hanafin at a candlelight vigil.

title: Flock cameras removed from Elgin Community College campus
description: Flock cameras have been removed from the campus at Elgin Community College.
content: Flock cameras have been removed from the campus at Elgin Community College.The school said staffers had to put bags over the controversial cameras after Flock refused to cancel their contract.The six license plate reader cameras were installed in April 2025, but the college said it grew concerned after reports of federal immigration officers accessing the cameras at other schools.Last fall, an ECC student was taken into custody by federal immgiraiton agents on campus during the Trump administration's Operation Midway Blitz immigration crackdown. The college said at the time it was not involved in the arrest and does not shared students' immigration status.ECC said attempts to shut down the cameras were unsuccessful until their contract ran out in April 2026. CBS News Chicago has reached out to Flock for comment and are waiting to hear back.

title: Judge orders temporary shutdown of Pullman Innovations feed plant amid lawsuit over foul odors
description: A Cook County judge has ordered an animal feed plant on the South Side of Chicago to temporarily shut down, after city and state officials accused the company of violating air pollution laws.
content: A Cook County judge has ordered an animal feed plant on the South Side of Chicago to temporarily shut down, after city and state officials accused the company of violating air pollution laws and causing hundreds of complaints from neighbors about foul odors.Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul and the City of Chicago obtained a temporary restraining order against Pullman Innovations on Wednesday, after filing a lawsuit against the company in August.Peggy Salazar, who lives near the plant in the South Deering neighborhood, said she has been dealing with foul odors from the plant for 40 years. "Think about sticking your head in a trash can on a 100-degree day and taking a big whiff," Salazar said. "You almost do feel like you do want to throw up. You know, it's gagging."The manufacturing facility about half a mile away has operated under different names over the years. It's currently Pullman Innovations. According to their website, they provide "highly nutritional, vegetable oil products formulated to meet your feed ingredient needs."In a lawsuit filed in August seeking to get Pullman Innovations to clean up its act, the city and state accused the plant of causing alleges air pollution in violation of permit conditions, construction of a boiler without a permit, failure to operate pollution control devices and more. "When it does come this way, I do smell it, and I say, 'Well, I know it's going to go away. So, what can I do?" said South Deering resident John Sandoval.On Wednesday, a judge granted the state's and city's request for a temporary restraining order, stopping odor-causing operations at the plant at least until Jan. 14, 2027, when the next hearing in the case is scheduled, or until the facility addresses the excessive odors and comes into compliance with environmental law before that date.Despite that court order, there was still a foul odor in the air around the plant on Thursday.The Illinois Environmental Protection Agency last inspected the facility in 2025, and reported the odors were so strong, it "made breathing difficult for the inspectors."Pullman Innovations did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: 10-year-old girl hospitalized after 8-year-old brother throws knife and hits chest, Lauderhill police say
description: Lauderhill police say the girl was conscious and breathing when taken to the hospital, and preliminary information indicates a small cut to her chest.
content: A 10-year-old girl was hospitalized after Lauderhill police said her 8-year-old brother threw a knife at her, which stabbed her in the chest Thursday afternoon. According to Lauderhill police, the incident occurred at an apartment complex in the 2900 block of Northwest 56th Avenue at approximately 3:30 p.m. The victim told police that she was cutting pizza and her brother became upset about not receiving his piece, so he grabbed the knife she was using and threw it at her. It struck her in the chest, according to police.The mother told police that she had stepped outside to get the mail when this occurred and found her daughter running out of the apartment, bleeding from her chest. She was transported to Broward Health Medical Center, and rescue personnel noted she was conscious and breathing. Preliminary information, according to police, indicates that she sustained a small cut to her chest. Detectives with the Lauderhill Police Department's Criminal Investigations Division have been notified, and the investigation remains ongoing. No additional information has been released.

title: Suspected jewelry thief fatally shot by security officer at Fort Worth shopping center, police say
description: Police say the man smashed a jewelry kiosk's glass before being shot. He fled across a parking lot and collapsed.
author_name: Doug  Myers, Marissa  Armas, Giles  Hudson, Felesha  Lee
content: A suspected smash-and-grab theft at a Fort Worth shopping center turned deadly when an armed security officer shot a man who was breaking the glass at a jewelry kiosk, police said.Officers responded shortly after 8:30 p.m. to the 4200 block of South Freeway near Seminary Drive, where La Gran Plaza is located, according to Fort Worth police.The man was seen using an object to break the glass at a jewelry kiosk inside the shopping center, police spokesperson Buddy Calzada said.An armed security officer nearby opened fire, striking the man at least once, Calzada said. The wounded man fled across the parking lot before collapsing.Shoppers, witnesses shakenResponding officers found the man and began lifesaving measures, including CPR, according to Calzada.Fort Worth Fire Department emergency medical personnel arrived and pronounced the man dead at the scene, police said.Wednesday, witnesses told CBS News Texas that the shooting happened near the entrance of the shopping center, on the south side. They said they heard four to five gunshots and saw the suspect running from the kiosk before they heard gunfire. Shopping center employees said the security guard worked for a private company hired by the jewelry business, not the plaza; however, CBS News Texas is still working to confirm that.Video captured on Wednesday shows glass boarded up near the entrance, where witnesses said the shooting happened.Next-day shoppers were left a little shaken."It's definitely really scary," said Jack Woods. "But we obviously want Fort Worth to be safe."Criminologist Alex Del Carmen said Texas law can allow the use of deadly force in certain circumstances to protect property. "What I've read so far, where the individual had already trespassed, the individual not only showed intent, but was actually removing property at the time illegally, that the respondent, in this case, the security guard that was hired by the company to protect that property, use lethal force, and that it is justified under the criminal statute in the state of Texas," Del Carmen said. "It's very unlikely, in my view, that this is going to be criminally prosecuted, because, in fact, in Texas, we're kind of unique in that sense, that as a state, we have this castle law, you know, principle that allows for individuals to defend property and people within that area."Some shoppers said they understand the security guard's response."Protecting property, self-defense, I mean the guy came in here, you don't know if he had a gun a weapon or something, he could hurt somebody," said Thomas Johnson. "So, I think it's kind of on him for making that decision for himself."CBS News Texas reached out to representatives at the plaza, but they said they had no comment.

title: Exclusive video offers insight into Cornell University Faculty Senate meeting
description: Exclusive video offers insight into Wednesday's high-stakes meeting at Cornell University.
content: Exclusive video offers insight into Wednesday's high-stakes meeting at Cornell University.The school's president, Michael Kotlikoff, faced questions from faculty Wednesday over the handling of sexual assault allegations as it considered a resolution of no confidence in the school's administration.This comes nearly two years after a student identified only as Jane Doe reported to campus police being gang-raped at a fraternity house. Earlier this month, the university announced former Deputy U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates will lead what they call a "comprehensive independent review" of its handling of sexual misconduct claims, including the 2024 case. Kotlikoff discussed the possibility of banning fraternities altogether at Cornell. He told the gathered faculty that he had just attended a town hall with alumni who had told him how important their fraternity and sorority experience was to them. Kotlikoff said the issue should be studied. "If at the end of the day fraternities can not exist in a safe environment, and we can't be convinced that they can be safe, then we should make that decision. But we should make it, it seems to me, based on data, and study, and expertise," Kotlikoff said. Additionally, on Tuesday, Kotlikoff announced sweeping changes, saying Cornell will work with New York State Police on an arrangement to bring in independent experts to investigate sexual assault allegations. The school has also banned fraternity parties for the rest of the academic year. At Wednesday's meeting, faculty debated whether they have confidence in the university's leadership handling of sexual assaults.The meeting was closed to reporters and the university said no cameras were allowed on the grounds that it would inhibit the debate, but CBS News New York investigative reporter Mahsa Saeidi obtained access through a source.Part of the video shows a speaker questioning the university president about the outside investigation."President Kotlikoff, can you name all of the different kinds of assaults, both sexual and otherwise, on men, women and children that the outside investigators will be examining, and how far will they go back in time in their investigations?" one speaker asks."That is a board review. I don't dictate that review. It's an open review. It does have a very broad mandate. I don't know how far back they're going to go, frankly, but I will say that we're open to anything they ask," Kotlikoff says.One speaker cited findings from the university's Title IX process, saying two students were found responsible for sexual assault but initially received temporary suspensions.Kotlikoff pushed back on the characterization of the cases, saying the students were not found responsible for the specific allegations described by the speaker."I have to say, the two people you say have been found responsible for rape. That is not the charge and that is not what they were found responsible for," Kotlikoff said. "And it's a process that's independent of the administration."The university has said that, following a Title IX investigation, two students were expelled after being found responsible for sexual assault, while two others were suspended for sexual misconduct.Some faculty members also question why the university's recent reforms were announced only after increased public scrutiny of the case."There's an article that comes out, then we get a statement. There's more information that comes out in the press, then we get another statement, and that's reactive as opposed to real leadership," said Faculty Senator Risa Lieberwitz.Additional video shows a separate exchange."We've seen this administration suppress our academic freedom, as well as our students' voices over the past few years," another speaker says."What academic speech has been restricted?" Kotlikoff asks the speaker."Since 2023, the administration has punished over 80 students for nonviolent speech," the speaker replies. Another meeting will take place on Oct. 28. After that, faculty members will have about one week to submit their vote on the no-confidence resolution.Even if approved, the measure would be symbolic because the faculty senate does not have the authority to remove the university president.Some faculty members told CBS News New York that the 2024 case is just the tip of the iceberg, saying other students and former students have shared their own experiences of sexual assault and they've been too afraid to report what happened.In September, Jane Doe sued the university, her sorority, the Chi Phi fraternity and seven now former Chi Phi members for allegedly assaulting her.All seven men have denied the allegations.Do you have a story that needs investigating? Let us know.

title: North Texas superintendent, school police chief on leave over unspecified allegations
description: Two top officials at Pilot Point ISD in Denton County are on paid leave as the district investigates a complaint
content: Two top officials at Pilot Point ISD in Denton County are on paid leave as the district investigates a complaint against them, according to a letter sent to parents on Wednesday.The letter, from the district's board of trustees, said the superintendent and the chief of the district's police department were placed on administrative leave "out of an abundance of caution" to allow an independent investigation. The letter did not provide any specifics about the complaint against Superintendent Shannon Fuller or PPISD Police Chief Eric Dortch. The board said it has identified someone to serve as the acting superintendent, who they will announce when an agreement is reached. PPISD police officer Dee Carter will serve as the acting police chief, the letter said."The Board is committed to ensuring this does not impact the operations of the District and its dedication to the continued success of its students, staff, and the community," the letter said.According to their respective LinkedIn pages, Fuller has been with Pilot Point ISD since March of 2024 and Dortch since August of 2024.

title: San Jacinto man nearly killed by fallen tree during intense winds
description: A father of four was nearly killed after intense winds knocked down part of a tree and crushed him on Saturday.
content: A father of four in San Jacinto was nearly killed after intense winds knocked down part of a tree and crushed him on Saturday."He's broken, but he's going to be great," said Alexandra Roldan, mother of the victim, Ricky Roldan. Roldan's son was cleaning up his kids' toys in his backyard last weekend when the winds suddenly picked up and broke off the part of the tree that crushed him."He said he heard something," Alexandra said. "When he looked up, that's when it fell on him."The tree landed on Ricky's back, breaking several vertebrae and ribs and pinning him to the ground. His wife Erica rushed out of their home to help him. The part of the tree was at least 20 feet long. "She tries to lift it up, but it's too heavy," Alexandra said. "She runs out in a panic to the neighbors, and she sees nobody. She runs back and picks up the tree. So my son was able to crawl out."Erica quickly called 911 after freeing her husband.Paramedics rushed Ricky to a local hospital where he underwent emergency surgery to save his life. "Right before he went into heart surgery, he told his sister, 'Please take care of my family. I'm not going to make it,'" Alexandra said. Several surgeries later, Ricky made it out alive and is now in recovery at a Moreno Valley hospital. Doctors expect him to make a full recovery. "Life is too short. Let the people you know that you love them," Alexandra said. "Let them know you love them."

title: Elk Grove Bond Road closed after deadly train crash
description: A 46-year-old man died Thursday after being hit by a train in Elk Grove, police said.
content: A 46-year-old man died Thursday after being hit by a train in Elk Grove, police said.The crash happened near Elk Grove Florin Road and Bond Road.Elk Grove police said Bond Road was closed in both directions just east of Elk Grove Florin Road while officers investigated. The train stopped after the crash but was not blocking the roadway.Officers noted that both crossing arms were lowered and the warning lights were on when the person walked onto the tracks. The name of the person who died has not been released by authorities.Police said Bond Road reopened in both directions around 2:30 p.m.

title: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia confirms she never passed bar exam after saying she's a lawyer
description: The White House described Katie Zacharia as "uniquely qualified" to be the new press secretary.
content: Washington — White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said Thursday that she never passed the bar, although she's called herself a lawyer and President Trump has referred to her as an attorney.Zacharia made the comment in an interview with conservative commentator Jack Posobiec after the Wall Street Journal reported that she failed the bar exam in California in 2011 and did not pass the bar in any other U.S. state in which she's lived. Zacharia graduated from Pepperdine University's law school.Zacharia told Posobiec she took the bar exam in California but didn't pass, saying she was distracted by her plans to get married and move to China for her husband's work around the same time. She said she "didn't think much" of the results, and said she didn't need to pass the exam to do her work in China. Zacharia also said she never described herself as an "attorney at law," and said there's a "lot of misinformation around the fact that I labeled myself a lawyer." She said she consulted with multiple experts. "I was very careful how I executed this. I never came across as someone who was an attorney at law," Zacharia said. Earlier this week, as President Trump was departing for a trip to Alaska, when reporters asked her where she had passed the bar exam, Zacharia responded, "I went to China," sparking confusion about her law background. A White House official said Zacharia earned her juris doctor from Pepperdine, which the university confirmed to CBS News. The White House official said Zacharia then moved to China with her husband for his job at an American private equity firm, while she worked on international transaction law.
