Zacharia told CBS News in a statement Thursday she "practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials," although it's not clear which credentials she meant. Only Chinese nationals may take the bar exam in China. On Fox News in April, Zacharia said she "lived in Beijing as a corporate lawyer for three years."Zacharia's Instagram bio also says that she is a lawyer. On Truth Social, Mr. Trump called her "a distinguished Graduate of Pepperdine University, and the Pepperdine Caruso School of Law, an attorney."But whether it's true that she can say she's an attorney or lawyer is being disputed — and it's a question Zacharia has considered. She told The New York Times that as she was beginning to appear on cable news, she talked with Pepperdine's president about how she could describe herself. The Times said, "She said she was warned not to use the words 'attorney" or 'esquire,' but that 'lawyer' was OK."But CNN on Thursday reported that Zacharia shared at least 15 social media posts identifying herself as an "attorney" over the last two years. The White House said Zacharia is "uniquely qualified" for the White House press secretary role. "Katie is a fabulous and wonderful addition to the team," White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement to CBS News. "She is uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his Administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as Press Secretary."On Wednesday, the Campaign for Accountability, a liberal nonprofit watchdog, filed a complaint with the State Bar of California, questioning whether she had violated California law in referring to herself as a lawyer without having passed the bar. She had been living in California with her family until she became White House press secretary. The Campaign for Accountability pointed to California Business and Professions Code Section 6126, which says, "Any person advertising or holding himself or herself out as practicing or entitled to practice law or otherwise practicing law who is not an active licensee of the State Bar, or otherwise authorized pursuant to statute or court rule to practice law in this state at the time of doing so, is guilty of a misdemeanor." "Ms. Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer repeatedly to buttress her reputation and credibility as a television legal commentator and now as the White House spokesperson, yet it seems it was all a lie," Campaign for Accountability executive director Michelle Kuppersmith said in a statement. "In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn't puffery; it's a crime. The State Bar should investigate whether Ms. Zacharia has misled the public about her credentials and hold her accountable if she has."Cheung blasted the left-leaning ethics group."This group that filed the 'complaint' is a radical leftist-organization run by rabid numbskulls suffering from a severe case of Trump Derangement Syndrome," Cheung posted to X. "Nobody takes them seriously because they are deranged low lifes."Nora Freeman Engstron, a law professor at Stanford Law School, said the language in California's law isn't ambiguous or unclear. "California law is crystal clear: You can't hold yourself out as a lawyer unless you're authorized to practice law," she told CBS News. "And the law doesn't just prohibit the unauthorized practice of law. It also prohibits the unauthorized pretense of being a lawyer.""California law doesn't just prohibit people from practicing law without a license," she added. "It also prohibits them from pretending they're entitled to practice law. You don't have to set foot in a courtroom or represent a single client to run afoul of the statute."

title: Maryland father and son accused of breeding, training dogs for dogfighting
description: A Maryland father and son have been indicted on federal charges for allegedly breeding, training and selling dogs for use in a dogfighting ring.
content: A Maryland father and son have been indicted on federal charges for allegedly breeding, training and selling dogs for use in a dogfighting ring.Theodore Lamont Stinson, 48, and his son, Theodore Lamont Stinson Jr., 25, both of Whiteford, face multiple charges, including conspiracy to engage in an animal fighting venture, according to the indictment.The charges also include buying, selling, delivering, possessing, training or transporting animals for participation in an animal fighting venture; using the mail or other interstate channels to promote or further an animal fighting venture; and interstate and foreign travel or transportation in aid of racketeering enterprises.According to the indictment, the father and son had been involved in buying, selling, breeding and training pit bull-type dogs for dogfighting since at least April 2016.The two allegedly operated a kennel called "KLK," which they used to advertise dogs for sale. They kept the animals on their property to sell, transport and breed dogs owned by them and their alleged co-conspirators.The indictment alleges that both men oversaw the dogs, with Stinson advising his son on their proper care.The father and son also allegedly arranged transportation for dogs involved in sales and breeding. Stinson often coordinated transportation for sales, while Stinson Jr. transported the dogs to their destinations, according to the indictment.44 dogs found during Harford County searchOn July 17, 2025, the Harford County Sheriff's Office and its Animal Control Unit executed search-and-seizure warrants at Stinson's residence.Investigators found 44 pit bull-type dogs, veterinary medications and supplies, a breeding stand, and a "spring pole/rope" accessory used to train and condition fighting dogs, according to the indictment. They also found paperwork related to dog sales and pedigrees.Potential prison sentencesIf convicted, Stinson and Stinson Jr. each face up to five years in federal prison for conspiracy to engage in an animal fighting venture and up to five years for buying, selling, delivering, possessing, training or transporting animals for participation in an animal fighting venture.

title: How do Flock cameras work? Former police captain questions criticism of Flock
description: A former Metro Detroit police captain is defending Flock cameras amid growing privacy concerns.
content: As controversy surrounding Flock license plate recognition cameras continues, a former Metro Detroit police captain says the technology is being misunderstood and that its crime-fighting benefits outweigh concerns about government surveillance.Mario Bastianelli, who spent 27 years in law enforcement and served as a captain with the Sterling Heights Police Department, says the cameras provide investigators with valuable information that can help solve crimes more quickly, particularly in departments with limited resources.Bastianelli, now chief administrative officer of Fortis Group, a Metro Detroit-based security solutions firm, says some of the public's concerns stem from a misunderstanding of how the technology works.How Flock cameras workFlock cameras are automated license plate readers that capture images of vehicles traveling on public roadways. The system records license plates and vehicle characteristics, allowing police departments to search for vehicles that may be connected to criminal investigations.Bastianelli explained that officers access the system via software with individual logins. Investigators can search for a specific license plate or use a general vehicle description to narrow down potential matches.For example, if a bank robbery suspect flees in a vehicle and witnesses provide only a description, investigators can search the database for vehicles matching that description.The system can also help police identify vehicles potentially involved in kidnappings, missing-person investigations and homicides."People have to understand it's an investigative tool," Bastianelli said. "It doesn't do facial recognition."He emphasized that identifying a vehicle does not automatically identify its driver or establish probable cause for an arrest."Just because there's a picture taken doesn't automatically equal probable cause for an arrest, and people need to understand that," Bastianelli said.Investigators must still corroborate the information, identify the person operating the vehicle and gather additional evidence.Privacy concerns and the potential for misuseDespite the potential benefits, Flock cameras have drawn criticism over concerns about government surveillance, data collection and the ability of police to track the movements of people who are not suspected of committing crimes.Critics question who can access the information, how long it is retained and whether officers could use the system for unauthorized purposes.Bastianelli acknowledges those concerns."I can understand the public's concern in regards to information that's being obtained about themselves," Bastianelli said.But he argues that the focus should be on how police departments use the information and whether adequate safeguards are in place."Just like any system, it could be abused and misused," Bastianelli said. "It's all about accountability. It's all about putting good policy in place."He said departments should establish clear policies, conduct regular audits and investigate allegations of improper use. Officers who misuse the technology should face appropriate consequences.Bastianelli also stressed the importance of transparency when problems occur.Comparing Flock cameras to existing police technologyBastianelli compared Flock cameras to Michigan's Law Enforcement Information Network, commonly known as LEIN, which police have used for years to access vehicle registration information and other law enforcement records.He said officers routinely check license plates through LEIN, and misuse of that system can result in disciplinary action, termination or criminal charges.While LEIN and Flock serve different functions, Bastianelli believes similar accountability measures should apply to both.He also questions what he sees as inconsistent public attitudes toward privacy.Bastianelli pointed to the amount of personal information collected through cellphones, internet searches and digital advertising.He said people routinely allow technology companies to collect information about their online activity, yet express strong objections to cameras photographing vehicles on public roads."That's way more concerning to me than the fact of cameras on a roadway that are taking pictures of cars that are traveling by," Bastianelli said.However, the comparison highlights an important distinction in the privacy debate: Unlike ordinary license plate checks, automated camera networks can create searchable records of vehicle sightings across multiple locations.That capability is central to concerns about how the technology could be used to reconstruct a person's movements over time.A valuable tool for smaller police departmentsBastianelli says one of the technology's biggest advantages is its ability to help smaller police departments investigate crimes without requiring additional personnel.Departments with limited staffing may not have the resources to dedicate multiple investigators to tracking down a suspect vehicle.Flock cameras, he said, can provide leads much more quickly."That is huge for small police departments that don't have a lot of resources," Bastianelli said.He believes the technology can be particularly valuable in time-sensitive investigations involving missing children, kidnappings and violent crimes.While acknowledging the potential for misuse, Bastianelli maintains that the benefits to public safety outweigh the risks when departments implement appropriate safeguards.He also urges residents to understand the technology before drawing conclusions or taking action against the cameras."Have proper information. Have facts in front of you before you make a knee-jerk, you know, decision and reaction, and go tearing down the Flock camera that's on your corner," Bastianelli said.For Bastianelli, the debate ultimately comes down to balancing public safety with privacy protections â and ensuring police departments remain accountable for how they use the information they collect.

title: Tombstone falls onto 6-year-old boy at Altadena cemetery
description: A 6-year-old was taken to the hospital after a tombstone pinned him down at an Altadena cemetery.
content: A tombstone at an Altadena cemetery toppled over and pinned a 6-year-old boy on Wednesday afternoon. Adonis Cordova, 6, is now walking on crutches after the scary ordeal. He said he was at the cemetery with his mom and family when he bent down to pick up his ball and the tombstone pinned him to the ground. "It fell on me and I felt a little scratch," he said. His mother Kaylyn Hampton said her son was scared when he couldn't get up. "He was actually pinned down, and I hear, 'Mom, I can't move.' The way he said it and the tone, I could hear the fear in him," she said. "His foot was blistered, and he was crying at the touch of it, and it was bleeding."Donte Fox, a family friend, said he tried to lift the tombstone off the kid's ankle and arm.The whole ordeal happened at Mountain View Cemetery, which released a statement."The monument has stood for approximately 100 years, and cemetery management is not aware of any prior incidents involving it," the cemetery wrote. "A full investigation is not yet complete, and the cause remains undetermined. Out of respect for the family and to ensure an accurate account, we will refrain from speculation until the circumstances are established."Cordova's family said they alerted cemetery staff immediately, but feel that they did not understand the severity of the situation."I understand situations happen, but I feel like the place should have taken more accountability or offered assistance to the family," Fox said. Cordova's family took him to the hospital, where he had X-rays that showed nothing appeared to be broken. While her son's ankle is still swollen and he's walking with crutches, Hampton shared her concerns that the headstones aren't being maintained properly. "He weighs 48 pounds and had some 100 pounds fall on him," she said.

title: Google data center clears site plan review by Van Buren Township Planning Commission
description: A proposed Google data center has taken another step forward, with the Van Buren Township Planning Commission voting to approve the final site plan.
content: A proposed Google data center in Wayne County, Michigan, took another step forward when the Van Buren Township Planning Commission voted on Wednesday to approve a final site plan for the campus, including a high-voltage switching station. Project Cannoli is a $2 billion data center investment that became public a few months ago. The 230-acre proposed data center is set to be located near Haggerty Road and Interstate 94. High-tech, data, and computer processing are permitted in the current zoning for the undeveloped property. The long-range campus plan calls for three data processing facilities, an office building and two network service buildings. "The project is designed to support the growing demand for secure, reliable digital infrastructure while delivering long-term fiscal benefits to the community with minimal operational impact," the developers previously said. "Project Cannoli is planned as a modern, low-impact facility that aligns with Township standards, prioritizes environmental stewardship, and contributes meaningfully to the local tax base." Wednesday's planning commission meeting included presentations from township staff and the developer, along with public comments. The commission voted on the site plan and on the switching station 5-1, with Commissioner Bernard Grant voting against both matters. "Saline tried to say no, and one month later, the courts built their data center for them. Van Buren was darn sure not going to let a courtroom decide what kind of building was built on our property," said Kevin McNamara, the Van Buren Township Supervisor. McNamara said he's visited many data centers across the country and thinks there's a real difference in how they're built. "The new ones, if you build them right, they can be very quiet. The ones that are marginal built, they are nightmares, and we're not going to have a nightmare one here," he said. McNamara said the township was able to negotiate the number of generators down from 150 to 20, secured updated cooling towers and implemented berms around the site that should make the building hard to see. "Without a drone you should not be able to see this, the access way is only off I-94 and you need to go down a windy drive you can't even look down the driveway we believe that this will be very low impact," he said. In March 2026, officials said that Google would be the company behind the project, which received a 5-2 site approval from the Van Buren Planning Commission in February. In the most recent step, the Wayne County commissioners overrode the Wayne County Executive's veto on tax incentives. That vote on Oct. 1 was 13-0, with two commissioners absent from the meeting. Van Buren Township officials previously approved $125 million in tax incentives for the project in May. Details made public about the project include what the developers called an "ultra-quiet fan package" for the dual-cell cooling towers, decorative security fencing where appropriate, and financial support for sidewalk construction along Haggerty Road. There will also be the creation of a Community Benefit Fund to help support senior services, low-income housing, and other needs in the county. The Michigan Public Service Commission also recently approved DTE's energy contract for the data center, with the condition that customers would not incur any costs associated with it. The Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes & Energy issued its joint wetlands permit on Aug. 19, township officials said. Reviews have also been conducted for the fire department and power line access.

title: Victim found shot to death in Plano alleyway, police say
description: The investigation remains ongoing.
content: Plano Police are investigating after officers said a person was shot and killed Tuesday evening.The department said officers responded to the 900 block of Middle Cove Drive around 5:30 p.m. for a reported shooting. They said they found the victim dead of a gunshot wound in an alleyway behind a home.Police said two 17-year-old suspects, Na'Treveon Deon Ward and Chauncey Kentrell Harris, have been arrested for capital murder. As of publication, the victim's identity is being withheld until the next of kin is notified.The investigation is ongoing.

title: Ousted general warned of years-long missile defense shortage before Iran war
description: Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George, later ousted by Defense Secretary Hegseth, said the shortage of missile defense munitions would extend into 2030.
content: Washington — In late December, two months before the U.S. war with Iran began, Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George warned that his service was critically short on missile defense munitions and that the shortage would last another five years, according to multiple U.S. officials familiar with the matter. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ousted George in April, as the Iran war was underway.George's risk analysis appeared in the Pentagon's Global Force Management Allocation Plan, a defense secretary-approved annual order determining where troops and weapons will be allocated across the globe, according to the U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News. He warned that the stockpile of Terminal High Altitude Area Defense batteries and Patriot missiles would continue to be strategically low until 2030. His assessment was written for the Defense Department's plan for fiscal year 2027 and before the outbreak of the U.S.-Israel-led war with Iran, now in its seventh month. U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News under condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly said his assessment stemmed from the transfer of Patriots to Ukraine after Russia's invasion in 2022, the expenditure of munitions to defend Israel, and the reduced capacity of the defense industrial base. CBS News is withholding the exact percentage figures conveyed by U.S. officials because of security concerns, and George declined to comment. U.S. officials say that while the U.S. possesses a significant stockpile of some offensive munitions, like the Joint Direct Attack Munition and Small Diameter Bombs, missile defense munitions used in Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD, batteries, and Patriot missile systems are at low strategic-risk levels. The THAAD system is one of the U.S. military's most advanced missile defense systems, designed to intercept and destroy incoming ballistic missiles during the final phase of their flight, either inside or just outside Earth's atmosphere. The Army has eight THAAD batteries. Each battery consists of 90 soldiers who operate six truck-mounted launchers, with each truck possessing eight launchers. A full battery controls 48 interceptors, according to a 2025 report from the nonpartisan Congressional Research Service. The Patriot air-defense system is designed to protect military installations, troops and other critical infrastructure from incoming ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as hostile aircraft. It can engage a broader range of aerial threats at lower altitudes than a THAAD battery, but when used together, they provide even more effective overlapping layers of defense against missile attacks. The Patriot munition at a critical low is the Patriot Advanced Capability-3, or PAC-3, a high-velocity surface-to-air interceptor designed to destroy incoming tactical ballistic missiles and cruise missiles by ramming into them. PAC-3s can also bring down enemy aircraft, according to U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News. "Those are the two Army munitions that would be most heavily used in a conflict with China," said Mark Cancian, a retired Marine colonel and CSIS Defense and Security senior adviser. "You're not gonna use that many Javelins, for example, because the amount of ground combat is going to be relatively limited, even artillery will be limited, but air defense — missile defense — that will be huge." An April estimate from the Center for Strategic and International Studies showed that it currently takes defense contractors four years and five months to complete delivery of new THAAD interceptor contracts. Patriot PAC-3 interceptor orders have an average delivery time of three and a half years. CSIS' estimate said that before the Iran war, the U.S. entered 2026 with roughly 2,300 or so Patriot interceptors and expended between 1,050 and 1,430 during the conflict, potentially consuming as much as 61% of its prewar inventory. Fewer than 500 replenishment munitions were expected to be delivered in fiscal year 2026. The stockpile for THAAD systems prior to the Iran war sat at around 355 interceptors, with the Iran war using between 190 to 290, or about 82% of its prewar inventory, according to CSIS. There were no expected deliveries for replenishment in fiscal year 2026. In the current fiscal year — 2027 — the U.S. has requested more than 800 THAADs. Two of the nation's largest defense contractors — Lockheed Martin and RTX, through its Raytheon business — are involved in manufacturing these systems and their key components. They've recently signed agreements aimed at accelerating production. In January, Lockheed Martin announced a plan to quadruple the production capacity of THAADs from 96 to 400 interceptors per year. While the war with Iran has caused missile defense munitions to be depleted at a much higher rate, decades of Pentagon spending decisions, a shrinking defense industrial base and successive military operations that consume weapons faster than manufacturers can replace them have contributed to the current shortages.One U.S. official told CBS News that even if the United States could avoid expending additional THAAD or Patriot munitions in Iran or in other conflicts, it would take until the midterm elections of the next presidential administration — 2030 — to replenish the stockpile to the already-low December 2025 levels. Contacted by CBS News, Pentagon chief spokesman Sean Parnell said, "Claims of U.S. munitions shortages are false. When the Fake News media irresponsibly amplifies these lies, the real-world consequences is clear: our enemies are emboldened to provide — or attack — American troops."He added that the U.S. still has "everything required to strike at the time and place of the President's choosing." "Across multiple combatant commands," Parnell said, "we have already executed successful operations while maintaining a deep, ready arsenal to defend our people and our interests."How munitions are used around the world The U.S. military is divided into 11 unified combatant commands, each responsible for either a region of the world or specialized military mission. For operations against Iran, U.S. Central Command, led by Navy Adm. Brad Cooper, is in charge. Each combatant command needs a certain number of troops and weapons. The Pentagon uses a framework known as Global Force Management to decide where American troops, their units and some of the military's most sought-after weapons are sent around the world. The Global Force Management Allocation Plan, or GFMAP, is at the center of the process, laying out which forces will be provided to combatant commanders, for what missions and for how long. The plan is typically organized around the federal fiscal year. Generally, the Pentagon enters a new fiscal year with an existing plan for many of the forces expected to deploy or remain deployed during the coming 12 to 24 months, rather than deciding from scratch each time a commander asks for troops or weapons. But the plan is not set in stone. Wars erupt, crises develop, missions end and commanders are faced with unanticipated events to address.For instance, the commander of U.S. European Command might want more Patriots in Poland at the same time that U.S. Central Command wants those same resources in Kuwait, while U.S. Indo-Pacific Command may also need the systems for contingencies involving China. There's a constant shuffling of troops and assets from one region to another — in one instance in April 2025, Adm. Samuel Paparo, the commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, told the Senate Armed Services Committee that the Army had transferred a Patriot battalion from his region to U.S. Central Command amid ongoing fighting with the Iranian-back Houthi rebels in Yemen. What led to the current weapons systems shortage?After the collapse of the Soviet Union, American military planners abandoned the assumption that the U.S. might need to fight a prolonged war against another superpower, explained Cancian. "After the Cold War, we planned on fighting short regional conflicts against countries like Iraq or North Korea. And for those countries we didn't need the large inventories that we had needed during the Cold War," Cancian said. "We needed much smaller inventories." He added: "We shrank the industrial base. There was the famous 'Last Supper' which was literally a dinner that the deputy defense secretary put on for the heads of the defense industry, and he told them there's not enough money to keep you all in business, so you're going to have to consolidate or move out of the business, which they did." The resulting mergers reduced the number of major aerospace and defense contractors from 51 to five, according to the CSIS analysis. Also, historically, the Pentagon's procurement decisions have reduced spending on ammunition and missiles to free up money for fighter jets, tanks and warships, even while acknowledging that those weapons are essential to war fighting. Cancian told CBS News that the consolidation of the defense industrial base shaped an industry that produces efficiently during peacetime but is not designed to surge production. "We squeezed all the surge out because it was seen as unnecessary. So, that's where we end up when the war in Ukraine begins," said Cancian. "And after six months or so, we realized that we just don't have enough munitions and equipment for a protracted conflict." Under the Biden administration, there was a renewed interest in building surge capabilities back into the defense industrial base but that would take time. As the war between Russia and Ukraine began in full, the U.S. transferred roughly 600 Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine. However, not all of those weapons came from American military stockpiles; some were manufactured through the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative or provided by European countries. Additionally, both Biden and Trump administrations used Patriot and THAAD missile interceptors to defend Israel against Iranian strikes. Six months before Gen. George's warning assessment, U.S. forces fired roughly 150 THAAD interceptors and almost 80 Patriot interceptors during the Twelve Day War. Cancian noted that the five-year timeline to bring Patriot and THAAD stockpiles just to the low pre-Iran war levels is based on the assumption that the production schedule stays on track — and that additional military operations do not further deplete the inventory.

title: Santa Ana wind event prompts Red Flag Warning for parts of Southern California as fire danger increases
description: Northeast to east winds could reach between 20 and 40 mph with gusts of 50 to 70 mph. The NWS says the strongest winds will likely occur Thursday afternoon through Friday afternoon.
content: A Red Flag Warning has been issued in Southern California after forecasters say a moderate to strong Santa Ana wind event is expected to increase critical fire danger through Saturday. The National Weather Service says the combination of hot temperatures and winds will create conditions that will cause a fire to spread if one ignites. The expected weather has prompted weather officials to issue a Red Flag Warning for most of Los Angeles and Ventura counties through 8 p.m. Saturday. A Red Flag Warning is typically issued when critical fire weather conditions are either occurring or will shortly. During a warning, weather officials urge residents to use extreme caution with anything that can spark a wildfire. Northeast to east winds could reach between 20 and 40 mph with gusts of 50 to 70 mph. The NWS says the strongest winds will likely occur Thursday afternoon through Friday afternoon. Winds will exhibit a typical pattern, which means they will start to ramp up a few hours before dawn and peak mid-morning before tapering off slightly in the afternoon and evening. The Santa Ana winds won't be the only thing impacting the region. Hot temperatures will ramp up as the week goes on.On Friday, temperatures in the valleys and along the coast will be in the upper 80s and 90s. There is also a chance that some areas could reach up to 100 degrees.

title: Judge finds Elon Musk, Kristi Noem engaged in premeditated campaign to smear ex-FEMA official
description: A federal magistrate judge said Elon Musk and former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem knowingly spread false information about Mary Comans, the former CFO of FEMA.
content: Washington — A federal judge on Tuesday found that billionaire Elon Musk and former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, as well as other senior Trump administration officials, engaged in a coordinated campaign to spread false information about a former FEMA official and impugn her integrity.U.S. Magistrate Judge William Fitzpatrick condemned the Trump administration for what he said was "outrageous" conduct targeting Mary Comans, who he said was "professionally targeted and personally attacked by government officials for no legitimate reason."Comans, a career civil servant, was most recently the chief financial officer at FEMA until she was fired in February 2025 without cause.While Comans was told that her firing was an exercise of the president's power to remove executive officials, the Department of Homeland Security published a press release that falsely accused her of "circumventing" agency leaders to make "egregious" payments to New York City for luxury hotels for undocumented migrants. The Trump administration also accused her of violating an executive order signed by President Trump on the first day of his second term that directed federal agencies to pause funding to nongovernmental organizations providing services to immigrants in the U.S. illegally.But the decision to continue payments to state and local governments, including two issued to New York City, was made by senior officials at DHS and FEMA, and was approved by employees with the Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE, the cost-cutting task force that was overseen by Musk, according to court records. Because of that approval, Comans was told to continue the payments to the state and local governments.Still, DHS and senior administration officials, including Noem, Musk and Corey Lewandowski, who served as a top aide to Noem, made a series of statements about Comans that they knew were false, the court found."These facts establish that high-ranking government officials, including then Secretary of DHS Kristi Noem and Elon Musk, engaged in a coordinated public relations campaign to impugn the personal and professional integrity of Ms. Comans," Fitzpatrick wrote. "For reasons unfathomable to this Court, officials chose to turn the power of the federal government against a singular employee with an impeccable record of public service."As part of its campaign targeting Comans, Musk, who served as a special government employee and oversaw DOGE, shared a photo of her on X and falsely accused Comans of engaging in "criminal action" by allegedly funneling millions of dollars to hotels in New York City. The court said Musk knew, or should've known, that his DOGE employees approved the payments. Fitzpatrick also said the social media post with Comans' photo and false characterization of her actions "was clearly intended to make her afraid." "Posting Ms. Comans' picture served no legitimate governmental interest and was little more than state sanctioned intimidation," Fitzpatrick wrote.The judge also said that Noem and Lewandowski provided false information to Laura Loomer, a far-right conspiracy theorist, about Comans with the expectation that she would disseminate it to her social media followers."Armed only with false statements, high-ranking government officials undertook a premeditated campaign to impugn the personal and professional integrity of Ms. Comans, a nonpartisan, career public servant," Fitzpatrick found. "Their intent was to disseminate false and derogatory information about Ms. Comans as widely as possible."The decision from Fitzpatrick stemmed from a name-clearing proceeding that was conducted after a federal judge ruled in July that Comans was fired without due process.Comans had filed a lawsuit in July 2025 that challenged her removal and argued that DHS and FEMA harmed her reputation by falsely accusing her of funneling millions of dollars to New York City for the hotels. The judge said all of the accusations leveled against Comans by Trump administration officials, including that she engaged in criminal activity, misspent federal funds and laundered "forbidden funding," were not true."The attacks against Ms. Comans were based entirely on false information, and many government officials knew the accusations were untrue at the time they were made," Fitzpatrick said. "With no regard for the truth and with no consideration for the personal and professional effect on Ms. Comans, government officials exploited their access to mass media outlets to broadcast false information."CBS News has reached out to DHS and to attorneys for Musk and Noem for comment.

title: Woman charged with DUI in fatal 2024 hit-and-run crash in Chicago's Rogers Park neighborhood
description: A woman has been charged with drunk driving in a fatal hit-and-run crash in 2024 in the Rogers Park neighborhood​ on the North Side of Chicago.
content: A woman has been charged with drunk driving in a fatal hit-and-run crash in 2024 in the Rogers Park neighborhood on the North Side of Chicago.Joscelyn Mercado, 20, of Streamwood has been charged with four counts of aggravated driving under the influence and one count of leaving the scene of a fatal accident.Cook County prosecutors said, on Aug. 17, 2024, Mercado was at a party with her cousin and friends, drinking and smoking marijuana, before leaving the party to meet up with other friends at Loyola BeachAfter stopping at a McDonald's, she ran multiple stop signs and hit several curbs before heading east on Howard Street, where she struck 67-year-old James Tillman Jr. as he was crossing the street in the 1900 block of West Howard Street, along the border between Chicago and Evanston.Prosecutors said Mercado did not stop, and dragged Tillman 5-7 feet before he was dislodged from under her pickup truck. Three people who were in the truck with Mercado had asked her to stop before the crash, and one of them posted a Snapchat story about it.Evanston police responded to the scene and Tillman was taken to the hospital, where he later was pronounced dead.Police POD cameras recorded Mercado's truck fleeing the scene and driving to Loyola Beach, where Chicago police found her in the driver's seat of the truck. Neither Mercado nor anyone in the truck had called 911 to report hitting Tillman.Prosecutors said blood and urine tests taken from Mercado were analyzed by the Illinois State Police, who determined her blood alcohol level at the time of the crash was between 0.108 and 0.164, over the legal limit for driving.DNA samples taken from the bumper of Mercado's truck matched to Tillman, and DNA from inside the vehicle matched to Mercado.However, Mercado was not charged until Wednesday. It was not immediately clear why Mercado was not charged until nearly two years after the crash.At her first court appearance on Thursday, a judge released Mercado on electronic monitoring, including a SCRAM device to monitor her alcohol levels. She also is prohibited from using alcohol, marijuana, or illegal drugs while awaiting trial.She is due back in court on Nov. 4.

title: Motorcyclist dies after crash on Kennedy Expressway, Illinois State Police say
description: A woman was killed in a motorcycle crash on the Kennedy Expressway on Wednesday afternoon.
content: A woman was killed in a motorcycle crash on the Kennedy Expressway on Wednesday afternoon. Illinois State Police said troopers responded to the crash just before 3 p.m. on southbound I-90 at Ohio Street. The motorcyclist was taken to an area hospital with injuries and was later pronounced dead. The victim has been identified as 29-year-old Kaitlin Wagner.State police did not say what led up to the crash. Multiple lanes on I-90 and the northbound Ohio feeder ramp were also shut down and have since reopened.Investigation into the crash remains ongoing.

title: Chicago police seek 3 who attacked CTA Red Line passenger, dragged them off train, sprayed their mouth with paint
description: Chicago police are looking for three people accused of a brutal attack at a CTA Red Line station in the Old Town neighborhood on the Near North Side.
content: Chicago police are looking for three people accused of a brutal attack at a CTA Red Line station in the Old Town neighborhood on the Near North Side.Police said, shortly after 2:30 p.m. on Oct. 9, the 65-year-old victim was beaten, dragged off a train at the Clark/Division stop, and spray-painted in the face and mouth.The attack was caught on surveillance cameras, and images released by police showed one of the three suspects had the numbers 5718 tattooed on the fingers of his left hand.Police asked anyone with information on the attack to contact detectives at 312-745-4477, or to submit an anonymous tip at CPDTIP.com and use reference #JK446326.

title: Man who stabbed Solano sheriff's K-9 sentenced to over 4 years in prison
description: A man convicted of stabbing a Solano County Sheriff's Office K-9 during a chase was sentenced to four years and eight months in state prison, prosecutors announced on Thursday.
content: A man convicted of stabbing a Solano County Sheriff's Office K-9 during a chase was sentenced to four years and eight months in state prison, prosecutors announced on Thursday.Back on Aug. 3, a jury found Harvey Harris guilty of personally inflicting serious injury on a police animal while armed with a knife and evading an officer with willful disregard, the Solano County District Attorney's Office said.The incident happened nearly four months prior, on April 7, when officials said Deputy Michael Ferrando spotted a vehicle traveling 25 miles per hour on Interstate 80 near Dixon Avenue.The deputy used his vehicle's PA system to call for the driver to speed up. When the driver did not comply, the deputy attempted to pull Harris over. Harris instead led deputies on a 35-minute chase before stopping just east of the Travis Boulevard exit in Fairfield.While stopped, Harris refused multiple orders to exit the vehicle, prompting Ferrando to deploy his K-9 partner, Ty.Moments after Ty entered Harris' vehicle, prosecutors said he began stabbing the K-9, resulting in a fracture and multiple stab wounds to the dog's neck.Ferrando and another deputy retrieved Ty from the vehicle, while Harris refused to drop the knife used in the stabbing. Officials said one of the deputies used a baton to knock the knife from Harris' grasp.Harris was then taken into custody.The district attorney's office said Ty survived and has since returned to work.

title: LAPD arrests 4-person graffiti crew, including a city employee, for alleged vandalism
description: Targeting high-profile locations, the crew allegedly racked up $175,000 in damage to commercial buildings and historic properties, using specialized climbing equipment and rappelling gear.
content: The Los Angeles Police Department arrested a four-person graffiti crew involved in an alleged "coordinated vandalism spree" targeting downtown LA and other locations throughout the region, LAPD Chief Jim McDonnell said during a Thursday news conference. "One aspect of this investigation that is especially disappointing to me, among those arrested, was a city employee," McDonnell said.Targeting high-profile locations, the crew allegedly racked up $175,000 in damage to commercial buildings and historic properties, using specialized climbing equipment and rappelling gear. According to prosecutors, the suspects used drones to record their vandalism, then profited from it. "To date, investigators have connected the suspects to acts of vandalism at 12 locations throughout our city, including 11 buildings in and around downtown Los Angeles and one location in the Mid-Wilshire area," McDonnell said. It took extensive investigative work to link the alleged suspects to the acts of vandalism, the chief said, with months of surveillance, search warrants, digital evidence, and social media analysis. The Department of Water and Power assisted in the investigation, McDonnell said, as one of its employees was a suspect and was subsequently arrested.Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman listed the variety of felony charges each of the four suspects face, including potentially years in prison.Javier Rezendez Rocha, 38, an LADWP employee, is charged with 12 felony counts of vandalism; Michael Ray Gonzales, 41, of Pico Rivera is charged with seven felony counts of vandalism; Francisco Rodriguez Aguilar, 37, of West Covina, and Richard Evan Ward II, 45, of Oceanside, are each charged with two felony counts of vandalism. "This isn't a bunch of kids that decided on some type of lark because they were bored one night to go ahead and grab some spray paint and tag some buildings," Hochman said. " No, these are grown men, adults who decided that they were going to profit over the desecration of buildings by their graffiti."

title: White House prepares plans to use weapon dubbed "mother of all bombs" on Iran, sources say
description: The White House and Pentagon have prepared plans to use a Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb to hit military sites in Iran if ordered by President Trump, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.
content: The White House and Pentagon have prepared plans to use a Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb to hit military sites in Iran if ordered by President Trump, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.A Pentagon official told CBS News: "The Department of War plans for a wide range of operational scenarios to execute Presidential and Secretary level direction and to ensure mission success in any operational environment."A White House spokesperson said: "We do not comment on sensitive military plans that may or may not exist. President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon."Last week, Mr. Trump said the U.S. would not attack Iran before the midterm elections. He also touted "productive conversations" with Iran, though he did not provide specifics.CNN first reported Thursday on the plans to use the Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, or MOAB, on Iran.Mr. Trump set a precedent for using the MOAB, also known as the "mother of all bombs," when it was used in 2017 to attack an Islamic State cave complex in Afghanistan. The bomb is the largest U.S. non-nuclear weapon, weighing upwards of 30,000 pounds at a cost of $170,000 per unit.Iran and the United States have largely held off on striking each other in recent weeks, after several months of on-and-off U.S. strikes on Iranian targets. But Mr. Trump has suggested the war could ramp back up if he is not able to secure a satisfactory agreement with the Iranian government.In a speech to the United Nations General Assembly last month, the president said he has a "big decision to make" on whether to strike a deal with Iran or "annihilate the Islamic Republic."Meanwhile, the U.S. is enforcing a blockade on Iranian ports and seeking to keep oil flowing through the Strait of Hormuz. But Iran has continued to threaten and strike ships in the key waterway, keeping global oil prices high.Over the summer, many of the U.S. strikes against Iran were concentrated on the country's conventional military capabilities near the Strait of Hormuz, including air defense sites and missile and drone storage, according to U.S. Central Command.Mr. Trump has also floated strikes on Iranian nuclear sites, including Pickaxe Mountain, a deeply buried site that analysts believe could be part of Iran's nuclear program.

title: Dublin home extensively damaged in early-morning fire
description: Two people and their dog were displaced from their Dublin home early Thurday when a fire in the garage spread to a large portion of the house, authorities said.
content: Two people and their dog were displaced from their Dublin home early Thurday when a fire in the garage spread to a large portion of the house, authorities said.The Alameda County Fire Department said in a social media post that crews responded at about 12:30 a.m. to the fire at a two-story house on Shady Creek Road, west of Dougherty Road and north of Alamo Creek Park.The fire, which appeared to have been started in the garage, caused extensive damage to the first floor and extended into the attic, the fire department said. The Livermore-Pleasanton Fire Department also responded to the fire, and firefighters prevented the fire from spreading to neighboring homes.Images of the fire showed a vehicle in the driveway that also went up in flames.Both adult residents of the home were alerted to the fire when their dog began barking, helping wake them up, the fire department said.No injuries were reported, and there was no word on the cause of the fire.

title: Georgia police chief facing felony charge for taking handgun meant for raffle, GBI says
description: A Georgia police chief is facing multiple charges after the GBI says he kept a gun donated to his station that was meant for a raffle.
content: The Georgia Bureau of Investigation has arrested one of the state's police chiefs accused of taking a donated handgun meant for a raffle.Quitman Police Chief Lawrence McGee, 44, is charged with one count of felony theft by taking and one count of violation of his oath of office, officials said.According to the GBI, the Brooks County Sheriff's Office asked the agency to investigate an alleged theft involving McGee of Feb. 3, 2026. Investigators say the Quitman Police Department received a donated handgun for a raffle during a regional traffic meeting, but McGee kept the gun for himself instead.GBI agents arrested McGee on Wednesday and booked him into the Brooks County Jail. An arrest warrant was issued for McGee following the return of an indictment by a Brooks County Grand Jury. McGee was arrested on October 14, 2026, and booked into the Brooks County Jail. He has since been released on bond.If you have any information that could help investigators, call the GBI's regional office in Thomasville at 229-225-4090 or the GBI Tipline at 800-597-8477.

title: City says River North high-rise with crumbling balconies is safe, for now; owner ordered to provide repair timeline
description: The Chicago Department of Buildings says a River North high-rise with crumbling balconies is safe, for now.
content: The Chicago Department of Buildings says a River North high-rise with crumbling balconies is safe, for now.Residents of 10 E. Ontario are concerned that chunks of concrete have been breaking off of their balconies for months. Balconies have visible exposed metal, some of which are rusted, which poses even more danger during winter, when temperature changes could cause the rust to expand and break loose even more concrete, experts said. The city said the building's owner and managers submitted a critical examination/ongoing inspection report which classified the façade as "Safe with a Repair and Maintenance Program." It also identified what repairs are needed. The city said the engineer reported no immediately unsafe or immediately hazardous conditions, there are temporary supports in place "at certain balcony railing locations."The city is now requiring the owners to provide a documented repair schedule for the balcony concrete, and engineer confirmation that the temporary supports will be effective until permanent repairs are made.

title: Florida attorney general sues Discord, alleging platform fails to protect minors from predators
description: The lawsuit cites eight incidents since 2022 in which adults sexually exploited minors through the platform, and Discord has not yet responded.
content: Attorney General James Uthmeier is bringing plenty of strife to Discord, the messaging and gaming platform.On Thursday, he filed a lawsuit against the online giant, which had 90 million active daily users as of 2025, according to its website, claiming the platform doesn't do enough to protect minors from sexual predators."Discord was marketing itself as a safe play, all fun and games. Indeed, it became a playground for young people," Uthmeier told reporters at an event in Tampa. "Unfortunately, today it is a playground for some of the most evil, heinous offenders." The lawsuit was filed in the 20th Judicial Circuit, which covers Charlotte, Collier, Glades, Hendry and Lee counties.In March, Uthmeier's office said it would investigate Discord and issued a subpoena seeking information from the company on marketing, age verification, content moderation, and parental control features.Discord did not immediately return an email seeking comment Thursday. On its website, the company says it has a "zero tolerance" policy towards child sexual abuse material and those who attempt to sexually groom users. Discord doesn't allow children under 13 to have an account, but it also doesn't verify users' ages."It's easy to talk anonymously," Uthmeier said. "Adults can get in with little to no age verification checks. Adults were able to pretend to be kids, prey upon kids, and unfortunately in too many cases, physically and sexually abuse kids." The lawsuit begins by listing eight incidents where an adult sexually exploited a minor through the Discord platform, all involving a Florida perpetrator or victim. All occurred between 2022 and 2026.It also notes that, while Discord has announced steps in recent weeks to improve safety for minors, those steps are "insufficient.""That late-breaking and insufficient announcement cannot undo the harm already caused in violation of Florida law; nor will it fully remedy the problem going forward," the lawsuit states.The lawsuit claims Discord violated Florida's Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act by marketing its platform as safe for minors, processing personal information of children, leading to substantial harm or privacy risks, and creating a public nuisance through its "unreasonable and unlawful conduct" that jeopardized the health and safety of children.Furthermore, the lawsuit asks the court to order Discord to stop marketing itself as safe without real age verification processes, to stop collecting data from children without parental consent, to impose $10,000 fines per violation of the Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act, and to impose $50,000 to $150,000 per every instance where Discord failed to protect children in online spaces."We need to send a message to Discord and all the other companies out there: Change your ways. Protect our kids," Uthmeier said. "Sure, make money and make profit, but do not choose profit over public safety. If you do that, we are going to make you pay a lot, and we are going to hold you accountable."

title: Ex-FBI agent sentenced in Detroit for defrauding investors in forex scheme
description: A former FBI agent was sentenced to almost 6 years in federal prison after having pleaded guilty to defrauding multiple investors, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Michigan said.
content: A former FBI agent was sentenced to almost 6 years in federal prison after having pleaded guilty to defrauding multiple investors, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Michigan said. Jeffrey Royer was an FBI agent from 1996 to 2001 and defrauded investors by falsely representing how their funds would be used and fabricating documents about their investments' performance, according to the district attorney's office.Royer told investors that their funds would be used for foreign currency (forex) and commodity futures trading, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office.Royer instead diverted some of the collected funds to personal expenses, made false assurances to investors that their funds were protected from losses and fabricated earnings statements showing significant gains when investors were losing money, the U.S. Attorney's Office says.Royer was ordered to pay restitution of $575,999.58 to his victims and to serve three years on supervised release after he completes his prison term.Royer had previously served a federal sentence that ended in 2012 for racketeering conspiracy, securities fraud conspiracy, securities fraud, obstruction of justice and witness tampering. "Once a respected member of law enforcement, Jeffrey Royer now stands as a repeat fraudster who abandoned every principle that badge was supposed to represent," said United States Attorney Jerome F. Gorgon, Jr. "Fraudsters like Royer abuse the trust others place in them and the positions they held. Abuse of the public trust will not be tolerated." "By choosing fraud over the oath he once took, Royer betrayed both the public and the law enforcement community," said Jennifer Runyan, special agent in charge of the FBI Detroit Field Office. "The sentence imposed today sends a clear message that misconduct, particularly by those who once held positions of trust, will be met with decisive action." The FBI investigated the case.

title: Popular Helen restaurant seriously damaged by fire; cause of blaze under investigation
description: A popular Helen, Georgia, restaurant is picking up the pieces after a fire severely damaged its building overnight.
content: Firefighters are investigating the cause of a blaze that damaged a Helen restaurant on Thursday morning.Officials say the fire broke out at Helen's Cowboys and Angels restaurant on Chattahoochee Strasse.According to authorities, Helen firefighters were returning to their station after another call when they spotted smoke and traced it to the restaurant, which had flames coming through its roof.The restaurant shared photos on Facebook of the building in flames and the damage caused by the fire."Tonight, we got knocked down! Tomorrow, we start building it back better, stronger, and bigger than ever before," owners Chris and Lauren Williams wrote. "Words can't begin to express the gratitude for the quick action of Helen Fire Department, Helen EMS, and Helen Police Department!" The Williams said that the rebuilding process will start quickly and that all scheduled catering events will still be honored.No injuries were reported in connection with the fire.The cause of the fire remains under investigation at this time.

title: Revitalization without gentrification in Southside Fort Worth: Hemphill No Se Vende
description: Hemphill No Se Vende in Southside Fort Worth advocates for a community and teaches others how to use their voice.
content: There are three words that can describe the mission of Hemphill No Se Vende: "Revitalization without gentrification." Hemphill No Se Vende is the Spanish saying for Hemphill is not for sale. It's a "coalition of community members working to defend the Southside from gentrification and displacement." Hemphill Street runs from West Lancaster Ave to SW Loop 820 in the Southside of Fort Worth. Community advocates are working to ensure that residents who have lived there for decades know their rights and have their voices heard by the city amid proposed developments in the area. You can see the saying in the windows of many local businesses and even on a mural as you pass through the area. "You can't take over our community without our say," community advocate Ricardo Avitia said. "Neighbors and businesses who know each other are coming together as a community to defend ourselves against unwanted development that is not made for us. And it's also a stance that we're not going to be overrun, just because we're from a minority community."History lost to developmentAvitia considers the Near Southside and Fairmount areas to be "prime examples and case studies of gentrification in Fort Worth." Most of the people who lived there for decades are no longer in the area. "Although our property market values have gone up, the people who were once there are not able to enjoy the benefits of those who are, you know, generating market values, for themselves and their families. Because they were unaware of what revitalization reunions for minority communities are," said Avitia. Avitia and fellow community advocate Angie Blochowicz say that the point of reaching out and educating residents is that the new growth and changes are created for the current population to enjoy and not just be pushed out. "It's beautiful what they've done. But we want that to come without pushing our community out," said Blochowicz. "A lot of us grew up here. Our parents still live in these homes. We live in homes on the same street, up the street, in the same neighborhood as our parents. You know, multiple kids, multiple houses. And we want to be sure that our kids might have that opportunity to live there as well when they get older." "I have memories from the Berry Theater, although it was vacant for many years. Decades," said Avitia. "You know, I had a story there... But those spaces, you know, our history is gone. It's erased."Community conversations and educationAvitia and Blochowicz engage in community conversations and build relationships. This includes workshops, meetings and connecting with people where they are. "Along with being informed about the zoning, there's so many things that are involved that usually, as working-class communities, we don't have time to invest in those other things because it doesn't have to do with me feeding my family or putting gas in my car, putting food on the table, you know," said Avitia. That's why Hemphill No Se Vende does their outreach on social media platforms, where they stream and post information that their community needs to know at the time that they do have. "A lot of these meetings are during the day, during times that our communities are driving home, are still at work," said Blochowicz. "And so we're really working with... the media movement... we can post, we can live it." Blochowicz also hosts programs at The Forkyard. A space for education, conversation and sharing culture. When it comes to conversations with the younger generations, Avitia believes that reframing the mindset of "leaving the hood" is an important distinction. "It's okay to be proud of where you come from," he said. "A lot of times we grew up wanting to leave the hood, not understanding that the hood is where it's at. Otherwise, so many people wouldn't want to be here, right? And I think that's important to, communicate that we can have nice things here in the hood."No Se VendeOne of the first efforts Hemphill No Se Vende is known for, is stopping rezoning on Hemphill Street. Blochowicz said, "A lot of people got a bad taste in their mouth and, not understanding why it was stopped, only thinking and seeing it as, 'Oh, they stopped progress.' And that's not how we see it, and that's not how the community saw it." "We give information, whether it's what we personally agree with or not. We are big on making sure that they have all the facts so that they can decide for themselves," she said in regards to the criticism. "We're growing, and we're learning, and we just want everyone on the Hemphill corridor to work together towards the same goal. And that's the point we're at with the Hemp Corridor Development Collaborative," she said. "Because we're not anti-development by no means," said Avitia. "We're pro community, pro positive development. Things are going to help our community feel safer." "We don't want to have to come back to visit. We want to be like, 'hey, this is how it happened. This is how it's done," he said. "We want to know our history, and we want to live that legacy so that everybody always knows, hey, no se vende."

title: LACoFD battles brushfire in the San Gabriel Valley, forward progress stopped
description: The blaze was reported around 1:09 p.m. in the area of N. San Gabriel Canyon Road and N. Ranch Road.
content: Crews with the Los Angeles County Fire Department are battling a roughly 50-acre brush fire in Azusa, known as the Peak Fire, with 31% contained. The blaze was reported around 1:09 p.m. in the area of N. San Gabriel Canyon Road and N. Ranch Road. Around 3:38 p.m., LACoFD said forward progress had stopped, Aerial footage showed water-dropping aircraft at the scene, with crews mobilizing in the adjacent neighborhood to enforce evacuation.An evacuation center for people impacted by the Peak Fire has been established at the Memorial Park Recreation Center at 340 N. Orange Place in Azusa. The blaze comes as a Red Flag Warning has been issued in Southern California. title: Woman and dog killed in shooting inside Jackson apartment, suspect charged with multiple felonies
description: A woman and a dog are dead after an early morning shooting on Oct. 14 at the Kennedy Meadows apartment complex.
content: A woman and a dog are dead after an early morning shooting on Oct. 14 at the Kennedy Meadows apartment complex, Jackson police said.Officers responded to the complex on New York Ranch Road after receiving a 911 call from a woman, who said "he's trying to shoot me" before the call disconnected. Sounds of shots being fired and a male voice speaking were audible in the background, police said.A Jackson police officer, along with personnel from other nearby law enforcement agencies, arrived at the scene and took cover after hearing sounds of suspected gunfire inside the apartment. Police said the suspect, identified as 39-year-old Michael Patrick O'Riley II, also called 911 and claimed there was an explosive device attached to the front door, and that he did not want to exit the residence. Following a brief standoff, O'Riley was convinced by a family member over the phone to surrender peacefully. Officers then went inside the apartment and discovered a woman, identified by officials as Kylene Douglas, who had been shot multiple times inside the primary bedroom. Despite efforts to save her life, Douglas ended up dying from her injuries. A dog that had also been shot was discovered dead inside the same room. O'Riley has been charged with multiple felonies, including premeditated murder, cruelty to an animal, and violating a domestic violence court order. Both O'Riley and Douglas were subject to court orders for peaceful contact with each other, the Amador County District Attorney's Office said.

title: Fort Lauderdale to consider tougher late-night rules as it cracks down on underage drinking
description: Police and fire rescue chiefs cite underage drinking, fights, and safety risks, and the mayor says commissioners will consider tougher late-night rules next week.
content: Fort Lauderdale announced it is cracking down on crime and underage drinking in the Himmarshee entertainment district, a popular area of bars and clubs just west of downtown."To the young people here, specifically to underage drinkers. You have been warned," Police Chief William Schultz said.Barricades now line the streets, and a light tower is in place."We are seeing concerning activity in the area, including underage drinking, fights, disorderly conduct, and large gatherings that create safety risks for businesses, residents, and visitors," Schultz said.Fire Rescue Chief Stephen Gollan said his department is seeing a significant increase in overnight calls."We're seeing a large uptick in call volume on the fire rescue side between 12 a.m. and 4 a.m., and the majority of those are pass-outs," Gollan said. About 30% of those calls involve people ages 18 to 24, he said.The city is adding patrols, including K-9 Units, mounted units, the Florida Highway Patrol, and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. Officers will closely watch bars and bartenders who serve underage patrons, and monitor overcrowding and parking-lot parties.Micah Harris, bar manager at Original Fat Cats in Himmarshee, supports the plan. He said late-night crowds have become more lawless."I think it's a fantastic idea; I think that it needs to be done. Certain businesses might be opening the door to these problems, and we're not one of them," Harris said."I would think that the kind of business that we want wouldn't be deterred by police presence, because they're not here to do anything wrong," Harris said.The announcement follows a number of shootings in the district, including one last December that sent five people to the hospital. The city banned open containers and outdoor drinking in all entertainment districts in January. According to FLPD, between Jan. 2026 and Oct. 2026, the department has made 124 arrests in the Himmarshee Entertainment DistriMayor Dean Trantalis said the City Commission is exploring more restrictions."Next week we will consider ordinance changes that would increase fines for alcohol-related violations and establish new requirements for businesses seeking to operate late at night. Those requirements would address security, alcohol safety, training, and the maintenance of areas surrounding their establishments," Trantalis said.City leaders said they will meet with business owners in the district and send notices to Broward County schools asking administrators to talk to students about the dangers of underage drinking.

title: Propositions 134 & 135 focus on sports and surgeries for transgender kids
description: On Nov. 3, Colorado voters will decide on sports and surgeries for transgender teens.
content: Editor's note: This summer, the American Medical Association's House of Delegates approved a new policy at its annual meeting that says the organization supports pediatric medical transition, including surgical interventions.Colorado has a reputation for being a trans-friendly state. Our laws, which outlaw discrimination based on gender identity, make it easy for people to change their gender on birth certificates and drivers' licenses, and require non-gender bathrooms in public buildings.But proponents of Propositions 134 and 135 say some of Colorado's laws go too far.A recent study by the State Legislative Council found there are about 56,000 transgender and nonbinary identifying individuals in Colorado, about 25-percent of whom are under the age of 18. It is those minors who would be impacted by Props 134 and 135.Since 2019, state lawmakers have passed 10 laws regarding transgender and nonbinary individuals, including a law in 2021 that gave them protected class status under the state's Anti-discrimination Act. That led many public schools to adopt new policies that, among other things, allow kids to use the restrooms, locker rooms, and dorms of the gender they identify with, and play on sports teams that correspond to their gender identity.Proposition 134 would change that. It would require all public schools - kindergarten through college - to designate sports teams as male-only and female-only and adopt policies that require students to play on the teams that align with their biological sex.The state education commissioner would enforce the law, which mirrors a new federal policy being challenged in the courts.Opponents say Prop 134 takes decision making away from parents and could lead to invasive exams to verify a kid's gender. They say the measure shames and isolates transgender students. Proponents say students who want to play sports are currently required to turn in forms signed by a doctor. Those forms, they say, can verify their gender.They say it's unfair for biological males to take roster spots, awards, and scholarships from girls and, they say, it's unsafe for them to play on girls' teams due to their strength and stature.Proposition 135 would ban certain surgeries for transgender kids.Kids under 18 years old could no longer undergo surgeries that alter biological sex characteristics if the surgeries are in response to their gender identity.It also bans the government and private insurance companies from paying for the surgeries.The Colorado Department of Health Care Policy and Financing, which administers Medicaid, says it spent $2.7 million on gender affirming care for kids between 2023 and 2025. It didn't have a breakdown of how much of that went to cover surgeries.Opponents say Proposition 135 - like Prop 134 - would take decision-making away from parents as well as doctors. They say it could lead to insurers refusing coverage for other gender affirming care and even prevent surgeries for non-transgender kids who have features different from their biological sex like boys with large breasts.Supporters note the measure makes exceptions for circumcisions, "medically verifiable disorders of sex development", and "acquired physical or chemical abnormalities". But it's unclear what disorders and abnormalities qualify.Treatments like hormone therapy and puberty-blocking drugs are exempt. Supporters say sex change operations shouldn't happen until kids have the maturity to make decisions that will impact them the rest of their lives.The American Society of Plastic Surgeons recommends waiting until age 19 for sex change operations.The Academy of Pediatrics says decisions about gender affirming care should be made by patients and physicians, not government mandates.Twenty-seven other states have laws in place similar to Propositions 134 and 135.The measures are statutory, not constitutional, so it takes a simple majority to pass them, and state lawmakers can change or repeal them.

title: Friday NEXT Weather Alert: Possible strong storms, damaging winds before weekend cold front
description: A NEXT Weather Alert is in effect for Friday in the Philadelphia area as strong thunderstorms with damaging wind gusts are possible ahead of a cold front.
content: A slightly enhanced severe weather threat across the Philadelphia region is developing ahead of a strong cold front. Scattered thunderstorms could produce damaging wind gusts, particularly Friday afternoon and evening.The exact timing and extent of the threat are still being refined.TODAY: Mostly sunny early, with increasing clouds this afternoon. Cooler and much less humid. High 66.TONIGHT: Mostly cloudy, with showers developing overnight, especially after midnight. Low 57.FRIDAY (NEXT WEATHER ALERT DAY): A few morning showers, then warmer and more humid with scattered thunderstorms possible later in the day. Some storms could be strong to severe, with damaging winds the primary concern. High near 80.NEXT big weather changesFriday is now a NEXT Weather Alert Day as the severe weather threat has increased. A powerful upper-level trough digging into the Northeast will drive a strong cold front across our region, with a slight risk (Level 2 out of 5) for severe thunderstorms across portions of eastern Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Delaware.The main concern is damaging wind gusts, but the latest outlook also indicates a marginal possibility of a brief tornado, particularly near the Delaware River Valley and Delmarva. Not everyone will see a severe storm, but the combination of increasing instability and strong wind shear makes this a threat worth taking seriously.Friday may start with showers before we get a break in the rain around midday. Southwest winds will bring warmer, more humid air into the region, pushing temperatures into the upper 70s and possibly near 80 degrees. That warmth and moisture will help fuel thunderstorms as the cold front approaches, with the greatest severe weather concern Friday afternoon into early evening, roughly 4-8 p.m.A line or broken line of storms could develop, producing locally damaging winds and potentially affecting the evening commute, high school football games and other outdoor plans.The wind will remain a concern even after the thunderstorms move out. As the front pushes offshore Friday evening, colder air will rush into the region on gusty northwest winds, with gusts of 30+ mph possible overnight into Saturday morning. That could bring down some smaller tree limbs or unsecured outdoor decorations, even outside any thunderstorms. At the Shore, conditions will become especially rough Friday night into Saturday, with strong winds and hazardous boating conditions.The weekend brings a dramatic return to chilly October weather. Saturday will be mostly sunny but blustery, with highs only in the mid-50s and northwest winds making it feel even colder. Sunday looks sunnier and less windy, with highs near 60 degrees, making it the more comfortable day for fall festivals, pumpkin picking and outdoor sports. We're also watching the potential for widespread frost and some freezing temperatures in colder suburbs Saturday night into Sunday morning, with lows falling into the 30s. Temperatures gradually moderate early next week, returning to the 60s Monday and Tuesday.The bottom line: Friday's NEXT Weather Alert Day brings a heightened threat for damaging thunderstorms, followed by strong winds and a dramatic weekend cooldown.Philadelphia 7-day forecast:Thursday: Showers south. High 68, Low 58Friday: Storms, wind. High 79, Low 61Saturday: Windy, colder. High 55, Low 49Sunday: Frosty start. High 60, Low 39Monday: Mostly sunny. High 66, Low 42Tuesday: Partly cloudy. High 70, Low 48Wednesday: Partly cloudy. High 70, Low 50NEXT Weather RadarsHourly ForecastGet the latest weather info on the CBS News Philadelphia app.

title: More workers are skipping medical and dental care over money worries, survey finds
description: Roughly a third of employees said they put off or skipped medical or dental care in the past year because of financial concerns, a new survey found.
content: Rising financial strains on American workers are forcing them to make painful trade-offs, such as skipping medical care, to make ends meet, new research shows. Financial security among U.S. employees dropped from 46% to 36% in 2026, its lowest level in seven years, according to a survey of 6,000 U.S. employees by benefits company Willis Towers Watson (WTW).While workers report feeling better physically and say their social connections have improved, their sense of well-being has moved in the opposite direction regarding money matters, the firm said.Barriers to healthcareFinancial pressures are also changing employees' attitudes toward seeking healthcare, shaping their views on retirement and affecting their performance at work, the survey found. Across all age groups, about one-third of employees say they put off or skipped a medical or dental appointment in the past year because of concerns over cost, and despite having health insurance, respondents told WTW. "They feel the cost of healthcare is huge and are facing high deductibles and high out-of-pocket costs," Courtney Stubblefield, a WTW health and benefits practice leader, told CBS News. "Those kinds of features are becoming barriers to them getting the care they need." Among different age groups, employees in their 40s reported feeling the least financially secure, according to the survey. Just 30% of workers in their 40s reported feeling financially secure, compared to half of workers 60 and over. More than 40% of people in their 40s said they delayed or skipped receiving medical care over money worries — the highest share among all age groups. Mid-career workers often balance multiple responsibilities, including caring for both children and aging parents, Stubblefield said."These people are more likely to have kids and family healthcare coverage, so it costs more," she said. "They're also part of what we call the sandwich generation, so they have kids in school or approaching college and are also caring for elderly parents. They have peak levels of obligation in that decade." Fading retirement dreamsRoughly two in three employees expect to be worse off in retirement than their parents' generation, citing healthcare costs as a barrier to saving for retirement, respondents told WTW.Separate research from Prudential Financial recently found that more than six in 10 retirees with at least $500,000 in investable assets do not feel comfortable spending money for enjoyment. Many cite inflation, the rising cost of living, and healthcare costs as barriers to spending on entertainment in retirement.Many older Americans are doing comparatively better than younger people. The 18 million households headed by someone 75 or older have the highest median net worth of any age group nationwide, according to Federal Reserve data. Americans in that demographic had a median net worth of $504,000 in 2025.Between 2022 and 2025, households headed by 65- to 74-year-olds saw their wealth increase by 37%, the Fed concluded.

title: Chicago-area man arrested after attempting to meet up with 15-year-old at Livonia park
