description: Court records say the person he had been messaging since Sept. 23 was an undercover officer. The man now faces a federal charge of travel with intent to engage in illicit sexual conduct.
content: A man who told an undercover officer he does maintenance work at a Chicago-area high school was arrested Monday at a Livonia, Michigan, park where he planned to meet someone he believed was a 15-year-old boy for sexual activity, according to federal court records.Christopher Thomas Mertens, 56, faces a federal charge of travel with intent to engage in illicit sexual conduct, according to a criminal complaint filed Tuesday in U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan.The person he had been messaging was an undercover officer with the Livonia Police Department who is assigned to the FBI's Southeast Michigan Trafficking and Exploitation Crimes Task Force, the complaint says.The officer was running an account on Taimi, a dating app, with the persona of a teenage boy as part of the Livonia Undercover Resistance to Exploitation Unit, known as LURE.On Sept. 23, the officer received a message on the app from a profile depicting a middle-aged man. The officer suggested moving the conversation to WhatsApp. During one of the early conversations, the officer said they were 15.Over the next few days, the two had numerous sexually explicit conversations, according to the affidavit. Mertens sent several explicit photos of himself and said he did maintenance work for a high school, the affidavit says.He said he lived and worked in the Chicago area but also had a home in Michigan, and he suggested they meet Oct. 12 because he would have the day off for Columbus Day.By then, the officer had gathered enough information to tentatively identify him and found a 2008 Ford Escape registered to his name in Michigan. Court records say the Flock license plate camera system showed the vehicle was often in the Chicago area.The two agreed to meet at Beverly Park, a neighborhood park on Hubbard Street in Livonia, and walk from there to the home of the teenager the officer was portraying, since the parents would be at work.On Monday, according to the complaint, officers used the Flock cameras to confirm the vehicle was in Chicago, and at about 7 a.m. tracked it eastbound on Interstate 94 near Gary, Indiana. Mertens then messaged that he would be at the meeting spot about 10:30 a.m. Livonia detectives set up surveillance at the park that morning and watched him arrive.He was taken into custody after he got out of his vehicle, the complaint says.

title: School bus driver fired after arrest for alleged possession of child pornography, Melissa ISD says
description: Melissa ISD fired Phillip Gates after learning of his arrest, the district said.
content: A now-former Melissa ISD bus driver was arrested this week in McKinney for alleged possession of child pornography, the district announced.According to a letter sent to parents from Melissa ISD police chief Chris Fontana, the district immediately fired Phillip Gates, 60, after learning of his arrest on Tuesday. "At this time, we have no information indicating a connection between this matter and Melissa ISD students," the letter said. "As a precaution, Melissa ISD is reviewing relevant information and is in close communication with local law enforcement to take any appropriate steps to support student safety."The district is urging any parents or students that have a concern to contact law enforcement or district administration.Court records show that Gates was arrested by the McKinney Police Department. McKinney PD has not released any information about the case or the circumstances of Gates' arrest. CBS News Texas has requested additional information from the department.Gates posted a $100,000 bond and was released from the Collin County Jail on Wednesday, records show.

title: Community mourns pilot among 6 dead in Wisconsin plane crash
description: The town of Woodville, Wisconsin, is mourning the loss of Ron Riek, a prominent businessman and pilot killed in a small plane crash Tuesday night near the Wisconsin Dells. Five of his passengers were also killed, including a child, according to the Sauk County Sheriff's Office.
content: The town of Woodville, Wisconsin, is mourning the loss of Ron Riek, a prominent businessman and pilot killed in a small plane crash Tuesday night near the Wisconsin Dells. Five of his passengers were also killed, including a child, according to the Sauk County Sheriff's Office.Riek owned a trucking company for over 30 years in Woodville. WCCO spoke with community members and found a common theme: he had a heart of gold.The crash occurred Tuesday night around 9:30 p.m., when the six-seat, single-engine Piper PA-46 he was piloting crashed about 10 miles southwest of the Wisconsin Dells.Authorities say Riek and his passengers were flying to Menominee from Kenosha, and the NTSB said Riek reported icing on the wings and needed to descend. Soon after air traffic controller approved the descent, communications were completely lost."Ron was a really outgoing guy. He would be very helpful with all his workers. Outside of work, he was just super nice," said Erin McMahon, who works at Woodville Cafe. "He'd go far and beyond for his workers."Several of the people WCCO spoke with Thursday said Riek was an experienced pilot, with safety always top of mind."To hear that he passed from flying, it's a shock," McMahon said.The NTSB says it will likely release a preliminary report within the next 30 days.

title: 9 fired FBI employees who worked on Trump documents case sue, alleging unlawful termination
description: Nine former FBI employees sued the bureau, saying they were unlawfully terminated for working on the investigation into President Trump's classified documents case.
content: Washington — Nine former FBI employees sued the bureau on Thursday, saying they were unlawfully terminated merely for working on former special counsel Jack Smith's investigation into President Trump's retention of classified records after his first term in the White House.The former special agents, intelligence analysts and staff operation specialists worked on counterintelligence investigations and were fired over the course of two days in February 2026 — just as the United States and Israel were set to begin military strikes against Iran.The nine plaintiffs represent the latest in a growing number of former FBI agents and other personnel who have filed lawsuits against the Justice Department and the bureau after they were abruptly terminated. Many of the fired employees worked on matters that displeased Mr. Trump and his allies.The plaintiffs "were unlawfully terminated not for any cause or any legitimate reason, but only to satisfy the President's personal vendetta," the lawsuit alleged."The firings did not follow any internal investigation or disciplinary process within the FBI, and Plaintiffs were not given any notice, a hearing, or an opportunity to appeal. Instead, Patel claimed to rely solely upon 'Article II' to support the firings," the suit said, referring to FBI Director Kash Patel and Article II of the Constitution, which lays out the president's executive powers.The 70-page lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia and names the FBI, Patel, Attorney General Todd Blanche and the Department of Justice as defendants. CBS News has reached out to the Justice Department and FBI for comment.FBI agents executed a search warrant at Mar-a-Lago in August 2022 and allegedly recovered more than 100 documents with classified markings. In 2023, Smith's office indicted Mr. Trump on more than three dozen charges related to his alleged retention of the records and efforts to obstruct the government's attempts to get them back. The charges were ultimately dismissed by the federal judge overseeing the case, who said Smith was unlawfully appointed special counsel. The Justice Department formally abandoned its appeal of the ruling after Mr. Trump won the 2024 election.Thursday's lawsuit cites public comments made by top Justice Department officials and the president directed toward the plaintiffs as evidence the firings were motivated by political animus. For example, Blanche, who was deputy attorney general when the employees were let go, stated that the administration had "cleaned house" at the FBI by firing employees associated with investigations involving the president.The lawsuit contains some new details about the circumstances surrounding the firings.In the case of counterintelligence section chief Jennifer Bacon, she learned she was being let go shortly after an agent named Miles Starr had requested access to the classified investigative files about Plasmic Echo, the codename given to the documents investigation.Starr, the lawsuit said, was a member of Kash Patel's Director's Advisory Team, a group staffed by agents from around the country who support his policy goals. He also was the lead case agent who testified in the since-dismissed indictment charging former FBI Director James Comey with lying to Congress. That testimony later was criticized by a federal magistrate judge, who accused the FBI of numerous missteps, including a failure to filter out potentially privileged materials.On Feb. 23, Starr emailed Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky to tell him that he urgently needed access to the Plasmic Echo case files, the lawsuit said. "Starr did not explain what he needed, but stated that he was on instructions from Patel to access the case file. Bacon granted him access to all Plasmic Echo files in the FBI's case management system, with the exception of one specific subfile. The files Starr had access to contained the names of all nine Plaintiffs," the lawsuit says.Less than 48 hours later, Bacon and the others were all fired.The lawsuit also suggested that the firings may have been an attempt to distract from negative press about Patel, who was spotted on Feb. 22 at the Olympic Games in Milan "chugging a beer and, in a display of wild immaturity and lack of personal control, flinging alcohol around the U.S. men's hockey team's locker room."A special agent in charge who was assigned to inform former special agent Zach Feldman he was being terminated even surmised that the firing might be "related to the news reports from earlier that day about Director Patel drinking alcohol at the Winter Olympics," the lawsuit said.The military strikes against Iran began on Feb. 28."This scandal proved politically perilous for Patel: he drew widespread criticism for his conduct, with numerous sources suggesting that his status with President Trump and position as Director of the FBI were in jeopardy as a result," the lawsuit said.On Feb. 25, Patel gave an interview to Reuters in which he disclosed that his phone records and those of White House chief of staff Susie Wiles were subpoenaed as part of Smith's investigations.Eight of the nine plaintiffs were fired the same day, and the ninth was fired the following day."With over a century of experience among them, these former FBI agents and analysts served our country with honor and distinction as they investigated leaks of national security and defense information, thwarted threats and attacks from our enemies, and responded to critical incidents like the Boston Marathon bombing," attorneys Margaret Donovan, Abbe Lowell and Rebecca Tinio said in a joint statement."In return for their service, they were fired because they did their jobs, as they always did, to follow the facts and the law without bias or favor."

title: ASU parts ways with hockey coach as player who collapsed at workout remains hospitalized
description: Matthew Mayich, a 21-year-old sophomore, collapsed during an Aug. 20 workout and had to be put on life support.
content: Arizona State University announced Thursday that it has reached a "mutual agreement to part ways" with hockey coach Greg Powers, nearly two months after 21-year-old sophomore Matthew Mayich collapsed during a workout and had to be put on life support."The university and Sun Devil Athletics are grateful for Coach Powers' work to establish ASU as a Division I hockey program and for his service over the past nearly two decades," ASU said in a statement.The school said it has hired Dave Hakstol as head hockey coach. Hakstol had previously been an assistant coach for the Colorado Avalanche in the NHL.Powers was placed on paid administrative leave late last month, after the parents of Mayich and several teammates demanded that the staff responsible for the workout that led to Mayich's collapse be removed while an investigation is conducted.Mayich was participating in an outdoor workout on Aug. 20 when he suffered heatstroke, according to Robert Carey, an attorney for his family. Carey has said Mayich was placed on life support and is "unlikely to recover," according to CBS affiliate KPHO-TV.Seven of his teammates later alleged in an anonymous letter that the school's description of the workout was inaccurate, claiming that Mayich was not given any water breaks and had shown signs of distress before the final exercise, during which he collapsed. They also said required emergency equipment, like cold-water immersion tubs, wasn't on the field. The school has asked former Arizona Supreme Court Chief Justice Scott Bales to oversee the independent investigation into the circumstances surrounding Mayich's collapse, KPHO-TV reported."Our focus remains where it has been since August 20, on Matthew, and making sure what happened to him is fully understood and never happens to another player," Mayich's family said in a statement Thursday. "It seems more like a negotiated agreement than accountability, and so we believe Justice Bales's investigation must continue with its full scope, gathering all digital evidence and covering everyone involved in that morning's workout and in approving it, and its findings must be made public. Coach Powers's departure should not limit his cooperation or anyone else's, and the players who have spoken up must be protected."Powers previously said in a statement when he was placed on leave that he intends to cooperate fully with the independent investigation into the incident.The workout, which the students say was run by an outside consultant named Tim Ziesel, was described in the letter as "grueling" and "military-style."Ziesel, in a statement released by his attorney, said, "There is no such thing as a military style workout other than calisthenics done to a cadence."

title: Decatur man accused of killing ex-girlfriend less than a month after his release on bond, DA says
description: Authorities say the Decatur man had a no-contact order as part of his bond for an arrest less than a month before his ex-girlfriend's killing.
content: A Decatur man has been indicted on charges of murder for the alleged killing of his ex-girlfriend.Authorities say 57-year-old Laharry Ward had a no-contact order as part of a bond agreement from a previous arrest.According to investigators, DeKalb County officers were called to an apartment complex on Friendly Heights Boulevard on the afternoon of July 21 after receiving reports of an unresponsive person.At the scene, they found 43-year-old Toyka Biggs lying on her apartment floor. Officials say Biggs had been stabbed and hit in the head multiple times.The DeKalb County District Attorney's Office said that surveillance video showed Ward at Biggs' apartment close to when she died. He had been arrested on a charge of battery - family violence against Biggs a month earlier and was prohibited from having any contact with her or returning to the apartment, officials said.Officers arrested Ward on July 29. He has remained in the DeKalb County Jail without bond ever since.On Tuesday, a grand jury indicted the Decatur man on charges of malice murder, felony murder, aggravated assault, and violating a family violence order.

title: Winter may bring snow and rain to some drought-stricken U.S. states, new forecast shows
description: NOAA's new winter weather outlook predicts wetter-than-usual conditions in some states plagued by long-standing drought.
content: The winter season may bring much-needed rain and snow to parts of the United States where both have been lacking, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's latest winter weather outlook. But wetter conditions expected in much of the South will unfold alongside drier-than-average winter months across the northern tier of the country, largely as a result of the exceedingly strong El Niño.NOAA's winter outlook, released Thursday, centered on temperature and precipitation forecasts for the U.S. from December to February. El Niño, a shifting climate pattern dictated by ocean temperatures in the tropical Pacific Ocean, influences weather around the world. Forecasters said it's going to play a significant role in how Americans experience the upcoming winter. Where to expect more snow and rainAlthough El Niño is considered the "warmer" phase of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation cycle, opposite the "cooler" La Niña, that doesn't necessarily mean its existence will lead to milder winter weather across the board, experts said."A strong El Niño does not reduce the severity of winter weather risks," said Ken Graham, director of NOAA's National Weather Service, at a briefing Thursday. Decades of observations taken from previous El Niño events point to stormier weather across the southern U.S. this winter, Graham added, increasing the chances that some areas plagued by drought earlier in the year will see relief in the form of rain and snow. But, he warned, "too much precipitation on dry soil can fuel destructive flash floods and mudslides," so communities in regions that could be affected are advised to prepare accordingly.The southern band of the U.S., including the Southwest, Southeast and portions of the East Coast, will likely experience wetter-than-average conditions through the winter as a result of El Niño, the outlook said. Meanwhile, portions of the Great Lakes, the northern Mountain West, Hawaii and much of Alaska may see drier-than-average winters this year.In some places, El Niño may not substantially impact the amount of rain or snow they receive in the coming months. According to the outlook, parts of the Intermountain West, northern Plains and Ohio Valley have equal chances of experiencing below-average, near-average or above-average amounts of rain and snow throughout the season.Warmer winters, for someFor some states, the winter season will bring more heat than usual. NOAA's outlook forecasts warmer-than-average temperatures for large swaths of the country, including parts of northern California, the Pacific Northwest, Midwest and Mississippi Valley, as well as much of the eastern U.S. Alaska will also see warmer conditions than usual.The lower half of the country is primarily expected to see temperatures hover around, or potentially just below, normal, with the outlook predicting near-normal temperatures across portions of the Southeast, including Florida. It said there are equal chances of below-average, near-average or above-average temperatures for much of the Southwest and Hawaii.Easing droughtThe upcoming winter weather is expected to ease drought conditions for huge stretches of the country, including drought-stricken portions of the Southwest, the southern Great Plains and parts of the East Coast. It may even bring drought to an end in some places, forecasters said.But drought conditions could also develop or worsen in other areas, including in some that have suffered from long periods without enough water, like Oregon and eastern Washington as well as parts of the northern Rockies.

title: Spotty showers possible in South Florida Thursday before heavy rain, flood threat arrives this weekend
description: It will be mostly sunny on Thursday with high temperatures near 90 degrees.
content: The dry season kicks off Thursday with mainly dry and breezy conditions across South Florida, and there is an isolated chance of seeing some showers during the day.It was a warm, steamy start to the day with feels-like temperatures in the low 90s across the Florida Keys and in Broward and Miami-Dade counties.It will be mostly sunny on Thursday with high temperatures near 90 degrees.Stay hydrated as heat indices will soar into the upper 90s and 100s in the afternoon hours when you factor in the humidity.The east breeze will build on Thursday with gusts of 15 to 20 miles per hour. There is a low risk of rip currents along our Atlantic beaches, and there are no advisories or alerts for boaters.As we head into the weekend, winds will increase and lead to hazardous beach and boating conditions.On Friday, spotty showers will blow in on the breeze. Highs will rise to the upper 80s, and it will feel like the upper 90s.This weekend will be wet and windy due to a frontal boundary, plenty of moisture and high pressure. Saturday is looking soggy with scattered storms that could produce some heavy downpours.The chance of rain is even higher on Sunday with more widespread storms and the potential for heavy rain and localized flooding.It will turn blustery at times with gusts possibly reaching 30 miles per hour or higher.We stay unsettled with high rain chances through early next week.

title: Violinist Anne Akiko Meyers joins Chicago Symphony Orchestra for 3 nights performing "Fandango"
description: Anne Akiko Meyers is joining the Chicago Symphony Orchestra starting Thursday night for three-performances of Arturo Marquez's concerto "Fandango."
content: Anne Akiko Meyers is joining the Chicago Symphony Orchestra starting Thursday night for three-performances of Arturo Marquez's concerto "Fandango."Meyers spoke with CBS News Chicago about her performance but also her ties to Chicago â which is where her father is from â as well as her work with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra and an upcoming project with rock band Aerosmith.Her performances of "Fandango" with the CSO begin Thursday, Oct. 15 and continue through Saturday, Oct. 17. The piece is inspired by the Spanish dance of the same name and its musical evolution through the new world. Marquez composed the piece specifically for Meyers to perform. The performances will be conducted by Giancarlo Guerrero.Tickets are available on the Chicago Symphony Orchestra website.

title: 6 dead, including child, in small plane crash near Wisconsin Dells, sheriff says
description: Six people are dead, including a child, in a small plane crash Tuesday night in south-central Wisconsin, according to the Sauk County Sheriff's Office​.
content: Six people are dead, including a child, in a small plane crash Tuesday night in south-central Wisconsin, according to the Sauk County Sheriff's Office.The Sauk County Sheriff's Office received multiple reports of a downed aircraft around 9:30 p.m. Authorities said the plane crashed in a wooded area near Mirror Lake State Park in the Town of Dellona, about 10 miles west of Wisconsin Dells, as rain fell and a thunderstorm moved through the area.Authorities said no structures were damaged and no one on the ground was hurt.Five adults and one child were on the plane and found dead, the sheriff's office said, including pilot Ron Riek, a businessman from the town of Woodville. The names of his passengers have not been released.Authorities say the plane was making a return trip from Kenosha to Menomonie. It was a six-seat, single-engine Piper PA-46.The National Transportation Safety Board said Wednesday that the pilot reported icing on the wings while the plane was flying at 24,000 feet and requested to descend. Air traffic control approved the descent, and the plane began a right descending turn that increased in rate until communications and tracking data were lost.The plane contacted an air traffic control tower before the crash, authorities said. The sheriff's office and the Federal Aviation Administration said investigators are reviewing those transmissions and whether weather played a role.A few families who live nearby said they were initially confused about what they heard at the time of the crash."It sounded like thunder, sounded like quiet thunder, and then all of a sudden you just hear sirens," said an area resident. "It's a sound you won't get out of your head." "I heard the crash and boom, and the weird thing is my pets all reacted to it," said another resident. "Usually they don't react to thunder, but I thought it was thunder."The NTSB is leading the investigation, and says a preliminary report should be available within 30 days.

title: Fire in East Hollywood rips through apartment building leaving nearly 100 residents displaced
description: A woman was rescued from the building and transported to a local hospital. No other injuries were reported.
content: A fire at a three-story apartment building in East Hollywood left nearly 100 displaced after it destroyed a large number of units on Thursday morning. Crews responded to the 500 block of Kingsley Drive around 4:24 a.m. and found smoke and flames coming from multiple floors of the building. The Los Angeles Fire Department said several apartment units were declared uninhabitable, leaving nearly 90 residents displaced. The American Red Cross is working to provide resources to those affected. A woman was rescued from the building and transported to a local hospital. No other injuries were reported.

title: 18-year-old to face first-degree murder charges in killing of 2 N.J. teens in hit-and-run
description: An 18-year-old faces murder charges for a fatal hit-and-run in Cranford, New Jersey​ last year.
content: An 18-year-old faces murder charges for a fatal hit-and-run in Cranford, New Jersey last year. Maria Niotis and Isabella Salas were both 17 when they were killed on Sept. 29, 2025. They were riding an e-bike when they were struck and killed by an SUV.Prosecutors say Vincent Battiloro, who was also 17 at the time, intentionally drove his vehicle into the girls. Over the summer, it was determined that Battiloro, who is now 18, would be tried as an adult. Prosecutors announced Thursday Battiloro has been indicted and will face two counts of first-degree murder. His next court date is Oct. 27. Attorneys for the families of the teen victims released a joint statement saying, "The families are hopeful that justice will be achieved and that a trial in open court will bring what happened to light."An attorney for Battiloro has not yet responded to CBS News New York's request for comment.

title: IHSA board discusses racism allegations against Lincoln-Way East girls' cross-country team
description: IHSA board discusses racism allegations against Lincoln-Way East girls' cross-country team
content: The Illinois High School Association board this week discussed the investigation into alleged racist behavior from the Lincoln-Way East High School girls' cross-country team in Chicago's south suburbs.Last month, the coach was accused of telling team members to "run past those monkeys," referring to runners from Homewood-Flossmoor High School.The Homewood-Flossmoor athletes said students from Lincoln-Way East then made racist noises and monkey-like gestures at them at a Sept. 4 meet.Lincoln-Way East officials said they investigated, but claimed it was all a misunderstanding.This was one of two times Lincoln-Way East school members were accused of racism within one weekend.Homewood-Flossmoor High School District 233 Supt. Dr. Jennifer Norrell said the first incident happened at a varsity football game on Friday when students reported that Lincoln-Way East fans mimicked monkeys while taunting Homewood-Flossmoor fans in the crowd.A video posted on social media appears to show some Lincoln-Way East students on the practice field making the inappropriate gestures. Homewood-Flossmoor leaders said the gestures were directed at Black students.Six Lincoln-Way students accused of racial harassment were ultimately allowed to withdraw from the school game incident, instead of being expelled.The incidents sparked a student walkout protest at Lincoln-Way East in support of Homewood-Flossmoor students.The IHSA said a statement regarding the completion of the investigation into the incidents would not be released until Friday.Lincoln-Way East is located in Frankfort, Illinois.

title: As David Jolly aims to turn Florida governor's office blue, he confronts his prior ties to an alleged fraudster
description: Shortly after David Jolly launched his campaign for Florida governor, his former boss was indicted for taking over $100 million from a disability nonprofit. Jolly says he wasn't aware of the scheme.
content: Less than two weeks after David Jolly launched his Democratic campaign for Florida governor last year, a Tampa grand jury indicted his former boss for allegedly siphoning over $100 million from a nonprofit set up to manage the assets of people with disabilities.Jolly has called the alleged actions of businessman Leo Govoni "raw cruelty." He has also distanced himself from Govoni, telling voters in a July video that he "was an employee of Mr. Govoni's at a separate company from which the theft later occurred," and "from public filings, his activities appear to have occurred almost exclusively after we left his employment."While Jolly didn't work at the nonprofit that was the source of the allegedly stolen money, he did work at a for-profit firm where the money was allegedly sent. Federal prosecutors said Govoni had used the firm to enrich himself. And a forensic accountant found that millions of dollars moved from the nonprofit to the firm during the period when Jolly worked there, according to filings from a related court case reviewed by CBS News.Nothing in the court documents suggests that Jolly knew about or was involved in the scheme laid out in the indictment, and he has not been accused of any wrongdoing. He told the Tampa Bay Times he was not aware of the transfers described by the indictment.Jolly campaign senior advisor Mark Riddle said in a statement: "Congressman Jolly has been forthright with the public and the press since he learned of this matter when the rest of the world did last year, upon the arrest and public filings against Leo Govoni. Congressman Jolly was one of over 100 W-2 employees among Govoni's many companies. He never served as an officer or in a position of any fiduciary responsibility, nor did he ever have any visibility into the finances of Mr. Govoni or his companies. Congressman Jolly has never been contacted by investigators in the criminal case against Mr. Govoni nor been a subject of the investigation."Jolly — a former Republican who left the party early in the Trump era — is vying for the governor's mansion against GOP Rep. Byron Donalds. Florida hasn't elected a Democratic governor in this century, but Jolly thinks discontent with the GOP could give him an opening.Jolly worked at Govoni's Boston Finance Group from 2012 until early 2014, when Jolly won his first election for a Tampa-area U.S. House seat. In 2013, the future congressman earned $250,000 at the firm, according to House financial disclosures. One 2013 statement from his House campaign describes Jolly as a vice president at Boston Finance Group.Govoni also donated to Jolly's various political campaigns and served as finance co-chair of Jolly's 2016 Senate run. Jolly's wife worked for another Govoni-run firm while he was a House member, and Govoni's son worked in Jolly's congressional office in 2014.Riddle told CBS News that Jolly "has done something that no Republican politician has done: returned Mr. Govoni's political contributions to his victims. Congressman Jolly calls on the other beneficiaries of Mr. Govoni's contributions to do the same."Govoni's alleged scheme left behind a trail of alleged victims. After Colorado resident Chase McMinn was shot at work, over $1 million from legal settlements was placed in a trust managed by Govoni's nonprofit to pay for his 24/7 care, according to his father. Between $200,000 and $360,000 disappeared, his father said, and it's not clear if it will ever be returned."What [Govoni] did was just so evil," Chase McMinn's father, Milt, told CBS News.An attorney for Govoni did not comment, saying he would let the case speak for itself. CBS News has reached out to Govoni's son for comment.Charges against Govoni mention firm where Jolly workedThe federal criminal charges against Govoni describe a complicated web of companies set up by the Clearwater-based businessman and his associates.At its center is the Center for Special Needs Trust Administration, or CSNT, a nonprofit co-founded by Govoni in 2000 to help manage and invest the financial assets of people with disabilities. Prosecutors say it eventually became one of the country's largest operations of its kind, managing around $200 million in assets across more than 2,000 trusts as of 2024.Between 2009 and 2012, prosecutors allege, CSNT agreed to lend up to $100 million to Boston Finance Group, a firm run by Govoni that was in the business of offering loans to other companies.After CSNT declared bankruptcy in 2024, a federally appointed trustee set out to track down the money and sued Boston Finance Group to claw back the loan.Court papers filed in that lawsuit show that the loan was set up as a revolving line of credit that allowed Boston Finance Group to borrow chunks of money from CSNT over time. In January 2012, Boston Finance Group was granted a $100 million credit line and was required to pay back the money by 2017, with quarterly interest payments until then.Boston Finance Group drew money from CSNT almost every quarter for a decade, starting in 2010, according to an analysis by a forensic accountant hired by the bankruptcy trustee who pored through both CSNT and Boston Finance Group's bank records.From March 2013 to February 2014, during Jolly's tenure at Boston Finance Group, the company drew down more than $10 million from CSNT, the accountant's analysis shows. Two accounting experts told CBS News the forensic accountant who carried out the analysis appeared to follow the correct procedures: Suresh Govindaraj, a professor at Rutgers Business School, and Francine McKenna, a professor at Montclair State University and independent journalist who covers accounting issues at public and pre-IPO companies.Court records do not mention Jolly or suggest that he was personally aware of those transfers.By late 2024, the accountant found, Boston Finance Group had borrowed just shy of $100 million from the nonprofit and only paid back around $19 million. The nonprofit was owed around $120 million net, including interest, the accountant said. A judge later found Boston Finance Group liable for the full sum, brushing off the firm's argument that it owed less.Federal prosecutors say the "overwhelming majority" of the money that Boston Finance Group borrowed from CSNT wasn't invested in order to help clients, and instead, much of it was "distributed … to other GOVONI-controlled entities for illegitimate, non-investment purposes, including the personal enrichment of the defendants and others."The indictment said Boston Finance Group "functioned as a slush fund and passthrough entity." It is not clear exactly what happened to the money that was transferred during Jolly's time at the firm, or whether those funds played a role in the alleged scheme. The indictment alleges several 2020 transfers from Boston Finance Group to other Govoni-linked entities constituted wire fraud."Govoni used his victims' money to live a lavish life, complete with luxury boxes at Tampa Bay Buccaneers games and the Kentucky Derby, pay off his own home mortgage, enable his use of private planes, and cover the living expenses of his friends and family," the Justice Department alleged in one court document last year. "He even distributed some of his victims' money directly into his own personal bank account."Federal prosecutors charged Govoni with conspiracy, fraud and other charges. He pleaded not guilty and was ordered detained ahead of a trial set for next year.Milt McMinn told CBS News his son Chase relied on money held by CSNT after he was shot in the head by a customer at an auto shop in the Denver area. The 2017 shooting left him quadriplegic, nonverbal and in need of 24/7 care."His life right now is basically a bed and a wheelchair," Milt McMinn said. He described his son as a "great young man."Chase McMinn's family was able to recover more than $1 million in legal settlements, and a judge directed the money to be managed by Govoni's nonprofit, his father said.In 2024, the FBI notified the family that it was investigating issues with the trust.Milt McMinn said he and his wife have had to pay for many of Chase's needs out of pocket, including a rehab center and expenses for Chase's daughter. The father said he is "really angry" about Govoni's alleged crimes."I just don't understand why he would do that," he said.Govoni and Jolly's relationshipOver the summer, Jolly told the Tampa Bay Times he met Govoni when they were both members of an elder affairs committee at Stetson University. He said Govoni initially brought him on as a consultant, and later hired him at Boston Finance Group in 2012 to help Govoni recover $30 million from a former business partner.Financial disclosures show Jolly worked at Boston Finance Group from some point in 2012 until March 11, 2014, when he won a special congressional election to replace his late boss, GOP Rep. Bill Young. Over that period, Jolly reported $468,750 in income from the firm.Govoni and employees of his companies donated thousands of dollars to Jolly's congressional campaigns, and Govoni served as finance co-chair for his 2016 Senate run. Govoni has donated to other politicians, a point Jolly raised over the summer, saying he "worked hard to surround himself with elected officials across Florida."After he was elected to Congress, Jolly says his wife also worked for Govoni. House financial disclosures list his wife as an employee of Boston Holding Company in 2015 and 2016.Meanwhile, Govoni's son worked for Jolly's office, the gubernatorial candidate said over the summer. According to his LinkedIn account, LJ Govoni worked as a senior legislative aide from April 2014 to December 2014. LJ Govoni's profile on the site doesn't mention that he worked for Jolly, but says his job "wasn't a career move — it was a personal ask." "When a close contact was elected to Congress, he asked me to come to Washington and help build the office: establish process, install leadership infrastructure, and make sure the operation ran the way a serious legislative office should," he wrote. "I came, did the work, and returned to the private sector when the foundation was set."

title: Crews battle Tujunga, La Tuna Canyon brush fire
description: Los Angeles Fire Department crews are battling a brush fire in Tujunga burning approximately 1 acre of medium to heavy brush south of the 210 Freeway, according to LAFD.
content: Los Angeles Fire Department crews are battling a brush fire in Tujunga burning approximately 1 acre of medium to heavy brush south of the 210 Freeway, according to LAFD. Aerial footage shows a heavy presence of firefighters on the ground. No structures are threatened, as light winds in the area fuel a moderate rate of spread. The wildfire's forward progress stopped around 1:23 p.m., according to LAFD.The blaze comes as a Red Flag Warning has been issued in Southern California. Forecasters say a moderate to strong Santa Ana wind event is expected to increase critical fire danger through Saturday.

title: Queens residents call on city to improve Union Turnpike intersection, alleging unsafe conditions
description: A busy intersection in Queens has neighbors saying they feel unsafe, and they want the city to step in.
content: NEW YORK â A busy intersection in Queens has neighbors saying they feel unsafe, and they want the city to step in.Residents say crashes are all too frequent at the dangerous intersection of Union Turnpike, Markwood Road and Park Lane, where Forest Hills and Kew Gardens share a border. It's a heavily used pedestrian and cyclist crossing to Forest Park.Speeding is a problem at Union Turnpike intersection, neighbors sayFor Connie Hau and her son Reese, neighborhood walks require extra precaution after a close call."I almost got hit by a car that just jumped the curb," she said."I have to run across because the cars are just rushing," 9-year-old Garison Ling said. For years, neighbors say they have witnessed crash after crash, with cars swerving to bypass a turn lane they say is poorly marked. Lisa Christopher says that twice her parked car was hit by vehicles that sped off."They're treating that one lane like two cars can fit there, and they're going so close and so fast," she said.The DOT denied Oded Horodniceanu's request for a speed camera back in 2020, claiming the area failed to meet criteria. He is now asking the city to consider a curb extension."Pedestrians wouldn't have to cross as far of a distance, and then, also, vehicles would have to slow down because there's a sidewalk there," he said.Neighbors call recent DOT upgrades "a Band-Aid"To make matters worse, locals say, faulty traffic lights regularly go dark, causing chaos.In a statement, the Department of Transportation told CBS New York in part, "We are aware of community concerns in the area and have made several recent improvements, including upgrading the signal infrastructure at Union Turnpike and Markwood Place last year, as well as implementing a street improvement project at Union Turnpike and Austin Street."Neighbors call the upgrades a Band-Aid, especially in light of a prolonged traffic light outage in recent weeks."We called 311 multiple times, and they said they resolved it, but the next day, the problem just came back," Gary Ling said.Council Member Lynn Schulman says making the corridor safe demands a multi-pronged approach."There's so many different parts of it. There's the lights. There's the parking," she said. "So we're asking the Department of Transportation to really take a close look at it."The DOT told CBS New York it will continue to monitor the area for improvements. While families wait for solutions, they hope no lives are lost.You can email Elle with Queens story ideas by CLICKING HERE.

title: Husband of Pennsylvania doctor charged with killing her, setting her on fire inside home
description: The husband of a Pennsylvania doctor is charged with murder after authorities said he strangled his wife and started a fire.
content: The husband of a Pennsylvania doctor is charged with murder after authorities said he strangled his wife at their home and started a fire while their daughter was inside. The Harrisburg Bureau of Police said in a news release that Jonathan Gatto was arrested and charged on Wednesday after a suspicious death and fire investigation at a home on Green Street. Man charged with killing wifePolice said the investigation revealed that the 41-year-old woman's death was not caused by the fire on Saturday. Gatto is now facing several charges, including murder, abuse of a corpse, endangering the welfare of children and aggravated arson. CBS affiliate WHP, citing court paperwork, reported that Gatto strangled his wife, 41-year-old Dr. Julia Pederson, and set her on fire while their 7-year-old daughter was asleep in the house.During an interview, Gatto told police that their marriage wasn't good and they were trying to figure out how to talk to their daughter about getting a separation, WHP said. Gatto told police that later that night he heard what sounded like a person falling down the stairs, but didn't find anyone, the TV station reported. He said he was awoken by the smoke detectors going off, and after getting their daughter out, he went back for Pederson but burned his hand, according to WHP.Court paperwork said the coroner ruled Pederson's cause of death as homicide by multiple traumatic injuries, WHP said. Victim remembered as "beloved pediatrician"In a statement to the TV station, UPMC said Pederson was a "beloved pediatrician" who "devoted her career to caring for children and supporting families."Pederson graduated from Harvard and earned her medical degree from Stanford School of Medicine, according to a GoFundMe set up in her name. "Beyond her career, Julia cherished the simple joys of life," the GoFundMe says. "She lived in Harrisburg with her family and enjoyed exploring local nature preserves, reading, and learning to crochet. She was so much more than her professional accomplishments, she was a daughter, a sister, a wife, and a mother whose presence and love meant so much to those closest to her." Court paperwork shows Gatto has a preliminary hearing scheduled for the morning of Oct. 28.

title: Minneapolis City Council fails to override mayor's veto on driverless vehicle ordinance
description: A vote to override Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey's veto of the City Council's rideshare ordinance that would require a human monitor in driverless vehicles failed Thursday morning at City Hall on a 7-5 vote.
content: A vote to override Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey's veto of the City Council's rideshare ordinance that would require a human monitor in driverless vehicles failed Thursday morning at City Hall on a 7-5 vote.The City Council passed the Workers Drive Minneapolis ordinance on Oct. 1 amid the rise in Waymo driverless vehicles in the city, focusing on the potential negative impacts on rideshare drivers and safety.The next day, Frey vetoed it, saying he "cannot support a back-door ban that belies our progressive tradition." He also highlighted the vital importance driverless vehicles could have on the livelihood of community members living with disabilities.Waymo officials echoed Frey's concerns earlier this month, calling the ordinance "a de facto ban on autonomous vehicles," noting its unprecedented in the 15 cities where the company currently operates."The veto of Workers Drive Minneapolis handed a win to Google, Elon Musk, and Jeff Bezos," said Councilmembers Robin Wonsley, Jamal Osman, Jason Chavez and Aurin Chowdhury in a joint statement. "Meanwhile, thousands of working-class families in Minneapolis are facing difficult conversations about how they will make ends meet if a breadwinner loses their income to a driverless robotaxi."After the vote, Wonsley, Osman, Chavez and Chowdhury said they would be restarting the legislative process to regulate driverless vehicles. While driverless vehicles have yet to hit St. Paul streets, its City Council proactively passed a resolution to study the potential impact on the workforce and public safety.

title: Soggy, chilly Thursday in the Twin Cities; season's first frost possible Saturday
description: A storm system rolls into Minnesota Thursday, bringing back the clouds and wet weather to the Twin Cities.
content: A storm system rolls into Minnesota Thursday, bringing back the clouds and wet weather to the Twin Cities.Rain moves into the metro and southern Minnesota through the morning commute and lingers into the afternoon. It wraps up by Thursday evening with a quarter-inch to half-inch of total precipitation, but very little for central and northern Minnesota.Highs will only reach the low-to-mid 50s both Thursday and Friday.Winds will pick up into Thursday night with gusts between 25-35 mph, driving in more cool air for Friday. Spotty showers are possible again early Friday, but the clouds clear into the afternoon. Saturday morning will be chilly with the metro's first good chance for frost.Lows will be in the mid 30s with lots of sunshine, getting the metro to near 60 by the afternoon. It will be a bit breezy this weekend with gusts near 30 mph.High pressure will drive the forecast with dry weather and pleasant temps into early next week. Expect highs back in the upper 60s and near 70 with morning lows in the 40s.

title: Cook County transforms high schools into early voting sites to help eligible students vote
description: Cook County transformed 27 suburban high schools into early voting sites for a "Teen Takeover for Democracy" event Thursday.
content: Cook County transformed 27 suburban high schools into early voting sites for a "Teen Takeover for Democracy" event Thursday.The program turns the schools into official voting sites where eligible students can take a break from their normal classes so they can cast early ballots for the 2026 general midterm election. Around 125 students were also certified as election judges.The program was developed in partnership with the Chicago Bears and the Cook County Clerk's Office. It was first launched for the 2026 March primary, in which the clerks' office said 1,136 ballots were cast in a single day at 24 participating high schools. That number, the clerk's office said, surpassed the combined total full week of early voting at six other traditional sites.

title: Georgia man says Coweta deputies used Flock cameras to track him after he sued them
description: The lawsuit alleges Coweta deputies used Flock Safety's license plate camera network to track a man in retaliation for suing them and accuses the company of failing to prevent improper searches.
content: A Georgia man is suing Flock Safety and Coweta County officials, alleging deputies used license plate cameras to track him in retaliation for an earlier lawsuit accusing them of excessive force.Tyler Murkerson filed the proposed class-action lawsuit on Oct. 8 in federal court in Newnan. It names Flock Group, which operates as Flock Safety, Coweta County, Sheriff Lenn Wood and sheriff's deputies as defendants.The lawsuit alleges deputies searched Murkerson's vehicle information without a legitimate investigative reason while his earlier civil rights case was pending. It also accuses Flock of failing to require safeguards that could prevent improper searches.According to the complaint, audit records show five searches attributed to the Coweta County Sheriff's Office that spanned more than 6,000 agency camera networks nationwide. The lawsuit describes a 197-day surveillance period involving Murkerson's vehicle.The only disclosed reasons entered for the searches were "info" and "37," neither of which identified an investigation, according to the lawsuit. Murkerson also alleges his vehicle was placed on an alert list that would notify users when it passed a camera.Murkerson's earlier lawsuit stemmed from a 2023 encounter in a gas station parking lot. He alleged deputies forced him to the ground, used a Taser on him and arrested him over an alleged seat belt violation. Criminal charges against him were dismissed in June 2023, and the civil case was resolved in 2026, according to his attorneys.The new lawsuit alleges Murkerson noticed increased deputy activity near his home, business and commute. He says he ended a six-year business relationship servicing a neighboring police department's vehicles because he no longer felt safe.Murkerson's lawsuit follows a separate internal audit that flagged Coweta Sheriff's Office employee accounts. Three employees resigned, and the sheriff's office requested a Georgia Bureau of Investigation inquiry. "We expect every employee with access to these systems to use them in a manner that is lawful, ethical and in accordance with agency policy," the sheriff's office said in its earlier statement about the audit.Murkerson is seeking damages and court-ordered safeguards, including documented investigative reasons for searches and regular reviews of users' activity. CBS News Atlanta has reached out to Flock Safety and the Coweta County Sheriff's Office for comment and will update this story when they respond.

title: Trump calls off plan to livestream Fort Hood shooter's execution, says people "would rather not watch him die"
description: "He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," President Trump wrote on Truth Social.
content: Washington — President Trump said Thursday that the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan will not be streamed, a decision that comes after his administration faced significant backlash over the Pentagon's initial plan to allow the American people to watch Hasan's death by firing squad."I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device," Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social. "He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed."The president said the immediate families of the victims can view the execution in person if they choose to."They deserve to witness JUSTICE!" he said.Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring more than 30 at Fort Hood in 2009, is set to be executed by firing squad at 1 p.m. on Dec. 3 at the Texas Army installation, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said earlier this month.The plan to allow the public to watch Hasan's execution was revealed by Hegseth last week in an interview with far-right political activist Jack Posobiec. "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public — because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," he said.Sean Parnell, the Pentagon's chief spokesman, said Hegseth and Mr. Trump spoke about the decision to cancel the planned livestream before the president announced it on social media."The Secretary supports the President's decision, and they are completely aligned," Parnell said in a statement.But the plan sparked broad outcry from Republicans and Democrats, who warned that livestreaming Hasan's death diminished the United States and could fuel radicalization.House Speaker Mike Johnson told CBS News national correspondent and chief Washington analyst Robert Costa that "the concern would be that you would create a video that would be a recruiting tool for future terrorists." Vice President JD Vance acknowledged that he would not watch the execution.CBS News reported Tuesday that Trump administration officials were leaning against streaming the death by firing squad.If the Trump administration had followed through with its plan, it would have placed the United States in a small group of nations carrying out public executions. Afghanistan and Iran are the only two nations that conducted known public executions last year, according to Amnesty International.It appears the last public execution in the U.S. took place in 1936. An estimated 20,000 people gathered to watch the hanging of Rainey Bethea, a Black man who confessed to the rape and murder of a 70-year-old White woman, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.The last military execution took place in 1961, when U.S. Army Private John Bennett was hanged. Hasan's death by firing squad would be the military's first using that method since 1945, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

title: Jackson officers shoot teen after he allegedly pointed a gun at them, police say
description: Jackson Police Officers shot a teen after he pointed a firearm at them, and he is now in critical condition, the Jackson Police Department says.
content: Jackson Police Officers shot a teen after he pointed a firearm at them, and he is now in critical condition, the Jackson Police Department says.Officers were dispatched to the 600 block of North Blackstone Street on Wednesday at about 2:43 p.m. for a personal welfare check on a juvenile reported missing, police say.Officers located the subject, identified as a 16-year-old Jackson resident, near the Jackson County Fairgrounds in the 200 block of North Ganson Street, according to police.According to police, officers spoke to the subject before he produced a handgun and fled on foot. During the foot pursuit, the subject pointed the firearm at officers, who then fired their weapons at the suspect and struck him, police say.The subject was transported to Henry Ford Hospital in critical condition, and the two officers involved were not injured, according to local police.Police say that all officers involved in the shooting have been placed on administrative leave pending the outcome of the investigation, which is being conducted by the Michigan State Police District 1 Team.

title: Cornell's Greek life should end permanently if found to be not safe, school president says
description: Cornell University's Faculty Senate met on Wednesday to debate a resolution of no confidence in the school administration.
content: Greek life at Cornell University should be ended permanently if leadership can't be convinced that fraternity gatherings there can be safe, the school's president, Michael Kotlikoff, said at a contentious meeting of the Faculty Senate on Wednesday night."I really appreciate the sentiment of a lot of faculty and a lot of leadership of the university that have said to me it's time for Greek life to go," Kotlikoff said at the meeting. "I do think as an academic institution we should study things, make decisions based on data and fact.""If at the end of the day, fraternities cannot exist in a safe environment and we can't be convinced that they can be safe, then we should make that decision," he continued. "But we should make it, it seems to me, based on data and study and expertise, not on emotion."Kotlikoff made the remarks at the start of a meeting where Faculty Senate members debated a resolution of no confidence in the school's administration. A vote on it is expected following another meeting Oct. 28.The meeting was closed to the media, but CBS News New York exclusively obtained video from the meeting before Cornell released audio of it early Thursday.More than 300 people attended, including about 100 in person and nearly 200 on Zoom, and it lasted over two hours, associate professor Ariana Kim said.The meeting was held in the wake of Jane Doe's civil lawsuit alleging she was drugged and sexually assaulted by multiple men at a fraternity house at Cornell in 2024. CBS News has reached out to attorneys for all of the accused; two responded and denied the allegations, while others have denied wrongdoing in comments elsewhere. None of the accused have been charged with a crime.In an opening statement at the meeting, Kotlikoff outlined the concern with fraternities on campus, saying it had become "quite clear" frats were now the center of social activity for students. "Many bars and areas without drinking in Collegetown shut down post-COVID," Kotlikoff said. "And we're now in a situation in which much of the social activity occurs in private houses. We don't have full ability to be confident that what goes on in those houses is safe."All fraternity parties have been suspended at Cornell through the end of the school year as an independent investigation — led by former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates — is now underway into "how the University prevents and responds to sexual harassment, sexual assault and related misconduct on campus," the school said in a statement. President questioned before "no confidence" debateThe school's administration has faced intense criticism over how it responded after Jane Doe first reported the alleged gang rape. The resolution to be voted on later this month states that the Faculty Senate "has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University." The resolution, which needs a simple majority to succeed, is largely symbolic as the Faculty Senate cannot fire anyone in the administration.At the meeting, one associate professor described the resolution as having "mostly strong support" and "some opposition."The Faculty Senate on Wednesday asked how Kotlikoff planned to regain the trust of students, alumni and the broader Cornell community, particularly following the arrests of people on campus during protests in recent years. "He really did not answer questions, and he really didn't take responsibility or accountability for problems that we have," said Risa Lieberwitz, a professor of labor and employment law, who relayed what happened during the closed portion of the Faculty Senate meeting.Faculty members pressed Kotlikoff on why it took "a long time" for him to speak out about the Jane Doe lawsuit, and how the statements he did make were "seemingly in response to the press.""I really reject the idea that I had no interest in it or was not concerned about it," Kotlikoff said. "That was my message to the community as soon as we learned about it, as soon as it was reported to the Title IX office, and that was the reason that we established this (independent) task force."The Q&A lasted for about 45 minutes before Kotlikoff left the building, and faculty members turned to the no-confidence resolution.Supporters of the resolution said they lacked confidence in the school's administration to make "systematic change" at Cornell, Lieberwitz said."People were talking about the lack of effective democratic governance on campus," she added.A smaller group, largely made up of faculty members from the math and physics departments, argued they needed "more information or data" before making a final decision, Kim said.Professor Paul Ortiz, the resolution's lead sponsor, said those who opposed the resolution know Kotlikoff well."They know him on a first-name basis," he said. "They have friendships like that with him that go back many years."Ortiz and Kim said they each received more than 100 messages from alumni on Wednesday, urging them to vote in favor of the resolution and "hold the administration accountable." Tommy Li, a Cornell student who spoke with CBS News outside the meeting, said he hoped the resolution would pass and described Kotlikoff's response to Jane Doe's allegations as a "horrible mishandling."The Faculty Senate will hold another hearing on Oct. 28 before its members vote on the resolution."If it were to be put to a vote today, I would say it — the resolution would pass," Ortiz said.

title: Modesto traffic safety operation nets 176 citations following string of deadly crashes
description: A single-day traffic safety operation in Modesto led to 176 citations being issued, police say.
content: A single-day traffic safety operation in Modesto led to 176 citations being issued, police said, after multiple deadly crashes happened in a short span of time. Police said that officers from Modesto, Newman, Patterson and Ceres worked together, starting with officers deploying to 16 schools in the city for enforcement. The operation then went city-wide and focused on speeding, distracted driving, pedestrian and bicycle-related violations, as well as unsafe movements and right-of-way violations. The operation came after the city saw multiple people killed in traffic incidents in October, including two girls that were struck and killed in a crosswalk on Coffee Road, and the death of a woman after a vehicle crashed into her residence on Fortuna Avenue.

title: No toll increases for Maryland drivers next year, Gov. Wes Moore announces
description: Gov. Wes Moore announced Wednesday he instructed the Maryland Transportation Authority to pause any toll increases for 2027.
content: Maryland drivers are catching a break next year. Gov. Wes Moore announced Wednesday he instructed the Maryland Transportation Authority to pause any toll increases for 2027. The increases were expected to offset financial losses from the Key Bridge collapse, but they are now expected to be pushed back until 2028.Moore said the move will save Marylanders at least $50 million. "Whether you're crossing the Bay Bridge, I-95, or traveling through one of Baltimore's tunnels, we're working to give Maryland families like yours just a little extra breathing room," the governor said in a video posted to social media. "I know that times are tough, and when costs go up, government should be looking for ways to bring them down," he continued. "So we're going to keep fighting to make Maryland more affordable and to deliver for the people who call Maryland home."State officials told our media partner, The Baltimore Banner, the pause will not impact funding for the bridge rebuild after a settlement was reached earlier this year with the owner and operator of the Dali cargo ship. Maryland last increased its tolls in 2013, according to The Banner. The most recent toll rates listed on the MTA website show the following prices for standard passenger vehicles with in-state E-ZPass: Bay Bridge: $2.50I-95: $6Baltimore Harbor Tunnel & Fort McHenry Tunnel: $4You can also use this online toll calculator to find your exact rate.

title: Inspection of Six Flags' Goliath roller coaster found no violations before deadly incident, officials say
description: Investigators are working around the clock to learn what led to the death of a man who fell off Six Flags Over Georgia's Goliath roller coaster.
content: Georgia Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner John King said that his office's regulators had inspected Six Flags Over Georgia's Goliath roller coaster months before the incident that killed one man and injured four minors on Monday.In an update, King said that his investigators were working diligently to learn what led to the death of 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem onboard the ride, and will continue to review the evidence, equipment, and relevant documentation.Witnesses told CBS News Atlanta that Kariem was ejected from the ride and struck other passengers as he fell. Officers working at the park responded to the scene around 3:58 p.m. Monday and found Kariem beneath the attraction, unresponsive and not breathing. Four juveniles also suffered non-life-threatening injuries and were taken to local hospitals."Our thoughts and prayers are with the family and loved ones of Hassan Kariem, as well as everyone affected by this heartbreaking incident," King said. "We recognize the unimaginable pain this family is experiencing, and they deserve answers. We have a solemn responsibility to determine what happened, and I want the people of Georgia to know that we are approaching this investigation with the urgency, diligence, and unwavering commitment to public safety that this tragedy demands."The Office of the Commissioner of Insurance and Safety Fire is responsible for inspecting and investigating the state's amusement rides. Officials say each ride is examined for compliance with state safety requirements annually before opening to the public."These inspections include reviews of required documentation, mechanical conditions, safety equipment, and the safe operation of rides in accordance with applicable standards and manufacturer specifications," the OCI said in a statement.According to the agency, Goliath's most recent inspection was March 16. Inspectors reported no violations, deficiencies, or red tags at that time. That inspection is now under a full review. "Georgia's safety laws exist for a reason, and we expect them to be followed to the letter," King said. "Our responsibility is to ensure that every applicable requirement is carefully examined and that the law is upheld. If our investigation identifies violations or failures to comply with state safety requirements, we will take the appropriate actions authorized under Georgia law. The safety of our citizens is not negotiable."Once the investigation is complete, officials say they will share their findings and determine what further actions may be necessary. Kariem was the second death connected with Goliath in the ride's 20 years of operations, according to data from Atlanta-based attorneys The Doan Law Firm. The first was in 2006, in which a 45-year-old man became unresponsive on the ride. The law firm said it appeared that the man suffered a fatal heart attack while on the ride and that his death was believed to be due to a congenital heart condition.The park is scheduled to reopen on Friday. It had been closed since Monday due to its weekend operations schedule. Goliath remains out of operation.

title: An Egyptian farmer found "an unusual stone." It led archaeologists to pieces of statues for an ancient king.
description: An Egyptian farmer was working on his land when he came across an unusual rock that turned his field into an archaeology dig.
content: Cairo — Egyptian farmer Khaled al-Shahat was working on his land when he came across something he hadn't seen before. The unusual pink rock led archaeologists to unearth pieces of statues for King Ramses II, who ruled Egypt from 1279 B.C. to 1213 B.C."I was working on my land on Friday when I came across an unusual stone," al-Shahat told CBS News. "I informed the relevant authorities, and they came to examine it."The stone turned out to be an ancient pink granite block measuring approximately 1.3 meters long (around 4.26 feet) and bearing two royal titles of Ramses II: "Nesw-Bity" (King of Upper and Lower Egypt) and "Sa-Ra" (Son of Ra, the sun god), the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities said.Archaeologists began excavations, and near the block they uncovered a colossal head of a statue of Ramses II, measuring approximately 1.6 meters high (around 5.25 feet). The king is depicted wearing the double crown, a symbol of the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt around 3100 B.C.On Wednesday, Minister of Tourism and Antiquities Sherif Fathy visited al-Shahat's hometown in Al Gharbia Governorate in the Nile Delta to honor him.The minister presented al-Shahat and his wife with certificates of appreciation, and awarded them a trip to Saudi Arabia to perform the Umrah pilgrimage in recognition of his honesty and responsible conduct for not keeping the discovery to himself."The minister insisted that the citizen be honored in his village, on his own land, and among his family and fellow villagers, in recognition of his honesty, awareness, and sense of responsibility," the ministry said in a statement.Archaeologists also unearthed the remains of the upper part of the statue's back pillar, bearing Ramses II's formal royal title, or Horus name: Hor Ka Nakht Mery Maat.The size of the head suggests the complete statue was about 28 feet tall, according to archaeologists."I was surprised and happy when they discovered more antiquities," al-Shahat told CBS News. "They told me this might change the history of the area."Most of a second royal statue, also believed to depict Ramses II, was uncovered. Measuring approximately 2.4 meters long (around 7.87 feet), it is missing its legs and base, as well as part of the upper section of its royal nemes headdress. Its head has clearly visible, well-preserved facial features resembling those of the first statue, the ministry said.Excavations and archaeological studies are continuing on al-Shahat's land to learn more about the statues, the area's history and its architectural development in ancient Egypt.

title: Rep. Ilhan Omar's office calls home search "an authoritarian move to silence an opponent"
description: The statement says the push to strip Omar of her citizenship "has no basis in the law and has no precedent." The Justice Department says agents executed a search warrant in an ongoing criminal investigation.
content: Rep. Ilhan Omar's office is accusing President Trump of using a federal search of her Washington, D.C., home to silence a political opponent weeks before the election.In a statement, a spokesperson for the Minnesota Democrat said the search was "politically motivated" and an escalation of Mr. Trump's "personal vendetta" against her that has lasted more than a decade. The statement called it "an authoritarian move to silence an opponent right before an election where he and his party will be rejected by Americans in historic proportions."Homeland Security Investigations agents executed a search warrant as part of "an ongoing federal criminal investigation," according to the Department of Homeland Security. Sources told CBS News the investigation centers on immigration paperwork from Omar's childhood that was completed by her late father, and that investigators are examining potential allegations of false statements and immigration fraud.Omar's spokesperson said Mr. Trump has "lied about her family, about her immigration history, and about her love of this country." The statement also said his push to strip Omar of her citizenship and deport her "has no basis in the law and has no precedent."Mr. Trump claimed to reporters Monday he "had nothing to do with" the search. "I think she's a terrible person, but that's really up to the DOJ," he said.Omar's office said she has "done nothing wrong" and called the raid an "outrageous abuse of power." Omar posted on social media Monday that she will "not be silenced."Relatives of Omar received grand jury subpoenas Friday, sources told CBS News, days before the search. Two sources said agents also took Omar's personal cell phone.The search has drawn criticism because of its timing. It appears to run contrary to Justice Department guidelines, which say prosecutors and agents "may never select the timing of any action" for the purpose of affecting an election. It's not clear why the government moved so close to the election, since some of the documents in question date to Omar's childhood. Sources told CBS News that Attorney General Todd Blanche was personally aware of the search.Omar is seeking reelection in a heavily Democratic district and is heavily favored to win. Supporters rallied in Minneapolis hours after the search.

title: 18-year-old driver killed in single-vehicle, fiery crash in Monroe County, deputies say
description: An 18-year-old Ida resident was killed after a fiery crash Thursday morning near Monroe, deputies said.
content: An 18-year-old Ida resident was killed after a fiery crash on Thursday morning in Monroe County, Michigan. The crash happened at about 6:54 a.m. on North Raisinville Road, north of Stewart Road, in Raisinville Township, the Monroe County Sheriff's Office said. This area is northwest of the city of Monroe limits. Garrett Siffer was driving a blue 2010 Ford Fusion northbound on North Raisinville Road when he lost control shortly after the Stewart Road intersection, deputies said. The car then went off the road to the east, went into a ditch and struck a tree. The car spun counter-clockwise and overturned, stopping on its roof. The car then caught fire. Lieutenant Ryan Sottile from the sheriff's office was the first emergency responder to arrive and used a fire extinguisher to put out the fire, deputies said. Siffer was pronounced dead at the scene, the report said. The London-Maybee-Raisinville Fire Department, Monroe Community Ambulance and the Monroe County Sheriff's Office Chaplain Program assisted on scene. Because of traffic disruptions, Raisinville Elementary School on North Raisinville Road urged families to approach its campus Thursday morning via Blue Blush Road rather than Stewart Road. Raisinville Elementary is part of the Monroe Public Schools district. The crash remains under investigation. Deputies ask that anyone who can assist in the review call the sheriff's office at 734-240-7725 or contact Crime Stoppers of Michigan at 800-SPEAK-UP.

title: Athletic trainer at San Jose school accused of sexual battery of student
description: An athletic trainer at a high school in San Jose was arrested for the alleged sexual assault of a student under his care and police believe there could be additional victims.
content: An athletic trainer at a high school in San Jose was arrested for the alleged sexual assault of a student under his care and police believe there could be additional victims.According to San Jose police, officers were called to a campus on the 5000 block of Mitty Way around 7:30 p.m. on Oct. 8. Police did not mention the school by name, but the campus of Archbishop Mitty High School is located at that address.Officers spoke to a 16-year-old female student, who said the suspect was providing care for her sports-related injury. The survivor told police the suspect sexually battered her and recorded the incident on his phone.Police identified the suspect as 31-year-old Kelvin Chiu, an athletic trainer for the school. Detectives with the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force began investigating and obtained search warrants for the suspect, residence and vehicles.The following day, detectives located Chiu and served a search warrant at his Fremont home. Detectives said that child sexual abuse material was found on Chiu's phone.Chiu was arrested and booked into Santa Clara County Jail on suspicion of annoying or molesting a minor, production and possession of child sexual abuse material and sexual battery.Police said that school administration was notified and that they were fully cooperating with the investigation.Cynthia Shaw of the Catholic Diocese of San Jose confirmed Chiu's employment as a member of the athletic training staff at Archbishop Mitty High School and that the victim's family notified the school on the same evening of the incident. Chiu was placed on administrative leave."Our first concern is for the student and family, and for all of our students and families. We recognize the impact a situation of this nature may have on our students, and the school's Counseling teams will be available to speak with students who may need additional support," Shaw told CBS News Bay Area.In a statement, the police department believes there could be additional victims due to Chiu's position of trust.Anyone with additional information is asked to contact Detective Camarillo or Detective Widmer of the Internet Crimes Against Children / Child Exploitation Detail Task Force over email or by calling 408-277-4102.

title: Medical cosmetic treatments in Mexico offer big savings. Why Americans are making the trip as potential risks remain
description: CBS California Investigates accompanied a group of women traveling from San Diego to Lipo Tijuana VIP, a medical spa that attracts patients from across the United States.
author_name: Kristine  Lazar, Amy  Corral, Chelsea  Hylton
content: As healthcare and living costs strain many household budgets, some Americans are looking beyond the U.S. border for cosmetic treatments they say they cannot afford at home.In Tijuana, Mexico, a growing number of medical tourists are seeking discounted procedures, including Botox injections, laser treatments and other aesthetic services. For some, even the cost of airfare and a hotel does not erase the potential savings.CBS California Investigates accompanied a group of women traveling from San Diego to Lipo Tijuana VIP, a medical spa that attracts patients from across the United States.The group included women from Mississippi, South Carolina and Southern California who traveled to the clinic for a range of cosmetic treatments.Alisha Thornlimb, known online as @hippie girl.modernworld, who organizes group trips for people seeking beauty treatments in Mexico, said she started the business after videos of her own experiences went viral on social media."I had a lot of ladies that were like, 'I want to go, but I'm scared. But take me with you,'" Thornlimb said.
