"We'll try it once and see how it goes, and the rest is kind of history."The price differences can be substantial, according to a comparison of treatments at Lipo Tijuana VIP and prices in the Los Angeles area.Thornlimb said carbon dioxide, or CO2, fractional laser treatment for the face, neck and chest that might cost about $1,800 where she lives was available in Tijuana for $220.Botox, another popular treatment, costs about $5 to $6 per unit at the Tijuana location, compared with $10 to $12 per unit in the U.S.Other prices cited in the comparison included:Sculptra: $585 per vial in Tijuana, compared with an estimated $800 to $950 in the Los Angeles area.Dysport: $250 for 50 units in Tijuana, compared with as much as $450 in Los Angeles.CO2 laser treatment: $595 for the face, neck and chest in Tijuana, compared with an estimated $1,200 to $1,500 in Los Angeles.HydroDiamond facial: $85 in Tijuana, compared with at least $175 in Los Angeles.Dr. Pedro Cota of Lipo Tijuana VIP said lower labor costs account for much of the difference."The product is the same, the quality standard and everything is the same," Cota said. "The only thing that changes is the labor because here the income is less, so the labor is cheaper."Cota said about 70% of his clientele comes from the U.S.For some patients, the lower prices make cosmetic procedures financially accessible.Shannon Watson traveled from Mississippi to receive treatments at the Tijuana clinic. She said the procedures would have been unaffordable for her at home."Definitely not," Watson said when asked whether she could afford the treatments in Mississippi. Even after accounting for airfare and hotel expenses, she said, the trip remained less expensive than receiving the same treatments at home. She added that her family initially questioned her decision to travel to Mexico for cosmetic care."They thought I was crazy," she said.Despite her family's concerns, Watson said she would consider returning for additional procedures and bringing her daughter along.Thornlimb said the trips appeal to women who want to spend money on themselves but cannot justify the cost of treatments in the U.S."It's an accessible thing, and then it makes everybody be able to feel maybe a little better about themselves that you maybe wouldn't be able to do before," she said.While lower prices can be appealing, experts caution that cosmetic procedures performed abroad carry risks, just as they do in the U.S.Stephanie Lopez says she learned that firsthand after receiving Botox at a different medical spa in Tijuana.Lopez said she initially noticed small bumps on her forehead after the injections but assumed they were caused by swelling. Later that night, she woke up with pain and larger bumps that felt bruised."I was really concerned," Lopez said.The bumps eventually disappeared, but Lopez said the experience changed her perspective on seeking cosmetic treatments abroad."You just never know," she said. "I'm glad it was just Botox. I'm glad that it wasn't something more extreme, something surgical. But still, not the best experience."Elizabeth Ziemba, president of Medical Tourism Training Inc., said patients should understand the risks before undergoing any medical procedure."There are risks with any kind of medical procedure that you have," Ziemba said. "It's changing your anatomy in some way, whether it's something as simple as a Botox injection or something as complicated as brain surgery or organ transplant."A 2022 study by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention found that of more than 93,000 medical tourists surveyed, 5% reported complications. That figure does not establish the risk for every procedure or destination, and patients should not assume that a low reported complication rate means a particular treatment is safe.Ziemba said patients can take steps to reduce their risk by researching providers and checking their qualifications."Make sure you've verified licensure and credentialing, you feel comfortable, you've asked a lot of questions," she said.Patients considering care abroad should also research the clinic, the practitioner's training and experience, the products being used, emergency procedures and what follow-up care would be available if complications develop after returning home.Insurance is another consideration. Although insurance options for medical travel exist, premiums and other costs could reduce the overall savings.Watson said she would consider undergoing plastic surgery under anesthesia in Mexico. Diane Way, who traveled from Lake Elsinore, said she was interested in returning for a procedure to remove loose skin.Their plans underscore the appeal of medical tourism for patients seeking treatment at a lower price. But experts say cost should not be the only factor in choosing where to receive care.

title: Blaine teen followed man from restaurant parking lot before shooting him on Highway 100, charges say
description: A teenager from Blaine, Minnesota, is accused of tailing a driver along Highway 100 in St. Louis Park​ and shooting him in the ankle.
content: A teenager from Blaine, Minnesota, is accused of tailing a driver along Highway 100 in St. Louis Park and shooting him in the ankle.According to the criminal complaint, the shooting happened on the southbound lane of the highway near Excelsior Boulevard shortly after 6 p.m. on Sept. 30. Officers saw six bullet strikes on a Honda Accord and saw several discharged cartridge casings along the road.Two people in the Honda Accord said they had gone out to eat in Columbia Heights and were on their way to Minnetonka. They noticed a black Hyundai Sonata with heavily tinted windows in the restaurant parking lot. The driver said he thought the Hyundai Sonata was following him, charges say.Video surveillance of the restaurant shows the Hyundai Sonata in the parking lot. It then exits the lot shortly after the Honda Accord leaves, according to documents.The Blaine teen is the registered owner of the Hyundai Sonata, and his cell phone data showed he was at the restaurant parking lot and along the highway, charges say.The casings found along the road match several other shootings, including one in Anoka County on Sept. 5 and one in Minneapolis on July 19. One of the casings matches a Burnsville shooting on Feb. 13, in which the St. Louis Park highway victim was also the target, charges say.The teenager is charged with drive-by shooting and second-degree assault. He is in custody.

title: Don Mattingly was Phillies' top choice for manager, Dombrowski says
description: Dave Dombrowski spoke at his end-of-season press conference just one day after naming Don Mattingly the full-time manager.
content: Philadelphia Phillies president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski spoke at his end-of-season press conference Thursday morning, just one day after naming Don Mattingly the full-time manager.Mattingly will stay on as the team's manager for at least the next two seasons, dropping his "interim" tag, the team announced Wednesday. He took over for Rob Thomson, who was fired in April when the team got off to a 9-19 start.Under Mattingly, the Phils went 79-55 and made their fifth-straight postseason appearance. The Phillies were ultimately eliminated by the Atlanta Braves in the National League Wild Card Series.Dombrowski said Mattingly was offered the full-time manager role just days after the Phillies were eliminated. The team delayed the announcement because the Eagles were playing that weekend and Mattingly had a family trip.Mattingly agreed to a two-year deal and was officially named manager Wednesday.Dombrowski emphasized that Mattingly was a leading candidate for the position and the first person offered the role.Dombrowski acknowledged the disappointing postseason and already promising changes.Dombrowski announced the team has hired former Mets manager Carlos Mendoza, who will serve as the team's infield and third-base coach. The Mets hired Mendoza ahead of the 2024 season. He only made the playoffs once as the Mets manager, when the team defeated the Thomson-led Phillies in the 2024 NLDS.The 46-year-old was dismissed from the Mets halfway through the 2026 season after a disastrous start, which included a 12-game losing streak in April. The Phillies also reportedly parted ways with hitting coach Kevin Long and infield coach Bobby Dickerson.

title: California High-Speed Rail consultants commute from out of state on taxpayers' dime, receipts show
description: Receipts also reveal a 23% pay increase for a key Denver-based consultant after Ian Coudri became CEO.
content: When an engineering firm won a $131 million contract to help design California's high-speed rail, track, and overhead electrical system, it promised that six key personnel positions would be based in Sacramento full time.Records obtained by CBS California show the consultants in three of those six key positions never relocated to Sacramento. Instead, taxpayers paid to fly them into the office — one from Texas and two from Denver — in some cases, almost every week.Records show the senior consultant was only in the office a few days a week, while his hourly billing rate rose nearly 23% under California High-Speed Rail Authority CEO Ian Choudri.Whistleblowers inside the authority say the absence of key decision-makers is stifling productivity, making it harder for state employees to get answers, hold meetings, and move the project forward.These revelations come after nearly three decades and more than $15 billion spent on California's High-Speed Rail project, yet California still hasn't laid a mile of high-speed rail track. The project recently lost $4 billion in federal funding and could run out of money by the end of 2027, even as the authority paid four consulting contractors more than $250 million over two fiscal years, all four of which were examined in an inspector general investigation into wasteful and unallowable travel expenses. This is the second installment of The Receipts, a CBS California investigative series examining consultant spending, oversight and influence over the state's multibillion-dollar high-speed rail project.After the inspector general uncovered widespread failures in consultant travel oversight, whistleblowers provided CBS California with some of the receipts and other materials that were the focus of the investigation.In Part 1, we revealed that highly paid consultants charged taxpayers for late-night and early morning rides back to their hotels from the CEO's home and nearby restaurants.On October 9, the High-Speed Rail Authority's board held a special meeting just hours after CBS California published that story. Board members did not directly question CEO Ian Choudri about the inspector general's findings or CBS California's, and Choudri declined to answer our questions after the meeting. The board ultimately voted 7-2 to restrict his independent contracting authority, requiring advance approval from the authority's attorneys for contract decisions within his $25 million delegated authority.As CBS California continues reviewing receipts and interviewing current and former high-speed rail employees, our findings raise new questions about consultant spending, influence, and oversight that the board will ultimately have to address.With the project under mounting financial pressure, the consultants responsible for helping design it now face questions about whether they delivered what California is paying for.Why is California paying consultants to fly to Sacramento when they were supposed to relocate there?CBS California reviewed approximately 6,000 pages of records associated with the SYSTRA|TYPSA Joint Venture, including its contract, invoices, travel claims, airline receipts, staffing records and internal office photographs. The joint venture is identified only as the "Track & Systems Design contractor" in the inspector general's report, but its office has since confirmed it is the contractor referenced.The firm has a $131.2 million contract to design track and overhead electrical systems for California's high-speed rail project.The inspector general found that the California High-Speed Rail Authority paid more than $76,000 for key personnel to travel from out of state between 2024 and 2026. Receipts obtained exclusively by CBS California Investigates reveal more.The firm's proposal said its key personnel were "100% committed to relocating to Sacramento." Travel records between July 2024 and May 2025 document repeated flights involving three key positions.The current digital manager is based in Denver, while the current design engineering manager travels from Austin, Texas. Both replaced employees originally named in the contract. Records indicate neither the original employees in those positions nor their replacements relocated to Sacramento.One consultant. Twenty-five trips. More than $31,000.Robert Kennah, SYSTRA's principal-in-charge, was one of the six original key consultants who signed an April 2024 letter committing to work full time in Sacramento. Instead, records show Kennah has been flying in to work in the office two to five times a month.CBS California identified 25 trips or travel claims between his Denver home and Sacramento from July 2024 through May 2025, with airfare, hotels and ground transportation billed to California taxpayers.After the rail authority's contract manager reminded SYSTRA of its Sacramento staffing requirements in December 2024, the trips dropped to about once a month, but taxpayers continued paying for them through May 2025.The inspector general found the same pattern. The contract manager told investigators that a senior consultant needed to work with a Denver-based team, but the watchdog questioned why taxpayers should cover travel costs driven by the firm's staffing arrangements.The authority did not answer our specific questions.Scheduled three days per week, billing for fiveWhistleblowers provided photographs covering about nine months of a Sacramento office whiteboard labeled "Who is in the Office?" The initials RK indicate when Kennah was expected to be in.Together, the photos and travel records detail a consistent three-day-per-week in-office pattern while billing for five days.The whiteboard isn't a verified attendance record and doesn't establish where he worked or whether he billed improperly, but it raises questions about how the authority verified his Sacramento staffing commitment and whether the correct billing rate was applied.Kennah's hourly billing rate jumped nearly 23%Shortly after Choudri was appointed CEO in 2024, Kennah's hourly billing rate increased by nearly 23% to $505.91, while California was still paying for his trips between Denver and Sacramento.The contract includes a calculation that pays eligible consultants more when they work from their home office rather than the Sacramento headquarters. However, the contract lists Sacramento as Kennah's office and specifies the lower rate.After Choudri took over, however, Kennah began consistently billing the higher rate, even when records indicate he was in Sacramento.The authority did not answer our specific questions about the higher billing rate, who approved it or whether Kennah was eligible for it.California paid more for the same number of hours under ChoudriThe difference becomes more apparent when comparing invoices.The state was billed nearly $13,000 more for 22 days' worth of work.The records also don't establish that either invoice contained an unauthorized charge, but they show how much the cost of one consultant's work and travel increased in less than a year.During much of that period, the authority was still paying for flights from Denver.What was California getting for the additional spending? The authority did not respond to our specific questions.The state rated the work "Very Good"Despite the findings involving travel and staffing, the authority's own performance evaluation praised the contractor.In July 2025, SYSTRA|TYPSA received a "Very Good" rating. The contract manager called the firm's work "superb."The June 2025 invoice included a $318,048.57 performance-fee adjustment. That positive assessment matters.The travel investigation doesn't establish that the firm's engineering designs were deficient and nothing in the records independently establishes that the performance adjustment was improper.However, the performance rating raises a separate accountability question.Was the authority evaluating only the work the contractor delivered, or also whether it fulfilled the staffing and travel commitments it made to win the contract?If those requirements weren't enforced, who was responsible?A quarter-billion dollars in consultant payments. Who's watching?Since Ian Choudri became CEO, California's high-speed rail project has fallen further behind, even as the authority said it is paying four major consulting contractors more than a quarter-billion dollars over two fiscal years.And that money wasn't for laying track.These contractors provide legal advice, financial guidance, program management and engineering design. Their work helps shape what gets built, how it gets built and what taxpayers pay.Whistleblowers inside the high-speed rail authority question whether the projected savings account for further delays and additional consultant work.The authority says it's revising designs and reducing the project's scope to cut costs. But the inspector general found the schedule slipped nine months in less than a year, while much of the projected savings came from plans to build less, including reducing sections of the railway from two tracks to one.Meanwhile, CBS California uncovered missed train-purchasing deadlines that cost the state $4 billion in federal funding.The authority says in-person work mattersIn its response to the inspector general's investigation, the California High-Speed Rail Authority defended paying to fly consultants into the office, citing Gov. Gavin Newsom's return-to-office executive order for state workers.But the inspector general noted that the order applies to state agencies and employees — not consultant travel.Further, the SYSTRA contract already required its key personnel to work in Sacramento. State employees aren't reimbursed for commuting to their regular workplace.In a response to CBS California, the authority said it is tightening travel oversight, updating reimbursement rules and requiring new training for consultants and contract managers before approving additional travel expenses."Only travel that is pre-approved, within contract scope and consistent with state regulations will be eligible for reimbursement," the authority said.Those broader savings figures don't explain why the authority paid prohibited international travel expenses or repeatedly reimbursed key personnel to travel to Sacramento.In a response to CBS California, the SYSTRA|TYPSA Joint Venture said: "We take all matters related to contract compliance, governance, and billing seriously, and we address them through established internal review and oversight processes," said Heather Hornyak, the firm's director of corporate communications.The joint venture declined to answer specific questions and did not explain why three key positions involved out-of-state travel despite its Sacramento staffing commitment, who approved Kennah's higher billing rate or why the authority was charged for travel the inspector general found prohibited under the contract.CBS California also sent Kennah detailed questions about his travel, billing rate and Sacramento work schedule. Kennah did not respond.The missing $250 million slideThe California High-Speed Rail Authority initially prepared a presentation responding to the inspector general's investigation that emphasized how little it spent on consultant travel compared with total consultant payments.The original presentation included a pie chart showing that the authority paid four consulting contractors approximately $252.7 million over two fiscal years. About $2 million went toward travel.The inspector general reviewed roughly half of that travel spending and found more than half was unallowable under state regulations or contract terms.But the pie chart disappeared from the presentation the authority ultimately delivered to its board.The revised version also removed the contract-by-contract payment totals.Asked why, an authority spokesperson said in an email, "The information was streamlined to keep the focus clear for the Board and the public."But whistleblowers inside the authority say the spending figures raise a much bigger accountability question.If California couldn't enforce basic travel and staffing requirements, who was overseeing the rest of the quarter-billion dollars paid to these consultants?The receipts in this investigation don't establish that Kennah or SYSTRA caused the project's delays, but they raise questions about whether the authority enforced the contracts with the consultants who are helping design it.We'll continue pushing for answers.

title: Illinois voter guide for the 2026 midterm election: How to register, vote by mail, find my polling place, more
description: The 2026 midterm election is on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. This is what you need to know about getting ready to vote in Illinois.
content: The 2026 midterm election will be held Tuesday, November 3, 2026, with parties vying for control of the Congress. Illinois voters will choose their next governor, as well as who will replace longtime representatives in the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate, including the successor to Senator Dick Durbin's seat. See our full 2026 Illinois election guide here.Here's everything you need to know to be ready to vote in Illinois for the the 2026 midterm election. When is Election Day?Election Day for the midterms is Tuesday, November 3, 2026.Polls are open from 6 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Election Day for in-person voting. Register to vote in IllinoisAll residents of Illinois who are U.S. citizens and over the age of 18 are eligible to vote in the 2026 midterm elections. Residents who are 17 at the time of the primary but who will be 18 by the day of the general election are also able to vote in both elections. That means if you're turning 18 on or before Nov. 3, 2026, you can still vote in the Illinois primaries.You also must have been a resident of the precinct in which you register to vote for at least 30 days before Election Day. To register to vote, you can visit the your nearest county clerk's office, the Illinois Board of Election Commissioner's Office, city, village and township offices, public libraries, schools, military recruitment offices and other locations specially designated by the state board of elections. You can also register to vote online. If you're not sure if you're already registered to vote, or if you think you need to update your existing registration, you can check and make changes online through the State Board of Elections. You can register to vote in Illinois up to 27 days before the election. However, Illinois offers grace period registration and voting all the way up to and on Election Day. To take advantage of that, you will need to register to vote and cast your ballot at the same time at the same location, in person.Grace period registration and voting starts the day after the deadline for regular registration and runs until polls close on Election Day. Does Illinois require ID to vote?If you register to vote in person or by mail, you will need to provide two forms of valid identification. These include a driver's license or state ID, government check or paycheck, bank statement, passport, utility bill, lease or mortgage, student ID and mail addressed to your current residence, or other government documents. At least one of the forms of ID you present must have your current address so you can be registered to the correct precinct.To register to vote online, or update your existing registration, you will need your full Illinois driver's license or state ID number, the last four digits of your social security number and the date your driver's license or state ID was issued. Illinois does not require a voter to present ID when casting a ballot outside a narrow set of circumstances. How do I find my polling place?You can find your polling place, where you will cast your ballot, on the Illinois Board of Elections website by clicking here. Most people will not need ID to vote on Election Day, but if you are registering in person during the grace period or on Election Day, or if your voting rights are challenged at your polling place, you will be asked for identification. It's advised to make sure you have at least one form of government ID, like a state ID or driver's license, on you when you go to vote.If you cannot prove your identity or eligibility, you can still cast a provisional ballot in Illinois. Illinois early voting hours and locationsEarly voting began on Sept. 24 statewide, 40 days before the general election Nov. 3. Most counties will have a temporary early voting location or locations for the beginning of early voting, with permanent locations opening a few weeks before Election Day, in early October. CBS News Chicago has a complete list of early voting sites in Chicago and the surrounding counties. For a complete list of all early voting locations in Illinois, visit the Illinois Board of Elections website.Any registered voter in Illinois can vote early for any reason. All you need to do is go to a designated early voting location. Click here to look up the early voting site near you. Most early voting sites also offer grace period registration if you're voting on Election Day. Illinois Vote by MailAll voters can request a vote by mail ballot for any Illinois election. The first day to file an application for the state to send a ballot for this year's elections was Dec. 17, 2025. All requests for a mail-in ballot must be received by the state Election Authority by Feb. 5, 2026. You can also get a vote by mail ballot in person at your election authority or from their website. Vote by mail starts 40 days before Election Day for regular voters and 45 days before Election day for military or overseas ballots. All vote by mail ballots must be postmarked no later than Election Day and received within 14 days of Election Day. However, the U.S. Postal Service quietly made changes to their postmarking process at the end of 2025 which means some mail may no longer get a same-day postmark, the result of cost cuts to USPS transportation operations that may delay the arrival of posted letters at its processing facilities, where the postmarks are issued. As such, anyone voting by mail is encouraged to send their completed ballot as soon as they can to ensure it gets a valid postmark.Illinois also allows voters to authorize any person to return their ballot to an election authority in person, a long as the voter has signed the affidavit on the envelope affirming they gave that authorization. You can also drop your vote by mail into collection site drop boxes before the close of polls on Election Day, postage-free.Who is on my ballot?You can look up sample ballot for your specific district on the Illinois Board of Elections website.

title: History Colorado Center is now the Colorado History Museum
description: The Colorado History Museum said the new name tells visitors that they will experience a museum dedicated to exploring Colorado's stories, cultures, and history.
content: History Colorado Center is now the Colorado History Museum. The state's history institution and museum network said the new name tells visitors that they will experience a museum dedicated to exploring Colorado's stories, cultures and history. "Museums are beloved institutions for their resilience, trust, and community power, and we are proud to be a long part of this tradition," said Dawn DiPrince, History Colorado President/CEO and State Historic Preservation Officer in a statement. "Colorado History Museum is wonderfully straightforward. Clarity builds bridges and creates access, which are bedrocks of our organizational values."History Colorado is a statewide organization with 11 museums, historic sites, collections care, research, historic preservation and archaeology, educational programs and community partnerships across Colorado. That name will remain the same; it's History Colorado Center, the specific location at 1200 Broadway in downtown Denver, that will undergo a name change. "Museums create spaces where people can connect with one another, encounter different perspectives and better understand the communities around them," said Kelly Brough, Chair of the History Colorado Board of Directors, in a statement. "The Board is proud to support a name that clearly and confidently reflects what this place is while opening the door to its future."The Colorado History Museum is open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Admission for kids 18 and under is free every day.

title: 2027 Sundance Film Festival passes on sale Oct. 15
description: The Sundance Film Festival's debut in Boulder is less than four months away and passes go on sale Oct. 15.
content: The Sundance Film Festival's debut in Boulder is less than four months away and passes go on sale Oct. 15. Festival passes and ticket packages will go on sale at 10 a.m. for both in-person and online screenings.The festival schedule will be available in early/mid December, with film screening selection for ticket package holders beginning Jan. 7, 2027. Single film tickets go on sale Jan. 8, 2027, with member pre-sale beginning the day before. Tens of thousands of people are expected to visit during the 11-day event in January. The 2027 Sundance Film Festival will take place Jan. 21–31, 2027, in Boulder. World premieres are scheduled Jan. 21 to Jan. 26. The winners of the Robert Redford Luminary Award will also be honored.The festival was founded in 1981 by Robert Redford and had previously been held in Park City, Utah.

title: South Side Chamber of Commerce says summer street festival helped decrease crime rates
description: In an effort to curb violence and crime on Pittsburgh's South Side, the South Side Street Festival was introduced, and it's believed to have worked.
content: In response to frequent violence and crime on Pittsburgh's South Side during the late-night hours, this summer, the South Side Street Festival was created to combat public safety issues. While there were mixed reactions at the time, the numbers are now backing up the idea. On one hand, people were supporting it with the hopes it would lower crime rates, while on the other, a petition was created to put an end to it. Now, the numbers show a declining crime rate. "The numbers don't lie," said Peter Margittai, president of the South Side Chamber of Commerce. "I think that it's a huge success from the public safety side." The South Side Street Festival closed a six-block stretch of East Carson Street to vehicle traffic on weekend nights. Entry was also restricted to anyone under 21. "I think the most telling numbers were arrests, which there were 62 arrests in 2025 and 25 in 2026," Margittai said. "So, a significant drop. The one that's phenomenal is firearms recovered. We had 33 in 2025 in that duration of time, and we only had two in 2026." The chamber also cited traffic stops being down 73%, traffic citations being down 35%, tows down 39%, and quality of life citations down 75%. However, critics argued the festival moved violence and traffic to the back streets, harming businesses. "The reason why the number is down is that no one was here," said Rich Cupka. "90% of the businesses down there were affected because the customers couldn't get to them because of the blockade." Margittai said he recognizes that complaint, and that there were bumps in the road, but overall, the festival's main goal was public safety, and they believe it worked. "We have not seen any kind of resurgence in crime, and we have not seen those numbers go up," he said. The chamber said there will be talks in the future about the festival and a return in 2027.

title: JD Vance to keynote GOP campaign rally in Monroe, Michigan
description: Vice President JD Vance will be the guest speaker at a Midterm Rally taking place on Thursday in Monroe, the Republican National Committee says.
content: Vice President JD Vance is headed to Monroe, Michigan, on Thursday for a midterm rally, the same day he sits down with "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil for a town hall with Michigan voters.The rally is at LevelUp Training Complex on Stewart Road, just east of U.S. 24/Telegraph Road. Doors open at 1 p.m. and the event begins at 2:45 p.m., according to the latest details from organizers. Vance's time at the podium was not provided. A sign-up link for the event was posted on the GOP website. LevelUp is an indoor sports complex and fitness center with spaces available for rent.The city of Monroe has posted road closures for Thursday afternoon in connection with Vance's visit. Vance's town hall, "Things That Matter: A Town Hall With Vice President JD Vance," airs at 8 p.m. ET/PT Saturday, Oct. 17, on the CBS Television Network and streams on Paramount+. The one-hour special will also be available afterward on CBSNews.com, YouTube and CBS News 24/7.The audience will be Michigan voters from across the political spectrum. Vance is expected to discuss the midterm races and the issues shaping voters' choices, including affordability, tariffs, immigration, health care, artificial intelligence, the war with Iran and the state of American democracy.Vance was last in Southeast Michigan on Aug. 31, when he spoke at an event in Sterling Heights.The Nov. 3 election is a midterm, not a presidential contest, but President Trump and Vance have both campaigned heavily for Republicans with so many U.S. Senate and congressional seats in contention.Michigan is closely watched in part because of the open Senate seat, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers are in a tight race.Paramount Skydance is the parent company of CBS News.

title: Cow shot by authorities after escaping truck on US-127 in Ingham County
description: A cow fell from a livestock trailer near the northbound US-127 exit ramp at Lake Lansing Road and was killed by local law enforcement on Wednesday, Ingham County Animal Control and Shelter (ICACS) says.
content: A cow fell from a livestock trailer near the northbound US-127 exit ramp at Lake Lansing Road and was killed by local law enforcement on Wednesday, Ingham County Animal Control and Shelter says.The cow was improperly secured during transport, and the individual transporting it was unaware the cow was missing until they arrived at their destination, over an hour away, the shelter says.ICACS officers were contacted by local law enforcement to assist with transporting the cow before it moved from the highway area into nearby residential neighborhoods to the east, which posed an ongoing public safety concern, according to the ICACS.ICACS officers then attempted to chemically immobilize the cow and contain and secure it, but the medications had little to no effect, and the cow moved into a densely populated residential area with an elementary school nearby, the shelter says.The shelter says that a veterinarian was brought to the scene to assist in another attempt to immobilize the cow chemically, but the attempt was unsuccessful, leading to the decision to kill the cow using a firearm by local law enforcement."This was an unfortunate outcome to a challenging situation," ICACS said. "Unfortunately, as the situation escalated, the safety of residents and the surrounding community had to remain the priority."

title: Pope Leo resumes some papal duties as he recovers from lung surgery, Vatican says
description: Pope Leo XIV has resumed some work, the Vatican said Thursday, after he had a piece of his right lung removed and received a diagnosis of lung cancer.
content: Pope Leo XIV has resumed some papal duties, the Vatican said Thursday, after he had a piece of his right lung removed and received a diagnosis of lung cancer earlier this week. A spokesperson for the Vatican said the pope celebrated Mass around noon and began "a little bit of work activity," including reading documents. The pontiff also met with Archbishop Paolo Rudelli, undersecretary of state, on Thursday, the Vatican said. Leo is set to be released from Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Oct. 20, one week after he was first admitted. The Vatican spokesperson said Leo would like to lead the Angelus prayer from the hospital on Sunday, but it's not clear yet whether that will happen. Leo also underwent routine checkups, including a chest X-ray, on Thursday, according to personal physician Dr. Luigi Carbone and thoracic surgeon Dr. Stefano Margaritora. Margaritora led the operation on the pontiff. The X-ray showed "good recovery of the operated lung," the two said in a statement, and the pope's "post-operative recovery is progressing as expected." The pope has also had at least one physiotherapy session, Carbone and Margaritora said. Candida Moss, the Edward Cadbury professor of theology at the University of Birmingham in England, told CBS News on Wednesday that it's typical for popes to stick to their schedules even amid health issues. Vatican protocols call for the pope's cardinals and aide to take over as many duties as possible, Moss said. "We have a long tradition of popes — not just Pope Francis, but also Pope John Paul II, who had Parkinson's for 10 years — who continued to remain as active as they could, and as active in Catholic liturgies as they could, right up until the end of their tenures," Moss said. The Vatican announced Leo had been diagnosed with lung cancer on Tuesday following his surgery.Preoperative tests had indicated the potential presence of the cancer, the Vatican said earlier this week. During the 90-minute operation, a lobe of the pontiff's right lung that had a nodular lesion was removed, the Vatican said. The Vatican has not shared any other details about Leo's cancer, such as its stage or genetic makeup.Leo is expected to travel to South America next month. The Vatican pointed to comments the pontiff made Sunday, when he said he is looking forward to going. The pope's audiences are canceled through Oct. 20.

title: Meet the Minnesota-based coconut oil company changing lives in the Philippines
description: Olsen says the primary industry in the area was coconut farming, and many farmers had found themselves tied to predatory loans, with interest rates as high as 200%.
content: Erik Olsen knew there was a mission to accomplish before he even knew what it was. It's what led him to leave a successful business venture for war-torn Iraq in 2003. "My mom thought I was going to come back in a coffin," he jokes decades later. From there, it led him to work with a team from Yemen, traveling the world help rescue victims of trafficking. But when he arrived in the Philippines, the mission was finally clear. "We just felt like there was more that could be done," Olsen said. "We knew there could be more impact in this area. So, we did a survey and we . . . We asked, we went to the different farmers and started asking them questions."It was then he realized the mission wasn't education, or a typhoon resistant home. It was freedom from debt â and it was tied to an industry you might not expect. Olsen says the primary industry in the area was coconut farming, and many farmers had found themselves tied to predatory loans, with interest rates as high as 200%. The result was 90% of farmers in the country living in poverty with virtually all of them drinking unclean water. Industry middlemen acted like a cartel, making sure things never had the potential to change. The solution: Dignity Made, a company that puts the control back in the hands of the farmers. Olsen and the team created a factory right in the heart of town â employing, and empowering, a community in the process. Now, the end result is an award-winning coconut product on thousands of store shelves across America. BIGGER THAN BELIEF Erik Olsen joins Adam Duxter on this week's episode of Bigger Than Belief, a weekly podcast exploring faith, belief, and religion â all through the stories of believers. With an emphasis on understanding belief through personal experience, we aim to create a conversation about faith that is fair, honest, and easy to understand, regardless of what you do (or don't) believe. We'll also take a journalistic approach to concepts and questions that are difficult to understand, while helping to make sense of current events impacting believers in our communities. You can find the entire episode now by searching Bigger Than Belief wherever you listen to podcasts.

title: Georgia school bus monitor, city council member accused of showing porn to children
description: A Georgia school bus monitor has been fired and arrested after he was accused of showing pornographic material to children while on the job.
content: A Georgia school bus monitor has been fired and arrested after he was accused of showing pornographic material to children while on the job.The Georgia Bureau of Investigation said that 70-year-old Jerry Alvin Sweat of Alma, Georgia, is charged with exhibiting harmful materials to minors.The GBI says its investigation began on Oct. 7, when the Bacon County School District asked the agency to investigate allegations that Sweat displayed the pornographic material to minors. At the time of the alleged incident, Sweat was working as a bus monitor for the school district.Sweat, who also represents District 3 on the Alma City Council, turned himself in to authorities on Tuesday and was booked into the Bacon County Jail. He was fired from his position as school bus monitor before his arrest.The investigation remains ongoing and officials are asking anyone with information on the case to call the GBI Regional Investigative Office in Douglas at 912-389-4103 or the agency's tip line at 1-800-597-8477.

title: Trump formally asserts executive privilege in legal fight over Kennedy Center's closure
description: President Trump has formally invoked executive privilege to shield certain records from a Democratic congresswoman who sits on the Kennedy Center board.
content: Washington — President Trump has formally invoked executive privilege to shield certain records from Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty of Ohio as part of her ongoing legal challenge to the president's effort to temporarily shutter the Kennedy Center for renovations. White House deputy counsel Joshua Hoyt informed a federal judge on Wednesday of Mr. Trump's formal assertion of the presidential communications privilege, a form of executive privilege. Hoyt said it covers information, documents or communications between Mr. Trump, his advisers and Kennedy Center employees about the president's duties and "the effective functioning" of the performing arts institution.Hoyt argued that because the president appoints members of the Kennedy Center's board and a related Advisory Committee on the Arts, he must "familiarize himself" with the institution's management, operations, fundraising efforts and planned activities."I believe that, without the protection of the presidential communications privilege over the communications described above, presidential advisors and their staff members would be chilled from gathering relevant information, exploring alternatives, and providing fully informed recommendations regarding the performance of the President's duties," the White House lawyer wrote in a declaration.In a separate filing, Justice Department lawyers accused Beatty of conducting a "fishing expedition" that raises separation-of-powers concerns."Even though the President's statutory duties and the Chairman's trust duties overlap, what matters for the purpose of executive privilege is that Plaintiff seeks information, documents, and communications concerning the President's actions in his official capacity," they argued.Executive privilege is not absolute and can be overcome by an adequate showing of need for the information at issue.The Kennedy Center's board of trustees, composed of Trump administration officials and the president's allies, elected Mr. Trump as its chairman last year, making him the first sitting president to hold the role. His effort to invoke executive privilege to shield records relating to the Kennedy Center raises new and untested questions of whether the protection extends to the president's actions as chairman of the performing arts institution, which was created by Congress in 1958 and is funded through a mix of federal dollars, ticket revenue and private donations.The president asserted executive privilege over a number of records relating to his attempt to close the Kennedy Center for two years to allow for renovations, its financial condition, the effort to add Mr. Trump's name to the building's facade and the possibility that the Kennedy Center could be demolished.Concerns that the building could be razed emerged after Mr. Trump said last month that the Kennedy Center will close and "end up being ripped down" if he and his administration did not get recognition for raising money and spearheading repairs to the institution.Mr. Trump was also photographed on Air Force One looking at a placard that appeared to say "Kennedy Center Demolished."The brewing fight over executive privilege comes as part of a lawsuit Beatty filed in December challenging the board's move to change the center's name to the Donald J. Trump and The John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts and shutter the institution for two years for renovations. Beatty is an ex officio member of the Kennedy Center's Board of Trustees.In May, U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper blocked the center's closure and ordered Mr. Trump's name to be removed from the building's facade. Construction crews stripped the president's name from the exterior in June, but the front portico of the building has since been covered by a tarp, concealing most of its name. Cooper has also allowed Beatty to collect information from the Kennedy Center about the decision to close the main building and any potential demolition, and to take depositions, a process known as discovery.But Beatty's lawyers said that the Justice Department sought to block her inquiries about any input and instructions Kennedy Center staff received from Mr. Trump in his capacity as the board's chair and refused to turn over any documents related to those communications.They accused the Justice Department of "improperly asserting a blanket privilege in an unprecedented fashion" and asked Cooper to order the Kennedy Center to turn over the material Beatty is seeking.In response to Beatty's inquiries, Justice Department lawyers said late last month that "to the extent the discovery requests seek communications involving the President or White House personnel, they are inappropriate because they may have the effect of seeking information protected by the presidential communications privilege."During a deposition with Matthew Floca, executive director and chief operating officer of the Kennedy Center, last week, a Justice Department lawyer repeatedly instructed Floca not to answer certain questions from one of Beatty's lawyers based on a protective assertion of executive privilege.

title: Fairfield police arrest man suspected of vandalizing campaign signs for local elections
description: A man has been arrested after multiple campaign signs for candidates in city elections were damaged, Fairfield police said.
content: A man has been arrested on a felony vandalism charge after multiple campaign signs for candidates in city elections were damaged, Fairfield police said on Thursday. Police said over the last several weeks, multiple campaign signs were reported to have been vandalized. City cameras and surveillance video from a local business were used to obtain an image of the suspect, identified as 68-year-old Jesus PiedraPiedra was arrested on Oct. 13 and booked into jail on a count of felony vandalism. The arrest comes just weeks before midterm elections on Nov. 3. Current Fairfield Vice Mayor Pam Bertani, who is a candidate in the city's mayoral race, applauded the arrest. "A huge THANK YOU to Officer Willie Smith, Chief Dan Marshall, and the entire Fairfield Police Department for their work on this investigation," Bertani wrote in a Facebook post. Piedra remains in custody with bail set at $25,000, according to county jail records.

title: Elk Grove Village to give $200 gift cards to all households after data center property sale
description: A $200 bonus is coming to thousands of households in the northwest Chicago suburb of Elk Grove Village.
content: A $200 bonus is coming to thousands of households in the northwest Chicago suburb of Elk Grove Village.The village is sending prepaid Visa gift cards to all of its 14,000 households. The money is coming from data centers, a hot-button issue in several suburbs.The sale of two data center properties for more than $1.4 billion generated more than $4 million in real estate transfer tax revenue, according to the village.Elk Grove Village has decided to pass along the windfall to residents."Our thriving business community helps us keep costs down for residents every day," Elk Grove Village Mayor Craig Johnson said in a news release. "But every so often, we get a chance to do something a little extra and share some of that success directly with our residents. That's a special opportunity, and we're glad to be able to do it."The village noted that it has provided direct financial relief to residents five times in the last six years. The village also issued $200 water bill credits to every household and waived certain business and license fees for its businesses during the COVID-19 pandemic, and also distributed $200 Visa prepaid gift cards to residents in 2022 and 2024.The 2024 gift card distribution was also funded by revenues involving a data center.

title: Minnesota Marine missing in action in WWII returns home after remains identified
description: A Minnesota man who served in the U.S. Marine Corps during WWII returned home Thursday morning after he was listed as missing in action for eight decades.
content: A Minnesota man who served in the U.S. Marine Corps during WWII returned home Thursday morning after he was listed as missing in action for eight decades.Ernest LaVerne Lund was born in Goodhue County in 1915, the second youngest child in a family of 14 siblings. He worked on farms until 1943, when he enlisted in the Marines.According to his obituary, Lund died on May 21, 1944 while working aboard LST-353 when it exploded in the West Loch Disaster at the Pearl Harbor Naval Base in Hawaii. The Navy, Army and Marines were staging ships in the area to prepare for a campaign to invade the Mariana Islands. An investigation never determined the cause of the explosion, but according to Naval History and Heritage Command, it is one of the greatest non-combat disasters in U.S. history. Lund was listed as missing in action.In 1985, a group of kayakers in Pearl Harbor spotted Lund's remains, but he wasn't identified until 2026 with the help of DNA samples from his family. "It's uplifted us all that he's finally coming home," said Roger McKelvey of Bloomington. "We're finally going to have closure about Ernest Lund, our hero in our family."His remains arrived in Minneapolis on Thursday morning and formal visitation will be held in Webster, Wisconsin on Friday. His funeral is scheduled for Saturday in Markville, Minnesota.

title: Jaemor Farms creates Dolly Parton-themed corn maze in North Georgia
description: At Jaemor Farms in North Georgia, creating a corn maze takes months of planning, a little patience and help from the experts.
content: Ever wonder how a cornfield becomes a giant puzzle you can actually walk through? At Jaemor Farms in North Georgia, creating a corn maze takes months of planning, a little patience and help from the experts.The farm's latest maze pays tribute to country music legend Dolly Parton, combining a fall favorite with a celebration of the singer's music and philanthropy.Jesse Gibson and her family have called Jaemor Farms home since 1912. What was once primarily farmland and cattle pastures has evolved into a destination for families looking for seasonal fun.Each year, Gibson and her family attend Corn Party, an annual convention for corn maze owners, where they decide on a theme for the next maze."We're part of a national maze company. We actually go to a corn party conference every year." Gibson said.This year, Gibson and her sister agreed that Parton was the perfect inspiration."My sister and I were both like, 'We've got to do Dolly. Everybody loves Dolly!'" Gibson said.Planning began in April, months before visitors would step into the maze. The timing proved especially fitting when Parton passed earlier this year."She's just had such an impact, not only on music, but in her giving spirit," Gibson said. "This was just a great way for us to partner with the causes that we feel, very, very pulled to," she added.Once the design is selected, the family plants the corn and waits for it to grow. Irrigation and favorable growing conditions help the field develop, but nature does not always cooperate."Then you kind of just wait. You irrigate it, you hope it grows," Gibson said.If portions of the field do not grow evenly, the family may replant those areas early enough in the season to allow the new corn to catch up.But growing the corn is only the beginning. Turning a field into a recognizable maze requires specialized planning and careful execution.That is where the experts come in. The maze company uses GPS devices and printed maps to plot the design directly onto the field. Workers then follow the planned routes with backpack sprayers, treating specific sections of corn to create the pathways."The maize company actually comes down and they go through the maze with some GPS and some printed paper," Gibson said.The process is precise, and the farm keeps some of the details under wraps to preserve the mystery for visitors.For Gibson, the months of preparation are worth it when families arrive to explore the finished maze."It's a lot of work that goes into it. But it's so much fun," she said. "It's just a great time for us to, you know, let people come out onto this piece of land that we have love for so many years and just be a part of our story."Of course, navigating the maze is a challenge of its own. Some visitors come prepared with a map on their phones, while others rely on trial and error. Jaemor Farms employee Lynn Lewis even has a strategy for those who start to feel trapped."The thing I like about the corn maze is … because I'm claustrophobic. You can just cut through the corn and get out of there!" Lewis said with a laugh.Other visitors may find themselves calling for help.And before anyone gets hungry while finding their way out, Gibson has one important warning: The corn is not meant to be eaten."We like to tell everybody … this is not edible corn!" she said. "You would not love it!"Instead, visitors can grab a map, bring their friends, and enjoy the challenge of finding their way through the field. And if all else fails, singing a Dolly Parton song might at least make the journey more entertaining.The Jaemor Farms corn maze is open through Nov. 8.

title: Teen girl dies after being found shot in the head in Belmont Cragin home, Chicago police say
description: Woman dies after being found shot in head in Chicago's Belmont Central neighborhood
content: An 18-year-old woman died after being found shot in a home in Chicago's Belmont Central neighborhood Wednesday night, police said.Chicago police said they were called to a home in the 2700 block of North Monitor Avenue at 8:53 p.m. Wednesday. When they arrived, they found an 18-year-old woman inside the home with a gunshot wound to the head. She was taken to Loyola University Medical Center in Maywood, police said, where she was later pronounced dead.The circumstances surrounding the incident were not immediately clear. Chicago police said Area Five detectives are investigating.

title: Man accused in Fox River boat crash that killed woman appears in court in civil case
description: Man accused in Fox River boat crash that killed woman appears in court
content: A man accused of drunkenly crashing his boat and killing a woman on the Fox River northwest of Chicago over the summer was back in court Thursday.Richard Steenson, 45, was charged with one count of first-degree murder, one count of reckless homicide, three counts of aggravated DUI, and four counts of operating a watercraft under the influence in the boat crash that killed Magdalena Jablonska, 48, on July 25. He has pleaded not guilty.He is also the defendant in a civil lawsuit alleging wrongful death.On Thursday, attorneys from Jablonska's estate were trying to get access to Stevenson's financial records for the civil case, and were seeking to amend their wrongful death lawsuit to allege willful and wanton conduct and pursue punitive damages.Authorities have said Stevenson had a blood alcohol level nearly three times the legal limit when he crashed his triple-engine pontoon boat into another boat on the Fox River, killing Jablonska. Prosecutors said Stevenson was going nearly 80 miles per hour in a no-wake zone at the time of the crash.Lawyers representing Jablonska's family and her fiancé, Alan Telmini, said they filed the wrongful death lawsuit against Stevenson to further investigate the circumstances that led to the fatal crash. They will look into whether Stevenson was overserved alcohol at a business before he drove the boat, and if the three engines powering the pontoon played a part in the crash.They also want to know if anyone knowingly allowed Stevenson to operate the boat despite a history of dangerous conduct, whether anyone who owned or controlled the boat negligently entrusted it to an unsafe driver, and whether any additional parties may share responsibility for Jablonska's death.

title: Person of interest identified in sexual assault at University of Chicago frat house
description: The University of Chicago announced Wednesday morning that it has identified a person of interest in a sexual assault at a fraternity house this past weekend.
author_name: Adam  Harrington, Darius  Johnson, Jermont  Terry, Sabrina  Franza
content: The University of Chicago announced Wednesday morning that it has identified a person of interest in a sexual assault at a fraternity house this past weekend.The person of interest was identified through witness statements and video evidence, all of which has been shared with the Chicago Police Department, the university said.The university said the person of interest is not a student or affiliated with the university but has been banned from campus. A source with knowledge of the investigation told CBS News Chicago that the university has banned multiple people associated with the incident from the university. Those people, the source said, were also not students. No one was in custody as of Thursday morning. The assault happened at the Alpha Epsilon Pi (AEPi) fraternity house at 5625 S. University Ave., across the street from the west side of UChicago's Main Quad in Hyde Park.According to a University of Chicago report, a 21-year-old woman reported she was sexually assaulted in a bathroom during a frat party at 1:50 a.m. Sunday. A UChicago alert issued this week said the woman was not affiliated with the university.The woman did not know her attacker, the university said. They said when someone intervened, the unidentified suspect ran off.Surveillance video in the area picked up someone matching the description running from the frat house, UChicago said.A University of Chicago police officer on patrol was flagged down to respond, and UCPD arranged for the woman to be transported to the University of Chicago Medical Center.Students described to CBS News Chicago what it's like along Fraternity Row on University Avenue during "rush season," the time of year when fraternities and sororities are actively recruiting new members. The student said at UChicago, rush season means frequent parties and other larger events. Video has surfaced online showing a woman, who identified herself as a friend of the 21-year-old victim, chasing down a man she claimed to be her friend's attacker and yelling that he assaulted her friend in a bathroom at a frat party.Later, the friend commented that the 21-year-old woman was "drugged and taken away from us against her will…practically incapacitated, being held to the ground with a man over her, kissing her and taking her clothes off."The video appears to have been taken near the Henry Crown Field House along 56th Street, about a block from AEPi. The woman pursues the man she says is the attacker around a corner onto a pathway between the fieldhouse and the Smart Museum of Art just to the west on 56th Street.CBS News Chicago as of Thursday morning was still trying to independently verify who was recorded and if those people were definitively involved."Sexual violence, in my opinion, on college campus is not a series of isolated incidents," said Jillian Furey, a clinical services supervisor for Resilience, a standalone rape crisis center in Chicago. "It is a pervasive public health crisis.""We're going to see survivors having to relive their trauma, potentially face their perpetrator in court, be questioned and disbelieved, know that they're facing a 4% chance of a conviction rate," Furey added. "Why would someone want to retraumatize themselves again?"Students are also speaking out about the incident. "There needs to be a serious look at the safety of frats in general and whether or not they should be kept around at all," one student said.Another student said the incident is likely to ruin the wrong reputations."It's going to follow the frat around, and I think that that's unfortunate in a sense of like, people who aren't culpable aren't forced to take responsibility, and the people who are responsible generally are not forced to take responsibility," the student said.The incident at the UChicago frat house comes amid the fallout from separate sexual assault allegations at the Chi Phi fraternity house at Cornell University, which is also raising questions about fraternity culture.The National AEPi organization has told this chapter to pause all events and programs while they cooperate with the investigation. In a statement, the fraternity said, "The chapter hurts for the person who was the victim in this incident." No charges have yet been filed against the person of interest.

title: Amazon launches new "personal AI" devices that can listen to your conversations and take notes
description: The products include a silicone wristband that can be clipped to clothing and a device that magnetically attaches to the back of a phone.
content: Amazon launched two new AI gadgets on Thursday that the company says can listen to conversations, compose notes and issue reminders. The first, the Bee Frontier, is a silicone wristband that can also be clipped to clothing and retails for $74.99. Amazon also announced the Bee Eclipse, a credit card-sized device that magnetically attaches to the back of a phone and goes for $99.99.The new tech offerings are engineered by Bee, an AI wearable maker that Amazon acquired last year. Equipped with microphones, Bee's "personal AI" devices transcribe meetings or everyday conversations, helping people document moments hands-free. The devices can then recommend "personalized goals and actions" based on the conversation, Amazon said."It takes note of the details you might otherwise forget and turns them into useful conversation summaries, to-dos, reminders, and insights," the company said in its release.If someone is on a phone call planning a vacation, for example, the Bee Frontier or Bee Eclipse will create a summary of the trip, documenting details such as flight times or hotel reservations. Amazon said users can also connect Bee to existing apps such as Gmail, Google Calendar, and Microsoft Outlook, allowing the AI technology to draft follow-up emails or create calendar invites based on what was discussed. The Bee devices can also be linked to Amazon's Alexa+ and Amazon.com. Users can get conversation summaries, recaps and 14 days of memory for free; if they want more advanced capabilities, such as integration with Alexa+ and Amazon.com and suggested to-dos, they'll need a Bee Pro subscription, which costs $11.99 per month.Amazon emphasized Bee's privacy protections, noting that "no one, including Amazon, can access your data." The audio recordings are deleted after the Bee devices transcribe them, and no one can access your data unless you share it, the company said.The Bee devices are part of a trillion-dollar market of AI gadgets that companies are marketing to consumers. Meta recently announced Muse, an AI assistant that comes in the form of a pocket-sized keychain. Microsoft, OpenAI and Samsung are among the other companies that have introduced AI-powered products aimed at consumers.

title: Plano dad delivers baby in hospital parking lot after wife goes into labor early
description: Emma Contreras wanted her husband to play a bigger role in the birth of their third child. Neither expected he'd be the one catching their newborn outside the hospital.
content: Emma and Diego Contreras of Plano had already decided that Diego would take a more hands-on role in the birth of their third child, who wasn't due until the following week.But Emma might be a little more careful about what she wishes for from now on.Diego ended up being far more involved in the delivery than either of them ever imagined."So whenever we were stuck at that red light, I think that's when my heart sank, and I thought, like, 'We're in trouble,'" Diego said. "But I still did not think the baby was coming."Baby Beni, however, had other plans. He arrived in his father's waiting hands in the parking lot of Medical City Plano."I guess he was crowning," Diego said. "I saw the top of the head. And so instinctively I just, like, squatted in front of him and I don't know how much time passed, but he just slipped out."But let's back up a bit.On the morning of Oct. 11, Emma began having what she thought might be contractions.Maybe."I told Diego that I'm going to go on a walk," Emma said, "and I don't know if these are real contractions. And so, I said, if I can't make it around the block, I think I'm in labor, but I did."Walk or not, Baby Beni decided he'd waited long enough."So, I used some techniques I knew to try and stall pushing," Emma said, "which is hard. But once we got to the hospital, it just got intense so fast."By the time Diego alerted emergency room staff and rushed back to the car, he said the "urgency" of the moment could no longer be denied."She said something like, 'He's here,'" he said. "And so, I pulled her pants down, and I saw... I guess he was crowning... I saw the top of the head."Mother, baby, and two busy big brothers are all doing fine. And what a story Diego will have to share with other dads."I'm really proud of him, honestly," Emma said. "Because I did, I really did, tell our doula I wanted him more involved."Then, with a laugh, she added: "Yeah, be careful what you wish for."And what a story they'll have to tell Baby Beni one day."And it's so funny because like I said, we walk there often to go to Starbucks. So now when we walk there with these guys, we can literally point and be like that," Diego said, as Emma finished the thought. "We can say where he was born.""Yeah," Diego said. "Usually, dads are pretty useless during delivery, so I'm glad that at least for this one, I contributed!"

title: 5 family members killed in apparent murder-suicide at Coffee County home identified as investigation continues
description: Officers say they arrived at the Coffee County home after responding to a 911 call and found four of the family members shot to death.
content: Investigators with the city of Douglas, Georgia have released the identities of the five adults killed in an apparent murder-suicide last week.Douglas police officers and Coffee County sheriff's deputies say they responded shortly after 11 p.m. on Oct. 9, to a report of an active shooter at a home on the 1800 block of Robin Lane in the Touchton Wood neighborhood.At the home, investigators say they found four adults dead. A fifth adult was rushed to Coffee Regional Medical Center, where they died.On Thursday, investigators shared a statement saying that they believe that 64-year-old John Anthony Fabrizio killed his four family members before shooting himself.The four victims were identified as 64-year-old Rachel Elizabeth Fabrizio, 28-year-old James Nicholas Fabrizio, 26-year-old Rosaida Figueroa Berrios, and 26-year-old William Christopher Fabrizio. All five individuals lived in the home, investigators said.In a press conference a day after the shooting, Douglas Police Chief Brannen Pruette said that the original 911 call had been placed by Rachel Elizabeth Fabrizio and that she had been complaining that John Anthony Fabrizio was smoking inside the home.The autopsies of the victims remain pending, officials said."The department extends its condolences to the victims' loved ones and recognizes the impact this loss has had on our community. We ask the public to respect the privacy of the families during this difficult time," the Douglas Police Department wrote on Facebook.The investigation remains ongoing and officials say that they will release additional information if it is deemed appropriate.Anyone with information that could help with the case is asked to call Inv. Brittany O'Steen at 912-384-2222 or email her at bosteen@cityofdouglasga.gov. Information can also be sent to the Douglas Police Department Tip Line, which is 912-260-3600.If you or someone you know is in emotional distress or a suicidal crisis, you can reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988. You can also chat with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline here.For more information about mental health care resources and support, The National Alliance on Mental Illness (NAMI) HelpLine can be reached Monday through Friday, 10 a.m.–10 p.m. ET, at 1-800-950-NAMI (6264) or email info@nami.org.

title: Monroe officials announce road closure for vice president's visit on Thursday
description: A road closure related to Vice President JD Vance's visit to Monroe will be in effect for several hours on Thursday.
content: A road closure related to Vice President JD Vance's visit to Monroe will be in effect for several hours on Thursday.Vance is the keynote speaker at a midterm rally for Republican candidates that is taking place at LevelUp Training Complex on Stewart Road, just east of U.S. 24/Telegraph Road. Doors open at 1 p.m. and the event begins at 2:45 p.m., according to the latest details from organizers. The Monroe Police Department and Monroe County Sheriff's Office announced on Wednesday that Stewart Road between North Roessler Street/Dazarow Drive and the west side of the CSX Railroad tracks crossing will be closed to through traffic from 1 to 6 p.m. Thursday. Businesses in that area can remain open during the road closure and will remain accessible.Stewart Road is along the north side of the city of Monroe limits, bordering Frenchtown Township, between U.S. 24 (Telegraph Road) and M-125 (North Monroe Street).Thursday is the same day that Vance will sit down with "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil for a town hall with Michigan voters at another location.Vance was last in Southeast Michigan on Aug. 31, when he spoke at an event in Sterling Heights. Michigan is closely watched in part because of the open Senate seat, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers are in a tight race. The above video originally aired on Oct. 13, 2026.

title: Second Kabob-It location among new dining offerings at University of Chicago
description: Second Kabob-It location among new dining offerings at University of Chicago
content: Back in the late 1990s and early 2000s, the Burton-Judson dining hall at the University of Chicago had the occasional theme night — including fried peanut butter and banana sandwiches and other fare to represent Elvis Presley's favorite foods more than 20 years after Presley had died.For a while, back in the author's first year of college, students could also eschew the cafeteria-style steam tables for Chef Bill's station, as he would cut a slice of roast beef and dress it with "midterm sauce."But in those days, students often complained about the dorm food. Some swore that a friend of a friend saw the "Grade D beef" truck pulling up behind the building — though no one really did, since it's just an urban legend.Others found any excuse to eschew their meal plan and spend a few Flex dollars at the Taco Bell in Hutchinson Commons at the Reynolds Club instead. There were other fast-food options at Hutch, but Taco Bell was easily the most popular.A lot has changed since then. U of C has now introduced a new menu lineup, featuring barbecue, Bahamian cuisine, and an expansion of a popular purveyor of kabobs.Maisha Oliver-Muhammad is the owner and chef at Kabob-It, located in Hutchinson Commons. The restaurant recently expanded to the Midway Café in the Renee Granville Grossman Residential Commons. Speaking to CBS News Chicago on Thursday morning, Oliver-Muhammad emphasized how a diverse variety of food offerings are culturally important at an institution that draws people from all over the world like UChicago."One of the things that I love about UChicago is that they have an offering for everyone. You have allergen-friendly stations, you have halal, you have kosher, you have a taqueria, you have a pasta station — they pretty much have an offering for everyone," she said.Oliver-Muhammad explained that she had been a dining hall manager on campus, and was tired of that position and wanted to start her own business."I pretty much did all the work that I needed to. I had a short time working in retail, and in one of those locations, I saw how much the vendors in the space were generating, and that sparked and motivated me to want to start my own business," she said. "UChicago gave me the opportunity because I'd been there for so long, and so that pretty much was the beginning of Kabob-It."In addition to the two UChicago campus locations, Kabob-It also now has a location at the Illinois Institute of Technology.As explained by the Polsky Center for Entrepreneurship and Innovation, Kabob-It pairs Mediterranean cuisine with African American influences and other flavors from around the world.Popular offerings include a salmon salad sandwich and a mango lemonade at Kabob-It Express at the Midway Café, and grilled chicken at Hutchinson Commons. Kabob-It also offers kabobs with chicken, salon, locally grown vegetables and fresh spices."We actually just won a competition with the Chicago Bears almost two years ago for our grilled chicken," she said.During her journey with Kabob-It, Oliver-Muhammad also enrolled with the Polsky Center's Small Business Growth Program, which pairs business owners from Chicago's South and West sides with U of C grad student consultants, faculty at the University of Chicago's Booth School of Business, and coaches.The Polsky Center noted that in working with the program, Oliver-Muhammad was able to improve her business by swapping open containers for three-compartment containers that divided rice, salad, and protein for every meal, which reduces food costs.Also newly opened this academic year on the UChicago campus is Little Betty Smokehouse, also in Hutchinson Commons. Little Betty is the brainchild of Dominique Leach, master of barbecue and founder of Lexington Betty Smokehouse in the Pullman neighborhood.Leach gained national notoriety as a contestant and judge on the Food Network. UChicago noted that she pairs time-honored smoking techniques, "bold, soulful flavors," and an "unmistakably Chicago point of view."At the Logan Center for the Arts, Café Logan recently underwent a transformation, partnering with the wife-and-wife team of Chef Lizz Wright and designer Monica Haslip, who operate Carver 47 Food & Wellness Market at the Little Black Pearl Art & Design Academy on 47th Street. The new café at the Logan Center is called The Hunt, honoring the late Chicago sculptor Richard Hunt.The menu at The Hunt features all-day breakfast, salads and bowls, and sandwiches.Meanwhile, Bahama Shack, which started at the University of Chicago, is on campus in food truck form. Bahamian-born Chef Courtney Neil operates Bahama Shack, serving up conch fritters, steamed or fried whole snapper, pigeon peas and rice, and other delicacies.As for Oliver-Muhammad, she is looking to expand to open an airport location.

title: Who is running for U.S. Senate in Michigan? Meet the candidates running to replace Gary Peters.
description: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, Republican Mike Rogers and candidates from four other parties will be on the November ballot for Michigan's U.S. Senate seat.
content: After the current U.S. Senator for Michigan, Gary Peters, announced in January 2025 that he would step down at the end of his Senate term, a key seat has opened up in the U.S. Senate for Michigan.Michigan's August primary saw Abdul El-Sayed win the Democratic primary against Congresswoman Haley Stevens. El-Sayed is now running in the general election against Republican Mike Rogers, who was unopposed in the Republican primary. Candidates from four other parties will also be on the November ballot.Who are the candidates running for U.S. Senate representing Michigan in 2026?Abdul El-SayedDemocratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed announced in April 2025 that he would be running for Michigan's U.S. Senate seat in the 2026 election.El-Sayed is a former Michigan health official who served as both the health officer and the director of Wayne County's Department of Health, Human and Veterans Services.Before that, he also served as Detroit's health commissioner and is an internationally known public health expert and healthcare advocate. Before his public service work, he earned his medical degree from Columbia University and a second doctorate at Oxford University.El-Sayed says in his campaign that he will "get money out of politics, put money in your pocket, and pass Medicare for All."He says he is fighting for an economy and healthcare system that work for everyone, affordable housing for all, clean air and water, accessible education and sensible foreign policy rooted in diplomacy and justice.Mike RogersThe Republican Party's candidate, Mike Rogers, announced his campaign for the U.S. Senate in April 2025.Rogers is a former congressman who ran in the 2024 race for the same seat but lost to the incumbent Democrat Elissa Slotkin.Rogers worked at a factory in Michigan before serving in the U.S. Army and working as an FBI agent.
