content: The state of Florida won a key court decision Wednesday that allows it to enforce a ban on social media accounts for kids under 14 and other restrictions.The law was one of the most restrictive in the U.S. on social media use by children when Gov. Ron DeSantis signed it in 2024.The law implicates the First Amendment, an appeals court said, but "likely does so in a content-neutral manner."It would likely survive a full legal challenge "because it doesn't burden substantially more speech than necessary to advance the important interest in protecting minors from social media addiction," a panel from the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals said in a 3-0 opinion.The law bans social media accounts for Florida children under 14 and requires parental consent for use by kids who are 14 or 15.Industry trade groups the Computer & Communications Industry Association and NetChoice sued Florida, arguing that the law violated the free-speech rights of social media providers and users. A judge in 2025 said the law likely was unconstitutional and granted an injunction. That injunction was put on hold while the appeals court heard the case. The lawsuit, with the injunction now overturned, will return to federal court in Tallahassee.The appeals court noted that the law covers social media platforms "that have been determined to induce heavy use by children, and applies only to platforms that use both algorithms and one of several addictive features."An email seeking comment from the Florida attorney general's office was not immediately answered. NetChoice said it was disappointed with the decision."We are currently evaluating all of our options as we continue the fight to ensure Floridians' rights to free expression online are protected, and parents remain in the driver's seat when it comes to making decisions for their families," said Paul Taske, a lawyer at NetChoice.

title: Menifee police find homemade .50-caliber firearm during call for service
description: Police said the fully functional homemade firearm capable of shooting .50-caliber Browning Machine Gun ammunition was lacking several important safety components.
content: A homemade gun capable of shooting .50-caliber Browning Machine Gun ammunition was discovered by police during a recent call for service at a home in Menifee. According to a news release from the Menifee Police Department, officers found the "fully functional homemade .50 BMG firearm" with several .50 BMG rifle rounds. "Due to the unusual construction and potential danger of the weapon, the Riverside County Sheriff's Department's Hazardous Device Team responded to assist ... in safely examining and clearing the firearm," the release said. Police said an additional concern was the lack of several important safety components typically found on commercially manufactured firearms, which they believed would increase the risk to anyone who tried to operate it. The suspect who allegedly had the weapon was prohibited from possessing firearms or ammunition, police said, adding that they were booked on multiple charges. They have not yet been identified.

title: Messi assists on De Paul goal as Inter Miami beats NYCFC 2-0 and returns to the MLS playoffs
description: Rodrigo De Paul scored on an assist from Lionel Messi and Germán Berterame added a goal to send reigning champion Inter Miami back to the MLS playoffs with a 2-0 win over New York City FC on Wednesday night.
content: Rodrigo De Paul scored on an assist from Lionel Messi, and Germán Berterame added a goal to send reigning champion Inter Miami back to the MLS playoffs with a 2-0 win over New York City FC on Wednesday night.Luis Suárez also assisted for Inter Miami, which has won back-to-back matches for the first time since July.Miami missed the postseason when Messi arrived in 2023, but has reached the playoffs the past three seasons, losing in the first round to Atlanta United in 2024, then beating Vancouver last year to win the club's first MLS Cup.Wednesday's victory came after Miami routed DC United 4-0 last Saturday on a pair of goals from Messi and Suárez, and it was the second league win for new coach Cristian "Kily" González, who took over Sept. 16. Berterame scored in the 20th minute for his eighth goal of the season. De Paul doubled Miami's lead right before the end of the first half. Dayne St. Clair denied Nicolás Fernández on a penalty in the final minute of the match for his second straight clean sheet.It has been a rollercoaster year for Messi, who led Argentina to its second straight World Cup final and announced his retirement from international soccer a month later. Now, he has a chance to cap it with another trophy.Up next NYCFC: Hosts LAFC on Saturday. Miami: At Atlanta United on Saturday. ___See AP's full MLS coverage here

title: James Talarico discussed flu conspiracy theories, was challenged about abortion on town hall
description: A nine-day campaign absence, a heated abortion debate and sharp criticism of ICE. James Talarico faced tough questions at CNN's Jubilee Town Hall.
content: Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico discussed his very publicized absence from the campaign trail so close to the election during a nationally televised town hall on CNN and Jubilee. Talarico said he had a nasty case of the flu and worked remotely from home and wouldn't change what he did. The state representative from Austin also used one of his overall campaign themes, blaming billionaires and encouraging Democrats, Independents, and Republicans to join his campaign, to sharply criticize all of the false claims and conspiracy theories about him online and social media that gained millions of views. "This is an example of what I call the rage economy," he said. "Conspiracy theorists can post anything they want on the internet. They get clicks. The billionaires who own these platforms get rich. We all get angry, and nobody's life gets any better. Conspiracy theories don't put food on the table. They don't put gas in the tank."Talarico debates town hall attendees on abortion, immigrationIn another segment of the CNN Jubilee Town Hall, various attendees were allowed to come onto the stage and challenge Talarico directly on an issue. Jody Hunt of Burleson, who is an Independent and orthodox Catholic, criticized Talarico's views on abortion, which he has talked about a lot during the campaign. Republicans have blasted Talarico's religious views for months and did so on social media during the town hall. While Talarico and Hunt agreed they want fewer abortions and unplanned pregnancies, they differed on what the Bible says about abortion. "The Bible is silent on the issue of abortion," Talarico said. "It means you and I both have to look at different scriptures to try to come to a conclusion." In response, Hunt said, "I just want to add that the Bible is not silent on abortion. There is the Ten Commandments, thou shalt not kill, and as Catholics, we take great insult sometimes when it's sounded that way." Talarico later replied, "You know I'm an educator like you, and if I believed that abortion was murder, that it violated the Ten Commandments, then I wouldn't support it. So, it is okay that you and I come to different conclusions about that."Talarico also said if elected, he would push for comprehensive immigration reform, which would include a pathway to citizenship for people who've been in the U.S. for a long time. He also repeated his criticism of ICE, calling it a secret police force. But he said he doesn't want to abolish ICE because the U.S. still needs immigration enforcement. During the show, CNN said that Republican Ken Paxton has not responded to their invitation to take part in a town hall, but that the invitation stands. Paxton has also not agreed to debate Talarico, despite multiple invitations from TV stations and Fox News, and even after President Trump said both candidates should debate.Talarico has said he will debate Paxton at any time and place. Paxton launches "Come and Take It" bus tourEarlier Wednesday, Paxton announced an 18-day bus tour across Texas. It begins in Rockwall on Saturday, and he will be in Allen on Monday. It's scheduled to end at the Alamo in San Antonio on Monday, Nov. 2, the day before the midterm election. Early voting begins Monday, Oct. 19. The Real Clear Politics average of polls shows Talarico leading Paxton by 2.6 percentage points, 48.1% to 45.5%. The Senate race is the classic definition of a toss-up, and both candidates are starting to get their supporters to the polls in what will be one of the hottest turnout elections in the country.Watch Eye On Politics at 7:30 Sunday morning on CBS News Texas on air and streaming

title: Snake Road in Illinois' Shawnee National Forest is only known road in U.S. to close for reptile migration
description: It's officially Forest Service Road 345 but it's far better known as Snake Road, an incredibly rare stretch Illinois' Shawnee National Forest that may be the only street in the U.S. to close for no-legged friends.
content: It's officially Forest Service Road 345 but it's far better known as Snake Road, an incredibly rare stretch Illinois' Shawnee National Forest that may be the only street in the U.S. to close for no-legged friends. Indiana Jones would shudder, but for herpetologist Scott Ballard, a slither doesn't produce a sliver of fear. "This is the best place to come and get rid of all your concerns and negative energy," he said. Snake Road is a rather straight road. It's the reptiles that provide the twists and turns. Why did the snake cross the road? To get to the other side â no joke. "This road is going in between their summer foraging areas in the swamp, and their fall hibernation areas in the bluffs," Ballard explained. "And they have to cross this road to get from one to the other." So every spring and every fall, Snake Road closes to cars. "That protects animals from being incidentally killed by vehicles running over them," explained U.S. Forest Service Officer Anderson Harris. "It's the only road in the U.S., to my knowledge, that we close for that migrations of the amphibians and reptiles." As snakes migrate across the road, people migrate to it. "People from around the world come here," said Harris. For so-called "herpers" â snake enthusiasts, that is â the biannual snake migration is a must-see. "It's definitely everything I thought it would be. It's great. Even if I didn't see any snakes, this is a gorgeous hike," said visitor Max Hicks. The hike is two and a half miles down and back, and it never gets old for Ballard. "My mom brought me home a snake for my 10th birthday and that started it," he recalled. Ballard ended up studying Snake Road for his Master's. "I said in my thesis, we need to close it longer, and so the Forest Service then incorporated my recommendations of two full months in the spring and two full months in the fall," he said. From Sept. 1 through Oct. 31, the reptiles have a clear path and people can get a clear view of more than 20 snake species. Three of those species are venomous, including the northern copperhead, which Ballard said are among the hardest venomous snakes to find in Southern Illinois. At the end of the day, Snake Road may not be up everyone's alley, but we can all agree it's good to unwind. Do you hear the Heartbeat of Chicago? We want to know about it. title: Federal judge blocks Trump administration's effort to close Maryland research center
description: The Beltsville Agricultural Research Center (BARC) in Prince George's County will remain open for now after a federal judge halted the Trump administration's effort to close the facility.
content: The Beltsville Agricultural Research Center (BARC) in Prince George's County, Maryland, will remain open for now after a federal judge halted the Trump administration's effort to close the facility.The ruling Tuesday temporarily blocks the administration's plan to restructure the U.S. Department of Agriculture, which included closing the flagship research center and transferring employees to other locations across the country.Maryland Democratic leaders praised the decision, saying BARC plays a critical role in supporting farmers nationwide and researching threats to agriculture and public health, including Cyclospora and avian flu.Prince George's County Executive Aisha Braveboy said the ruling prevents the administration from permanently closing the facility."I applaud the decision of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, which granted a stay pursuant to 5 U.S.C. Â§ 705, halting the Trump Administration's effort to restructure and reorganize the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA)," Braveboy said.Braveboy also said BARC supports an estimated 1,000 jobs and warned that permanently closing the center would reduce Maryland's gross domestic product by roughly $450 million."As County Executive, I will continue to fight for federal employees and federal jobs," Braveboy said. "We know that people don't take federal jobs just for the money, they take them because they believe in public service and the important missions of their agencies."Maryland's Democratic congressional delegation also welcomed the ruling. U.S. Sens. Chris Van Hollen and Angela Alsobrooks, along with Reps. Glenn Ivey, Steny Hoyer, Kweisi Mfume, Jamie Raskin, Sarah Elfreth, April McClain Delaney and Johnny Olszewski, issued a joint statement praising the court's decision."As we've said time and again, this Administration's attempts to shutter BARC are not only unwise â they're illegal," the lawmakers said in a joint statement. "BARC conducts critical research that helps farmers across our nation put food on the table for American families â including combatting serious threats to our agriculture, like Cyclospora and avian flu."The lawmakers said the ruling makes clear that the administration's efforts conflict with congressional intent and pledged to continue opposing the closure.The court's decision halts the effort for now, leaving BARC open while the legal challenge continues.CBS News Baltimore reached out to the White House for a comment but has not heard back.

title: Top U.S. DOJ official orders California to review list of possible noncitizens who received mail ballots
description: The Justice Department has ordered California to review a list of people who the federal government believes may have received mail-in ballots for the upcoming election despite not being U.S. citizens.
content: Washington — The Justice Department has ordered California to review a list of people who the federal government believes may have received mail-in ballots for the upcoming November election despite not being U.S. citizens, according to a letter reviewed by CBS News.In the Oct. 13 letter, acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter imposed a 48-hour deadline to review the list of names, which were provided on a password-protected thumb drive, to determine the citizenship status of each individual."For individuals whom you cannot independently confirm citizenship status, we request that you immediately instruct the appropriate elections official to segregate — not cancel — those individuals' vote-by-mail ballots until their citizenship status can be determined," McCotter wrote. "If individuals on the list have not yet been sent a vote-by-mail ballot, take all immediate and reasonable steps to not provide a ballot to those individuals until we confirm their citizenship status," he added.In a statement, California Secretary of State Shirley Weber confirmed that her office received a letter from the Justice Department, but said the federal government "did not provide the list [of alleged noncitizens] to our office.""The USDOJ's relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states' protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections," Weber said.Dean Logan, the registrar-recorder/county clerk of Los Angeles County, confirmed he had received the letter but said the records were on a USB drive that his office had not yet accessed. "The letter included a USB drive purportedly containing the referenced records, along with a handwritten note providing a password. We have not accessed the drive because doing so would conflict with established data privacy and information security protocols," Logan said in a statement. "We do not consider the device a secure medium. Additionally, the letter does not specify the number of individuals involved or describe the information contained in the records."He added: "Federal and state laws are clear on how voter eligibility is established — and any action to remove a voter from eligibility must be based on verifiable information, not assertions of unconfirmed data matching."Similar letters were also mailed out to other counties in the state, a person with knowledge of the matter said. The move comes after Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin in July told California's secretary of state that the government believed there were noncitizens listed on its voter rolls.Reuters was the first to report on the letter.McCotter's demands represent the latest effort by the Trump administration to press blue states on whether they have people who are unlawfully registered to vote on their rolls.The Justice Department's Civil Rights Division filed 31 lawsuits in an effort to force states to hand over unredacted copies of their voter rolls. The division has said it wants to ensure states are keeping clean voter lists, but it has since acknowledged that it also intends to share the data with the Department of Homeland Security so that the lists can be screened for noncitizens.Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general for the Civil Rights Division, sent letters to all 50 states in July threatening to take criminal action if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their voter rolls.So far, the Justice Department has lost 26 of those cases, and has not achieved one legal victory to date. It has resorted to using publicly available voter lists and other investigative means to try to identify noncitizens who may be registered in those states.Since President Trump took office, the department has criminally charged more than 100 people with voter fraud-related crimes. The crackdown comes as the president has continued to allege, without evidence, that the 2020 election was stolen due to voter fraud.Experts have repeatedly found across multiple studies that the incidents of voter fraud are minimal and have not been numerous enough to impact the outcome of an election. A data analysis published last month by Reuters found that states may have added more than 30,000 self-declared noncitizens to voter rolls since 2000 because of software glitches and clerical errors that came about during the processing of driver's licenses and state IDs.That figure is small relative to the number of registered voters. In the 2024 election, Census data showed there were about 174 million people registered to vote.

title: Rancho Cucamonga brewery that irked neighbors to become fire station after city's $8M purchase
description: A controversial brewery located in the middle of a Rancho Cucamonga neighborhood, often drawing the irritation of neighbors, is set to become a fire station after the property was purchased by the city for nearly $8 million.
content: A controversial brewery located in the middle of a Rancho Cucamonga neighborhood, often drawing the irritation of neighbors, is set to become a fire station after the property was purchased by the city for nearly $8 million. The Hamilton Family Brewery opened last year, on Eighth Street and Archibald, and since then Armando Moreno says he's dealt with a slew of issues in his usually quiet neighborhood of nearly 40 years. "I think we've lost a lot of what is considered a neighborhood feel," Moreno said. "We couldn't find parking; that was one of the issues. Another issue was people urinating on the street."After several neighborhood protests, the Rancho Cucamonga City Council approved a purchase agreement for $7.8 million between the Rancho Cucamonga Fire District and the brewery's owners. The city is now set to turn it into a fire house after it began looking into complaints against the brewery in March."Initially, the idea of selling something we worked so hard to build and all the blood and sweat and tears and sacrifice that went into that location? It was like, 'Heck no,'" said brewery owner Josh Hamilton.Hamilton said the brewery moved after outgrowing their old location, and despite the initial reluctance, he believes the sale is a win for everyone."The neighbors would be happy. Our customers would be happy to have extra parking. I would be happy to not have the stress of dealing with the neighbors," Hamilton said. Fire officials say the new fire house would improve response times, but many residents have questioned the staggering price tag for the property. While the fire department will fund most of it, some of the money will come from the city.Hamilton said he bought the property for $2.5 million, but invested millions more to turn it into a fully functioning brewery. "Some people see the purchase price; double that went into it, essentially," he said, adding that he's expecting to return to his old location on Seventh Street, where he'll build a tasting room. Moreno said the cost is worth the peace, hopeful now that he and his neighbors will return to their quiet way of life. "Instead of having to deal with this every day, it's good for the community, cause we don't have one nearby," Moreno said of the fire house.Rancho Cucamonga Fire District officials say they already purchased a separate plot of land for a new fire house, which they plan to sell. The city council approved the sale last week, but the deal still needs to go through escrow.

title: Dodgers on brink of elimination after 6-2 loss to Brewers in NLCS Game 3
description: The Los Angeles Dodgers are on the brink of elimination after losing 6-2 to the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 3 of the National League Championship Series on Wednesday night.
content: After sweeping the Milwaukee Brewers in last year's National League Championship Series, the Los Angeles Dodgers are on the brink of elimination after losing 6-2 in Game 3 on Wednesday night.Now down 3-0 and on the verge of a Brewers sweep, the Boys in Blue will fight to stay in the postseason and continue their quest for back-to-back-to-back World Series championships. With lefty ace Blake Snell on the mound for the start, the Brewers were largely held in check despite Jackson Chourio's solo shot on the first pitch of the game. From there, Snell limited the Brewers to just one hit over the next five innings. After the Dodgers answered back in the sixth inning with Will Smith's bases-loaded, two-run double to take the lead, Snell allowed a two-run homer to Newport Beach native Jake Bauers after an 11-pitch battle. Outfielder Garrett Mitchell followed up with a solo shot in the very next at-bat, giving the Brew Crew a 4-2 lead in the seventh.Milwaukee scored again in the eighth inning when Brice Turang, who had previously reached base on a single, scored on a wild pitch from Justin Wrobleski. They tacked on another insurance run in the top of the ninth on a Joey Ortiz single, also off Wrobleski.Rookie Robert Gasser got the start for the Brewers, hurling five shutout innings while allowing just three runs and striking out three. Outside of the two runs Abner Uribe allowed in the sixth, via three walks and a hit, Milwaukee's bullpen held the Dodgers to just one baserunner after Gasser was taken out.Snell finished the game with nine strikeouts in six innings, allowing four runs and walking two.Shohei Ohtani reached base three times while batting sixth for the Dodgers, first on a hit by pitch in his second at-bat and again with a single. Before the game, he was hitting just .150 in the postseason with zero home runs and no RBIs. It's only the second time the Dodgers have faced a 3-0 hole in the postseason. The last time was in 1966, when the Baltimore Orioles swept them in the World Series. Manager Dave Roberts hasn't lost hope. During his playing career, he was a key member of the 2004 Boston Red Sox that came back from a three-game deficit against the New York Yankees to become the only team in MLB history to complete a four-game comeback in a best-of-seven series."We've won four in a row a number of times this year," Roberts said. "We've got to win tomorrow. That's our only focus."Up nextThe teams meet again for Game 4 on Thursday at 5 p.m. at Chavez Ravine. With their season and pursuit of history on the line, the Boys in Blue are slated to send Tyler Glasnow to the mound against Milwaukee, which hasn't yet announced a probable starter.This is a developing story. Check back for details.

title: Video shows Hollywood sinkhole swallowing Spectrum van
description: A large stream of water flowed through the area on Wednesday morning.
author_name: Austin  Turner, Laurie  Perez, Jasmine  Viel, Dean  Fioresi
content: Wild aerial footage showed a sinkhole that swallowed a van in Hollywood after a water main burst on Wednesday.The footage was captured near the intersection of Franklin and Normandie avenues, near the John Sowden House, just before noon. The front half of a Spectrum van was entirely underground, with its back tires anchored at street level.Spectrum told CBS LA in a statement that a technician was working in the area when the sinkhole opened up, and the individual was uninjured."We're working with local officials and first responders, and we'll support them however we can as they assess the situation," a Spectrum spokesperson said.A neighbor said the Spectrum technician was working in the rear of the truck when the van started to sink. A spokesperson for the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power told CBS LA that a water main broke in the area around 11:10 a.m., causing a six-foot hole to open in the street."The affected main is 8 inches in diameter, with approximately 30 services impacted," the spokesperson said, adding that the main was installed in 1938. As repair work continued, LADWP noted that Normandie Avenue would be closed between Franklin and De Mille Drive. They set a preliminary service return time of midnight, and crews were still investigating what caused the main break. During the outage, LADWP handed out water to affected residents. The Spectrum vehicle had been removed by 4 p.m., LADWP officials said. Video posted to the Citizen app showed a large stream of water flowing through the area on Wednesday morning."The whole ground was shaking, and you could hear the water running under the house," said a woman named Gayle, who said she's worried her house could be the next thing to sink into the ground. Some neighbors told CBS LA that the water issues in the area go back years, with the most recent evidence of a leak coming two weeks ago when water was spotted seeping through the pavement in an alleyway. Crews were in the area then to repair the issue.LADWP officials say there's no indication that work is related to the main break. "There are many contributing factors in why our water mains break, age being one of them," said LADWP spokesperson Caesar Rubio, who added that the agency proactively replaces approximately 45 miles of pipe every year. He says that LADWP also has a dedicated leak detection team that works to identify leaks before they happen. So far this year, he says they've found nearly 100.

title: Denver police can't issue traffic citations to autonomous vehicles
description: Denver police department can't issue traffic citations to autonomous vehicles, lawmaker raises concerns
content: Autonomous vehicles are here in Denver with plans to expand even further, in fact more of these autonomous vehicle companies could be eyeing a launch in the Mile High City. So, we wanted to know who's responsible when things don't go as planned.Waymo has gotten off to an interesting start here in Denver. "It just stopped in the middle of the road, it just stopped," a man told CBS Colorado a few weeks ago after he was involved in a crash with one.Bystanders have also taken footage of the cars making their way through a road with wet pavement, and a popular Denver farmers market."It's important topic because there's absolutely a need for guardrails on autonomous vehicles," said State Representative Sheila Lieder, a Democrat from Jefferson County.These real-life scenarios prompted us to take a look into accountability and parameters, and we learned there's a gray area with autonomous vehicles. "My mind is who gets the ticket?" said Lieder.Denver police say, "if there's no driver in an autonomous vehicle, there currently isn't a mechanism within state law for issuing a citation for a traffic infraction."Denver's Department of Transportation and Infrastructure says it can issue an autonomous vehicle a parking citation, but can't put a limit on how many autonomous vehicle companies can operate in the city. "2017, it, you know, was probably a good fit, but we have Waymo's running all over now," said LiederLieder is referring to the bill signed into law roughly a decade ago that gave the green light for these vehicles to come to Colorado. She's since sponsored legislation to place parameters on autonomous semis, and is not only working to bring back a similar bill back this session, but is taking a look at what else should be established as state law. "We're looking at all different types of options, and we got a lot of stakeholdering to do."

title: Plano ISD pledges up to $250 million for Dallas Stars arena, raising school funding questions
description: District officials say future tax revenue and state funding adjustments could produce a net financial gain, but critics question the risks.
content: Plano ISD says it will contribute up to $250 million toward the proposed Dallas Stars arena at the former Shops at Willow Bend site. That would be in addition to the $700 million the city has proposed for the project.But where is the school district's money coming from, and could the deal affect school funding?Plano ISD is partnering with the city on a tax increment reinvestment zone, or TIRZ, agreement. The district says its contribution will come from a portion of future tax revenue generated by new development in the zone, rather than existing classroom funds.Under Texas' school funding system, commonly known as the "recapture program" or "Robin Hood," property-wealthy districts such as Plano ISD must send a portion of their local property tax revenue to the state to help fund public education.The district expects to contribute up to $250 million over an estimated 18 years. The money would go into a city-administered fund for public improvements in the redevelopment zone, which includes the Stars arena.Plano ISD says the agreement is expected to be offset through adjustments to the amount it owes the state under current law. The district projects it will receive about $438 million over the same period, or $188 million more than its projected contribution. Those figures are projections, not guarantees.The city has proposed contributing $700 million toward the arena through a venue tax that voters will decide on in the upcoming election.The agreement also could allow Plano ISD to hold graduation ceremonies at the proposed arena instead of the Ford Center at The Star in Frisco.The district approved the agreement in August, and the Plano City Council approved it on Oct. 12.Some residents remain concerned about using school district resources for an arena project."I've been a resident of Plano my whole life. I grew up and went to Plano East Senior High School. You know, go Panthers. And I really am not too keen on the idea of moving money away from the schools," said Bryan Beck.Finance expert Sriram Villapura said the district's potential financial benefit depends on whether the redevelopment delivers the expected results."So the bigger question is this, 'Will the Plano ISD really benefit?'" Villapura said. "If there is better enrollment, yes, they'll benefit from the extra money. Otherwise, I'm not very sure what's the point of that extra money coming back to Plano ISD from the new tax base. My concern is that it could potentially be more money might be going out of Plano ISD."Plano ISD projects the redevelopment could grow its tax base by $7.3 billion. The district says the agreement will help spur development and generate long-term revenue for schools, but the financial projections depend on future property values, economic conditions, and state law.

title: DeSoto works to address utility billing issues as residents demand answers
description: Several residents say their water bills don't match their online accounts, and getting answers over the phone has been difficult.
content: As utility billing problems continue for some DeSoto residents, on Wednesday night, city staff met with them to address their concerns. Several residents say their water bills don't match their online accounts, and getting answers over the phone has been difficult."It's like you can't get any answers," LaTanya Maxwell said. "Everyone keeps saying that they have a new system going on, be patient with us, but I think we've been patient enough." "I would just tell everyone, the city is not sitting idle on this," City of DeSoto Public Utilities Director Brandon Lacy said. City staff says they've requested on-site support from Tyler Technologies, the vendor behind the new billing system. They say problems surfaced after its launch that hadn't appeared during testing. In a video last week, the city's interim city manager addressed the ongoing problems, telling residents if they've noticed a past due notice on their current bill, disregard it. Even if they paid their previous bill, he says the new system is incorrectly carrying that amount forward. "We will not be turning off anybody's water during this period until we get back to normal operations," Lacy said. While all of this is sorted out, the city has brought in additional customer service representatives to help with the high volume of calls."When you call on the phone, you're expecting to get an answer and we understand that," Lacy said.Another town hall is scheduled for Oct. 21 at 6 p.m. and it will be held virtually.

title: Data shows violent crime dropping in Minnesota despite recent concerns about gang violence
description: The report was published right before shootings in Bloomington, Eden Prairie and Edina that local law enforcement attribute to Somali gang violence.
content: Amidst an outcry at the local level about recent gun violence, annual reporting at the state and federal level shows violent crime is continuing to drop in Minnesota. Christopher Dotson, the special agent in charge leading the FBI Field Office in Minneapolis, said that he expects the positive trend to continue. He said that he has spent time with five field offices over the course of his career, but he's never seen the level of collaboration he's witnessed between law enforcement agencies in Minnesota. He said that teamwork is, in his opinion, largely to thank for the numbers moving in the right direction. "I can tell you as a state, as a whole, it's gone down significantly," Dotson told WCCO, "those are good news stories that I think we gotta remember." In September, the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension published its 2025 Uniform Crime Report, which helps feed the FBI's crime data. The report shows that overall crime dropped by 9% between 2024 and 2025. The number of murders dropped from 172 to 130, an approximate 25% drop, and aggravated assaults dropped by 11%, going from 9,842 to 8,762 statewide. The report was published right before shootings in Bloomington, Eden Prairie and Edina that local law enforcement attribute to Somali gang violence. In community meetings that followed, some residents expressed that they no longer feel safe and believe the problem is getting worse."When we say violence is down but there's a shooting in your neighborhood, I know that's a hard pill to swallow," Dotson said. Dotson said that from his perspective at the FBI, it's a manageable problem that he believes can be brought under control. He said that he does not know the specifics of what is being proposed, but supports the general idea of local law enforcement organizing a Somali gang-focused task force.Dotson said he also agreed that the gangs under the spotlight are unique given the lack of focus on moving money or drugs or defending turf; however, he noted that the gang distinction can help involve federal partners given the possibility of investigating conspiracy-based crimes. He also echoed sentiments from local leaders to avoid painting an entire community with the same brush. "I do not think that a couple of lone acts or violent offenders should be used to define a community. Again, when we define this community or identify where the subject is coming from, we are also identifying part of the solution. It's an opportunity for outreach and it could be a plea for partnership," Dotson said. At the moment, he did not indicate whether the FBI was directly involved in investigating recent gang activity in the suburbs beyond the general commitment to share information and resources.

title: Crew targets more than 20 small businesses in overnight burglaries, most on Northwest Side
description: The thieves aren't getting away with much, with one owner saying they may have gotten away with $10.
content: Chicago police are searching for the people responsible for more than 20 overnight business break-ins.At the center of it all â a red sedan.The thieves aren't getting away with much, but they're causing a lot of expensive damage for the small business owners.Piles of shattered storefront glass are what more than 20 small business owners faced Wednesday morning.Around 6 a.m., a barista at Terra Coffee in Avondale hid for cover as a brick came flying through the front door. She then came face to face with the intruder â both ran away in different directions."They more than spooked her, they traumatized her. That's a very scary experience to have gone through and she was here by herself," said co-owner Jocelyn Telles.Two other businesses, including Subway and a nail salon in the shopping plaza, were also broken into Wednesday morning. Despite the sign outside of Terra warning potential intruders that they don't have cash and security cameras are recording, they burglarized Telles business anyway. "Unfortunately, this is just one of the realities of running a business in Chicago," Telles said.At Fry the Coop in Portage Park, about $4,000 in damage was done in seconds and the register was ripped out. This was not the first time, according to the restaurant's general manager Lewis Tovar."They probably got away with 10 bucks tops," he said.Chicago police said that a group of four people used a brick and other heavy objects to smash the glass of the businesses. They say a red sedan, believed to be stolen, was used in the overnight break-ins. One of the suspects, wearing a sweatshirt with this distinctive design, was seen inside several of the stores, including Migos Fine Foods, also in Portage Park."We are trying to build a community. We are trying to help people. We are trying to make a living, but where do we go from here?" said Azazi Morsi with Migos Fine Foods. "What is being done to change these things?"There is plenty of surveillance video from all of the targeted businesses, but so far, no arrests have been made.

title: Cloquet police search for missing 16-year-old girl last seen near Loring Park
description: The Cloquet Police Department says Juliet Nunez, who may also be going by the name Seraphina, was last seen on Monday near Loring Park in Minneapolis.
content: Authorities in northeastern Minnesota are asking for the public's help in locating a 16-year-old girl last seen in Minneapolis.The Cloquet Police Department says Juliet Nunez, who may also be going by the name Seraphina, was last seen on Monday near Loring Park in Minneapolis.Nunez is described as 5 feet 7 inches tall and weighing 143 pounds, with blue hair and brown eyes.Authorities say there is concern for Nunez's well-being.Anyone who has seen or knows the whereabouts of Nunez is asked to contact the Cloquet Police Department at 218-879-1247 or call 911.

title: Old Denver golf course gets new life as a park
description: Denver plans to designate the old Park Hill Golf Course as parkland.
content: Denver's former Park Hill Golf Course is entering a new chapter, with city leaders announcing plans to permanently designate the property as parkland, break ground in 2027, and bring in a nationally recognized designer to lead the project.Mayor Mike Johnston and Councilwoman Shontel Lewis announced the three developments and outlined a vision for the long-debated property's future."We will announce the plan to work with the council to formally designate this space as park space," Johnston said.Under the proposed designation, the land would be protected for park use under city ordinance."What it means in our city ordinance is that when we formally designate something as a park space, it can only and forever be used as a park space," Johnston said.The city also announced that Michael Van Valkenburgh will lead the park's design. His firm is known for projects including Brooklyn Bridge Park in New York and the Obama Presidential Center in Chicago."What we know is really a once-in-a-century opportunity. This would be the largest piece of private land ever converted into a public park in the city," Johnston said.But for some neighbors, the announcement brings excitement alongside concerns about how the project will serve the surrounding community.Deronn Turner, a longtime Park Hill resident and parent of a child with Down syndrome, said she wants the design to prioritize accessibility and preserve the neighborhood's history."I say cautiously because I've seen a lot of things happen in terms of gentrifying areas, and the whole is not looked at," Turner said.Turner, who also works with children with special needs, said she wants residents to have a meaningful role in shaping the park. Her priorities include accessible playground equipment, quiet spaces for people with sensory needs, and preserving Black history."For me, it would take more conversations and boots on the ground," Turner said.Van Valkenburgh told Turner that accessibility would be part of the design process."You can count on us for what you just asked to happen. I promise," he said.The design vision also includes reducing water use through native and drought-tolerant plants.City officials say community input will help guide the project, noting that thousands of people have already responded to a city survey.Denver acquired the former golf course in 2025 after voters rejected proposed plans to redevelop portions of the property.With groundbreaking targeted for 2027, the next phase will focus on turning the long-contested land into a public park that reflects the surrounding community's needs and history.

title: South Florida nonprofit proposes turning Broward hotel into affordable housing for veterans
description: The nonprofit would buy and renovate the hotel on University Drive, with studios and one-bedrooms renting for $1,000 to $1,200 a month, utilities included, pending city review in November and December.
content: A new proposal moving forward in Coral Springs aims to address one of the most pressing issues facing South Florida veterans: the rising cost of housing.With rents continuing to climb, finding an affordable place to live has become increasingly difficult for military service members returning home and veterans living on limited incomes.To help tackle the issue, the Tunnel to Towers Foundation, a nonprofit organization, is offering to purchase and renovate the La Quinta Inn on University Drive, north of Sample Road, converting the hotel into apartments for veterans.The sale is not yet complete, and the city of Coral Springs will finish vetting the proposal in November and December.For local veterans, the initiative comes at a critical time. Bob Lavoie, a Vietnam veteran who served as an Army specialist, said housing affordability is a dominant topic of discussion."It's unaffordable. The prices are crazy," Lavoie said. "I know a veteran who's paying $1,800 for one room."To qualify for a unit, veterans must have an honorable discharge and agree to a background check. The proposed studio and one-bedroom units would rent for between $1,000 and $1,200 a month, with all utilities included.Community members are also working to support the effort. Kerri Gordon with Mission BBQ is raising money for the Tunnel to Towers Foundation by selling promotional cups to help make the development a reality."It can be permanent housing, or it can be a stepping stone," Gordon said.

title: Denver seeks comment on new draft plan of Burnham Yard redevelopment
description: Denver released a draft plan of development of Burnham Yard for new Broncos stadium.
content: A new draft plan for Burnham Yard, the preferred site for the Denver Broncos' proposed new stadium, outlines major changes that could reshape surrounding neighborhoods.The city's plan includes proposals for safer streets, improved access to the South Platte River, affordable housing, and historic preservation.The plan would guide development of the 58-acre rail yard and surrounding areas in the La Alma and Lincoln Park neighborhoods. The broader planning area covers nearly 800 acres, stretching from Alameda Avenue to Colfax Avenue and from the South Platte River to Santa Fe Drive.The small area plan was prompted by the Broncos' large development review proposal. The city is leading the planning process to ensure community concerns and priorities are reflected in the area's future."I think really the plan is trying to solve several issues with trying to retain the local character and history of the communities," said John Deffenbaugh, CEO of Historic Denver.Historic Denver, a nonprofit focused on historic preservation, has participated in discussions as the plan has taken shape."Historic Denver has been part of this, so we attended a bunch of meetings as the plan was emerging," said Deffenbaugh. The draft plan aims to connect surrounding neighborhoods to the site while minimizing the displacement of residents and businesses. It also identifies six key development areas, including the area around 13th Avenue and Zuni Street, which is important to Historic Denver."I think the biggest challenge is to find the sweet spot between community interest and history and creating a regional and nationwide attraction for the benefit of the whole city," said Deffenbaugh. One proposal that has drawn interest from Historic Denver is the potential adaptive reuse of the Zuni Steam Plant, which could become a cultural hub within the development."We were excited to see the Zuni Steam Plant in the plan for adaptive reuse. That's important and really can be an anchor for the site," he said.The area currently includes industrial properties and underused sites, including warehouses. The draft plan envisions a multimodal spine and community corridor, with opportunities to preserve historic features while improving connections throughout the area.Historic railroad features, including a locomotive and turntable, could help tell the story of Burnham Yard's past to future visitors.LINK: Draft Plan for the Redevelopment of Burnham YardsThose preservation efforts could help ensure that new development reflects the site's history as the surrounding area evolves.The plan remains in draft form, and the city is seeking public feedback. Residents have until Oct. 28 to submit comments before the plan moves through the approval process.

title: Suspect arrested in connection with shooting at LIRR Bellport station
description: A 19-year-old man has been arrested and charged with attempted murder in connection with last Friday's shooting at the Long Island Rail Road's Bellport station, authorities said.
content: A 19-year-old man has been arrested and charged with attempted murder in connection with a shooting at the Long Island Rail Road's Bellport station last Friday, authorities said.The incident began around 2:25 a.m. when a group of four passengers exited a train, and one person in the group turned and fired a gun toward passengers, striking a 17-year-old.Officials said the bullet passed through the teen and struck a second person, a 40-year-old man who was boarding the train with his bicycle. The man was hit in the shoulder and taken to the hospital.Law enforcement agencies launched an extensive search for the suspects, using drones and other resources to help locate them.Officials later tracked down the 17-year-old, whom police identified as the intended target.He was arrested by Suffolk County police on an unrelated warrant. Investigators said he was found with an untreated gunshot wound to the chest from the night of the shooting.Officials said they believe the shooting stemmed from a dispute involving a girl.Authorities said no other passengers or bystanders were injured in the incident.Officials described the incident as an isolated event.After being released from the hospital, the 40-year-old man was arrested by the MTA Police Department on an outstanding warrant unrelated to Friday's shooting, according to authorities.

title: Colorado residents in Longmont say cellphones have become nearly unusable
description: Some Longmont residents say their cellphones have become nearly unusable in recent weeks.
content: Some Longmont residents say their cellphones have become nearly unusable in recent weeks, leaving them unable to reliably make calls, contact their children's schools or reach family members. The problems are drawing complaints from residents and pressure from Colorado lawmakers for a solution.Alyssaa Bustamante-Harrison said she has struggled to get service across her neighborhood, sometimes leaving her unable to make calls even when she's away from home."I tried to call the school. It failed. I tried to call my mom. It failed," Bustamante-Harrison explained.Bustamante-Harrison estimates she goes without service for about 75% of her drive."Just a lot of stress knowing that, if I'm away from home or not on Wi-Fi, that I might not be able to get a hold of my daughter's school or vice versa," Bustamante-Harrison said, "I've even stopped running errands during the day because I want to make sure that I'm home," she said.Bustamante-Harrison is among dozens of Longmont residents who have raised concerns about cellular service. Colorado officials report that more than 100 people across Boulder County have also complained to the Federal Communications Commission.Local officials believe the service problems are connected to the Table Mountain Radio Quiet Zone, a federally regulated area north of Boulder that protects sensitive scientific research from radio-frequency interference.The quiet zone has been in place for decades and protects research by federal agencies, including the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and the U.S. Geological Survey.But, as the region's population has grown and cellular networks have expanded, carriers have faced challenges balancing service needs with federal restrictions on radio transmissions.Jake Marsing, a Longmont City Council member, said residents are dealing with more than occasional dead zones."We're experiencing not just dead zones, but, essentially, phones that are effectively unusable," Marsing said. "I mean, we've got a good portion of our community that are dealing with bricks."Marsing said the need for cellular service has changed as more people move into the area and rely on mobile phones."As cell service providers have really increased in prevalence, and, then, as our area has increased in population density, the signal needs have changed," he said.Marsing said carriers had about a year and a half of notice to comply with the requirements, but the changes did not happen at the same pace for every provider. Hes said many of the concerns he's heard involve T-Mobile, the carrier Bustamante-Harrison uses."I don't know what to do in the meantime, and we're still expected to pay our phone bill even if our phone isn't working in half of the town," Bustamante-Harrison said.T-Mobile told CBS Colorado that it has met the required federal thresholds but is continuing to work on longer-term network solutions.T-Mobile sent a statement that said in part, "We have now achieved the required federal thresholds … Teams are continuing to work on longer-term network solutions … That requires coordination with the federal government, so we don't have a firm completion date …"The service problems have prompted action from Colorado's congressional delegation. U.S. Rep. Joe Neguse and Sens. Michael Bennet and John Hickenlooper sent a letter to the National Telecommunications and Information Administration and the FCC, urging the agencies to meet with cellular carriers and work to resolve the reported outages.The lawmakers pointed to signal adjustments made to comply with federal rules protecting the Table Mountain Radio Quiet Zone."We write to urge your agencies to assist in resolving major reported cellular network outages in Boulder County, Colorado, following signal adjustments made to comply with National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) regulations protecting the Table Mountain Radio Quiet Zone," the lawmakers wrote.State Sen. Katie Wallace, who represents east Boulder County and western Weld County, said she believes improvements are possible."I don't think that this has to be the reality moving forward," Wallace said. "I think that there are ways that the carriers should catch up on their infrastructure in order to meet these new regulations that, again, were rolled out more than almost two years ago, right?" She said cellular companies need to invest in infrastructure that can meet federal requirements while providing effective service to customers. Wallace said lawmakers are working to connect with local governments, county officials and federal agencies while asking carriers to address the problems.Marsing said, in Longmont, local officials need a clear list of what would help carriers restore service."We need to know from the carriers what they need, specifically what T-Mobile needs in order to restore effective service. If those are, you know, 'Hey, we need cell phone boosters,' if we need fast track permitting, if we need, you know. We just need the list," Marsing said.The Boulder County Office of Disaster Management said it has not received reports from residents who were unable to reach 911 because of the cellular service issues. "Even if your phone shows no bars from your carrier, a 911 call can still connect using any available tower, regardless of which company you pay for service," the office said in a statement. The county's 911 centers are also not seeing an increase in failed calls. Even so, officials recommend residents consider backup ways to communicate in case cell service is unreliable.The Boulder Office of Disaster Management recommends the following options:Use a landline or voice-over-internet-protocol (VoIP) phoneEnable Wi-Fi callingCheck whether your phone supports satellite callingText instead of calling when possibleConsider ham radio and keep an all-hazards weather radioOfficials caution that no single communication method is guaranteed to work in every single situation. Residents should check which options are available to them before an emergency.For Bustamante-Harrison and other residents dealing with spotty service, the central question remains when they will be able to depend on their phones again.

title: Miami-Dade father arrested, accused of starving and locking up his two children, deputies say
description: According to an arrest report, the children told deputies they went days without food and were locked in their rooms, and the father is held on a child neglect charge.
content: A northeast Miami-Dade father was arrested Tuesday after authorities said he starved his two children because he believed the government was putting stuff in their food.According to his arrest report, Wendy Louis, 40, also locked the children in their bedrooms for days at a time, forcing them to use a bucket as a toilet and withholding schooling from them. Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office deputies responded to Louis's home on Northeast 175th Street on Tuesday to conduct a welfare check after family members contacted law enforcement, the report said. The relatives said that the children reached out, telling them that they had not been fed in days, were locked inside their rooms, were forbidden from using the bathroom, and were forced to drink water directly from the shower head. When deputies arrived and interviewed both victims, the children confirmed the horrific conditions, the report said, as routinely going days without food because their father claimed "the government is putting stuff in the food"; they were locked inside their rooms for days at a time and forced to use a bucket as a toilet. They also described that their father didn't allow them to shower daily and forced them to drink the shower water when they were thirsty. They also told law enforcement, according to the report, that they had not attended school since August 2023, when Louis withdrew them from classes, and that they were not receiving any form of homeschooling. Deputies on scene noted in the report that both children appeared "extremely small and thin for their age," with unkempt and matted hair. The kids' ages were not clear in the report. Upon being taken into custody, Louis refused to be interviewed by investigators. Authorities noted he failed to provide necessary care, supervision, food, and medical oversight to maintain his children's physical and mental health. He is facing charges of child neglect, domestic violence, and resisting an officer without violence. His bond was set for the two charges of child neglect without great bodily harm at $5000, and a judge ordered him to stay away from the children. As of Wednesday afternoon, he remains behind bars at Turner Guilford Knight Correctional Center.

title: Big Bear bald eagle Jackie's cause of death revealed
description: Big Bear bald eagle Jackie's cause of death has been revealed nearly two months after she died in August, following weeks of testing and rehabilitation.
content: Big Bear bald eagle Jackie's cause of death has been revealed nearly two months after she died in August, following weeks of testing and rehabilitation. According to the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, a necropsy and additional testing determined that Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza, or HPAI, was the "primary underlying cause of her decline.""In an uncommon presentation of the virus, the infection caused a severe ulcer in her stomach that led to persistent internal bleeding, anemia, and the development of bacterial sepsis," said Steve Kubiski, the Director of Disease Investigations with the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, which performed the necropsy. Jackie, who was estimated to be around 14 years old, died nearly a month after she was rescued from the Big Bear Lake shoreline, where she was found after being seen in a fight with two subadult eagles in July. A team of veterinary experts at the Ojai Raptor Center oversaw her care in the weeks that followed, documenting the process as they tried to nurse her back to health. Despite undergoing a blood transfusion, which briefly provided a glimpse of hope, Jackie continued to suffer setbacks in her recovery due to the sickness, which remained a mystery until Wednesday's announcement by California wildlife officials. "Jackie showed signs of chronic disease involving the ventriculus, the muscular portion of a bird's stomach, commonly called the gizzard. The damaged and ulcerated tissue contributed to ongoing blood loss and her persistent severe anemia," the CDFW release said. "It also allowed bacteria to enter the body, resulting in a serious secondary bacterial infection." Officials said that additional testing also revealed severe inflammation and blood clot formation in Jackie's heart and several major blood vessels, and that the HPAI virus genetic material was present in several tissues throughout her body, including the ulcerated tissue in her ventriculus. Other tests showed Jackie was negative for West Nile Virus, and heavy metal levels were within acceptable limits.While toxicology screening detected brodifacoum, an anticoagulant rodenticide, in Jackie's liver, the necropsy did not find uncontrolled bleeding typically associated with the chemical pesticide, so it was not identified as her primary cause of illness or death. "Together, the findings showed that Jackie was suffering from multiple severe and interconnected disease processes that had been developing over time and ultimately led to her decline and death," CDFW's release said.Jackie's remains were cremated by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's National Eagle Repository, following the established procedures intended to prevent the transmission of HPAI to wildlife or humans, the release said. "The story of the Big Bear bald eagle reflects the powerful connection people feel to these iconic birds," said a statement from CDFW Director Meghan Hertel. "We're grateful to everyone who cared for her and worked to support her well-being. Understanding the results of these tests is an important part of learning from this case and can help inform the care and treatment of other eagles and wildlife in the future."Jackie was an iconic fixture in Southern California, drawing the attention of millions across the United States thanks to the 24/7 livestream camera documenting her life and that of her partner, Shadow, from above Big Bear Lake. Over the years, the duo parented several clutches of eaglets, most recently Sandy and Luna. CDFW officials said that based on camera data, they have no evidence to suggest that Shadow or the eaglets were sick."Jackie's story brought unprecedented public attention to bald eagles and the importance of protecting the habitats they depend on," the release from CDFW said. "Her life and the public's connection to her highlights the powerful role that wildlife can play in connecting people to conservation."In the weeks since her death, Jackie has been honored with a massive memorial service in Big Bear, a life-size monument at a park in the San Bernardino Mountains and an Ontario Tower Buzzers minor league baseball game dedicated to celebrating her life. California state legislators also passed a resolution in her honor, proclaiming September 4 as California Wildlife Day.

title: Marcus Reus has goal, assist to back JT Marcinkowski as Galaxy blank Timbers 2-0
description: Marco Reus had a goal and an assist to back JT Marcinkowski and the Los Angeles Galaxy beat the Portland Timbers 2-0.
content: Marco Reus had a goal and an assist to back JT Marcinkowski and the Los Angeles Galaxy beat the Portland Timbers 2-0 on Wednesday night.Reus staked the Galaxy (10-11-9) to a 1-0 lead in the 17th minute when he used assists from Robert Taylor and Pablo Ruiz to score his eighth goal of the campaign.That's where the score stood until Reus set up up Justin Haak in the 80th minute for his second goal this season and his fourth in 110 career matches. It was the career-high 11th assist for Reus.Marcinkowski finished with five saves for Los Angeles. It was his fourth clean sheet in 24 starts this season.James Pantemis stopped three shots for Portland (9-14-6).The two clubs played to a 1-1 draw in Portland to close out March.The Galaxy improve to 6-4-5 at home, while the Timbers fall to 2-10-3 on the road.Portland has gone 1-4-2 since the start of September.Up nextPortland: Hosts Colorado Rapids on Saturday.Los Angeles: Hosts San Diego FC on Saturday.

title: Hollywood officials warn Amendment 3 could cost city $34 million and force cuts or higher fees
description: At a public meeting, a deputy city manager said no service is safe from potential cuts, and city officials estimate the first tax reduction alone would cost $34 million.
content: The city of Hollywood hosted a public meeting to give residents an opportunity to ask questions and learn more about Amendment 3, a ballot proposal aimed at drastically slashing property taxes.Under Amendment 3, the taxable value of a primary homestead property would drop by $150,000 in 2027 and by $250,000 in 2028. Following those reductions, the state Legislature would decide whether to eliminate property taxes on primary residences altogether.City officials warn the proposal could significantly impact local municipal budgets. Hollywood stands to lose $34 million in revenue with the initial cut alone."What's really important for people to understand is that nothing is safe from potential cuts," said Adam Reichbach, deputy city manager in Hollywood. "Ultimately, cities are going to have to make decisions about whether we cut services or programs or raise taxes and fees or maybe some combination of both, but ultimately we have to balance our budget every year."Tax revenue currently makes up 46% of Hollywood's general fund. If property tax revenue drops, property owners without a homestead exemption could face tax increases to offset the losses.The potential revenue loss comes as municipal operating costs continue to rise sharply."Landscaping contracts are up over 25%. Police vehicles are up 25%. Medical supplies are up 160%," Reichbach said. "These are real numbers that cities are going to have to deal with. Look at gas prices, right? All of our police vehicles, all of our fire units, they all rely on that."

title: Denis Bouanga and Son Heung-min propel LAFC to 3-1 victory over Austin
description: Denis Bouanga and Son Heung-min both contributed to all three goals for Los Angeles FC in a 3-1 victory over Austin FC.
content: Denis Bouanga and Son Heung-min both contributed to all three goals for Los Angeles FC in a 3-1 victory over Austin FC on Wednesday night.Neither team found the net until Bouanga took a pass from Son seven minutes into the second half and scored to give LAFC (12-9-9) the lead. Brandon VÃ¡zquez scored for the second time this season â using an assist from Myrto Uzuni to knot the score in the 66th minute.Bouanga answered the following minute with his 17th netter off another assist from Son â his league-leading 15th of the season â and LAFC went back in front 2-1.Bouanga returned the favor when he notched his eighth assist on Son's goal â his sixth â in the 72nd minute for a two-score advantage. Bouanga's assist was his eighth and Jacob Shaffelburg picked up his career-high fifth.Hugo Lloris totaled three saves for Los Angeles, now 2-2-3 since the start of September.Brad Stuver stopped 10 shots â one off his career high â for Austin (7-11-11), which has lost two straight following an eight-match unbeaten streak.LAFC improves to 9-3-3 at home, while Austin drops to 3-8-4 on the road.The two clubs played to a scoreless draw in Austin to close out March.Up nextAustin: Hosts Vancouver Whitecaps on Saturday.Los Angeles: At New York City FC on Saturday.

title: Santa Monica's Mel's Drive-In could be demolished for new housing
description: A new filing hopes to stop a property owner's plan to turn Mel's Drive-In in Santa Monica into an apartment complex.
content: At the corner of Olympic and Lincoln Boulevards, sits a roadside postcard and a nod to history at Mel's Drive-In."Having places that tell stories that survive over time is something that everybody understands," said Nina Fresco, Vice President of the Santa Monica Conservancy. Fresco and the conservancy are playing a part in writing the location's next chapter. "We want to bring landmarks into the future," Fresco said. The Santa Monica and Los Angeles Conservancies filed a nomination application in August, asking the city to designate the 1959 googie-style diner a landmark. They said it would protect key features and set standards for any changes, but wouldn't rule out new housing. In September, the property's owner, ValueRock, followed up with a preliminary application for a 138-unit apartment complex. The city said it's not a formal housing application and no demolition permit has been filed. "My client believes the highest and best use for this property is a housing project," said Dave Rand, the property owner's attorney.Rand said the application proposes demolishing the building at this time, but calls it a very early first step and adds that the owner is open to a compromise."Things change and evolve, but that doesn't mean we can'tkeep some of the great things about this site that people love," Rand said. The project could potentially include a ground-floor cafe that looks and feels like the existing one. Fresco said she's taking a wait-and-see approach. "I need to see or hear more because it's not what you want to do; it's how you do it," Fresco said. "Something that looks like it is not preservation."Rand said he's asked the Santa Monica Conservancy for a meeting. Both sides, including LA Conservancy, said housing and preservation can coexist at the location. "I don't think it has to be an either or," said Andrew Salimian, a director at the LA Conservancy.Mel's Drive-In remains open with the manager telling the LA Times that the lease runs through 2029. The city expects the Landmarks Commission to review the nomination application on Dec. 14, with any appeal going to the city council. "I think we can create a new building here that very much respects and embraces and celebrates the past," Rand said.

title: Car found in Colorado lake renews debate over proposed traffic gate in Bow Mar community
description: A car found in Bowles Lake Wednesday morning is renewing concerns about traffic safety in Bow Mar.
content: A car found in Bowles Lake Wednesday morning is renewing concerns about traffic safety in Bow Mar, where residents are pushing for a gate to limit access to the town. But neighboring cities Denver and Littleton say any gate could push traffic concerns onto their public roads.The car was discovered in the lake around 7 a.m. South Metro Fire Rescue crews, including the South Metro Dive Team, confirmed no one was inside the vehicle, and no one was hurt. First responder scanner traffic indicated the car's license plates came back as stolen. Columbine Valley Police Department covers Bow Mar and did not provide any details beyond South Metro Fire's update that officials were looking for the suspect.For Liz Manning, a Bow Mar resident and the town trustee, the incident highlights what she believes is a pattern of unsafe driving in Bow Mar."The concerns I have is that, at some point, this is going to involve a pedestrian and not just the lake," Manning said.The town has proposed installing a gate near Sheridan Boulevard as part of its efforts to address traffic concerns. However, leaders in Denver and Littleton have pushed back against the proposal, arguing that restricting access to public streets could shift traffic problems into neighboring communities.After opposition from residents and leaders in Denver and Littleton, Bow Mar has refined their plans and now intends to start with one gate instead of the originally proposed three.Manning said the town has already tried several measures to slow traffic, as the town's traffic studies show more drivers coming through Bow Mar, with a majority of drivers believed to not be residents."We have slowed our speed limit to 20 miles an hour," Manning said. "We have installed a multitude of speed bumps. We've narrowed our roads. We've increased enforcement, and we're still having these issues, and so the next phase of our traffic mitigation efforts are a gate at Sheridan."Columbine Valley Police Department did not respond to CBS Colorado's request for data on Wednesday but Bow Mar's traffic reports that cite police data show the town saw close to 300 traffic violations last year, slightly less than in 2024. The town's 2025 traffic study also shows the average vehicle speeding near Sheridan was going close to 30 miles per hour where the speed limit is 20 mile per hour.Denver City Councilman Kevin Flynn argues Bow Mar should work with neighboring communities rather than restrict access to its streets altogether. Flynn shared concerns that a gate near Sheridan could back traffic up into a busy intersection at Quincy."(Bow Mar officials) want to solve their traffic hazards on the backs of my residents by giving them the traffic hazards," Flynn said.Columbine Valley Police did not clarify whether Bow Mar residents or non-residents are responsible for specific traffic violations."You know what (Bow Mar officials) haven't tried? They haven't tried cooperating with Denver and Littleton. That's what they haven't tried," Flynn said, "How many of those crashes are Bow Mar residents? How do we know that the guy who crashed into the lake isn't a Bow Mar resident?"Flynn warned that installing a gate could prompt Denver to consider a similar measure on the city's side of the road, effectively blocking Bow Mar's access to its own gate.Manning said Bow Mar residents are demanding action, as the town continues to see crashes and more cars driving through town."I appreciate (Denver and Littleton's) position within their respective towns. I think we're at a point where our residents are demanding action," Manning said, "We're trying to avoid a fatality."Manning said, if the single gate is installed, the town plans to monitor its impact on traffic.Littleton's mayor also opposes Bow Mar's proposed gate, but says Littleton's existing gate operates differently. Littleton Mayor Kyle Schlachter says his city's gate has limited closure periods during rush hour, when access is limited to emergency vehicles. It does not restrict access exclusively to Littleton residents.Bow Mar is expected to discuss its gate proposal at the town's next meeting on Monday, Oct. 19.

title: New dinosaur species, a T. rex cousin that "would have chased us," identified from fossil found 100 years ago
description: A fossil discovered 100 years ago in the U.K. has been identified as a previously unknown cousin of the T. rex, and it "definitely would have chased us."
content: London — A previously unknown species of dinosaur — a "long-clawed predator the size of a tiger" and a cousin of the Tyrannosaurus rex — has been identified from a fossil originally found 100 years ago, but which remained hidden away in a British museum until recently.The species has been named Invictibellatrix amberina, and it belongs to a group of two-legged carnivores known as megaraptorans according to an article published in the Royal Society Open Science research journal. Megaraptorans were closely related to the group of dinosaurs T. rex originated from, the tyrannosaurs. Unlike T. rex, however, scientists say Invictibellatrix did not attack prey with its mouth, but with its long arms and giant curved claws.Researchers believe the dinosaur would have been between 10 and 13 feet long and almost 5 feet tall. Its body would have had feathers, and it would have hunted smaller dinosaurs, lizards and mammals.The fossil that led to the discovery sat in a drawer at the Natural History Museum in London for nearly 100 years, having first been obtained by the vaunted institution in 1924. Dr. Cassius Morrison of University College London, the lead author of the article that announced the discovery, called it a "real mystery that the fossil was overlooked for so long."Morrison wrote that while Invictibellatrix "was not the apex predator of its time," it would have been a formidable threat to humans if they had coexisted with the species — even "more dangerous than a T. rex." "We would have been perfectly sized prey, about a third of their body weight," he said. "They definitely would have chased us. A T. rex would not have bothered, as we would have been too small."The fossil itself is a chunk of the back of a skull. It was one of 1,000 specimens originally discovered by Reginald Walter Tooley on the Isle of Wight, off the south coast of England, and it was then acquired by the Natural History Museum.Invictibellatrix lived during the Early Cretaceous period, around 120 million years ago, and is one of the smallest and earliest known members of the megaraptoran group.To understand Invictibellatrix, researchers first took a CT scan of the fossil to create a 3D model of that part of its skull. The results were compared with the skulls of other two-legged meat-eating dinosaurs, such as tyrannosaurs, spinosaurs and raptors. A number of unique features led researchers to conclude they had discovered a new species.Invictibellatrix is Latin for "unconquered female warrior" and amberina refers to the amber found in the rocks where the fossil was discovered. The researchers said by naming the dinosaur Invictibellatrix, they wanted to "give hope and strength to all those who are bullied, discriminated, victimized, and oppressed that tomorrow will be theirs and not to give up in the face of such odds."

title: Mystery of Amelia Earhart's missing plane could be solved in days, researchers say
description: A group of American researchers believes it may be days away from finding what remains of the missing plane of legendary aviator Amelia Earhart off a remote island in the South Pacific.
content: A group of American researchers believes it may be days away from finding what remains of the missing plane of legendary aviator Amelia Earhart off a remote island in the South Pacific. An expedition team led by Steve Schultz from Purdue University and Richard Pettigrew from the Archaeological Legacy Institute on Wednesday began the painstaking search for what could be Earhart's Lockheed Electra 10-E plane. "We're looking at the land, we're looking for artifacts that might relate to Amelia Earhart," Pettigrew told CBS News on Wednesday. "We're still very much in the data-gathering phase," Schultz added. Members of the expedition are searching a lagoon off the coast of Nikumaroro. They are focused on inspecting what is known as the Taraia Object, a visual anomaly that has been visible in aerial photos dating back to 1938 but was first noticed in satellite imagery in 2020. That satellite imagery is what inspired the new expedition. Stormy weather hindered their efforts on Wednesday, but expedition members said they expect to have a definitive answer on the object in the coming days. The search area is so remote, it took the 17-member expedition team five days at sea to reach it. However, the team is confident it will be able to say in just a matter of days whether they have found Earhart's plane. "Our next step is complete analysis of the data that we gathered and then to begin using a hydraulic dredge to remove sediment from the bottom," Pettigrew said. Earhart went missing on July 2, 1937, while attempting to become the first person to fly around the equator. Earhart and her navigator, Fred Noonan, vanished 22,000 miles into their expedition. Nikumaroro is part of the archipelago country of Kiribati, which is located about halfway between Australia and Hawaii. It's about 400 miles southeast of Howland Island, which, according to researchers, was the final destination of Earhart and Noonan's journey around the equator.
