But critics warn that the information could also be used to track immigrants, people seeking abortions outside their home states, and survivors fleeing abusive partners.Ashley Ortiz, a member of the activist group The Wolves, said she fears the technology could put domestic violence survivors at risk."We're going to be seeing them tracked by their domestic violence abusers," Ortiz said.She pointed to concerns about law enforcement officers misusing surveillance systems to access information for personal reasons, potentially exposing a survivor's location to an abusive partner.The concerns extend beyond Flock itself, said Manny, an organizer with Deflock San Francisco, who argued that interconnected surveillance systems create broader risks when data is shared across agencies."All of these surveillance systems are feeding into a network that is designed to data share," Manny said.Flock did not respond to a request for an on-camera interview. The company says it has no contract with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and that ICE cannot directly access its cameras or customer data.Langley has also denied that Flock helps authorities target people seeking abortions. The company says its safeguards are designed to prevent misuse.Law enforcement agencies across the Bay Area have pointed to Flock cameras as tools that can help investigators quickly identify suspects after crimes are committed. San Francisco has approved the use of Flock cameras for public safety, setting up a debate over how to balance investigative benefits with civil liberties protections.For protesters, the risks outweigh those benefits without stronger oversight.Suleiman said changing public attitudes about surveillance begins with conversations that encourage people to question how the technology works and who can access the information it collects."Nobody ever stumbles into political consciousness, right? It's often relational," she said.She hopes the demonstration will also pressure local officials to reconsider how they approach surveillance technology."[We want] to push, you know, our local lawmakers to stop catering to the whims of tech billionaires and actually listen to the San Franciscans who call this place home," Suleiman said.Flock Safety is now valued at nearly $8.5 billion, underscoring the growing commercial stakes surrounding public safety technology as communities debate its reach and oversight.

title: Clairton Bears football team will miss 3rd Friday night game of the season
description: For the second week in a row and the third time this season, the Clairton Bears football team won't be playing under the Friday Night Lights.
content: For the second week in a row and the third time this season, the Clairton Bears football team won't be playing under the Friday Night Lights.This Friday, the Bears were set to take on the Leechburg Blue Devils. But the Leechburg Area School District released a statement saying in part, "Due to recent injuries and resulting roster constraints, our coaching and administrative staff have determined that we cannot safely field a team for this contest. The health, safety, and physical well-being of our student-athletes will always be our highest priority.""It just sucks that the kids are practicing and they don't get to play," said Athena Brant, whose son plays for the Clairton Bears. "I don't understand. I mean, I understand the shortage of players, but I mean, I hope no other teams do it."KDKA-TV reported in September that the Bears announced their regret to forfeit their game against Steel Valley High School due to "personnel matters." WPIAL officials confirmed to KDKA-TV on Wednesday that the game was postponed on Sept. 4 because the coach was unavailable to coach.Last week, the Bears' game against Springdale was postponed along with their game this week against Leechburg.WPIAL officials confirmed to KDKA-TV that both games were postponed due to Springdale and Leechburg not having enough eligible players on the team."The games were not forfeited. They were postponed," said WPIAL spokesperson Matthew Manz."It's sad for the seniors too, because this is their last year. So hopefully they get to play," Brant said.Clairton is the defending WPIAL and PIAA Class 1A Champion.Manz said the schools have until Oct. 31 to make up the games."If they're not made up, the league will decide if the games are forfeited," Manz said.KDKA-TV reached out to the Clairton superintendent and athletic director to learn more about when or if those games will be rescheduled. We did not hear back.The Bears' next game is set for Oct. 23 against Greensburg Central Catholic.

title: Six Flags Over Georgia to reopen on Friday after deadly incident on Goliath roller coaster
description: Six Flags Over Georgia will reopen later this week as the investigation into the deadly incident onboard its Goliath roller coaster continues.
content: Six Flags Over Georgia will reopen as scheduled later this week as the investigation into the deadly incident onboard one of the park's roller coasters continues.In a statement to CBS News Atlanta, park officials said Six Flags Over Georgia will be open on Friday. The park has been closed since Monday due to its weekend operations schedule. While the park will be reopened, its Goliath roller coaster will remain closed after the death of 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem onboard the ride on Monday afternoon. Witnesses say that Kariem was ejected from the ride and struck other passengers as he fell.State investigators and the ride's manufacturer, Bolliger & Mabillard, are investigating the deadly incident. The park's parent company has shut down multiple similar rides across the country out of caution.Kariem was the second death connected with Goliath in the ride's 20 years of operations, according to data from Atlanta-based attorneys The Doan Law Firm. The first was in 2006, in which a 45-year-old man became unresponsive on the ride. The law firm said it appeared that the man suffered a fatal heart attack while on the ride and that his death was believed to be due to a congenital heart condition.Riders injured in incident identified as juvenilesOn Wednesday, the Cobb County Police Department shared a new statement about the other passengers who were injured during the deadly incident."All of them were transported by ambulance to various area hospitals with non-life-threatening injuries," the police department said. "Because they were all juveniles, no further information can be shared."Family of man killed at Six Flags warns about donation scamsKariem was an IT manager, teacher, and robotics coach at Atlanta charter school Wesley International Academy.On Facebook, the school described Kariem as a "beloved colleague, friend, and integral part of the Wesley family for more than 12 years.""His love for Wesley, dedication to our students, and commitment to our school community were evident in everything he did," the post read. "Mr. Kariem was deeply loved and respected, and his absence will be felt throughout our school community. Our hearts are with his family, friends, colleagues, students, and all who knew and loved him as we mourn this tremendous loss."On Wednesday, Kariem's family released a statement asking for privacy while noting that they have not created or authorized any crowdfunding accounts or fundraising appeals in his name."Please do not donate to requests posted in groups, on pages or through personal or professional accounts," the statement read in part. "If his mother decides to establish a scholarship or fund in his honor, she will announce it publicly through her designated official representative."

title: Bay Area woman's nonprofit provides sexual violence survivors with dignity along with essentials
description: A San Jose woman's nonprofit is clothing people with warmth and comfort when they surrender their own clothes as forensic evidence in sexual abuse investigations.
content: A San Jose woman's nonprofit is clothing people with warmth and comfort when they surrender their own clothes as forensic evidence in sexual abuse investigations.Lisa Blanchard clothes people with dignity and love. She knew she'd found the right career fit after a woman told her that survivors of sexual violence give up what they're wearing for DNA evidence."So if you give up all your clothes, what are you going to wear home, right?" said Blanchard. "So I remember when this woman told me this, feeling utterly horrified. Like, I felt like I immediately had to get up and change that."So Blanchard started The Grateful Garment Project in 2011. It was her college capstone assignment. Then it transformed into a San Jose-based nonprofit. It's collected and given away clothing to more than 34,000 sexual abuse survivors, from infants to adults."Someone cares," said Blanchard. "I want those people to know that they are not alone in that moment."Volunteers from The Grateful Garment Project help serve more than 100 partner agencies including hospitals and shelters in 45 California counties.Blanchard says the most-needed items, bras, are also the least donated. The nonprofit also gives away toiletries, toys, books and backpacks.Because of privacy concerns, Blanchard rarely meets the recipients but she did get an unexpected shout-out from Chanel Miller who was sexually assaulted in 2015 on the Stanford University campus. Miller woke up disoriented and alone in the hospital; her clothes were surrendered as evidence."I was left naked except for a flimsy hospital gown and my boots," Miller said in a social media post. "If I had had to leave the hospital in that state, I imagine I would have felt completely exposed, vulnerable and humiliated."In her memoir, Know My Name, Miller describes choosing an outfit from The Grateful Garment Project and says she still cherishes the sweatshirt."It's a shield of armor. It's proof there's still good in the world," she described in her video post.The acknowledgment touched Blanchard's heart."It made me cry actually. It still makes me cry to think about it," she said of Miller's video. "It is a rare treasure to receive validation from an actual survivor."The nonprofit receives no government money and is 100% donor-funded, said Blanchard. The group recently held Its annual fundraising luncheon, DigniTea, in Cupertino.The Grateful Garment Project also offers internships for high school and college students, honoring the nonprofit's origins as her college assignment.Jessica Ramirez of the Sonoma County Rape Crisis Center, Verity, noted how Blanchard went out of her way to furnish a survivor's new apartment.Each donated object, Ramirez noted, is tagged with a message that someone cares."It definitely helps them be seen," Ramirez said. "So they know where it came from, it came from love. They truly do care and want to support survivors of sexual assault."

title: Penn State leaders recommend ending 47 degree programs
description: Students at Penn State University and its branch campuses may soon have fewer programs to choose from.
content: Students at Penn State University and its branch campuses may soon have fewer programs to choose from.After an "Academic Portfolio and Program Review," leaders announced that the final recommendations include ending 47 of its bachelor's and associate degree offerings, or nearly 12%, in the coming years.Administrators said the main reasons come down to low student enrollment and limited employment opportunities. According to Penn State, 784 students, or 1.1% of the undergrad student population, enrolled in these programs in spring 2026. The university said they will all be able to complete their degrees.Currently, there is no one enrolled in nine of the 47 programs, and they've started phasing out or not accepting new students into 15 of them. Twenty-four would continue to be offered at another campus.About three-quarters or the majority of the programs impacted are at branch campuses, which recently faced years of debate over their sustainability, with seven of them set to close next spring, including Fayette, New Kensington and Shenango.About a third of the programs recommended for closure are in the humanities and arts, and some degrees would disappear at all campuses, including American studies and security and risk analysis.The recommendations now await final approval by Executive Vice President and Provost Fotis Sotiropoulos.In a statement, he called the review a "healthy practice" in higher education, and went on to say, "Regular program reviews will help us to be nimble and responsive as the world continues to change, and as we continue to face the reality of changing demographics, stagnant state support for our students, and rising costs."It's an exercise administrators said will continue as they develop an ongoing review cycle.So far, there's been no word on potential faculty layoffs or on how much money Penn State could save from these cuts.More information can be found on Penn State's website.

title: Communities across Pittsburgh area look for relief amid rising salt costs
description: While winter isn't here yet, its impact is already being felt in the wallets of municipalities across the Pittsburgh region.
content: While winter isn't here yet, its impact is already being felt in the wallets of municipalities across the Pittsburgh region. The bid for prices almost doubled, and leaders were looking for cheaper options.When KDKA-TV first reported the issue a few weeks ago, some governments were looking to find better prices. Some did, but they are still paying significantly more than they did last year.The South Hills Area Council of Governments, or SHACOG, does the salt bid for about 100 communities across Allegheny and Butler counties. This year the bid was $152 per ton from American Rock Salt, up from $88 per ton last year with Compass, which had delivery issues.SHACOG president and West Mifflin Council Vice President Dan Davis says only 30% of municipalities took this bid."That's significantly lower than we've had in the past. Usually, we were running 90-95% acceptance of the bid pricing that we had," Davis said.Places like Brackenridge took the bid. On the phone, their borough manager told KDKA-TV that nothing else was concrete. To make up the cost difference, they will have to take money from their paving.On the flip side, West Mifflin is one of the 70% of communities that didn't take the bid. They partnered with eight other municipalities to get $134 a ton with Morton."Even for us larger communities, who did buy extra salt at the end of the year through our Compass contract, it's still a significant increase. A one-hundred percent increase is a large impact on your communities," Davis said.What has Davis not too happy is that a cooperative purchasing program with the state got a bid closer to $90 a ton with American Rock Salt, just a couple of months before SHACOG put out their bid. This contract is only for one year."Next year, we're trying to do a one plus two, and bid it a little earlier so we do have better pricing. So, we're hoping that will get resolved next year a little bit better," Davis said about future bids.KDKA-TV reached out to American Rock Salt for comment, but has not heard back as of Wednesday evening.

title: Prisco's Family Market in Aurora celebrates century in operation
description: The celebration comes as the market survived some of the hardest chapters in American history and a few of its own.
content: They've been feeding Aurora for a full century.Now, the city leaders plan to celebrate Prisco's Family Market Friday, with a party showcasing some of their vendors, handing out free hot dogs and issuing a special proclamation.The celebration comes as the market survived some of the hardest chapters in American history and a few of its own.A hundred years of history, told through the generations of grocery bags and the photos on the walls."We used to climb up in the truck and the sit on the wheel walls amongst all the groceries, which is kind of funny because that would never be accepted today, but we loved it in our my grandpa loved having us along," said Beth Guzauskas, owner of Prisco's Family Market.Beth traces Prisco's Family Market history through her own family tree. Her mom and dad were the second generation.Started as a produce store on wheels, a fourth generation has now pulled up a plate."This place is my childhood," said market president Andy Guzauskas. "My great grandma watched me in our old store while mom was at work."Andy says he stocked and cleaned shelves through school and briefly considered another path."I sat through the first class. I went to my counselor and said I need to change it. It's not for me," he said, laughing.But this is more than business â it's about his community."It's very important to us," Andy said. "A lot of statistics show that neighborhoods with independent groceries in them tend to have a better quality of life."They've fed Aurora through lean times â two World Wars, the Great Depression, recession and COVID, but storm damage last year was their biggest challenge yet."I just stood there and cried. I just really did," Beth said.And when they needed it, their customers came back, ready to help them rebuild."We were flabbergasted. I was like, I don't know what I'm doing back there, so I can't ask you to go back there, but we'll see what insurance says first," Andy said.As for what the future holds, with little room left for more photos. "We'll have to go to the next wall," Beth said.They're not sure what's next, but they know how far they've come."It's amazing. I think my grandparents would be proud," Andy said.

title: A.J. Brown returns to Patriots practice for first time since suffering ankle injury in Week 1
description: Wide receiver A.J. Brown practiced Wednesday for the first time since suffering a high-ankle sprain in the team's season opener.
content: The Patriots are one step closer to getting a key piece back on the field. A.J. Brown practiced Wednesday for the first time since suffering a high-ankle sprain in the team's season opener. Brown was placed on injured reserve after suffering the ankle injury against the Seattle Seahawks in Week 1, meaning he had to miss at least four games. The Patriots have now played four games since, going 3-1 so far while Brown has been on IR.Reports at the time indicated that the team expected Brown to miss four to six weeks following the injury.On Wednesday, the Patriots opened Brown's practice window, which means they now have 21 days to add him to the team's active roster.Head coach Mike Vrabel said it's too early to tell if Brown will play this week against the New York Jets. After Sunday's game, the Patriots have a quick turnaround. They play the Chicago Bears on Thursday Night Football Oct. 22."He hasn't been out there for four weeks. So we'll get him back out there practicing, see if he's ready to go in a couple days. If not, then 21-day window and we'll go from there," Vrabel said before practice.Vrabel was asked about Brown's rehabilitation process."I think he's stayed engaged. I think it's difficult sometimes to stay engaged. But his routine was really good," Vrabel said. "His ability to be around guys in the meetings and also focus on his rehab, treat everything as a pro, be where he's supposed to be and do everything to get back."Brown's return would be a boost for New England's wide receiver room, as Mack Hollins is currently on injured reserve with a calf injury. On the team's practice report, Brown was officially listed as a limited participant. Cornerback Christian Gonzalez, who has missed the last two games with a shoulder injury, was also on the practice field Wednesday in a limited capacity.Vrabel also said offensive lineman Marcus Bryant's practice window is being opened. He's been on injured reserve after suffering an ankle injury during the preseason.TreVeyon Henderson, who suffered a high-ankle sprain against the Raiders, and Will Campbell, who injured his knee in the game, were both on the field and limited on Wednesday.

title: New renderings show vision for The Stitch, but funding questions remain for Atlanta highway park
description: New renderings of The Stitch offer a closer look at the proposed transformation of downtown Atlanta, but significant questions remain about funding and when construction of the highway park could begin.
content: A stretch of Atlanta's Downtown Connector could one day look dramatically different, with trees, walking paths, and public gathering spaces built above the traffic.New renderings of The Stitch offer a closer look at the proposed transformation, which aims to reconnect parts of downtown separated by Interstate 75/85.But while the designs show what is possible, significant questions remain about funding and when construction of the highway park could begin.For Geraldine Robinson Smith, who has lived at Centennial Place Apartments for nearly eight years, the project represents an opportunity to make the downtown area more connected."Right near, we are downtown, in the middle of downtown, but at the same time, we got the highways right there. And they need to be connected," Smith said.Smith, who walks to work, said she would welcome more trees and greenery in the area."I would like to see more greenery. You know, I would like to see more greenery, more, you know, forest look, more trees," she said.The proposed project would create approximately 17 acres of public space in three phases, with the first phase focused on roughly five acres near Peachtree and Courtland streets.The renderings show green lawns, walking paths, and gathering places above portions of the interstate. Traffic would continue moving beneath the proposed park.Smith said additional recreational space could also benefit children in nearby neighborhoods."So if you get more parks, because over here in the complex where I live, there's a lot of kids," Smith said. "So that would even be better for the kids if they had a park right here where they can actually go and do things, do activities."The proposed first phase is not located directly beside Smith's apartment complex, but she said the broader idea of creating more public space appeals to her.When shown the renderings, Smith responded, "Oh, yeah. Yes. That would be nice. Very nice."Not everyone is convinced the project should be a priority.Brittany Wade, who lives near 14th Street and the Downtown Connector, said she has watched traffic increase as the surrounding area continues to develop."A lot of traffic, a lot more people, city's growing," Wade said.While Wade sees potential benefits in additional green space, she questioned whether the money could be better spent addressing existing infrastructure. The entire project is estimated to cost between $750 million and $1 billion."Seven hundred million is a lot of money. I don't know. Maybe get some more opinions," Wade said. "I think some of the roads could use a little bit more work than maybe bringing in green spaces, honestly."The first phase's cost alone is estimated at $250 million to $275 million. The larger project would require substantially more funding.The Stitch also faces a financial setback after losing more than $150 million in previously awarded federal funding. Project leaders have pursued an additional $60 million federal grant as they work to advance the plan.Street and pedestrian improvements could begin as early as late 2027, but construction of the park above the interstate does not have a confirmed start date.For residents like Smith, the idea of transforming space above one of Atlanta's busiest highways offers a glimpse of what downtown could become.For Wade, the question is whether that transformation should come before other pressing needs.Both perspectives highlight the challenge facing The Stitch: turning an ambitious vision for downtown into a project that can be funded and built.

title: Long-awaited Sellers Avenue Bridge reopening brings relief to Ridley Park businesses
description: After four years of construction and detours, the Sellers Avenue Bridge in Ridley Park is reopening to traffic on Thursday.
content: After four years of construction and detours, the Sellers Avenue Bridge in Ridley Park, Pennsylvania, is reopening, bringing relief to business owners who said the closure took a toll on their livelihoods.PennDOT is wrapping up a $10 million construction project, with a ribbon-cutting ceremony planned for Thursday at 1:30 p.m. to celebrate the completion of the bridge."I could not be more excited," Jennifer Kearney, who owns a photography studio in the middle of the construction zone, said.The construction noise sometimes made it difficult to work."It's a little bit hard to do a newborn photo shoot when there's a jackhammer right outside," she said.The bridge was built in 1904 and rebuilt in 1952. PennDOT abruptly closed it in July 2022 after determining it was no longer safe for drivers or pedestrians.Business owners said they are ready for a fresh start."I am so thrilled about parking being more available, and there's parking wars around here for sure," Machele Kortum, owner of Lux & Roses, said, "and those roads being closed by the bridge is not helping."The new bridge has two travel lanes and a sidewalk on each side.PennDOT also made traffic signal upgrades, installed ADA ramps and completed other improvements designed to accommodate higher traffic volumes."The bridge was replaced with a 75-foot-long concrete box beam bridge and a solid-faced barrier capped with curved fencing on the barrier was installed with the bridge, so there are some safety features," Helen Reinbrecht, community relations coordinator for PennDOT, said. "We did keep a lot of the historic elements of the bridge, so ornamented lighting and plaques. And the masonry abutments will all look familiar to drivers and pedestrians."Before its closure, the bridge carried about 3,400 vehicles a day, with trains running underneath. Pedestrians can already use the new bridge. Vehicle traffic is set to return Thursday.Kearney hopes the reopening will make it easier for people to visit her studio, and said she is grateful to the clients who continued to support her throughout the construction."There were times when I was kind of ready to throw in the towel and just say, you know what? I'm done, I'm going to find another space," she said. "But then it got to a point where I thought, if I've made it this far, I want to see the completion."

title: Lamar Jackson absent again at practice for the Ravens, Hendrickson returns
description: Lamar Jackson was absent again at practice Wednesday, as the Baltimore star deals with an ankle injury that has already caused him to miss one game.
content: Lamar Jackson was absent again at practice Wednesday, as the Baltimore star deals with an ankle injury that has already caused him to miss one game.Jackson was injured two weekends ago in a victory over Tennessee. The Ravens were able to win at Atlanta on Sunday night with Tyler Huntley at quarterback. They play at Cleveland on Sunday.Baltimore (4-1) has some margin for error after a solid start. That's in contrast to last season, when Jackson was hurt early on and didn't come back until the team was 2-5. He rarely looked great after that, so there's some risk in bringing him back too soon."I think it's definitely day to day," coach Jesse Minter said. "I think a lot of times, right when those things happen, you're not sure, and as you gather information, you look at stuff. ... He's doing everything he can to be out here, and when he's able to be, then he will."Huntley has won all three of his starts for the Ravens since the beginning of last season.The Ravens did have edge rusher Trey Hendrickson (finger) back as a full participant in practice after he missed the last two games. Rookie receiver Ja'Kobi Lane, who is still on injured reserve because of a wrist injury, practiced fully as well.Several players were limited, including recently acquired center Cam Jurgens (concussion)."We'll make sure that all the medical stuff goes the way we want it to go, and if it does, he'll be ready. If not, then we'll be ready to play without him," Minter said. "The medical side will really determine his availability, but he's done an amazing job mentally to really learn everything and be ready to roll."Tight end Matthew Hibner (hand) did not practice.

title: Pennsylvania lawmakers propose bail reforms following murder of Pittsburgh-area doctor
description: A group of lawmakers is introducing legislation that aims to strengthen the bail process and protect potential victims of violence from offenders with prior violent convictions or charges.
content: A group of state lawmakers is introducing legislation that aims to strengthen the bail process and protect potential victims of violence from offenders with prior violent convictions or charges. They gathered in Moon Park Wednesday to announce the legislation, while also calling for reform of pre-trial bail procedures in Allegheny County.Republican state Reps. Jeremy Shaffer, Natalie Mihalek, Valerie Gaydos, Jason Ortitay and Andrew Kuzma are co-sponsoring two separate pieces of legislation following the recent murder of Dr. Idris Evans, a pediatrician at UPMC Children's Hospital of Pittsburgh who was killed during an attack at his Edgewood home.House Bill 2856, introduced by Shaffer, requires consideration of prior violent convictions, burglary convictions, other pending criminal charges and protection from abuse orders when a decision is made regarding bail."The question must be asked: How is a person with a violent past released on bail without stronger safeguards?" said Shaffer in a written statement. "The tragic murder of Dr. Evans makes it crystal clear that assessing danger to the community must be a central part of any bail decision."Mihalek also plans to introduce legislation requiring a complete and current criminal history report, including in-state, out-of-state and federal records, to be provided to judges or magistrates before bail is set or modified."This issue has exposed a simple truth about the Allegheny County bail system â there is no one looking out for victims in this case, the general public," Mihalek said in the statement.That claim was echoed by Kelly Rae Robertson, a former Allegheny County Court employee of more than 14 years, who worked as a bail investigator at the Allegheny County Jail. Robertson said she witnessed pressure to recommend release of high-risk offenders, due to grants received from outside sources with the intent of keeping jail population numbers low. Because of those non-monetary bail releases, Robertson alleges several violent offenders were allowed to go free and then went on to allegedly commit more violent attacks."There's not enough time today to tell all the stories like these or to name all the people who are now dead because the priority was the grant metrics and a lower jail count rather than public safety," said Robertson.State Sen. Devlin Robinson, R-Allegheny County, also introduced Senate Bill 490, which calls for an examination of the bail process. The bill, which had bipartisan co-sponsors, passed the state Senate in March."Pennsylvanians deserve a criminal justice system that takes the threat of violent crime seriously and puts the safety of victims and communities at the forefront of bail decisions," said Robinson.The lawmakers also pointed to other violent murders in the county at the hands of violent offenders, like the murder of Benjamin Brallier, an off-duty Liquor Control Enforcement agent who was stabbed on the Montour Trail. Anthony Quesen, who had been previously released on non-monetary bail for a robbery charge the previous year, was sentenced to 16 to 42 years for Brallier's murder.Shaffer said the bill's main objective is to ensure cases like this never happen again."We owe that to the Evans family," Shaffer said. "We owe that to the families whose names we will never have to learn if we get this right."

title: Cornell faculty debates no-confidence vote in university's administration
description: Cornell University's Faculty Senate began debating over a resolution of no confidence in the school's administration on Wednesday.
content: Cornell University's Faculty Senate on Wednesday began a debate over a resolution of no confidence in the school's administration. Dozens of members of Cornell's faculty are considering whether the university's administration can effectively address sexual assault at the school.Last month, a female student filed a lawsuit saying she was drugged and raped by multiple men at a fraternity house there in 2024. CBS News New York has reached out to attorneys for all of the accused. Two have gotten back to us and denied the allegations.Since then, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul tapped Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor to look into the case. Cornell has also hired Sally Yates to lead an independent investigation into its response.The first of two meetings took place Wednesday. A second hearing will take place on Oct. 28. After that hearing, a vote will take place. Cornell's president Michael Kotlikoff attended Wednesday's meeting, along with other members of Cornell's administration. "It would be a massive statement to the upper administration and hopefully signal to them you need to resign, step down, make room for new leadership who can better understand and more holistically lead this institution," Professor Ariana Kim previously said. Kim introduced the resolution of no confidence that is being debated.Ahead of Wednesday's meeting, Kotlikoff gave his first interview about how the administration handled the investigation into the 2024 alleged gang rape and told The New York Times he has no intention of stepping down."The fact that Jane Doe experienced what she experienced at Cornell is something that I am personally sorry for," Kotlikoff told The Times.Cornell's Title IX investigation at the time found two men responsible for sexual assault and expelled them."I do think it's important to understand we have more information now than we had at that time," Kotlikoff told The Times.He also acknowledged drugs and alcohol remain a problem at the Ivy League school."I think that this is a problem that relates to 20-year-olds, 21-year-olds leaving home for the first time, coming into an environment where there's access to alcohol, where there is, unfortunately, in some cases, access to drugs. And they're not prepared," Kotlikoff said. "This is a challenge for us. We have to respond by building character, judgment, responsibility, care for each other."On Tuesday, Cornell University announced it was suspending parties and social events at fraternity houses for the rest of the academic year. The school also gave state police a role in investigating sex crimes on campus.

title: More quiet fall weather Wednesday in Twin Cities; rain on deck early Thursday
description: More quiet fall weather is on tap Wednesday in Twin Cities, with rain on deck early Thursday.
content: Aside from perhaps a little more sunshine later, Wednesday is going to look and feel a lot like Tuesday in the Twin Cities.Expect a mix of clouds and sun with highs near 60 degrees in the afternoon.Showers are possible in the metro Thursday morning through the overnight hours, with a period of steady rain between the afternoon and evening. The metro can expect around a quarter inch, with less up north. Southern and southeastern Minnesota, however, could see a half inch or more. Winds will pick up through Thursday evening with gusts of up to 35 mph, driving in more cool air for Friday. Some showers are possible in the Arrowhead early Friday with the potential for a few flakes to mix in.Friday will be windy and cold with highs near 50 degrees and gusts exceeding 30 mph.Saturday morning will be chilly, possibly bringing the metro its first freeze of the season. Lows will be in the mid 30s with lots of sunshine, which will help push temps into the low 60s by the afternoon.It will be a bit breezy this weekend with gusts near 30 mph. Dry and late-summer temps are expected through at least midweek. Highs look to rebound into the upper 60s and near 70, with morning lows in the 40s.

title: How Arden Hills' Rice Creek Commons is akin to creating city out of thin air in Twin Cities' core
description: Rice Creek Commons, a project 13 years in the making, came to fruition Wednesday in Arden Hills, Minnesota, marking the first major development at the former site of the Twin Cities Army Ammunition Plant.
content: Rice Creek Commons, a project 13 years in the making, came to fruition Wednesday in Arden Hills, Minnesota, marking the first major development at the former site of the Twin Cities Army Ammunition Plant.Ramsey County commissioners, city leaders and members of the business community were on hand for the grand opening of the new, 157,000-square-foot headquarters of Micro Control.It's a 10-acre site, but it's staggering considering the entirety of the redevelopment is more than 450 acres. The county bought the old plant from the U.S. government in 2013 and spent years cleaning decades of hazardous waste from the property. Construction began with an April 2025 groundbreaking, when officials said the redevelopment was expected to have a future economic impact of $1 billion, WCCO reported. The Ramsey County Board approved the sale of a portion of the land in January 2024.Rafael Ortega, chair of the Ramsey County Board of Commissioners, says he's already thinking about what's next. "When you think about it, this almost doubles the size of Arden Hills in terms of the city," Ortega said. He said the project also increases the county's tax base and gives residents a chance to live close to where they work.Ramsey County is already preparing to cut the ribbon on a new county road. Work on new places to live, shop and eat is to follow.

title: Neighbors say proposal to expand Twin Rivers development would strain rural area in Anne Arundel County
description: Residents in Anne Arundel County say the development would bring more traffic to already congested rural roads and take away green space they were promised.
content: A decade-old agreement is at the center of a development dispute in western Anne Arundel County, where neighbors are fighting a proposal to add hundreds of homes to the Two Rivers community.Residents say the additional development would bring more traffic to already congested rural roads and take away green space they were promised."Feels like we're being pushed out"For lifelong resident Andrew Meyer, the fight is personal. His family has called the area home for more than a century. He said his great-grandfather purchased the property in 1899 and moved his family there the following spring."My father was born on this property, and I was born on this property, and my kids were born on this property," Meyer said.Now, residents say they're concerned their way of life is at risk. "It almost feels like we're being pushed out, slowly," said Jim Holman, president of the Forks of the Patuxent Improvement Association.Promises madeAt the center of the dispute is a proposal to build 377 additional homes in the neighboring Two Rivers development.Residents point to a 2016 agreement between the developer and the Forks of the Patuxent Improvement Association that explicitly caps the development at 2,060 homes.The agreement was negotiated after years of discussions over the development's size and impact on the surrounding community.Residents say the proposed additional homes would also be built on land known as Parcel O, which they understood was supposed to become an environmental park with walking trails.Even some residents of Two Rivers say they feel misled."There is a pattern of breaking promises and advertising. I call it bait and switch," said Jan Randall, a Two Rivers resident who said she moved to the community, in part, because of the promised environmental park.Friends of Two Rivers Committee Chair, Ed Riel, said, "You made an agreement 10 years ago, I think you should honor it."Crowding concernsBeyond the potential loss of green space, neighbors worry hundreds of additional homes would put even more pressure on the area's narrow, rural roads."It's one way in and one way out, and it's already overcrowded," Meyer said.Residents say much of the additional traffic would travel through the intersection of Conway Road, Meyers Station Road and Patuxent Road before heading toward Route 3, an area they say already experiences significant congestion."The infrastructure is not able to keep up with the amount of development," Holman said.Anne Arundel County has not yet approved the proposed 377 additional homes.Legal fight underwayMeanwhile, the Forks of the Patuxent Improvement Association is already engaged in a legal battle with the developer, Two Rivers Associates, over alleged violations of the agreement.The association has accused the developer of building homes closer to existing properties than the 600-foot separation required under the covenant.Residents say the developer is also seeking to have the agreement invalidated, arguing that the neighborhood association breached its terms.CBS News Baltimore reached out to the developer and its legal team for comment but has not received a response.Another court hearing is scheduled for Oct. 22.The neighborhood association is relying on donations to help cover its legal expenses, as residents continue their fight to preserve the character of their community."This is a fight that we don't plan on giving up," Holman said. "We plan on taking it to the very end until the court rules one way or the other."

title: 72-year-old woman charged in deadly wrong-way Mon/Fayette Expressway crash
description: Maciola Newman has been charged with homicide by vehicle in a wrong-way crash that killed Jacob Huber earlier this year.
content: A 72-year-old woman from Ohio has been charged in connection with a deadly wrong-way crash that happened on the Mon/Fayette Expressway earlier this year.Maciola Newman, 72, of Pickering, Ohio, is facing multiple charges, including homicide by vehicle in connection with the crash that happened around 4:30 a.m. on July 14, 2026, near the Interstate 70 interchange of the expressway.Jacob Huber, 24, was killed in the crash. Huber was a young lineman for West Penn Power. His obituary remembered him as a friend to anyone in need.Investigators said he was driving southbound on the expressway when he was hit by a vehicle traveling the wrong way.According to court paperwork, Newman and her passenger in their vehicle were each seriously injured in the crash and flown to Allegheny General Hospital. The state trooper who responded described catastrophic damage to Huber's car, the criminal complaint said.Investigators documented tire marks, debris and where both cars came to rest. The complaint also says Huber's speedometer was stuck at 80 miles an hour after the impact.A state police crash reconstruction confirmed, investigators say, that Newman had been driving north in the southbound lanes, causing the crash.Newman's charges include homicide by vehicle, involuntary manslaughter, reckless endangerment and traffic offenses. Court records show that Newman has a court appearance for a preliminary hearing scheduled for next week.

title: South Sacramento neighbors call for safety changes on Valley Hi Drive months after fatal crash
description: South Sacramento neighbors along Valley Hi Drive say repeated crashes, damaged vehicles and a deadly collision have left them afraid for their safety and eager for changes.
content: South Sacramento neighbors along Valley Hi Drive say repeated crashes, damaged vehicles and a deadly collision have left them afraid for their safety and eager for changes. The crashes, which span more than a year, have been caught on one family's security cameras. They said they have had thousands of dollars in damages as speeding cars have blasted parked vehicles outside their home and damaged their property. Tragedy struck back in April 2026, when Ariana Ayala was a passenger in the vehicle that crashed into a parked car and a fence on Valley Hi Drive. Sacramento police said the driver was a 19-year-old male friend of Ayala's.The crash was caught on home security cameras. In just split seconds, a speeding car going sideways comes to a crashing stop.Ayala was killed in the crash. Her mother, Betsy Lopez, spoke to CBS News Sacramento in June and said she was compelled to advocate for safer streets after her daughter's death. Months later, there are still no safety changes on Valley Hi Drive. "Dangerous, scary to walk or even visit my family," said one father who lives at a home damaged by repeated crashes. His family installed a metal fence to protect the yard and home from speeding cars. Isaac Gonzalez, a traffic safety advocate and founder of Slow Down Sacramento, said roads like Valley Hi Drive were built wide and open, which can lead to drivers ignoring speed limits. "It creates a comfort for a driver to drive as fast as they want," Gonzalez said.A city spokesperson said officials are aware of the concerns about speeding on Valley Hi Drive. Solutions are in the works to make the road safer, they say, including reviewing speed limits and implementing traffic calming measures.

title: Howard County police investigate burglaries at 9 businesses across county
description: Howard County police are investigating a string of burglaries that targeted nine businesses across the county Sunday night into early Monday morning.
content: Howard County police are investigating a string of burglaries that targeted nine businesses across the county Sunday night into early Monday morning.Investigators believe two suspects, who were seen traveling in a vehicle, were responsible for the break-ins. Police are asking residents and business owners to check their security cameras for footage that could help identify them.The burglaries spanned Howard County, from Columbia and Clarksville to Elkridge, Ellicott City, Fulton and Highland. The businesses targeted included liquor stores, restaurants, and gas stations.9 businesses targeted across Howard CountyPolice said the following businesses were burglarized:Columbia: Cash and drinks were stolen from Pizza Boli's on Oakland Mills Road.Clarksville: Lottery tickets were stolen from 108 Wine & Spirits on Clarksville Pike. Cash, a safe and alcohol were taken from Village Liquors on the same road.Elkridge: Cash was stolen from America's Best Wings on Montgomery Road, and alcohol was taken from Howard Wine & Spirits on Hearthside Way.Ellicott City: Cash, cigarettes and alcohol were stolen from Olde Tyme Liquors on Triadelphia Road.Fulton: Cash and tobacco products were stolen from High's on Lime Kiln Road. A McDonald's in the 8100 block of Westside Boulevard was also burglarized, with a cash register targeted.Highland: Alcohol was stolen from Highland Wine & Spirits on Clarksville Pike.Security video shows masked suspect breaking into liquor storeFor some business owners, the burglaries are part of a frustrating pattern of crime that has repeatedly affected small businesses.Mr. Shah, the owner of Olde Tyme Liquors in Ellicott City, said several of his convenience and liquor stores have been targeted before."It is frustrating. We work hard for every penny, and then they just come and take the stuff," Shah said.Security video obtained by WJZ shows a masked man smashing the front door of 108 Wine & Spirits in Clarksville. The suspect runs inside, grabs rolls of lottery tickets, stuffs them into a bag and runs out.Kevin Jo, the store's owner, said the burglary happened in a matter of seconds."It's very unusual to happen to us, and I really worry about the store, and then hopefully not anybody gets injured," Jo said. "They took like not even 30 seconds, like 10 seconds."Business owners face costly repairs after break-insWhile stolen merchandise adds to their losses, business owners said the cost of repairing damaged storefronts can be even greater."Those items don't value that much, but the stress that I have to come in at 3 o'clock [in the morning] and clean up everything, plus my windows and doors cost a lot more than what they stole," Shah said. "It's a nightmare."Business owners share security tips to prevent future burglariesBusiness owners said they are sharing information and security tips with one another in hopes of preventing additional burglaries."We are trying to hope it's not going to happen to another liquor store," Jo said.Shah said the problem extends beyond the recent string of break-ins."We have so many friends. They own retail stores, and it's happening all the time. This is nothing new," he said.Police search for two suspects in burglary spreeHoward County police said investigators believe two suspects were responsible for the burglaries. The department is asking homeowners and business owners in the affected areas to review security footage that could help investigators trace the suspects' movements."We see the same suspects. We see the same vehicle, which we can't quite identify yet," said Seth Hoffman, a public information officer with the Howard County Police Department.Police plan to expand access to security camera footagePolice also said businesses will soon be able to connect their security cameras to the department's Real Time Information Center, allowing investigators to monitor incidents as they unfold."That will give us another ability to be able to target these when they're happening," Hoffman said.The department also offers security consultations to help businesses identify vulnerabilities and improve their safety measures.

title: Man killed after argument turned to shooting inside Miami-Dade business, authorities say
description: Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office confirmed that the victim died at the hospital after being airlifted for treatment.
author_name: Steven  Yablonski, Manuel  Bojorquez, Ana Maria  Soler
content: A man is dead after police said a heated argument led to a shooting at a Miami-Dade business on Wednesday morning, deputies say. According to Medley police, officers responded to a truck yard business in the area of Northwest 109th Street and South River Drive for reports of a shooting.When officers arrived at the scene, they said they learned that a verbal argument between two people inside led to the incident."Two individuals got into a verbal altercation at which time one of them armed themselves with a firearm and ended up shooting the victim," said Sgt. Luis Rivera of the Medley Police Department.Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said the victim was rushed to a hospital on a medical helicopter for treatment. The Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office confirmed that the victim later died Wednesday afternoon and they will be taking over the investigation now that it's a fatal shooting. It remains unclear whether the two individuals were employees or visitors. However, authorities emphasized there is no broader threat to the community."We do want to make it clear that there is no threat to the public or any business in the area. Our officers have the investigation and the scene contained, and as of now we're continuing our investigation oere," Rivera said.The shooter has not been identified. Deputies said the suspect was also transported to the hospital for medical treatment and is expected to be charged following release.

title: MVA releases new rookie driver materials to assist motorists and instructors
description: The goal is to make the information clearer, more accessible, and more engaging for new motorists.
content: If you're learning to drive and hope to get your license soon, updated materials could help you simplify the process.Earlier this month, the Motor Vehicle Administration announced an update to the Maryland Rookie Driver curriculum.The goal is to make the information clearer, more accessible, and more engaging for new motorists.WJZ took a closer look at the new materials which provide information about work zone safety, technology in modern vehicles, and help improve driver education in classrooms.The MVA got input from safety advocates and consulted with driving schools to develop the curriculum.These changes represent the first comprehensive update since 2017. MVA Administrator Chrissy Nizer says the "updated curriculum gives instructors new tools and students information that reflects the realities they will encounter on today's roads."To access the updated Maryland Rookie Driver Manual, visit this website.Other MVA driver safety videos included in the new curriculum can be found here.

title: Trial of ex-Massachusetts cop charged in Sandra Birchmore's death focuses on police investigation
description: Testimony in the trial of former Stoughton, Massachusetts police officer Matthew Farwell resumed for a second day Wednesday at federal court in South Boston.
author_name: Penny  Kmitt, Kristina  Rex, Neal  Riley
content: Testimony in the trial of former Stoughton, Massachusetts police officer Matthew Farwell resumed for a second day Wednesday at federal court in South Boston. A state investigation into Sandra Birchmore's death was at the center of testimony, with prosecutors describing it as insufficient. Farwell is accused of killing the 23-year-old Birchmore and her unborn baby in her Canton apartment in February 2021. Her death was initially ruled a suicide, but friends didn't believe it.Farwell was later charged in 2024 with a federal count of killing a witness or victim. In 2025, he was also charged with causing the death of an unborn child. If convicted, he faces a mandatory sentence of life in prison. He has pleaded not guilty to both charges.Massachusetts State Police Trooper Matthew Dunne was back on the witness stand for more than five hours Wednesday before completing his testimony. He's one of the investigators who initially looked into Birchmore's death and ruled it a suicide. No suicide note foundJurors saw more graphic photos of Birchmore in her apartment, hanging from the closet door with a duffle bag strap. They also saw a photo of an ultrasound image that was on her refrigerator."No suicide note was located," Dunne testified.He also told prosecutors that he did not speak to anyone who lived next door or preserve certain items in the apartment. He said he did not report the incident as a suspicious death.Investigators interview Matthew FarwellDunne testified that he did not attend Birchmore's autopsy.He did visit Birchmore's school where she worked and learned through interviews that she was in a relationship with Farwell. He interviewed Farwell on Feb. 6 in the parking lot of a Stoughton school. It was not recorded on body camera and no one took notes."These were tactical decisions to prevent the defendant from just telling us he wasn't going to talk to us," Dunne said.Farwell said his sexual relationship with Birchmore had been going on for about two to three years. "I believe he said he was intoxicated at some point and they encountered each other," Dunne said. Farwell also acknowleged going to Birchmore's apartment before her death."The account he provided was that he went over there to break up with her," Dunne said.Dunne said that he did not interview any of Farwell's coworkers in Stoughton because "our investigation was more focused on the Birchmore side of things.""So you were more interested in looking into Birchmore than the man at her apartment in a mask?" the prosecutor asked.The defense objected to the question, and the judge said it would not be answered. A second interview of Farwell happened again in a parking lot on Feb. 11. Neither Dunne or his supervisor, Sgt. John Fanning, who knew Farwell, took notes, Dunne said.The prosecutor asked Dunne if he was aware that data showed Birchmore's phone had stopped moving before Farwell left her apartment. Dunne said yes."This piece of information was given weight, but it's got to be factored in with everything else we know about the investigation as well," he said.Dunne was also asked if Farwell's false statements about when he started having sex with Birchmore were factors in the investigation."All of this has to be taken into context with the full investigation, but they were definitely given weight," he said.Trooper says no signs of struggleDuring cross-examination, Farwell's defense attorney Kimberly Stevens asked Dunne about what he saw in the bedroom."Did you see signs of the struggle in the room?" she asked."No," Dunne replied.He also testified that coworkers at Birchmore's school told police that she suffered from anxiety and depression, and the principal told police that he decided she would not be brought back last year because of poor attendance.Birchmore's aunt also told police that she had taken medication for bipolar disorder when she was young and that she said she was going to kill herself when the home she once shared with her mother and grandmother were being sold. Dunne said that Farwell volunteered on his own accord that the had been at Birchmore's apartment on Feb. 1. He said he was there to tell Birchmore it wasn't his child, Dunne said.Dunne also said investigators found a suicide note authored by Birchmore that was dated in 2017, along with a list that appeared to reference ways in which to commit suicide, including rope. Stoughton police officer testifiesIn the afternoon, the prosecution called Stoughton Police Sgt. Robert Kuhn to the stand. He said he was friends with Farwell outside of work. Kuhn met Birchmore when she was in the youth explorers program and also interacted with her as the resource officer at Stoughton High School. He described her as "incredibly impressionable.""She really looked up to police officers and had an affinity for law enforcement," Kuhn said.Testimony finished for the day at 4 p.m., and Kuhn will be back on the stand Thursday.Matthew Farwell trialThe first day of testimony Tuesday featured several witnesses who were close to Birchmore and surveillance video from her apartment building the day she died.Jurors can expect to hear from a friend of Birchmore, a Stoughton police detective and the former Stoughton police chief in the coming days. Investigators said Farwell started sexually abusing Birchmore when she was 15 and he was 27. They met when she joined the police department's explorers' program.Prosecutors said Birchmore learned she was pregnant in December 2020 and told Farwell he was the father. The defense said DNA testing confirmed Farwell was not the father.The video played in court Tuesday showed Farwell, wearing a hood and mask, entering the lobby of Birchmore's apartment building and getting on an elevator at 9:28 p.m. on February 1, 2021. Prosecutors said Farwell strangled Birchmore and staged it as a suicide. He left about a half-hour later.Farwell's attorney did not deny her client and Birchmore had an affair, but she said Farwell never thought the baby was his and when he broke up with Birchmore, she killed herself.The trial is expected to last about five weeks. No cameras are allowed in federal court so it is not being broadcast or livestreamed.

title: Mary Cassatt exhibit at Art Institute aims to recreate lost mural from 1893 World's Fair
description: Cassatt now has her own exhibit at the Art Institute, which aims to recreate the form and spirit of the long-lost mural.
content: The 1893 World's Fair looms large in Chicago history.Now, one of its groundbreaking works of art is a centerpiece of a new exhibit at the Art Institute of Chicago — but there is one big problem.At the heart of this exhibit at the Art Institute is a work that no longer exists. "It's a tough problem for a curator to have, to center this story about a monumental mural without the mural," said Annelise Madsen with the Art Institute.That mural, "Modern Woman" by Mary Cassatt, was from the 1893 World's Fair."It was Cassatt really scaling up her subject matter, what she had built her career portraying, the lives of everyday women, but giving that a sense of import, a sense of grandeur," Madsen said.Cassatt now has her own exhibit at the Art Institute, which aims to recreate the form and spirit of the long-lost mural."What we do have are a lot of enticing traces," Madsen said. "We have archival material. We have reproductions of the mural that are in fair publications from the 1890s. We have letters by Cassatt."The exhibit covers a lifetime of Cassatt's work beyond the missing mural — like the iconic painting, "The Child's Bath," from 1893."She was a fierce, independent woman and an artist of the time," Madsen said. "I think she was, first of all, showing us the impact of human connection."Her impact still felt, even through a mural that we can't see. "It's a Chicago story, and we, for that reason alone, we must embrace it. It's part of the history of this city." Mary Cassatt actually helped the art institute get one of its signature works — El Greco's "The Assumption of the Virgin."In 1905, Cassatt wrote to the institute's president when the painting became available, saying it belonged there. Cassatt's exhibit runs through January 3, 2027.

title: Armored car courier robbed near bank in Cicero, Illinois
description: Armored car courier robbed near bank in Cicero, Illinois
content: An armored car courier was robbed Wednesday afternoon in the west Chicago suburb of Cicero.At 12:20 p.m., Cicero police were called for an armed robbery in the 4800 block of West Cermak Road. They learned an armored car courier was leaving a bank on the block and going to an armored truck parked nearby, the Town of Cicero said.Multiple people came up and robbed the courier, the town said. No shots were fired, and no one was injured, the town said.Video from CBS Skywatch showed crime scene tape around a Brinks truck outside a PNC Bank branch.Cicero police were coordinating with the FBI for the investigation.

title: High-stakes pitches: Tech startups compete for $475,000 at Venture Atlanta conference
description: Hundreds of startup founders are pitching their companies face-to-face to big-name investors at Venture Atlanta, all hoping to find someone ready to bet on their vision and take home the grand prize of $475,000 in funding.
content: For Southern tech entrepreneurs, a few moments in front of the right investors can turn a big idea into a billion-dollar business. That high-stakes opportunity kicked off Wednesday morning in Midtown as the annual Venture Atlanta conference returned to the Woodruff Arts Center and Atlanta Symphony Hall.Over the two-day event, about 600 startup founders are pitching their companies face-to-face to big-name investors, all hoping to find someone ready to bet on their vision and take home the grand prize of $475,000 in funding.Connection and capital are the two main draws at this year's conference, where innovators across artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, healthcare, and robotics are taking the stage to make their case for growth funding.Among the founders hoping to secure investment is Eric Truitt, an Atlanta native and Georgia Tech alumnus who now serves as CEO and founder of Mantis Space."I was raised in Atlanta, went to school at Georgia Tech, and getting to come back in our community..." Truitt said of the opportunity to pitch in his hometown.His company is tackling a growing problem in orbit, keeping satellites powered when they lose sunlight."Right now, there's thousands of satellites in orbit, and all of those satellites run on sunlight," Truitt explained. "But every 90 minutes, nearly every one of those satellites goes into the dark. So we're building the first power grid for space to keep the lights on for every one of those 10,000 satellites."Also eagerly awaiting their turn on the main stage are Daniella and Rob Sladen, founders of the aerospace defense startup Zulu Pods. The company is aiming to solve critical supply chain issues in the defense sector with a specialized orange prototype designed to lubricate unmanned aircraft."We focus on components for affordable mass, so there's a lot of drones and missiles that are being bought these days, and it creates a massive supply chain bottleneck," Rob Sladen said.Their compact prototype holds enough oil to keep a drone or similar flying device in the air for an hour.Now in its 19th year, Venture Atlanta has established itself as a premier launchpad for dozens of profitable companies across the region.According to Venture Atlanta CEO Allyson Eman, the conference has supported 1,100 companies over the past nearly two decades, helping them raise more than $9 billion in capital and achieve $22 billion in exits.Some of Atlanta's most recognizable tech names got their start on the conference stage, including parking app giant ParkMobile."ParkMobile actually pitched on our stage in 2009," Eman noted.Another notable alum is Bark Technologies, a company dedicated to online child safety that secured funding through the event."It's a fantastic company, I love what they're doing to help kids and safety," Eman said. "And they've been growing ever since they've been on Venture Atlanta."The Venture Atlanta conference continues through Thursday, when the winning startup will be awarded $475,000 in funding. This story will be updated once a winning company is announced.

title: Life-saving lung transplant gives Long Island mom second chance at life
description: A Long Island mother of five who once feared she might not survive long enough to receive a lung transplant is now home recovering and looking forward to the future after a community effort helped change her life.
content: A Long Island mother of five who once feared she might not survive long enough to receive a lung transplant is now home recovering and looking forward to the future after a community effort helped change her life.One year ago, Annamarie Patterson was battling severe lung disease. she weighed about 90 pounds, relied on oxygen, and was running out of options.Patterson needed a lung transplant, but three hospitals declined to move forward because she was living in a shelter and lacked stable housing for post-operative care."I almost died three times," Patterson said.The situation left her family facing an uncertain future.After CBS News New York shared her story, viewers donated to help her cause. Those contributions, along with support coordinated by Legacy Development Corporation, helped secure housing and financial assistance needed for her transplant journey.Patterson was able to receive a life-saving lung transplant in June."I'm feeling okay, happy I'm not on any machines. That's most important," she said.Patterson is now living in her own apartment in Patchogue, where she is adjusting to life after surgery.While her recovery continues, she still relies on oxygen at times and attends physical therapy sessions. She also faces the challenges that come with transplant recovery, including managing a weakened immune system and a strict regimen of medications.Patterson also expressed gratitude to the people who contributed to her recovery."I want to thank them so much because without them, I don't know if I would have been here talking to you right now," Patterson said.Dr. Keith Pettus, founder and CEO of Legacy Development Corporation, said public support surged after Patterson's story aired."Once you all came, the story became bigger than life and people began giving," Pettus said.Pettus said watching Patterson's progress and seeing her family in a home of their own has been especially meaningful after a period that once seemed hopeless.Patterson is not yet able to return to work, but she is celebrating milestones she once thought might be impossible."I can blow out my candles this year," she said.

title: Chicago City Council falls one vote shy of overriding Mayor Brandon Johnson's veto on new threshold for city debt
description: The Chicago City Council on Wednesday fell one vote shy of overriding Mayor Brandon Johnson's veto of an ordinance that would have required a higher threshold for the city to borrow money.
content: The Chicago City Council on Wednesday fell one vote shy of overriding Mayor Brandon Johnson's veto of an ordinance that would have required a higher threshold for the city to borrow money, in an effort to make it more difficult to add to the city's massive pile of debt.The measure would raise the threshold for taking on debt from a simple 26-vote majority to a 30-vote supermajority of the City Council. Alders approved the measure last month by a 32-15 vote, but Johnson vetoed the ordinance last week.The City Council voted 33-17 on Wednesday to override Johnson's veto, one vote shy of the 34 required to do so.Ald. Jason Ervin (28th), the mayor's City Council floor leader, argued that the proposal would have diluted the power of Black and Latino alderpeople, and allowed a minority of the City Council to "hold the key to how the city can invest in itself.""For as long as I can remember, 26 votes ruled the day in this body. That's how democracy works. You win with the majority, and you move on," Ervin said.Opponents of the measure said, while they want the city to rely less on borrowing money, the bid to raise the threshold for doing so was aimed more at weakening Johnson ahead of the upcoming election than fixing the city's debt problems."This is not going to be better governance. This is not going to fix your issue. You know, unless you're just trying to give the mayor a black eye, this is pretty unnecessary. We could actually fix this in a different way," said Ald. Maria Hadden (48th).However, supporters of the ordinance said it would have made the City Council more independent of the mayor, and required the mayor to be more collaborative with alderpeople when seeking to borrow money.With debt payments and employee pension obligations making up approximately 40% of the city's annual operating budget, supporters of the higher threshold for borrowing argued it was necessary to improve the city's fiscal discipline."In order to become a truly independent council, we have to change the rules," said Ald. Marty Quinn, who led the effort to raise the threshold for taking on more city debt. "The ordinance before us today forces the mayor, whoever that mayor may be, to find four more votes on city debt issues. That's it."Quinn noted the Illinois General Assembly already requires a three-fifths majority vote by both the House and Senate to pass all debt-related legislation.However, after last month's City Council vote, Johnson argued raising the threshold for borrowing is not "a useful way to grow our economy.""The last thing that people want is government to get in the way of itself," he said. "There are definitely major concerns there, you know, and I will address it accordingly."Johnson argued that issuing bonds is a necessary tool to boost economic development and affordable housing in long neglected neighborhoods on the South and West sides. He echoed that argument in a letter accompanying his veto."Neighborhoods with the greatest infrastructure needs should not face additional barriers to securing essential public investment," Johnson wrote in a letter accompanying his veto. "Delaying infrastructure projects can increase construction costs, worsen deterioration, and ultimately cost taxpayers more. While this ordinance increases a voting threshold, it does not put into place any additional measures around debt affordability, reporting requirements, or financial oversight."Ald. Bill Conway (34th), an investment banker, argued that the Johnson administration has left borrowing power authorized by the City Council last year languish for months before actually issuing bonds. He noted the City Council authorized $1.8 billion in bonds for capital infrastructure improvements last December, but City Hall only recently started issuing those bonds. "The notion that requiring 30 votes instead of 26 will somehow delay infrastructure investment simply doesn't square with the facts. If there is any delay in this area, it is with the executive branch, certainly not City Council," Conway said.City Council gives final approval to $261 million settlement for 17 wrongful murder convictionsMeantime, the City Council unanimously approved a massive $261 million settlement over multiple wrongful conviction cases, the largest police misconduct deal in Chicago history.The eye-popping settlement would resolve 16 lawsuits filed by 17 men who say they were framed for murder by notorious former Chicago Police Detective Reynaldo Guevara.City attorneys said all but two of the men have received certificates of innocence. Of the two who have not, one has applied for one, but a judge has yet to rule on the request, and the other has not yet sought a certificate of innocence.The massive payout is only part of the growing costs related to Guevara, who has been linked to dozens of wrongful convictions. Beyond the 17 men whose cases are being settled under the deal, Deputy Corporation Counsel Jessica Felker told aldermen there are still two more Guevara-related lawsuits in settlement talks, with 23 other Guevara lawsuits still pending which will likely end up being settled.Nine other men are challenging convictions in cases Guevara handled, but have yet to sue the city.Those cases likely will cost the city hundreds of millions of dollars more.City attorneys told aldermen if Guevara's victims each pursued their own lawsuits and took the cases to trial, unpredictable juries could expose taxpayers to even higher costs.In the cases being settled under the $261 million deal approved on Wednesday, city attorneys estimated the move would save taxpayers between $300 million and $400 million compared to the risk of taking the cases to trial. The settlement would be paid in two installments in 2027 and 2028. Alders formally oppose Amtrak's controversial plan to build new maintenance yard in BridgeportThe City Council also is expected to approve a resolution opposing Amtrak's plan to move its maintenance facility from the South Loop to Bridgeport near Rate Field.The resolution calls on Amtrak to pause plans for a $900 million Midwest maintenance facility until environmental studies are made public and a public hearing takes place.Ald. Nicole Lee (11th), whose ward includes Bridgeport, has said the chosen site is too close to existing homes."Where it is now is totally industrial. Within 500 yards of that yard where they sit now, 26 people live. Within 500 feet of this yard where they want to move to, 6,741 [people live]," she said.Lee has said Amtrak plans on moving forward with the Bridgeport maintenance facility under federal authority than can bypass local zoning, building, and environmental regulations.While the resolution alders plan to pass on Wednesday does not carry any legal authority to stop the project, local leaders are hoping the vocal opposition from neighbors and elected officials convinces Amtrak to slow down and reconsider the project.Amtrak has said, while it looked at rebuilding the maintenance yard in its current location or moving elsewhere, it selected the proposed Canal Street site in Bridgeport for its new maintenance yard because of its proximity to Union Station. It was the right size and shape, and ultimately, there was a willing seller.The project is closely tied to plans for a potential new White Sox stadium in the South Loop.White Sox minority owner Justin Ishbia's company, Canal Edge, is the private development and delivery partner for the Amtrak project and is providing $125 million in private capital.City Council launches next phase of Chicago-Cook County domestic violence task forceA local task force created to address the rising rates of domestic violence and strengthen support for survivors will soon be brought back for a second phase.Back in July, the Chicago-Cook County Violence Against Women Task Force released a report that identified gaps in the justice system that often failed survivors.The task force said survivors of abuse and domestic violence are often left to navigate a confusing system where agencies don't share information and, in many cases, don't even collect the same data.While the task force couldn't access key data, CBS News Chicago did. In 2024, we obtained a decade of Cook County records. Our investigation found only about 25% of protection orders were being served, meaning many survivors never got the protections judges ordered.Task force members said that investigation helped expose a critical weakness that has since seen improvement.The development of the report was phase one of the work of the task force. Phase two would work to implement recommendations made in the report.The City Council Public Safety approved the second phase of the task force last week, and the full City Council gave the measure final approval on Wednesday.Alders to expand "Smart Streets" program to ticket cars blocking bike and bus lanesA pilot program that uses cameras on city vehicles and CTA buses to automatically ticket drivers blocking bus and bike lanes downtown will be expanded citywide over the next two years, after a unanimous City Council vote.The Smart Streets program was first launched in November 2024 in an area bounded by Roosevelt Road, Ashland Avenue, North Avenue, and Lake Michigan. The program allows the city to install cameras on CTA buses, city vehicles, and utility and light poles to catch drivers who park in bike lanes, bus-only lanes, bus stops, and crosswalks.Tickets for blocking a bus lane cost $90. Tickets for stopping or parking at a bus stop run $100. Blocking a bike lane can result in a $250 fine.Earlier this year, the pilot area was expanded north to an area bound by Roosevelt Road, Ashland Avenue, Irving Park Road, and Lake Michigan.On Wednesday, the City Council approved a measure to make the program permanent and expand it citywide in three phases in 2027 and 2028.City officials and aldermen have said the program is designed to provide more reliable bus service, and eliminate hazards for bicyclists, who are often forced out of bike lanes and into the same lanes as cars and other vehicles when someone blocks a bike lane.

title: Data center developer offers residents of Kansas town $1,000 each for 10 years
description: Digital Realty is offering utility and property tax credits to residents of De Soto, Kansas, in a bid to win public support for a data center facility.
content: Amid a pronounced public backlash against data center construction in the U.S., one real estate developer is making an offer it hopes will win over one Kansas community: money.Digital Realty is offering every household in De Soto, Kansas, where it plans to build a data center, $1,000 in utility and property tax credits for 10 years. "Digital Realty builds critical infrastructure that enables the modern economy, and we believe we also have a responsibility to help strengthen the communities that make this growth possible," Andy Power, the developer's president and CEO, said in a statement on Wednesday. The offer is part of a $20 million community investment Digital Realty is pledging in De Soto as the company paves the way for a 280-acre data center site. The company said the project, which will eventually cover 1,400 acres, will provide recurring tax revenue, create jobs and deliver other economic benefits to local residents. Digital Realty, a publicly traded company based in Austin, Texas, with a market worth of more than $67 billion, said in a news release that it is working with De Soto to finalize distribution of the $1,000 credits to households.
