The company, whose clients include Amazon Web Services, Microsoft and Nvidia, expects to create 250 permanent jobs for local suppliers and contractors once the site is complete. The initial phase of development will also support "thousands of construction jobs over time," Digital Realty said in its news release.A recent CBS News poll found that more Americans oppose than favor building a new data center in their area, citing concerns that the facilities harm the environment, drain local resources and raise utility costs.

title: Palatine teen arrested for alleged mass shooting plot that may have targeted Aurora Hindu temple
description: A 19-year-old Palatine man has been arrested after an investigation into threats involving a potential mass shooting that may have targeted a Hindu temple.
content: A 19-year-old Palatine man has been arrested after an investigation into threats involving a potential mass shooting that may have targeted a Hindu temple.Palatine police said on Sunday afternoon that they were contacted by Mount Prospect police, who said they had been tipped off to a possible mass shooting by someone who received "concerning electronic communications" from Alexandros Paporakis of Palatine.Paporakis was arrested outside his home in the 1300 block of North Baldwin Court Sunday evening by Palatine and Mount Prospect police.While searching his home, police said they found a rifle, multiple loaded rifle magazines, hundreds of additional rounds of rifle ammunition, tactical equipment, a tactical vest containing body armor and a patch with imagery associated with white supremacist extremism."They recovered a rifle, they recovered loaded magazines, hundreds of rounds of rifle ammunition as well as a body armor," said Palatine Police Chief William Nord. With help from the FBI, police said they were able to examine Paporakis' electronics and electronic communication, and said they found a manifesto in which he self-identified as a white supremacist and wrote about his hatred for non-white people, including Jewish people, African Americans, Indians and other non-white people. "Reading through the manifesto, he did state some extremist ideologies and talked about violence, he talked about mass killings and how he wanted to carry out this mass shooting," Nord said. The Cook County State's Attorney's Office charged Paporakis with one count of making a terrorist threat and one count of unlawful possession of a weapon for possessing a rifle with a barrel less than 16 inches long, both felonies.In court Wednesday, prosecutors said Paporakis' coworker told police he had openly talked about being a white supremacist at his job at Taco Bell, making disparaging comments about people of other races. The coworker also told police he had discussed Nazis and an armed struggle, and expressed a particular hatred toward people from India.Prosecutors said on Saturday, Paporakis told a coworker he was planning "it" at the largest Hindu temple in Aurora, then told another coworker that Sunday "was going to be a special day."Prosecutors said early Sunday afternoon Paporakis texted his coworker and asked him to call him. When he did, prosecutors said Paporakis told his coworker his gun jammed and "he got out of there 'super-fast.'" After the call, he sent the coworker messages on Signal showing an AR-style rifle, showing how the gun failed to fire when he pulled the trigger, and a photo of himself in a tactical vest, according to prosecutors. Prosecutors also said during this chat he sent the coworker a copy of his eight-page manifesto. He also told them that he planned to carry out the attack later.After they spoke over the phone, this coworker and another colleague called 911 to report the incident, prosecutors said.Palatine police said the specific intended location in Paporakis' alleged threats has not been confirmed and an investigation into that remains open. The Aurora police were notified of the threat, who then coordinated outreach to Hindu places of worship in the area to make them aware. The FBI was also involved in the investigation.Court documents say Paporakis suffered from mental and emotional health issues and had been without prescribed medication. A judge ordered Paporakis detained while awaiting trial.

title: Opening statements begin in former Oakland Mayor Sheng Thao's trial on corruption charges
description: Opening statements in the corruption trial of former Oakland Mayor Sheng Thao and three others began on Wednesday morning after jury selection wrapped up on Tuesday evening.
content: Opening statements in the corruption trial of former Oakland Mayor Sheng Thao and three others began on Wednesday morning after jury selection wrapped up on Tuesday evening.Seven women and five men were seated as jurors following a day-long session of questioning Tuesday from Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, federal prosecutors and defense attorneys. The jurors and six alternate jurors were chosen from a pool about 70 potential jurors questioned.Assistant U.S. Attorney Abraham Fine began to lay out the government case Wednesday morning during his opening statements, opening with a forceful characterization of Thao."Public official who put her power up for sale, who put greed first, who put her own monetary interest above the people she was supposed to serve," Fine said. Thao, her boyfriend Andre Jones, local businessman David Duong, and his son Andy Duong face federal charges in a wide-ranging indictment alleging bribery, mail and wire fraud, and conspiracy. The allegations point to a pay-to-play corruption scheme to use the levers of municipal government to benefit themselves.Prosecutors say that just before the November 2022 election that would bring her into office, Thao conspired with the Duongs to use her future position as mayor to benefit their business dealings, including extending the city's recycling contracts with the company they ran, Cal Waste Solutions. The Duongs also allegedly bankrolled a negative campaign mailer targeting Thao's rivals in the mayoral race.The indictment alleges that following the election, Thao, Jones, Andy Duong and other co-conspirators arranged for Jones to be paid compensation disguised as wages through a "no-show" job. In 2023 Thao allegedly proposed using emergency powers to buy housing units from a company linked to the Duongs without going through standard competitive bidding. The conspiracy also involved getting a preferred, high-level official into a city role to benefit the Duong's business interests, and having sponsors associated with the Vietnamese American Business Association - founded by David Duong and run by his inner circle - to cover travel expenses and perks for Jones and other city workers, according to the complaint. In his opening statement, defense attorney Jeffrey Tsai argued that prosecutors were presenting a misleading story driven by local businessman and political operative Mario Juarez, expected to be the government's central witness in the case and who has cooperated with prosecutors in exchange for a reduced sentence. "Justice Department will ask you to believe Thao is the main character in the story is a new mayor who immediately sold her office," Tsai said. "The narrator of the story is named Mario Juarez. The story is pure fiction."Tsai characterized Juarez as the driving force behind the allegations and maintained that Thao was never involved in a bribery agreement.In June 2024, the FBI raided Thao's home that she shared with Jones, as well as properties linked to the Duong family, including Cal Waste Solutions. The federal indictment, announced in January 2025, came months after Oakland voters recalled Thao from office. All four defendants have pleaded not guilty to the charges.Legal analyst Steven Clark told CBS News Bay Area that the turmoil associated with Thao's tenure as mayor would be a challenge for the defense."The big problem for Miss Thao is this abuse of public trust that she's accused of, and that's something that's going to be difficult for the defense to deal with in this trial because she comes into the trial with a lot of baggage," Clarke said.The trial is expected to last about a month. If convicted of all charges, the defendants face up to 35 years in prison.

title: Judge dismisses Bill Quinlan's lawsuit alleging double-dipping in Chicago mayoral election; he vows appeal
description: A Cook County Circuit Court judge dismissed Chicago mayoral candidate Bill Quinlan's lawsuit accusing some of his opponents of illegally double-dipping by running for mayor while running for state office.
content: A Cook County Circuit Court judge dismissed Chicago mayoral candidate Bill Quinlan's lawsuit accusing some of his opponents of illegally double-dipping by running for mayor while running for state office.The lawsuit named rivals Alexi Giannoulias, Mike Quigley and Maria Pappas. Giannoulias and Quigley have both formally declared they're running for mayor; Pappas has not. Giannoulias is also running for re-election as Illinois Secretary of State, Quigley for re-election to federal office as U.S. congressman for Illinois' 5th District, and Pappas for re-election a Cook County Treasurer.The core of Quinlan's argument revolved around changes in Illinois election law in 2024, which now says that if a person's name is presented as a candidate for two or more incompatible offices – meaning they cannot serve in both roles at the same time – they must withdraw from all but one.Candidates will file to appear on the ballot as a Chicago mayoral candidate in 2027 from Oct. 19 through 26, while they are on the ballot for their other races in the Nov. 3 midterm election. Before the 2024 state law change, mayoral candidates could not begin filing their nominating petitions until after the previous year's general election. The new law requires the petitions to be filed by Oct. 26.Wednesday, Judge Eve M. Reilly dismissed the case, saying it was filed prematurely. She did not rule on the merits.Quinlan announced after the hearing that he will appeal the ruling. "Today's ruling was about timing, not substance," he said in a statement. "The court did not rule on whether Alexi Giannoulias, Mike Quigley and Maria Pappas can run for two incompatible offices at once. That question is still wide open, which is why we will appeal and seek a definitive answer before voters cast their ballots on Nov. 3."

title: Danza Alegría uses traditional Mexican dance to preserve culture in Baltimore
description: Every step, every color and every flip of the skirt tells a story. Danza means dance, and alegría means joy.
content: Every step, every color and every flip of the skirt tells a story. Danza means dance, and alegrÃ­a means joy.In Baltimore, the group Danza AlegrÃ­a is using traditional Mexican folklÃ³rico dance, music and colorful costumes to help a new generation growing up in America stay connected to its roots."As an immigrant mom, I miss a lot of my culture, and I'm interested in my kids learning about their roots, and that's why I teach dance in my community," said Alexandra Gonzales, founder of Danza AlegrÃ­a.Gonzales began dancing Mexican folklÃ³rico at just 3 years old in Puebla, Mexico. What started as a lifelong love of dance has grown into a mission to preserve her heritage and share it with others.That mission starts at home with her 15-year-old daughter, Melissa Colin."When my mom was teaching, I wasn't originally dancing," Colin said. "I saw her dancing, and as I saw her, I learned how to do the footwork and stuff."Now, six years after the group formed, Colin helps teach other Latino children about their culture, even as they grow up thousands of miles from their families' homelands."My mom is from Mexico, and I'm from Mexico too, and I like to be in this culture because it teaches us how to dance," said Alexandra, an 8-year-old dancer. "We're with our friends, we can dance together, and that's why I love my culture."Through regional dances, traditional music and vibrant costumes, students learn more than choreography. They learn about their families' histories and how to carry those traditions into the future."Hopefully, we continue showing our roots," said dancer Salma Ruiz. "Some of us are first generation. So we just want to continue showing everyone our culture and continue going through generation and generation."The next generation is already imagining a future in which they pass those traditions on to others."Maybe when I'm older I can teach little kids how to dance and all that stuff," said 7-year-old dancer Andrea.And the lessons extend beyond the stage.Danza AlegrÃ­a welcomes people from different backgrounds, using dance as a way to bring cultures together and build understanding."I love to share my culture and feel part of my country is with me," Gonzales said. "Bringing with me how I feel proud of my country. I feel free to share it with other cultures here in the United States."For Gonzales and her dancers, culture isn't just inherited. It's shared, celebrated and passed down from one generation to the next.You can find their performances on its website.

title: Eden Prairie adds new security measures to football games in wake of homecoming shooting
description: Changes include two designated secure entrances with metal detectors, a ban on face coverings except for religious or documented medical reasons, and a no-re-entry policy.
content: Fans attending Eden Prairie High School football games will face a much different security experience for the rest of the season following a shooting at the school's homecoming game earlier this month.The district's new security rules mirror measures commonly seen at Minnesota Vikings games. Large purses and backpacks are no longer allowed inside the stadium. Fans may only bring clear bags or small personal bags.Additional changes include two designated secure entrances with metal detectors, a ban on face coverings except for religious or documented medical reasons, and a no re-entry policy. "The metal detectors are good, but what I think we really need is security out in the parking lots," Eden Prairie senior Gavin Motzko said. "I think that's going to go a long ways."Stadium gates will close at halftime, students must present school identification to enter and must attend a school participating in the game."I'm here for it," Motzko said. "I think it keeps everyone safe. It keeps the game good and enjoyable for everybody."The new procedures come after the shooting in the parking lot during the Eagles' homecoming game a week and a half ago. The incident sent a crowd of more than 1,000 spectators scrambling for safety. Two teenagers were injured. Authorities later arrested and charged an 18-year-old suspect in the shooting.This week, prosecutors also charged four additional men with riot-related offenses tied to the disturbance.According to a criminal complaint, "several of the participants were making gang signs during the disturbance." Law enforcement officials have connected the shooting to a recent increase in Somali gang-related violence reported in several Twin Cities suburbs."They're not dealing with money, there's no drugs, they're purchasing legal firearms," Bloomington Police Chief Booker Hodges said last week. "These aren't the '80s, '90s gangs. These kids are different."The enhanced security measures will extend beyond football. Eden Prairie school officials said extra security measures will also be in place at Eagles basketball games and that security procedures for school events will continue to be reviewed."I think we'll get used to it," Motzko said. "I think it will be different. I think it will be a little bit of, you know, something new every day."

title: Philadelphia doctors say early detection crucial as Pope Leo XIV reveals lung cancer diagnosis
description: Philadelphia-area experts say early testing and detection are important ways to protect against lung cancer.
content: A day after lung cancer surgery, Pope Leo XIV is reported to be walking around his room, eating a regular diet and having respiratory physical therapy.The Vatican says post-operative blood tests and a chest X-ray show no immediate complications. Doctors say the prognosis for the 71-year-old pontiff is good.CBS News Philadelphia talked to doctors in the Philadelphia area about the pope's condition.Dr. Thomas Meyer with Main Line Health said he was in a recent audience with the pope, who's said to be healthy and active."I saw him personally about two weeks ago in Rome; he looked quite robust and happy," Meyer said.Leo had the most common type of lung cancer — adenocarcinoma — that was removed with the lower lobe of his right lung in a 90-minute operation."We know that the rise of adenocarcinoma in non-smokers is significant, and smoking is no longer the only way that you acquire lung cancer," Dr. Patrick Ross, a thoracic surgeon at Main Line Health, said.Ross said exposure to secondhand smoke and radon can also increase the risk of lung cancer. More testing will show if the pope's cancer has spread, which will determine whether more treatment is needed."If the stage is early, there's an excellent prognosis," Ross said.Doctors say the pope's case is helping raise awareness about the leading cancer killer."The tricky thing with lung cancer is that most of the time patients are without symptoms," Dr. Stacey Su, chief of thoracic surgery at Fox Chase Cancer Center, said.That's why people at risk — including former smokers and people with a family history of lung cancer — are encouraged to get early testing, Su said.Temple Health has a Healthy Chest Initiative to find lung cancer early when it's curable, and most healthcare systems have similar programs. In a statement, Philadelphia Archbishop Nelson Pérez said he was grateful to learn that the pope's prognosis "remains highly optimistic." He asked people in the archdiocese to continue to pray for the pope.

title: Woodland teen soccer star Da'vian Kimbrough honors his Mexican roots
description: Da'vian Kimbrough made history at just 13 years old when he signed with Sacramento Republic FC, becoming the youngest professional soccer player in American history.
content: Da'vian Kimbrough made history at just 13 years old when he signed with Sacramento Republic FC, becoming the youngest professional soccer player in American history.Now 16, Kimbrough continues to build his career on the field while embracing his Mexican heritage. After spending this year with North Texas SC, the young forward has also represented Mexico's Under-17 national team.For Kimbrough, wearing Mexico's jersey is about more than soccer. It's an opportunity to honor his family and connect with a heritage that has shaped his life."Not everyone gets a chance to represent," Kimbrough said. "And I think those are probably one of my better moments, as well as the stuff I've done with Sac."His connection to Mexico begins at home, through his mother's side of the family and the traditions passed down by his grandfather, who grew up in MichoacÃ¡n."My mom's side is Mexican, and my grandpa, he grew up in MichoacÃ¡n," Kimbrough said. "Growing up with him, whether it was watching Liga MX games or eating the food he cooks, traditional dishes, that's kind of where I take most of my main heritage."Those everyday experiences helped shape Kimbrough's understanding of his roots. Now, he hopes to take that connection a step further by visiting the place where his grandfather grew up."We want to take a trip down to Mexico, where my grandpa grew up, because we feel like it's important to visit and see where he was kind of had the foundation of the heritage," Kimbrough said.As he continues to develop as a professional athlete, Kimbrough also recognizes the importance of representation, especially for young people who share his background."There are Mexicans all around the world, not all just in Mexico," he said. "So I'm happy that I get the chance to showcase that. And, yeah, hopefully I can be someone they can look up to."Kimbrough will remain on the offseason roster for North Texas until a final decision is made on his transfer option before the 2027 season begins.At just 16, he is continuing to make his mark in soccer while carrying his family's story and Mexican heritage with him.

title: Baltimore inspector general says fire department gave backpay to officers before their start date
description: Baltimore's Office of the Inspector General (OIG) has issued a new report alleging that the fire department provided backpay to promoted officers based on the date a vacancy was posted, not the date when employees began working in the position.
content: Baltimore's Office of the Inspector General (OIG) has issued a new report alleging that the fire department provided backpay to promoted officers based on the date a vacancy was posted, not the date when employees began working in the position. The mishandled backpay "resulted in thousands of dollars paid for work that was never done by the recipient of the monies," said the report, which was released Wednesday.A review of retroactive payments made to employees promoted in 2024 to the positions of pump operator and emergency vehicle driver showed that more than $30,000 had been paid in total backpay, according to the report. The OIG noted that union agreements used by the Baltimore City Fire Department (BCFD) "do not contain clear language mandating the promotional backpay process for employees." However, providing backpay from the time the promotion positions were first posted "has continued as a past practice."Some department vacancies remained open for yearsBecause of the length of the BCFD promotion process, vacancies can remain open for months, or sometimes even years, according to the OIG report."Backing the pay to the start of posting caused the city to pay multiple times for the same shifts and pay employees for work they did not perform and were also ineligible to perform during the period in question," it said.The OIG found the practice to be a waste of taxpayer dollars and the report said the agency was referring its findings to the city's Department of Audits so that it can review the practice. The OIG report noted it concluded that the practice "allegedly occurred for decades."Fire department issues responseA response from the BCFD was released along with the report. "BCFD generally agrees with your ultimate recommendation to discontinue the process of backdating promotions to the date of vacancy as a matter of course, and where the date of vacancy precedes a current promotional list," said the response. "We believe BCFD had the full discretion and the responsibility to discontinue the process, which, as noted in the report, BCFD did, effective August 8, 2025," it added. The OIG stated that the report was completed prior to the city restoring the agency's access to records. Before the restoration happened, Baltimore officials had feuded for months with Inspector General Isabel Cumming over access to city records and computer systems.

title: Jury deliberations begin in 2022 rowhome fire that killed 3 Baltimore firefighters
description: The fate of James Barnett, a man on trial in a 2022 fire​ that killed three Baltimore firefighters​, now lies in the hands of the jury.
content: The fate of James Barnett, a man on trial in a 2022 fire that killed three Baltimore firefighters, now lies in the hands of the jury.Barnett is accused of setting a Stricker Street rowhome on fire back in January 2022, resulting in the deaths of Baltimore Fire Lieutenants Kelsey Sadler and Paul Butrim and Firefighter/EMT Kenny Lacayo.Lawyers for both sides presented their closing arguments Wednesday, before the jury began deliberating.The judge emphasized to jurors they are only looking at three charges against Barnett: Second-degree arson, involuntary manslaughter and reckless endangerment. On Tuesday, the judge dropped three counts of second-degree murder in the case.Deliberations have now ended for the day and will resume Thursday morning.Prosecutors say "there is no doubt"Prosecutors with the Baltimore City State's Attorney's Office began the closing arguments Wednesday, reviewing what they said are the facts of the case.They said Barnett created at least four flashes of flames, setting fire to a dilapidated home on Stricker Street, and walked away after being in the house for about eight minutes.Assistant State's Attorney Matthew Galey said four cameras captured Barnett the night before the Jan. 24, 2022 fire. Galey said the fire started in the exact location where Barnett created those flashes."There is no doubt that what he did inside caused the fire," Galey said in court, going on to say, "We don't just have the evidence, we have the statements of the defendant."Galey also said Barnett made conflicting statements in his interview with police.In a video recording, you can hear Barnett saying a picture of the person of interest is not him but looks like a younger version of him. He also says he may have worn the jacket that appears in the picture."Everything he said in that interview is a lie," said Baltimore City Assistant State's Attorney Daniel Salem. "He's trying to hide the fact that he burned the house down."Galey added the fire didn't start any other way, noting BGE reported no gas was on at the home."What he did was such disregard for human life," said Galey. "It's despicable."Defense argues Barnett is "completely innocent"Barnett's defense attorney Jason Rodriguez argued there's no evidence to support the charges against his client.Rodriguez said it's hard to prove arson, as there was no "willful or malicious intent." He said the person in the video, not naming his client, left the home on Stricker Street when there was no fire."We're being disingenuous when Barnett said, 'I was there,'" Rodriguez said. Rodriguez said Barnett was referring to being at the rowhome a month or so prior, not the night before."James Barnett is completely innocent of all the charges before you," he added.Rodriguez claimed the person of interest that detectives identified appears to be younger than Barnett. He said it's hard to get a good look at the person's face, arguing it's hard to prove that it's Barnett. Rodriguez even claimed the color of the jacket didn't match up. He said Barnett wore a blue and gold jacket. The state claimed the jacket was blue and yellow.Barnett did not testify during the trial.

title: 2 men plead not guilty to allegedly stabbing off-duty NYPD detective
description: Two men were arraigned Wednesday after police said they stabbed an off-duty detective 10 times before fleeing in the Bronx.
content: Two men accused of stabbing an off-duty NYPD detective pleaded not guilty in court Wednesday.D'Angelo Rafael Jean Caraballo, 25, and Sneider Mejia Bautista, 24, are facing several charges, including attempted murder in connection with the brutal attack on Det. Jose Mercedes on Oct. 2 on East 206th Street and Rochambeau Avenue in the Bronx.Prosecutors allege Mejia approached Mercedes and brandished a knife. Caraballo, they allege, then got off a scooter and ripped two chains from Mercedes' neck.Mejia is accused of stabbing Mercedes 10 times.Prosecutors told the judge Mercedes identified himself as an NYPD detective six times during the attack.Mercedes spoke about the harrowing ordeal on Tuesday afternoon."I was on vacation, I was on my day off, and I was not expecting this," he said. "It was a very, very scary sight to me. I've been investigating crime for a long time, and at this time, I just wanted to enjoy my vacation, my time off. I wasn't expecting this."Mercedes said he identified himself in both English and Spanish to the men."I thought I was going to die," he said.Prosecutors allege in the days after the attack, the men tried to evade capture by not using their phones and by cutting their hair "in an attempt to disguise themselves."Caraballo and Bautista were arrested in Massachusetts, where they were found hiding in the basement of a house, police said. They were extradited to New York to face criminal charges.Defense attorneys for both men didn't say much Wednesday, other than they were waiting to file a bail application."I'm going to reserve my bail application until I have a chance to interview his family, who is here in court, and get a better picture of his life," an attorney for Caraballo said.Members of Mejia's family sat in the courtroom but said nothing to reporters.Both were remanded and will be back in court in early December.The Department of Homeland Security said both men are from the Dominican Republic and are living in the United States illegally.

title: Shania Bennett, ex-Parker staffer, challenges former boss in Philadelphia mayoral race
description: Shania Bennett, who previously worked for Philadelphia Mayor Cherelle Parker, says her campaign will focus on quality of life issues.
content: Near the corner of Broad Street and Snyder Avenue in South Philadelphia, Shania Bennett shakes hands with a daycare owner. The two talk about the smoke shop that opened nearby, and Bennett pops her head in the door to take a look around.It's an area the 26-year-old knows well. Growing up nearby, Bennett said she used to hop on SEPTA at this intersection almost every day. But it's the same corner where her brother was killed in 2021. "He was a beautiful person. I kid you not. Beautiful," she said. "I watch how the lack of investment in this corridor, the crime that's happened here, ongoing. Things that just, kids that when they get out of school shouldn't have to deal with."CBS News Philadelphia met with Bennett on this corner on Oct. 8, a little more than a week after she launched her bid for mayor.The soon-to-be 27-year-old is the first to issue a challenge to Mayor Cherelle Parker, who is Bennett's former boss. Bennett served as the Parker administration's director of youth engagement.While Bennett says she did see progress being made in certain areas, she didn't feel it was equally distributed across the city. She compared it to looking at a report card."If we're getting a trash thing right in South Philly, and it's an A, but it's an F in North Philly, our overall grade point average is going to be a D. If we're lucky, a C," Bennett said. "And so, I think when we look at Philadelphia from a quality of life standpoint, quality of life, protection of life, enhancement of life, I was like, we can keep our A's, A's, pull our bad grades up, and really focus on how Philadelphia holistically scores."So far, Bennett has not released a full platform. But she told CBS News Philadelphia her campaign and messages will focus on three categories."All of my pillars will fall into quality of life, enhancement of life, and protection of life," Bennett said. "From businesses to moving away from just gun violence. When we're looking at gun violence, we're talking about access to jobs. We're talking about training our workforce."Bennett also said she would want to create public dashboards showing how the city is working to solve problems."Let's take a pothole for an example," Bennett said. "I want people to see how many times that pothole has been reported. How long it took for it to be completed. And are people satisfied?"Bennett's challenge is an uphill climb. No sitting mayor seeking reelection has lost in Philadelphia since at least the Home Rule Charter was passed in 1951. At 26, Bennett will be one of the youngest mayoral candidates the city has seen. It's something she acknowledges has come up."At first it was an issue," Bennett said. "And now that I've been outside, getting out of the echo chamber of social media, people are like, 'We want someone young. We want someone with fresh ideas. We want innovation.'"As for experience, Bennett said she has worked in the offices of both state Rep. Jordan Harris and state Sen. Nikil Saval. She was elected a committee person in South Philly at age 18.Bennett said, as mayor, she would lean on experts and what she hears from residents."I believe in myself. And I believe in the ability of me to be able to lean on other strong leaders and appoint strong leaders to the table to be able to make quality decisions to see the change we want to see, while also listening to the community."CBS News Philadelphia reached out to representatives from Mayor Parker's campaign, who declined to comment for our story.The 2027 primary election in Pennsylvania is slated for May 18.

title: Detroit leaders mobilize resources to combat recent shootings as overall gun violence declines
description: Seven shootings occurred in Detroit over a seven-day period, with most happening on the city's east side, according to Detroit Police.
content: Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield and Police Chief Todd Bettison said they are coordinating law enforcement and community resources to combat a recent wave of shootings across the city, including an incident that left a 7-year-old girl and her mother wounded.Seven shootings occurred in Detroit over a seven-day period, with most happening on the city's east side, according to Detroit Police.Sheffield said addressing violence requires a collective effort to protect young people."It takes a comprehensive, holistic and overall approach from everyone to ensure that we're protecting the lives of our young people," Sheffield said.One of the recent incidents involved a 7-year-old girl and her mother, who were shot after a dispute between children escalated into gunfire. The shooting occurred on Detroit's east side. The father of one of the children pulled out a gun and shot the mother and her child. Both victims are expected to survive.Chief Bettison said the suspect in that case was taken into custody less than 24 hours after the shooting, crediting community members with helping police identify him."Community members told us that night who he was," Bettison said.Chief Bettison said the department is working with state and federal law enforcement agencies and local prosecutors to hold people accountable for violent crimes.Bettison cited cooperation with the Michigan State Police, the U.S. attorney's office and Wayne County Prosecutor Kym Worthy as part of the broader effort to curb gun violence."It is a collective," Bettison said, warning that people who commit crimes in Detroit will face accountability.Mayor Sheffield also pointed to summer programming and other community initiatives as part of the city's strategy to prevent violence before it occurs.Mayor Sheffield said community involvement remains essential to those efforts.City leaders said the goal is to prevent shootings as well as respond quickly when violence occurs.Despite the recent incidents, overall shootings in Detroit are down compared with the same period last year, according to Chief Bettison.

title: Horse carriage advocates, opponents speak out as NYC ban looms
description: New York City Council will vote Oct. 22 on whether to ban the horse carriage industry, sparking debate.
content: A New York City tradition is on the verge of ending as the City Council will soon decide whether to ban the horse carriage industry.Council Speaker Julie Menin said Wednesday that city officials will be voting on Romanch's Law on Oct. 22. The bill, named after a teen killed during a horse carriage accident, will phase out the industry by June 2028."There are the votes within the council to support this. This has been a long time coming," Menin said.The plan would also prohibit new horse carriage licenses; the horses would be retired, and the city would develop a transition program to help drivers find new jobs."I'm also appointing a working group to work through some of these issues, because under the bill, we have until June of 2028 to complete the transition, which involves everything from making sure the horses are going to a humane place, making sure that we get the workers jobs, and making sure that we're working with the medallion owners," Menin said.Gov. Kathy Hochul also weighed in on the proposed ban, saying she supports the measure.The carriage industry called the proposed ban unconstitutional and is vowing to fight back.Transport Workers Union President John Samuelsen said Menin is using the death of a tourist to contrive a public safety crisis."Council Speaker Menin's bill has no meaningful economic relief for workers," Samuelsen said. "This is disgraceful political opportunism, and [Mayor] Zohran [Mamdani] should not simply go along with it, particularly when immigrant families' livelihoods are being destroyed. This entire situation is reprehensible.""This bill will be devastating for carriage drivers and carriage owners. People will be evicted, people will lose their houses. They have mortgages and bills they need to pay. They have children," industry spokesperson Christina Hansen added.The drivers and their union say the council bill is short on details of how to take care of those left without jobs. They are running ads slamming Menin for what they call "empty promises.""The bill has no guarantees, only references to potential job counseling, job fairs, job referrals, and possible financial compensation for medallion owners. The bill doesn't protect workers. It destroys them," one ad says.The proposed legislation leaves it up to Mayor Zohran Mamdani to devise a plan to find a soft landing for the 160 horses and 200 drivers. CBS News New York's Marcia Kramer asked him what he plans to do."I think that we have a civic responsibility to ensure that we are not leaving anybody out to dry," Mamdani said.The mayor said there's still time to find solutions before the bill takes effect in June 2028."It is the kind of runway that's required to ensure that we can fulfill all of these different obligations," Mamdani said.Horse carriage drivers in Central Park on Wednesday had a lot to say on the issue."You're 40 years coming to work and then you're told one day you don't have a job," Tony Moran said."When I got here in this industry, it was everything to me," Mario Angelucci added. "I'm doing it because I love what I do. Horses, it's something beautiful. It's an amazing, creative [industry] to be a part of. They can just bring joy to people, children."Meanwhile, MTA Chairman Janno Lieber said he would be open to finding jobs for the drivers, and a spokesperson for the mayor insisted the bill prevents the horses from becoming carriage horses elsewhere or being sent to slaughter.

title: Daejon Love, man accused of posing as 49ers player, indicted in alleged fraud scheme
description: Daejon Love, the Sacramento County man accused of posing as a San Francisco 49ers player and wealthy real estate investor to defraud victims, has been formally indicted on a federal wire fraud conspiracy charge, officials said.
content: Daejon Love, the Sacramento County man accused of posing as a San Francisco 49ers player and wealthy real estate investor to defraud victims, has been formally indicted on a federal wire fraud conspiracy charge, officials said Wednesday.Love, 35, appeared in federal court in Portland, Oregon, on Tuesday. The U.S. Attorney's Office in the District of Oregon said Love pleaded not guilty and was ordered detained pending trial, which is scheduled to begin on Dec. 15.Federal prosecutors said Love and an alleged co-conspirator — 18-year-old Taylor Jamie Chan — solicited money from victims by promoting fraudulent high-yield investment opportunities, including an "expedited account" promising unusually large returns in a short period of time. Both men were arrested in late August.Federal prosecutors allege Love used online dating profiles and social media accounts containing fake personal and financial information to gain victims' trust. He allegedly presented himself as a wealthy real estate investor or a current or former NFL player and developed romantic relationships with some victims.The indictment also alleges Love staged displays of wealth to persuade people to send him cash or wire money for investments. Prosecutors say he then used the money for personal expenses, including travel, expensive cars, clothing, and jewelry.One woman described recognizing warning signs in Love's claims, saying they seemed "too good to be true."Federal authorities said the alleged scheme involved more than two dozen women and approximately $1.3 million.If convicted, Love faces up to 20 years in federal prison, up to three years of supervised release and a $250,000 fine, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office. Federal prosecutors said he would also be required to forfeit any property obtained through the alleged scheme.

title: AI-assisted adaptive radiation therapy acts like a GPS as it targets areas impacted by breast cancer, doctors say
description: A new weapon against breast cancer is using AI to make radiation more precise, sparing healthy breast tissue.
content: A new weapon against breast cancer is using artificial intelligence to make radiation more precise, sparing healthy breast tissue.CBS News New York recently met one of the first patients on Long Island to receive this high-tech treatment.Natalie Calderon, a 49-year-old Rosedale accountant, had avoided mammograms for a few years, until she says a vivid dream convinced her to get checked."It's time to listen to your body, listen to your intuition," Calderon said. "I was faced with a doctor and he basically put his hand here and said go get checked."She listened, and was diagnosed with stage 1 breast cancer.Cutting-edge science known as AI-assisted adaptive radiation therapy treated her after a lumpectomy. The treatment helps doctors at Northwell Health Radiation Medicine by precisely targeting only the area where cancer was removed."In the moment, while the patient is on the treatment table, tailor and adapt their radiation treatment plan to their anatomy on that day, in that moment," said Dr. Fleur Gallant, a Northwell Health radiation oncologist.Like a GPS that recalculates its route."Conditions can change and sometimes we need to recalculate a different route and that's what we do with adaptive therapy. It's a much smaller area with a lot of sparing of normal surrounding breast tissue," Gallant said.The benefit of less radiation is less time away from family and work and a better cosmetic result, because whole breast radiation can cause scarring and breast asymmetry."By shrinking the footprint of the radiation therapy in the breast, you're getting less of that scarring, a softer and more natural breast and one that has less cosmetic detriment from the radiation," Gallant said.Calderon, who was sidelined by the radiation for only five days, is now cancer free. She is encouraging other women not to wait for a wake-up call."Cancer treatment is evolving, basically, so I would say don't be scared. It could be a chapter in your life, but it's not your entire story," she said.Adaptive radiation therapy is also used to more precisely target other cancers, doctors say.

title: South Florida influencers take on political issues, measures as expert urges clearer disclosure rules
description: Creator Pascal Okoh says he has not been paid for political videos, and consultant Christian Ulvert says disclosure rules may need updating.
content: Social media influencers are increasingly using their platforms to discuss political issues and ballot measures, a trend that is reaching South Florida as election season intensifies.For voters scrolling through Instagram, TikTok, and other platforms, distinguishing between independent commentary and paid political advertising is becoming increasingly difficult.Pascal Okoh, a South Florida creator known online as @directedbyjunior, built his following highlighting local restaurants, attractions, and community hotspots. Recently, he expanded his content to cover local political issues and ballot initiatives."People will watch me for what I do, who I am," Okoh said. "I'm not here to choose a side. It's more just bringing information out to people."Okoh said he feels a responsibility to share information with his audience when issues affect their communities."With my platform, my page, it would be an injustice to not get that word out there," he said.One of his recent videos explaining a beach zoning vote in Hollywood received nearly 400,000 views.As creators take on political topics, questions often surface about whether influencers are being compensated. When asked whether he had been paid to make political videos, Okoh said, "Absolutely not."However, political experts say the growing role of influencers in campaigns raises important concerns."Influencers are putting their reach to work on campaigns. Some, like me, question it," said Christian Ulvert, a longtime political consultant and analyst.Ulvert believes disclosure rules for online political content may need to evolve as technology changes."I think it's time our legislators look at updating the rules," Ulvert said. "As a voter, I want to know if I'm being influenced, if it's authentic and organic, or if it's because that person is being paid."Beyond sponsorship questions, Ulvert warned that algorithms can reinforce existing beliefs by serving users repetitive content."If we just create echo chambers without the validity behind it and authenticity of information, it does hurt societal norms in a very big way," Ulvert said.To ensure accuracy, Okoh said he researches his topics and consults local experts before sharing videos online."Be very careful. Do your research. Ask around to see what's really going on before you put a video out there," Okoh said.As voters prepare for upcoming elections, Ulvert recommends consuming news from multiple sourcesâincluding traditional news outletsâand discussing political information directly with friends, family, and community members.

title: North Texas teen accused of possessing, uploading AI-generated child sexual abuse material to TikTok, deputies say
description: The Parker County Sheriff's Office said TikTok shared information with the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children about the material.
content: A North Texas teen is facing a handful of charges after the Parker County Sheriff's Office said the teen used artificial intelligence to generate nude images of another child before uploading them to TikTok.The sheriff's office said the Celina Police Department sent them information in September after receiving a tip from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) in July. The sheriff's office said TikTok had alerted the NCMEC that a user had shared the images on the platform, and the NCMEC then gave the information to Celina Police, as it was initially believed the user lived there. However, information about the user's internet provider later led investigators to Parker County in late September.Parker County deputies said they executed a search warrant on Oct. 1 at a residence there and learned that the user was 16 years old. Two more search warrants were carried out for the TikTok account, and during an interview, deputies said the teen confessed to taking photos of a younger child and using AI to alter the images to make the child appear nude. The sheriff's office also said evidence indicated the suspect had used photos of at least three other victims for the same purpose, and that investigators identified all of the victims and notified their families.The teen suspect was processed at the Parker County Sheriff's Office on Oct. 8, and deputies said the teen was released to their parents under state law. The suspect is now charged with possession of child pornography â a second-degree felony â along with voyeurism of a child victim and possession of certain visual material depicting a child, both of which are state jail felonies. Parker County deputies note the suspect now awaits juvenile court proceedings.

title: Arlington care home operator pleads guilty after client deaths, court filing shows
description: Police found at least 20 clients who died and said there could be more.
content: The Arlington businesswoman who operated an illegal home-based healthcare company and was under investigation after at least 20 clients of hers died, pleaded guilty and was sentenced to at least 18 years in prison for multiple crimes, according to officials.Arlington police investigated Regla "Su" Becquer for months and her unlicensed company, "Love & Caring for People LLC," which operated community living homes. Authorities learned that her company, which claimed to provide supervised personal care for adults in need throughout five homes in Tarrant County, was actually abusing and neglecting clients and committing fraud. Police found at least 20 clients of hers who died since September 2022 and said there could be more. Most of the victims were cremated or buried, and only two had autopsies. One of those autopsies revealed that 60-year-old Steven "Kelly" Pankratz died from mixed drug toxicity while under Becquer's care. In addition to the deaths, investigators found evidence of Becquer taking possession of clients' phones, cars and even houses. The Tarrant County District Attorney's Office said Becquer was sentenced to 18 years in prison for financial abuse of the elderly, 10 years in prison for abandoning or endangering an individual, and 2 years in state jail for criminally negligent homicide. "These sentences will end Becquer's infamous business scheme and bring justice for victims who went unknown for so long," said Anna Tinsley Williams, with the Tarrant County DA's Office.The DA's office did not say whether the sentences would run concurrently.

title: How pet food inflation is hitting owners in their wallets
description: Pet food prices have risen 20% since 2022, leaving nearly one in three Dallas pet owners struggling to afford food for their animals, according to a PetSmart Charities survey.
content: Inflation isn't just affecting the cost of food for humans. It's hitting pet parents' wallets as well.A new PetSmart Charities survey found Dallas had the highest rate of pet food affordability concerns out of all the cities surveyed, with almost one in three pet owners reporting having problems buying pet food.The saying is, "A dog is a man's best friend," but it's getting more expensive to feed our furry friends. The consumer price index shows the cost of pet food has gone up 20% since 2022.Maria Koegl is the executive director of Don't Forget to Feed Me Pet Food Bank in Fort Worth. The non-profit supplies pet food to 45 different organizations."At the end of the month, we usually don't have any inventory left," Koegl said. "This year we actually have about 10 to 15 organizations on our waitlist that have reached out and said we've had a significant increase in clients asking for pet food assistance, and we can't meet that need."The Fort Worth HOPE Center is one of the partners they work with. Warehouse manager Terri Schenk said the non-profit has given more than 58,000 pounds of pet food to families this year."I've been with the Fort Worth HOPE Center for nine years, and this is the biggest need that we've ever seen," Schenk said. "They don't have money to pay bills, and they have to make a choice. If they can't provide the pet food, then they'll feed the dog their food, and then they don't have enough to eat."Don't Forget to Feed Me Pet Food Bank has been around since 2008. They said this is the most demand they've seen in their 18-year history."We're seeing at least 10% of our current partners are asking for an increase in the pet food that they need to be able to serve the clients they have at the capacity that they're requesting," Koegl said.The pet food bank is also seeing a decrease in donations as people struggle to feed their own pets."The less donations we get of pet food, the more we have to buy," Koegl said.It's a cause the non-profit tries to keep up with to help keep pets in their homes and out of local shelters.Free drive-thru pet food is available at the Dallas Animal Services pet food pantry on the second and fourth Wednesdays of every month from 8 to 9 a.m.

title: Lamar Cook, former Maura Healey staffer facing gun and drug charges, now accused of SNAP fraud
description: Lamar Cook, a former staffer for Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey who was fired after his arrest on cocaine and gun charges last year, has been arrested again.
content: Lamar Cook, a former staffer for Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey who was fired after his arrest on cocaine and gun charges last year, has been arrested again. This time, Cook is facing federal charges for alleged Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) fraud.Cook, 46, is the former deputy director of the governor's western Massachusetts office. He was fired in November 2025 after being arrested on state charges. Prosecutors said at the time that Cook allegedly had cocaine delivered to a state building in Springfield where he was working. On Wednesday, U.S. Attorney for Massachusetts Leah Foley announced federal charges against Cook. He is charged with one count of SNAP fraud and wire fraud.Cook appeared in federal court in South Boston Wednesday afternoon.Despite the judge calling the allegations "distasteful," Cook was able to leave the courtroom on personal recognizance following his arraignment.Prosecutors say Cook violated bail on his state charges and will try to have it revoked in a Springfield courtroom on Thursday. Cook did answer any questions from reporters as he left the courthouse.Prosecutors said Cook was making a $130,227 year while working for Healey and received $22,374.29 for accrued vacation time when he was fired. The state later "realized an error" in paying Cook for the accrued vacation time, and unsuccessfully tried to reverse the direct deposits.The state was unable to get the money back because Cook did not have enough money in his accounts.Lamar Cook federal chargesThe U.S. Attorney said Cook's bank account held balances of about $13,000 in January 2026 and $8,800 in April 2026.Prosecutors say that Cook's mother won $1 million in the Massachusetts Lottery in early 2026. She made payments to Cook totaling about $12,000 between May and June 2026.On April 6, 2026, Cook applied for SNAP benefits and allegedly claimed zero income, less than $100 in his bank account, and said he was living in a two-person household with only himself and his child.Cook allegedly failed to disclose that his fiancée and her mother lived with him at his Springfield home. In addition, investigators say his fiancée was making more than $80,000 as an employee of Springfield Public Schools.After applying to the program, Cook received nearly $550 per month in SNAP benefits. Prosecutors said he used them regularly at grocery and retail stores and also during a trip to Disney World in Florida this past July. U.S. Attorney calls allegations "simply egregious" If convicted of SNAP fraud, Cook faces up to five years in prison. A wire fraud conviction would mean a sentence of up to 20 years."The alleged conduct is simply egregious. SNAP benefits are intended to put food on the table for struggling families who cannot make ends meet, not for those who allegedly hide income to circumvent the financial requirements, much less travel to Disney World," Foley said in a statement Wednesday.She called it "disturbing" that the state couldn't stop the alleged SNAP fraud from happening and could not recover the $22,000 it mistakenly paid Cook for his vacation time.During an event on Wednesday, Healey was asked about the latest charges against Cook."Good. That's a federal program. Those are federal taxpayer dollars. And I'm glad that the U.S. Attorney's office has taken action," Healey said.Healey is currently running for re-election. Her opponent, Mike Minogue, released a statement following Cook's arrest."Maura Healey appointed this man. This is a failure at every level. Families in this state are cutting back at the grocery store while this administration can't even track its own payroll. Governor Healey is about to spend a record-breaking $298 billion over her four-year term, and Cook's case proves we can no longer afford to let her hide what's going on with the numbers," Minogue said.
