title: How The Lighthouse keeps neighbors fed: "It's hard out there"
description: Here's how the KDKA Turkey Fund helps our neighbors in need.
content: Believe it or not, we're already on week four of the 45th Annual KDKA Turkey Fund, and it's your generous donations year after year that help us help our neighbors at Thanksgiving.But if you're wondering just who you're helping, we thought we'd introduce you to one of them. Derrick is a Butler County native who visits The Lighthouse in Valencia every other week for food and other supplies. He's been going there for about five years.Derrick, like so many others, says he just can't afford to make ends meet in the current economy."I got here due to family situations and matters. I was having hard times with certain bills and things like that," Derrick said.For him, The Lighthouse is a beacon of hope."They have everything you need," he said. "You shop around. You get what you want. They walk you around here like it's a regular store. It's a community thing, and they treat you like family when you come here. Everything is good. They make everybody feel welcome."Many people who struggle with food insecurity are ashamed to admit it, largely because of the stigma surrounding it or the misconceptions about it. But Derrick says he is not embarrassed and urges others who are afraid to simply put aside their pride and ask for help."Just don't feel ashamed about it. They're here to help, and that's what they do. That's their whole goal. It's to make sure that everybody who's in need gets help," Derrick said.Food distributions at The Lighthouse are a well-oiled machine with staff and volunteers who genuinely care about each neighbor who walks through the door."It trickles all the way down from the top to the bottom, and it shows," Derrick said. "It's nice to have that safety net, especially for food and items that you know you can't get to support your family and to get that care," he said. Derrick calls The Lighthouse a blessing."Without this, a lot of people would be hurting," he said. "It helps people stay afloat in life, and it really helps give them faith and hope."He says he's grateful not only for The Lighthouse but for every day he's given."I just want everybody in life to stay blessed and keep the faith," he said. "Just know that there are people out there from different programs. Ask for help if you need it. Don't feel shameful. Just feel blessed that you get to see another day and that there are things like this out there to support the communities, especially in our area. Because it's hard out here. And people have to do what they have to do, but when you have this support, you can't go wrong."And here's how you can donate to the KDKA Turkey Fund to help folks like Derrick.You can go to any PNC Bank. If you donate in person, they'll match all donations, up to $100,000. You can donate online at kdkaturkeyfund.com. You can text "kdturkey" to 50155. Or you can mail a check to P.O. Box Thanks, Pittsburgh, PA 15230.From all of us at KDKA-TV, thank you!

title: 4th District race in Illinois pits Democrat Patty Garcia against Republican Lupe Castillo
description: U.S. Rep. Jesus "Chuy" Garcia is retiring at the end of his term, and four candidates have lined up to run for his seat in Illinois' 4th Congressional District in the upcoming November election.
content: U.S. Rep. Jesus "Chuy" Garcia is retiring at the end of his term, and four candidates have lined up to run for his seat in Illinois' 4th Congressional District in the upcoming November election.Garcia has represented the district, which covers parts of the Southwest Side of Chicago and southwest suburbs, since 2019.He filed petitions to run again this year, but dropped out of the race at the last minute, citing family health issues.That left his chief of staff, Patty Garcia, who is not related to the congressman, as the only candidate on the ballot in the Democratic primary in March.Some called the maneuver a bait and switch, and Congressman Garcia has accepted some criticism, and it's now a central issue in the race for his seat.Republican candidate Lupe Castillo said the way Congressman Garcia left the race shows he's not trustworthy and still does things the "Democratic machine way." "Doing it through the back, coming up with things that aren't fair for anybody else," she said. "The way that he did it on the last day, he made the announcement at the last hour, was not fair."Patty Garcia said the congressman's last-minute decision to drop out of the race left her with "a very hard hand to handle" in her decision to transition from chief of staff to candidate."I had less than 24 hours to make that decision," she said.While some have viewed the congressman's decision as a move to clear the field for his favored candidate for his seat, but Patty Garcia said there was nothing fortunate about her boss' decision."It is not fortunate to wish that someone would be ill to the point that they can't serve," she said. She noted there are also two third-party candidates who were able to get on the ballot after the congressman left the race, despite facing stricter requirements for their nominating petitions.Lyons Mayor Chris Getty is running as an independent candidate, and Lindblom High School science teacher Ed Hershey is running as the Working Class Party candidate.Castillo acknowledged she faces an steep challenge to win the race as a Republican in a heavily Democratic district."Oh, yes it is," she said.Castillo grew up in Bridgeport, worked as a pharmacist and a baker, and has made Little Village home for decades."It's sort of turning around, but I don't think it's turning around fast enough," she said. "It's doing it very slow, because of what's going on in the neighborhood with the undocumented people that we have here."Asked how she views Operation Midway Blitz, the Trump administration's immigration crackdown in Chicago last year, Castillo said, "it's neither here nor there. It could have been handled a little bit better."While Castillo said she's in favor of large parts of the Trump administration's immigration enforcement efforts, she stopped short of calling for another wave of immigration raids in Chicago."I wouldn't say to that extent, you know, the way they came in," she said. "There is no right way to do it. Nobody's going to like it, no matter what."For her part, Patty Garcia said it's time to abolish U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement."I know it's controversial for some folks, but what's radical for me is that we're taking food from seniors, taking food from kids, and instead wasting it on this rogue agency that has gone out there with a blank check and gone unchecked," she said.She also voiced her support for impeaching President Trump if she is elected to Congress."I've been vocal about my intention to hold ICE accountable, but that also includes Trump, that includes any of the folks around him, any of his cabinet secretaries," she said.

title: JewishGen revamps online database to help people uncover their family histories
description: The genealogy resource, which holds nearly 33 million records, is launching an upgraded website to help users trace their roots, from immigration to the Holocaust.
content: For people trying to piece together their family histories, a single record can change everything.Karen Lichtman, an independent filmmaker from Bay Ridge, Brooklyn, spent decades believing her grandparents were the first in her family to immigrate to the United States from Eastern Europe. Then, research through the website JewishGen led her to a relative she never knew about: her great-grandfather, Harry Aron Berger, who was born in 1862 in what is now Ukraine and is buried just 4 miles from her home."I can't express it. It's hard to put into words," Lichtman said as she stood beside his fallen tombstone at Washington Cemetery.She read the Jewish mourner's prayer over the grave, believing she was likely the first person in her family to visit in decades."I have to fix it. He's not forgotten about. He might have been misplaced in all my family stories, but now I have him," she told Brooklyn reporter Hannah Kliger.Lichtman's discovery highlights the role of JewishGen, one of the world's largest online resources for Jewish genealogy. Based at the Museum of Jewish Heritage in New York City, the organization is preparing to launch an updated website next week to help users navigate millions of historical records.The database contains just shy of 33 million individual records, according to Caitlin Hollander Waas, chief genealogist at the Museum's Kalikow Jewish Genealogy Research Center."There's a saying in genealogy that, 'When do people start doing their family research? When it's too late to ask,'" Hollander Waas said.JewishGen was among the earliest online genealogy communities when it began nearly 40 years ago. Its records help people trace family histories through immigration, displacement and the Holocaust, offering a way to reconnect with histories that may have been lost across generations.The updated website aims to make that research more accessible, particularly for younger users who will carry the work forward."The concern is always, you know, who's going to take care of this when I'm gone? Who's going to continue to work? Who's going to keep photographing graves all over the world?" Hollander Waas said. "I think that's the big thing, is making it more accessible for the next generation of users."For Lichtman, the research has already reshaped her understanding of her family's journey to America. She hopes to visit Ukraine once the war is over, traveling to the place where her great-grandfather's story began."I was told for decades, 'Your grandparents are from countries that no longer exist and everyone else is dead,'" she said.Now, she has a new connection to the past."That trip to Ukraine started with a trip up Bay Parkway to visit a relative who I had no clue came here," Lichtman said. "His immigrant story is my immigrant story."Have a story idea or tip in Brooklyn? Email Hannah by CLICKING HERE.

title: Large stretch of Southern California under Red Flag Warning as Santa Ana winds bring elevated fire risk
description: In the warning, the National Weather Service said the Santa Ana winds will "dry out any helpful effects of the recent rains."
content: Santa Ana winds are leaving much of Los Angeles and Ventura counties with elevated wildfire risk on Thursday and Friday, leading to a National Weather Service warning that any blazes could spread quickly."If fire ignition occurs, conditions are favorable for extreme fire behavior which would threaten life and property," a NWS Red Flag Warning says. "A Red Flag Warning means that critical fire weather conditions are either occurring now, or will shortly. Use extreme caution with anything that can spark a wildfire."As a result of the Santa Ana wind event, which could bring fire danger in combination with low humidity, CBS LA has issued a Next Weather Alert for Thursday and Friday. The alert spans the Ventura County mountains and valleys, Malibu, the Santa Monica Mountains, San Fernando Valley, San Gabriel and San Bernardino mountains, the Inland Empire and Orange County."If a fire were to start, it could spread rapidly because of the weather conditions," said CBS LA Chief Meteorologist Paul Deanno. The NWS says those winds will "dry out any helpful effects of the recent rains" Southern California received."The winds are coming in from the desert, pushing through into the mountains, through the canyons and the passes. Finally, when it trickles down into our wind-prone areas, that's what helps dries us out," said CBS LA Meteorologist Amber Lee.Forecasters indicate that wind gusts Thursday and Friday can reach upwards of 70 miles per hour in mountain areas. Inland, they're expected to come from the northeast between 20 and 40 mph.Santa Ana winds are likely to peak on Friday, according to the NWS.Southern California prepares emergency measuresSouthern California Edison is considering public safety power shutoffs for roughly 224,500 customers in Los Angeles and Ventura counties amid the heightened fire risks.Residents can view their outage status here.The LA County Sheriff's Department issued an advisory that potential outages could "disrupt communications, traffic signals and electrically powered medical equipment" and urged residents to prepare."We urge residents to remain vigilant, stay informed, have an emergency plan, and follow the guidance of public safety officials," LA County Sheriff Robert Luna said. "Preparedness and collaboration are essential to keeping our communities safe." The LA County Fire Department also stated that they are prepositioning personnel and aerial resources ahead of the Santa Ana winds."With strong winds capable of driving rapid wildfire growth, we urge residents to prepare immediately," LA County Fire Chief Anthony Marrone said. "Review the Ready! Set! Go! program, identify your evacuation zone, and be prepared to evacuate without delay." Drawing on the lessons from the January 2025 wildfires, LA County's emergency management team said they are already coordinating with different departments ahead of the wind event. "The January 2025 wildfires underscored the importance of early coordination, clear public information and planning for people who need additional assistance," said Kevin McGowan, director of the emergency management office. "Our responsibility is to coordinate the County's response and provide actionable information. To prepare for a potential emergency, residents can visit protect.genasys.com to find their evacuation zone. LA County officials urged residents to find more than one route out of their neighborhood, learn how to open garage doors during a potential power outage, and pack supplies, including medication, in case they need to evacuate at a moment's notice."Residents can help protect themselves and their neighbors by preparing now, staying informed, and being ready to evacuate," McGowan said. LA County officials urged residents to avoid parking on narrow roads, sharp curves and any areas that can block roadways for first responders and trap other residents during an evacuation. Ready SoCalCBS LA has prepared guides for emergency preparedness during wind events and wildfires. Here are some checklists and guides to keep in mind: Evacuation orders can happen at a moment's notice; here are things to remember to grabSteps to lower your risk and increase chances of insurance coverage for wind damageA car might be your only lifeline during a wildfire; here's how to drive safeFamily remembers loved one lost in Eaton Fire and warns of the need to prepareWhat you should have at home to stay safe during dangerous windsWildfire checklists: what you need to know to stay safeStrong winds checklist: steps to protect your home

title: Student arrested after loaded gun found at Woodlawn High School in Baltimore County
description: A student was arrested at Baltimore County's Woodlawn High School on Wednesday after the individual was found to be in possession of a loaded gun.
content: A student was arrested at Baltimore County's Woodlawn High School on Wednesday after the individual was found to be in possession of a loaded gun. The weapon was found after two students got into a verbal altercation at the school, said a statement sent to community members and shared with CBS News Baltimore. The altercation ended when staff members were able to separate the two students, the statement said. As part of the school's investigation into the incident, an allegation was made that one of the students may have had a gun.A search was initiated, and one of the students was found to be carrying a weapon. "Our School Resource Officer responded and confiscated the weapon, and the student was arrested," the statement said. "Additional Baltimore County police officers also responded to the school to assist. This is now a police matter, and an investigation is underway."A statement from the Baltimore County Police Department confirmed that the loaded weapon was found after a search. "No weapon was discharged, and no student was injured during the incident," the police statement said. "The investigation remains ongoing." School officials thanked staff members for acting quickly to maintain the safety of students. "Weapons of any kind are strictly prohibited on school property, and the student will receive serious school consequences in addition to law enforcement action," the statement continued. The school offered assistance from counselors if any students needed it. Parents were urged to speak with their children "about the importance of making safe choices and reporting any safety concerns to a trusted adult right away," the statement said.

title: Reality TV star "Kash" fatally shot by sister during fight in Oakland, DA says
description: The sister of reality TV star Mackayla "Kash" Paige fatally shot her during an attempt to help in a fight, Oakland police said.
content: Reality TV star Mackayla "Kash" Paige was fatally shot by her sister during an attempt to protect her after a fight broke out, Oakland police said Wednesday.Vernika Dunbar was arrested, police said, about an hour after the shooting, which took place around 1:35 a.m. on Sunday near the 270 block of 14th Street. According to police, Dunbar, Paige and two others were in the area when a verbal and physical altercation occurred, and Paige and an unknown woman began to fight. In an attempt to help Paige, Dunbar got a gun from one of the people in their group and approached Paige and the other woman, police said; Dunbar then began to try to pistol-whip the other woman but ended up shooting Paige. Police said Dunbar waived her rights and told investigators what happened, which was corroborated by surveillance video. The Alameda County District Attorney's Office said she was charged with involuntary manslaughter, assault with a firearm, carrying a loaded firearm in public, and brandishing a firearm in public. Mackayla "Kash" PaigePaige appeared on reality shows such as "Real West Coast Baddies" and "Young and Reckless." Fans knew her as "Kash," and family said on Monday that Paige appreciated those who supported her. "If you were a fan of her, she appreciated you. She loved you. All she wanted to do was make people happy," her cousin said.

title: St. Paul City Council approves plan to study impact of robotaxis on workforce, public safety
description: Twin Cities leaders on both sides of the Mississippi River want to press the brakes before driverless vehicles hit the road.
content: Twin Cities leaders on both sides of the Mississippi River want to press the brakes before driverless vehicles hit the road. Many rideshare drivers believe that robotaxis will take their jobs. St. Paul city leaders are trying to get ahead of the rideshare debate. They want St. Paul's transportation to be shaped by community members, not by big tech."This is a question of who we value as a city. Do we ensure thousands of drivers and workers can support their families and put food on the table or are we siding with billionaire taxi CEO's who think they can ignore our regulations and undercut workers to pad their pockets," said HwaJeong Kim. The St. Paul City Council will recommend community protections in advance of autonomous cars coming to the capitol city.No timeline was put on resolution but the author, Rebecca Noecker, says it's more important to make sure the study is done right. They'll look at the impact of these vehicles on transportation workers, public safety, emergency response and how they work in winter weather."I would expect a full study would take certainly no less than six months or maybe up to a year to be done to completion," Noecker said. St. Paul is also looking across the river at Minneapolis. The Minneapolis City Council approved an ordinance earlier this month that mandates a human monitor in driverless cars."It could be a driver in one of those cars. Don't let innovation leave us behind. We're here. We want to be here," said rideshare driver Mardis Washington. It's something Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey opposes. He vetoed the ordinance."We know from a local state study that about 10,000 drivers in our state pay their rent and feed their families with income that they make driving rideshare," said Ward 2 City Council Member Robin Wonsley. Minneapolis council members want to protect jobs and say safety is a big issue when driverless cars are on city streets.Waymo, the Silicon Valley-based company, calls the move by Minneapolis a defacto ban.Its cars have been seen throughout the Twin Cities mapping routes.Thursday, the Minneapolis City Council will vote to uphold Frey's veto or override it.

title: Baltimore police officers convicted of misconduct charges after chase leads to assault
description: Two Baltimore Police Department (BPD) officers have been convicted on misconduct charges, the state's attorney's office for Baltimore City announced on Wednesday.
content: Two Baltimore Police Department (BPD) officers have been convicted on misconduct charges, the state's attorney's office for Baltimore City announced on Wednesday. Officer Mordechai Mandelbaum was found guilty of making a false statement, making a false report and two counts of misconduct in office, said a statement by the state's attorney's office.Officer Menachem Rosenbloom was found guilty of second-degree assault and one count of misconduct in office.The charges relating to false reports and false statements carry a penalty of up to six months and/or a $500 fine, the statement said. Second-degree assault carries a penalty of up to 10 years and/or a fine of $2,500. Misconduct in office has no maximum penalty. Sentencing in the case has been scheduled for Dec. 16. Officer made statements "with the intent to deceive"Officer Mandelbaum allegedly made false statements to Officer Rosenbloom on June 26, 2025, with the intent to deceive, the indictment documents showed. The statements were made during an incident at the 700 block of E. Chase Street, after Officer Rosenbloom allegedly assaulted a man.The officers noticed a man had left his apartment, leaving his two young children unattended, according to the indictment. The officers initiated a vehicle pursuit of the man, who traveled on foot in and around I-83.After a foot chase, Officer Mandelbaum allegedly ran a few steps toward the man before losing his balance and falling forward onto the sidewalk. Officer Mandelbaum was accused of falsely reporting to Officer Rosenbloom that the man "tripped" him, causing him to fall, further stating that the man "kicked" his foot.After the officers found the man again, Officer Rosenbloom got out of the patrol car and started a foot chase, according to the indictment. Eventually, the man stopped running, stood in a corner behind residential buildings, and raised both hands in surrender.Officer Rosenbloom then allegedly deployed his pepper spray into the man's face several times without legal justification.State's attorney: Such cases "undermines public trust" Officer Mandelbaum falsely reported that the man assaulted him as soon as he exited the patrol vehicle, the documents showed. Officer Mandelbaum repeated his false assertion that the man "kicked him" at least three separate times, the indictment said.Baltimore State's Attorney Ivan J. Bates issued a statement on the convictions. "Police officers are entrusted with tremendous authority and a responsibility to uphold the law," Bates said. "When that authority is abused, through excessive force, false statements, or misconduct in office, it undermines public trust and threatens the integrity of our justice system. These guilty verdicts reaffirm that no one is above the law, and our office will continue to hold individuals accountable for their actions, regardless of their position or badge," he added.

title: 140-year sentence given to Baltimore woman found guilty in 2025 triple shooting
description: A Baltimore woman has been sentenced to 140 years in prison after being found guilty of murder in a triple shooting in 2025 that killed a teacher's aide and injured two others, including an 11-year-old child.
content: A Baltimore woman has been sentenced to 140 years in prison after being found guilty of murder in a triple shooting in 2025 that killed a teacher's aide and injured two others, including an 11-year-old child. The sentence, imposed on 38-year-old Cassandra McRae, was announced Wednesday by the Baltimore City State's Attorney's Office. A judge ordered McRae to serve 140 years of the sentence, with the first 25 years being without the possibility of parole, said a statement issued by the State's Attorney, Ivan Bates. McRae was charged with second-degree murder, four counts of conspiracy to commit murder, four counts of attempted murder in the second degree, five counts of use of a firearm in the commission of a felony or crime of violence, and reckless endangerment.The shooting involving McRae led to the death of 52-year-old Anntoinette Jennings, a grandmother and pre-K teacher' aide at Waverly Elementary/Middle School.Surveillance footage used as evidenceSecurity footage revealed the shooting resulted from an altercation at a children's basketball game involving Jennings' family and a woman, later identified as McRae. The defendant entered a grey sedan, which followed the victims' vehicle to the scene of the shooting, the State's Attorney's statement said. The security footage showed that McRae exited the sedan and approached the victims' vehicle at the rear passenger side. At the same time, two male suspects approached the vehicle on the driver's side. McRae touched the vehicle's rear and stated: "There they go right there, there they go right there." Moments later, shots were fired into the victims' vehicle by one of the male suspects. All three suspects then fled the scene. During the course of the investigation, Tavon Singleton was identified as one of the male suspects. The other suspect remains at large. Singleton was ultimately acquitted of all charges, the statement said. Defendant proclaimed her innocenceInside the courtroom, McRae proclaimed her innocence, according to our media partner, the Baltimore Banner. "I have been wrongfully convicted on all charges, and I have committed no crime. I am innocent," McRae said. "I want justice for your family, just as much as you do."However, Baltimore Circuit Judge Dana Middleton described McRae as the catalyst for the deadly shooting, saying she was responsible for what happened even though she did not pull the trigger, the Banner reported.The charges stem from a shsooting that occurred on January 22, 2025, in the 5400 block of York Road, where multiple people suffered from gunshot wounds inside a vehicle. The incident killed 52-year-old Anntoinette Jennings and injured two others, including an 11-year-old. Two other people inside the vehicle, including a 6-year-old, were not injured.State's Attorney Ivan J. Bates issued a statement on the sentence. "A sentence of 140 years reflects the devastating consequences of this Defendant's actions," he said. "Her willingness to engage in conduct that took the life of a grandmother and injured two other people, including an 11-year-old child, demonstrates a shocking disregard for human life and the safety of innocent children," Bates added.

title: Gas, airfare costs have signficantly increased, but travel is still in high demand, Minnesota agency says
description: MEA weekend gives a lot of families a final chance to travel before winter if they can afford to do so.
content: New labor data shows gas prices are now more than 34% higher than a year ago. Airfare is up 22% from this time last year. With a rise in travel costs overall, a Coon Rapids travel agency says travel remains in demand."We have seen a ton of demand for fall travel. People want to go everywhere," said Maggie Brandt of Riverdale Travel, an agency that has been in the business for 100 years.MEA weekend gives a lot of families a final chance to travel before winter if they can afford to do so."There's been some unique deals I've been able to find. Staying with friends or not having food outings as my main form of entertainment," said Kristen Ostrem of Minneapolis.Riverdale Travel says families are finding ways to make it work and this is the busiest they've ever been."People aren't necessarily cutting corners when it comes to vacations, they might be saving money in other places to afford their experiences," Brandt added.Airfare isn't cheap. New data shows airfare is up more than 20% from just last year. The CEO of Delta Air Lines says they have no choice but to pass on higher fuel costs."We expect oil prices to be $6 billion higher than they were a year ago, and that's a substantial shock" said Delta CEO Ed Bastian.Thinking about a road trip instead? AAA says the average price for regular gas in Minnesota is roughly $4.25, where last year's average was $2.89. That's a 47% increase.If you're sticking around Minnesota for the long weekend, here are some ideas:The Science Museum of Minnesota has a new nature exhibit.The Minnesota Zoo has its annual Jack-O'-Lantern Spectacular.Minnesota Department of Natural Resources reminds you that parks are open and fall colors are bright.

title: Car crashes into Buena Park apartment building, woman in critical condition
description: Orange County Fire Authority crews responded to the building at 8th Street and Rostrata Avenue and extricated a woman trapped under the vehicle inside the structure.
content: A car crashed into a Buena Park apartment building on Wednesday afternoon, leaving one woman in critical condition.Orange County Fire Authority crews responded to the building at 8th Street and Rostrata Avenue and extricated a woman trapped under the vehicle inside the structure.The vehicle's two occupants were not injured, according to OCFA.Aerial footage showed a silver sedan with extensive front-end damage, pulled out of a first-floor apartment that had been destroyed.The driver and passenger were detained and released pending further investigation. title: Bed-Stuy native trades gun for camera, becomes National Geographic Explorer
description: Wildlife photographer George McKenzie Jr. of Brooklyn is bringing his work to some of the world's most remote places and inspiring young people through photography workshops.
content: Most people walk by a pigeon without stopping to admire its beauty. Others go out of their way to avoid New York City rats entirely.But for wildlife photographer George McKenzie Jr., the overlooked and unadmired wildlife of the five boroughs became his first photography subjects.McKenzie grew up in Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn, where gun violence and the pressures of street life shaped his childhood. Today, he travels the world photographing wildlife as a National Geographic Explorer, from the Arctic to Africa."My camera definitely opened up so many doors for me," McKenzie said.One of the few African-American wildlife photographers in his field, McKenzie said he rarely saw people who looked like him while he pursued his dream."I'll always tell people, if you can find me a Black wildlife photographer from an urban environment who speaks English as their first language, I'll give them a certain dollar amount. And I haven't lost that bet," he said.But McKenzie's career didn't begin in exotic or remote locations. It started on his childhood block."It's not where you're from, it's what you have access to. I have access to some of the smartest birds. They're really beautiful," McKenzie said.He grew up surrounded by examples of the life he would eventually leave behind. He dropped out of high school and said the threat of gun violence was a constant presence."I would go to school with a gun in my backpack," McKenzie said. "The friends I kept at the time were living that lifestyle. I had cousins that lived that lifestyle. I had so many examples in front in front of me."The profession initially caught McKenzie's attention for a more unexpected reason."I got into photography because at an early age I figured out women like photography," he said.Over time, the camera became a gateway to a different future, one that took him far beyond the streets where he grew up.His longtime friend, Perry Easton, a Bed-Stuy artist, said he remembers the challenges facing young people in the neighborhood."Drugs, prostitution, gangs," Easton said.Watching McKenzie's career take off inspired Easton to explore his own artistic talents, he said. McKenzie's success also showed him that the circumstances of their upbringing did not have to determine their futures."You can easily be fooled and you think this is all I can amount to in life. And that's not true," Easton said.Now, McKenzie is the subject of a documentary, "Book of George," a Jackson Wild Earth Alliance Impact Pitch finalist. He's also working to help other young people discover opportunities beyond their immediate surroundings. Through his Unseen Story Foundation, he offers free photography camps and workshops that introduce young people to careers in conservation storytelling.McKenzie said his own story helps him connect with the students he teaches."They understand where I come from. Because a lot of them come from the same kind of backgrounds," he said.A camera changed the way McKenzie saw the world. Now, he hopes to change the way young people see themselves.Have a story idea or tip in Brooklyn? Email Hannah by CLICKING HERE.

title: The real story behind the iconic "Don't Mess With Texas" slogan, 40 years later
description: The iconic "Don't Mess With Texas" slogan turns 40 this year, but its origins and original purpose may surprise those who associate it with Texas pride.
content: Every Texan knows the phrase "Don't Mess With Texas." It evokes a sense of Texas pride, a puffed-out chest and a tip of the hat. But with the endless appearances on signs and merchandise, it can be easy to forget what Don't Mess With Texas is all about.The answer is self-evident, but may be hard to catch at first. It's about the word "mess," in the literal sense of making a mess. In 2026, the Texas Department of Transportation (TxDOT) is celebrating the phrase's 40th anniversary as a potent marketing tool against roadside litter.A solution to an expensive problemThe idea for the a marketing campaign was sparked in 1984, after TxDOT had to spend $20 million to clean up roadside litter, the equivalent of more than $64 million today."This litter was a massive growing problem, but especially along highways and rural roads. And the majority of the litter was fast food wrappers, cans and bottles often thrown out of vehicles, which was super dangerous to drivers," TxDOT spokesperson Laura Butterbrodt said in a recent interview.TxDOT hired Austin-based marketing agency GSD&M for the campaign, which was headed by Mike Blair and Tim McClure. They wanted to create a slogan that would connect with Texans, especially those that might be more prone to littering; McClure called them "bubbas in pickup trucks" and those that believed it was their "God-given right" to litter. On an early walk one morning, McClure noticed trash in his neighborhood and said he heard his mother's voice in the back of his head saying it looked like a mess, much like his room growing up. That was a lightbulb moment for him. Texans don't say litter, they'd say it's a mess. So he took it to TxDOT and "Don't Mess With Texas" became the slogan of the campaign. To turn the idea into a memorable message to the public, Blair knew they needed big names and attention-grabbing commercials. The first one, released in 1986, featured Stevie Ray Vaughan playing guitar in front of a huge Texas flag and uttering the now-famous slogan into the camera.From there, the phrase exploded into the mainstream and Blair directed more and more commercials with Texas celebrities and athletes. The campaign has featured the likes of Willie Nelson, George Strait, Matthew McConaughey, Joe Jonas, and now Post Malone.Don't Mess With Texas successThe campaign was not only catchy, it actually worked. After one year, roadside litter decreased 29%. By the 1990s, it was down 72% and the numbers continue to decline.Despite that, there is a reason the campaign is still around 40 years later: About 362 million pieces of trash accumulate on Texas roads every year, about half of it coming from motorists, TxDOT said.Roadside litter is mostly things like cans and water bottles, but micro-litter is also a big problem, TxDOT said. Any piece of trash that's smaller than 2 inches is considered micro-litter, with cigarette butts being the most common."Litter is any trash that is not disposed of in a trash can. Gum is litter. Even compostable things like banana peels and an apple core is litter when you throw it out a car window or on the ground. Also trash that flies out of a car window or out of a truck bed, even if it's an accident, that's still littering," Butterbrodt said.Throwing litter out of a car can be hazardous to other drivers. Research done by AAA in 2016 showed that at the time, 500 people died and 39,000 people were injured from accidents caused by objects being tossed out of a window, or from trying to avoid roadside debris. Most of those incidents were along interstates. Littering can also be costly for Texas drivers, in addition to the millions the state spends on cleaning it up. Someone caught littering can face a fine of up to $2,000.Throwing a piece of garbage out of the window affects every Texan, polluting water and soil and affecting wildlife. Think of what Big Bend would look like with a mountain of trash, or Fredericksburg vineyards strung with litter instead of grapes. Wading through plastic bottles to see Big Tex or the Alamo. These places are Texas heritage and the pride and joy of Texans. Such a beautiful and diverse landscape doesn't deserve to be messed with.

title: Suspect in fatal Atlanta Beltline stabbing not competent to stand trial, judge rules
description: The suspect in a stabbing that killed a 29-year-old on the Atlanta Beltline​ has been deemed not competent to stand trial, a Fulton County judge has ruled.
content: The suspect in a deadly stabbing on the Atlanta Beltline in August has been deemed not competent to stand trial, a Fulton County judge has ruled.Court records obtained by CBS News Atlanta reveal that a judge declared 54-year-old Jonathan Hamby incompetent, putting him on a separate competency docket. The records showed that he was also looking for new counsel in his case.According to a post on the Superior Court of Fulton County's website, the Competency Docket involves the judge, attorneys for the prosecution and defense, and mental health experts as part of a "restoration process." If a defendant is "not restorable" they can ultimately be committed.Hamby has been charged with murder, possession of a knife during the commission of a felony, aggravated assault, and terroristic threats in the death of 29-year-old Ramon Harris on the Beltline on Aug. 23, 2026.Body camera footage showed officers arriving at the scene and ordering Hamby to get on the ground. Hamby is heard in the footage telling officers that he was defending himself.Jail records show Hamby has been booked dozens of times since 2011 on charges that included obstruction, battery, criminal trespass, interference with government property, aggravated assault and possession of a knife during the commission of a felony. In a statement following his arrest, Hamby's family said he had a long history of severe mental illness and active psychosis and had repeatedly tried to get him treatment."We spent years desperately fighting a broken system to prevent this exact tragedy from happening," the family wrote.Court documents show that Hamby is scheduled to be in court for a pre-indictment preliminary hearing on Dec. 17, 2026 with a status conference on Feb. 11, 2027.As of Wednesday, Hamby remains in custody at the Fulton County Jail.

title: "Aggressive" great white shark prompts closure of Huntington Beach coastline
description: An "aggressive" great white shark spotted off the Huntington Beach coastline prompted the temporary closure of the beach on Tuesday.
content: An "aggressive" great white shark spotted off the Huntington Beach coastline prompted the temporary closure of the beach on Tuesday. In a social media post, Huntington Beach Fire Department officials said they received a "credible report" of a 10- to 12-foot great white shark near Lifeguard Tower 16. "The shark was reportedly circling, a behavior classified as aggressive under Marine Safety's shark response protocols," the post said. Out of an abundance of caution, city officials opted to close the beach from Seapoint to the Huntington Beach Pier, approximately a mile north and south of the lifeguard tower. "We do see animals from time to time. So, is it unusual? No. But the size of the shark is bigger than we normally encounter," said HBFD Battalion Chief Doug Leach. Firefighters said the stretch of beach would remain closed until at least 3 p.m. on Wednesday. "Please follow all posted signs and instructions from lifeguards. Public safety remains our top priority," the post said. City marine safety personnel were expected to continue monitoring the situation after posting warning signs on the beach and notifying beachgoers.On Wednesday, the surfer who spotted the shark spoke with CBS LA. "When the wave stood up, you could see the sun through the back, and so then I saw the shark fully through the back of the wave swimming basically straight towards me," said Patrick, who was foil surfing Tuesday afternoon when the shark suddenly appeared. "It was probably 20 to 40 feet away from me."He said he doesn't believe the shark was coming after him; rather, they were just crossing paths. He said he beelined for the shore after seeing the shark with something in its mouth. Chris Lowe, a California State Long Beach Marine Biology Professor and Shark Lab Director, said this is typically the time of year when sharks move up and down the coast. With El NiÃ±o now impacting the oceans, what was a "sharky summer" is turning into a "sharky fall." "It's not over yet. So, we're just getting into the thick of the season, so this could go well into December," Lowe said.

title: Sacramento airport therapy dogs, known as the BARC team, help to ease travel stress
description: People flying in and out of Sacramento International Airport have a four-legged team of volunteers to help reduce the stress of travel in the BARC team.
content: Travelling can be stressful, especially around the busy holidays. People flying in and out of Sacramento International Airport have a four-legged team of volunteers to help reduce that stress.The Boarding Area Relaxation Corps, or BARC for short, are volunteer airport therapy dogs who have been easing the stress of traveling for the last decade. Their owners volunteer through an organization called Lend a Heart, a volunteer group that trains the dogs for this kind of therapy."We see a huge decrease in stress. I think it's made a huge impact here and a great impact on us too," Christine Hale with Lend a Heart said.The dogs even get airport nametags. When their shift is done, they get a treat to enjoy on the tram ride home. You can find BARC at the Sacramento airport on Wednesdays, Fridays and Sundays once you get through TSA security.Hale says, "We found that's the best place as people come through TSA, they just see us right there, and glom onto us. We also wander the terminal and gates and can find you that way."That was the case for some Sacramento State women's soccer players, including seniors Lexi Schroeder and Ellie Farber."I love it because I am an anxious flyer, so when I saw the dogs, oh my gosh â I need to pet them, it's just what I needed," Schroeder said.The dogs don't mind the attention either."We dropped our bags and came back, so cute," Farber said.Volunteers would love to see more dogs and shifts here, but they say they could use more recruits to meet demand. Lend a Heart hopes there are some dogs and owners out there willing to be a part of the endeavor. People interested in letting their canine volunteer with BARC can contact the Lend a Heart team through their website.

title: Questions remain over the future of Flock camera use in Detroit
description: Flock says that the audit-assistance tool will be mandatory by the end of the year.
content: Madison Heights has disconnected its city-run automated license plate readers while it reviews privacy and data-security concerns.In Detroit, Police Commissioner Victoria Camille says the board's oversight is limited after approval."Through the ordinance, we're responsible for approving the surveillance technical specification reports before DPD can go out to bid, and then after that, we really don't have too much oversight except for asking questions," said Camille.Camille says she asked for DPD's Flock audits in August and still hasn't received them.She also says DPD disclosed that an officer used the database to search his wife's license plate for personal reasons.CBS News Detroit reached out to DPD for comment, but a spokesperson said there was no update or information to give at this time.Flock says every search is logged — showing who searched, when and why."Earlier this year, we launched audit assistance, and that flags anomalies to an administrator for review if it's something that could be misused. Doesn't mean it's automatically misused," said spokesperson Courtney Terlecki.Flock says that the audit-assistance tool will be mandatory by the end of the year.It also says Detroit's data is stored in the AWS Cloud in the U.S., and DPD controls who can access it and can revoke sharing at any time.However, Flock says DPD is the best source for which agencies currently have access.Camille says she hasn't seen a current list."Not at all. There's not enough transparency. And if you think about surveillance, surveillance by nature is intended to be secret, and public oversight of these types of things is really important," said Camille.The request for DPD's audit information remains outstanding.

title: Man charged after 21 dead cats found inside Pennsylvania home
description: A man is facing charges after police said 21 cats were found dead at a home in Westmoreland County.
content: A man is facing charges after police said 21 cats were found dead at a home in Westmoreland County.A woman called police after finding all of her cats dead and "in various stages of decomposition" at a home on North Second Street in West Newton, the Westmoreland County District Attorney's Office said in a press release on Wednesday. The homeowner told investigators that Jonathan Hodgetts of Jeannette was supposed to be caring for the cats while she was taking care of another sick cat, the district attorney's office said. The woman said she had sent supplies to the home, and Hodgetts sent her photos and assured her the cats were fine. The district attorney's office said a veterinarian performed a necropsy on the cats and determined they died of starvation. The woman told investigators that Hodgetts was rescuing the cats and getting them fixed, and the two of them had plans to turn a detached garage into a cat sanctuary. She had last seen the cats alive in July, the district attorney's office said. Hodgetts is facing charges of aggravated cruelty to animals, cruelty to animals and neglect.

title: Noel Night to return to Midtown Detroit after 1-year hiatus
description: One of Detroit's most beloved holiday traditions is making a comeback.
content: One of Detroit's most beloved holiday traditions is making a comeback. After a one-year hiatus, Noel Night will return to Midtown Detroit on Dec. 5, bringing back the shopping, entertainment and family friendly activities that have made the event a holiday staple for generations.Organizers with Midtown Detroit say they spent the past year gathering feedback from businesses, cultural institutions and community members to better understand what people want from the event going forward."We really heard a lot that people loved a holiday atmosphere," said Melanie Markowicz, executive director of Midtown Detroit. "They love decorations. They love holiday music, and they love unique gifts, performances and to support the arts community. They are so vibrant in Detroit."Noel Night, which began in 1973, has long drawn families to Midtown for holiday shopping, arts and cultural experiences, live entertainment and seasonal festivities.This year, organizers are also expanding holiday programming with a new event.The inaugural New Center Holiday Market at the Fisher Building is scheduled for Dec. 12 and will feature local artists, makers and vendors, along with seasonal performances and holiday-themed experiences."It'll be a unique shopping experience with classical music, choirs and we also have two showings at Broadway at the Fisher of the musical "BOOP." So that's gonna be really fun too," Markowicz said.Organizers say the return of Noel Night is about more than holiday shopping. They hope the event continues to provide free, family-friendly experiences for Detroit residents while showcasing the city's vibrant arts community."This was a special opportunity for families to come for a free, family-friendly event that had all kinds of activities, arts, music and to be outdoors and enjoy and explore all the neighborhoods in Midtown and the Cultural Center," Markowicz said.Midtown Detroit is currently accepting applications from artists, makers, food vendors, performers and small businesses interested in participating in one or both events. Applications are due Oct. 19.Noel Night will take place Dec. 5 in Midtown Detroit, while the New Center Holiday Market at the Fisher Building is set for Dec. 12.

title: Four arrested in California, Georgia in shooting of 49ers player Keion White in February
description: Four people were arrested in California and Georgia in connection with a shooting that injured San Francisco 49ers player Keion White earlier this year, authorities said Wednesday.
content: Four people were arrested in California and Georgia in connection with a shooting that injured San Francisco 49ers player Keion White earlier this year, authorities said on Wednesday.The shooting happened on Feb. 9 at about 4 a.m. at the Dahlia Club in San Francisco's Mission District. White, a defensive end who joined the 49ers in a trade with the New England Patriots last October, was shot in the ankle during a private party he was hosting at the club after attending the Super Bowl earlier in the day at Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara.White told reporters last month that his injury wasn't serious and that he didn't even realize he had been shot right away."I didn't know I got shot until like five minutes after, as I was walking around," White said.There were no arrests at the time and the San Francisco Police Department said the shooting was preceded by a verbal altercation between two groups of people."Operation D-Line" results in arrestsOn Wednesday, the department announced the arrests following a months-long investigation dubbed "Operation D-Line" which involved dozens of search warrants and help from multiple law enforcement jurisdictions and the San Francisco District Attorney's Office. "Our investigators identified multiple people involved in the incident," Police Chief Derrick Lew said at a press conference on Wednesday. "It started when multiple suspects, some brandishing firearms, confronted the 49ers player, which then led to a physical altercation between the group and the victim, who was shot in the leg."On Oct. 7, the Atlanta Police Department, acting on a SFPD warrant, arrested 38-year-old Marquis Davis at his home. During the arrest, officers also seized an illegal firearm, 820 grams of MDMA, 1,026 grams of methamphetamine, 979 grams of cocaine, and 3,842 grams of fentanyl, according to San Francisco police. On the same day, San Francisco police officers and San Joaquin County Sheriff's deputies arrested 36-year-old Antoine Washington in Stockton, California, and also recovered a loaded gun, over 120 oxycodone pills, and nearly $7,000 in cash. Also on Oct. 7, SFPD officers took 35-year-old Curtis Green into custody in Irvine, California with the help of the Irvine Police Department. On Oct. 9, the Los Angeles Police Department arrested 36-year-old San Joaquin County resident Gregory Walker in Southern California.Two defendants charged in Keion White shootingWalker and Green were brought back to San Francisco and booked into county jail on Monday and the two were arraigned on Wednesday. Walker was charged with assault with a semi-automatic firearm, with allegations that he personally discharged a firearm and inflicted great bodily injury, along with being a felon in possession of a firearm, the District Attorney's Office said. Green was charged with misdemeanor gun charges, including brandishing a firearm and carrying a loaded gun in public.District Attorney Brooke Jenkins said her office would move to have Walker detained pending trial without bail because of the public safety risk he poses. San Francisco Police Chief Derrick Lew said his department and DA's Office were working with the other jurisdictions to arrange for Davis and Washington to be brought to San Francisco. He added that the circumstances surrounding the shooting were still being investigated."We are actively pursuing evidence to continue to clarify the motivations behind this violent incident and to hold those responsible accountable for their actions," Lew said at a press conference on Wednesday.Lew acknowledged the assistance of the Atlanta Police Department, Cobb County Police Department, Georgia State Patrol, Irvine Police Department, Los Angeles Police Department, and San Joaquin County Sheriff's Office for their assistance in the case.Police asked for any additional witnesses or victims in the incident to come forward and contact the department.It was the second time in two years that a 49ers player was shot during the offseason. On Aug. 31, 2024, wide receiver Ricky Pearsall was shot in the chest during an attempted robbery in the city's Union Square just before the start of his rookie season.

title: 16-year-old girl killed in Detroit drive-by shooting identified
description: The family of 16-year-old Kayliah Embery did not want to comment on camera at this time, but told CBS News Detroit that they are heartbroken by what happened.
content: A teenage girl who was shot and killed Tuesday in a drive-by shooting on Detroit's east side has been identified by her family.The family of 16-year-old Kayliah Embery did not want to comment on camera at this time, but told CBS News Detroit that they are heartbroken by what happened.Detroit police detectives walked the east side of Detroit Wednesday afternoon, looking for more evidence and eyewitnesses. The remnants of police caution tape wrapped around utility poles are the only sign of the tragic and senseless shooting that killed Kayliah.On Tuesday, Police Chief Todd Bettison said four people, including Kayliah, were inside a Jeep Cherokee when a dark-colored sedan drove by and fired multiple gunshots into the vehicle.Police say Kayliah was hit more than once, and another person was shot in the hip. The two other people in the Jeep were not injured.The investigation continues, but the people living in this neighborhood located near Chalmers Street and East Forest Avenue are stunned by what happened. Neighbors didn't want to talk on camera.One woman who says she knows the family well says they have suffered a lot of loss in the last few years, but with Kayliah being the youngest, it's even more devastating.No arrests have been made, and there is no suspect information. Police say there is a $5,000 reward for information leading to the arrest of the suspect. Tips can be submitted on DetroitRewards.tv.

title: St. Sabina Church asking public for help to keep social service center in operation
description: Father Pfleger says they see about 200 people each day at the St. Sabina Service Center amid the high cost of living.
content: Saint Sabina's Social Service Center celebrated its second year in operation in the Auburn Gresham neighborhood on Tuesday.While they've fed many in the neighborhood, the church says it's coming at a high cost.Father Michael Pfleger says they see about 200 people each day at the St. Sabina Service Center, proving the cost of living is high and the crowd on Wednesday showed that need."Yeah, this is in walking distance, but the other place you gotta take the bus, the L," said Theordora Reed.Saint Sabina Service Center is a place Reed visits almost every day. "I come here all the time, I come here all the time. I just walk down the street and I'm right here." Stocking up on essential items from rice to flour. Inside the food pantry, other shoppers like Lavell Cunningham."I just think that it's needed, like on a regular. Like we just need to continue the whole solidarity, unity and communication," he said.Saint Sabina celebrated two years of its food pantry with a special party on Wednesday morning. The pantry started in October 2024 after Catholic Charities closed the pantry the month before. Two weeks later, the church reopened it.Father Pfleger says it's been a huge expense to keep it up and running."I didn't realize the amount of cost for staff, for rent, for garbage pickup, for security, for all of the things we need here. It's a huge expense of around $500,000 a year," he said.Reed recalls the vast difference. "They didn't have the stuff that they got now, so, and they didn't have the help. Plus, they got services for people that's homeless or people that have problems with their life," she said.The pantry also has several agencies that help with resources for those experiencing homelessness, health, medical plans, rent and other case management programs. Unfortunately, Father Pfleger says they've had to turn people away because they ran out of food. "So on our second anniversary, I'm asking people in Chicago, if you can donate food, businesses, if you can donate funds so we can get food. We need Chicago's help to keep going." The service center is open five days a week, from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m.

title: Man's call about mother-in-law leads to arrest of suspected scammer in Paulding County, deputies say
description: A man's concern for his mother-in-law helped deputies arrest a woman accused of scamming more than $60,000 from her elderly victim.
content: A man's concern for his mother-in-law helped deputies arrest a woman accused of scamming more than $60,000 from her elderly victim.Officials with the Paulding County Sheriff's Office say their investigation began on Oct. 7, when a man called 911 to report his belief that his mother-in-law was being scammed.During the investigation, authorities say they learned the scammers had convinced the victim that they were from the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, and asked for gift cards, wire transfers, cash, and bitcoin.According to officials, detectives learned that the suspects were expecting the victim to drop off several thousands of dollars in cash and notified deputies."The suspects set a time and place for the drop, and we quickly assembled in the area to arrest the suspect," the sheriff's office told CBS News Atlanta.The suspect, identified as 58-year-old Zishan Zeng, was charged with two counts of elder exploitation and two counts of theft by deception. Investigators say the Duluth woman also is facing charges in Douglas County.Zeng is currently being held in the Paulding County Jail without bond.The investigation remains ongoing.

title: Michigan communities pump hundreds of millions into rivers, betting on economic payoff
description: From the Rouge to the Kalamazoo, communities and the state are funding cleanups, parks and restored rapids. Some projects have studies showing returns, and others have no economic analysis.
content: On a recent sunny fall morning, a couple dozen people paddled in bright-colored kayaks past factories, a docked freighter and miniature mountains of industrial materials on southeast Michigan's Lower Rouge River."This is really exciting to have this many people out here kayaking the Rouge because, when I was a kid, the Rouge was so dirty they told you, 'Don't touch it,'" said Sally Petrella, watershed ecologist with Friends of the Rouge, which organized the paddling event.The river was once so polluted it famously caught on fire. Petrella told attendees it has "a long way to go," but restoration efforts have made it "safe enough for you to be out here paddling."Communities across the state are pumping hundreds of millions of dollars into rivers like the Rouge, hoping for both environmental and economic returns.Battle Creek has pitched a project to renaturalize part of the Kalamazoo River that runs over concrete. Grand Rapids is working to restore rapids to the Grand River downtown. A state park is being built around Flint's riverfront. The state announced earlier this month it's investing $89 million to clean up the Detroit, Kalamazoo and other rivers.Backers envision more riverside development bringing tourists to kayak, fish and otherwise enjoy cleaner waterways that are more hospitable to native plants and animals.Economic impact studies aren't always completed for such projects, but many point to a 2007 Brookings Institution study that predicted a $3 return for every $1 invested in waterway restoration. A study on the Huron River in 2017 found the river produced $53.5 million in economic activity annually, while a 2023 White River study pegged its economic impact at $20 million."We've actually done studies in Muskegon that have showed a 6-to-1 return on investment," said Alan Steinman, a professor at Grand Valley State University's Annis Water Resources Institute and a co-author of the Michigan Blue Economy report. "The number is less important than the concept that, 'Oh my God, these properties really do have inherent value, cultural value and economic value that had none associated with (them) prior to the restoration effort.'"Kris Martin, an urban planner with Battle Creek Unlimited, the firm helping to look into whether part of the Kalamazoo river should be renaturalized, said removing the aging concrete channel would make the river "a greater amenity to the downtown.""Right now, it's not accessible for the public at all," he said. "And it's quite dangerous."Martin said costs for the project will depend on the path forward but are expected to be "in the millions." An economic cost-benefit analysis is expected to be a component in the next report released by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers.For the Flint state park project, an economic analysis is not currently planned, because it would cost money, but project spending includes $30.2 million plus a $41 million endowment for future operations and maintenance.As for Grand Rapids, the project is estimated to cost at least $19 million. Economic impact for the project as it stands today has not been publicized.Even when the economic impact is not calculated, administrators say river restoration projects can be a worthwhile investment.Starting in the mid-2000s, the Traverse City area began what has been deemed the largest dam removal project in Michigan's history. Three dams along the Boardman River were taken out to reconnect coldwater streams and restore fish habitat. The project cost more than $27 million.Conservation Resource Alliance**,** which served as the project manager and financial administrator for the effort**,** said it doesn't actually know what the economic benefits have been."It's something that's really hard to quantify and would take a lot of time and investment from the partner collective that removed those dams to do so," said Gavin MacDonald, communications manager for Conservation Resource Alliance.But MacDonald said that, anecdotally, the payoff is that the dam removals restored a more free-flowing river that benefits fish and people."The river is now navigable, so you can paddle large stretches of the Boardman River," MacDonald said. "It's made it more accessible for the people that live in the region and the people that visit to explore and be more connected with nature."Sometimes the payoff is known.For decades, prime downtown waterfront property in Detroit included vacant buildings and abandoned lots. The area has now been transformed to a nationally recognized waterfront that includes greenways and parks, more than eight miles of trails, places to get a drink and go sledding. About $2 billion in public and private dollars have been invested into the project so far and the Detroit Riverfront Conservancy says visitors spend $82 million a year.The Huron River's water trail was designated a part of the National Water Trail System in 2015. Elizabeth Riggs, deputy director at the Huron River Watershed Council at the time, had a hunch that the water trail and other restoration work benefited the river, but she wanted proof."I and others working on the campaign were keen on trying to tell that story of (the river) in dollar terms â which is, as we know, a good way to tell a story â to try to reach as many people as possible, and to help convince decision-makers to invest in rivers and protecting them and restoring them," she said.The watershed council commissioned a study, published in 2017 by Grand Valley State University, to evaluate the economic impact of the Huron River. Researchers found that the river and its water trail were estimated to generate $53.5 million in economic output annually and that the river provided $150 million a year in economic value services through recreation, flood reduction, harboring rare organisms and more.In 2023, Grand Valley State University also published an economic assessment of the White River. The river is located in west Michigan and runs through the Huron-Manistee National Forests. It's fed by coldwater streams and can support salmon and trout.The study found that nearly 70,000 visitors came to the White River in a year and that the river's total economic impact was valued at $20 million."It's a good number to know," said John Stivers, secretary of the White River Watershed Partnership.But he said that, when it comes to the White River, it's a little complicated.The river was designated as a Country-Scenic River by the Michigan Natural Resources Commission in 1975. Development on certain stretches needs to go through a Natural Rivers Zoning Review Board, he said, and the river is further protected because it runs through national forest land.Stivers said some people see the White River as a secret and they want to keep it that way."There are a lot of people that love it the way it is and aren't really too interested in turning it into a high economic engine," he said. "It's a balance."

title: Woman describes encounter with Philadelphia suspected serial killer R.C. Horsch: "The devil in disguise"
description: A woman spoke with CBS News Philadelphia about creepy interactions she had with Horsch and his son Eugene Horsch​.
content: Police and the FBI were back at the so-called "house of horrors" in Philadelphia's Olney neighborhood Wednesday, sifting for human remains in the investigation into suspected serial killer Raymond "R.C." Horsch.A Jane Doe spoke with CBS News Philadelphia about creepy interactions she had with Horsch and his son Eugene Horsch."The devil in disguise," Jane Doe said. "I honestly believe he was the devil in disguise."The woman, who wants to remain anonymous, told CBS News Philadelphia that she met R.C. Horsch five years ago. She said he took this photo.The Jane Doe remembered eerie details of a second-floor bedroom at 417 West Chew Ave."That room that they took me in was a crazy room," she said.She said she first met R.C. Horsch's son, Eugene Horsch. He pulled over while she was standing at a bus stop. She said she recognized a woman in the front passenger seat of Eugene Horsch's car."She called me over to the car," she said, "and I was asked if I would be interested in a few dollars to take some pictures."She said she visited the Horsch residence only one time. She said back then, she was in active addiction. She described that dark bedroom in detail."It had this old bed, like the old-time hospital beds with metal frames and the metal bars, and it had a set of handcuffs hanging off the side," she said. "That bed really freaked me out."She recalled feeling uncomfortable with the line of questions R.C. Horsch was asking, including about her family and friends."I did [feel in danger] once the questions started being asked," she said. "I started being asked questions about my life, about getting high, as far as where I go, who I associate with."She said she feels lucky while watching news reports showing police digging up the property for human remains as their search drags on for traces of more than half a dozen women whom police say have ties to the Horsch home.Police have put up parking regulation notices on the block, saying they're extending the investigation into a third week.

title: Top U.S. banks dropped customers over political and religious views, regulator says
description: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency said nine of the top U.S. banks "debanked" customers over their political or religious views.
content: Top U.S. banks have "debanked" customers because of their political or religious views, as well as their business activities, according to a report from the Treasury Department's Office of the Comptroller of the Currency. The report, released on Wednesday, examines a practice that President Trump has claimed discriminates against conservatives over their views. Debanking has also been highlighted by some cryptocurrency investors, who claim their accounts have been closed because banks are uncomfortable working with crypto industry clients. The OCC said the report was in accordance with Mr. Trump's 2025 executive order requiring federal banking regulators to review complaints to identify financial institutions that had declined business with clients because of their views.Some conservatives have argued that they've been unfairly targeted by financial institutions, although the OCC found that some banks had also refused to do business with Democratic-leaning organizations. Debanking can also occur for legal and regulatory reasons, such as if a bank detects potentially fraudulent activity or an account is overdrawn. The OCC, which reviewed 100,000 complaints and hundreds of bank decisions between 2020 and September 2025, found that the nine largest national banks it supervises had policies that swayed their decisions based on political, religious or business activities. "Americans should have access to financial services regardless of their beliefs, affiliations or political views. Fair access to financial services is not a mantra — it is a mandate," said Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan V. Gould in a statement on Wednesday.The incidents cited in the report include the payment processor WePay, which is now defunct and was acquired by JPMorgan Chase in 2017. WePay closed the accounts of several merchants selling MAGA- or Trump-related items, the OCC said."Our policies prohibit discrimination against customers based on political or religious views," a JPMorgan spokesperson said. WePay's processes "did not meet our expectations. We identified it, corrected it, and the business no longer operates."The OCC also found that some banks turned away customers due to their industries. For instance, businesses involved in oil and gas exploration, coal mining or firearms were restricted from some financial services, the agency concluded.Other banks cited in the report, including Citibank and Wells Fargo, declined to comment and pointed to a statement from the Bank Policy Institute, a trade group for the banking industry. "The banking industry supports fair access to banking services and has been working to ensure that government regulations and policies enable banks to serve law-abiding customers," the Bank Policy Institute said in response to the OCC's findings. The group added, "We support efforts to establish clear and consistent standards that promote access while maintaining sound risk management, including the administration's recent efforts to prioritize supervisory attention on material financial risk and rather than reputational risk."

title: Cook County State's Attorney Eileen Burke says murder of CTA janitor proof that electronic monitoring system is broken
description: Cook County State's Attorney Eileen Burke, who has been critical of the county's electronic monitoring system, said the recent murder of a CTA janitor at a Green Line station​ is the latest example that the system is broken.
content: Cook County State's Attorney Eileen Burke, who has been critical of the county's electronic monitoring system, said the recent murder of a CTA janitor at a Green Line station is the latest example that the system is broken."Electronic monitoring is not monitoring at all right now," Burke said.Chevazz Campbell, the man charged with killing CTA janitor Justin Mobley earlier this month at the Damen stop on the Green Line, was wearing a court-ordered ankle monitor at the time for a recent retail theft case.Cook County prosecutors have said Campbell had repeatedly broken curfew with his ankle monitor before the attack, and was out of compliance for hours at a time. Burke's office asked for him to be brought in, but it never happened. Burke said it's proof the current electronic monitoring system is broken.The Chief Judge's office, which runs the county's electronic monitoring system, said they enforced the law by issuing warrants for Campbell's violations, but said it was law enforcement which failed to enforce those warrants. Burke wants state law changed."Violent criminals shouldn't be on electronic monitoring; when a warrant is issued, that it is actually executed upon; and that they don't get day-for-day credit for time they spent in their home," she said.Speaking at the Lincoln Forum at the Union League Club of Chicago, Burke was asked when she will seek that change in legislation from the Illinois General Assembly. "We are working daily with our legislative committee, and how we are going to pose these, but it's running into a brick wall in the legislature," she said.Campbell has a lengthy criminal history, including a three-year sentence for stabbing another person in 2018. As for why he wasn't picked up when new warrants were issued for his recent electronic monitoring violations, the sheriff's office prioritizes warrants for violent crimes. Before he allegedly killed Mobley, Cambpell was on electronic monitoring for a retail theft charge, a non-violent crime.Burke was also asked Wednesday why her office has not filed criminal charges against any federal agents for their actions during Operation Midway Blitz, as some high-profile figures have pushed for – including former Mayor Lori Lightfoot and Judge Ruben Castillo, who chairs the Illinois Accountability Commission, which was tasked by the governor with investigating the feds' conduct during that immigration crackdown."You have to be okay with people not being happy with your decision," Burke said. "I will never make decisions in this office based on who is screaming the loudest. I will only make decisions in this office based on the law and the facts that are presented to me."

title: Severe storms threaten North Texas ahead of cold front bringing 40-degree temperature drop
description: The timing of the front looks to be speeding up, with it moving in late Thursday and pushing south of us on Friday.
content: North Texas was off to another warm start Wednesday morning, with temperatures in the 70s and 80s and partly to mostly cloudy skies. Feels-like temperatures this afternoon will reach 103°. There is a 20% chance of an isolated shower or thunderstorm this afternoon, with better coverage north and west of the metroplex into Wednesday night.The big story will be the strong cold front moving in by Thursday afternoon. The timing of the front looks to be speeding up, with it moving in late Thursday and pushing south of us on Friday. Ahead of this, there is a chance for isolated strong to severe storms tonight, mainly north and west of the metroplex. Damaging winds will be the main threat.On Thursday, highs will be in the 80s, then will quickly fall overnight into the low 60s. There is a chance of isolated showers and thunderstorms Thursday afternoon into the overnight as that front pushes in, with most of the shower and thunderstorm activity staying just west of I-35, but we're not ruling out some early shower activity Friday morning. On Friday, the two stories will be the strong winds gusting up to 40 mph and the noticeably cooler temperatures.Highs Friday likely stay into the 60s area-wide, with temperatures on Saturday morning dipping into the 40s. Saturday afternoon and Sunday morning will likely feature lows in the 40s and highs in the 60s once again. By Sunday afternoon, we start warming back up into the 70s, and the 80s return by next week.

title: Monroe Public Schools adopts new policy banning transgender females from girls sports
description: The updated policy, which passed 5-2 on Tuesday, only allows biological female students to play girls sports and use girls locker rooms.
content: The Monroe Public Schools board moved forward with updating its girls athletic participation policy after a parent claimed the district violated Title IX protections when it hosted Ann Arbor Skyline, which had an alleged transgender athlete on the team. The updated policy, which passed 5-2 on Tuesday, only allows biological female students to play girls sports and use girls locker rooms. A federal lawsuit against the district aims to prevent MPS from reversing that policy and to award damages to one of its families."Just because they changed the policy last night doesn't mean they can't change the policy again. So, we want to make sure there's a court that looks at that and says you can't do this anymore," said Thomas More Law Center attorney Richard Thompson.Sean Lechner filed his federal lawsuit against the district earlier last week, claiming school officials failed to tell families that a transgender female athlete would be competing against his daughter's varsity volleyball team last year. An independent investigation found no Title IX violations back in April, but Lechner's attorney says the investigation was flawed."It was a report that was predestined to find unsubstantiated. This law firm that they used was a friendly law firm. They knew what the results were going to be," Thompson said.Monroe Public Schools Superintendent Andrew Shaw says that while they've yet to be served with the lawsuit, he said in part, "We remain steadfast in our commitment to adhering to all state and federal guidelines and laws while upholding student safety."While Thompson says he feels the school board did the right thing by changing its policy, the ACLU says it violates Michigan's civil rights laws."Our state civil rights laws explicitly prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity and gender expression in education.
