We believe that such a policy is in violation of the Elliott-Larsen Civil Rights Act," said Jay Kaplan, attorney for the ACLU Michigan LGBTQ+ project.Even though a Trump administration executive order supports the district's new policy, Kaplan says it doesn't have the power to supersede Michigan's civil rights laws.

title: Man accused of threatening to shoot up Holly outdoor music event
description: A man was charged after allegedly making threats of shooting people at an outdoor live music event in Holly, according to Oakland County Prosecutor Karen D. McDonald.
content: A man is accused of making threats of shooting people at an outdoor live music event in Holly, Oakland County Prosecutor Karen D. McDonald announced. Daniel James Gibson, 26, was charged with one count of false report or threat of terrorism after allegedly threatening to "shoot the place up" at the reopening of Andy's Place in Holly, according to prosecutors.On Saturday afternoon, Gibson reportedly attempted to bring his own alcohol to the event and repeatedly climbed over the fence surrounding the event after organizers removed him, prosecutors say.According to prosecutors, Gibson allegedly threatened to "shoot every person in there" or "shoot the place up" while reaching into his backpack.Police recovered a knife and several containers of alcohol from the backpack, prosecutors say."There is no such thing as an 'idle threat' of mass violence," McDonald said. "A community gathered to enjoy music and celebrate the reopening of a local business has a right to safety. The defendant's alleged actions, while intoxicated and carrying a weapon, could have caused a panic and endangered everyone at this event."False report or threat of terrorism is a felony punishable by up to 20 years in prison, a $20,000 fine or both.

title: Man charged with holding woman's head underwater in koi pond at Old Orchard shopping center
description: Man charged with holding woman's head underwater at Old Orchard
content: A man was charged with attempted murder and other felonies Wednesday after police said he attacked a woman and held her head underwater in a pond at Westfield Old Orchard shopping center in Skokie, Illinois, the day before.William Dobbs, 35, of Skokie, was charged with one count each of attempted murder, aggravated battery to a senior citizen, and aggravated battery with great bodily harm.He was to appear Wednesday for a detention hearing at the Skokie Cook County Courthouse.Skokie police said shortly after 11 a.m. Tuesday, officers responded to reports of an attempted robbery at the shopping center. Police said a man hit a woman he didn't know with a bag before pushing her into the koi pond on the north end of the mall.Witnesses intervened and separated the pair before officers arrived.One witness who didn't want to be identified said she saw the woman completely submerged in the water while the man had her in a headlock."We thought he was just swimming by himself until we came closer and saw a woman underneath the water," she said.The woman was taken to the hospital to be treated for injuries from the attack.The woman's age has not been specified, but the charges imply she was a senior citizen.

title: Stockton City Council votes to remove Jason Lee as vice mayor
description: Before the vice mayor vote, a substitute motion that would have allowed Lee to resign from the position instead was considered. Lee supported the motion, but it failed in a 4-3 vote.
content: The Stockton City Council voted to remove Jason Lee as vice mayor and from the city's Audit Committee, escalating a dispute over his leadership role amid ongoing tensions at city hall.The council voted 4-2 to remove Lee as vice mayor. Lee did not vote on that measure.A separate vote removed Lee from the Audit Committee by a 6-1 margin, with Lee casting the only opposing vote.Before the vice mayor vote, a substitute motion that would have allowed Lee to resign from the position instead was considered. Lee supported the motion, but it failed in a 4-3 vote.The decisions come amid months of friction between Lee, Mayor Christina Fugazi and other council members over leadership, committee assignments and the conduct of city business.The council's internal conflicts have also drawn scrutiny from a civil grand jury, which criticized the body over infighting, treatment of staff and allowing political disputes to interfere with city business.In recent weeks, the city largely agreed with findings that public feuds among council members erode public trust and distract from the council's responsibilities."At last night's meeting, I offered my resignation as Vice Mayor to avoid spending final weeks over political theater while Stockton has real issues in front of it. The council continued political chaos despite the grand jury's recommendation to turn down political turmoil," Lee said in a statement released through a PR firm on Wednesday. "While the Council spent hours on a title, two young people in our city committed suicide last week and we are coming up on a year of the mass shooting in our city. We need to keep our focus on the safety of our community, not on political attacks." During the discussion, Lee questioned why council members were seeking to change his committee assignments and remove his vice mayor title. Fugazi said the changes were within her authority and emphasized that the decision was not personal.Lee also questioned whether the city had the legal authority to remove him from the vice mayor position.Ahead of the meeting, Lee released the following statement: "The Council unanimously ratified my appointment as Vice Mayor through December 31, 2026, as the City Charter provides. The City's own staff report acknowledges that its reconsideration procedures do not, on their own, authorize removing a sitting Vice Mayor.Before the Council acts, I'm asking the City Attorney to identify in writing the legal authority for these items. It's a simple question, and residents deserve a clear answer.With less than three months left in this term, our time is better spent implementing the Civil Grand Jury's recommendations and cooperating fully with the State Controller's audit. My commitment to District 6 has never depended on a title, and I'll keep doing the work."The dispute follows a series of controversies involving Lee, including clashes with local leaders and law enforcement over records handling, heated exchanges with the mayor and other council members, and scrutiny over city payments for a comedy show featuring Lee.He has also accused the city of silencing him after he was blocked from attending meetings remotely.Councilmember Michelle Padilla called the vice mayor agenda item a "charade" and criticized the actions as bullying."I am sick of being bullied, and the employees and the departments of Stockton are sick of being bullied as well," she said.The votes remove Lee from the vice mayor role and the Audit Committee. The votes did not affect his status as a member of the Stockton City Council."I remain the Councilmember for District 6, with a full vote on this Council, and my commitment to the residents who elected me hasn't changed," Lee said Wednesday. "I'll keep pushing for the Grand Jury's good governance and full cooperation with the State Controller's current audit, and the investments our neighborhoods need, prioritizing the people of Stockton over politics."

title: Man convicted of 2020 attempted murder of Sacramento police officers
description: A jury convicted Malcolm Wilcox of multiple counts, including the attempted murder of two Sacramento police officers.
content: A jury convicted a man on Oct. 13 of multiple counts, including the attempted murder of two Sacramento Police Department officers, prosecutors said. The Sacramento County District Attorney's Office said the convictions stem from an incident that happened on April 11, 2020, where a police officer attempted to pull over Malcolm Wilcox, who had a warrant for attempted murder in Yuba County. Wilcox initially fled from the officer at high speeds before he abruptly stopped, exited his vehicle and began firing shots at the officer with a semi-automatic firearm, according to prosecutors.Another officer arrived at the scene and both officers shot Wilcox, who continued to shoot at the officers until he ran out of ammunition and surrendered.Wilcox's sentencing is scheduled for Nov. 13, 2026. At this hearing, an allegation regarding a prior strike for first-degree burglary will be determined. He is facing up to 74 years to life in prison.

title: Armed suspect at Dallas motel fatally shoots self during police encounter, officers say
description: The department said no officers were injured in the incident.
author_name: Matthew  Ablon, Steve  Pickett, Giles  Hudson
content: An investigation is underway after the Dallas Police Department said a shooting involving an officer ended with an armed suspect dead after reportedly turning the gun on himself on Wednesday afternoon.Initial details were limited, but in a post on X, the department said officers were confronted by an armed suspect at the Mustang Inn along the 400 block of South RL Thornton Freeway, just off I-35E. Dallas Police initially said the suspect was struck after officers opened fire, though new details emerged during a news briefing around 2 p.m.Executive Assistant Chief Terrence Rhodes said the suspect, identified only as a man in his mid-30s, had multiple warrants out for narcotics and parole violations. Officers, Rhodes said, used Flock technology to track him down. When they arrived, Rhodes said officers encountered the man armed with a long rifle and ordered him to stand down. Rhodes noted one officer fired a weapon at the man, but it's not known now if that shot hit the suspect.After that, Rhodes said the suspect produced another gun and fatally shot himself.The department also said no officers were hurt. It is unclear if the suspect fired at officers during the encounter.The investigation remains ongoing. CBS News Texas will update this article as new details are shared.

title: The songs of Patsy Cline come alive at the Lone Tree Arts Center
description: Lone Tree Arts Center is putting on "Always... Patsy Cline," a memory play about the friendship between the country superstar and one of her fans.
content: "Always...Patsy Cline" is heartfelt celebration of one of the most influential singers of the 20th century as well as a powerful story about friendship. A new production of the musical is on stage at the Lone Tree Arts Center proving that Patsy Cline is as powerful today as she was at the height of her career. The show follows the memories of Louise Seger as she falls in love with Cline's voice on the radio, then meets her in person, and the friendship that is born out of that one meeting. "She was an ordinary person...Louise, and here's this extraordinary star who just kind of falls into her life with this brief encounter. And, they maintained a friendship until the end of Patsy Cline's life," said Emma Messenger, who plays Louise Steger in Lone Tree Arts Center's production. Seger tells her story through the iconic music catalog of Patsy Cline, who was one of the most popular female country singers in recording history. Playing Patsy Cline in this musical is no easy feat. "It's a huge responsibility and also an absolute blast," said Adriane Leigh Robinson, who plays Patsy Cline. Robinson sings 26 songs throughout the show including all the hits as well as a couple of deep tracks. "I live in kind of the same register that she does. She's this rich, warm alto, so individually no, the songs are not difficult, but when you squeeze them all together in 2-and-a-half-hours," Robinson said. Kelly Van Oosbree directs the show. She wants audiences to understand how grounded Patsy Cline was in the face of extraordinary fame. "My favorite moment between the two of them is when they meet for the first time and the reaction that Louise has to meeting her idol," Van Oosbree told CBS Colorado. "She had that seminal iconic voice that people recognize and probably will for the test of time."While Patsy Cline's music may be the draw for this production, audiences will leave "Always...Patsy Cline" with a wonderful message about friendship.LINK: For Tickets & Information for "Always...Patsy Cline" at the Lone Tree Arts Center"Always...Patsy Cline" is running from October 8 - 25, 2026 at the Lone Tree Arts Center.

title: Affordability, immigration and Iran war shape race for Florida's 26th Congressional District
description: Republican incumbent Mario Diaz-Balart faces Democrat Nicole Locklin and independent candidate Deborah Ann Meidinger Hosey in Florida's 26th District.
content: From the rising cost of living to immigration and the war with Iran, voters across South Florida's 26th Congressional District have several issues to consider as they prepare to head to the polls in for the 2026 midterms in November.Longtime Republican Rep. Mario Diaz-Balart faces two challengers. They are Democrat Nicole Locklin, and no-party-affiliation candidate Deborah Ann Meidinger Hosey.The district includes portions of northwest Miami-Dade and southwest Broward counties, including communities near Hialeah, Miami Lakes and Doral.CBS News Miami spoke with all three candidates and voters across the district about the issues shaping the race.Affordability is at top of mind for many in South Florida"Affordability of anything, everything is so expensive, gas up to five dollar, groceries up the roof," said district voter Luzmar Fernandez.Each candidate is offering a different approach to bringing those costs down.Diaz-Balart has represented South Florida in Congress for more than two decades. He won reelection in 2024 by nearly 42 percentage points, but the district has since been redrawn, dropping Collier County and adding portions of southwest Broward County.The Republican incumbent is campaigning on his record in Washington, D.C., including efforts to cut federal spending."Because I get things done, whether it's cutting waste, and I have a record of cutting waste," Diaz-Balart said, pointing to $12 billion in spending cuts through a congressional subcommittee he chairs.On affordability, Diaz-Balart highlights recently passed federal tax breaks for tipped workers and seniors.Locklin says the district needs a new option. The attorney, who moved to South Florida from California, says her own experience shapes her views on policy. "I would say that I am bringing the experience of real life as a successful professional who is still struggling despite being better off than most people," Locklin said.She supports lowering tariffs and shifting more of the tax burden to billionaires and large corporations.Hosey, who is running without a party affiliation, says voters deserve an alternative to the two major parties."So it's not a matter of join the red team, join the blue team. Let's take a look at the purple team and see if we can focus on what the problem is, and let's bring the solution forward," she said.Hosey said her experience in education and local government work involving seniors has convinced her that Congress needs to prioritize programs aimed at reducing the cost of housing, food, utilities and child care.Fuel prices another concern among voters"Gas, too much," said Khani Lozier, who estimates he spends about $100 filling up his vehicle every three days.All three candidates link higher fuel costs to the war with Iran, but disagree on what should happen next.Locklin wants an immediate end to the war.Diaz-Balart said U.S. military action was necessary to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. He also supports increasing domestic energy production and refining capacity.Hosey wants Congress to debate the war and supports additional negotiations with U.S. allies.Immigration is another major issue in a district that includes communities with large immigrant populations. Recent U.S. Census data shows more than 70% of residents in both Doral and Hialeah are foreign-born."I feel bad for a lot people who are scared to go out, especially in Doral, the Venezuelans, and just stay home," said district voter Ramon Alonzo.Diaz-Balart says securing the border was necessary but describes some of the immigration enforcement that followed as an "overreaction."He supports legislation that would allow undocumented immigrants from certain countries to have their cases reviewed individually.Locklin wants to abolish U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), expand legal pathways to immigration and hire more immigration judges.Hosey said her experience in education and local government work involving seniors has convinced her that Congress needs to prioritize programs aimed at reducing the cost of housing, food, utilities and childcare.Despite their different proposals, the candidates are competing for the support of voters who say they want meaningful relief from the financial pressures affecting their daily lives.For Fernandez, the priority is straightforward. She says whoever represents the district in Washington should help make life more affordable."Give us a way to actually live and not just survive," she said.Voters will decide who represents Florida's 26th Congressional District in the Nov. 3rd general election.

title: Don Mattingly staying on as Philadelphia Phillies' manager, losing "interim" title
description: Don Mattingly will stay on as the Phillies manager and lose his "interim" title for the upcoming season, according to the team.
content: Don Mattingly is staying on as the Philadelphia Phillies' manager for at least the next two seasons, and the team has dropped his "interim" tag.Phillies president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski made the announcement Wednesday morning, confirming earlier reports. He said Mattingly has signed a two-year deal.Mattingly, lovingly referred to as "Donnie Baseball," is the father of Phillies vice president and general manager Preston Mattingly and has 12 seasons as an MLB manager under his belt between the Dodgers and Marlins.Taking over after a disastrous start to the 2026 season, the Phils went 79-55 under Mattingly and made the postseason on the last day of the regular season.He was previously serving as the team's bench coach before the team fired manager Rob Thomson. Mattingly was under contract as the club's bench coach for 2027 before signing on as full-time manager.Mattingly, 65, will take the reins ahead of the 2027 season, which could be at risk of being delayed or shortened pending negotiations of MLB's collective bargaining agreement, CBS Sports reports.The Phillies are looking to turn around their fortunes and advance further into the MLB postseason with their highly paid — and aging — core of stars. The Fightins were eliminated by the Braves in the National League Wild Card Series on Oct. 1. Earlier this month, Alex Cora reportedly turned down Dave Dombrowski's offer to become the Phillies' manager. Cora was initially offered the job in April after he was let go by the Red Sox, with the Phillies position open following Thomson's firing.The news was first reported by The Athletic.

title: Triple shooting in Mesquite family dispute leaves 2 teens dead, man wounded, police say
description: The investigation is still active.
content: The Mesquite Police Department is investigating after a triple shooting overnight left two teens dead and a man in the hospital.Officers said they responded to a reported shooting along the 2200 block of Amber Springs Drive just after midnight, though the department notes it was reported earlier that it unfolded along the 2800 block of Clearwater Drive. When officers arrived, they said they found two 18-year-old residents suffering from gunshot wounds. Lifesaving measures were attempted at the scene before both were taken to a Dallas-area hospital. The department said both victims died of their injuries.Mesquite Police said a third person, identified as a 20-year-old man, arrived separately at a nearby emergency room, also suffering from gunshot wounds. Investigators said they believe he is tied to the shooting. His injuries were deemed non-life-threatening, and police said he is being taken to a Dallas-area hospital for further treatment.The department said all three victims are in the same family and that an argument over a haircut escalated into a physical altercation, during which police said guns were drawn and shots were fired.As of publication, nobody involved has been publicly identified, including the victims who died. Mesquite Police have promised to share more information as it becomes available.

title: Climate change pushed Earth to its limits in 2026 as certain "vital signs" reach record extremes, report says
description: Climate change has pushed the planet's environmental systems "deeper into uncharted territory," researchers said in a new report centered on the state of Earth's climate in 2026.
content: Climate change pushed the Earth's environmental system to, and perhaps beyond, its limits in 2026, as several of its "vital signs" reached record extremes, researchers said in a new report on the state of the global climate. Of the 16 climate markers that researchers consider integral measures of how the Earth is doing, seven are currently at record extremes, while multiple others show evidence of accelerating or abruptly shifting, the report published Wednesday in the peer-reviewed journal BioScience said.The markers include greenhouse gases, temperature, glacier mass, oceans, wildfires and the planet's energy imbalance, which refers to the difference between the amount of energy the Earth absorbs and the amount it radiates back out into the atmosphere.Researchers warned in the report that the planet's climate "is moving deeper into uncharted territory.""Earth's life-support systems are being pushed beyond stable limits, with changes unfolding faster than our ability to respond," the report said. "Across the globe, extreme heat, floods, droughts, storms, and wildfires are no longer rare events but defining features of a changing planet."A record yearJuly 2026 broke records as the warmest month ever for the contiguous United States, while the country as a whole was experiencing what turned out to be the hottest summer it had ever seen. Globally, ocean temperatures also reached new heights in July, the report said, while data show that carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere are higher now than at any other time in the last 2 million years. Heat waves scorched Europe, killing an estimated 14,000, and baked portions of the U.S., too, fueling wildfires that burned millions of acres of land.Climate change appears to be accelerating, and its effects are becoming more intense, the researchers warned. They noted that the patterns they'd observed while compiling the report had raised concerns about their potential to cross a point of no return, one at which their impacts on various ecosystems would be irreversible. In 2025, coral reefs became the first environmental system on Earth to reach a climate "tipping point," with researchers saying the damage could be permanent.Global warming is happening more quickly now than it was a few decades ago, according to the new climate report, which said the rate of warming has sped up, increasing from roughly 0.05 degrees Celsius per decade between 1880 and 1970, to 0.19 degrees Celsius per decade between 1970 and 2010, and 0.36 degrees Celsius per decade between 2010 and 2024."Rapid destabilization"Faster warming increases the likelihood of crossing tipping points from which different environments can't bounce back, and it also risks destabilizing the delicate balance between them, researchers said.For example, greenhouse gas emissions from melting permafrost, wildfires, or other natural sources, which are all triggered by the temperatures associated with global warming, could essentially become a cycle that fuels itself. Amplified sea ice loss, ecosystem degradation and carbon emissions could also begin to create their own self-perpetuating feedback loop — the crux of the "hothouse" climate trajectory, where various tipping points act as catalysts that push global warming far past humans' control."We are witnessing the rapid destabilization of the Earth's climate system," the researchers said. "This is no longer a warning for the future; it is a diagnosis of the present."However, the report noted that worsening trends in fossil fuel combustion and other emissions, the main drivers of the extreme changes it centers on, have been accompanied by positive shifts in renewable energy use. But the researchers emphasized that any progress seen so far "remains far below the scale and speed needed to stabilize Earth's climate system.""Rapid reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, effective adaptation, ecosystem protection, and transformative societal change remain essential to reducing climate risks and securing a more resilient and sustainable future," they said.

title: Watchdog says PFAS found in 100% of Minnesota water testing sites
description: Minnesota's chapter of the Environment America Research and Policy Center​ says all of the 91 waterways across the state it tested for PFAS came back positive for some level of contamination.
content: Minnesota's chapter of the Environment America Research and Policy Center says all of the 91 waterways across the state it tested for PFAS came back positive for some level of contamination.Experts say forever chemicals can have a major impact on your health, compromising immunity, decreasing fertility, causing developmental delays in children and increasing the risk of certain kinds of cancers. "As one of the nation's longest rivers, the Mississippi supports a number of complex ecosystems across Minnesota, providing habitats for bass and catfish, mammals like otters, beavers and muskrats and countless other animals," Rolfes said. "We shouldn't have to worry about tainted drinking water or catching and eating contaminated fish." Rolfes says a lot of the PFAS discharge comes from sewage sludge on farm lands, but also the 3M facility in Hastings."These results are likely just the tip of the toxic iceberg since sources we used may not include all PFAS data in Minnesota," she said. Experts say they are especially concerned about the areas that are contaminated even when there's no clear source of forever chemicals. In 2024, 3M agreed to a country-wide, multi-billion-dollar settlement over PFAS-related water pollution. Kris Hansen, a former 3M employee, told WCCO that same year the Maplewood-based company knew about the dangers caused by PFAS as far back as 1975. 3M only moved to discontinue PFAS manufacturing in 2022, ceasing all usage of the forever chemical just last year.

title: New Jersey officials identify man fatally shot by police in Middle Township, New Jersey, last month
description: Andre Moore was armed with a knife when he was shot and killed by police in Rio Grande, New Jersey, the attorney general's office said.
content: Officials in New Jersey are sharing more about a man who was shot and killed by police in Cape May County in September. Middle Township police officers encountered a disabled vehicle at the intersection of Route 9 and Satt Boulevard in Rio Grande around 10:20 a.m. on Sept. 25, New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport's office said. Officers had previously tried to stop the car but were not successful. As officers approached the car at the intersection near the Walmart Supercenter, they heard a woman screaming, according to an update from the AG's office released Wednesday.Inside the car, police found a man whom the AG's office identified as 37-year-old Andre Moore, of Cape May Court House. Moore was allegedly holding a knife to the woman, the attorney general's office said. Middle Township officers Christopher Rudy and Ty Pettit discharged their firearms, striking Moore, who was pronounced dead at the scene, according to the attorney general. The woman was taken to an area hospital for treatment for multiple stab wounds.The attorney general's office is investigating the shooting as required by state law.

title: Human DNA found at Olney "house of horrors" in Philadelphia after investigators used luminol to search home, sources say
description: Human DNA was found at the Olney "house of horrors" in Philadelphia after investigators used luminol to search the home on West Chew Avenue, police sources said Tuesday.
content: Human DNA was found at the Olney "house of horrors" in Philadelphia after investigators sprayed luminol to search the home on West Chew Avenue, police sources said Tuesday. Philadelphia police and the FBI were back at the home Monday night, using luminol to search for signs of human blood. Police sources said Tuesday the human DNA found at the Olney house will be tested further. It was found in several locations of the residence at the center of a massive investigation, according to police sources. On Tuesday, police are digging up the backyard of the Olney home with heavy equipment to search for human remains. Roughly a dozen agents from Quantico, Virginia, and Philadelphia homicide detectives are processing the home and surrounding the property. The agents are removing each layer of soil in the backyard and treating it as if it were a mass grave. The front yard is set to be excavated Wednesday. The home, which was owned by Raymond "R.C." Horsch until he died in 2025, and his son, Eugene Horsch, is linked to as many as seven missing women. Five of them are presumed dead. So far, no human remains have been found. Investigators tore down a shed in the backyard Tuesday so that they could dig beneath it. They found numerous animal carcasses in that area of the property. What is luminol? Retired FBI supervisor Richard Marx said luminol is a "presumptive test for blood."Marx oversaw evidence recovery in some of the most complicated federal investigations, including Pulse nightclub and the World Trade Center."When sprayed on trace amounts of what is believed to be blood, it gives off a very faint luminescence, a blue light," Marx said. "It has to be relatively dark in the room to see the light because it's a very faint chemical reaction."Olney "house of horrors" investigation ramps upThe investigation into the Olney "house of horrors" has ramped up over the last week as law enforcement continues to search for signs of foul play and any human remains. Investigators have been coming and going from the Horsch home for months. Recently, the investigation has taken up the 400 block of West Chew Avenue as police dismantle the home. Police sources say they've recovered valuable evidence inside.Last week, investigators used K-9s trained to detect hidden thumb drives and file-storage drives and cards, and to smell oils on those devices, even when they're hidden. A source close to the investigation told CBS News Philadelphia the basement was broken into a number of rooms and resembled an old high school science lab. A 55-gallon drum was removed from the basement months ago, shortly after the investigation began, along with a couple of dozen containers that police said were filled with an oily, sludge-like material.Investigators removed two clogged sewer laterals from the property in July, sources said. The sewer laterals connected the home to the main sewer line. One of the pipes was abandoned and out of service due to clogging. Sources did not speculate on what the pipes could contain, but both were taken to a lab for extensive testing.Investigators continue to search for evidence to corroborate some of the disturbing content they say they've recovered from reviewing a fraction of the 1 million pieces of photographic and video evidence taken from 417 Chew Ave.Who are Raymond and Eugene Horsch? Raymond Horsch lived at the home on West Chew Avenue until he died in 2025. Law enforcement sources say Raymond Horsch is considered a "suspected serial killer." He created dark pornographic films, self-published several books and referred to himself as an empathetic serial killer. CBS News Philadelphia reviewed hundreds of pages of books that Horsch wrote and published, which have since been yanked from Amazon. Much of the material is graphic, disturbing, sexually explicit and violent.In one book, Horsch claims he murdered a woman and disposed of her body through a chemical process.The investigation into the Olney house started after Raymond's son, Eugene Horsch, was arrested following a traffic stop in June at 6th and Market streets. He was pulled over after a nearby park ranger heard a woman say to him, "You're going to hurt me." Inside Eugene Horsch's vehicle, police found crack cocaine and guns — a .40 caliber and .38 Special, according to court documents. He also had fake Drug Enforcement Administration credentials in the trunk of his car. The woman with Eugene Horsch had Blair Tonzelli's identification on her. Sources and investigators have since said that set off alarms because Tonzelli was reported missing in 2023. Eugene Horsch remains locked up on drug and weapons charges, pending a federal trial. His attorney has declined to talk about the case or comment on whether Eugene has spoken with investigators.Missing women linked to Olney "house of horrors"Seven missing women, including five who are presumed dead, are linked to the Olney "house of horrors." Two more women known to frequent the home haven't been seen in years. Nicole Fusaro, Maribel Fresses, Gabrielle Amarando, Amy McHale and Tonzelli have ties to the home. Fusaro has been missing since 2018. In August, police said in a news conference that they recovered "graphic and dark" evidence that Fresses and Amarando are presumed dead. Fresses was last seen in February 2018, and Amarando has been missing since September 2012. The Olney home is the last known location of McHale, who was previously married to Raymond Horsch and disappeared in 2016.

title: Michael Penix Jr. "feeling better" after rib injury, expected to start Falcons-Bears game
description: Michael Penix Jr. is feeling better after injuring his ribs against Baltimore, and the Atlanta Falcons expect him to start Sunday against the Chicago Bears if his recovery goes as planned.
content: Michael Penix Jr. is feeling better after injuring his ribs against Baltimore, and the Atlanta Falcons expect him to start Sunday against the Chicago Bears if his recovery goes as planned.Coach Kevin Stefanski said Wednesday that Penix would practice on a limited basis, with his workload determined by how he feels."Yes, as long as everything goes according to plan," Stefanski said when asked whether Penix would start Sunday.Stefanski declined to discuss the specifics of the rib injury."With any injury like this, you want to make sure, as they move around, how they're feeling," he said. "It could be all, some, none. We shall see."Penix was injured on a sack by Baltimore's Tavius Robinson with about 19 seconds left in regulation Sunday night. He missed one play, briefly returned and threw an incomplete pass, but did not play in overtime.Tua Tagovailoa replaced him for the extra period. After Baltimore scored a touchdown on its opening possession, Tagovailoa threw an interception that sealed the Falcons' 30-23 loss.Stefanski also said defensive end Za'Darius Smith is working his way back from a neck injury. Cornerback C.J. Henderson would not practice Wednesday but is improving, the coach said. Both will be evaluated as the week progresses.Atlanta is preparing to host a Bears team that Stefanski described as talented and well coached."It's a huge challenge for our football team," he said.

title: How technology is changing the detection of breast cancer
description: Dr. Rachel Brem tells Norah O'Donnell how AI is helping detect breast cancer earlier, and what younger women need to know about starting mammograms.
content: Dr. Rachel Brem decided at age 12 that she wanted to cure cancer after her mom was diagnosed with breast cancer. It was early detection that led to her mother living way past her prognosis of six months. Now, Brem is working to improve breast cancer screening for all women.Brem is a board-certified diagnostic radiologist and director of Breast Imaging and Intervention at George Washington University. She created the Brem Foundation to help prevent breast cancer from taking more lives. On this week's episode of "Healthful," she discussed the innovation that makes her hopeful.Artificial intelligence and breast imaging"AI is going to change everything in medicine, and certainly breast cancer detection," Brem said.In addition to her work with George Washington University's Breast Imaging and Intervention unit, Brem collaborates with ScreenPoint Medical to develop Transpara, an AI breast cancer screening software.Already there is significant scientific research showing mammograms paired with AI evaluations "can find cancer up to five years earlier," she said, by detecting warning signs in women that might be missed with just mammograms alone. The software can also predict future risk of breast cancer even when none is detected in a mammogram."Imagine what the impact of that is going to be on survival therapy," Brem said.If women begin getting screened at age 35 with AI-enhanced readings, she noted the software will constantly teach itself how to improve in detecting breast cancer with each analysis. That's younger than the starting age recommended by several major medical organizations.At George Washington University, Brem said, "we've been using AI for over four years in every mammogram," adding that using the software does not cost extra.The FDA has cleared some AI technology to predict risk of or detect breast cancer. However, nationwide, just 20% of practices use AI with their mammogram procedures. Often, the AI readings cost extra, which may make the option inaccessible for some."There is nothing you can do to absolutely prevent breast cancer," Brem acknowledged.But she said, "One of the things AI can do is really equalize the inequalities," referring to the racial disparities that affect diagnosis and treatment for many women."Black women die at a 40% higher rate [from breast cancer] than White women," Brem noted, and women with fewer resources have less access to mammograms. Brem wants to change this with her foundation, which for the past 20 years has championed early detection through innovative screening, increased education and awareness, and equitable access."I look forward to the more wide-reaching implementation of AI to help not only find more cancers, but with healthcare," she said.A breast cancer breath test?Brem is helping to develop a breath test that could detect breast cancer. Diseased tissues give off a chemical compound that becomes gas and, scientists believe, could be used as a noninvasive way to assess who needs further screening. These tests are still in the experimental and clinical trial phases. They are not cleared by the FDA for screening. "It's not available yet, but I'm really excited about having no pain, no compression, and no injection way of diagnosing if you're accurately diagnosed," Brem said. And there's hope it could someday help beyond breast cancer. "The next step on our roadmap is not just breast cancer but a women's health panel where you could do one breath and get all these tests done," Brem said. The current state of breast cancer screeningThe guidelines from the American College of Physicians stated in 2026 that women over the age of 50 should get a mammogram every other year. The United States Preventive Services Task Force recommends that women should start screening every other year at the age of 40. To Brem, "This is a travesty.""Women will die if they listen to that."From her research, women should get checked for breast cancer annually starting at the age of 40. For those with a history of breast cancer in their family, they should start at 35.This is all easier said than done. Women often cite anxiety as a reason they delay or skip getting screened. The thought of receiving a positive test result understandably makes women nervous, but as Brem notes, "We don't get rid of the disease by not knowing we have it."Early detection of breast cancer leads to significantly better outcomes compared to cases where breast cancer is found in its later stages. "Ninety-nine percent of women with early breast cancer survive and thrive," Brem said, but this outcome can only be possible if women screen for it early and regularly.In addition to the recommended mammograms, Brem also believes "you absolutely, unequivocally definitely need more exams" if you have dense breasts. Half of women have dense breasts, and mammograms might not be able to pick up potentially deadly tumors hiding behind the tissue. Ultrasounds, MRIs or contrast-enhanced mammograms are necessary for those with dense breasts to get a complete view of their risks.Supplemental screening isn't always standard with some doctors. Brem advised that it is "really important" for women to insist that their doctors order these extra exams. The mammograms are not enough.Demand more, get educated, and "be badass"Brem is adamant in her belief that women can be proactive now to better their health and improve their breast cancer outcomes. If you have dense breasts, demand additional screening. For those under 40 who think they have time until they need to start screening for breast cancer, think again."You're not too young to have breast cancer," Brem warns.Having the conversation now about your plan for breast cancer screenings and seeking out additional exams is essential in early detection and better prognosis. "If you find it early, even if you're young, it's curable," Brem said.Rates of cancer are rising in younger women and awareness is the first step to being proactive about your health. Her foundation provides resources to educate women. But what do you do with this information? Brem urges you to advocate for yourself at the doctor's office."We tell women to be badass," she said. "You need to advocate for yourself. It is a fundamental principle. It's your right. It's what you deserve, and it's not a maybe."

title: Netflix is cutting 6% of its workforce as its revenue growth slows
description: The layoffs will affect the company's product, tech, legal and HR teams, Netflix leaders said in a memo to employees.
content: Netflix said it is laying off roughly 6% of its workforce, according to a memo to employees obtained by CBS News.The cuts will impact the company's product, technology, legal and human resources departments, Netflix co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters wrote in the memo. "Our business is strong and growing, and we remain on track to deliver our full-year forecast," Sarandos and Peters said. "We'll continue to invest aggressively in high-impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation. Doing that means making focused choices across the business so we can keep delivering for our members, partners, employees, and investors."Netflix declined further comment on the planned layoffs.The news was first reported by the Wall Street Journal. The news outlet said Netflix's job cuts will impact roughly 1,000 positions globally, the company's largest workforce reduction since 2022.Netflix had roughly 16,000 full-time employees as of December 2025, according to a securities filing.Netflix remains profitable. In its second financial quarter, the company earned $3.4 billion on revenue of nearly $12.6 billion, up 9% and 13%, respectively, from the year-ago period. S&P Global estimates that Netflix had 327.7 million subscribers at the end of last year, up 8.6% from a year earlier.Yet Netflix's growth has slowed in recent years amid mounting competition from other streaming platforms and a saturated North American market. Netflix shares, which traded at just below $70 each on Wednesday, have fallen nearly 43% over the last 12 months. The company is scheduled to release its next earnings report on Oct. 20.

title: Man accused of pushing woman, baby from 15th-floor Bronx balcony arraigned
description: Angel Carrasco, 31, was arraigned Wednesday after police said he pushed his 23-year-old ex-girlfriend and their baby off a balcony in the Bronx last week.
content: The man accused of pushing a woman and her baby off a Bronx balcony was arraigned on Wednesday.Police say Angel Carrasco, 31, pushed Nathaly Ramirez, 23, off a 15th-floor balcony as she was holding on to their 8-month-old daughter. Ramirez was killed, and her baby was seriously injured.Carrasco allegedly ran from the scene but was eventually found at a home after a close acquaintance alerted authorities.For several days, he has been undergoing evaluations at hospital, which is where he was arraigned from via video on charges of murder, attempted murder and assault.Carrasco did not enter a plea Wednesday. His next court date is scheduled for Nov. 4.The alleged crime has left the neighborhood shocked, hurt and outraged.Many came to mourn at candlelight vigils, remembering the young mother and shining a light on domestic violence.According to police sources, the couple had a domestic-related history with police, and neighbors reported hearing screams and desperate pleas from Ramirez's apartment before the deadly push.Friends and family of Ramirez had been frustrated over how long it took Carrasco to face a judge. They say the wait for justice was adding to their pain.

title: Testing of voting machines underway in Miami-Dade ahead of start of early voting Monday
description: Miami-Dade Supervisor of Elections Alina Garcia said security measures are in place to ensure the safety of votes.
content: We're only a few weeks away from the midterm elections, and on Wednesday, officials were busy testing voting machines to make sure there are no issues when voters head to the polls to begin early voting next week.So, how do you make sure your vote counts in the upcoming Florida midterm election?CBS News Miami got a behind-the-scenes look at how the process works in Miami-Dade County.Crews spotted workers putting ballots through a percentage of the machines that will be used during the election to make sure the machines not only accurately count the total amount of ballots, but the ballots that were used on Wednesday had a pre-determined outcome.Security measures in place to ensure election safety"The logic and accuracy test, it's mandated by the state of Florida," Miami-Dade Supervisor of Elections Alina Garcia said. "It's part of law, and we do this."She said the state of Florida goes above and beyond."There's a lot of security measures that we do take," she said. "For example: the vote-by-mail ballots. In order to receive a vote by mail ballot, you have to request it. We ask for information to ensure that it's you. Once we receive that ballot, we check the signature to ensure that it is you. So we do a lot of things that other states do not do."And she said that voters should feel confident that their vote counts."I just want to reiterate that we're not connected to the internet, and there's no way of hacking our system because we are not connected to the internet," Garcia said.How to vote early in the Florida midterm election"So there's three ways of voting," she said. "You can vote-by-mail, you can vote early, or you can vote on Election Day. There's no excuse, so please vote."And Garcia wants to emphasize that Election Day is the last day to vote."You can vote-by-mail. You would need to request your vote by mail ballot before the 22nd of October. That is the last day to request your vote by mail ballot. You can also vote early voting, which commences next next Monday, the 19th, until the 1st of November. We will be open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. And of course, the last day to vote is on Election Day."

title: Miracle League of South Fulton builds confidence and friendships, one swing at a time
description: At the Miracle League of South Fulton, children and adults with disabilities get a turn at bat and a place to belong.
content: On Saturdays, the gym at Burdett Park Recreation Center becomes a ballpark, filled with the crack of the bat, family cheers, and players heading home.There are no balls, strikes, or scores to keep. At the Miracle League of South Fulton, children and adults with disabilities get a turn at bat and a place to belong."This is a place for our players to be themselves. If they stim, if they yell, if they roll on the floor, it's safe for them," executive board member Karen Nunnally said. For families, what happens between the bases can make a difference long after the game ends.Karla Hood's son, Cairo, started last season in tears. Now in his second season with the league, he has had a complete turnaround. He loves to play and cheer on his teammates. "Even though he has a difference, he still gets to be a part and be accepted for who he is," Hood said.Dana Brown's son is just beginning his time with the league. His first game brought a sense of accomplishment for both mother and son."It's a sense of pride, and it makes me happy because it makes him happy and he's getting used to playing recreational sports," Brown said.Volunteers, known as Angels in the Outfield, help players take swings and round the bases. For Forest Park High School student Natasha Mata, being there is something to look forward to. "This is one of my favorite Saturdays if I'm being honest," she said.Friends and teammates Carl Mumford and Jalen Johnson bring big swings and a little friendly competition."This kid - he tried to destroy me in baseball because he made a bunch of home runs, but my home runs was better," Carl said of his friend. For Johnson, the friendships are part of what makes the league special."It's important because we meet each other and play," he said.Interim League President Dr. Ronald Tolbert sees those connections as an essential part of the experience. He has been part of the league with his son Moses since the beginning. "Moses has developed friends for life," Tolbert said.Beyond the game, Tolbert said the league gives players opportunities to practice social skills and grow more comfortable around others."He needs to experience social events that will help him develop good manners, good appropriate behaviors, and that's part of what we're trying to teach these kids."The league is also working toward a new goal: raising money for a field and playground of its own, with equipment designed to meet players' physical and sensory needs.Nunnally said that requires more than a traditional accessible space. Plans include equipment that accommodates wheelchairs and sensory features for players who need movement or tactile experiences."People think a Miracle League field and an ADA field is the same thing. It absolutely is not," she said.While that goal is still ahead, Tolbert said the growth happening inside the gym is already clear."A lot of these kids were very shy when they came here. Now you're looking at kids that are outgoing, have more confidence in themselves, and not afraid to show up and show out," he said."They just need an outlet where they can enjoy themselves, where they can make friends, where they can be free and do things that they are meant to do."For Miracle League players and families, every Saturday offers another chance at bat. And every time they round the bases, someone is cheering them home.You can learn more about the Miracle League of South Fulton on their website.

title: How a $6,500 Zelle scam targeting a Florida couple led investigators to a Georgia woman
description: A Georgia woman was arrested after authorities said a Florida Keys couple lost $6,500 in a Zelle scam involving callers posing as law enforcement officials.
content: A Georgia woman has been arrested after authorities said she was involved in a scam in which a couple in the Florida Keys was tricked into paying $6,500 to people posing as law enforcement officials.Johnay Monique Barnett, 37, of Roswell, Georgia, was charged with grand theft and booked into the Monroe County jail on Tuesday, according to the Monroe County Sheriff's Office.The investigation began in December 2025, when a couple in Key Haven, near Key West, reported receiving calls from people claiming to work for the Seminole County jail. Seminole County is located in the Orlando area.According to authorities, the callers told the couple that their son had been arrested and that they needed to pay $6,500 for an ankle monitor he would be required to wear upon his release.Believing the claims, the couple transferred the money through Zelle, an online payment platform, deputies said.The scammers later contacted the couple again, demanding an additional $9,000. This time, the couple refused to pay, cut off communication and reported the incident to the sheriff's office.Investigation leads Florida authorities to GeorgiaInvestigators worked with several Georgia law enforcement agencies, including the Forsyth County Sheriff's Office, Atlanta Police Department and Alpharetta Police Department, to identify a suspect.Authorities also obtained assistance from multiple banks and reviewed security camera footage, financial records and body camera footage from previous investigations involving similar scams.The evidence ultimately led investigators to obtain an arrest warrant for Barnett.She was arrested and transferred to Monroe County, where she was booked into jail on Tuesday, Oct. 13.The Monroe County Sheriff's Office did not specify whether any of the stolen money had been recovered or whether additional suspects were being sought.

title: ​World's oldest shipwreck found off Turkey, archaeologists say: "Time capsule at the bottom of the sea"
description: ​Archaeologists in Turkey have dated the shipwreck to between 4,400 and 4,700 years old.
content: Archaeologists have discovered the world's oldest shipwreck off the coast of Turkey, dating it to between 4,400 and 4,700 years old.The structure of the ship has not survived the nearly five millennia underwater, but its contents of clay jars have been preserved surprisingly well, with some still containing traces of what they transported over 4,000 years ago.The archaeologists who found the vessel said that it was a nearly 33-foot-long trade ship transporting goods across the Mediterranean Sea and originated somewhere on the eastern Mediterranean coast.The wreck dates back to the same time period as when the Pyramids of Giza were being built, and will "offer insights into ancient trading connections and the everyday lives of seafarers," according to Turkey's Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy."The shipwreck is a time capsule at the bottom of the sea," Hakan Öniz, an associate professor at Turkey's Akdeniz University who oversaw the expedition to uncover the ship, told CBS News' partner network BBC News.Alongside the 30 ceramic storage jars in the wreckage, called amphorae, three stone anchors were also discovered.Öniz told CBS News that when his team first found the wreck four years ago, the amphorae only appeared to be a century or two old."However, we later became excited when we saw the same amphora forms in a publication on Egyptian archaeology and returned to the site," Öniz said. "Indeed, they were similar to those found at the Giza pyramids in Egypt. We were incredibly excited." The design of these amphorae — with two handles, a flat base and a ridge in the middle — was distinctive to pottery from that period of history.Karin Sowada, an archaeologist at Australia's Macquarie University, examined the pots after they were brought to the surface. She told the BBC that there was still a viscous, glossy residue inside some of the amphorae."I looked inside and nearly fainted. I could not believe how much [residue] was visible. It wasn't just like spots … a lot of this material was still remaining," she said.Analysis of the clay used to make the jars suggests that they were produced in workshops in the Middle East's Jordan Valley, located along Jordan's border with Israel and the West Bank."It appears the vessel sank while transporting olive oil or wine from that region westward — perhaps to Troy or to the Minoan civilization in Crete," Öniz told CBS News.Similar examples of amphorae have also been found in Egypt, Troy and Crete, according to Ersoy.Öniz told the BBC that when he was diving for the wreck, his first thoughts were on the lives of the many people connected to the ship."We are the first humans who [have] touched these objects after 5,000 years," he said."We are always thinking of the sailors ... the producers of the amphora and the person who carried the amphora on their shoulders to the ship, and the women who were waiting for their husbands, and they unfortunately couldn't go back."The discovery has taken the record of the world's oldest shipwreck from the previous holder in the Aegean Sea located near Greece, which was dated to 4,200 years ago.

title: 2 arrested after robbery near Live Oak Skate Park
description: Two men were arrested after an armed robbery was reported Tuesday night near Live Oak Skate Park, the Sutter County Sheriff's Office said.
content: Two men were arrested after an armed robbery was reported Tuesday night near Live Oak Skate Park, the Sutter County Sheriff's Office said.The sheriff's office said the victim of the robbery reported that they were accosted by two men, who threatened the victim with a firearm and robbed them before fleeing on foot.The two suspects, 22-year-old Hugo Diaz Chavez of Live Oak and 25-year-old Francisco Ramos of Live Oak, were arrested following interviews by detectives, the sheriff's office said on Wednesday. Chavez was booked on multiple charges including assault with a firearm, robbery, conspiracy, and multiple narcotics charges. Ramos was booked on robbery and conspiracy charges.

title: World's largest in-water sailboat show returns to City Dock in Annapolis
description: The Annapolis Sailboat Show -- the largest in the world of its kind -- is returning to City Dock for four days beginning on Thursday.
content: The Annapolis Sailboat Show -- the largest in the world of its kind -- is returning to City Dock for four days beginning on Thursday.Visitors attending the show can board more than 150 sailboats and meet with hundreds of vendors who are "showcasing marine electronics, rigging, safety equipment, apparel, accessories, and services," a news release announced. Attendees can also compare boats and layouts, meet manufacturers and dealers, and find all sorts of sailing resources.Show hours run Thursday through Saturday from 10 a.m. until 6:30 p.m. On Sunday, the hours are from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Organizers say the event is the largest in-water sailboat show in the world. General admission tickets for adults are $32. Children 7-15 years of age pay $10, while kids 6 and under get in for free. On Sunday, military personnel and first responders in uniform will be admitted for free, or get discounted tickets with a valid military ID.The boat show "brings together sailing enthusiasts, prospective buyers and industry professionals to celebrate life on the water and explore the latest in sailing," the news release said. "This is the moment when Annapolis becomes a boating town in the truest sense," said Sheila Jones, Annapolis Boat Show's general manager. "The docks are full, the boats are ready, and there is something happening everywhere you turn. Come shop for your next boat, get out on the water, learn something new, or simply enjoy a great fall weekend in Annapolis!" New to this year's show will be courses that are part of the Cruisers University program, an educational resource visitors can choose to join. The program offers seminars and hands-on courses aimed at building confidence and improving sailing skills, according to the news release. Because of ongoing construction work along City Dock, the show will feature an updated layout. This will include tents for family-friendly activities, while still maintaining the in-water display.Attendees are encouraged to order tickets in advance from annapolisboatshows.com and plan for additional travel time due to traffic and construction restrictions in downtown Annapolis.

title: Chicago's Congress Theater renovation could start by winter after federal loan approved, alderman says
description: Long-anticipated renovation on the Congress Theater in Chicago's Logan Square neighborhood could start by this winter, according to the 1st Ward alderman.
content: Long-anticipated renovation on the Congress Theater in Chicago's Logan Square neighborhood could start by this winter, according to the 1st Ward alderman.In a newsletter to his constituents, Ald. Daniel La Spata said the HUD 108 federal loan that was needed to begin construction has been approved. Since approval, La Spata said the site is undergoing a required federal environmental review and the owners are submitting plans for transportation and landscaping requested by the Chicago Department of Transportation, but "we are moving steadily forward."La Spata said the goal is to have "people working on the building before winter comes."The theater has been closed since 2013. In August, 16 teenagers were arrested for trespassing at the Congress. The weekend before, social media posts showed hundreds of people attending an illegal rave inside.La Spata, who has championed the historic theater's renovation, warned at the time in another newsletter that "participants did significant damage to the building – substantially increasing the cost of its rehabilitation."Please note: The above video is from a previous report.

title: Man accused of assault, attempted kidnapping of 2 children near Oakland's Lake Merritt
description: A man has been arrested in connection with the assault and attempted kidnapping of children in two separate incidents near Lake Merritt in Oakland on Monday morning.
content: A man has been arrested in connection with the assault and attempted kidnapping of children in two separate incidents near Lake Merritt in Oakland on Monday morning.According to Oakland police, both incidents took place shortly before 9 a.m. near Grand Avenue and Harrison Street. According to the preliminary investigation, a child in a stroller was attacked by a suspect who later left on foot.Soon after, police said the same person attempted to remove another child from a stroller before leaving on foot. Neither child needed medical attention.Officers arrested a suspect, an adult male, in connection with both incidents. The suspect's name has not been released.Additional details about the incidents were not immediately available.Anyone with additional information about the case is asked to contact the Oakland Police Department's Felony Assault Unit at 510-238-3426 or to email cidvideos@oaklandca.gov.

title: Remains found in Annapolis park identified as man missing since January
description: The human remains found in Truxton Park in Annapolis have been identified as belonging to a man reported missing in January.
content: Human remains found last month in Truxton Park in Annapolis have been identified as those of a man reported missing in January. Nicholas Bradley Patterson, 33, of Annapolis was reported missing by family members on January 21.In September, human remains were found in a wooded area of Truxton Park. Part of the park was closed to the public while police searched for evidence and processed the scene. At the time, police said there was no danger to the public. Annapolis Police said this week that the medical examiner's office has now identified those remains as Patterson's. Police detectives are continuing to investigate the case. The department said there is no reason to believe foul play was involved and the official cause of death will be determined, pending a final report from the medical examiner's office.Anyone with information about the case is urged to call Annapolis police at 410-260-3439.

title: Denver working group on data centers says they're off to promising start, "it exceeded my expectations"
description: Denver's working group on data centers has officially begun meeting with the goal of creating policy recommendations for the city.
content: Denver's working group on data centers has officially begun meeting with the goal of creating policy recommendations for the city.The group, diversely composed of community members and experts in a multitude of industries, was created after the city council approved a moratorium to pause the construction of data centers in Denver."This is an opportunity to be a part of democracy in action to help set the rules that we haven't had for these kinds of developments, and to make sure we're protecting Denver's resources and putting Denverites first," said Mark Orrs, who's on the working group.Orrs is an associate professor at Colorado School of Mines, and he's bringing his expertise to the table."My training is in sustainable development, and I teach responsible engineering, specifically engineering for social and environmental responsibility," he explained. And one of the core questions at the center of the conversation is whether 'sustainable' and 'data centers' can exist in the same sentence."There are new kinds of technologies coming out every day that might make them more sustainable," Orrs said. "But to date, what we've seen is a lot of unsustainable development in this area."Orrs is one of 26 individuals with diverse backgrounds chosen to participate from more than 250 applicants. But with honor comes enormous responsibility. "We know that others are looking to us, and to see how we decide to proceed, and that they will follow," said Orrs."We are and have been the tip of the spear on this discussion," said Councilman Darrell Watson. "We are one of the first large municipalities to do a moratorium. We're one of maybe one that are building a working group with this very extensive application process."Watson represents District 9, where the controversial CoreSite facility in Globeville was recently built, which became the catalyst for the moratorium. "I think we have a unique process, and I do believe we're going to come up with a commonsense approach to regulating data centers," said Watson. For now, the working group is just getting started and met for the first time last week."I thought it went about as well as I could have expected," said Orrs. "In fact, I said it exceeded my expectations."The next working group meeting will be on October 29, and although they are slated to meet through May, Watson says they'll continue to meet as long as necessary for the city council to create legislation.

title: Metra's new battery-powered trains will run on the Beverly Branch of the Rock Island Line
description: Metra and Cook County officials unveiled new lithium ion battery-powered trains that will first run on a stretch of the Beverly Branch of the Rock Island Line.
content: Metra and Cook County officials unveiled new lithium ion battery-powered trains that will first run on a stretch of the Beverly Branch of the Rock Island Line.Metra leaders and Cook County Board President Toni Preckwinkle, along with other officials, officially rolled out the new trains Wednesday morning at a news conference at the LaSalle St. Station. The trainsets are made by Stadler, a Swiss railway rolling stock manufacturing company, and are part of their Fast Light Innovative Regional Train, or FLIRT, models. Metra is purchasing eight four-car FLIRT trainsets from Stadler U.S., which is based in Salt Lake City, and also has the option to buy eight more if the first set are successful.The trains rely on onboard lithium-ion batteries. Stadler boasts its FLIRT platform is modular and flexible, which they say make it ideal for a wide range of needs. "These will be the first battery-powered trainsets to operate in North America, and they're unlike anything Metra has operated before," said Metra CEO Jim Derwinski. "These zero-emission trainsets will be cleaner and quieter, and we hope they will play a key role in helping Metra to operate more frequent, all-day service and improve connectivity with CTA and Pace." The trains will have single-level cars with low-level boarding and lifts to make them ADA compliant, the agency said. They will come in four-car sets that can seat 208 people each, and have open gangways so passengers can easily move car-to-car.The trains will also have bike racks, luggage racks, USB outlets and two ADA-accessible bathrooms. They will charge using existing cables in yards and terminals, and can recover energy through regenerative braking, but Metra also said it will have dedicated charging infrastructure. Metra plans to put the trains into service in 2028, with the first of them running the 16-and-a-half mile stretch between LaSalle St. and Blue Island on the Beverly Branch of the Rock Island Line. The new trains are on display at LaSalle St. Station Wednesday from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. and Thursday from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m.

title: Judge blocks Trump's White House ban targeting CNN, MS NOW and Politico, saying it likely violated First Amendment
description: U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly said the White House's revocation of hard passes for CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists likely violated their First and Fifth Amendment rights.
content: Washington — A federal judge on Tuesday blocked President Trump's attempt to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, maintaining access to the grounds for reporters from the three news organizations indefinitely.U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, who was appointed by Mr. Trump, granted the outlets' request for a preliminary injunction, which will remain in place while the case moves forward. In a 26-page decision, Kelly found that the revocation of their journalists' hard passes likely violated their Fifth and First Amendment rights."It is likely that President Trump's revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes is the sort of action that would deter a reasonable reporter or news organization from publishing stories to which he objects," Kelly wrote in his decision. "The revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes matters a lot as to how, whether, and to what extent they can do their jobs."The judge said Mr. Trump's comments "suggest that he intended the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes to alter their reporting on him, bolstering the case that his action here is sufficient to deter a reporter of ordinary firmness from reporting in the same way she had before."The Justice Department is appealing the decision."The Fake News has no place demanding a spot in the President's Oval Office," a White House official said in a statement. "The lies they smear are a disservice to the American public and tear at the very fabric of our Democracy. They're completely capable of reporting from directly outside."Theodore Boutrous, lawyer for CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, said the court was right to block the White House from enforcing Mr. Trump's ban."When the President issued his 'ban on the free press,' he blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment," Boutrous said in a statement. "Since then, the President has repeatedly, candidly, and consistently admitted in public that he banned our clients from the White House to punish reporting he doesn't like and to try to force journalists to cover him in ways he prefers. The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound."The president announced last month his decision to ban journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House grounds because of what he said was their "constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS." Reporters from the three outlets who showed up at the White House the day after the ban was announced were turned away and had their press credentials taken by the U.S. Secret Service.The news organizations filed their lawsuit on Sept. 21 and argued the president's ban retaliated against them because of their news coverage, in violation of the First Amendment. CNN, MS NOW and Politico also argued their reporters were denied their Fifth Amendment right to due process because they were not provided notice that their reporting could lead to their White House access being revoked or the opportunity to respond.The day after the outlets filed their suit, the White House Press Office sent them letters informing them of the president's initial decision to revoke their journalists' press credentials and setting a Sept. 25 deadline for them to respond. The White House argued that reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico violated standards of professionalism and published articles that raised national security concerns.The White House provided the outlets with lists of pieces that it said "threatened national security and/or spread falsehoods." But most of the articles were written by journalists who do not have White House hard passes. One of the flagged stories from Politico, which was published in June, was based on a press call organized by the White House. During the call, reporters were instructed to attribute quotes to a "senior administration official," according to court records.The news outlets asked Kelly to grant them temporary relief and restore their journalists' access to the White House, which the judge agreed to do late last month.His decision then was based on the press organizations' due process argument. Kelly did not address their First Amendment claims.CNN, MS NOW and Politico also asked Kelly to grant them longer-term relief, which would remain in place as the litigation plays out. In a hearing last week, the judge pressed a Justice Department lawyer on the Trump administration's justifications for the ban and why the government's argument in court appeared to differ from Mr. Trump's public justification.The Justice Department has argued that the president determined the outlets should be denied access to the White House because they violated standards of professionalism and threatened national security. But Mr. Trump has repeatedly attacked the outlets for "negative" coverage of his administration and for publishing "constantly bad stories."Mr. Trump "seems to have said publicly and on several occasions" that he was taking action "because of X and Y, and now the government is coming to court saying no, it was actually Z," Kelly said.The judge also said the due-process concerns were "the biggest hurdle" for the Justice Department to surmount.In his decision, Kelly said the Trump administration failed to put forward evidence that Mr. Trump's decision to revoke hard passes for CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists initially was based on national security grounds, and reiterated that the reporting cited by the White House as raising issues is "commonplace, for better or worse.""When he announced the ban with his post on September 18, he did not mention national security. When he was asked later that day about the 'particular reason' for his action, he did not mention national security. And while it is true, days later, that he used the phrase 'national security' in subsequent social media posts about the ban, that expression appears to have been simply another way for him to describe Plaintiffs' alleged inaccuracies and unfairness in their reporting about topics like his achievements or electoral success," he wrote.Addressing the letters the White House sent to each of the outlets informing them of the ban, Kelly wrote that they "appear to conflate concerns about otherwise protected speech ('trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about ... other issues') with national security concerns."Mr. Trump has for years denounced the media over coverage that he dislikes, calling news outlets "fake news" and lobbing attacks against individual reporters. The president stopped the Associated Press from attending certain events at the White House over its refusal to use the name "Gulf of America" after his executive order changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico.The AP sued and a federal appeals court allowed Mr. Trump to restrict its access to the Oval Office and Air Force One, places where only a subset of the White House press corps goes. But the appeals court has not yet ruled on the legal merits of the White House's ban targeting AP journalists.Mr. Trump's decision to keep CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists from the entire White House campus marked an escalation of his yearslong feud with the press. When he announced the ban targeting the three outlets, the president warned he could revoke access for "other Fake News Media Outlets."CNN and CBS News are both part of Skydance, the parent company formed by the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. title: John Skelton pretrial rescheduled for December, murder trial could take 30 days
description: A pretrial was adjourned to Dec. 16 in the murder case against John Skelton of Lenawee County, whose three young sons were last seen in 2010.
content: The jury trial in the case of a Southeast Michigan man accused of murder in the deaths of his three young boys is expected to last for 30 days. That's according to notes placed in the Lenawee County 39th Circuit Court docket on Wednesday after attorneys met with the judge for a pretrial conference on the charges against John Skelton. He faces open murder charges in connection with the disappearance of Andrew, Alexander and Tanner Skelton, last seen in November 2010.The pretrial was adjourned to Dec. 16 to allow for completion of transcripts from the preliminary exam that concluded on Sept. 3 in the Lenawee County 2A District Court and to prepare for any motions to be filed, the court docket indicated. Skelton's attorney also told court officials that he expects the case to be scheduled for a 30-day jury trial. Background on the Skelton case The Skelton boys, who were ages 9, 7, and 5 at the time they were reported missing, have never been found. There were repeated searches in Michigan and Ohio, and attempts to match them to human remains found in Montana in 2017 and remains found in Tennessee in 2026. The Skelton boys were legally declared dead in March 2025, upon the request of their mother, Tanya Zuvers. Their father was charged Nov. 12 with three counts of open murder and three counts of tampering with evidence. Those charges were filed about two weeks before his expected release from prison on earlier charges stemming from the investigation of the whereabouts of the boys. The Michigan State Police led the investigation. The above video originally aired on Sept. 3, 2026.

title: Small Minnesota school mourns 3 current and former students in a matter of days
description: A senior, a graduate who became a South Dakota deputy and another graduate have died in a matter of days. The school says its students become graduates, and its graduates become neighbors.
content: Three current and former Dawson-Boyd students have died in a matter of days, leaving a small school community in far western Minnesota grieving a football player who died in a crash and a graduate who was a South Dakota deputy shot and killed in the line of duty.Senior Carter Monaghan was the football player. Katherine Frank, a 2018 Dawson-Boyd graduate, was a Minnehaha County deputy. The third was Aaron Gebur, a graduate whose mother previously served students at the school as a paraprofessional. The school's message did not say how Gebur died or detail the circumstances of any of the deaths."Three lives. Three families. Countless connections throughout our community," the school said in a message to its community.The losses weigh heavily in a small school, the message said.
