"Our students become our graduates, our graduates become our neighbors."Frank was shot Friday and died Monday, surrounded by family and loved ones, according to a GoFundMe page organized by the Minnehaha County Deputies Association."Katherine was more than her badge," the page said, adding she was a sister, daughter, granddaughter, girlfriend and friend.Her family describes her as incredibly funny and someone who gets along with just about everybody. Outside of work, she enjoyed spending time with her two dogs, Ares and Aspen, reading, cooking and playing video games. She leaves behind five siblings, ages 15 to 28, her grandparents and her boyfriend.The association is raising money for funeral costs and the family's financial stability. As of Wednesday, the fundraiser had collected more than $80,000 in 811 donations, above its $60,000 goal."There are no words that can take away the pain," the school said, offering "compassion, our presence, and our care for one another." It urged people to remember that grief looks different for everyone, to extend grace and to check on one another.The school said each of the three will remain part of its "Blackjack family."

title: Iran and Russia-linked hybrid attacks in Europe are mounting, U.K. spy chief says. Here's a look at recent incidents.
description: Britain's domestic spy chief says "hybrid tactics" used by Russia and Iran are evolving. Here are some of the most notable incidents of 2026.
content: London — The head of Britain's top domestic spy agency MI5, Sir Ken McCallum, painted a dark picture Tuesday of the changing national security threats facing the U.K. and the world. "We have entered a new era of national security, requiring a new response," he said in his annual threat update at MI5 headquarters in London. "Those who mean the U.K. harm aren't attacking things government owns or controls. They're aiming at people, businesses, communities." McCallum said that among state threats, "Russia remains aggressor number one," while intelligence analysts have also seen a "major shift" in "Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets." Both countries, he said, have adopted more and evolving "hybrid tactics" as they target everything from air force bases to synagogues across the U.K. and Europe. Below is a look at some of the incidents that fit that description over the last year alone.IranIran has used and continues "using criminal proxies to try to intimidate oppositionists, Iranian media organizations, and Israeli sites," McCallum said. But as the U.S. war with Iran nears the eight month mark, analysts have also seen the Iranian regime, "like Russia, attempting to expand their hybrid campaign," he said, leading to more than 50 arrests in the U.K. over the last year alone. "Sadly, much of this aggression has been aimed at British Jewish communities," McCallum said, speaking of incidents this year that included "a wave of arson and sabotage incidents targeting Jewish communities in the U.K. and other European nations," but also acts targeting "harder targets, like military sites."Many of these attacks were claimed by a group calling itself Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), or the Islamic Movement of the Companions of the Right, which U.K. authorities have sanctioned and said is tied directly to the elite Quds Force of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which Britain considers a terrorist organization. A CBS News investigation in March found the group appeared to have links to Iran, and a member said it would "keep threatening U.S. and Israeli interests worldwide until we've avenged every child in Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, and the resistance nations … We urge people to stay away from Zionist and American interests and individuals to keep themselves safe."These Iran-linked attacks include:Liège, Belgium: March 9. An explosive device detonated at a synagogue, causing no casualties. Attack claimed by HAYI.Rotterdam, The Netherlands: March 13. The firebombing of a synagogue. Attack claimed by HAYI. Dutch authorities say they're investigating Iranian links to the incident.Amsterdam, The Netherlands: March 14. A device detonated outside a Jewish school. Attack claimed by HAYI.Golders Green, London: March 23. Four ambulances belonging to a Jewish volunteer ambulance service set on fire. Attack claimed by HAYI.Antwerp, Belgium: March 24. A car set on fire in a Jewish quarter of the city. Attack claimed by HAYI.Paris, France: March 28. 17-year-old allegedly tries to place an explosive device at the Bank of America headquarters. French authorities suspect HAYI was behind the attack, though the link was not confirmed. Nijkerk, The Netherlands: April 4. A device detonated outside the premises of a group called Christians For Israel. Attack claimed by HAYI.Finchley, London: April 15. Molotov cocktails and a brick thrown at Finchley Reform Synagogue. Attack claimed by HAYI.Park Royal, London: April 15. An attempted arson attack against Persian-language news outlet Iran International. Responsibility for the incident was never claimed. In March 2024, a journalist for the channel, Pouria Zeraati, was stabbed outside his home in London. According to The Guardian, counterterrorism police and security services in Britain believed the Iranian regime used criminal proxies to carry out the attack.Hendon, London: April 17. Attempted arson at the former premises of charity Jewish Futures. Attack claimed by HAYI.Harrow, London: April 18–19. A suspected arson attack at a synagogue in Harrow, then a bottle containing accelerant was thrown at the Kenton United Synagogue a day later. Attack claimed by HAYI.Golders Green, London: April 29. Two Hasidic Jewish men stabbed in the north of the capital. Attack claimed by HAYI.RAF Fairford, England: Sept. 27. Suspected plot involving British base used by U.S. bombers to strike Iran. Gasoline was found in vehicles, but no viable explosives. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the incident was "almost certainly" directed by Iran.Manchester, England: Oct. 2. Two Iranian nationals are charged with terrorism offenses following an alleged plot targeting a Jewish community in the northern city of Manchester. RussiaFor now, Russia remains the biggest threat to security, according to the U.K. spy chief's Tuesday briefing."The Russian military and intelligence services are once again escalating their attempts at hybrid warfare," McCallum said, adding that Moscow was "being careful to stay below the NATO Article 5 threshold" with its actions, which would trigger the alliance's collective defense principle."It'd be foolish for them to cross" that line, he said, and so far Russia "is using tactics that stop short — though sometimes not much short — of conventional conflict."Incidents linked to Russia this year include:Off Vaindloo Island, Estonia: March 19. Russian SU-30 fighter allegedly violates Estonian airspace – NATO scrambles aircraft in response. Hutthurm, Germany: March. Authorities thwarted a Russian-ordered assassination attempt targeting the head of a Germany defense company, according to Die Zeit.Norwegian waters, near the U.K.: Reported April 9. The U.K. and Norway deployed military vessels to deter Russian submarines found to have lingered for over a month from attacking undersea cables. Over the last few years there have been several incidents of alleged Russian sabotage of such cables. Labege, France: June 1. Molotov cocktails thrown at a drone factory that supplies the French and Ukrainian armed forces. French authorities are investigating Russian links, according to Le Monde.Leipzig, Germany: Aug. 4. An explosive-laden drone is found near cargo facilities and Ukrainian aircraft. German authorities explicitly attributed the incident to Russia.Skarzysko-Kamienna, Poland: August. Fire at a WB Electronics factory that produces drones and other military components. EBU reports that authorities believe Russia used "low-level operatives" to carry out the attack, but authorities do not identify those responsible.Tallinn, Estonia: Aug. 15. Arson attack on Milrem Robotics, a defense company that supplies robotic military vehicles to Ukraine. Estonian authorities attributed the attack to Russia in late September.Swindon, England: Sept. 9. Joshua Cammidge charged over allegedly sharing locations of drone factories with people linked to Russian military intelligence and offering to carry out sabotage attacks.Wola Krobowska, Poland: Sept. 23. Arson attack on a Starlink satellite ground station, which Poland officially blames on Russia in October.Lithuania, September. Drone carrying explosive device crossed Belarusian border is shot down by NATO aircraft. Italian defense minister says it "most probably" came from Russia. Denmark: Oct. 7. A Danish intelligence official says Russia attempted acts of sabotage against defense industry companies supplying Ukraine over summer.

title: Georgia officer who shot, killed HeeHaw the donkey asks judge to throw out owner's lawsuit
description: The Cedartown officer who shot and killed HeeHaw the donkey argues that bodycam video shows he acted to protect a colleague. HeeHaw's owner says the donkey posed no threat.
content: Body-camera video obtained by CBS News Atlanta shows HeeHaw the donkey galloping toward officers before a Cedartown police officer shoots him during a search for a missing girl. The officer is now using the footage in a request to dismiss the owner's lawsuit.Officer Trenton Ryan Garner filed the request Oct. 7 in federal court in Rome, arguing that he reasonably believed the donkey posed an immediate threat to another officer. HeeHaw's owner, Hannah Michelle Israel, alleges officers entered her fenced pasture without a warrant or permission and shot the donkey without provocation. Her complaint describes HeeHaw as "young, small, and tranquil" and says he "posed no threat," according to Garner's filing. The shooting happened shortly after midnight Aug. 30 while officers were helping search for a missing 12-year-old girl in Polk County.The recording initially has no sound. Garner's filing explains that the camera preserved 30 seconds of video before recording was activated, without audio. After the shooting, Garner tells dispatch: "Firearm discharged at a donkey. It was trying to attack us in the pasture and on the track." Officers then continue the search. Garner's attorney, J. Scott Key, argues the video shows HeeHaw getting within a body length of another officer before Garner fired. He is asking the judge to consider the recording and dismiss all three claims against Garner.The defense also argues that crossing the pasture did not violate Israel's constitutional rights and that Garner should be protected from the lawsuit because he reasonably believed another officer was in danger. These are the officer's legal arguments; the supplied documents do not include a ruling on the request. In his incident report, Garner said another officer activated a Taser's electrical arc to try to scare HeeHaw away, but the donkey continued approaching. Garner wrote that he fired once, and HeeHaw turned, moved uphill and collapsed.Israel told officers she had bottle-fed HeeHaw since he was young and that he had never acted aggressively or tried to bite anyone. In a statement posted by Elsberry Riding and Farm, she described herself as "heartbroken and traumatized" and said she was seeking answers and accountability.Since the matter remains under investigation, the City of Cedartown told CBS News Atlanta that it will not comment on it.

title: Maryland deadline to request mail-in ballots for 2026 election is fast approaching. Here's what to know.
description: The deadline for Maryland residents to request a mail-in ballot for the 2026 general election is fast approaching, and officials are urging voters to plan accordingly.
content: The deadline for Maryland residents to request a mail-in ballot for the 2026 general election is fast approaching, and officials are urging voters to plan accordingly. Mail-in ballots requested via mail or fax must be received – not just sent – by Oct. 27, said a statement issued by the Maryland State Board of Elections (SBE). Voters wishing to receive a mail-in ballot via email must submit a request by Oct. 30.Mail-in ballots can be requested online here."Safe, secure and convenient"Last month, election officials announced that 590,922 Maryland voters had requested mail-in ballots for the 2026 general election. That total included voters who requested ballots delivered by mail, as well as those who requested print-at-home ballots via email, the SBE said."With the General Election just weeks away, I encourage all Maryland voters to take a few moments now to make their voting plans," State Administrator of Elections Jared DeMarinis said. "Voting by mail remains a safe, secure and convenient way to participate in the democratic process. Voters who plan to cast their ballots by mail should be mindful of the upcoming request deadlines to ensure they have ample time to receive and return their ballots," DeMarinis added.When and where to return mail-in ballotsMail-in ballots returned by mail must be postmarked by or before 8 p.m. on Election Day, Nov. 3. If returning by hand, ballots must be submitted at an early voting center during the early voting period, or dropped at a ballot drop box or local board of elections by 8 p.m. on Nov. 3, the SBE said. The early voting period runs from Oct. 22 through Oct. 29. A list of locations can be found at vote.md.gov/vote2026.

title: Colorado deputies stop wrong way driver on I-25 in Castle Rock
description: Deputies in Douglas County had to shut down Interstate 25 in order to stop a wrong-way driver.
content: Deputies in Douglas County had to shut down Interstate 25 in order to stop a wrong-way driver. According to investigators, it all started when deputies responded to reports of a vehicle traveling the wrong way on the interstate in Castle Rock about 4:45 a.m. Tuesday. When deputies tried to pull over the vehicle, the driver, a male, accelerated to more than 80 mph while continuing to drive the wrong way. That's when deputies worked with the Lone Tree Police Department to shut down I-25 ahead of the vehicle and then stopped it with a Tactical Vehicle Intervention. The driver was taken into custody. Deputies said they saw multiple indicators that the driver was impaired and charges are pending. During the investigation, they discovered the driver, not from Douglas County, has an extensive criminal history in Colorado, including seven driving under the influence or driving while ability impaired charges spanning decades. At the time the suspect was captured, deputies said records showed he had a suspended license. "Wrong-way drivers create an immediate and potentially catastrophic danger for everyone on the roadway. I'm proud of the quick decisions, teamwork, and professionalism demonstrated by our deputies and our partners at the Lone Tree Police Department. Their actions helped prevent what could have been a tragic outcome and kept our community safe. Let me be clear: we will not tolerate impaired driving in Douglas County," said Douglas County Sheriff Weekly.

title: 1 killed after Ford F-150 crashes into Colorado State Patrol vehicle, semi on I-70
description: A 19-year-old male died after suffering life-threatening injuries in a crash when the Ford F-150 he was riding in crashed into a Colorado State Patrol vehicle on I-70 and then into a semi that was involved in a previous crash.
content: A 19-year-old male died after suffering life-threatening injuries in a crash when the Ford F-150 he was riding in crashed into a Colorado State Patrol vehicle on Interstate 70 and then into a semi. According to investigators, the crash happened about 6:45 a.m. while troopers were investigating a single-vehicle semi crash in the same area. The semi crash happened in the westbound lanes of I-70 near mile marker 321 east of Byers. During that investigation, the trooper's patrol vehicle was struck by a Ford F-150. The initial investigation shows the trooper was partially blocking the left lane of travel while tow trucks were removing the semi from the center median. That's when the driver of the Ford, an 18-year-old male, lost control and struck the patrol vehicle. Troopers said the truck continued westbound before entering the center median, striking the guardrail and then striking the rear driver's side of the semi. The driver of the truck was rushed to the hospital for serious injuries. The passenger of the truck was rushed to the hospital with life-threatening injuries and died. The trooper was rushed to the hospital for a precautionary medical evaluation. No other injuries were reported at the scene. The name of the crash victim has not been released. The Colorado State Patrol Vehicular Crimes Unit is investigating this crash.

title: 2026 Gold Glove Finalists include Cubs' Bregman, Crow-Armstrong, Happ, Swanson, and Suzuki; and White Sox's Meidroth
description: Five Chicago Cubs players and one Chicago White Sox player have been named as finalists for Gold Glove Awards in 2026 as the best defensive players at their position.
content: Five Chicago Cubs players and one Chicago White Sox player have been named as finalists for Gold Glove Awards in 2026 as the best defensive players at their position. Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman, shortstop Dansby Swanson, left fielder Ian Happ, center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong, and right fielder Seiya Suzuki all were named as Gold Glove finalists in the National League.Chicago White Sox second baseman Chase Meidroth also was named an American League Gold Glove finalist.With Gold Glove five finalists, the Cubs are tied with the Toronto Blue Jays for the most in Major League Baseball. The Cubs also led MLB in Gold Glove finalists last year with six, and won a league-leading three in 2025.Bregman has one previous Gold Glove Award while he was with the Houston Astros. He finished 2026 with +9 outs above average, second among all third basemen behind Padres third baseman Manny Machado. Swanson has two previous Gold Glove Awards in 2022 and 2023. He finished the season with +16 outs above average, more than all but three qualified shortstops.For Happ, a Gold Glove Award this year would be his fifth consecutive win. He had nine outfield assists in 2026, tie for eighth most in MLB.Crow-Amrstrong, largely considered the best defensive player in MLB, led the majors in outs above average (+26), FanGraphs' "defensive runs" metric (+23), and Statcasts's fielding run value (+26).Suzuki made a significant improvement in defense this season, recording a +8 fielding run value in 2026, after a negative rating in his first four seasons. His +14 defensive runs saved rank second among all MLB right fielders.Meidroth, who spent a majority of his rookie season in 2025 at shortstop, moved to second base in 2026, and led all American League second basemen with a +10 in Statcast's fielding run value metric.

title: Man gets life prison sentence for Silver Lake Trader Joe's employee shooting death
description: Gene Evin Atkins, 36, was convicted of 41 counts, including second-degree murder, assault with a semi-automatic firearm on a peace officer, attempted carjacking, and mayhem for the July, 2018 crime spree.
content: The man who was found responsible for the Silver Lake shooting death of a 27-year-old Trader Joe's assistant manager was sentenced to more than 200 years to life in prison.Gene Evin Atkins, 36, was convicted of 41 counts, including second-degree murder, assault with a semi-automatic firearm on a peace officer, attempted carjacking, and mayhem for the July, 2018 crime spree. Atkins set off a chain of events that led to the death of Melyda "Mely" Maricela Corado. Though he was not the person who fatally shot Corado, he was charged with her killing under the theory that Corado's death was the result of his actions.Albert Corado, Mely's father, spoke outside the courthouse following sentencing on Wednesday. "The result doesn't matter. My daughter is still not here," Corado said. "He took an angel … My entire family, he changed us forever."Prosecutors say Atkins first shot his 76-year-old grandmother and 17-year-old girlfriend in South Los Angeles before taking his grandmother's vehicle and leading police on a wild chase, ending at the Trader Joe's store as he dashed inside, firing at police.Police returned fire and struck and killed Corado. Atkins ultimately surrendered to police after a four-hour standoff inside the store where he held employees and customers hostage.Earlier this year, a jury convicted Atkins of 40 counts, including 24 counts of false imprisonment of a hostage involving Trader Joe's employees and customers, three counts of attempted murder and four counts of assault with a firearm on an officer.He was acquitted of the most serious charge of first-degree murder, while the jury deadlocked on the second-degree murder charge involving the death of Corado, resulting in a retrial. The second jury found him guilty of second-degree murder and found true allegations that he personally used and discharged a firearm during the crime.

title: How do I know if I have been exposed to measles? Pittsburgh-area medical experts explain the symptoms.
description: Being exposed to measles is extremely serious, especially if you haven't been vaccinated.
content: Many health experts find themselves increasingly concerned about the outbreak of measles in Pennsylvania. Now, with a confirmed case in Allegheny County, there is little doubt that other cases are out there and that it is extremely contagious. When someone is infected with measles, they can be contagious and not even know the risk. As an airborne virus, measles flies on the fall breeze, and we have no way of knowing it's there. "It's the most contagious virus that we know; we have no other viral infection like this," said Dr. Robert Jacobson of the Mayo Clinic. "One of the other tricks of this virus, this respiratory particle, is that it can hang in the air for two hours after the infected person leaves the room," Dr. Robert Jacobson said. "This means an unrecognized case of measles - a person who just has runny, watery eyes, nose, and a cough with a fever those first few days - they're spreading the respiratory droplets in every room and hallway they're in and leaving it hanging in the air.""It's in the air, you breathe it in, and there you go," added Dr. Jillian Irwin, the Allegheny County Health Department's medical director. When is measles contagious?Dr. Irwin said it can be anywhere between 7 and 21 days from exposure before you start showing symptoms."Four days before they get the telltale rash, and four days after," Dr. Irwin said of the contagious period. "The day you get the rash is [day] zero."According to Dr. Irwin, if you've received the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine or had measles as a child, you should be OK. She said that 9 out of 10 people who have not been vaccinated will contract measles. According to the CDC, one out of five of those people will end up in the hospital. If you know that you have been exposed to measles but haven't been vaccinated, you can get the vaccine within three days. Measles infection can be serious"There's no guarantee that you're going to know if you are exposed within three days," Dr. Irwin explained. "That is why it's not worth the risk. People can get pneumonia; they can get brain swelling; it's a pretty severe situation. While it's not common, it's why we worry about measles." When it comes to the case of the child being exposed to measles at Target in McCandless, Dr. Irwin said they knew they were cutting it close with the warning. "There was one more day before people could potentially get immunoglobulin to help prevent measles," she said. That window is now closed. Dr. Irwin said this is very serious as now five people in Pennsylvania have died during this outbreak of measles. She said don't just assume it's a cold if you get a cough, runny nose, and watery eyes -- they could be symptoms leading up to the measles rash. Editor's note: A previous version of this article referred to Dr. Robert Jacobson of the Mayo Clinic as Dr. Robert Jackson. The article has since been corrected.

title: German police seize humanoid robot that allegedly groped teen girl, and phones of young men who had it
description: German police have seized a humanoid robot after it allegedly touched a 16-year-old girl in an indecent manner and made sexually suggestive gestures.
content: Berlin — German police have seized a humanoid robot after it allegedly touched a 16-year-old girl in an indecent manner and made sexually suggestive gestures toward her. Investigators were trying to determine Wednesday whether the robot's actions were deliberately controlled by two young men who apparently livestreamed the incident in the western city of Cologne on social media.The unusual incident occurred on Oct. 10, shortly before midnight near a fast-food restaurant on a bustling nightlife strip in Cologne, according to a police statement released Monday.Videos shared online appear to show the teenage girl standing with two friends, aged 17 and 18, when a red-and-gold robot in athletic wear, about 4 feet tall, approaches her from behind. According to police, and as the videos appear to show, the robot touches the 16-year-old's buttocks and repeatedly makes thrusting movements toward her.The owner of the robot, a 16-year-old male, and his 19-year-old companion are said to have recorded and livestreamed the encounter themselves, while commenting on it live on social media.Police officers alerted to the incident encountered the two young men nearby shortly after it was reported. At that point, the robot was already in the trunk of a Volkswagen, but the police say they seized both the robot and the two suspects' smartphones as evidence.German media identified the robot as a commercially available humanoid model that costs around 5,000 euros, or about $5,600. One of the individuals involved later claimed on TikTok that the robot had accidentally collided with a woman while trying to avoid another passerby. But longer videos circulating online appear to show the robot performing sexually suggestive movements after the contact with the girl.Investigators are analyzing surveillance video and online recordings to reconstruct the exact sequence of events, the police said. They also hope to determine whether the robot's actions were controlled remotely, whether specific movements were programmed, or whether the machine acted on its own.The incident raises some unusual legal questions. Under German law, the criminal offense of sexual harassment generally requires direct physical contact between people. Legal experts told the television network RTL that the use of a robot could therefore make it difficult to prosecute the robot's owners under existing harassment laws.Instead, police are investigating the case on suspicion of a sexually motivated insult. Possible violations involving the unauthorized publication of images may also be examined.No charges have been filed against either of the two suspects so far.The case highlights new challenges for law enforcement agencies as increasingly powerful humanoid robots become more accessible to private individuals, bringing new questions about where responsibility lies when machines are used to commit potentially criminal acts.

title: JD Vance greets supporters at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport
description: Vice President JD Vance attended a meet-and-greet Wednesday morning at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport.
content: Vice President JD Vance attended a meet-and-greet Wednesday morning at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport.Vance shook hands and posed for photos with supporters, who greeted him with chants of "48," a reference to a potential presidential run in 2028.The event began around 10:50 a.m. at Southwest Airlines Cargo, 3400 North Interloop Road, and was held outdoors on the airport tarmac.Vance did not hold a formal news conference. He was seen speaking with U.S. Rep. Mike Collins, who is challenging Democratic U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff, and Republican lieutenant governor candidate Josh Dolezal, among others.

title: Irish Partnership of Pittsburgh asking for public's help as financial pressure jeopardizes annual festival
description: The Irish Partnership of Pittsburgh's campaign looks to raise $200,000 after years of financial pressure.
content: A Pittsburgh tradition that has celebrated Irish culture for decades is facing an uncertain future as organizers turn to the community for help. The Irish Partnership of Pittsburgh is launching a campaign to raise $200,000 after years of financial pressures put the Pittsburgh Irish Festival in jeopardy."We just really hit a financial place that has put the event in jeopardy for the first time in over 35 years," said Executive Director of the Irish Partnership of Pittsburgh, Mairin Petrone.Organizers said several setbacks have contributed to the financial challenges, including severe flooding in 2018, relocation expenses, inflation and intense weather during last month's festival."We lost about eight hours of our most important hours of our festival weekend," said Petrone.At the same time, the cost of putting on the festival has continued to climb, especially after rising costs due to the COVID-19 pandemic."We typically see a 2-3% increase in expenses year after year. During COVID, those numbers were 11-12%, and they didn't go away," said Petrone.The challenges put more than the annual festival at risk. The Irish Partnership of Pittsburgh also works to keep Irish culture alive in the region through community and educational programs."It's not just our organization that's impacted by this. There's a significant ripple effect. To think about the fact this is in jeopardy is humbling. It's scary. It's embarrassing. We hate to have to turn to the community, but we're hoping there are folks out there who want to keep this tradition alive," said Petrone.Organizers say there are several ways people can help, including making donations, participating in raffles for trips to Ireland, attending local cultural events, or becoming legacy donors. They have launched a site that is accepting donations at this link.They are also asking supporters to help spread the word about the fundraising effort if a monetary donation is not an option."Share this with your friends and family. Share the post on Instagram or Facebook," said Petrone. "Any little bit helps create awareness about what we're trying to do."There is no set timeline for the fundraising campaign, but organizers hope to secure the money as soon as possible to help ensure the festival's future.For more information about the festival, you can go to their website here.

title: 16-year-old girl shot and killed in Detroit drive-by shooting, police say
description: Chief Todd Bettison says a second person was shot in the hip and was taken to a hospital.
content: Detroit police say a 16-year-old girl was killed on Tuesday in a drive-by shooting on Detroit's east side.Police say officers responded to the 4700 block of Chalmers Street after receiving a 911 call at about 6:49 p.m. A preliminary investigation found that four people were inside a Jeep Cherokee when a dark-colored sedan drove by the Jeep, and someone inside the sedan fired shots.The teen girl's name has not been released. A description of a suspect has not been released.Chief Todd Bettison says a second person was shot in the hip and was taken to a hospital. Their current condition is unknown. The two other people who were in the Jeep were not hurt and are considered witnesses, Bettison says.An investigation is ongoing."I'm very angry about this," Bettison said. "We're sick of the violence. We're tired. Enough is enough."The shooting comes one day after a 7-year-old girl and her mother were shot Monday evening. Police say a suspect was taken into custody on Tuesday. The shooting is believed to have stemmed from an argument over a group of young children, ages 7 and 8, who had been fighting earlier in the day. Police say the father of one of the children confronted the adult victim and shot her before fleeing the scene. The bullet went through the woman's arm and struck her daughter in the shoulder. Both the mother and child are expected to recover.Last week, an 11-year-old was shot by their sibling with an unsecured gun. The father is facing firearms – safe storage violation and felony firearm charges. Police say three children were home alone at the time of the shooting."No family should have to endure the devastation and pain that this brings. And no child's life or future should be cut short because of senseless gun violence," Sheffield said of Tuesday's shooting. "We encourage anybody in this community, in our city, to speak up."Anyone with information about Tuesday's shooting is asked to call Crime Stoppers at 800-Speak Up.

title: Evanston-Skokie School District 65 make final recommendation to close 2 schools
description: Lincolnwood and Dewey Elementary Schools were chosen to be closed as leaders say enrollment was down 33% at both.
content: After weeks of preparing the community for school closures, Evanston-Skokie School District 65 made the recommendation Tuesday to shut down two more schools.But the closures are just the start of cuts for staff and students. District leaders held several meetings last month updating the community about a $5 million deficit, which they felt was only going to get worse because of declining enrollment and aging buildings.They told parents and staff members weeks ago that schools would need to close, but did not announce which schools would be impacted until a school board meeting Tuesday night, during which teachers and staff members sat anxiously as they waited to find out.The announcement ultimately came that Lincolnwood Elementary School, at 2600 Colfax St. in Evanston, and Dewey Elementary School, at 1551 Wesley Ave. in Evanston, were chosen to shut down. Leaders say enrollment was down 33% at both.The move would force 713 students to change schools district-wide. At Dewey, parents and even the principal were caught off guard by the proposal to close their building by the end of the school year. They knew the district was looking to shutter schools to save money, but did not expect theirs to be on the chopping block."We recognize that this recommendation may come as more of a surprise to the Dewey community, as Dewey was not as prominently represented in last year's school closure discussions," Evanston-Skokie School District 65 Interim Supt. Eric Witherspoon wrote in an email.This is the second consecutive year that District 65 has announced closures, The district does not plan to sell the properties. Instead, leaders say they could be renovated in the future once the sinking ship is righted.Dewey Elementary School principal Anna Marie Newsome wasted no time sending an email home letting parents know that she is not fully sure of the next steps for their children's transition. She called the decision to close Dewey "unexpected" and "difficult news."The grandmother of a Dewey second grader said she wasn't sure when she would break the news to her grandson that his school is closing."Little by little, we'll try to explain it, and hopefully, it doesn't happen," said Edilma Gillett, "because he loves his school and he loves his teacher."Gillett said she is still confused why Dewey is even on the list."I can't figure out what are the reasons for closing Dewey," she said. "Seems like attendance is high. Morale is good. We have good teachers."Evanston dad Ned Bothfeld was disappointed in the district's choice to close schools for the second year in a row."Overall, I think it's a huge embarrassment to the community," Bothfeld said. "It's really a shame."Bothfeld added that his embarrassment started with District 65's former superintendent, Devon Horton, who left to lead a school district in Georgia.Earlier this month, Horton pleaded guilty to wire fraud, embezzlement, and tax charges stemming from his time at District 65. On Wednesday, two former vendors for District 65 admitted to receiving kickbacks from Horton.Meanwhile, the cuts at Evanston-Skokie School District 65 run deeper than just school doors now."They're looking at numbers," said Natalie Copper, president of Evanston Child Care Professionals. "We're looking at hearts." Copper works with a school-age child care program that provides on-site before- and after-school care for kindergarten through 5th graders. It too is getting cut, eliminating more than 30 positions."Even though it's not mandated, grocery stores aren't mandated, but we need them," she said. "So we need school-age child care for families as well."District leaders say cuts to child care in addition to early start will net $1.2 million in savings, but Copper says it's bigger than dollars."They're forgetting that they work for families," she said. "They work for children and the fact parents pay to have a child in the school age program should say something."The district is also going as far as to eliminate all transportation for pre-K. It estimates the savings at $700,000. With the school closures and additional cuts, leaders say they will save $2.9 million annually and $58 million over 20 years. "They need to do a better job at managing," Copper said.The board will vote on a final decision on the cuts on Monday, Nov. 9.

title: Woman remains missing after her vehicle found crashed near Huron River, police say
description: A Southgate woman remains missing after her vehicle was found crashed into the backyard of a home in Huron Township.
content: A Southgate woman remains missing after her vehicle was found crashed into the backyard of a home in Huron Township, Michigan. The Huron Township Police Department said it was called about 5:34 p.m. Saturday on a report that a vehicle had crashed near a home in the 18000 block of Hannan Road, near the Huron River. The driver, later identified as 43-year-old Kimberly McGrath, could not be found. McGrath was not found at her home in Southgate, and family members told police they last had contact with her on Friday. The Huron Township Fire Department searched accessible areas of the Huron River. Law enforcement drone and K-9 searches, working with the Huron Township police and fire departments, Metroparks Police Department and Michigan State Police also searched the area. But she has not been found. "Our fear is that Kimberly could be injured from the crash," Huron Township Department of Public Safety Director Everette Robbins said. "Our number one priority is to locate her and make sure she is safe. We ask residents who live in that area to check their outbuildings or anywhere on your property where an injured person may seek shelter. We continue to investigate and use every resource available to us. Her family desperately wants her home, so if you know where she is, please call us." Police ask that anyone who has information about McGrath's whereabouts contact the Huron Township Police Department at 734-753-4400.

title: Minnesota State may shift up to $25 million a year from colleges to help 2 struggling universities
description: The plan would send $10 million to St. Cloud State and $4.8 million to Bemidji State, with most of the money coming from two-year schools. Trustees vote Oct. 14. College presidents, students and employees have objected.
content: Minnesota State is considering a plan to shift millions of dollars from its colleges to help two financially unstable universities â a move college presidents, students and employees condemned as the school system considers longer-term fixes to a growing financial crisis. The proposal, headed to the Board of Trustees for a final vote on Oct. 14, comes as the 270,000-student system grapples with broader budgetary distress that has officials weighing campus closures or mergers across its 26 colleges and seven universities. If approved, the proposal would allow the system to reallocate up to $25 million each year for the next four years â with reapproval required each spring â to "financially challenged institutions," taking a majority of the money from two-year schools.St. Cloud State University and Bemidji State University would together receive about $15 million. Both universities are running dangerously low on cash reserves despite steep budget cuts.System officials describe the proposal as a "stopgap" and hope it will act as a bridge until they tackle underlying financial problems driving a $31.5 million systemwide deficit that, if left unaddressed, is projected to more than triple by summer 2028.Bill Maki, the system's vice chancellor for facilities and finance, acknowledged the plan is "somewhat unprecedented" in the system's three-decade history. But he told MinnPost it's a matter of "crisis for a couple of institutions." "Action needs to be taken," he said. "This is not by any means a perfect solution. It is temporary."The proposal would send $10 million to St. Cloud State University in central Minnesota, an institution that has lost about 5,400 students in the past two decades. The university has already reduced its workforce by 40% in 15 years and suspended admission to nearly 200 academic majors, minors and certificates since 2023.Those cuts have not offset the lost tuition revenue from declining enrollment and other budget pressures, however. By this summer, a school spokesperson said, St. Cloud State will have "depleted" its reserve funding pool, a savings account that held nearly $19 million a decade ago. It also already took a $2 million loan from the system office. College presidents, students and employees staunchly opposed the proposal when the Board of Trustees first considered it in June.Now is not the time for a "temporary funding bandage," said Rose Sargent, the LeadMN student organization treasurer, in June."While the intent may be to stabilize struggling universities, reallocating resources away from colleges will not solve the root cause of those challenges," added the organization's then-vice president Marco Loera Alvarez. "Instead, it risks creating similar financial pressures for the very institutions that are currently serving students effectively."MinnPost contacted all college and university presidents in the Minnesota State system; most declined to comment on the proposal or did not answer.Lori Kloos, president of St. Cloud Technical and Community College, told the trustees in June it would be "extremely challenging" to manage a budget reduction. She questioned the decision to move ahead with taking money from community colleges before the system develops a long-term strategy to shore up its finances."A 5% reduction might not sound like a lot, but when 80% to 85% of our operating budgets are salary, there's an impact," Kloos said at the board meeting.It's not the first time Minnesota State has shifted money to help struggling schools: between 2005 and 2015, the system dedicated $5.5 million to eight colleges and one university in response to financial issues. But that money didn't come from the individual budgets of peer institutions.The board's vote comes on the heels of an announcement from Minnesota State Chancellor Scott Olson last month of a systemwide redesign that will likely include campus closures, mergers or consolidated administrative services. System officials will present initial options in January.Maki said work on the larger overhaul was accelerated, in part, due to concerns about the plan to move money from two-year schools. "I don't want to minimize those concerns," he said, adding that it's not possible to 100% avoid unintended consequences â including the potential to "weaken other institutions." In his Sept. 21 memo, Olson said the system needs to "urgently" cut costs. Eight institutions, five of which are universities, are projected to have ended fiscal year 2026 in poor financial health, according to system officials. Restructuring the system is critical to Minnesota State's future, Olson noted. He said cuts at individual colleges won't cover systemwide budget holes, which he attributed to "constrained" state funding, declining enrollment, inflation and reluctance to make Minnesota State unaffordable by continuing to raise tuition.In public meetings since Olson's announcement, employees demanded the system act transparently as it makes decisions affecting tens of thousands of people. During a Wednesday town hall at Century College, one professor raised the idea of shutting down St. Cloud State University, saying the university's financials appear to suggest it is "screaming for closure."In response, Olson noted that St. Cloud State is one of the largest universities in the system â it enrolls about 10,600 students â and said its closure would "strand all kinds of people." "Given their scale, given what they mean to the economy of central Minnesota, I guess I believe it's worth another try at saving them," he said. "Not everybody agrees with that."Kevin Lindstrom, president of the Minnesota State College Faculty, has spent months worrying about the consequences of the funding reallocation proposal on two-year colleges, especially smaller institutions in greater Minnesota. "Those places work really hard to stay afloat and to serve their communities," Lindstrom said in an interview. "They don't have a margin for error, and this will impact them disproportionately."System leaders have been discussing the potential to shift money to bolster the most-struggling institutions in public meetings since February. That plan was one of five draft proposals presented in June aimed at addressing systemwide financial troubles. A group of Minnesota State College and University presidents spent the summer tweaking the proposal with system officials, based on public feedback.Under the latest proposal that trustees will vote on, schools with smaller cash balances would contribute less toward an emergency fund used to help struggling institutions. If approved, the board would annually reassess the proposal through fiscal year 2031. For fiscal year 2028, colleges and universities would contribute between $121,000 and $1.8 million. Overall, two-year colleges would contribute about three times as much money as four-year universities, according to a MinnPost analysis.The system would then distribute $10 million to St. Cloud State University and $4.8 million to Bemidji State University.Bemidji, which educates about 4,000 students in northern Minnesota, has cut several academic programs, three dozen positions and one third of its faculty, spokesperson Andy Bartlett said. Despite raising new money and growing enrollment, reductions in state funding, coupled with salary increases, have resulted in "enduring deficits," Bartlett said. Other universities have also cut jobs, frozen hiring, consolidated operations, delayed investments and spent down reserves, Kenneth Janz, head of Winona State University, said during the June Board of Trustees meeting. He spoke as a representative for university presidents. University presidents support the reallocation proposal, he said then, because it "recognizes the seriousness of the current condition." But he does not want it to act as a substitute for broader financial fixes the system must make.Winona State University reduced its budget by $40 million in the past 15 years. Janz said the pandemic, which cut into revenue from in-person services like housing, meal plans and athletics, is one reason universities, in particular, are struggling."We cannot cut our way to sustainability," Janz said. On Wednesday, board members will consider another proposal to take $24.3 million from all institutions, through summer 2032, to demolish excess facilities. Because schools would otherwise use that money to buy equipment, the proposal would most affect two-year technical schools with equipment-intensive programs like welding or automotive programs., Olson said during a recent town hall.A draft of Minnesota State's budget request for the upcoming legislative session shows the system will ask lawmakers for $25 million in one-time funding to support struggling institutions, as well as $25 million for building demolition. The draft needs final approval from trustees in November and would be submitted to lawmakers for consideration. The board decisions come as the system examines other ways to cut costs, like getting rid of unused buildings to reduce maintenance and utilities expenses, redesigning the formula for dividing state funding across all schools, and sharing IT, cybersecurity and other services systemwide.Olson's announcement about a broader system restructure adds yet another layer onto those goals. Just last week, Minnesota State Community and Technical College announced it would close its Detroit Lakes campus, which educates just over 100 students near Fargo. That move, officials said, will save $1 million per year and $18 million in future costs, like maintenance, utilities and insurance.While Olson's memo created an enhanced sense of urgency, there have been warning signs of systemic financial problems for over a decade.A 2016 internal report warned that Minnesota State could face multimillion dollar budget holes and "a future that is financially unsustainable" due to factors like declining enrollment, excess buildings and diminishing state support."We cannot and must not wait until 2025 to begin to make changes or we will only compound the challenges of achieving financial sustainability," the report said.At a Century College town hall last week, Olson said that report "was put on a shelf." "It should have been dealt with. It wasn't," he said. "Now we have to deal with it. But it's not too late."

title: Newton County woman indicted for murder after boyfriend's remains found in shallow grave
description: A Covington woman is facing charges of murder, identity theft, and more after investigators say her boyfriend's remains were found in a shallow grave behind a home.
content: A woman is in custody without bond after officials say the remains of her boyfriend were found in a shallow grave in a Newton County home's backyard.In October, a Newton County grand jury indicted 43-year-old Taiesha Wilson on charges of malice murder, murder, concealing the death of another, identity theft, and more.Investigators say that the charges come after the remains of a man were found behind a home on Brighton Ridge Lane on July 5, a few days after the sheriff's office received intelligence reporting that 47-year-old Dee Dee O'Hara had been killed.The same day the man's body was found, authorities arrested Wilson, O'Hara's girlfriend, charging her with making false statements to Newton County investigators. She has been in custody at the Newton County Jail ever since.The Georgia Bureau of Investigation's Medical Examiner's Office identified the remains as O'Hara in August, and investigators say they learned he was killed in a "domestic-related" incident."The Newton County Sheriff's Office extends its deepest condolences to the family and loved ones of Dee Dee O'Hara during this difficult time," said Sheriff Brown. "Our agency remains committed to thoroughly investigating violent crimes and pursuing justice for victims and their families. We appreciate the assistance and collaboration of our partner agencies throughout this investigation."The investigation remains ongoing. Authorities are asking anyone with information to email Investigator Clinton French at clfrench@newtonsheriffga.org or calling the Newton County Sheriff's Office tip line at 678-625-1585.

title: U.S. blasts "embarrassing" complaint filed against Lebanon's ambassador
description: The Trump administration sharply criticized a legal complaint filed in Lebanon against the country's ambassador to Washington over her reported outreach to her Israeli counterpart.
content: Washington — The Trump administration sharply criticized a legal complaint filed in Lebanon against the country's ambassador to Washington over her reported outreach to her Israeli counterpart, accusing Hezbollah-linked actors of seeking to obstruct U.S.-led efforts to foster diplomatic contacts between the two countries.The complaint against Lebanese Ambassador Nada Hamadeh Moawad was filed with Lebanon's military judiciary by a lawyer the U.S. described as "pro-Hizbollah," in response to a report in Lebanese media that Moawad contacted Israeli Ambassador Yechiel Leiter after his son was seriously injured in a car-ramming terror attack in the West Bank last month."It is embarrassing that a military court is handling a complaint against the Lebanese Ambassador in Washington for carrying out the policy of their legitimate government and engaging in U.S.-led negotiations," a State Department spokesperson told CBS News late Tuesday, in an unusually pointed statement. The two diplomats have been participating in U.S.-brokered talks aimed at improving relations between Israel and Lebanon — an effort that has faced resistance from Iranian-backed Hezbollah. Lebanon and Israel held their first direct diplomatic talks in decades in Washington in April, with the Israeli and Lebanese ambassadors to the U.S. sitting alongside their American counterparts. Pictures of Secretary of State Marco Rubio with the ambassadors drew scorn from Hezbollah supporters in Lebanon."The Lebanese military judiciary should use its limited resources to prosecute Hizballah operatives plotting against the Lebanese government and people instead of working on their behalf," said the State Department official, who also called for the repeal of laws and practices that enable the "politicized targeting" of civilians and diplomats while shielding Hezbollah. "We have no patience for obstruction," the official said. That appeared to be a reference to a 1955-era anti-normalization law which was part of a broader Arab League boycott of Israel and prohibits any contact between Lebanese and Israeli citizens.A diplomatic source told CBS News that the law is outdated and has become a tool used by Hezbollah to suppress those who seek peace and normal relations with Israel.CBS News has reached out to the Israeli Embassy for comment.It is unclear whether the complaint against Moawad will result in formal proceedings. It comes amid a sustained push by the Trump administration to bring the longtime adversaries, still formally at war, closer together. In April, Secretary of State Marco Rubio hosted the two ambassadors for direct talks, acknowledging at the time that the U.S. was working against "decades of history and complexities." In June, the two countries signed a framework agreement meant to lay the groundwork for lasting peace, based on a gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces from southern Lebanon alongside the disarmament of Hezbollah and deployment of Lebanese government forces. Implementation of the agreement has stalled amid disagreements over the sequencing and verification of those steps. The last formal round of talks, held in Rome in August, ended without a breakthrough. The ambassadors met most recently at the State Department in September, and another round of negotiations is expected this month in Rome.

title: All 55 decomposing bodies found at South Chicago Chapel funeral home identified by Cook County Medical Examiner's Office
description: More than two months after authorities found dozens of decomposing bodies at the South Chicago Chapel funeral home, the Cook County Medical Examiner's office has identified all 55 people whose bodies were found inside.
content: More than two months after authorities found dozens of decomposing bodies inside the South Chicago Chapel on the Far South Side, the Cook County Medical Examiner's office has identified all 55 people whose bodies were found inside the funeral home.Officials previously said that 56 bodies were found inside the funeral home, but have since determined it was actually 55.The medical examiner's office said that there were 55 decomposing bodies found, and one bag of organs that authorities originally believed to be a different person, but that DNA testing confirmed belonged to one of the 55 bodies.South Chicago Chapel's funeral director's license was suspended in early August, when state regulators found decomposing bodies were being kept in "deplorable conditions" that included rodent and maggot infestations.According to the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation records, the state suspended the license of funeral director Johanna Morgan due to a finding that the facility's "continued practice is a danger to the public safety, interest and welfare."Records show Morgan had been "allowing multiple decedents to be kept in an unrefrigerated area with deplorable conditions including rodent infestation, causing decomposition and maggot infestation of the bodies."Her husband, Clark Morgan, previously was caught improperly handling bodies at the Heights Crematory in south suburban Chicago Heights in March 2025. After that discovery, the Illinois State Comptroller's office, which regulates crematoriums, tried over and over and over again to get the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation, which regulates funeral homes, to suspend Johanna's funeral director license. For their part, the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation said they filed formal disciplinary charges against Johanna Morgan in October 2025. But the agency has yet to agree to an interview to help explain why she still had her license before it was suspended in August 2026.In May 2025, after shutting down Heights Crematory, the Comptroller's office asked why the Morgans hadn't faced any criminal charges. According to emails CBS News Chicago obtained through records requests, Illinois State Police forwarded a long list of possible charges to the Cook County States Attorney's Office:443 potential violations of the Crematory Regulation Act 715 counts involving the Integrity in Death Care Act. And 8 counts of abuse of a corpse. But a spokesperson for the Cook County States Attorney's office said in August that, upon receiving the info from state police, they "recommended that ISP continue their investigation and consider the possibility of financial crimes." Last month, the city of Chicago filed a lawsuit against Clark and Johanna Morgan and several of their business entities, accusing them of 23 building code violations at South Chicago Chapel. Among other allegations, the lawsuit accuses them of failing to keep the building "clean, sanitary and safe," failing to install fire alarms or carbon monoxide detectors anywhere in the building, and unpermitted construction on the second floor. The city is asking a judge to fine the owners $11,500 per day for every day the violations go uncorrected.

title: Keller: Deaton brought fire against Markey in Massachusetts Senate debate, but math not in his favor
description: Democratic Senator Ed Markey and Republican challenger John Deaton met in their first and only debate before the November election.
content: The opinions expressed below are Jon Keller's, not those of WBZ-TV, CBS News or Skydance.Republican Massachusetts Senate nominee John Deaton is not stupid. He knows he's a massive underdog in his race against incumbent Ed Markey, trailing by a RealClearPolitics polling average of 23 points, a yawning gap that has never shown any sign of closing.And he can read the national polls too. "We all know that the Democrats are going to win the House, and the Democrats are going to win the Senate," Deaton said in Tuesday night's WBZ debate. "You have a chance to send a nonpartisan person like me [to Washington] who will really put America first and decide, 'Is it good for Massachusetts and America?' And if it is, I'll support it."This is the choice cut from Deaton's beef with Markey - his argument, aimed at independents and disgruntled Democrats, that Markey is too partisan to be trusted. After agreeing with Markey that Donald Trump's war with Iran is illegal and foolish, Deaton cited military ventures under Democratic presidents that "you never said a word [about] because they wear Democrat jerseys. I wear an American jersey. I call President Trump out, I'll call a Democrat president out."Unfortunately for Deaton, the math is not in his favor. Mr. Trump's job approval in Massachusetts is at a record low in the most recent polling last month, third worst in the nation. Just 7% of Democrats approve, along with a pitiful 12% of independents. Even among Republicans, approval of Mr. Trump has tumbled to 64%, down from 79% in August.And by emphasizing his distaste for much of the Trump agenda and his refusal to vote for Mr. Trump, Deaton has even shrunk the available pool of Republican votes, not that they amount to much.So, it was no wonder that Markey made a run at the world record for disparaging references to Mr. Trump in an hourlong debate set by Gov. Maura Healey just last week. Trump has "declared war on the Massachusetts economy" and "targeted" Markey's neighbors in Malden, he said. And right off the top he cast Deaton as "the elephant in the room," a poseur who "gave $350,000 to the Republican Party in order to buy this nomination. He's got an R on his jersey, he bought that R … He's trying to pretend that he's an independent and that he's a Republican at the same time. That's an oxymoron. It's like trying to be a carnivorous vegetarian, you just can't get away with that."Ouch.Deaton was well-prepared, brought the fire, and landed a number of blows that at times appeared to make Markey wince. But the incumbent never took the bait, pivoting away from every taunt with a Trump-related counter.In this state, this year, with this president insisting voters pretend he's on the ballot, that should be more than enough.

title: Flint man convicted of firing into home, paralyzing ex-girlfriend
description: A 23-year-old Flint man accused of firing into a home and paralyzing his 17-year-old ex-girlfriend has been convicted, Genesee County Prosecutor David Leyton said.
content: A 23-year-old Flint man accused of firing into a home and paralyzing his 17-year-old ex-girlfriend has been convicted, Genesee County Prosecutor David Leyton said.Mario Devon White Jr. was found guilty of discharging a firearm in or at a building causing serious impairment of a body function, felony firearm and domestic violence, according to the prosecutor's office.White will be sentenced on Nov. 9 and faces up to 20 years in prison, as well as a mandatory two-year sentence for felony firearm.Prosecutors say that on March 23, 2025, the victim was at her home with a man who was playing a video game and talking in an online group chat when White joined the chat. White heard the victim talking in the background and threatened her physically before the man with her replied that White would have to go through him to get to her, prosecutors say.Video footage showed that White arrived at the victim's home shortly afterward and that he and the man got into a fistfight outside before the man went back inside, prosecutors say.The victim then opened the front door, saw White outside with a gun, shouted a warning to the others in the house and slammed the door shut, according to prosecutors. Prosecutors say that White fired at the house, and at least four shots struck it, with two going through the front door. One of the shots struck the victim, leaving her paralyzed, and she spent several months in the hospital, prosecutors say."What started as an argument in an online chat ended with a 17-year-old paralyzed inside her own home. None of this had to happen. A disagreement like this one should end with words, never with someone coming to the door and firing into the house. Our thoughts are with her and her family as she faces a long road ahead," Leyton said. The jury found White not guilty of assault with intent to commit murder and an accompanying count of felony firearm.

title: College Park man posed as child to manipulate young girls to send him nude photos, prosecutors say
description: Prosecutors say the 23-year-old Georgia man had chatted with hundreds of girls as young as 9 online while pretending to be a boy their age.
content: A College Park man will spend over a decade in federal prison for posing as a child online to manipulate underage girls into sending him sexually explicit photos and videos, officials say.Dye'Shuan Green, 23, pleaded guilty to one count of production of child sexual abuse material and four counts of enticement to create child sexual abuse material in June.Prosecutors say the investigation into Green began in 2022, when a Columbus mother reported to local police that her daughter had been manipulated by a man to send him nude images. An investigation led by the FBI revealed Green had young victims around the country, officials said.According to investigators, Green found young girls on social media and gaming sites while pretending to be a boy their age. Once they started talking, Green befriended his victims and said that he wanted to have a relationship with them. He then allegedly begged and threatened the girls to send him sexually explicit photos.Authorities say Green has chatted with hundreds of young girls online. His victims were allegedly as young as 9 years old."Posing as a child and then pressuring children, among the most vulnerable members of our society, to produce sexually explicit and harmful material is unconscionable," said Marlo Graham, special agent in charge of FBI Atlanta. On Tuesday, a U.S. district court judge sentenced Green to 16 years and 10 months in prison, followed by 15 years of supervised release."The Court's sentence holds a predator accountable for his reprehensible acts and ensures he won't victimize another child for most of the next two decades," said U.S. Attorney Theodore S. Hertzberg, "This case also serves as a reminder to parents and caretakers about the dangers deviant criminals like Green pose to young people online."

title: Chicago students organize care package for Pope Leo following lung cancer diagnosis
description: Chicago students who met with Pope Leo in Rome last year are showing support following his lung cancer diagnosis.
content: Chicago students who met with Pope Leo in Rome last year are showing support following his lung cancer diagnosis. The Vatican said doctors removed the lower lobe of the Pope's right lung. Testing during the operation confirmed lung cancer. Doctors have not released the cancer's stage, whether it has spread, or what additional treatment he may need. Students at Our Lady of Mount Carmel Academy are preparing a special care package, including a White Sox blanket, so he has a little piece of home as he recovers in the hospital. "I want to make sure that he knows that we all love him and we want him to feel good," eighth-grader Lucas Knudsen said. "We are with him, and we can walk together with God." They're part of Team 14, a 40-member student group named in honor of Pope Leo. The group formed after students went viral for holding a mock papal election in their classroom.That eventually led to a trip to Rome, where students and their families met the Pope.The students continue to take part in monthly prayer and service projects, including food drives for a west-side pantry. Now, they are coming together to pray for the Pope and make get-well cards. Their teacher, Allison Foerster said this is about showing appreciation. "We want him to know he's in our prayers and that we appreciate him and that we wish him well," Foerster said.

title: Kelly Clarkson's art store incident caught on video as debate rages
description: The viral spat​ between a Brooklyn store and singer Kelly Clarkson continues as the store released surveillance video of the alleged incident.
content: The viral spat between a Brooklyn store and music superstar Kelly Clarkson continues as the store released surveillance video of the alleged incident. Clarkson accused staff at Art of Play in Brooklyn Heights of treating her poorly, which blew up on social media. The video has no audio but shows the interaction between Clarkson and two store employees. Clarkson is seen walking into the store with a yellow shirt and a baseball hat on. She looks around before going over to the animatronic singing bird that she wanted to buy.She is seen pointing to the object, which is hung on the wall. Then it looks like Clarkson calls an employee over.They talk briefly while he leans against a counter before she walks back to the entryway of the store. When she is at the front, Clarkson turns to a person who was behind a counter and looks agitated.The singer throws her hands up and walks out. She only spent about five minutes in the store, according to timecode on the video.The feud began when Clarkson posted on social media that an employee at the store looked at her as if she couldn't afford the $15,000 bird. "Wow, dude. You're an idiot and just lost a huge sale. But y'all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts character in Pretty Woman," she wrote, in part.Art of Play said the bird wasn't for sale, but staff offered to show her a different mechanical bird. Employees also said the bird's creator said he would be willing to sell Clarkson a nearly identical bird. In an interview with Inside Edition, Art of Play owner Adam Rubin said he fears for his staff after the situation blew up."We are afraid for the safety of our shopkeepers. Kelly Clarkson has put us in danger," he said.The Retail, Wholesale and Department Store Union also spoke out, saying that whether it is a celebrity or a regular person, "no customer has the right to abuse retail workers on the floor or mobilize online harassment against them."

title: Postage still owed on mailers supporting Sheng Thao during Oakland mayoral race
description: Many questions remain about the raid at Oakland Mayor Sheng Thao's home including why the Postal Inspection Service also took part.
content: Many questions remain about the raid at Oakland Mayor Sheng Thao's home including why the Postal Inspection Service also took part.And while the Postal Inspection Service has declined to comment on why it was involved, CBS News Bay Area learned the USPS is owed tens of thousands dollars after delivering campaign mailers that aimed to benefit Thao when she was running for mayor. Samari Johnson owns Butterfly Direct Marketing, a direct mailing agency in Oakland. Johnson said his company printed the attack flyers and mailed them out in 2022.Johnson said a couple of weeks before the November 2022 general election, a long-time customer, Mario Juarez, contracted him to print roughly 170,000 attack mailers targeting Oakland mayoral candidates Ignacio De La Fuente and Loren Taylor."The picture of me was doctored up. My skin is darkened. My eyes are turned red. The eyebrows are pointy, sort of invoking images of a devil or something like that," recalled Taylor.Johnson said the attack ads went out about one week before the election. He said Juarez paid him $31,200 for his service and gave him three checks to pay the U.S. Postal Service for the postage. After the mailers went out, he said all three checks bounced, totaling more than $53,000.Johnson said with interest, Juarez now owes the US government roughly $60,000."It's been very heartbreaking, very disturbing, very emotional," said Johnson. "The USPS put a postal stop on my business direct mail permit."He said his permit remains suspended.The fine prints on the mailers said they were funded by Juarez and his independent expenditure or I.E. account called California Forward Now. CBS News Bay Area checked to see who donated money to that I.E. account. But it did not appear Juarez filed any paperwork to identify the donors, which is required by campaign financing laws.But Renia Webb, Thao's former chief of staff, said she knows who paid for those flyers. Webb served as Thao's chief of staff when Thao was the District 4 councilmember. She also volunteered on Thao's mayoral campaign.However, Webb resigned from Thao's office after Thao won the election citing concerns over public corruption. CBS News Bay Area did an extensive report on Webb's pay-to-play allegations against the mayor and her boyfriend, Andre Jones."The post office is involved with this investigation because it was the mail fraud with them using the funding to get those flyers sent out," said Webb.Webb said Andy Duong of California Waste Solutions was backing Thao for mayor. Webb claimed Duong was paying Juarez to attack Thao's chief rivals, De La Fuente and Taylor.She recalled one meeting between Thao, Duong, and Juarez at a Jack London Square restaurant."Andy was like, 'Yeah, I need to talk to you about something.' And Mario was like, 'Yeah, I need some more money.' That was his exact words. And he and Sheng and Mario went off to the corner right outside of Seabreeze where the Jack London (cabin) is. And they stood right there and talked maybe for about 15 minutes," said Webb. "I know that they're not supposed to be doing that. During campaigns, the campaign and that I.E. account are never supposed to work together. They're supposed to be two separate total entities."Webb and Johnson believed the unpaid postage or the mailers could be one reason why the U.S. Postal Inspection Service was involved in last week's raid."I can't speak to the U.S. Postal Service investigation. But what I can say is that to stiff a small business based in Oakland, a Black-owned business out of $60,000 is shameful," said Taylor.The U.S. Postal Inspection Service deferred all questions to the FBI, which had declined to comment on the raids.FBI investigators have not accused Thao, Duong, or Juarez of any wrongdoing. But the Alameda County District Attorney charged Juarez with one count of felony for passing bad checks.As for Johnson, he's used to printing mud-slinging ads, but he's not happy he's caught up in one."And it's also an embarrassment to my business to be involved in this type of situation," said Johnson.Thao's spokesperson released a statement that read, "as Mayor Thao has previously said, she is committed to cooperating with the investigation and looks forward to the opportunity to vindicate herself. But she will not indulge rumor and innuendo. We expect there will be an opportunity to say more, but now is not the time."CBS News Bay Area contacted California Waste Solutions to get a comment from Andy Duong. CBS News Bay Area also contacted Mario Juarez. They did not respond back before publication deadline.Taylor lost the 2022 mayoral election to Thao by less than 700 votes. Taylor is assemblying a team to run for the mayoral seat if Thao is ousted. Thao insisted at a recent press conference she would not resign.But she is facing a recall in the November election."If the best way for me to serve my city and make sure that we get on top of these issues is to place my name on the ballot for mayor, then that's what you'll likely see," said Taylor. If voters recall Thao in the November election, the city council president would serve as the interim mayor. The county election's office would then have 120 days to set up a special election to elect a new mayor.

title: Colorado storm brings mountain snow, beneficial rain and a chance for widespread frost
description: Mountain travel could turn difficult Wednesday night as snow increases at higher elevations. Denver and the northern Front Range could see much-needed rain before a sharp cooldown brings frost and freeze concerns by Friday morning.
content: Widespread snow is expected across Colorado's mountains, with some rain for the Front Range.Timing out the stormRain and snow will become more widespread Tuesday night, mainly across the high country. A few bands will escape the mountains, bringing light to moderate rain across the Eastern Plains.The mountains will see the most widespread rain and snow Wednesday all day Wednesday. For Denver and the northern Front Range, the best chance for widespread rain arrives Wednesday evening, potentially lasting into Thursday morning.And now for something you hear with every storm: Track is key.A northern storm track would keep moisture around Denver, Boulder and Fort Collins longer into Thursday morning. A southern track, which the American model is currently showing, could leave northern Colorado with much less rain.I'm favoring the northern track right now, but that's the little "boom or bust" factor with this storm.Rain and snow totalsSnow could fall as low as 8,500 feet Wednesday night into Thursday. Most mountain roads should remain wet, but slick conditions are possible above 9,000 feet, especially after dark.Winter Weather Advisories will go into effect Wednesday at 6:00 a.m. until 6 a.m. Thursday. This storm is all about elevation. The higher you go, the faster snow totals will increase. Travel could become difficult across some of Colorado's highest mountain passes.For the northern Front Range, we're expecting some very beneficial rain. Denver, Boulder and Fort Collins could pick up anywhere from a third of an inch to 1 inch, assuming the northern storm track holds.A big cooldown is on the wayTemperatures will continue dropping through the week, with the biggest cooldown arriving Thursday night into Friday morning. By Friday morning, lows will be below freezing in the high country, with 30s and lower 40s across the Western Slope and Front Range. That brings the potential for the first widespread frost of the season, with a freeze possible in colder areas. If you still have sensitive plants outside, bring them inside or cover them Thursday night. Winter is coming!

title: Rush University System and Endeavor Health announce merger, would create largest health system in Chicago
description: Rush University System for Health and Endeavor Health announced they will merge into a single integrated academic health system, creating the largest health system in Chicago.
content: Rush University System for Health and Endeavor Health announced they will merge into a single integrated academic health system, creating the largest health system in Chicago.The combined system will have 12 award-winning hospitals and more than 400 care sites, the merger announcement said. Endeavor Health will also fund an incremental $1 billion investment to advance community impact, academics and research, and care innovations across the Chicagoland region. The announcement said a "significant portion" of that investment will be spent on community partnership to address "social determinants of health" and creating infrastructure to support underserved patients and communities.The combined health system will operate under the Rush name, officials said. Endeavor Health president and CEO J.P Gallagher will be named president and CEO of the unified system once the merger is complete; current president and CEO of Rush, Dr. Omar Lateef, will remain in place through close, then serve as CEO Emeritus and Strategic Advisor to the CEO. The health system will be governed by a 20-person board appointed equally from the Rush and Endeavor systems, and led by a chair from Rush.Rush University System is a nonprofit health system including Rush University Medical Center, Rush University, Rush Copley Medical Center and Rush Oak Park Hospital. Endeavor is Illinois' third-largest health system based in the Chicago area and serving seven northeast Illinois counties.
