Their hospitals include Edward, Elmhurst, Evanston, Glenbrook, Highland Park, Northwest Community, Skokie and Swedish Hospital. Endeavor Health also recently announced a new partnership with the Lynn Sage Breast Cancer Foundation, joining their multi-institution Chicago Breast Cancer Research Consortium. Rush is already a member of the group, as are Northwestern Medicine and University of Chicago Medicine. The health systems estimate the future combined organization will have more than 46,00 0 employees and serve more than 2 million patients each year in Northern Illinois and Northwest Indiana.Rush and Endeavor said they expect to complete the merger in early 2027 after regulatory review and approval.

title: Colorado rain totals: more rain and mountain snow expected
description: Wednesday is a First Alert Weather Day as a strong fall storm brings a blast of much colder air, widespread rain across the Denver metro area and heavy snow to the mountains.
content: Wednesday is a First Alert Weather Day as a strong fall storm brings a blast of much colder air, widespread rain across the Denver metro area, and heavy snow to the mountains. As of Wednesday morning, many communities across Colorado have picked up measurable precipitation, with more to come.Latest Rain Reports Across Colorado: Durango: 2.04 inchesSilverton: 1.71 inches Golden: 1.37 inchesBoulder: 1.25 inchesArvada: 1.14 inchesPagosa Springs: 1.01 inches Evergreen: 0.99 inches Morrison: 0.88 inches Superior: 0.80 inches Littleton: 0.77 inchesDenver: 0.38 inchesRain and mountain snow will increase in coverage Wednesday afternoon and continue into Wednesday night. Temperatures will remain chilly, with highs mainly in the 40s across much of the Denver metro area. Snow levels are expected to drop to around 7,000 feet by Thursday morning. The heaviest snow is forecast above 9,000 to 10,000 feet, where several inches of accumulation are possible.Higher mountain elevations could receive 4 to 12 inches of snow, while mountain valleys and higher foothills may see lighter accumulations, including at least a dusting in some areas.The combination of accumulating snow and potentially slick roads could affect travel in the mountains from Wednesday afternoon through Thursday morning. Drivers heading over mountain passes should be prepared for changing road conditions. The first Winter Weather Advisory of the season is posted for the mountains starting Wednesday afternoon through Thursday morning. Rain could also linger along the Interstate 25 corridor and across the eastern plains Thursday morning as cooler air moves into the region. Precipitation is expected to gradually taper off Thursday afternoon as the storm system moves east and weakens.Behind the storm, colder overnight temperatures could bring the first freeze of the season to much of Colorado's eastern plains. Temperatures are expected to drop to freezing or below late Thursday night into early Friday morning across much of the plains. Those with sensitive plants, outdoor vegetation, or exposed plumbing should prepare for the possibility of freezing temperatures. A Freeze Warning is in place from midnight tonight through Thursday morning for the San Luis Valley, where temperatures could drop into the mid-20s to lower 30s. A Freeze Watch is in place Thursday night through Friday morning for El Paso and Kiowa counties, with overnight lows dipping into the upper 20s to lower 30s.The colder weather will be short-lived, however, as drier conditions and a warming trend return. By Friday, skies should begin clearing and temperatures will gradually moderate. A mostly dry forecast is expected to continue through the weekend, with temperatures climbing back above seasonal averages. Above-normal temperatures are also expected to continue into early next week.

title: How this new safety technology is helping some students at Pennsylvania School for the Deaf in Germantown
description: Some students at the Pennsylvania School for the Deaf in Germantown have new safety technology.
content: Some students at the Pennsylvania School for the Deaf in Germantown have new safety technology. It's needed because most alarms are sound-based, which doesn't help people who are deaf. Now, a special group of students has new technology that turns sounds into lights, words and vibrations.I'zariah Jennings, 18, is learning about new safety technology for people like her, who are deaf.When a smoke detector goes off, the device flashes a light. The screen says "smoke," and there's a vibrating piece to alert the person.In addition to alerting for fires, the HomeAware device can also signal for things like doorbells and phone calls. "It definitely makes me feel more safe because I have the vibration and the light to give me information," Jennings said through an interpreter. "I really love this technology. It's great because you can avoid dangerous situations if something happens. If nobody is with you in the house, I can do it independently."Jennings is among the students at the Pennsylvania School for the Deaf and the Transition Academy who received the devices in partnership with Children's Hospital of Philadelphia's Center for Childhood Communication, which provided a $10,000 grant."I love it. It's very much needed for our students," said Kim Stephan, who is the supervisor of outreach services.Melissa Draganac-Hawk, the head of the school, said the donation is a huge benefit. "Clearly, as a deaf person, it's important that we have access to alarms," Draganac-Hawk said. "I'm thrilled for the students, for their additional opportunity for independence and growth, to not have that dependence on their families and for the family's concern and worry about their students."The devices can also be programmed for 20 different sounds, including a baby crying and storm alerts that can be life-saving for people who can't hear.

title: Students, volunteers partner to improve Southwest Detroit school
description: Ally Financial employees and volunteers joined leaders from Detroit Public Schools Community District and the DPSCD Foundation for a Day of Service.
content: Students at Neinas Dual Language Learning Academy got a firsthand lesson in community service as volunteers worked side by side with them to improve their school on Tuesday.Ally Financial employees and volunteers joined leaders from Detroit Public Schools Community District and the DPSCD Foundation for a Day of Service focused on supporting students, families and educators at the Southwest Detroit school.Projects stretched across the campus, including the beautification of the school's community garden, the assembly of hundreds of snack packs for families and a makeover of the teachers' lounge.For students like Juan Angulo, the garden renovation is especially meaningful."I finally can see a change in the garden and how it's, it helps better for the little kids, so that way they can enjoy it like I did," Angulo said.The community garden has long been a gathering place for students, who help maintain the space and participate in activities there throughout the school year."I think it's very cool because when the kids come out, they're able to see all the new plants and like the flowers and everything that's going on," student Dulce Rodriguez said. "And it's a part of our community, so it's like an important space for us."The event was made possible through a partnership between Ally Financial and the DPSCD Foundation, which works to connect schools with community partners that can help meet specific needs identified by school leaders."This is what we want alumni to do, to come back, give back, show our current students that they are supported from people that walk through the same door as they get," said Kerrie Mitchell Campbell-Mabins, president and CEO of the DPSCD Foundation.One of those alumni is Kathie Patterson, Ally Financial's chief human resources and corporate citizenship officer. Patterson attended Detroit Public Schools and once walked the halls of Neinas herself."I have goosebumps," Patterson said. "I don't think I realized how powerful of an emotional feeling I'd have walking through those school doors."In addition to providing volunteer support, Ally Financial also donated $50,000 to support DPSCD initiatives.Organizers hope the effort inspires more businesses to partner with local schools, demonstrating how community investment can create lasting benefits for students, teachers and families.

title: Colorado voters guide to all the ballot measures
description: Colorado voters will decide on 14 statewide ballot measures this November, covering issues ranging from taxes and crime to election rules and civil rights.
content: Colorado voters will decide ballot measures regarding everything from taxes and crime to election rules and civil rights this November.The Secretary of State's Office says 13 citizen-initiated measures have qualified for the ballot. Democratic lawmakers in the state legislature also referred a measure.The measures address familiar issues, including immigration enforcement, crime penalties and transgender rights. Others would establish constitutional rights related to natural gas and hunting and fishing. There are also questions for voters to answer about taxes and government spending.The measures generally fall into four broad categories: taxes, criminal justice, elections and voting, and civil rights. Four measures would reshape Colorado's tax structure and government spending limits. Proposition 136 would permanently cap Colorado's flat income tax rate at its current 4.4%. Amendment 87 would replace the flat tax with a graduated system that raises taxes on households earning more than $500,000 annually while lowering taxes on those earning less. Backers estimate the change would generate roughly $2 billion in additional revenue during its first year, with funds dedicated to education, healthcare and childcare. The revenue would be exempt from Taxpayer's Bill of Rights (TABOR) spending limits. If both Proposition 136 and Amendment 87 pass, the measure receiving the higher vote total would determine whether the 4.4% cap remains in effect. Proposition NN would allow the state to retain and spend an estimated $4.5 billion or more that would otherwise be refunded to taxpayers under TABOR. During the first decade, the money would be directed toward education and children's programs. After that, lawmakers would decide how to spend the funds. Proposition 137 would require revenue from taxes on sporting goods and outdoor equipment, estimated at $175 million annually, to fund wildfire mitigation and conservation programs exclusively. Three proposals focus on crime and law enforcement. Proposition 132 would make possession of any amount of fentanyl a felony punishable by up to eight years in prison. Distribution offenses could carry sentences of up to 32 years. Defendants found with less than one gram who complete treatment programs could have charges reduced to misdemeanors.Proposition 133 would increase penalties for child sex trafficking, allowing sentences of life in prison without parole. Amendment 81 would require state and local law enforcement agencies to notify federal immigration authorities when a person whose immigration status cannot be verified is charged with a violent crime or has a prior felony conviction. Two constitutional amendments address election administration and redistricting. Amendment 84 would require voters casting ballots by mail in state and federal elections to provide either the last four digits of their Social Security number, a driver's license number, or a state-issued identification number. In-person voting procedures would remain unchanged. Amendment 86 would prohibit congressional district boundaries from being redrawn to favor one political party over another and would require approval from Colorado's Independent Congressional Redistricting Commission before changes could be made outside the normal census cycle.Four measures deal with civil rights. Proposition 134 would require schools at all levels, from elementary schools through colleges and universities, to limit girls' sports to biological females and boys' sports to biological males. Current Colorado law allows students to participate on teams that align with their gender identity. Proposition 135 would prohibit gender-transition surgeries for minors when performed in response to a perceived gender identity. The measure would also prohibit insurance providers and state or federal government programs from paying for such procedures.Amendment 82 establishes a constitutional right to buy and sell natural gas in Colorado. Amendment 83 would create a constitutional right to hunt and fish and designate hunting and fishing as the preferred methods for managing wildlife populations in the state. Finally, Amendment 85 would require ballot titles to be written at an eighth grade reading level. The proposal would also prevent the Legislature from requiring specific wording that could interfere with that standard. With measures touching on taxes, public safety, elections, energy policy and social issues, Colorado voters will face one of the most diverse statewide ballots in recent years when they cast their votes in November.

title: Crash-and-grab burglars take ATM from Shell Gas station in Highland Park
description: Crash-and-grab burglars targeted a Shell Gas station in Highland Park, Illinois, overnight.
content: Crash-and-grab burglars targeted a Shell Gas station in Highland Park, Illinois, early Wednesday morning. Highland Park officials said police responded to the Rmarts convenience store at the gas station in the 1400 block of Park Ave, along U.S. Route 41, just before 3:30 a.mOfficials said officers found extensive damage to the front of the business and a black Jeep Cherokee with rear-end damage. Video from inside the store shows four masked people wearing gloves taking the ATM. The store owner told CBS News Chicago the burglars took an ATM with $2,000 inside. Officials confirmed the Jeep was later reported stolen from of Chicago. An investigation is ongoing.

title: Democrat Jared Moskowitz taking on Republican Scott Singer in race for Florida's District 25
description: The race for Florida's newly redrawn Congressional District 25 is set to be the most expensive race in the U.S.
content: We're just about three weeks away from knowing who will be representing the newly redrawn Florida Congressional District 25, which is set to be the most expensive race in the nation.It runs from Miami Beach to Delray Beach in South Florida, and both candidates and voters spoke with CBS News Miami.Voters have their concerns and say they've been hit hard in the wallet."A cut of beef that used to be $70, if you're entertaining people and you're just getting some steaks or something, now it's $170," said Nino de la Osa.Other voters say they have concerns about immigration policy."It's immigration. I'm concerned about that," Shilean Lopez said. "The economy, the gas, that stuff I'm really concerned about."Democrat incumbent Jared Moskowitz is facing off with former Republican Boca Raton Mayor Scott Singer."We have to lower costs for the American people," Moskowitz said. "When they go into the grocery store, they don't see partisanship, they just see prices."Singer is focusing on the economy as well, as the two battle it out for the District 25 congressional seat."We need to get that spending under control," Singer said. "We need to put more money back in the taxpayers wallets."Moskowitz is the former Florida emergency management director, appointed by Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis."When I agree with the Democrats on an idea, I vote with my party. When I think my party's wrong, I vote against it. I have a very independent record," he said.He said Singer will vote however President Donald Trump tells him to."He's gonna be a rubber stamp for the Trump administration, and I'm gonna be independent," Moskowitz said.That's not true," Singer said. "I'm not a rubber stamp for anyone. I, as mayor, I had broad bipartisan support and didn't agree with everyone 100% of the time," Singer said.Singer says it's Moskowitz who will vote party line."Jared Moskowitz is going to vote for whoever Democratic leadership tells him. And unfortunately, the socialist wing seems to be taking over the Democratic Party race by race," he said.CBS News Miami asked Singer if he agrees with current immigration enforcement. He says Congress has to focus on sane policy."When you have a hangover from President Biden of more than 10 million people coming in illegally, it's going to be challenging to get some of those people out. It's up to the executive to make sure that they're administering the laws," he said.Moskowitz points out what he calls broken promises from Mr. Trump."He said he was going to only go after criminals when it came to immigration, and yet he broke his promise on TPS to Venezuelans, he broke his promise on TPS to Haitians. And now you've got ICE operating in Miami, you know, rounding up people from the Cuban community," Moskowitz said.Singer is challenging Moskowitz to a televised debate, but said his opponent refused.Moskowitz says the two will face off on a Zoom with the Sun Sentinel and at two community forums.

title: Social Security sets its 2027 COLA increase at 3.6%. Here's what that means for your benefits.
description: The 2027 cost-of-living adjustment is the largest since 2023. Here's how it will impact the typical benefit check starting early next year.
content: More than 75 million Americans will get a 3.6% boost to their monthly Social Security benefits next year, due to a cost-of-living adjustment announced Wednesday by the Social Security Administration. The 2027 cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, represents the largest annual boost for Social Security recipients in four years. The bigger increase is meant to keep pace with higher inflation this year, driven in part by soaring fuel prices sparked by the war in Iran. Starting in January, next year's COLA will increase the average Social Security payment by roughly $75 to $2,170 a month, the Social Security Administration said. The Labor Department said Wednesday that the Consumer Price Index, a closely watched inflation gauge, rose at an annual rate of 3.7% in September. The annual COLA helps older Americans, people with disabilities and other Social Security beneficiaries stay ahead of rising prices, ensuring their benefits don't lose purchasing power. Yet critics say the measure may fall short for many seniors struggling to cope with rising costs following a 2.8% benefits adjustment in 2026 — a rate that has lagged the CPI for the last seven months. "While a 3.6% COLA is certainly welcome, it wouldn't necessarily restore the purchasing power seniors have already lost," Shannon Benton, executive director of the advocacy group Senior Citizens League, told CBS News. "The COLAs are designed to keep pace with inflation, not make up for years of falling behind." She added, "The bottom line is that seniors aren't getting ahead. They're getting a slightly bigger check to pay bills that have gotten even bigger." About 7.3 million people who receive Supplemental Security Income will see the new COLA reflected starting on Dec. 31, 2026, the agency said. The 3.6% COLA lags September's inflation data, noted Nancy Altman, president of Social Security Works, an advocacy group for the program. "People are getting crushed by prices," Altman said in an email. "As important as the Social Security COLA is, it is not keeping up with prices." How Social Security calculates the COLA Each fall, the Social Security Administration announces its inflation adjustment based on a metric known as the "Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers," or CPI-W, which tracks the average change in prices paid by workers for a basket of commonly purchased goods and services. The COLA is based on that inflation data from July through September. However, some advocates for senior citizens say that the CPI-W doesn't accurately reflect spending by older Americans, who tend to spend more on healthcare than younger people. Those costs have tended to rise faster than overall inflation. As such, some experts support using different measures to make Social Security's annual adjustment. "We favor the adoption of the CPI-E (Consumer Price Index for the Elderly), which calculates the impact of inflation on seniors' true living costs," Max Richtman, president of the National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare, told CBS News. The advocacy group has endorsed two congressional bills — the Social Security Expansion Act and the Social Security 2100 Act — that would make the switch to the CPI-E. "Without adopting a more adequate COLA formula, seniors likely will continue to tread water or fall behind rather than 'catch up,'" Richtman said. Medicare has not yet announced its 2027 premiums, which could eat into Social Security's inflation adjustment, experts said. Part B premiums, which pay for doctor visits and outpatient care, are automatically deducted from seniors' monthly Social Security checks. "For some retirees, a significant portion of their COLA increase can be absorbed by healthcare costs before they even have a chance to spend it elsewhere," Tyler End, a certified financial planner and CEO of retirement planning firm Retirable, told CBS News. End added, "Healthcare inflation runs 5.8% annually, while COLA averages 2.4%. Even on paper, a 3.6% COLA only goes so far if the costs retirees face most heavily continue to rise faster than their benefits." More senior citizens in poverty Social Security is the largest antipoverty program in the U.S., the Census Bureau said last month. However, the poverty rate among seniors has been inching higher for several years, rising to 15.4% last year from 14.2% in 2022, according to government data. Experts attribute that increase partly to issues such as rising healthcare costs, lagging Social Security benefits and insufficient retirement savings. In an AARP survey taken ahead of the COLA announcement, about three-quarters of older Americans said a 3.5% inflation adjustment in their Social Security benefits wouldn't be enough to keep up with rising prices. "There's a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans: 1 in 5 have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last," AARP CEO Myechia Minter-Jordan said in a statement on Wednesday. At the same time, Social Security's trust fund is projected to become insolvent in six years. Unless lawmakers agree on remedies, all Social Security recipients will see a benefit cut of more than 20% in 2032. "Americans cannot afford cuts to the benefits they have earned, whether through changes to their hard-earned payments or the COLA," Minter-Jordan said.

title: Route 66 dedicated as National Historic Civil Engineering Landmark in Chicago
description: Route 66 dedicated as National Historic Civil Engineering Landmark
content: The historic Route 66 was recognized Wednesday with a special dedication at Navy Pier.The American Society of Civil Engineers dedicated the highway as a National Historic Civil Engineering Landmark at the event Wednesday morning. The group said it will recognize how the road impacted the development of modern America through commerce and tourism."This recognition honors not only extraordinary achievement, but also the vision and ingenuity that transformed a road into an enduring part of the American story," Nora Gainer, executive director of Civic Relations and Partnerships at the Art Institute of Chicago, said at the dedication ceremony.American Society of Civil Engineers president Marsha Anderson Bomar, Assistant Illinois Department of Transportation Secretary Tom Carney, and Chicago Department of Transportation Commissioner William Cheaks Jr. also all attended the dedication ceremony. There are only three other National Historic Civil Engineering landmarks in Chicago — one commemorating the event of the Reversal of the flow of the Chicago River in 1900, one honoring the Chicago water supply and its Lake Michigan intake system as designed by engineer Ellis Chesbrough, and one celebrating the Cortland Street trunnion-bascule drawbridge, which was the first of its kind, and which is now closed for a complex restoration effort.The iconic Route 66, born officially as U.S. Highway 66 in 1926, ran more than 2,000 miles — connecting the West Coast to the Midwest by road for the first time. The Illinois portion stretches 301 miles, from Chicago to the Mississippi River.Illinois was also the first state to complete its section of Route 66, Carney said at the event Wednesday.The original route started along Jackson Boulevard in downtown Chicago. When Jackson Boulevard was made one-way eastbound in 1955, the Chicago path of Route 66 was split between that street and Adams Street a block to the north, starting and ending near the Art Institute of Chicago at Michigan Avenue.To celebrate its centennial this year, the symbolic starting point of Route 66 was extended north and east to Navy Pier. The idea was to create a pier-to-pier connection for the highway, with Santa Monica Pier right outside of Los Angeles serving as the other terminus.In Chicago, Route 66 goes on to follow Ogden Avenue through the city's West Side and near west suburbs, and heads southwest through downstate Illinois before crossing into Missouri, Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona before terminating in Southern California.During the highway's glory days, Route 66 was a muse. "(Get Your Kicks on) Route 66" has been part of the American songbook since Nat King Cole first released it in 1946. Chuck Berry, a native of the Route 66 city of St. Louis, released a cover version in 1961.In the literary realm, Route 66 is a powerful symbol in John Steinbeck's 1939 novel "The Grapes of Wrath," representing a pathway to hope from the Dust Bowl.Route 66 was decommissioned as a federal highway in 1985.The National Historic Civil Engineering landmark dedication ceremony was set to be held at 10 a.m.

title: Lighted CPKC Holiday Train expected to pass through Southeast Michigan on Nov. 22
description: The train travels between concert stops in Windsor, Ontario, and a Chicago suburb. It is expected to pass Romulus, Belleville, Milan and Adrian on the evening or night of Nov. 22.
content: Southeast Michigan train enthusiasts can put Nov. 22 on their calendar as the likely date to look for the lighted CPKC Holiday Train as it travels between concert stops.The Canadian Pacific Kansas City (CPKC) company announced on Wednesday that its train tours will begin Nov. 19 in Montreal, Quebec. As in recent years, there are two train routes with scheduled stops in 182 communities across Canada and the United States. This annual tradition provides live performances and holiday cheer while promoting donations to community food pantries.None of the performances in recent years have included Southeast Michigan. But area residents are known to host watch parties and wait near railroad tracks in hopes of seeing the holiday lights on the traveling train cars.If it follows the expected route, one of the two CPKC trains will pass several Southeast Michigan communities, including Romulus, Belleville, Milan and Adrian, during the evening or night of Nov. 22. That train has a performance at 5 p.m. ET on Nov. 22 in Windsor, Ontario, and a performance at 5:30 p.m. CT Nov. 23 in a suburb of Chicago, Illinois, according to the tour schedule.The rail company said it will post updates on its Facebook page and other social media platforms as the tour takes place. The rail company asks people to stay 50 feet away from tracks when watching for the lighted train.The Holiday Train tradition began in 1999 and has raised more than $28.3 million and collected more than 5.6 million pounds of food for community food banks in Canada and the U.S.

title: Red Wings sign Alex DeBrincat to 7-year contract worth $13 million per year
description: The Detroit Red Wings have signed two-time All-Star forward Alex DeBrincat to a seven-year contract worth $13 million per season.
content: The Detroit Red Wings signed two-time All-Star forward Alex DeBrincat to a seven-year contract worth $13 million per season on Wednesday.The move provided desperately needed good news for a franchise mired in a decade-long postseason drought with an interim general manager, a former captain in limbo and an unsigned restricted free agent.The 28-year-old DeBrincat has established himself as a productive offensive player in the NHL with 298 career goals and 603 points. He led the team and set a career high with 85 points last season and matched his career high with 41 goals, becoming the first player to have at least 40 goals for the Red Wings since Marian Hossa in 2009.DeBrincat leads the Red Wings with four goals and eight points this season, but they have lost five of their first six games. Detroit hosts Philadelphia on Thursday night.Chicago selected DeBrincat in the second round of the 2016 draft. He was an All-Star with the Blackhawks during the 2022 season and was traded to Toronto the following offseason. The Red Wings acquired the Farmington Hills, Michigan, native from the Ottawa Senators in 2023, and he was an All-Star in his first season in Detroit.DeBrincat's extension is a positive development for a franchise that has had a string of negative news.Detroit demoted former general manager Steve Yzerman in July, giving him an advisory role to owner and CEO Chris Ilitch, and named Shawn Horcoff interim GM after failing to hire one during a search.Dylan Larkin asked for a trade during the offseason, and after the team did not move the 30-year-old center, he was stripped of his captaincy. Larkin was booed when he was introduced before the season-opening game while he was not in uniform, recovering from an upper-body injury. When the Red Wings were preparing to start the season earlier this month, defenseman Simon Edvinsson was seen training with a team in his native Sweden. The 23-year-old restricted free agent had nine goals and 25 points in 72 games last year, his second full season in the NHL. Detroit drafted him No. 6 overall in 2021, and he has 19 career goals and 60 points in 175 games.

title: Georgia Tech linebacker Kyle Efford retires from football after years of injuries
description: Georgia Tech senior linebacker Kyle Efford says he is retiring for health reasons.
content: Georgia Tech senior linebacker Kyle Efford, the first player in 24 years to lead the team in tackles in three consecutive seasons, announced Tuesday he is retiring for health reasons.Efford said he made the decision due to an accumulation of injuries during his career."Over the past few years, my body has taken more damage than I can continue to ignore," Efford said in a statement released by the school. "Damage that will continue to remind me of the sport that I love many years down the road. And while my heart and mind still have so much more to give, I've reached a point where I have to start thinking about the life I have ahead of me."This isn't how I imagined my football career coming to an end, but I am at peace. I can say with complete confidence that I gave this game every single piece of me. There is nothing left in the tank, and there are no regrets in my heart."Efford finished his career with 250 tackles, including 222 from 2023 through 2025 when he led the team in tackles three consecutive seasons. He had 81 tackles in 2023 when he became the Yellow Jackets' first freshman to lead the team in tackles outright since 1999.A surgically repaired shoulder limited Efford to three games this season. He had 27 tackles while matching his career high with 13 in Georgia Tech's 14-13 loss to Colorado to open the season. Efford had six tackles in last week's 28-25 win over Duke after missing the previous two games."We'll miss having number 44 in the middle of our defense, but know that he'll continue to make an impact on this team with his leadership and presence," Georgia Tech coach Brent Key said. "He might not be on the field for us moving forward, but he'll always be a part of the Georgia Tech football program."Efford was voted a team captain in 2024 and again this season.

title: Water and cancer, once taboo in Iowa politics, are now front and center in campaigns
description: Back-to-back years of water restrictions in the Des Moines area and a growing "Make America Healthy Again" movement have pushed a once-avoided issue into debates, ads and roundtables for candidates in both parties.
content: Iowa is facing a budget deficit, high costs and economic strain from trade disputes that have squeezed farmers.But problems that have simmered for decades â water quality and cancer rates â have been forced to the forefront of state politics this year. They are the focus of debate questions, roundtable events and campaign advertisements for candidates from both parties, up and down the ballot.The issue has historically been politically taboo for fear of pointing fingers at the powerful agricultural industry in Iowa, one of the country's top producers of corn, soybeans and hogs. Chemical fertilizers and animal waste contain nitrates and phosphorus that can get washed with rain or snowmelt into the state's web of rivers.The problem has long caused tension between Iowa's more liberal urban centers, which rely on rivers and lakes for drinking water, and mostly conservative stewards of its rich farmland. Farmers are increasingly participating in practices to prevent runoff, although critics say the lack of regulation forces downstream Iowans to pay for the pollution.The spotlight has grown, and the political calculus has shifted, after back-to-back years of restrictions on water use in the Des Moines area coupled with a burgeoning "Make America Healthy Again" movement in Iowa's small towns and rural communities.Iowa has the second highest rate of newly diagnosed cancers in the country. Specific diagnoses, like prostate, breast and lung cancer, are increasing in Iowa faster than in the U.S. overall. It's affecting urban and rural parts of the state.New state-funded research at the University of Iowa shows most, but not all, of Iowa's above-normal rates for five cancers can be explained by demographic and behavioral factors, such as smoking and binge drinking. Researchers next assess environmental factors, including nitrate levels."The real issue is the water and the nitrates," said Democrat Josh Turek, who is running for U.S. Senate, as he talked with cancer patients last week. "Every Iowan deserves when they turn on the tap to ensure that their water is clean and not giving them cancer."Some studies have found a link between nitrates in drinking water and certain diseases, but it remains an area of debate. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency does not currently classify nitrates as a cancer risk. The agency initiated a plan to review that assessment in 2017, but it's been stalled, revived and stalled again under different White House administrations.The Republican congresswoman running against Turek, Ashley Hinson, recently gathered farmers, researchers and local officials to discuss Iowa's water problems. She said there is an ongoing need for investments in infrastructure, water quality monitoring and conservation programs to ensure Iowans have safe drinking water. She also said people can feel safe because treated tap water meets federal regulations."We all know that we have some challenges here in Iowa," she said. "I don't think water quality is a partisan issue."It's been more than a decade since the Des Moines area's water utility, fed up with paying roughly $16,000 per day to remove nitrates from water, sued counties further upstream to get them to help cover the cost. The complaint was ultimately dismissed, and Iowa's Republican leaders celebrated the ruling.Last year, Central Iowa Water Works issued its first-ever ban on lawn watering to reduce demand on its nitrate removal facilities, and state politicians rejected any suggestion of a "blame game" that would implicate farmers. Iowa had been investing nearly $100 million annually in its nutrient reduction strategy in recent years.In May, though, Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds and lawmakers committed an additional $320 million for water infrastructure, conservation initiative incentives and other projects, including millions to Central Iowa Water Works to update equipment."Water quality isn't a farm issue. It isn't a city issue, and it isn't a political issue," Reynolds said. "But it absolutely is non-negotiable."Still, criticism of slow progress has continued, including from candidates running to replace Reynolds.Republican Zach Lahn and Democrat Rob Sand both emphasize that the state needs to better prioritize the water problem, though neither has called for mandating farming conservation practices that reduce runoff.Lahn, who was endorsed early in his primary by the political committee MAHA Action, has diverged from many of his Republican peers in directly linking polluted water and agrochemicals to Iowa's cancer crisis.At Lahn's agriculture-focused town hall in northeast Iowa in August, one attendee raised the issue."Right now the farmers, I would say, are really getting blamed for the high cancer rate in Iowa," she said. "Even our daughter calls from Des Moines and says: 'Should we be drinking this water?'"Lahn said he knows certain agrochemicals are important "tools in the tool chest.""We're not here to ban products," he said, "but we do have to address the water quality issue."Federal regulations say drinking water is safe with a maximum nitrate level of 10 milligrams per liter. That threshold was set to prevent what's known as blue baby syndrome, a condition when an infant's blood doesn't have enough oxygen, but more scientific studies are now analyzing the relationship between nitrate-laden water below that threshold and certain cancers.Lahn said he tested the nitrate levels from his well water and creek in rural east-central Iowa, finding both well above the federal limit.Central Iowa Water Works ran its nitrate removal treatment for a record 193 days straight earlier this year, and the treated water's nitrate levels hovered around eight to nine milligrams per liter in the heart of summer.Sand usually references water early in his stump speech, naming one reason he initially registered as a Democrat is the party's advocacy for clean water because he likes to fish. He said Tuesday after meeting with cancer survivors and parents of children with cancer that he's seen the topic rise in the public consciousness over the past few years."I hear from people regularly who are so concerned about it that they wonder whether or not they want to be in Iowa," Sand said.Twenty years ago, research scientist Chris Jones said he'd give his boss at Des Moines' water utility updates on the rivers' nitrate levels."He'd say to me, 'Where's the outrage?'" Jones recalled. "Now, the outrage has arrived."Jones, who later worked on water quality monitors at the University of Iowa, says it's a huge failure of the state for Iowans to lose faith in drinking water.Jones is a Democrat running in the election to be Iowa's secretary of agriculture, trying to unseat incumbent Republican Mike Naig.Chief among their differences is whether conservation solutions should be mandatory. In a debate, Naig said Jones is an outlier in demanding farmers be required to adopt conservation practices. Iowa's agricultural industry resists mandates, in part because not all farmers own the land they farm and some conservation efforts might lead to profit loss, at least initially.Naig, who previously worked for chemical manufacturer Monsanto, highlighted the records that his department has set under Reynolds' leadership and said conservation work is being scaled up to accelerate progress."It's been a hot topic on the campaign trail," Naig said, but "we have to have a long view of these things, and we're making progress."

title: Suspect in Gilroy attempted murder case may be in Mexico, police say
description: Authorities in the South Bay said a man suspected of stabbing an acquaintance earlier this month may have left the country.
content: Authorities in the South Bay said a man suspected of stabbing an acquaintance earlier this month may have left the country.According to the Gilroy Police Department, a man was stabbed on the 7300 block of Church Street, between 6th and 7th streets, shortly before 9 p.m. on Oct. 2. Police said the victim, a 45-year-old man, was found with what was described as a "serious" stab wound to his abdomen.The victim was taken to a local trauma center with life-threatening injuries and underwent emergency surgery.In a statement, police said 35-year-old Jose Antonio Mateo Ruiz was identified as the suspect following witness interviews, collection of physical evidence and additional follow-up. Detectives obtained an arrest warrant for Mateo Ruiz for attempted murder. Investigators determined that Mateo Ruiz and the victim were acquaintances who spent time earlier in the day. The stabbing took place after an argument broke out between the two in the evening.Mateo Ruiz left the area before police arrived. With the help of license plate readers, investigators were able to locate Mateo Ruiz's vehicle in Santa Cruz County, but he has not been found.Investigators said they received information suggesting Mateo Ruiz may have left the country for Mexico after the stabbing.Police described Mateo Ruiz as standing about 5' tall, weighing about 155 pounds, with short dark hair and brown eyes.Anyone with information on Mateo Ruiz's whereabouts or the case is asked to contact Detective Cat Fraide of the Gilroy Police Department by calling 408-846-0335 or emailing Cat.Fraide@CityofGilroy.org.

title: Pope Leo recovering "as expected" after surgery and lung cancer diagnosis, Vatican says
description: Pope Leo XIV is recovering "as expected" and has begun respiratory physiotherapy after tests confirmed a lung cancer diagnosis following surgery, the Vatican says.
content: Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer after undergoing surgery on Tuesday to remove a nodular lesion from his right lung, the Vatican announced. The 71-year-old pontiff was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican said in a news release following the surgery, describing the operation as "successful" and with "no complications." It said the diagnosis of lung cancer was confirmed during the surgery, which lasted 90 minutes. In an update shared Wednesday by the Vatican, doctors leading the pope's care at Rome's Gemelli Hospital said he had undergone blood tests and a chest X-ray as scheduled following the surgery and that the results "confirm a normal post-operative course: the values are within the expected range for the type of procedure performed.""The Holy Father has carried out respiratory physiotherapy and has begun walking around his room," they added. "He has resumed a regular diet, having both breakfast and lunch. His recovery is proceeding as expected."A Vatican spokesperson said Wednesday that the pope was expected to remain hospitalized for a week from the point of his admission on Tuesday. In its earlier statement on the surgery, the Vatican said that, "to ensure a radical resection, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique," and "intraoperative histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of pulmonary adenocarcinoma, as suspected from pre-operative tests."According to the Vatican, Leo "regained consciousness normally" following the procedure and was then taken back to his room on the 10th floor of the Gemelli Hospital, which has long provided medical care for popes. "The Vatican tends to keep these things under wraps, so there'll be a lot of reading between the lines to try and detect what is the state of the pope's health," Candida Moss, the Edward Cadbury professor of theology at the University of Birmingham in England, told CBS News. "We're going to need to get more information on his pathology," Dr. David Jones, chief of thoracic surgery at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, told CBS News. "Were lymph nodes involved? What's some of the molecular pathology that's going to be done that can help dictate what therapy, if any, is indicated?"Leo, who was born in Chicago, is known for living an active and healthy lifestyle, including swimming and playing tennis, all factors that likely worked in his favor going into the surgery. He has maintained a busy schedule since becoming pope a year and a half ago.Leo entered the Gemelli Hospital in the Italian capital through the main entrance earlier in the day and waved to dozens of well-wishers who had gathered to greet him. According to the Vatican, the team that performed the surgery was led by Dr. Stefano Margaritora, Gemelli's chief thoracic surgeon. The Vatican on Monday canceled all Leo's audiences through Oct. 20. There was no word on whether Leo would be able to keep his planned trip to South America next month. The typical recommendation for a procedure of this kind is to avoid air travel for about three weeks, which would put the pope right up against the start of that trip, which is scheduled for Nov. 6. Moss told CBS News that Vatican protocol calls for the pope's cardinals and aides to step in and take up many of his duties as needed. "We should also expect that, inasmuch as is possible, Pope Leo is going to continue to work," Moss said. "We have a long tradition of popes — not just Pope Francis, but also Pope John Paul II, who had Parkinson's for 10 years — who continued to remain as active as they could, and as active in Catholic liturgies as they could, right up until the end of their tenures." While Gemelli has a specific papal apartment that past popes have used, complete with a private chapel on the 10th floor, Leo will actually be staying in a nearby room since the papal apartment is undergoing renovations, according to the Vatican press office. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a social media post that he and his wife were "united in prayer" for the pope. "May the Lord give him strength and the Holy Spirit guide the medical professionals taking care of the Holy Father," Rubio wrote. The Vatican had announced on Sunday that Leo would undergo surgery after a nodular lesion was found in his lung. According to the American Thoracic Society, a lung nodule usually measures less than half an inch in size and is discovered using a CT scan. Fewer than 5% turn out to be cancer, according to the thoracic society. If a nodule is determined to be cancerous, it is usually a sign of early-stage lung cancer. "The doctors believe it's best to take action, so, following their advice, I've decided to have surgery to remove it," Leo said in remarks during his Sunday noon blessing. "Thank you for your spiritual support, and I entrust myself to your prayers."Lung adenocarcinoma is the most common type of lung cancer in the United States, according to the Lung Cancer Foundation of America, and makes up about 40% of all diagnosed lung cancers.It forms in glandular cells on the outer parts of the lung and is likely to be diagnosed earlier than other lung cancers because it spreads more slowly, the LCFA said. Symptoms can include fatigue, shortness of breath and upper back and chest pain. Treatments can include surgery, chemotherapy, immunotherapy and radiation. One of Pope Leo's 2 brothers also battling cancerLouis Prevost, Pope Leo's older brother who resides in Florida, has multiple myeloma and is undergoing treatment, his wife, Deborah Prevost, told CBS News on Tuesday. Multiple myeloma is a form of blood cancer, according to the Mayo Clinic. It forms in plasma cells, which are a type of white blood cell, and then builds up in the bone marrow. Deborah Prevost did not share what stage her husband's cancer is in, but said he is currently in a clinical trial at a local hospital where he is being treated.She said her husband was first diagnosed with multiple myeloma in 2017 but was able to maintain it at a "very low level" after undergoing treatment in 2019 that included stem cell treatment and a clinical trial. He "fell out of remission" three months ago, she said. Deborah Prevost could not comment on the specifics of Pope Leo's condition, but said her husband and his brother spoke last week before Louis Prevost went in for his clinical trial. Pope Leo also informed his brother of his own situation. "He [Pope Leo] called to let us know what would be happening," Deborah Prevost told CBS News. "We keep praying, keeping spirits up for both of them."

title: Liquor store burglary caught on surveillance video on Chicago's Northwest Side
description: A liquor store burglary was caught on camera on Chicago's Northwest Side overnight.
content: Multiple business break-ins are under investigation on Chicago's Northwest Side overnight. A liquor store burglary was caught on camera in Forest Glen. Surveillance video captured two people breaking into Bottles and Cans Edgebrook in the 6400 block of North Central Avenue around 5:20 a.m. The video shows a person using a brick to break the glass on the door.A person is seen in the video running out of the liquor store with a cash register. Chicago police said the two people took a cash box from inside the store before driving away in a red sedan. Just a few stores down, police were investigating break-ins in the 5300 block of West Devon Avenue. Police said a group of four to five people broke the door and window of Chocolate Shoppe Ice Cream around 5:23 a.m. Police said the group did not appear to enter the business. Police said the group left the scene in a red car. The front door was also smashed at S&J Nails on the same block. No arrests have been made. Area Five detectives are investigating.

title: Giannis Antetokounmpo, Miami Heat could be a perfect title-chasing pairing
description: Giannis Antetokounmpo joined the Miami Heat after 13 seasons with the Milwaukee Bucks and believes this change will bring out the best in him.
content: Giannis Antetokounmpo ran off the floor about an hour into the first Miami Heat training camp session of the season. He had already sweated through his practice uniform and wanted to change into a fresh one.Someone let him into an adjacent room, and he found a place to change."Much better," Antetokounmpo said. With that, he sprinted back to practice.Change, he believes, can be good. After 13 seasons with the Milwaukee Bucks — with 10 All-Star selections, nine All-NBA picks, two Most Valuable Player awards and one NBA title during that span — the 6-foot-11 Greek forward is starting anew with the Heat, who have a lot in common with Antetokounmpo. Both have been to the top of the NBA mountain, and now, both are counting on the other to help them reach that height again.But why now? Put simply, Antetokounmpo just wanted a fresh uniform.Miami Heat gave up a ton to make deal happen"I feel like I was in my comfort zone for many years and I just wanted just a new challenge," Antetokounmpo told The Associated Press. "And I feel that with where I am in my career, Miami is the organization that will bring the best out of me. It's an organization that loves to compete. Every single game, every single minute. And I'm the same. I'm the same person, so hopefully this — me being here — allows me to compete, allows me to help my team win games and get to the ultimate goal, which is winning the championship."The Heat gave up a ton to make the deal happen. The full trade, finalized in July, brought Antetokounmpo and Bobby Portis Jr. to Miami in exchange for Tyler Herro, Kasparas Jakucionis, Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kel'el Ware, three first-round picks, a first-round pick swap and a second-round pick. Miami won't finish paying off the trade, in terms of the draft capital, until 2033.And then there's the not-so-small matter of Antetokounmpo's next contract, one that could be worth as much as $275 million over four seasons if he ends up with a max extension sometime in the coming months.It is a ransom. But if this goes as Miami hopes, the price could seem like a bargain."I feel lucky to be his teammate, especially at this stage of my career," said new Heat guard Klay Thompson, a four-time champion from his time with Golden State. "I couldn't ask for a better opportunity. I've played against Giannis for many years, but now to be able to build chemistry with him and watch him hopefully have another MVP-like season is just a joy for me. And Heat fans should be ecstatic because when your best player is one of your hardest workers, it's contagious and it's just great to be a part of."He has averaged 24.1 points and 9.9 rebounds per game in his career, something only eight other players — Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Elgin Baylor, Larry Bird, Wilt Chamberlain, Anthony Davis, Joel Embiid, Karl Malone and Bob Pettit — either have done or are doing (since Davis and Embiid are still active).And over the last 10 seasons, Antetokounmpo ranks first in total points and fourth in total rebounds. Injuries limited him last season — he wanted to play more than he did and grew frustrated that the Bucks had a differing stance — but his stat averages haven't dipped. Antetokounmpo's game is elite, by any and all measures"If you're going to turn the page to a new chapter, it's extremely exciting to be able to add a two-time MVP, somebody that is fully in his prime," Heat coach Erik Spoelstra said. "His competitive spirit is aligned with ours. It's so tough to be able to get a player of his caliber. To be able to do that, for him to choose this to be the place he wants, for us to choose him ... and the possibilities of what we can accomplish together, then yes, that is exciting."Antetokounmpo wasted no time in starting to rave about the Heat culture, a phrase that has become a lightning rod for criticism from talking heads around the NBA — especially after the franchise slapped the word across shirts and jerseys. But the culture, the noncommercial version, still exists, brought in by Pat Riley more than three decades ago and protected by Spoelstra and others still today.It's simple: Work harder than everyone else and see what happens. Antetokounmpo spoke highly of it from afar for years. He's raving about it even more now."I love the culture and I want to be in a place that can bring the best out of me," Antetokounmpo said. "I want to play as many games as I can, be available for my teammates as much as I can. I'm always going to be honest. Last year, when I played, I thought I played at a very high level. The first 15 games, I thought I could be in the MVP discussion."Sometimes, things don't work out the way you want and sometimes, when you think things don't work out the way that you want, they actually do. I know when I'm healthy and I have the right mindset, I'm very hard to deal with."He speaks Greek, English and some Nigerian, plus has made a vow to learn Spanish — which makes tons of sense for someone who just moved to Miami. He says he already has learned to love much of what Miami has to offer (with iguanas the notable exception). He's building relationships within the organization and insists that the acclimation process is far from complete.He sees the potential. He wants another title. The Heat want another title. It's a match."I'm just trying to fit in," Antetokounmpo said. "And when I find the time to kind of be myself, I will be myself."

title: AI-generated videos of deadly Fort Hood shooting are spreading online. Here's what they get wrong.
description: AI-generated videos depicting the 2009 Fort Hood shooting are circulating on social media, but they contain numerous inaccuracies and false claims.
content: Videos generated by artificial intelligence about the 2009 Fort Hood shooting, which left 13 people dead, are appearing in social media feeds. Some contain numerous factual errors.A Facebook page called "Why Is It Like That?" posted a two-part series of AI-generated videos that purportedly depict the shooting and its aftermath. Both are riddled with mistakes and falsehoods.Who is behind the videos? The page lists an Austin address that belongs to a tattoo and piercing shop. CBS News Texas called the shop, and an employee who answered said she had never heard of the page.A phone number listed on the "Why Is It Like That?" Facebook page belongs to an Austin home remodeling company. An email sent to the address associated with the page was returned as undeliverable.CBS News Texas could not verify the identity associated with the page and it appears to be fake, much like the AI-generated videos people have been watching, sharing and commenting on.Debunking AI-generated videos about 2009 Fort Hood shootingOne of the videos is titled "The Day Fort Hood Changed."The caption reads: "A historical look into the events and investigation surrounding the 2009 Fort Hood tragedy. This video is intended solely for education, documentary and historical analysis purposes."The video begins with Fort Hood misspelled and shows a man standing in front of a building with what appear to be Humvees parked outside.Next, it cuts to a room where soldiers sit in rows, wearing dark green camouflage uniforms with a newer pattern. In November 2009, soldiers at Fort Hood wore Army Combat Uniforms, or ACUs, which featured a gray-green pixelated pattern.Later, the scene cuts to a clipboard covered in gibberish.The video then shows a man portraying the convicted shooter, Nidal Hasan, opening fire inside the room before cutting to the exterior of a building with more gibberish on its sign.A second video also contains numerous inaccuracies.It begins with the shooting and shows firefighters entering the building while gunfire is underway. That is inaccurate. The first responders that day were police officers who encountered Hasan outside.The video then shows soldiers rushing to help victims while wearing combat gear, another inaccuracy. Such gear is worn in combat, not as everyday attire on an Army post.The video also depicts a woman portraying Sgt. Kimberly Munley running toward the scene inside a building.At the time of the shooting, Munley was a member of Fort Hood's civilian police department. She was directing traffic nearby when the shooting began and rushed to the scene.Munley encountered Hasan outside the readiness center. The two exchanged gunfire, and she was shot in the thigh and knee and wounded in her index finger.But it was Sgt. Mark Todd, another civilian police officer at Fort Hood, who ultimately ended the shooting. He is not featured in the AI-generated video.Todd rounded the corner of a building shortly afterward and ordered Hasan to surrender. The two exchanged gunfire before Todd shot and handcuffed Hasan, ending the rampage.Fort Hood covers approximately 340 square miles, an area larger than New York City's five boroughs combined. The installation's front gate is about four miles from the readiness center where the shooting occurred, making the scene depicted outside the front gate in the video unlikely.AI-generated videos continue to circulateThe videos have been viewed and shared numerous times. Both are labeled as "true crime documentaries," but CBS News Texas has been unable to trace them to a specific individual.CBS News Texas has reached out to the Army about the AI-generated videos and is awaiting a response.The two videos are just a snapshot of the many AI-generated depictions currently circulating online.

title: Royal Caribbean cruise passenger who went overboard rescued after she spent 20 hours at sea, Greek coast guard says
description: The incident occurred when the Royal Caribbean ship Odyssey of the Seas was sailing southwest of the island of Zakynthos, the Greek coast guard said.
content: A woman who allegedly jumped off a cruise ship into the Ionian Sea was rescued over the weekend after 20 hours in the water, the Greek coast guard said. The incident occurred early on Friday when the Royal Caribbean Cruises ship Odyssey of the Seas was sailing southwest of the island of Zakynthos, the coast guard said. The 44-year-old Salvadorian woman subsequently told her rescuers she had jumped because "she wanted to disembark," a coast guard spokesperson told AFP. "She was 20 hours at sea," the officer said. After an alert went out early on Friday, two coast guard boats and a navy helicopter were dispatched to the area and other nearby ships were rerouted. The Odyssey of the Seas also joined the search, the officer said. A passing freighter eventually located the woman, fully conscious, in a life ring early on Saturday and she was picked up by a Greek coast guard patrol boat. A video released by the coast guard shows a crew throwing a rope to a woman floating inside an orange life ring in the water in the dark.She was taken to the port of Katakolo and then to hospital in the nearby city of Pyrgos for health tests that include a psychiatric evaluation ordered by a local prosecutor, the officer said.According to Royal Caribbean, Odyssey of the Seas is 1,138 feet long and can accommodate 4,198 guests. The ship offers seasonal cruises to the Greek Isles.Last year, a man jumped off a Royal Caribbean cruise ship near the Port of San Juan — allegedly to avoid paying off more than $16,000 in gambling debt to the cruise line. Jey Gonzalez-Diaz jumped into the water as the ship disembarked, during U.S. Customs and Border Protection inspection, according to a criminal complaint. He was then brought to shore by someone passing by on a jet ski, and later charged with attempting to avoid monetary reporting requirements when traveling into the U.S.

title: Trump meme coin buyers vie for dinner with the president. Many appear to be overseas.
description: At least 52 $TRUMP holders moved funds through crypto exchanges that bar U.S. customers.
author_name: Gabe  Kaminsky, Madeleine  May, Steve  Reilly
content: More than half of the top holders listed as competing for seats at President Trump's next meme coin dinner have used cryptocurrency exchanges that prohibit U.S. customers, indicating that many of the buyers are based overseas, according to a CBS News analysis.The gala, set for Nov. 22 at the Trump National Golf Club outside Washington, D.C., will seat the 185 largest holders of the $TRUMP meme coin, according to the website for Fight Fight Fight LLC, the company behind the coin. A public leaderboard for the event only lists the top 100 holders.Mr. Trump is billed as the featured speaker alongside three yet-to-be-named "legends." The top 29 holders will get upfront seating and a VIP reception with the president, the website says.The upcoming dinner is the latest example of the unprecedented intermingling of business and politics during Mr. Trump's second term.Mr. Trump earned at least $635 million in royalties last year from a licensing deal tied to the $TRUMP token, according to his financial disclosure. Mr. Trump stands to earn more money from the coin, since an affiliate of the Trump Organization earns revenue whenever the coin is traded, according to the meme coin's website. "Foreign actors used to need a back door to try to influence a president," said Zach Everson, a researcher for the progressive consumer rights advocacy group Public Citizen. "Trump is holding the front door open and inviting them in for a steak dinner."Out of the 100 top holders listed as competing for seats, at least 52 moved funds through crypto exchanges that bar U.S. customers, including Binance, Bybit and MEXC, according to the CBS News analysis.Because exchanges like Binance bar U.S. customers, analysts typically treat accounts that use them as likely belonging to people outside the U.S., said Matt Fiebach, co-founder of the crypto data firm Entropy Advisors."All you can know with certainty is that a non-U.S. person or entity sent funds," Fiebach said.A cryptocurrency exchange is a company, much like a stock brokerage, where customers trade dollars or other currencies for crypto. CIC Digital LLC, a Trump Organization affiliate, and another company, Fight Fight Fight, together own 80% of the total $TRUMP supply, according to the project's website. The parent company of Fight Fight Fight, Celebration Cards LLC, uses Mr. Trump's name and likeness under a licensing agreement, the website adds.At least 44 of the users on the leaderboard transacted through Binance prior to purchasing $TRUMP, the analysis found.CBS News examined the transaction histories of the crypto wallets listed on the gala leaderboard using data from the blockchain intelligence firm Arkham. While it's not possible to see who owns specific wallets, it is possible to identify which exchanges are being used to purchase crypto tokens. The users that transacted on the exchanges that bar U.S. customers account for nearly $6.8 million of the more than $15 million in value reflected on the coin leaderboard as of Wednesday. A meme coin is a type of asset that is typically used for commemorative purposes or comedic value, and not a currency. In 2023, Binance was forced to offload its U.S. customers after it pleaded guilty to federal charges that included failure to prevent money laundering on its platform and sanctions violations.Its co-founder, Changpeng Zhao, also pleaded guilty to failing to maintain an effective anti-money-laundering program. (Mr. Trump granted a pardon to Zhao in October 2025, claiming the crypto billionaire was a victim of a political prosecution under President Biden). Exchanges can also shed light on who might be making moves to sell their tokens. The largest holder of $TRUMP moved about $70 million worth of the coin in September to an account where it could be sold, just before the gala dinner contest was announced, The Washington Sun reported.The coin's total market value has dropped more than 95% since its peak in January 2025, to about $532 million, data show.Democrats and progressive watchdog groups have raised foreign influence questions about the $TRUMP coin, warning that people overseas could be paying for access to the president. While it may be possible for a U.S.-based user to circumvent foreign exchange prohibitions by masking their location using a virtual private network, or VPN, many exchanges say they take measures intended to prevent this. The Trump Organization did not respond to requests for comment. A White House official said in a statement that the Trump administration only acts in the "best interest of the American people." The official added that the meme coin event is "a private event, not a government function, and there is no promise of official government action in exchange for attending."This wouldn't be the first time the president has headlined a $TRUMP coin gala. Mr. Trump appeared at a similar meme coin dinner in May 2025 at his golf club in Virginia, and another this April at his Mar-a-Lago resort.The meme coin has been a financial boon to Mr. Trump, who raked in more than $1.4 billion last year from crypto-related ventures, according to his financial disclosure. The current top spot on the Trump gala leaderboard is occupied by a wallet that holds about 1.5 million $TRUMP tokens, valued at nearly $3 million. That wallet received its $TRUMP holdings in two transfers on Oct. 8 — the largest of which came from another wallet that has used the Binance exchange. It's unclear whether the same person controls both."As was the case with Trump's previous meme coin gala, it appears that the majority of $TRUMP investors are purchasing his meme coin through overseas exchanges," said Virginia Canter, who worked as an ethics lawyer in Republican and Democratic presidential administrations. "Foreign actors are literally buying a seat at the president's own table." Within days of its January 2025 launch, the Trump token reached a peak value of $75.35. It has since fallen dramatically — to roughly $2 as of Wednesday. The sharp decline in value has led Democrats to call it an alleged "pump-and-dump" scheme.Mr. Trump's ties to crypto are expected to be a top oversight area for Democrats should they take a majority in the House or Senate in the 2026 midterm elections.The Trump family co-founded and holds a stake in World Liberty Financial, a separate crypto company launched in 2024. It generated hundreds of millions in revenue for Mr. Trump last year, his financial disclosure shows. World Liberty Financial drew scrutiny in 2025 after MGX, an investment firm backed by the Abu Dhabi government, used World Liberty's stablecoin to make a $2 billion investment in Binance. Both Binance and Mr. Trump denied the pardon for Zhao, the Binance co-founder, was connected to the transaction. "I don't know who he is," Mr. Trump told CBS News days after pardoning the crypto billionaire.

title: 2 CHP officers injured while investigating deadly I-80 crash near Fairfield
description: A Tesla hit a CHP patrol car about an hour after a separate crash killed a 19-year-old driver.
content: A 19-year-old driver died in a crash on Interstate 80 near Fairfield Tuesday night, and two California Highway Patrol officers investigating that crash were injured about an hour later when a Tesla hit their patrol car.The first crash happened around 10:45 p.m. on eastbound I-80 west of Air Base Parkway.CHP said a 19-year-old San Pablo man driving a Honda Civic lost control for an unknown reason and was then hit by a Chevrolet Tahoe driven by a 47-year-old Sacramento man.The Civic driver was taken to a hospital, where he died. CHP said alcohol does not appear to have been a factor.Around 11:45 p.m., four CHP officers were still investigating the crash with four lanes closed and traffic being diverted into the slow lane.Investigators said a Tesla driven by a 22-year-old Sacramento man went through a flare and cone pattern and hit a CHP Dodge Charger with two officers inside.Both officers were taken to NorthBay Hospital in Fairfield and have since been released.CHP said it is not yet known whether the Tesla's Full Self-Driving feature was active at the time of the crash.All eastbound lanes reopened around 8:30 a.m. Wednesday.

title: Trump promised to lower prices for Americans. Here's what the data shows.
description: Just weeks before the midterm elections, 90% of Americans say prices in the U.S. are the main factor shaping their view of the economy. These charts show why.
author_name: Aimee  Picchi, Megan  Cerullo, Mary  Cunningham
content: President Trump campaigned in 2024 on promises to lower Americans' cost of living, vowing to push gasoline prices below $2 a gallon and to deliver 2% mortgage rates. Two years later, consumers face sharply higher costs for many of the necessities he pledged to make more affordable.Less than a month before the midterm elections, the gap between Mr. Trump's promises and the financial realities facing many Americans is fueling voter frustration over the economy. Although economic growth is solid and unemployment remains low, nine in 10 Americans say prices are the most important factor shaping their views of the economy, according to a recent CBS News poll.The financial pressures affecting Americans predate Mr. Trump's return to the White House last year. Consumers are reeling from the cumulative impact of five years of post-pandemic inflation, economists note. But his campaign promises raised hopes that he would lower consumer prices.At the same time, some of Mr. Trump's policies have exacerbated inflation. His tariff regime contributed about 2.9 percentage points to inflation through February, according to new research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Without the tariffs, the price of goods would have declined, the researchers said.Mr. Trump's decision to attack Iran in February has also led to a drawn-out conflict that has disrupted oil shipments and sharply driven up the price of oil, gas and diesel."It's undeniable that several of these supply shocks that the U.S. economy has been navigating through come from policy decisions made by the administration — namely, decisions to intervene in Iran and decisions to impose tariffs," Greg Daco, chief economist at investment advisory firm EY-Parthenon, told CBS News.Inflation in September is forecast to have risen at an annual rate of 3.6%, up from 3.4% in August, according to economists polled by FactSet — well above the Federal Reserve's 2% annual target. Ryan Bourne, an economist at the libertarian Cato Institute, said that consumers "judge the prices they're paying against the prices they paid four or five years ago, and are still shocked by it."He added, "As a result of that, they think the economy's doing very, very badly."The White House said that Mr. Trump's agenda "stopped Biden's inflation crisis" while creating jobs and economic growth. The administration's policies "will continue to deliver economic wins over the next two years," White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers told CBS News."The President has delivered tangible wins for American families: He signed the largest working-class tax cuts in history, cut the cost of prescription drugs, added more than one million private-sector jobs, locked in nearly 20 trade deals that put American workers first and sent 401(k)s to record highs," Rogers added.The following charts show how U.S. costs have changed for expenses ranging from groceries to car insurance.Groceries "A vote for Trump means your groceries will be cheaper." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Pittsburgh on Nov. 4, 2024.For consumers, each visit to the supermarket is a fresh reminder of inflation's impact on food costs, which have continued to rise since Mr. Trump vowed to lower grocery prices. The cost of food prepared at home has climbed 4% since November 2024, according to Consumer Price Index data, when Mr. Trump said a vote for him would lead to lower costs. That increase comes on top of a 23% jump in food prices during the prior four years. Because consumers tend to remember what they spent on groceries before the pandemic, they get a jolt each time they visit the supermarket, said Daco of EY-Parthenon. "Whether it's talking about gas prices or grocery prices or restaurant prices or travel prices, everybody talks about inflation," he said. "The salience of prices is what is driving this downbeat consumer morale."Food costs are continuing to rise due to a number of factors, ranging from the elevated price of gas and diesel, which are needed to fuel farm equipment and ship items to stores, to the Trump administration's tariffs, economists said.Gasoline "Energy is going to bring us back. That means we're going down and getting gasoline below $2 a gallon, bring down the price of everything from electricity rates to groceries, airfares, and housing costs." — Mr. Trump in a speech at the Economic Club of New York on Sept. 5, 2024.Gas prices have surged since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February. As of Oct. 9, the national average price for a gallon of gasoline was $4.37. That's up 47% from $2.98 on Feb. 27, one day before the war began, according to CBS News data. Prices at the pump are at a record high for October, according to AAA.Diesel prices rose to a record high of $6.53 per gallon on Sept. 22 and now hover around $6.28. Diesel, which is widely used in the trucking, agriculture and construction sectors, is a factor in consumer prices for nearly every type of good, including groceries.Gas prices tend to have an outsized impact on consumer sentiment, influencing their views on future inflation and the broader economy, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco.Energy and electricity "By contrast, I'm announcing today that under my leadership, the United States will commit to the ambitious goal of slashing energy and electricity prices by half, at least half." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Asheville, North Carolina, on August 14, 2024.Consumers' energy bills have continued to increase this year. Data from the Energy Information Administration (EIA) shows that average monthly residential electricity costs rose 12.5% between December 2024 and July of this year. Electricity bills are rising as utilities spend more to upgrade the nation's aging power grid, and overall energy demand grows amid the data center buildout. Natural gas is also more expensive. Average monthly residential prices for natural gas rose 106% between December 2024 and July 2025, according to the EIA. Energy Innovation, a nonpartisan policy and research firm, attributes the jump to geopolitical conflict, an increase in domestic exports, extreme weather linked to climate change and rising infrastructure costs.A July report from advocacy groups The Century Foundation and Protect Borrowers found that the national average utility bill reached $280 per month in early 2026, up 12% since the end of 2024, just before Mr. Trump took office. Many people could face even higher energy prices this winter. Americans are forecast to spend an average of $1,030 to heat their homes between mid-November and mid-March 2027, according to the National Energy Assistance Directors Association, a policy organization. Homeowners who use heating oil are projected to pay an average of $2,627 over that three-month period, up roughly 50% from last year, the group said.Car insurance "Car insurance is up 70% to 100%, and you can't get it. … But prices will come down. You just watch, they'll come down, and they'll come down fast." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Asheville, North Carolina, on August 14, 2024.Car insurance costs are one area where consumers are seeing some modest relief. Data shows motorists are paying 5.5% less for vehicle coverage since premiums hit a recent high in February. Still, insurance prices have soared in recent years along with the cost of both new and used vehicles. Yelena Shulyatyeva, senior U.S. economist for The Conference Board, a nonprofit that represents businesses, attributed the recent dip in premiums to increased industry competition, rather than public policy actions."Some of the deceleration was a result of a pushback from consumers, rather than some legislative or other action," Shulyatyeva told CBS News.Housing and mortgage costs"We will drive down the rates so you will be able to pay 2% again, and we will be able to finance or refinance your homes drastically at much lower costs." — Mr. Trump at a campaign rally in Tucson, Arizona, on Sept. 12, 2024.Mortgage rates were climbing from pandemic-era lows for several years before President Trump returned to office in January of 2025. The average rate on a conventional 30-year mortgage now stands at 7.28%, up from 7.04% when Mr. Trump took office, according to Freddie Mac.But home loan rates have been volatile, briefly dipping below 5% in February before climbing amid surging government bond yields, rising inflation and geopolitical tensions. Borrowing costs are just one side of the struggle: Home buyers are also contending with high prices, keeping many on the sidelines as they wait for more affordable options. The median list price for a home in August was $408,333, up 4% from $392,967 since Mr. Trump took office, according to Zillow. The gap between the income needed to afford a home, $126,487, and the U.S. median income, $86,490, is now the widest since 2005, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta.Credit card rates"We're going to put a temporary cap on credit card interest rates. We're going to cap it around 10%.
