We can't let them make 25% and 30%." — Mr. Trump in a campaign speech in Uniondale, New York, on Sept. 18, 2024.President Trump proposed capping credit card interest rates at 10% while campaigning, an issue he also highlighted after taking office in 2025. But while the effort drew bipartisan support, the proposal fizzled.Currently, the average credit card rate across all commercial bank accounts is 20.94%, down from 21.58% when Mr. Trump resumed office, according to Federal Reserve data. Credit experts said the rate-cap proposal would have hindered consumers' access to credit. "Obviously, we'd love for everyone to have low rates and be free from debt. But the unintended consequence of a 10% cap would be the loss of access to credit, because banks say they wouldn't be profitable with it capped at that low rate," Ted Rossman, principal consumer finance analyst at Money Management International, a nonprofit credit counseling firm, told CBS News.Airfare"We're going [to] … bring down the price of everything from electricity rates to groceries, airfares and housing costs." — Mr. Trump in a speech at the New York Economic Club on Sept. 5, 2024.Along with promising to reduce energy prices, Mr. Trump pledged to lower airfare costs for travelers. In recent months, fares have eased slightly, although CPI data shows that they remain 17% higher than in January 2025. The war in Iran has disrupted global oil supplies and raised jet fuel costs, which are the second- biggest expense for airlines after labor costs. Facing significantly larger fuel bills, carriers are raising prices to cover the added costs. Jet fuel now costs $4.34 a gallon, up 85% from an average of $2.35 per gallon in January 2025, according to the Energy Information Administration. Aviation analysts also point to the May shutdown of budget carrier Spirit Airlines as another factor behind higher fares. ACA health insurance"I will make the ACA much, much, much better for far less money (or cost) to our greatest American citizens. …" — Mr. Trump in a Truth Social post on March 26, 2024.Millions of Americans with an Affordable Care Act health insurance plan face sharply higher costs than a year ago. Average monthly premiums have risen to $178, or $2,136 per year, up 58% from 2025, according to a May analysis from nonprofit health group KFF. Obamacare plan deductibles have soared from an average of $1,027 per person to $3,786, up 37% over the same period, KFF found. Prices for ACA plans spiked after Congress allowed a tax subsidy designed to lower plan costs to expire at the end of last year.In an effort to offer relief, the Trump administration began sending $500 checks in September to nearly 1 million ACA participants in 30 states.Prescription drugs "When reelected as president, I will continue my efforts to protect Americans from unaffordable drug prices …" — Mr. Trump in an interview with AARP Magazine on Oct. 2, 2024.Prescription drug prices have dropped since Mr. Trump took office in his second term, falling 3.9% after peaking in February 2025, government data show. Mr. Trump has credited his policies lowering drug costs, with the White House stating in August that the president "has delivered" on his campaign promise. The administration cited policies such as its "most favored nation" approach, which links U.S. drug prices to those paid in other developed nations. Experts said that while the Trump administration's policies have helped, other factors are also at play. For instance, manufacturers of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are cutting their prices amid increased competition, while the nonpartisan Brookings Institution notes that more generic drugs are entering the marketplace, tempering healthcare costs.

title: Community mourns 42-year-old educator who died in fall from Six Flags roller coaster: "Beloved colleague, friend"
description: Hassan Kariem was a 42-year-old IT manager in the Atlanta Public Schools system, which is remembering him as a "cherished member" of the school community.
content: Friends and loved ones are mourning the man who fell to his death Monday while riding a roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia. Witnesses say Hassan Kariem was ejected from "The Goliath" and struck other passengers as he fell.The 42-year-old was an IT manager in the Atlanta Public Schools system, which is remembering him as a "cherished member" of the school community "whose presence and impact will be deeply missed."Wesley International Academy, the Atlanta charter school where Kariem worked, described him as "a beloved colleague, friend, and integral part of the Wesley family for more than 12 years.""Throughout his time at Wesley, Mr. Kariem served as our IT manager, a technology teacher, and a robotics coach, leaving a lasting impact on generations of students and colleagues," the school said. Family members told local media he was a passionate educator and had survived two bouts of cancer and a fiery car crash. They say he was at Six Flags with family when the horrific accident happened.Vanessa and Fred Sowemimo, who had just gotten off the same ride, described what they saw, saying Kariem "flew out of his seat."Others who were there were frantic, and some were crying, said Fred Sowemimo. "There was a young lady … she had, like, blood all over her white skirt, it was in that moment, at least for me, I was like, 'Oh wow, this actually did happen,'" he said.State investigators and the ride's manufacturer, Bolliger & Mabillard, are investigating the incident. Six Flags has temporarily shut down Goliath, as well as nine similar rides across six of its parks — temporary closures that are "out of an abundance of caution," a spokesperson said. Seaworld Orlando's Mako roller coaster, which is also made by Bolliger & Mabillard, has also shut down as a precaution. Matthew Miller, a theme park safety expert, said the closures are about taking a pause to see what comes out of the investigative report, and then reopening as soon as possible.For the Sowemimos, there is relief that they're safe, but also heartbreak for Kariem's family. "Someone did not go home yesterday. And I just want to say to pray for them," said Vanessa Sowemimo. "Just pray for these people who were truly impacted."Bolliger & Mabillard said it is "deeply saddened by this tragic accident," adding, "Our thoughts are with the family and those affected." Six Flags also said it is "deeply saddened" and cooperating fully with authorities.

title: Atlanta lifts remaining boil water advisory following water main repairs and testing
description: Residents and businesses in South Fulton, Fairburn, Union City, Chattahoochee Hills and Palmetto can use tap water without boiling it after Atlanta officials lifted the boil water advisory Wednesday morning.
content: Residents and businesses in South Fulton, Fairburn, Union City, Chattahoochee Hills and Palmetto can use tap water without boiling it after Atlanta officials lifted the boil water advisory Wednesday morning.The Atlanta Department of Watershed Management lifted the advisory at 8 a.m. after testing found no contamination in the public water system. Water can now be used for all purposes without boiling, the department said.The advisory had already been lifted for southwest and northwest Atlanta at 3:30 p.m. Tuesday after tests found no contamination there.Officials issued the advisory Sunday, Oct. 11, following a water supply interruption affecting the Chattahoochee Water Treatment Plant. Crews later completed repairs to a broken water main near the plant.The department said the city's drinking water meets or exceeds federal standards and that the Georgia Environmental Protection Division has been notified.

title: More than 70 firefighters, support crews, working to contain wildfires in Upper Peninsula
description: Two wildfires that were discovered on Friday in Michigan's Upper Peninsula are about 20% contained each, the DNR says.
content: More than 70 firefighters and support crews remain on assignment in Michigan's Upper Peninsula as two wildfires continue to burn. The Ridge Fire has burned about 450 acres and is about 20% contained, while the Craig Lake Fire has burned about 600 acres and is about 20% contained, the Michigan Department of Natural Resources said on Tuesday evening. Both fires were discovered on Friday by a DNR pilot. The Ridge Fire is burning in rugged terrain north of the Dead River Basin, which is a reservoir about 10 miles northwest of Marquette. The Craig Lake Fire is burning north of Craig Lake State Park. That site is considered the most remote of Michigan's state park system, with trails, backcountry camping and six small lakes. The cause of the Craig Lake Fire has been confirmed to be a lightning strike that smoldered until high winds caused it to ignite in a remote area of the U.P. Weather conditions late last week were warm and dry, with high winds. Rainfall has significantly lowered the fire activity, the DNR said Tuesday. But the terrain is treacherous with muddy roads and slippery rocks. Drought conditions have fed the fires burning as much as 2 feet deep in the duff layer, forcing trees that appear green above ground to fall without warning. Those who are in the North Basin Drive are urged to remain on alert for updates. The "Ready, Set, Go!" instructions for that region remain at "ready." The Noquemanon Trail system west of the County Road 510 trailhead remains closed. In addition, a Temporary Flight Restriction (TFR) is in place near the fire zone at a 5-nautical-mile radius, below 3,500 feet. Drones are strictly prohibited, as they would halt air operations. The above video originally aired on Oct. 13, 2026.

title: Georgia early voting opens with record first-day midterm turnout, secretary of state says
description: Georgia voters set a first-day early voting record for a midterm election Tuesday, casting more than 188,600 in-person ballots, according to the secretary of state's office.
content: Georgia voters set a first-day early voting record for a midterm election Tuesday, casting more than 188,600 in-person ballots, according to the secretary of state's office.Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger reported 188,667 early in-person votes, up from 134,962 on the first day in 2022. That is an increase of 53,705 voters, or about 40%. In 2018, the first-day total was 70,849."This record-breaking turnout proves that voters have confidence in the integrity of our elections," Raffensperger said in a statement. "It's a testament to our strong election system overseen by 159 of the best county election officials in the country."The office also reported that 10,267 absentee ballots had been accepted.Voters can find early voting locations and hours for their county on the state's My Voter Page. Updated turnout figures are available through the secretary of state's Election Data Hub.

title: Groundbreaking held for new entrance at South Portico of Griffin Museum of Science and Industry
description: Groundbreaking held for new entrance at South Portico of Griffin Museum of Science and Industry
content: Groundbreaking was held Tuesday for a project to turn the South Portico of the Griffin Museum of Science and Industry into an active entrance.The $22 million renovation will add an outdoor café, a public gathering space, and a terrace overlooking Jackson Park. The entrance would also be ADA accessible.The South Portico is architecturally identical to the North Portico of the museum, with its row of limestone laurel wreaths, statuary, and of course, stately Ionic columns perfect for the museum where visitors can learn about ionic bonds in chemistry — among many other topics, of course.The North Portico faces 57th Drive and the Hyde Park neighborhood, and used to have a surface parking lot in front of it before the parking lot was buried and the land turned into green space in the late '90s. The South Portico faces the pond known as the Columbia Basin in Jackson Park, but has not been a way in or out at any point since the building has been the Museum of Science and Industry — which will celebrate its centennial in 2033.The area, for all intents and purposes, has always functioned as the back of the museum.But as Chicago kids learn in elementary school, the Griffin Museum of Science and Industry started out as the Palace of Fine Arts at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition. During the fair, when an assortment of other Beaux Arts structures stood proudly all around Jackson Park, people traveled through gondolas through the lagoon and walked up the South Portico stairs to visit what is now the Griffin MSI, museum president and chief executive officer Chevy Humphrey explained.More than 130 years later, Jackson Park is seeing a renaissance with the opening of the Obama Presidential Center just to the south of the Griffin MSI. Speaking to CBS News Chicago Political Reporter Chris Tye in August, Humphrey said it is time to connect the museum with the park."No one can enter from Jackson Park," Humphrey said in August. "You see how beautiful Jackson Park is, with the Japanese gardens, this incredible lagoon, and now with the Obama Presidential Center, there needs to be the opening that we need for our visitors."The idea to reopen the building's south entrance came from the surrounding community in Woodlawn and Hyde Park."I went out and met with over 1,000 people my first year and had many community meetings, and community members actually said, 'Why are your doors closed to us when we're visiting Jackson Park?'" Humphrey said in August.The South Portico is set to open in the winter of 2027.Recently, the Griffin MSI also announced plans for alterations to the North Portico where the main entrance has always been, in the form of a welcome hall.As described by Urbanize Chicago, the Welcome Hall will feature a low-slung archway that connects to the museum building by a glass structure. Renderings appear to show visitors entering the museum through the welcome hall both at grade level and by going up the stairs.Part of the central area of the front stairs would be carved out for the accessible ground-level entrance, Urbanize Chicago reported.The plan for the Welcome Hall will also include an adjacent outdoor Science Gardens, which will be open to the public without admission, the Griffin MSI said.The existing underground entry hall will become additional exhibition space, the Griffin MSI said.Both the changes to the South Portico and the planned welcome hall at the North Portico have been less than welcomed by some critics. In the Chicago Tribune, City of Chicago cultural historian emeritus Tim Samuelson wrote that the changes to the entrances would be "the most seriously damaging" alteration he has ever witnessed to the Griffin MSI, with the only thing worse being the demolition of entire historic buildings."With the approved alterations to the Griffin Museum of Science and Industry, the building will essentially remain standing," Samuelson wrote in the Tribune this week. "But the changes will destroy the essence of what makes the building rare and special. It's all about an elusive quality known as perfection."Samuelson wrote that as the Palace of Fine Arts during the World's Fair, what became the Griffin MSI building was "repeatedly singled out for being as near to perfection as could be humanly achievable in its architectural composition and the relationship to its site." He also noted that when the building became the Museum of Science and Industry after falling into abandonment and ruin, its plaster exterior was rebuilt down to every detail in limestone.With the changes coming to the North and South Porticos, Samuelson wrote, the staircases on both sides will be "punctured" to leave a "gap-toothed large hole" at the center, while the porticos themselves will be glassed in.In the Chicago Sun-Times last month, architecture critic Lee Bey also took issue with the welcome center plan for the Griffin MSI's North Portico. He called the welcome hall an "ungainly and unattractive pavilion that visually overpowers the building's historic north entrance and its beautiful, open front lawn," and compared it to "a big old wide-brimmed hat blocking the screen at the movie theater."However, Bey wrote that the South Portico alterations seemed to be "more appropriate and less monumental in approach, according to the latest renderings."

title: Hochul, Blakeman clash over immigration, economy in New York governor's race debate
description: Gov. Kathy Hochul and Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman sparred over affordability, immigration and energy policy during a debate Tuesday.
content: Gov. Kathy Hochul and Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman sparred over affordability, immigration and energy policy during their first, and only, debate Tuesday night.In opening remarks, Blakeman criticized Hochul's handling of migrant-related spending and argued New Yorkers are struggling under high taxes and utility costsThe exchanges became heated as Hochul tied Blakeman to President Donald Trump and criticized his policy positions."He says that he's going to bring Trump-style leadership to Albany," Hochul said. "He says he's going to cut Medicaid in half."Hochul also accused Blakeman of supporting aggressive immigration enforcement policies.Blakeman focused much of his criticism on affordability, arguing that New Yorkers are struggling with high taxes, utility costs and energy prices.He pointed to neighboring Pennsylvania, claiming its energy policies have helped keep costs lower for residents."On the Pennsylvania side of the border, people are driving around in brand-new Cadillac Escalades," Blakeman said. "And on the New York side of the border, they're driving around 25-year-old rusted-out pickup trucks because of your policies."Hochul defended her record and pushed back against Blakeman's criticisms. She highlighted her administration's efforts on public safety and repeatedly challenged his support for Mr. Trump.During one exchange, Hochul referenced comments Blakeman made praising Mr. Trump at a rally."You called my moratorium crazy," Hochul said. "Donald Trump says it's only for dumb, poor people who would support that. You support what Donald Trump said there as well?"Later, Hochul questioned why Blakeman had described Mr. Trump as "the greatest president of your lifetime."Blakeman replied that political rallies are often meant to energize supporters."At a rally, it's a cheering section, and you say things to get the crowd worked up," he said. "I think Donald Trump deserves accolades for many of the things that he's done."The candidates also clashed over New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, with Blakeman criticizing the mayor and Hochul countering that her opponent has failed to challenge Mr. Trump on issues affecting New Yorkers.This was the only debate the two candidates agreed to before the election.Hochul enters the final stretch with a lead in recent polls, while Blakeman is trying to win over independents and voters looking for a change. Early voting begins Oct. 24 with Election Day on Nov. 3.
